items.question: The Spanish Heir (What If Carlos II had a son?)
human_answers: I'm very interested to see how the Habsburgs continue to manage their Mediterranean and American possessions. It might be too much to hope for, but perhaps if the final decades of his reign are less frantic, he might be a little more relaxed and not outlaw the use of Nahuatl and Quechua within the administration of the American colonies. Beyond that, continuing spanish rivalry with France will be interesting- I'd assume if Spain can get it's act together they'll be looking for a return of the franche comté. But as they're not as much of a land power as Austria, they might end up losing Belgium to France. Corsica and Tuscany are also up for grabs this century, which could confirm them as masters of all Italy. In the Mediterranean, Spanish support might lead to a longer lasting Catholic Morea, whether under the Venetians or under the Spanish themselves- and given how much the spanish the like Catholicism, it might scare the orthodox within the ottoman empire into closer association with the ottoman state. Austrian-ottoman wars in the beginning of the 18th century will be altered should the Spanish coordinate with their cousins by sea- Crete, Cyprus and even Rhodes could be targets here. The age of dynastic partitions is mainly over, but one more might just be on the cards- either Castile and the colonies Vs Aragon and the Mediterranean, or Spain and the colonies Vs Italy and the Mediterranean.

I: The Habsburg Miracles The Battle of Vienna (1683) ​ On September 8, 1683, the nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary arrived in Vienna. On this holy day, priests, citizens, and soldiers alike poured into the churches of Vienna or failing that, their steps, and prayed. For unlike any previous nativity, this one had been one that many expected to live to see. For two months, Vienna had been surrounded by more than 150,000 Turkish soldiers commanded by the Grand Vizier, Kara Mustafa, Pasha, himself. This mighty host had cut off Vienna entirely from the rest of the Christian world and bombarded it daily while the Ottoman trenches steadily advanced upon the city. The Austrian army and band of citizens that had been left behind by their frightened Emperor Leopold numbered less than 20,000. Their situation was desperate and even their stalwart garrison commander, Ernst Rudiger von Starhemberg, could sense that the city would not survive much longer, and once the Ottomans broke through its walls everyone knew that only a bloody execution awaited every one of them. In the grips of this terrible situation, Starhemberg and the defenders of Vienna could do nothing more than pray for deliverance from the Blessed Virgin Mary. That same Wednesday night those prayers were answered when the daily signal rockets of Vienna were answered by five rockets from Kahlenberg Hill in the west. Those five brilliant flashes signaled that the relief that Vienna had long-awaited and desperately needed was presently on its way. However, on Thursday, the only banners that waved in the fields around Vienna were the banners of the Ottomans and the soldiers beneath those banners remained in place, not diverted to fight some other foe. Of greatest concern, the cannonades against Vienna slackened, which only ever happened when the Ottomans were preparing a direct attack on the city. That afternoon, with the western horizon still devoid of signs of Christendom, an explosion rocked the western defenses of Vienna when a mine cratered part of Lobl Bastion. Soon after, hundreds of Ottoman soldiers charged up the slope toward Vienna's walls to wrench Lobl Bastion out of the defenders' hands. Starhemberg's expectation of this attack meant that the breach in Lobl's wall had been stuffed with Austrian soldiers. Even after close to sixty days of unending and horrific investment, the Austrians stood strong and drove back the Ottomans twice. The toll that the Austrians inflicted on their attacks was so severe that the Grand Vizier declined sending the third assault. Afterward, Starhemberg quickly organized the repairing and retrenchment of the outer defenses of Vienna. Additionally, Starhemberg backed up these fortifications with chains and barricades in the streets and homes behind the walls. Whether the signals of the day before were true precursors to a timely relief or not, Starhemberg had no intention of surrendering Austria's capital to the enemy. Death was a more palatable alternative. Those signals had not been for naught. A relief army had been formed and was in fact on its way. For the previous two months, just a mere 20,000 Imperial soldiers had remained within touching distance of Vienna to provide the vague suggestion of relief. But over the last weeks of August, that 20,000 men had been dramatically increased to create a real army. First, came 11,000 Bavarians under the personal command of the twenty-one-year-old Elector Maximilian II Emanuel. Unlike any other contingent, even the Emperor's own soldiers, Max Emanuel and his Bavarians had not demanded some incredible subsidy upfront or alternative reward to come to the aid of Vienna. The money could wait until Austria was not in the grips of catastrophe. For now, all Max Emanuel and the Bavarians required was an opportunity to demonstrate their bravery and prove their honor by saving the beleaguered city of Vienna. Shortly after the Bavarians arrived came an army of 6,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry from the Franconian and Swabian Circles. They had only come after weeks of careful negotiation between Emperor Leopold and the Circles, which ended with Emperor Leopold agreeing to pay them a large sum for their services. Next, came 7,000 foot and 2,000 horse of Saxony, who like the Bavarians were commanded by their ruler, Elector Johann Georg IV. While the Bavarians brought with them an impressive train of field artillery, the Saxons brought an essential set of light and mobile artillery pieces. Finally, some smaller units of Germans such as that of Julius Franz of Saxony-Lauenberg added to the army. The last piece of this army was 24,000 Polish footmen and hussars led by King Jan III Sobieski. This eastern army outdid the contribution of any single Imperial prince, even exceeding the army of Emperor Leopold himself. And this number was not even all of it. Some days behind the Poles lagged thousands of the Lithuanian subjects of King Jan III. Bringing this considerable army away from the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and then all the way to the Danube had left the Commonwealth itself practically defenseless. In fact, the only defense that King Jan III could offer was a stern warning and a threat of devastating retaliation against the Ottoman partisan Imre Thokoly if he attacked the Commonwealth in the King's absence. However, putting his home in danger was without a doubt necessary to give Christendom a chance to save Vienna. Without the Poles, the Imperial army counted only 50,000 men whereas, with them, the Christians numbered close to 75,000 soldiers. Although this final number was just half that of the Ottomans, it was far better than being only a third. With a King and two Imperial Electors holding commands within this great Christian army, the threat of splintered focus and disorganized tactics was high. Although Emperor Leopold was technically superior to each of them as the Holy Roman Emperor, his previous flight from Vienna had proven that the battlefield was not where his talents lay. Fortunately, the man who Emperor Leopold gave command of his soldiers to, Duke Charles V of Lorraine, proved to be the perfect individual to navigate this multinational army's complicated hierarchy. As the exiled ruler of an occupied duchy Charles of Lorraine's only vocation for the past decade had been being an Imperial general. Through this experience managing the Austrian army's diverse officer corps, Charles of Lorraine learned how to bring an army together around a singular goal through personally connecting with each and every commander of importance. Whereas others were brash and offensive or deferential and meek, Charles of Lorraine was straightforward and easy-going, which was a welcomed ideal among soldiers and commanders alike. Quickly, Charles of Lorraine gained the confidence of the Christian army's generals and bound them to the goal of rescuing Vienna above all else. Under Charles of Lorraine's guidance, Jan Sobieski, Max Emanuel, and Johann Georg all agreed to ignore Emperor Leopold's directive that the relief army should take a longer approach through the gentle grounds to the southwest of Vienna. Instead, in their eagerness to save Vienna, the relief army determined to reach the city as quickly as possible by taking the shortest path across the rocky outcrop of the Wienerwald. With all appropriate haste, the relief army soon cut its way through the forest to Vienna's northwest and then crossed the Danube dangerously close to the Ottoman outriders. By September 8, the army had made its way to Tulln, just 22 miles from Vienna, and was readying its final approach toward Vienna. That night they sent off the signal rockets to inform Vienna of their coming and inspire just a few more days of resistance from the city. When the relief army finally entered the Wienerwald on September 9, it was confronted by an unruly wilderness that had grown out of hand since the Habsburg Emperors had denied the forest to anyone but themselves. As a consequence, the relief army lost its cohesion as it filtered through the forest and up its steep slopes. No man found comfort as he marched or rode through the crowded woods and its sprawling undergrowth, all the while thoughts of a terrible battle hung over him. To make matters worse, a German scouting party spotted Ottomans holding part of the ridgeline in the way of the army's approach. The Ottomans, however, lacked the foresight to either fortify or sufficiently man that ridgeline. This allowed the Christians to pounce on the Ottoman position between dawn on September 11 and wrest control of the ridgeline before the Ottomans could realize their mistake. Yet this victory was not complete as several Ottomans managed to escape from the skirmish and flee back to the main camp where they made the Grand Vizier aware of the relief army's imminent approach. Ottoman scouts had already revealed the relief army to the Grand Vizier two days prior to this attack on the ridge. However, the survivors of the attack were able to confirm the whereabouts of the relief army and its size, which verified the Ottoman belief that the relief army intended to come straight at them from the west and that no attack should be expected from the south where the patrols had still not encountered any Christian soldiers. The narrow geography of the Wienerwald meant that the best avenue for an attack was straight at the center of the Ottoman position. This position could be defended by a series of mannered ridges, hills, and villages. Although the Grand Vizier decided against enhancing the natural defenses provided by the topography with either trenches or palisades, the series of obstacles still presented a formidable challenge. The Christians would have to funnel themselves into multiple zones of fire and if the Ottomans held their ground then it would be a slaughter. Another set of obstacles and an even greater challenge for the Christian army would have to be overcome before they could even reach the Ottoman defenses. After the morning's victory, the Christians were able to occupy the ridge of Kalhenburg and look down toward Vienna. The maps had led them to believe that between that ridge and Vienna lay gentle slopes and clear ploughed fields. Instead, the rocky and uneven ground that had begrudged them in the Wienerwald continued on all the way to the edge of Vienna. The lines that separated the fields were not low wooden fences but haphazard stone walls and thick hedgerows that could not easily be traversed. These demarcations enclosed not open fields of crops but thick and twisted vines of unharvested grapes. Further complicating this approach was a set of deep ravines, small streams, and some scattered villages. Any of these alone was an impediment, but all of them together formed a veritable wall against an assault. As the Christians piloted this difficult terrain they would be easy targets for the Ottoman cannons and muskets. The cavalrymen high up on their horses would be particularly exposed as they slowly negotiated the convoluted ground. All in all, the Christians would have no hope of sending in straight lines of pikemen and musketeers or charging forth coherent blocks of horsemen. Instead, the Christians would have to advance slowly and carefully across the difficult ground and under heavy fire before throwing themselves against prepared defenses and ready defenders. In the face of this adversity, the Christians did not cower. They had come all this way to save Vienna and they would do their damnedest to try, even with so much going against them. However, the Christians' willingness to push on was not the result of confidence or of faith. Many Christian soldiers spent that night sleepless and unable to stomach any food. Even Charles of Lorraine was nervous on the precipice of this battle. They all understood that the likelihood of their victory was low and believed that many of their souls would depart on the morrow. It would be a red day, all they could do was hope it would not be a black day too. On Sunday, September 12, 1683, the great battle for Vienna began when hundreds of Ottoman skirmishers began climbing up the slope toward Kalhenburg and opened fire on the Christian army at around 5 am. With men dropping left and right, the Christians could not hold still and simply return fire. Instead, the Saxon infantrymen abandoned their positions and drove down the hill toward the Ottomans. The whole left flank of the Christian army joined the Saxons in this counterattack that swept away the eastern skirmishers. Although the first Ottoman attack was thrown back, the left flank of the Christian army had placed itself well ahead of the rest of the army in doing so, which left it vulnerable to an Ottoman counterattack. Charles of Lorraine took quick notice of the danger and ordered the left to slow its advance while the rest of the Christian army was ordered to catch up. Although the Saxons had dragged the rest of the army out of its strong positions along the ridge, the earlier success had inspired the men with confidence and even Charles of Lorraine could feel something. The order for a general attack was given. As the Christians crowded around the Ottoman stronghold of Nussberg, they cried out "Ave Maria!" and the Ottomans threw back "Allah, Allah Akbar!" These screams and shouts were drowned out by the overwhelming sound of muskets firing, cannons blasting, and swords clattering. The fighting was vicious and uncertain. But at that particular spot, the Christians found themselves more numerous than the Ottomans and steadily overcame their Ottoman forest. Of great importance were the Saxon light cannons that had been successfully dragged down the slope to directly fire into the Ottoman formations. Within the Ottoman camp, the Grand Vizier was well-aware of the unfolding battle and committed his reserve to saving Nussberg and holding back the Christians. However, the Grand Vizier failed to organize a larger reinforcement from other parts of the army because he could not coordinate with the various pashas and Tatar chiefs. In contrast, even with the dreadful terrain and multinational nature of the army, Charles of Lorraine had maintained decent lines and formations. Close to noon, Johann Georg's cavalry was unleashed on the Ottoman sipahis, which allowed the Saxon infantrymen to wrest Nussberg away from the Ottomans. Still, the Saxons had to fight the Ottomans for each and every house in that village. the continuance of this attack faltered as the Saxons once more overextended themselves in the chase. But once the Christians regrouped they renewed their attack and took the next Ottoman stronghold in front of them. At this point, Charles of Lorraine called for the army to hold to avoid another overextension. He needed to ensure that the army did not lose its cohesion and under the hot summer sun, Charles of Lorraine was worried about his soldiers suffering from exhaustion and thirst. This pause allowed the thousands of Polish cavalry to make their way down the slopes from the Wienerwald and toward the southern edge of the Ottoman position. With the Christian army having successfully made it down the slopes and having already broken one Ottoman position, the Christians finally found themselves at the advantage. Even though the Ottoman army as a whole was larger than the Christian one, on those fields to the west of Vienna, the Christians were superior in number. And now that they had made it down the slope, those numbers could be fully deployed against the Ottomans. Both Charles of Lorraine and Jan Sobieski could feel this shift. To the northeast, Charles of Lorraine asked the German commanders if they wished to push on or whether they should delay the battle to the next day. To the south, Jan Sobieski asked his own commanders the same question. In both councils, the answer was the same: March on. With this order shouted out, the Christians moved forward once again and pushed up to the remaining positions. In the north, the Imperial soldiers led by the Bavarians and Saxons assaulted the Ottoman formations and after an hour and a half, conquered them. All the enemies within them were slaughtered. To the south, the Poles sent a forlorn hope forth to test the Ottoman positions. Although this lonesome company was mauled by the far more numerous Ottomans, their charge still shook the Ottomans just enough for Jan Sobieski to order the entirety of his hussars and the rest of the cavalry to charge the Ottomans. When the Poles bore down on them, the Ottomans did not present themselves as the vicious conquerors of Constantinople. Instead, demoralized by the morning and afternoon's travails, the Ottomans were a disorderly mess that lacked the spirit and discipline necessary to hold against a cavalry charge. The Poles punched through the Ottomans and began to cut them to pieces. Quickly, the Ottomans lost the last of their courage and began to flee. Meanwhile, the Germans to the north continued to stomp over the Ottomans in front of them. Within the hour, the Ottoman army was broken and sent into flight. The citizens of Vienna rejoiced when Charles of Lorraine's official messenger pronounced that "Vienna was relieved". Thousands exited their homes and cried out in jubilation in the streets while others exited the city to set their eyes on their glorious saviours. Everywhere music played and tears of joy and relief painted faces. Although the army remained on alert for the rest of the night in case the Ottomans came back, all knew that no such thing would happen. By some miracle of God, an army of fewer than 75,000 men had secured a true and complete victory over an army of more than 150,000. Vienna was saved and the Ottomans were shattered [1] . While this miracle on the Danube saved Emperor Leopold from suffering the same ignominy of losing Vienna as his ancestor Emperor Frederick III, it was not the only miracle to bless the House of Habsburg on that day. More than a thousand miles away in the heart of Spain at the Royal Alcazar of Madrid, another miracle was delivered to the Habsburgs. There, after twelve hours of screaming and crying, Queen Marie Louise of Spain gave birth to the long-awaited first child of King Carlos II of Spain [2] . Better yet, she gave birth to a son who could inherit the many crowns of Spain without any dispute. Thus, Marie Louise ended nearly two decades of uncertainty over who would next possess the crown of Spain. Just as the victory over the Ottomans was celebrated by all within Vienna, the birth of a son, a crown prince, was celebrated by all within Madrid. To them, there could be no greater miracle than that which saved them from a dozen European rulers laying claim to some piece of the Spanish empire once the sickly King Carlos II's heart finally gave out. Thus, both halves of the Habsburg dynasty were saved on the fateful day of September 12, 1683. [1] This is a retelling of the historical relief of Vienna. There is no alteration to make note of. [2] This is the Point of Divergence, Marie Louise produces an heir. There is at least one rumored pregnancy for Marie Louise during her marriage to Carlos II. Unlike the rumored pregnancies of her successor Maria Anna of Neuburg, this rumored pregnancy was taken seriously and not believed to be completely chimerical. One reason for that difference in reactions was that although Carlos II was never conventionally healthy, he was far more relatively healthy while married to Marie Louise. During this time, the only believed issue with conception was his premature ejaculation. Later, when married to Maria Anna, Carlos II was suffering from increasing health issues including atrophy. Here, the suggestion is that Carlos II and Marie Louise manage to get lucky and overcome his premature ejaculation to produce an heir. Alternatively, you are welcome to believe that Marie Louise found another partner. Or even that this is a legitimate miracle from God. Either way, she has produced a child whom Spain will accept as the heir.
items.model_answer:
If Carlos II of Spain had produced a legitimate surviving son, the biggest immediate consequence is that the War of the Spanish Succession probably does not happen in the form we know it, because the central trigger of the crisis was the extinction of the Spanish Habsburg line in 1700. A son would have provided a clear dynastic continuation, and in a monarchy where legitimacy mattered enormously, that alone would have strengthened internal stability across Castile, Aragon, Naples, Sicily, Milan, and the Spanish Netherlands. Spain would still have been weak, fiscally strained, and administratively cumbersome, but it would not have faced the same sudden international struggle over who should inherit its composite empire.

That does not mean Europe would have accepted this quietly. Everything would depend on who the mother was, when the son was born, and whether the child seemed likely to survive. If the heir were born to María Luisa of Orléans or Mariana of Neuburg and clearly recognized by the Spanish political nation, then both Bourbon France and Habsburg Austria would lose their strongest legal claims. Louis XIV could no longer plausibly expect his grandson Philip of Anjou to inherit Spain, and Emperor Leopold I would likewise find it harder to promote the Austrian Archduke Charles. The other powers, especially England and the Dutch Republic, would probably welcome a legitimate Spanish heir, because their overriding fear was not Spain itself but the absorption of the Spanish monarchy by either France or Austria. A native Spanish Habsburg continuation would preserve the balance of power better than either a Bourbon or Austrian takeover.

The real question is whether this son would have been healthy and politically viable. Carlos II was notoriously sickly, and the broader Habsburg family had severe dynastic weaknesses because of generations of inbreeding. A son might easily have been frail, disabled, or infertile himself, creating not a solved succession but a delayed one. If the child were a minor when Carlos died, a regency would be unavoidable, and then the struggle would shift from inheritance to control of the regency. That could be dangerous. France, Austria, and domestic Spanish factions would all try to dominate the court, and Spain’s territories might split over which foreign power to trust. So the existence of a son does not automatically guarantee peace; it more likely changes a clean succession crisis into a regency crisis.

If the son survived into adulthood and was reasonably competent, the Spanish monarchy might remain under a Spanish Habsburg branch into the eighteenth century. In that case, the Bourbon reforms associated with Philip V would probably not occur, or at least not in the same form. Historically, the Bourbons centralized administration, weakened the old constitutional distinctions within Spain, and introduced more French-style statecraft. A surviving Habsburg heir would likely preserve more of the older polycentric system, with separate laws and privileges in the Crown of Aragon, and perhaps a slower, less coherent reform process. Spain might therefore avoid the devastations of the succession war, but at the cost of remaining administratively weaker and less modernized.

This matters for the wider map of Europe. Without the War of the Spanish Succession, Britain likely does not gain Gibraltar and Minorca in the same way, and Austria may not acquire the Spanish Netherlands, Naples, Milan, and other Spanish Italian possessions through a peace settlement. That means the eighteenth-century balance in Italy and the Low Countries would look very different. France, too, would be checked in a different way: Louis XIV would lose the opportunity to place a Bourbon on the Spanish throne, but he might also avoid the enormous military and financial burden of the war. Britain might emerge somewhat less dramatically as a Mediterranean and commercial power, at least in the short term, because Utrecht was crucial to that rise.

For Spain’s empire overseas, a son of Carlos II would probably mean continuity rather than transformation. The American empire would stay attached to Madrid under familiar institutions. Yet here again there is a paradox. Avoiding the war could preserve resources and legitimacy, which is good for imperial cohesion, but avoiding Bourbon rule might also mean no Bourbon imperial reforms, which historically tightened control and increased revenue in the eighteenth century. So Spain’s empire might be more stable initially but less capable of long-term recovery.

The most plausible overall outcome is this: a son of Carlos II prevents the immediate extinction crisis and probably averts the specific Bourbon-Habsburg partition struggle that produced the War of the Spanish Succession, but he does not restore Spain to greatness. He would give the monarchy breathing room, preserve the Spanish Habsburg line, and likely maintain European balance more peacefully for a time. But unless this heir were unexpectedly robust and talented, Spain would still confront the same structural problems of military weakness, fiscal fragility, and dynastic uncertainty. In other words, a son for Carlos II likely postpones and softens the collapse of Habsburg Spain rather than fully reversing it.

items.original_question: What if Umar ibn Hafsun defeats the Umayyads - Mozarab/Muladí Al-Andalus One of my favorite historical subjects to research is Al-Andalus, the Muslim-ruled realms of the Iberian peninsula that existed between the 8th and 15th centuries. A land where East met West, Al-Andalus represented a rare example of Islamic Arab rule of Western European territory, resulting in the blending of cultures, religion, knowledge, and languages that proved to be massively influential on the development of European civilization and human history as a whole. Even though it was swept out of Iberia by the Reconquista, the influence of Al-Andalus can still be felt today, through Hispanic language, culture, art, and cuisine. For example, there are many Arabic loanwords in the Spanish language, tacos have middle eastern roots, and I remember a story my grandfather would tell me about when he met Bedouin tribesmen while deployed as a U.S. Marine during the Gulf War, and while they could not understand the English language, they could understand his Spanish. In the late 9th century, the once-Caliphs of the entire Muslim world, the Arab Umayyad dynasty, ruled over the vast majority of the Iberian peninsula from the prosperous city of Cordoba. Their rule would last for 300 years, but would not be without resistance. Although they comprised a small portion of the population, the ruling class of Al-Andalus was almost exclusively Arab. Mozarabs, local Iberians who remained Christian under Muslim rule, and Muladí, Iberians who had converted to Islam, resented the discriminatory racial and taxation policies of their Arab overlords, creating a degree of instability within Al-Andalus. Born around 850, Umar ibn Hafsun was a prominent leader of Iberian resistance to Umayyad rule. Simultaneously described as being of both North African and Visigothic descent, the rogue-ish and opportunistic ibn Hafsun attracted a following of disaffected Mozarab and Muladí alike, and alongside fellow rebels such as ibn Marwan and the Banu Qasi clan, would contest Umayyad rule from his fortress, Bobastro. While he would experience much success early on, several defeats against the Umayyads, such as at the Battle of Poley in 891, as well as his conversion to Christianity in 899, in what appeared to be a bid to attract the support of the Christian King of Asturias, would weaken his following. He would fight to the very end, dying in 917, and his sons would continue his fight until 928, when Bobastro fell to Emir Abd-ar-Rahman III. Umar ibn Hafsun remains somewhat of a tragic figure in Iberian history, but he also represents a glimpse into what could have been. Had he succeeded in supplanting the minority Arab ruling class with Mozarabs and Muladí, perhaps by winning battles such as the Battle of Poley, ibn Hafsun could have ensured the creation of a stronger, multicultural and multireligious Al-Andalus. This creates an interesting scenario for speculation. Could this alt-Andalus survive for longer, perhaps even to the present? What would the society of alt-Andalus look like? Would religious and ethnic differences eventually shatter this state, or would it strengthen it, combining the best of the Christian and Islamic worlds? Would alt-Andalus fall to neighboring Christian and Muslim invaders, or would it become one of the leading powers in Europe and the Mediterranean, an even greater conduit for the exchange of trade, knowledge, and culture than the Al-Andalus of OTL? And how would this alt-Andalus impact the development of Hispanic culture, and European and world history as a whole?

If Umar ibn Hafsun had decisively defeated the Umayyads and replaced their authority in al-Andalus, the most plausible result would have been a more fragmented, frontier-style state centered on the southern uplands rather than the later strong, centralized Umayyad emirate and caliphate based in Córdoba. His victory would likely have changed both the political structure of Muslim Iberia and the balance between Arab, Berber, Muladí, and Mozarab communities.

Umar ibn Hafsun’s revolt drew much of its strength from groups that were often marginalized by the Umayyad elite: local converts to Islam, rural strongmen, discontented Berbers, and in some phases Christians, especially Mozarabs. That means a Hafsunid victory would probably not have produced a simple continuation of Umayyad Andalusi rule under a new dynasty. Instead, it likely would have created a coalition regime with weaker claims to universal legitimacy and more dependence on local loyalties. Córdoba might have remained important, but it is hard to imagine it becoming the same commanding center it later became under Abd al-Rahman III.

A Hafsunid al-Andalus would probably have been less Arab-aristocratic and more socially mixed in its ruling culture. Muladí elites would likely have gained political prominence much earlier and more fully. Mozarabs might also have had a somewhat stronger position, especially if Hafsun continued using anti-Córdoban alliances across confessional lines. Since Ibn Hafsun himself reportedly converted to Christianity late in life, one of the biggest possibilities is that his state might have blurred the confessional hierarchy that structured Umayyad rule. That would not necessarily mean a “Christian” al-Andalus, but it could have meant a polity in which local Christian elites and Islamized Iberian elites shared power more openly than under the Umayyads.

Even so, this would have come at a cost. The Umayyads were effective state-builders: they imposed taxation, built bureaucracy, disciplined frontier defense, and eventually reasserted control over rebellious provinces. Ibn Hafsun’s movement was powerful precisely because the state was weak in some regions, but that does not mean he could easily have replaced the Umayyads with an equally durable regime. A victory over Córdoba might therefore have led not to a stable Hafsunid kingdom over all al-Andalus, but to a looser confederation of regional lords. Seville, Toledo, Zaragoza, Mérida, and other centers might have behaved almost independently, acknowledging Hafsunid supremacy only when convenient.

That fragmentation would have had major consequences for Christian polities in the north. Without a restored, centralized Umayyad state, León, Navarre, and the Catalan counties would likely have faced a weaker and more divided Muslim south. The famous tenth-century Umayyad revival, including the proclamation of the Caliphate of Córdoba and later military pressure on the northern kingdoms, probably would not have happened in the same way. Christian expansion southward might have begun earlier or proceeded more steadily, especially in border regions where local Muslim and Christian rulers often made pragmatic alliances anyway.

Culturally, the consequences are mixed. On one hand, a less centralized state might have meant less of the spectacular court culture associated with Córdoba at its height: fewer grand monuments on the scale of Madinat al-Zahra, less concentrated patronage of philosophy, poetry, and high administration, and weaker projection of Andalusi prestige across the western Islamic world. On the other hand, local hybrid cultures might have become even more pronounced. A Hafsunid order rooted in Muladí and Mozarab society could have accelerated the development of a more distinctly Iberian Islamicate culture, less tied to Arab lineage and eastern models and more shaped by local language, local aristocracies, and cross-confessional exchange.

Religion would be especially important. If Ibn Hafsun’s Christian turn became central to the regime, the result could have been explosive. Many Muslim supporters might have abandoned him, while Mozarabs and northern Christian kingdoms might have embraced him opportunistically. In that scenario, al-Andalus might even have split into competing Muslim and Christian successor states much earlier, with religious identity becoming a sharper political dividing line sooner than it did historically. If, however, his conversion remained politically secondary and his regime stayed basically pragmatic, then the more likely outcome is not religious reversal but a less rigidly Umayyad, more locally negotiated Andalusi order.

In the long run, the most likely big-picture effect is that there would be no Córdoba caliphate in its historical form. Instead of a tenth-century peak of centralized Andalusi power followed by taifa fragmentation in the eleventh century, Iberia might have entered a taifa-like era a century earlier. Muladí and Mozarab actors would probably have had more room to shape politics, but that would have been within a weaker, more divided political system. So Umar ibn Hafsun defeating the Umayyads would probably have meant a more locally rooted but less stable al-Andalus, less dominated by the Umayyad Arab elite, more open to Mozarab and Muladí participation, and ultimately more vulnerable to both internal breakup and northern Christian expansion.

AHC: Best timeline for Catholicism

Without changing integral doctrine or dogma, attempt to make the best timeline for the Catholic Church. That means, a stronger Church, the most amount of catholics/catholic states, and crippling the opposition as much as possible. A few important changes that could be made to this end is preventing the Schism of 1054, preventing the Reformation/a highly successful counterreformation, and having Islam either never exist or fail to conquer outside of Arabia. The consequences of any of these scenarios alone are immense. Other smaller things to change could be making states like Japan convert.
items.model_answer:
A plausible “best timeline” for Catholicism would not be one where it dominates more completely, but one where it preserves its spiritual depth while avoiding the biggest self-inflicted wounds that weakened its moral authority and fractured Western Christianity.

The strongest version probably begins with a less politically entangled Church after Constantine. In this timeline, Christianity is legalized and protected, but the bishops of Rome do not become so deeply tied to imperial and later feudal power. Catholicism keeps its sacramental, intellectual, and charitable life, but avoids becoming too much like a state apparatus. That would likely reduce corruption, simony, and the long habit of treating dissent primarily as a political threat.

A second major improvement would be a successful avoidance of the Great Schism of 1054. If Rome and Constantinople had managed a durable compromise over papal authority and theology, Christianity might have remained institutionally united across Latin and Greek worlds. That would have been enormously beneficial: less civilizational rivalry between East and West, potentially a more coordinated response to later invasions and crises, and a broader, richer Christian tradition developing together rather than in competition.

The next crucial turning point is the late medieval Church. In the best timeline, reform happens before the Protestant Reformation rather than because of it. If the papacy had curbed financial abuses, improved clerical education, enforced discipline, and tolerated a somewhat wider range of theological debate in the fifteenth century, Martin Luther might have become a reforming voice within the Church rather than the catalyst for a permanent schism. Catholicism could then have remained the main institutional home of Western Christianity while still undergoing serious renewal. That would probably mean fewer wars of religion, less confessional fragmentation in Europe, and a much stronger shared Christian intellectual culture.

Relatedly, this best timeline would avoid the harshest forms of persecution and coercion. No Inquisition in its most notorious form, less use of forced conversion, and a clearer earlier commitment to the idea that faith cannot be compelled. Catholicism would retain missionary energy, but spread more through persuasion, education, charity, and cultural adaptation than through alliance with colonial force. This would greatly improve its long-term moral credibility, especially outside Europe.

Another major improvement would be a better response to science and modernity. In the ideal timeline, the Church does not mishandle the Galileo affair and becomes an early patron of a clear synthesis between faith and scientific inquiry. Then, in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, Catholicism resists both reactionary anti-modernism and total accommodation. It accepts constitutionalism, religious liberty, and democratic participation earlier, while still defending its moral teachings and social vision. In effect, it becomes a stabilizing moral voice in modern society rather than often appearing as its opponent.

In the twentieth century, something like Vatican II still happens, but earlier and with less polarization. The Church renews liturgy, biblical study, and engagement with the modern world without creating as much internal chaos or backlash. It also develops stronger systems of accountability much sooner, especially regarding clerical abuse. If the abuse crisis had been confronted decisively generations earlier, Catholicism would likely have retained far more trust in Europe and North America.

So the “best timeline” for Catholicism is probably this: united with the East, internally reformed before Luther, less coercive, less politically compromised, more intellectually open, earlier in embracing religious liberty and democracy, and much more morally serious about accountability. In that world, Catholicism would likely still be one of the largest religions on earth, but more importantly it would be more credible, less divided from other Christians, and better able to present itself as a universal church in substance rather than only in claim.

human_answers: Wouldn't Philip Jr.'s surname be "Tudor-Palatinate"? While he was a male-line member of the House of Wittelsbach, Philip was the Duke of Palatinate-Neuburg (and his brother would become Elector Palatine after the death of their childless uncle) and Wittelsbach was mostly used for the Bavarian branch of the family, with the Palatine branches mostly using "Palatine-X" as their house name (like the Spanish Hapsburgs who used "of Austria" as their surname) Looking forward to see what will be Philip's religious education, although seeing as his father is Lutheran and his uncle would support protestant tutors he will probably be on the "low-key protestant" side of things. EDIT: Also will be interesting to see how the Palatine inheritance will work out on this TL, Philip the Contentious's older brother Otto-Henry became Elector Palatine in 1556 after their uncle, Frederick, died childless. And Otto-Henry would himself die childless in 1559 (he was married from 1529 to 1543, but no children were born, he was probably the one sterile since his wife had 11 children from a previous marriage). In OTL Philip died childless in the 1540s, meaning that the Electoral title passed to a cousin, but since in this TL he has children, I'm curious to see if there will be a personal union between England and the Palatinate or Mary will have a second son so they can divide the inheritance

For the last six years of her father's reign, Mary and Philip largely stayed out of court affairs, only returning for King Henry's last two marriages and Christmastide celebrations. While Mary's relationship with Kitty Howard was scarcely remarked upon before and after the unfortunate queen was executed, she and Catherine Parr had become close friends, with Catherine being godmother to Mary's third daughter, Mary just as Anna of Cleves was godmother to little Elizabeth. However, Mary's relationship with her father seemed to deteriorate as it was becoming quite clear that Henry was disappointed that he only had granddaughters. He even suggested that little Katherine should be raised in her aunt's household to make sure she didn't become as insolent as her namesake. Mary refused to speak to her father for a almost four months after that and it was only through Catherine Parr's intervention did Henry not go through with drawing up an act of succession that would skip over Mary and her daughters. When King Henry passed away in January 1547, Mary discovered she was pregnant again. Six months after her father's death, she gave birth to a son. She named him Philip after his father who greeted the birth of his son just as happily as he had the birth of his three daughters. There was some discussion over whether or not the boy would take his father's surname or his mother's as King Henry had decreed when Philip and Mary were first married. As his Uncle Edward's heir, some even wanted the boy to be raised somewhere else. Mary put her foot down, saying that if her husband's name was good enough for their daughters, it was good enough for her sons. She did not say a word about Phillip being taken from her. Of course, she hardly needed to as the Duke of Somerset, the Lady Elizabeth, Anna of Cleves and the Dowager Queen Catherine made it extremely clear to Edward, how utterly awful that would be. The boy-king himself wasn't too keen on the idea, considering he had never known his mother. In the end, Philip, Earl of Cambridge was known as Philip of Bedford and he would grow up in the Somerset household until he was six-years-old and started his formal schooling in Hatfield. Family tree: Philip, Duke of Somerset (b. 1503-) m. Mary of England (b. 1516). 1. Katherine of Somerset (b. 1540) 2. Elizabeth of Somerset (b. 1542). 3. Mary of Somerset (b. 1545). 4. Philip, Earl of Cambridge (b. 1547).
items.original_question: What if Princess Mary Tudor married Philip of Bavaria After a short courtship, King Henry announced that his daughter Lady Mary's engagement to Philip, Duke of Palatinate-Neuburg. Philip and Mary marry in early March in a small ceremony attended by the royal family and a few favored courtiers. Many expressed their displeasure at the match, chief among them the Imperial ambassador who wrote to the Holy Roman Emperor, lamenting that his poor cousin was now tied to a German Heathen who has no royal to speak of. The Earl of Hertford was similarly was not pleased with the marriage viewing any children Mary had as potential rivals to his nephew Prince Edward. Despite going through the process of getting a divorce from Anna of Cleves, King Henry remained on good terms with his son-in-law, even granting him the Duchy of Somerset once he abdicated his own duchy to his brother so he and Mary can stay in England. He was even happier to learn that Mary was pregnant with his first grandchild, requesting that the unborn son be named Henry for him. He was quite disappointed when on December 23, Mary had a daughter named Katherine instead.
items.model_answer:
If Princess Mary Tudor had married Philip of Bavaria instead of Philip of Spain, the biggest change is that England would likely have been pulled much less deeply into Habsburg dynastic politics, and Mary’s reign might have been somewhat less unpopular at home, though many of her central religious policies would probably still have remained the same.

Mary’s actual marriage to Philip of Spain was controversial because many English people feared foreign domination, Habsburg entanglement, and the subordination of English interests to Spain. A Bavarian match would still have been a Catholic foreign marriage, so it would not have removed xenophobic or nationalist anxieties entirely, but it would have been less threatening than a marriage to the heir of the vast Spanish and Habsburg world. Philip of Bavaria was not the head of a giant imperial system, so Parliament and the political nation would have been less likely to see the marriage as a route to English dependence on a superpower. That might have reduced the intensity of resistance such as Wyatt’s Rebellion, or at least changed its scale and tone.

Religiously, Mary still would almost certainly have tried to restore Roman Catholicism. Her commitment to reversing the English Reformation did not depend on marrying Philip of Spain. A Bavarian husband, being Catholic, would probably have supported that goal. So the Marian restoration, including reunion with Rome and persecution of Protestants, might still have happened. However, without the strong Spanish association, English Protestant propaganda might have found it slightly harder to fuse anti-Catholicism with anti-Spanish feeling. Mary might therefore have faced somewhat less political damage from the image of being a ruler serving foreign Catholic interests.

In foreign policy, the effects could have been more significant. The Spanish marriage helped draw England into Habsburg-Valois conflict, contributing to war with France and ultimately the loss of Calais in 1558. A Bavarian marriage would likely not have created the same pressure to align with Spain against France. England might have stayed more diplomatically flexible, and the disastrous loss of Calais might possibly have been avoided. If that happened, Mary’s historical reputation would be less bleak, since Calais became a symbol of failure. Avoiding that war would be one of the most important practical consequences of the alternate marriage.

Dynastically, much would depend on whether Mary still had a child. If Mary and Philip of Bavaria produced a Catholic heir, English history could have changed dramatically. Elizabeth might never have become queen, and England could have remained on a more firmly Catholic path for much longer. In that case, the Elizabethan religious settlement, the particular shape of English Protestant identity, and even later conflicts with Spain could all have unfolded very differently. If, however, Mary still died childless, then Elizabeth would probably still have succeeded her, and many of Mary’s changes would likely have been reversed much as they were in reality.

Bavaria itself was an important Catholic princely house in the Empire, but not one able to guarantee the same military and diplomatic backing that Spain offered. So Mary would gain a respectable Catholic alliance, but not the enormous prestige or strategic clout of a Spanish-Habsburg marriage. That could be an advantage domestically, because it would appear less threatening, but a disadvantage internationally, because it would give England less leverage in European power politics.

So in summary, a marriage between Mary Tudor and Philip of Bavaria would probably have made her reign less identified with Spain and less politically toxic in England, while leaving her Catholic program broadly intact. The most likely major differences would be reduced fear of foreign domination, a lower chance of being dragged into war on Spain’s terms, and therefore a better chance of avoiding the loss of Calais. The truly transformative consequence would still hinge on the succession: if the marriage produced a surviving Catholic heir, English history might be radically different; if not, the long-term outcome might remain surprisingly close to what actually happened.

items.question: What If Have a Christian or Post-Christian religion incorporate as many "apocrypha" into its canon as possible
human_answers: I suppose the first question is what is meant by apocrypha? Because it can mean different things and they're all different to address. Is it what many Protestants and Rabbinic Judaism call apocrypha? That is the additional books of the Old Testament that are instead considered Deuterocanon in Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy? At its core, these are books found in the LXX (Septuagint), but not found in the Masoretic text and are considered canonical texts for the majority of the Christian world. Removing the Protestant Masoretic preference resolves that part easily. Is it the broader Second Temple literature, often called Jewish Apocrypha? This is largely apocalyptic literature and includes things like Enoch, the somewhat related Jubilees, Esdras A (or III Ezra, or I Esdras...) , the Apocalypse of Esdra (IV Ezra/II Esdras), the various Baruchs, but also includes Wisdom literature like Psalms 151-155, Wisdom of Sirach, and the Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs. Some of these were contained in LXX translations (Sirach, the Esdras, Psalms 151-155, etc), while others weren't (Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs, II Baruch, Enoch). This is a mixed bag for canonical status, some of them made it in due to being in existing Greek collections (the LXX), while others weren't. Enoch certainly saw a lot of respect in the early church, but it ultimately lost its status over time and only remained in Ethiopia; which itself has weird canon, the Ethiopic Bible includes Enoch and Jubilees before the Esdras, and also includes the 3 Books of Meqabyan (Ethiopic Maccabees), while disincluding the actual Books of Maccabees (and the Ethiopic books are not at all related, they aren't about martyrs at all in fact, and are almost certainly written in the Middle Ages in Ge'ez originally). A lot of these are interesting books that could have significant impact on theology, but most of them are written quite late too, which was a large part of why they weren't included in any canon; most were know pseudepigrapha even at the time. Then we have the New Testament apocrypha, which ranges from things like gnostic literature and known pseudepigrapha with little chance of incorporation to the antilegomena, many of which had good chance of inclusion. Those not included, but that could have been are the Gospel of the Hebrews (scholars think there's actually 3 different works under this title, and they're all lost), the Apocalypse of Peter, the Acts of Paul, the Shepherd of Hermas, the Epistle of Barnabas and the Didache. Worth stating is that the antilegomena weren't "removed," there was heavy debate early in Christianity of what was and wasn't canonical. Different churches used different books. Some were popular in one place, but unknown in others. Worth stating for the record: the Council of Nicea had NOTHING to do with canonical formation and this was still getting discussed for centuries after. The Church Father Jerome is one of the most important figures in the Old Testament canon development, he was highly influential in the West and was one of the main reasons for why the Catholic and Orthodox Deuterocanons are slightly different. As far as the New Testament, most of the Acts of the Apostyles genre were known pseudepigrapha and very clearly non-canonical even in content. They were popular literature and very clearly derived from the Greek novel tradition. Acts of Paul being one exception to this, it was deeply popular and some argued canonical, but in a canon that includes the Pastorals (and even the Deutero-Paulines), it just didn't fit with the theology of the Pauline letters (although I'd argue it fits quite well with the Authentic Pauline corpus). The Apocylpse of Peter wasn't actually well regarded by most priests and theologians though, but it was certainly popular. Its essentially an early Dante's Inferno. The Shepherd/Hermas, Barnabas (NOT the Gospel of Barnabas, which is a medieval forgery), and the Didache I think are the easiest bunch, although not entirely without problem. The Shepherd is deeply allegorical, but was known to not be apostolic (not insurmountable, as Hebrews made it in, but apostolic lineage was important) and has an arguably binitarian lean to it. Barnabas is also allegorical and also deeply anti-jewish. It is essentially saying that the Jews misread their own books, and this is what the Jewish laws really mean - a lot of these require some serious contortion, to say the least. The Didache is interesting since its the first book of the genre of "Church Orders," which are basically moral and litergical texts. In some ways, its an early version of the genre that would become the Anglican Book of Common Prayer. Some other possibilities are the Odes of Solomon, which are a Judeo-Christian work, likely from the Qumran community, with a pretty strong connection to the Johannine literature.

Another work to consider is the Ascension of Isaiah, a christian work written as a series of visions/prophecies of the prophet Isaiah. Also, the Book of Adam and Eve could become part of the Bible, it discusses what happens to Adam and Eve after Genesis, which is interesting. I doubt the distinction of a so-called "Thomasine" branch of anything, seeing as the gospel of Thomas is a late forgery, dating from the 2nd Century, and not originating from any known centers of Christianity claiming Thomasine origin, Kerala, Edessa or Bactria. The chance of the Didache becoming part of the Bible seems slight to me, seeing as its genre isnt really saying it should be, its just a how to book, thought to be directed to clergy. I would agree the best chance to expand is going to be the Apostolic fathers works: Letters of Ignatius, Polycarp, possibly Papias' work might make it in as a supplement to Acts of the Apostles.

Something to keep in mind, is that "canon" actually has different meanings. And what you mean by "canon" could have major implications on just how big it can get. To general Protestants, the Biblical Canon means that these are only 66 divinely inspired books, period, no more, no less (the familiar Protestant Canon). The Catholic teaching is a bit more nuanced. It states that there are at least 73 divinely inspired books (which make up the Catholic Canon). This does actual leave open the possibility that there are other books that could be divinely inspire but just are not included. That said, there are some individual books that have been rule as incompatible with canon & not divinely inspired. For most of the other Christian sects, the concept of canon is a bit "fuzzier." With many of the books falling into a category that could best be described as "potentially divinely inspired, but since it we see no problems with it we don't need to bother making any further determinations". Thus they are still included in the canon list.

Yes I am including those (potentially). It's a challenge though so it's more of a "would it be realistic" thing. And no real timeline, could be very early or very late. No, as long as there is a somewhat notable text that does consider them canonical. For instance 1 Enoch is not considered orthodox by the majority of Christians but there is at least one denomination that does consider it such. I see. That does make sense. Apparently a lot of stories that have become Christian folklore (of sorts) are from books like the Infancy Gospel that are not usually considered canon, but there are traces throughout art and popular imagination (and even in Islam). Some of the non-canonical Gospels and Acts for instance, additional pseudo-Pauline epistles (and letters by other figures). Could be a fairly small but still notable enough to make it into the historical record and maybe persist as a niche sect.
items.original_question:
AHC: Have a Christian or Post-Christian religion incorporate as many "apocrypha" into its canon as possible

The definition of "apocrypha" obviously varies across denomination, e.g. 1 Enoch is canon according to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church but not any other major denominations. But I'm thinking more along the lines of having some denomination which recognizes as many texts as possible which are not in every Biblical canon IOTL (and possible none), e.g. Acts of various specific figures (as distinct from Acts of the Apostles), Gospel of Thomas, etc. etc.
items.model_answer:
If a Christian or post-Christian religion tried to incorporate as many “apocrypha” as possible into its canon, the result would probably be a much broader, more plural, and more internally tension-filled religion than most historic churches. “Apocrypha” here could mean several layers: the Deuterocanonical books accepted by Catholics and Orthodox but not most Protestants, Jewish pseudepigrapha like 1 Enoch and Jubilees, New Testament apocrypha like the Gospel of Thomas or Protoevangelium of James, later apocalypses, acts, infancy gospels, and even some medieval visionary material. A canon built to maximize inclusion would look less like the tightly bounded Bible familiar in mainstream Christianity and more like a library of sacred witness.

The first major effect would be theological expansion. Traditional Christian doctrine is shaped by a relatively small set of texts that achieved canonical status. If you add many apocryphal works, you immediately widen the range of available beliefs about angels, demons, cosmology, the afterlife, Mary, Jesus’s childhood, secret teachings, apostolic missions, and the end times. For example, books like 1 Enoch would amplify angelology and demonology; the Protoevangelium of James would strengthen traditions about Mary’s holiness and early life; the Gospel of Thomas might foreground sayings-based spirituality and inner enlightenment; apocalyptic texts would diversify ideas about resurrection, judgment, and heavenly journeys. Such a religion would likely tolerate multiple theological voices rather than insisting on one systematic doctrine.

Second, authority would change. In historic Christianity, canon helps define orthodoxy by excluding certain texts. A maximal-apocrypha canon would weaken that sharp boundary. Religious leaders would have to decide whether all included texts are equally authoritative or whether there are tiers: perhaps a core canon, a secondary canon, and edifying but nonbinding writings. Without some hierarchy, contradictions would become very difficult to manage. One text might support bodily resurrection, another a more mystical interpretation of salvation; one might emphasize church order, another private revelation. So in practice, even a highly inclusive religion would probably develop a layered canon rather than treating every text identically.

Third, ritual and devotional life would become richer and stranger. Many apocryphal texts are vivid, story-driven, and liturgically suggestive. They supply names, scenes, and legends that mainstream Christians often know through tradition rather than scripture: the names of Mary’s parents, expanded stories of the apostles, dramatic descents into hell, elaborate heavenly visions. If these became canonical, feast days, prayers, icons, drama, pilgrimage traditions, and moral teaching would multiply. The religion might look more imaginative and mythically textured than text-centered Protestantism, perhaps closer in feel to some forms of Orthodoxy, Catholicism, or esoteric Christianity, but even more expansive.

Fourth, identity would shift from exclusivity to curation. A religion that canonized many apocrypha would almost have to present itself as preserving the fullness of Christian memory rather than the purified original deposit of faith. It might claim that the early church narrowed the canon too much, and that divine revelation is broader than later orthodoxy allowed. This could make it attractive to people dissatisfied with rigid dogma, especially in a post-Christian setting where seekers often prefer spiritual plurality, hidden traditions, and suppressed voices. It could present itself as the “great archive” of Christian possibility.

At the same time, there would be serious problems. The more texts included, the harder it is to maintain doctrinal clarity, communal unity, and historical credibility. Some apocrypha were written much later than the apostolic age, reflect strongly sectarian agendas, or contain legendary embellishments. A church that declared all of them canonical would face immediate questions: why these texts and not others? On what grounds are obviously conflicting writings all sacred? Is historical truth required, or only spiritual usefulness? The religion would need a robust theory of revelation—perhaps saying that inspiration is multivocal, symbolic, and cumulative rather than uniform and literal.

If this were a post-Christian religion rather than a church trying to remain conventionally Christian, the outcome could be even more radical. It might treat Jesus not as the sole center of a closed revelation but as the focal figure in a vast sacred ecosystem of writings. Canon would function less as a fixed rule of faith and more as an expanding constellation. Such a movement could blend Christian apocrypha with Gnostic, mystical, esoteric, and even non-Christian texts, creating something like a Christian-adjacent wisdom tradition. In that case, “canon” would mean recognized sacred literature, not a strict doctrinal boundary.

So the most likely answer is that incorporating as many apocrypha as possible would produce a religion that is broader, more imaginative, more mystical, and more inclusive of neglected traditions, but also much less doctrinally tidy. It would probably survive only by adopting a layered view of authority, where some texts are foundational and others are interpretive, visionary, or devotional. Without that structure, the canon would become so large and internally diverse that it would be less a single scripture than a sacred library.

items.question: What If Greek royal family that is ethnically Greek
human_answers: "What factors allowed the European powers to accept native princes in Serbia" is a false question because it presumes the European powers had a role in allowing native princes there to begin with. With the exception of Russia during the First Serbian Uprising, there were no other powers involved beyond the Ottomans. Had it ended with the First Serbian Uprising, whether in Ičko's Peace in 1807 or by 1813 otherwise, we would've seen the Ottomans consenting to a native prince in the region, in the form of Karađorđe, by themselves, and that'd be the end of it. Karađorđe was already attempting to consolidate power for himself in those latter years, even while he had opposition, so he was already set to be uncontested. Which brings forth two questions: had the Greeks fought alone, would it have increased the odds of a native prince being put in power, and would they have even chosen to be a monarchy? As others have argued so far, there was too much conflict between the various revolutionaries to allow for something like that, and it's also why OTL there actually wasn't a monarchy in Greece after the revolution until Greece's stability was brought under question and it was decided by the Great Powers that it should be a monarchy with a foreign prince in power to bolster it. This ignores some of the historical facts surrounding the dynastic conflict in Serbia. Obrenović didn't just decide he was going to challenge Karađorđe's claim to authority over the Serbs, he had become a leader in his own right, rallied the people to another uprising, and won, by the time Karađorđe attempted to come back. He had received what Karađorđe would've gotten had the First Serbian Uprising won, effectively, and he wasn't going to let him challenge that, least of all because of fears of what the Ottomans might do in response. Had the Greek War of Independence seen a decisively unifying leader like Karađorđe or Obrenović from its outset, there's no reason to assume that you'd have other leaders contesting their claim to power by wishing to assert themselves instead - when Karađorđe attempted to consolidate power, he received pushback on it, and it's likely a Greek-equivalent situation would see a similar conflict, where the consolidating leader would receive pushback from his revolutionary peers. But as everyone else has pointed out, revolutionary leadership was a lot more diffuse and filled with conflict, so there's no chance you'd have a unifying leader like that emerge. Really, the case of Serbia should highlight the fact that, had the Greek War of Independence not been a war for independence, but a war for greater autonomy ala the First Serbian Uprising up to 1807, in a TL where it was successful, depending on who's Sultan at the time, the same privileges extended in Ičko's Peace to the Serbs might be extended to the Greeks too, which means that the Ottomans would've demanded the Greeks decide on who to be prince among their leaders.
items.original_question:
AHC: Greek royal family that is ethnically Greek

Greece became independent from the Ottoman Empire in 1821. Two different European dynasties ruled it - the Bavarians (whose only king of Greece was the unpopular King Otto) and the Danish. Neither of these dynasties were of Greek heritage. However, there was a sizable Greek aristocracy in the Ottoman Empire, such as the Phanariotes of Constantinople. What if an ethnically Greek family (such as one of the Phanariot families) was chosen to rule Greece? Can you think of some candidates for a possible ethnically Greek royal family for 19th century Greece?
items.model_answer:
If the Greek royal family had been ethnically Greek rather than originally drawn from foreign dynasties, Greek monarchy would likely have had stronger symbolic legitimacy, especially in the 19th and early 20th centuries. One of the main problems of the Greek crown was that it was widely seen as an imported institution, first under the Bavarian Otto and then under the Danish Glücksburg line. A native Greek dynasty could have made the monarchy appear more closely tied to the national struggle for independence, Orthodox identity, and popular political culture.

That might have reduced some of the recurring distrust between crown, politicians, and public. A more culturally rooted monarchy may have been better able to present itself as the natural representative of the nation rather than as a Great Power imposition. In turn, this could have softened the chronic instability that marked modern Greek history, including coups, forced abdications, and sharp divisions between royalists and anti-royalists.

However, ethnicity alone would not have solved the monarchy’s deeper structural problems. Greece still faced weak institutions, foreign intervention, military influence in politics, economic strain, territorial ambitions, and intense factional conflict. The National Schism during World War I, for example, was not just about whether the king seemed foreign; it was about real strategic and constitutional conflict between the monarchy and Venizelos. Even an ethnically Greek king could still have clashed with elected governments, the army, or outside powers.

It is possible that a Greek royal house would have survived longer, perhaps by becoming more clearly constitutional and less identified with outside interests. The monarchy might have developed into something more like a stable national institution, comparable to other European constitutional monarchies. But it is also possible that the same pressures that eventually destroyed the monarchy in Greece would still have prevailed, because the decisive issue was often political behavior, not ancestry.

So the most likely counterfactual is this: an ethnically Greek royal family would probably have enjoyed greater initial acceptance and stronger nationalist legitimacy, which may have reduced some anti-monarchical feeling, but it would not by itself have guaranteed a stable or lasting Greek monarchy.

items.question: What If Peter of Castile (Pedro the Cruel) marries an English princess in 1360s
human_answers: Oh that's very flattering. Thank you I think the TL you're proposing is plausible and interesting re: the development of ATL Castile and Caroline War. I'm not sure the marriage with Philippa of Clarence is the way to achieve it, though. I don't share others' concerns about her inheritance, but it doesn't necessarily fit into Edward III's plans to create spheres of influence for his sons. Philippa, if she's not marrying Mortimer (who had some smaller land claims in Ireland before inheriting the Burke estates through Philippa) would seem to make more sense for a Fitzgerald or Butler or a knight of the Garter who Edward wanted to establish as a peer without alienating anything from the crown. You could argue that I am overestimating the importance of these spheres of influence. (This is around the time that Lionel gets a Visconti bride -- an arrangement negotiated to put pressure on the papacy to approve the Langley-Flanders marriage, which demonstrates that Edward III still had an overarching and interconnected dynastic plan.) But this is a period in which the Black Prince set out his own foreign policy. He does not simply rubber-stamp his father's agreements. It is TBP's decision to end the Castilian alliance when Pedro executed the prisoners from Nájera. Just a few years later, TBP vetoed his father's alliance with Charles the Bad. All of which is to ask, how would it matter to the Black Prince that his niece is queen of Castile? Or would TBP end the alliance anyway if Pedro acts the way he did in OTL? Then there is also the issue of Pedro's not-great treatment of his wives. We don't know much about Lionel (relative to his four more famous brothers), but we see Edward III and Gaunt have very close relationships with their daughters. Edward made his favorite daughter one of the greatest landholders in England and Gaunt was so fond of his eldest daughter (apparently because she reminded him of his late first wife) that he didn't marry her off until her mid 20s. If Lionel has this sort of affection for Philippa then he may not be willing to entrust his daughter to a king like Pedro. (Though, honestly, I think this is a less important point. Not only only is it entirely speculative of Lionel's personal affections, but Lionel does demonstrate a commitment to his father's plans in going through with the Visconti match for the main purpose of furthering his brother's marriage prospects in Flanders. Still, I don't thin Pedro's treatment of his wives can be entirely discounted.) I very strongly suspect that the marriage contract handed the Ulster estate over to Lionel in its entirety and entailed it to his heirs, regardless of remarriage. Heiresses in weak negotiating positions often lost everything to their husbands and, considering both that a) Elizabeth de Burgh only became an heiress because her father was assassinated by his cousin -- i.e., the man who would inherit if Elizabeth did not -- and b) that Elizabeth's guardian was her mother, Maud of Lancaster, who was a member of the English royal family herself, it just seems very likely that the marriage contract gave Lionel everything. Maud was predisposed to favor the royal family as a relative herself and would be very strongly predisposed to screw over the Burghs who murdered her husband by disinheriting them in favor of Lionel.

To be fair, when the negotiations presumably happen (1366 or 1367 the latest) Philippa's father Lionel is alive, healthy and about to be married for the second time. I don’t think the perspective of Philippa inheriting his estates looks all that close at this point. Moreover, I don’t think that the perspective of Pedro potentially inheriting domains in England and Ireland should scare Edward all that much. If anything, they could potentially serve as a hook to ensure the favorable Castilian policy towards England or otherwise they can be easily confiscated (it’s not like Castile can really try retain those estates against the wishes of Plantagenets). If after Lionel dies Edward really wants to revert these estates back to the crown (although as mentioned before there are arguments for Edward not to do it), I think there is a really neat way to do it. Presumably Philippa’s dowry however large can it be (BTW how large can it be? Up to £10,000 perhaps?) would not be enough to pay for Black Prince’s army (even if ITTL Edward, helping the future husband of his niece, can be a bit more moderate in his pricing). While Pedro can raise some money on his own (he was ready to pay de Guesclin 200000 gold coins – presumably florins - in 1369, so he had some money, although of course it wouldn’t be enough to settle his OTL bill with Edward), he would probably still need to pledge some his territories in lieu of the rest of the payment. So, after Philippa inherits her father’s estates, the mortgage can be rearranged with English and Irish estates now serving as a collateral instead of Castilian territories. Or even perhaps these estates can be given to the Black Prince staight away in lieu of the rest of the debt. @material_boy , what do you think about the proposed PoD and some of its consequences? I have been toying with the victorious Pedro for several years now, but the perspective of modeling the alternative HYW always seemed to daunting. It was your amazing TL that inspired me to approach it. So your opinion would be especially appreciated (although of course I would be happy to hear feedback from everyone).
items.original_question: What if Peter of Castile (Pedro the Cruel) marries an English princess in 1360s UPD: I have updated both the PoD and who is the most likely bride for Pedro. See up-to-date details here and further ( link ). However all the potential consequences of Pedro surviving described in the second part of this message are still very much valid. UPD 2: Please find the TL draft for 1362-1364 in this message ( link ) I've always had a soft spot for Pedro the Cruel (aka Pedro the Just) of Castile. His victory over Henry of Trastamara would have monumental consequences both for Iberian Kingdoms and for Europe in general (I will list some of them further down). While there are a few threads on the forum discussing the possibility of his victory over Henry they are all rather short and usually either discuss earlier PoDs (e. g. Joan of England surviving and marrying Pedro) or more decisive battle of Najera (with Henry being killed or captured in battle). The former is definitely plausible, but would alter 1350s and 1360s quite a bit, while the later doesn’t strike me as all that consequential (after all in 1367 Henry has a son as well as two brothers who could potentially lead the Trastamara party to victory even without Henry). IMHO the main reason for Pedro losing the Castilian Civil War were not particular mistakes on his part or successful moves on Henry’s, but rather the military dominance of du Guesclin’s routier army over Castilian one. So, if we want Pedro to retain his throne, we need to either occupy or counterbalance routiers until the Caroline Phase of the Hundred Years’ War starts. The latter was successfully done IOTL with the help of Edward the Black Prince in 1367, but the relations between Pedro and Edward quickly deteriorated mainly because Edward didn’t receive his pay as per treaty of Libourne and thus Pedro was left to his own devices in 1368-1369 and was defeated and killed. Presumably Pedro didn’t pay Edward simply because he was unable to raise such an enormous sum. The PoD I present is Pedro marrying Philippa of Clarence as part of negotiations with English. Philippa is the eldest granddaughter of Edward III and has just reached marriageable age in 1367. IOTL, she married Edmund Mortimer but of course king of Castile is a way more prestigious match (there are conflicting records about when exactly Philippa was betrothed to Edmund IOTL, but for the purpose of this PoD let us pick the latest option 1368). Pedro on the other hand is in his thirties, has not legitimate issue and both his wife and his beloved mistress are dead since 1361. The purpose of the marriage is twofold: firstly, to bring Castile closer to England and secondly to be a neat way to subsidize Edward’s expedition. I am not sure how large Philippa’s dowry was IOTL, but presumably if she has a royal marriage, it definitely should be quite large. So Edward’s army can at least partly be subsidized with his niece’s dowry. I am not sure if such an arrangement is plausible, but if it does happen consequences are massive. Presumably if the relationship between the Black Prince and Pedro is unstrained (or at least is significantly better than IOTL), the second invasion of Henry and de Guesclin would seem futile and probably doesn’t happen. In 1369 the Caroline Phase begins (even if IOTL Charles V summoned Edward because he already realized that Castille would fall to Henry, which is debatable, ITTL Charles presumably understands that Edward would help Pedro no matter what and thus he might as well go on with his plan). Thus, Henry would have very little military support and will stand no chance against Pedro and his allies. Possible consequences of the PoD: 1. Castille itself has a radically different social structure. a. IOTL Henry and his heirs had to give out large parts of royal domain for their supporters from lesser nobility that formed new aristocratic elites (since pedristas were active until mid-1380s Trastamaras needed their continous support for an extended period of time and thus royal domain suffered greatly). Quoting from Teofilo F.
