It is difficult to ascertain how the French in Canada felt, as they lived in a quasi-medieval subsistence economy. Although not under full-blown feudalism, their society was paternalistic, hierarchical, and agrarian. The Church and the seigneurs (many of the seigneuries were owned by religious orders) were the pillars of authority. This is crucial in explaining the lack of widespread revolutionary fervour. However, in the late eighteenth century, there remained a cultural and sentimental connection to France, particularly to the Ancien Régime and the monarchy. After the executions of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, masses were said for them, and the French press in Quebec noted this. They were mourning the grandson of their last French sovereign, not celebrating the secular republic that executed him. In December 1778, from Boston, French Admiral d’Estaing called on the Canadiens to rise and rejoin their motherland, but this was difficult as Canada was where most British forces were stationed. It is unclear whether they wished to return to France, but the Continental Congress felt uneasy about the French returning to North America. Because the Canadiens were largely illiterate (literacy was still below 40% in 1850), it is difficult to say whether they were politically sophisticated, as the colony had been largely marginal and lacked a large merchant class under French rule. Education was not widespread and was largely controlled by seminaries or convents. It was even less politically sophisticated than the Spanish colonies in the Americas. My guess is that independence would have been the least likely of options, unless the Bishop of Quebec assumed the role of head of government.

Then the place will find a way to get out of American control ASAP. Mismatched expectations and all that because of a fundamental misreading by the Continental Army/Congress of the situation, particularly WRT the Quebec Act. The French never wanted to retain Canada après la Conquête because the sugar colonies in the Caribbean were far more valuable, plus lots of bad blood between the Canadiens and Versailles about which direction their part of New France should go. You'd basically be accelerating the French Revolution's TL but with a Canadien cause - and this time the British would come off as the good guys by allying with the habitants, whether or not it takes it back under its wing or accepts it as an independent country but under the British sphere of influence. And it finds a way to get out of the US ASAP, particularly if the initial military occupation goes as OTL and they basically alienated everyone. More probable than getting annexed by the US. Considering Quebec in this case would be a direct cause for the French Revolution ITTL, that's easy to remark on. While still predominantly Francophone (albeit with Canadian French given the same recognition as, say, Brazilian Portuguese), society and culture would take a more, say, Argentine or Uruguayan-like direction but w/ its own quirks (including probably far more indigenous influence) and probably different relationships among groups that would be relatively more egalitarian and opposed to reinstating the colonial relationship. Considering the British would still be next door viz. Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, as well as the HBC doing its thing, British influence would remain strong and that would include the cultural sphere, too.

It depends on how the Americans treat the Canadiens, and how they handle the Iroquois. If the Americans can't keep the Iroquois mostly neutral, and if they prevent them from trading with the Canadiens, then Quebec will want want to leave in a hurry. If the Americans could be deft in the administration of Quebec, better in battle, luckier with allied victories, and more skillful in peace negotiation I think there is a good chance that the Canadiens would want to be in a confederacy, or a customs union with a mutual defense pact. The centralizing reforms of the Constitution would likely have been opposed by the Canadiens as antifederalism, which brings me to the next point, though it is possible they could remain in the union if it transitions from Articles of Confederation to Constitution. While the Canadiens would most likely have forbade slavery, that doesn't mean they would have been abolitionists in the vein of the northeastern Calvinists and Quakers. While they could have been like the 1840s and 1850s Free Soilers, their antifederalism and relative lack of industrialization might have moved them into common cause with Southern states. The Canadiens also could have been aligned with the "Westerners" in looking for federally funded internal developments to help with their access to Atlantic ports, and their access to settling Upper Canada and Indiana/Illinois Territory. Being so close to Nova Scotia and Newfoundland the Canadiens could also be interested in a strong navy. So perhaps an American Quebec could be allied with someone like Calhoun. As for the issue of Loyalist Migration, their emigration would likely have been reduced if they didn't have British Upper Canada as a destination. Many of the Loyalists would have resigned themselves to life in the new government. There still would have been Loyalist emigration from both America and Lower Canada, and there would still be a movement of Loyalists to Upper Canada and other territories despite them being no longer British Empire owned. So those populations would have thrown a new political impulse into the country later especially after the Constitution is ratified.

I'd assume a French route with independence after the French revolution. Maybe some nobility or rich flee to Quebec during the revolution. I'd think US keeps what it would get otl plus Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward island. Ontario might go to the U.S. While Newfoundland and Labrador goes to Quebec. The American loyalists could be moved into western Canada to try to colonize Western Canada. England might be more harsh in dealing with the Oregon territory. You could see a war over it with Quebec siding with a side. Should U.S. Win they might get British Columbia in the treaty. Quebec might get islands in Nunavut. Russia in this timeline would probably favor selling Alaska to England. With more northern territory. I can see the South looking for more Mexican territory. There's a possibility the slave and free state addition could continue on longer. This causes a delay of the civil war potentially.
items.original_question: What if Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop? So having just watched a new video from Blue, it gave me an idea of dusting off an old topic I used to talk about In 1775, the Continental Army under Generals, Richard Montgomery, Daniel Morgan, James Livingston, and Benedict Arnold (Yes, that Benedict Arnold) marched north into Canada in an attempt to capture Quebec from the British and persuade the French Canadians in joining the revolution. It went well for part of the expedition at first, with Montgomery nearly capturing British Govenor Guy Carleton in Montreal. Meanwhile Arnold's part journeyed through the wilderness to get to Quebec City, which was very difficult. However, by the time the Americans gotten to Quebec, a snowstorm occurred and the battle turned into an utter disaster. Montgomery got killed, Arnold was wounded, smallpox plagued the Americans, the British suffered few causalities, and the Americans managed to alienate the Canadians. Meanwhile, Carleton received reinforcements and made a counter offensive that drove the Americans back to Fort Ticonderoga. For context, what if the Americans captured Quebec? Say Montgomery captured Govenor Guy Carleton and the Americans managed to catch Quebec City by surprise. In my previous thread about the fate of Quebec (Roughly around Lower Canada; Upper Canada is a whole other can of worms), there were four possibilities I gave, but we're going to talk about three: A) French route- The Americans offer Quebec back to France for support in their war, meaning France regains Quebec by the end of the war B) American route- The Americans annex Quebec, making Quebec part of the USA. C) Independent route- The Americans make Quebec into a sister republic, making Quebec independent by the end of the war. (There's no British route since that OTL) Now, I want to focus on one particular aspect of the fate of Quebec: Culture. If Quebec wasn't under the British/TTL Canada, what would culture be like for the French Canadians. Depending on the route we take, how would culture, society, art, cuisine, fashion, etc, develop for the French Canadians? In the French route, how would Quebec be affected by the French Revolution? In the American route, how would Quebec develop under the USA? In the Independent route, how would Quebec develop stuck between the British and Americans while having access to the St Lawrence?
items.model_answer:
If the Americans had captured Quebec in 1775 and held it, Quebec would probably still have remained overwhelmingly French-speaking and Catholic for a long time, but its political identity would have developed very differently. Instead of becoming the core of a British Canadian state, it would have been folded into the revolutionary world of the United States. That would not mean rapid assimilation into Anglo-America, though. In the late eighteenth century the American rebels were not in a strong position to replace Quebec’s population, religion, or legal customs overnight, and they would have had good reasons to conciliate the French Canadian majority.

The first big issue would have been religion and law. One of the main reasons the Continental Congress tried to win over Quebec in the first place was by promising liberties rather than forced cultural change. If the Americans had succeeded, they likely would have had to preserve Catholic worship, tolerate the Church, and probably leave much of French civil law and seigneurial landholding in place, at least temporarily. Otherwise they would have faced constant resistance from a population that was already wary of both British and American Protestants. So in the short run, Quebec might have resembled a more northern version of later Louisiana: politically attached to the United States, but socially and legally distinct.

That said, integration into the United States would still have changed Quebec’s trajectory in major ways. The American Revolution and the political culture that followed were less accepting of corporate privileges, aristocratic hierarchy, and established church influence than either old France or the British imperial settlement in Quebec. Over time, American state-building would likely have weakened the seigneurial system earlier, reduced the political power of the Catholic clergy, and promoted elected institutions more aggressively. Quebec society might therefore have become more republican and locally political earlier than it did under British rule, but not necessarily more culturally English at first.

Language would be the central long-term question. Under British Canada, French survived in large part because Quebec became the demographic and institutional center of French Canada. If Quebec became part of the United States, French would probably remain dominant locally for decades, especially in the countryside and parish life, but it would face stronger pressure from English over the nineteenth century. Migration from New England and New York into the St. Lawrence valley would likely be heavier than in actual history, especially after independence and westward expansion stabilized. American commercial networks, courts, newspapers, and politics would reward English. French would survive, but probably in a more regionally confined and defensive way, rather than as the language of a future province leading a bilingual federation.

This means Quebec’s culture might evolve into something like a large-scale northern analogue of Cajun or Creole Louisiana, though more populous and therefore more resilient. French Canadian identity would still exist, but perhaps less as the basis for a quasi-national project and more as an ethnic, regional, and religious identity inside the United States. Instead of becoming one of the “founding peoples” of Canada, French speakers in Quebec might become one of several major American minority cultures. Their institutions—schools, churches, local courts, presses—could still be substantial, but they would likely have to fight harder to preserve them against pressures for linguistic and civic standardization.

There is also the question of slavery, race, and continental politics. If Quebec joined the United States early, it would almost certainly enter as a free or gradually freeing region, since slavery there was limited and the climate and economy did not favor plantation development. That would place it in the northern political orbit. In the nineteenth century, a French Catholic Quebec inside the United States might become associated with northern anti-slavery politics, immigrant Catholic politics, and resistance to nativist Protestant movements. Its Catholics would likely face the same anti-Catholic suspicion that Irish and other Catholic groups later encountered, but because Quebec’s population was older, rooted, and regionally concentrated, it could respond with stronger local solidarity.

The biggest difference from real history is that there would probably be no Confederation in the form we know it, and no Quebec as the principal French-speaking province within Canada. Without British Quebec anchoring a northern empire, the rest of British North America might fragment, shrink, or reorganize around the Maritimes and the far interior. That matters because real Quebec’s culture was preserved not only by local stubbornness but by its constitutional place in Canada. Inside the United States, Quebec would lack that same kind of guaranteed national bargaining position. It might still keep its language and faith, but with less formal protection and more dependence on local majorities and state rights.

So the most likely outcome is not that Quebec becomes instantly “Americanized,” nor that it remains unchanged. Rather, it becomes a French-speaking, Catholic, increasingly republican society inside the early United States, preserving much of its local culture at first but gradually experiencing stronger assimilationist pressure than it did in Canada. By the late nineteenth or twentieth century, it would probably still be recognizably French in language, memory, and religion, but less institutionally secure, less nationally central, and more like a powerful regional minority culture than a coequal national one.

items.original_question: Administration of British colonies in North America if the USA would have never existed? I have seen several maps of North America in alternate history scenarios where the 13 colonies lost in 1775/1776. IF England would have won, how would they have administered their colonies in North America afterwards in the late 18th, the 19th, and the 20th century? Would they have administered their colonies separately (Pensilvania, Massachusetts, Newfoundland, Quebec, "Canada?", Florida, Louisiana, Oregon etc.) or would they have united them sooner or later in a big north american british dominion? Also, would they have eventually taken oregon/nootka? what about louisiana and alaska from france and russia respectively? PS: Yes I know there are a lot of "What if the US lost the war of 1776..." threads here but this is mostly about the administration of these colonies
items.model_answer:
If the United States had never come into existence, the British colonies in North America would probably have remained under British imperial administration at first, but they would not likely have stayed forever as tightly controlled colonies. The most plausible long-term outcome is that they would have evolved into something like Canada, Australia, or New Zealand: self-governing British dominions within the Empire, and eventually independent states or a federated North American dominion.

In the short term, administration would have continued through the British system already in place before independence. London governed through the Crown, the Board of Trade, colonial governors, and local assemblies. Each colony had its own charter, governor or lieutenant governor, courts, and elected assembly, but ultimate authority rested with Parliament and the Crown. Britain had already been trying after the Seven Years’ War to tighten imperial control, raise revenue, station troops, and regulate westward expansion. If no American break had occurred, this central oversight likely would have continued for some time, though Britain would probably have had to compromise more with colonial elites to keep the colonies stable.

Over time, the colonies would likely have gained more internal self-government. The British Empire in the nineteenth century increasingly shifted toward granting settler colonies control over domestic affairs while Britain retained authority over foreign policy, defense, and constitutional matters. In that scenario, the mainland colonies might have followed a path similar to British North America after 1776: provincial governments first, then perhaps regional unions, and eventually a larger federation. A single “British North America” stretching far beyond historical Canada is conceivable, though not guaranteed; regional divisions between New England, the Middle Colonies, the South, and the frontier might also have produced multiple dominions rather than one.

Slavery would have made administration especially complicated. Since Britain abolished slavery in most of its empire in the 1830s, a British North America that still included the southern mainland colonies would almost certainly have faced imperial emancipation. That could have caused major political conflict, perhaps even rebellion by slaveholding colonies, and might have led to some kind of restructuring or separation within British North America. So even if the USA never existed, the mainland colonies might not have remained one unified political unit.

Westward expansion would also have been different. Britain had tried to limit settlement beyond the Appalachians in 1763, partly to reduce conflict with Indigenous nations. Without an independent United States pushing aggressively westward as it did historically, expansion may have been slower, more negotiated, and more directly shaped by imperial strategy. But it would still probably have happened eventually, especially given settler population growth and imperial rivalry with Spain, France, and later Russia in North America.

By the late nineteenth or early twentieth century, the most likely administrative form would have been a dominion or a set of dominions under the British Crown, with responsible parliamentary government modeled on Westminster. In the very long run, these entities would probably have become fully sovereign, as Canada did, while perhaps retaining the monarch as head of state for some time.

So the simplest answer is: if the USA had never existed, Britain would probably not have ruled the North American colonies forever as old-style colonies. They would most likely have moved from crown-and-parliament administration, to self-governing dominions within the British Empire, and eventually to independence, either as one large federated British North American state or as several successor states.

items.question: What If the Southern Ming had survived?
human_answers: I foresee a successful Chinese expedition to retake the North within a decade or two. Sichuan was perhaps ironically where the most effective anti-Qing forces were based in OTL. Remnants of Zhang Xianzhong and Li Zicheng’s forces continued fighting there for decades until well into Kangxi’s reign IOTL. The site saw repeated struggles between different forces for many decades. It’s actually the reason for the significant decline in the population of Sichuan IOTL, not Zhang Xianzhong’s Sichuan massacre. Population wise, the Qing Dynasty would have difficulty regrowing the population of the north due to lack of food. The North has always been a basket case since the end of the Northern Song Dynasty. During the Ming Dynasty, Southern China had at least two times the population of the North. And that is before the collapse of the Ming Dynasty Which saw massive fighting. You see plenty of areas throughout Northern China eating rice as staples today, but the truth was that this is evidence for how much northerners have come to rely on Southern grain. Rice does not grow in the North, and has to be imported from the South. Before the Sui-Tang Dynasties when the Grand Canal was not built, Northern diet was based on wheat. Still is to a lesser extent today. After this period, they became increasingly reliant on Southern crops until from the Ming Dynasty onwards, they became entirely reliant on it. Northern Qing can’t just regrow when they don’t even have the rice to feed the people. As time goes on, even by the 17th century, warfare is gonna increasingly dependant upon firearms, meaning population,technology and economy is gonna become decisive in eventual Southern victory. Individual prowess of the troops that the Manchus relied heavily on will become less relevant,especially as the Qing simply does not have Manchu population to supply large armies to both stamp out rebellions or to fight the Southern dynasty. The Manchus iotl exploited a critical window before that was gonna be a problem to conquer the South.

This is what I have in mind: 1. In OTL, as I understand it, by this point the Ming dynasty’s North China had been devastated, the population had grown unevenly, and the state had come to depend heavily on Jiangnan’s grain resources. In that situation, if the Qing were to occupy only North China while the Ming retained control of Jiangnan, the Qing would likely suffer from serious food shortages. Under such conditions, I think it is highly likely that the Qing would resort to massacres in North China similar to the Yangzhou massacre seen in OTL. However, in the end, the Qing might later face the problem of overpopulation once again. Personally, when it comes to the Malthusian trap, I think the Northern Qing would suffer from it more severely than the Southern Ming. What do you think? 2. In OTL, the Dzungars were destroyed by Qing expeditions. However, in this timeline, the Dzungars would likely expand their power significantly across Mongolia and Tibet. Unlike in OTL, the Qing would probably remain largely on the defensive. As a result, the Dzungars would not be destroyed and would likely enjoy a substantial imperial existence until they were eventually conquered by the Russian Empire. Russia, too, would likely push into Manchuria more frequently and more deeply than it did in OTL. The Qing would have a much harder time containing them and would probably have to request military assistance from Joseon more often than in OTL . It is even possible that, unlike the Treaty of Nerchinsk, Russia might succeed in extracting territorial gains much deeper inside the region. And here is the next question. In your view, assuming that the Southern Ming and the Northern Qing both survived until the mid-18th century, which state do you think would collapse first? And in what ways do you think each polity would face its respective crises? First of all, in OTL, the course of the Yellow River changed in the 1850s. This could also have significant effects on China.

Why do you say they will sinicise faster? By contrast, I think they’d sinicise even slower, as they can’t hope to match the southern Ming in chineseness and so would have to rely on other pillars of legitimacy to prop up their rule, perhaps leaning further into Tibetan Buddhism. Edit- looking more into how Tibetan Buddhism had spread so deeply into Mongol society in the late 16th century, people seem to say that the Qing need to appeal to Taoist and Confucian ideologies meant they could not be called a primarily Buddhist state. Ittl, I think the Qing would lean much more heavily into buddhist kingship, and this might also make their policy towards Han people less racist- there would be a way for Han people to politically abandon the Confucian-Taoist kingship embodied by the Ming, by adopting Tibetan Buddhism, which would make them part of the ruling group without becoming Manchu. Why do you say it didn’t happen in India? As an aside, there was a mid 17th century equivalent to the treaty of Westphalia in Central Asia, the Great Code of 1640, by which various Oirat and Mongol clans agreed to act as a collective body to uphold general peace and a universal legal code, while upholding the sovereignty of the individual tribes. Otl, it became irrelevant once the Qing got rid of any form of Mongol sovereignty by defeating the Dzunghars and winning the Khalkha Mongols to their cause, but in a world where the Qing aren’t so powerful, the “Holy Mongol Empire” likely maintains its constitutional structure for longer. Instead of a Dzunghar khanate, we’d therefore talk Ming China allying with the Western Yuan Dynasty to hold back the Qing, and perhaps the federal Yuan would be more successful than the Dzunghar were otl in their wars against the Kazakhs/the Khanates of Bukhara. Or perhaps, the Qing end up functioning as the Austria analogue- personally controlling by far the most land and people, but still unable to strip away the autonomy of the various Mongol and oirat ulus’, who regularly meet and would all revolt against imperial overreach.
items.original_question: If the Southern Ming had survived? Thread 'Perpetual Brightness: Surviving Southern Ming' Apr 12, 2006 Once, the Confucian school outside Quanzhou had bustled with students and scholars. Some of China’s greatest administrators had come from there, and in its day the school had been a center of learning. But since the famines, and the Manchu invasion, the school had grown quiet. The buildings were dilapidated, with peeling paint and rotten timber. There was only one man there, in the dark of night, standing by a fire. The man watched as the flames cast a red glow over the temple, as it consumed the robes of a scholar. An Empire was collapsing outside its walls, but inside the silence was... Faeelin Replies: 168 Forum: Alternate History Discussion: Before 1900 In OTL, after an empire collapsed in China, there were many cases where it was not completely destroyed and replaced by another empire, but instead split into northern and southern regimes. Even before the Qing dynasty, the Jurchen states themselves formed a northern empire, while the Southern Song continued to exist in the south. In the 17th century, the Ming dynasty, like the Song before it, also established the Southern Ming. However, it ultimately fell after only twenty years. Was there no way for the Southern Ming to survive? The problems of the Southern Ming, as I see them, are as follows. 1. In the case of the Southern Song, all other imperial claimants were captured by the Jurchens, and as a result, a person low in the line of succession became the only remaining claimant. This, paradoxically, allowed him to secure a certain degree of legitimacy and take power. By contrast, the Southern Ming began in a situation where the legitimate imperial princes had largely been captured from the outset, while there were still too many lower-ranking imperial relatives remaining. This excess of potential claimants triggered disputes over the imperial succession. 2. In the case of the Jin dynasty, it had not yet fully subdued the Western Xia or the Mongols. In particular, the Mongols were later unified by Genghis Khan, who went on to establish the most powerful nomadic empire in history. At the time, the Goryeo dynasty was nominally a tributary state of the Jin, but it had not been decisively subdued through war. The Jin lacked the capacity to invade Goryeo and had no choice but to settle for maintaining relatively moderate relations. In other words, the Jin dynasty could not devote all of its national strength to the conquest of the Southern Song. By contrast, the Qing dynasty had already conquered the Chahar Mongols and had invaded the capital of the Joseon dynasty, forcing it into clear submission. Although the Dzungars and Russia would later enter the Chinese arena, this occurred only after the game had effectively already been decided. 3. The Southern Song was able to survive thanks to outstanding generals such as Yue Fei and Han Shizhong, who successfully defeated the Jurchen armies. By contrast, on the eve of the Ming dynasty’s collapse, Wu Sangui’s forces—virtually the only remaining elite army—defected outright to the Qing side. As a result, the Southern Ming was forced to struggle on with inadequate military strength, trapped in a situation where incompetent warlords fought among themselves in constant internal conflict. Taking these factors into account, I think that for the Southern Ming to have survived for a long time, things would have had to be different from the very beginning. “Before the fall of Beijing, the Chongzhen Emperor decides to transfer the capital to Nanjing. Abandoning Beijing, he withdraws south, and Wu Sangui’s army joins the emperor’s entourage and moves to Nanjing as well.” In effect, this would mean that the Chongzhen Emperor is “ceding North China to the Jurchens,” but even so, the southern regions would be far more securely preserved. However, he did not do so. The reasons lie here. In short, he was an “indecisive and irresolute emperor,” and as a result, instead of taking responsibility for such a momentous decision, he merely kept postponing it. What I am curious about is this: 1. If the Chongzhen Emperor were to decide on relocating the capital, what kind of POD (point of divergence) would need to occur? 2. If the Southern Ming had survived at least until the 19th century, how would East Asian history from the 17th to the 19th centuries have changed? Assuming the Southern Ming succeeded in repelling the initial Qing offensives, who would be in the more advantageous position thereafter? If the Southern Ming were to endure, how would Western powers in the 19th century approach China?
items.model_answer:
If the Southern Ming had survived, the most plausible result is not a simple “China stays the same but without the Qing,” but a very different early modern East Asia in which China remained a Han-ruled, maritime-facing, fiscally strained empire that probably survived only by reforming more than the late Ming ever had.

The first question is what “survived” means. If the Southern Ming merely held on in the far south for a while, then it would likely have become a reduced regional state, perhaps centered on the lower Yangzi, Fujian, Guangdong, or the southwest, coexisting uneasily with a Qing north. But if we mean that it successfully resisted the Manchus and reestablished control over most of China, then the long-term consequences would have been much larger.

In that stronger scenario, the biggest immediate difference is political legitimacy. The Qing solved the dynastic crisis by conquering China and then building a durable imperial order that combined Manchu military power with Confucian statecraft. A surviving Southern Ming would instead have had to restore legitimacy after catastrophic collapse. That would likely require punishing factionalism, rebuilding central authority, and finding a way to reconcile scholar-official elites, regional commanders, and powerful merchants. In other words, the dynasty would survive only if it became less like the late Ming in its final decades. A restored Southern Ming probably would have been more militarized, more dependent on regional armies and naval forces, and more willing to tolerate practical reforms in taxation, defense, and trade.

That matters because the late Ming state had serious structural weaknesses: fiscal shortfalls, elite tax evasion, military decay, and intense court factionalism. The Qing inherited these problems but also benefited from conquest institutions and a relatively disciplined ruling coalition. The Southern Ming did not have that advantage. So survival would probably mean a more reformist and less ideologically rigid regime than the pre-1644 Ming. It might have strengthened coastal defense, integrated maritime commerce into state revenue, and worked more closely with powerful southeast commercial networks.

This leads to one of the clearest counterfactual effects: maritime policy. The Qing, especially in the early decades, imposed severe coastal evacuations and restrictions because of anti-Qing resistance such as Zheng Chenggong’s movement on Taiwan. A surviving Southern Ming would have had every reason to do the opposite. It would probably have leaned heavily on naval power, overseas Chinese merchant networks, and customs revenue. That could have produced a more outward-looking state, especially in Fujian and Guangdong, and perhaps a stronger official engagement with trade in Southeast Asia, Japan, and European merchants. China might not have become “modern” early in any simple sense, but its political economy could have been more commercially integrated and sea-oriented than under the early Qing.

Taiwan would also likely have developed differently. Under a surviving Southern Ming, the Zheng regime might have remained not as an anti-dynastic refuge but as a strategic maritime base within a broader Ming restoration. Taiwan might have been incorporated earlier and more deliberately into a Chinese imperial system, perhaps as a naval frontier rather than as a marginal prefecture. That could have shifted the island’s demographic and political development significantly.

Another major difference concerns Inner Asia. The Qing was not just a Chinese dynasty; it was also an Inner Asian empire. It conquered and governed Mongolia, Tibet, and Xinjiang in ways that profoundly shaped the borders of modern China. A surviving Southern Ming would have had a much harder time doing this. The Ming lacked the Qing’s Manchu-Mongol political networks, banner institutions, and steppe legitimacy. So even if the Southern Ming recovered China proper, it is far from certain that it would have incorporated Xinjiang, Tibet, and Mongolia to the same degree. The map of modern China might therefore be much smaller or at least much looser in those frontier zones. This is probably the single biggest long-term geopolitical difference.

Relations with Europe would also change, but not necessarily in the simplistic direction of “better modernization.” The Southern Ming already existed in a world where Jesuits, silver trade, firearms, and maritime commerce were important. A surviving regime may have been more open to using European artillery specialists, merchants, and diplomatic intermediaries. It may also have been less inclined than the Qing to tightly regulate foreign contact in the early period. But openness to trade is not the same as industrialization or military revolution. The court would still be a Confucian agrarian empire with strong reasons to fear disorder and foreign influence. So one should expect selective engagement, not a sudden transformation into a naval-capitalist power.

Still, in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the absence of the Qing could matter a great deal. The Qing’s high-Qing prosperity and territorial expansion gave China great scale and prestige, but later the dynasty also became identified with ethnic tensions, frontier overstretch, and the challenge of ruling a huge multiethnic empire under mounting Western pressure. A Southern Ming China, if more compact and more maritime, might have faced a different set of nineteenth-century crises. It might have been more vulnerable at sea but less burdened by Inner Asian commitments. It might have had stronger merchant institutions and coastal militaries, which could have helped in confronting Western powers. On the other hand, if it remained fiscally weak and regionally fragmented, it might have succumbed even earlier to internal rebellion or foreign pressure.

Culturally, the consequences would be significant but subtler than people often assume. Many features commonly associated with “traditional China” in the West were shaped by the Qing, including hairstyle regulations like the queue, banner institutions, and certain forms of ethnic hierarchy. Without Qing rule, those features disappear or look very different. Elite culture might show more continuity with late Ming tastes: stronger urban commercial culture, literati individualism, and perhaps more visible links between high culture and merchant wealth. But Confucian orthodoxy, civil examinations, and gentry dominance would likely remain central unless the regime undertook unusually deep reforms.

So the most likely answer is this: if the Southern Ming had truly survived and restored itself, China would probably have remained a major unified empire, but one that was more Han-identified, more coastal and commercial, less successful in Inner Asian expansion, and forced into earlier military-fiscal reform. East Asia would be reshaped accordingly: Taiwan’s role would change, maritime trade might become more central, and the territorial foundations of modern China could be very different. The best-case version is a more adaptive, sea-oriented Ming revival. The worst-case version is a brittle, faction-ridden remnant state that survives temporarily but fails to match the Qing’s territorial and institutional achievements.

items.question: What If the British won the 1812 War?
human_answers: As far as the political landscape is concerned, I think the Federalists are routed as per OTL. They'll be blamed for losing the war, even if theyre ultimately vindicated over the long haul about being right about how the war would go. The whole post-war love affair that existed OTL is going to be gone, and I think the eight years following the war are going to be politically toxic. Depending on the border shuffling, the US might lose multiple free states which will affect the long term sectional rivalry already in development. Illinois might flip to a slave state due to butterflies if the slavers back a single candidate upon the state's formation. The Virginian dynasty probably crumbles and Monroe probably stays put as Secretary of State instead of seeking the presidency. If the Battle of New Orleans doeant take place Jackson's path to power is much longer and more arduous, if he even seeks the office at all. Theres a not unreasonable chance that the capital moves to Philadelphia and stays there. America may seek to purchase Texas around the time they signed the Adams-Onis Treaty of OTL, they could afford it, and if Monroe is still Secretary of State they're probably dabbling more in that area as it was already a pet project of his. If Texas isn't purchased, I think there's going to be a greater push against annexation by the Whigs given the greater disparity between free and slave states. A lot depends on the peace treaty, though.

I would consider OTL to be a tie, and I think spin city can depict it as such at the time. I've seen threads arguing it was a USAmerican victory because Britain wasn't able to conquer them. What does winning look like? Typically, it means taking something from the loser. Since USA never gained anything during the war, there's nothing they can be forced to give back. So, it would have to be something they held prior (or had claim to). Retaking control of any of the lost colonies is largely devoid of reality. Border adjustments in Maine/Vermont/New York are on the table. Making the old Northwest part of Canada, perhaps as a Native Reserve, is a possibility. Would Britain keep New Orleans if they had taken it prior to truce and/or the rest of Louisiana? Give it back to Spain? Trade it for full control of the NW, if they haven't secured control of that already? Realistically, how much could Britain gain? But, I think OP wants to discuss political ramifications if the war ends with there being zero doubt which side won. There could be a major territorial concession which is bound to completely change the USA even if it rebounds spectacularly (such as loss of New Orleans/Louisiana), in which case political ramifications are a secondary concern. Or, territorial concessions are more limited, leaving things a bit more recognizable. A lot of things left unsettled by the ARW, are going to be settled in Britain's favor. Trade agreements may emerge also favoring Britain. Depending on the severity of the peace, politics will also be severely affected far beyond a 'USA lost, unequivocally, but otherwise everything is the same' . So, yeah, we need to know the scope of the peace. The OP needs to be fleshed out more.
items.original_question: What if the British won the 1812 War? How would this influence the US political landscape? My opinion is: 1840 Democratic (Jacksonian, pro-States´ Rights) Whig (Anti-Jacksonian, pro-States´ Rights) Federalist (Anti-Jacksonian, anti-States´ Rights)
items.model_answer:
If Britain had clearly “won” the War of 1812, the biggest immediate effect would probably have been a much weaker United States and a stronger British position in North America, but not the permanent destruction of the U.S. A British victory could have taken several forms—holding more American territory, forcing concessions in a peace treaty, strengthening Native buffer states in the Old Northwest, or humiliating the U.S. badly enough to change its politics for a generation.

The most likely major consequence would have been on the western frontier. One of Britain’s war aims, especially late in the conflict, was to support the creation of a Native American buffer state between the United States and Canada. If Britain had won decisively enough to impose terms, that idea might have survived. In that case, U.S. expansion into the Great Lakes and upper Midwest would have slowed dramatically. Figures like Tecumseh might have become even more historically central, and Native resistance to U.S. settlement would have had much stronger backing. This would not necessarily have stopped U.S. expansion forever, but it could have delayed it by decades and changed the map of the interior.

In Canada, a British victory would have strengthened loyalty to the empire and deepened the sense that British North America had successfully resisted U.S. invasion. Canadian identity already drew heavily from that experience; a clearer British triumph would have made that even stronger. The border might also have become more militarized and politically important much earlier.

Inside the United States, the political consequences could have been severe. The war was already controversial, especially in New England. A humiliating defeat might have discredited the “War Hawks” and the Republican leadership under Madison. The Federalists, instead of collapsing after the Hartford Convention, might have revived as the party of commercial stability and anti-war caution. American nationalism, which in actual history was energized by the war’s symbolic victories, might have developed more slowly and more defensively.

That matters because the War of 1812 helped create a story that the U.S. had fought Britain to a draw and earned international respect. If Britain had clearly won, that sense of national self-confidence would have been shaken. Mythic events like Andrew Jackson’s rise after New Orleans might never have had the same power. Jackson himself might not have become a national hero, which could have altered the future of American democracy, Indian removal, and party politics in the 1820s and 1830s.

Economically, a British victory might have kept the United States more vulnerable to British commercial pressure. The U.S. would still likely have grown, because its population and land resources were enormous, but its leaders might have been more cautious in challenging Britain at sea and in foreign trade. American industrialization, which got a boost from wartime disruption and postwar nationalism, may have proceeded more unevenly.

In foreign affairs, Britain would have emerged with greater prestige and leverage in North America, though probably not with a desire to reconquer the United States. By 1812–1815 Britain was more concerned with Napoleon and global strategy than with restoring the old colonies. So even in victory, Britain likely would have sought a stable, subordinate U.S., not annexation. The Monroe Doctrine, issued in 1823, might have been weaker, delayed, or less credible if the U.S. had recently suffered defeat by Britain.

In the long run, the U.S. probably still becomes a large and powerful country because of its demographics, resources, and distance from Europe. But a British victory could have produced a North America where Canada was more secure, Native confederacies remained stronger for longer, U.S. western expansion slowed, and American nationalism matured later and with less confidence. In short, Britain winning the War of 1812 would most likely not have erased the United States, but it could have made the 19th-century continent more British, more Indigenous in the interior for a time, and less decisively dominated by the U.S.

items.question: What If the English Armada of 1589 had succeeded in destroying Spain's remaining Atlantic fleet and triggering a Portuguese revolt?
human_answers: Actually, I think one could argue the opposite: that it's magically deterministic to assume that, in some unspecified way, this crisis will send the whole country into a downward spiral that will lead to its implosion. I mean, once you go over the list of changes, there isn't too much difference: yes, the Spanish Navy has been severely damaged; yes, Portugal has become independent; yes, Spain has lost all its possessions in Europe that are outside the Iberian Peninsula... but really the only significant difference from OTL is that Portugal became independent earlier, the burden that the Netherlands represented is now "someone else's problem," the remaining Spanish Navy is much smaller, and now Portugal has very serious reasons to hate England for keeping the Azores "because we can." The American Empire remains intact, it is doubtful that the English will be more successful in appropriating anything than in OTL, and they are possibly too busy antagonizing someone else once they see that the possibility of another Invincible Armada is not going to happen in the near future. OTL Spain recovered from that, even if 200 years later they declined for other reasons, but this alone should not condemn them to failure.

Spanish resilience at the time was incredible, considering how Philip II expended so many resources on fronts that ultimately yielded no tangible gains beyond preserving his honor (which was the sole reason he remained in the Flanders War). Even if England were to seize the Azores, I do not believe this would satisfy the Portuguese nobility and bourgeoisie—the main factions Antonio, Prior of Crato, would need in order to legitimize his rule. Furthermore, if Spain was able to rebuild a second fleet within two or three years—not as large as the first, but still significant—we must not forget that while the English might capture a treasure fleet, they could not always be expected to capture all of them. If there was one defining trait of Spanish admirals regarding their treasure fleets, it was their elusiveness. Even so, a Spain under Philip II, burdened by numerous problems, could compel Philip III to reconsider his policies and explore the possibility of a genuine peace with the Dutch Republic—something that could ultimately benefit Spain in the long run.

While I agree the OP is going way too far and too fast, I'd say 1589 had the potential to screw Spain over far worse than it did in OTL. I'd say your best POD is probably for Antonio to die on the way to the Iberian Peninsula, but too late for the fleet to turn back. To get out of that pickle, Drake and Norris opt to just try to do as much damage to Spain's fleet and resources as they can. In that they proved far more successful than in OTL, even temporarily occupying some of the Azores and capturing the treasure fleet. Spain has even more money problems than in OTL. The rebuilding of the Spanish fleet is an even bigger task than in OTL, and the Royal Navy does start to gain a reputation for invincibility. In France, Henri III's OTL assassin made his attempt when the Royalists celebrated the English successes, and the butterflies ensured Henri III survived ITTL. Henri III retakes Paris, and the wheel starts to come off the Catholic League significantly earlier than OTL, especially since the retaking of the capital is quickly followed by Henri of Navarre also winning the ITTL version of the battle of Arques. Spain is stuck providing far more resources to sustain the elements of the Catholic League than it had to in OTL until significantly later, when it has less resources available in the first place. And all over the Western World, the Habsburgs' enemies are taking heart... Colapse might be too strong a word but the ruin of Philip II's continental ambitions would probably come earlier, and cost more to Spain in the long run, than in OTL.
items.original_question: What if Spanish "collapse" in 1589 One of the most famous failures in modern European history, the 1588 Spanish Armada destroyed a big part of the Spanish naval forces, and was a major humiliation for Philip II. Yet England, one year later, completely blew its chance to fully wreck the Spanish by launching the ill-fated English Armada, which sought three main objectives: 1) Destroy the remaining Atlantic fleet of Spain 2) Incite a rebellion in Portugal against Philip II 3) Seize the Azores and turn it into a permanent English possession It failed in all of these objectives. Yet, the POD is not a minor or major decision, it is simple: somehow England succeeds. The remaining fleet of Spain that survived the 1588 Armada is destroyed in a series of naval battles, a landing is made in Portugal and António Prior of Crato is installed King of Portugal, starting a Portuguese Restoration War 50 years before OTL, and finally England manages to seize the Azores from Philip II's forces. Say that the Spanish naval forces are completely obliterated by the English; Portugal gains independence from Spain in 1590 with heavy English backing; the Azores (through negotiation with Portugal) become a English territory. What would happen with England, Spain, Portugal and the rest of Europe? How might the colonization of the New World be altered by a successful English Armada? Let's not get into details on **how** this happens, but assuming that it just does happen
items.model_answer:
If the English Armada of 1589 had succeeded in destroying Spain’s remaining Atlantic fleet and also sparked a major Portuguese revolt, the balance of power in western Europe could have shifted dramatically and much earlier than it did in actual history.

The immediate result would likely have been a severe blow to Philip II’s monarchy. Spain in 1589 was still immensely powerful, but its strength depended on maritime communications, silver shipments, and the ability to move troops and supplies across a sprawling empire. Losing the surviving Atlantic fleet just a year after the failure of the Spanish Armada would have created a true naval crisis, not just an embarrassment. It would have weakened Spain’s ability to defend the Iberian coast, escort treasure fleets, reinforce the Spanish Netherlands, and challenge England at sea.

If the expedition had also triggered a successful Portuguese revolt, the consequences could have been even greater. Portugal had only recently been absorbed into the Spanish monarchy in 1580. A revolt backed by England and centered on Dom António might have restored Portuguese independence decades earlier than the actual restoration of 1640. That would have deprived Philip II of Portuguese ports, ships, colonial resources, and strategic access to the Atlantic and Indian Ocean worlds. Instead of ruling the whole Iberian Peninsula, the Spanish crown would have faced a hostile or at least unreliable Portugal on its western flank.

For England, this would have been a major strategic triumph. Elizabeth I’s government would no longer be merely surviving Spain’s challenge; it would be actively dismantling Habsburg power. English prestige would have risen sharply. The crown might have gained easier access to Portuguese Atlantic islands or ports, more freedom for privateering, and possibly an earlier opening for English commercial expansion into areas where Portugal had previously dominated. It also would have strengthened the political position of those in England who favored an aggressive Protestant and maritime policy.

In the Netherlands, a weakened Spain might have struggled even more to sustain the war against the Dutch Revolt. One of Spain’s persistent problems was the cost and difficulty of supplying armies in the Low Countries. A shattered Atlantic naval system and the loss of Portuguese resources would have intensified that strain. The Dutch might have secured effective independence sooner, and anti-Habsburg coalitions in Europe would have been encouraged by the sense that Spain was no longer invincible.

In France, the effects are a bit more uncertain, but still important. Philip II was heavily involved in the French Wars of Religion, especially in support of the Catholic League. A deeper crisis at sea and in Portugal might have reduced Spain’s capacity to intervene in France. That could have made it easier for Henry of Navarre to consolidate power as Henry IV, potentially stabilizing France sooner and limiting Spanish influence there.

Globally, an early Portuguese break from Spain would have mattered enormously. Under the Iberian Union, Spain and Portugal were joined under one crown, which helped pull Portuguese overseas interests into Spain’s broader wars. If Portugal had broken away in 1589, its empire in Brazil, Africa, and Asia might have followed a different trajectory. England and the Dutch would still have challenged Portuguese power overseas, but they might have done so under different diplomatic conditions, perhaps sometimes as Portuguese allies against Spain rather than simply as predators on a weakened Iberian world-system. At the same time, Spain without Portugal would have had fewer imperial assets to draw on, reducing its ability to sustain global rivalry.

That said, success would not automatically have meant Spain’s collapse. Spain still possessed great wealth, a formidable army, and resilient institutions. The Habsburg monarchy had shown an ability to recover from disasters. A Portuguese revolt could also have turned into a long civil and military conflict rather than a clean restoration. England, too, was financially strained, and holding gains on the Iberian Peninsula would have been difficult. So the most plausible outcome is not total English domination, but a significant acceleration of Spain’s relative decline and of England’s and the Dutch Republic’s rise.

In short, a successful English Armada in 1589 could have transformed the failed follow-up to 1588 into one of the decisive turning points of early modern Europe. It might have ended the Iberian Union, weakened Spanish intervention across Europe, strengthened England and the Dutch, and produced an earlier shift from Habsburg predominance toward a more contested Atlantic order.

items.question: What If Britain pursued a more hostile stance against the American Colonies following the Boston Tea Party, going on the offensive in 1774?
human_answers: This is why it might have been shortsighted for the British Empire to put so much investment in achieving the total conquest and liquidation of the French Colonial position in the Ohio Country and Canada in the 1754-1763 timeframe, to disproportionate benefit of their Colonial 'Fortunate Sons'. While for Britain, it had the side benefit of defeating French forces, which feels nice, and drawing French fleets out for fights they would lose, and capturing some value from the fur trade, Britain particularly "got over its skis" in providing all this support for the Colonies *without* first compelling the Colonies, then under some fears for their frontier populations, to revise their Charters to accept the principle and practice of taxation by the Westminster Parliament, as a regular, reliable contribution to common defense of the empire, its frontiers, and its trade-based prosperity. Instead, by 1763, Britain brought home French North America like Christmas toys and puppies on its own schilling (though Colonial Assemblies chipped in some from their allowance, but often got reimbursed). But then, late 1763 turned out to be a cold, cold, bitter post-Christmas January hangover, when London Parliament started to tell the Colonies, "now start paying tax for all your presents........oh and by the way, sorry, can't let you play with the new Christmas puppy (settle the new lands in the Ohio, west of the Alleghenies), because it turns out the puppy bites and scratches and we can't afford to keep going to the clinic." ---The Americans certainly were not going to react well to the new message of 'fun's over, time to pay up'. While Britain and the American colonies had certain minimum legal rights, even for tenant farmers (still far less than for small freeholders though) I certainly do not think the three protections you mentioned were observed universally, neither in Britain nor even in all the Colonies, in the 1700s pre and post independence. Making this assertion might be a bit of falling for and repeating English/British self-congratulatory propaganda. Evictions were a fact of life in the English-speaking world in the 1700s and all other centuries. The 1700s were known for the enclosure of common lands [yes, that by itself is not eviction but can lead to starvation-inducing poverty even if one is in a cottage, but it can also lead to failure to meet rent obligations and consequent eviction] and consequent driving of English peasants from the countryside to create an ever increasing town and urban laboring population for industry. White tenants on southern landholdings in the Colonies could be subject to evictions as could tenants in Hudson Valley patroonships. Yes, I'm thinking this is descriptive of the Scandinavian situation until after 1800, or nearly that late, which made it, legally speaking more like serfdom systems East of the Elbe than like tenancy systems in Britain or Western Europe. Serfs lacking really any rights of appeal or any rights at all, whereas tenants in England, parts of France, and I would think the Low Countries and Switzerland would have some rights of appeal, even though their landlords would have superior rights through the 1600s and 1700s.

If the British objective was to set off a full-scale war in every colony right off the bat in which they would lose that is exactly what they should do. The British had no means to do what you're suggesting. The incident that set off the fighting was the British trying to disarm the colonists. In the first year of the war the British lost control in all 13 Colonies. Britian had to spend a year mobilizing an army 1/3 of which were German mercenaries for the invasion of the New York. After winning a number of tactical victories they were unable to bring a single colony back under their control. At no time were they ever able to bring even 10% of the population under occupation. After 1777 all they could hold were coastal enclaves, although there was fratricidal warfare in Georgia & South Carolina. They could hold no territory without the Presence of British or Hessian regulars. Loyalist forces were weak everywhere. The coastal enclaves they held became shells eventually with most of the people leaving, and little trade with the interior. What had brought about the war were British policies to control American trade to force them to trade only with England. That alienated the merchant class. Planters had to sell into a closed market were the buyers set the price, and controlled credit terms. That alienated the planter class. They tried to strangle early industrialization so the colonies could only sell raw materials, and buy English finished goods. That alienated the rising manufacturing class. They blocked westward expansion beyond the Proclamation Line. That alienated the landed class. The overall effect was to squeeze specie out of the colonies creating a growing barter system which alienated everyone. Closing courts, and assemblies, and finally trying to disarm the militia left the colonies with the choice of ether abject surrender or rebellion. It wasn't easy but the British Crown went from being very popular in 1765 to every colony taking up arms against them in 1775.

There are tons of things they could do. They could dissolve the militias and ban the Americans from owning weapons. They could introduce an actual tax to fund a permanent military presence - the Americans paid no land rent, only tarriffs. They could abolished the American right to elect judges and sheriffs, instead appointing crown loyalists by decree. They could have given soldiers immunity from local prosecution and law enforcement, instead tasking their commanding officers (who would of course do pretty much nothing) with upholding the law for their soldiers. They could have created an American trading company owned by the crown and banned Americans from any imports and exports except through this company and cracked down on smuggling. The facts are that the Americans enjoyed the most liberal and democratic system in the world at the time of their revolt. They wanted something even more democratic and liberal. But to most people at the time, especially colonial subjects, they would seem like spoiled toddlers throwing a tantrum. Swedish peasants paid roughly 30-40% of the value of an average harvest in land rent at this time. Icelanders could only trade with the very corrupt royal Danish tradign company, which paid aroudn 5% of the value of their wool and forced the Icelanders to buy moldy flour in return. Austrian and Prussian peasants were banned from owning arms, and their courts were handled by government-appointed bailiffs, unless nobility had the right to neck and hand (to be police, prosecutor, judge and executioner all in one, Judge Dredd style) on their estate.

This is a quote from Wikipedia, as of January 20th, 2026: "With the ascension of peace in 1763 the army was dramatically reduced to a peacetime home establishment of just over 11,000 men, with a further 9,750 for the Irish establishment and 10,000 for the colonies. This meant 20 regiments of infantry totaling just over 11,000 men were stationed in Great Britain, 21 regiments were stationed in Ireland, 18 regiments were stationed in the Americas, and 7 regiments were stationed in Gibraltar. Alongside this, the army could call on 16 regiments of the cavalrymen and 2,712 men in the artillery. This gave a theoretical strength of just over 46,000 men exclusive of the artillery." British Army during the American Revolutionary War - Wikipedia en.wikipedia.org Source as listed in the footnote is here: The British Army at the Start of the Revolution - AmericanRevolution.org Learn about the formation and makeup of the British Army at the start of the American Revolution, with this book chapter from E. Curtis, Ph.D. www.americanrevolution.org "The English establishment comprised 25,871 infantry organized into 46 regiments and 20 independent companies; 4,151 cavalry organized into 16 regiments; and 2,256 artillerymen organized into one regiment of 4 battalions." "The Irish establishment consisted of 13,423 infantry divided into 28 regiments; 2,718 cavalry divided into 12 regiments; and 228 artillerymen embodied into one regiment of four companies. "Such were the numbers of the British army in 1775 and such they had approximately been ever since the close of the Seven Years’ War. "An examination of the location of the British army in 1775 reveals the fact that while small detachments of it were to be found in many distant quarters of the globe, the bulk of it was distributed unequally among three different countries. There were roughly speaking 15,000 men in England, 12,000 in Ireland, and 8,000 in America. The remaining 10,000 were distributed among the West Indies, Africa, Minorca, Gibraltar, and Scotland." Each regiment had a listed strength of 477 men. The British concentrated four of these, or just under 2,000 men, in Boston in 1773 to close the port and essentially establish martial law in Massachusetts. This was achieved by moving them New York City, where these regiments had been stationed. The other 6,000 to 8,000 men to cover Canada, Fort Ticonderoga, the forts around the Great Lakes, Florida, Jamaica, and the West Indies. After abandoning Boston, in 1776 the British increased the size of their army from roughly 45,000 to 60,000 troops, mainly be recruiting in Germany. Out of these, they were able to concentrate about 40,000 to take New York, including troops that had been sent to and which failed to take Charleston. Another 10,000 or so chased the Americans out of Canada. Peak strength of the Briitsh army during the American War of Independence was around 80,000. Note that the British were expecting a rematch with France during this time. In fact, Amherst, the commander of the British army, pointed out that the British simply didn't have the strength to garrison the thirteen colonies and advised against trying to reconquer them. The point is that in 1773, the British had the strength to do a show of force in Boston only. And since 90% of the disturbances were coming from New England, the calculation had to be that this would be sufficient. It was only in New England where the situation was turning violent, and it was only after the formation of the Continental Army, and armed clashes between British and American troops, that they declared all thirteen colonies to be in rebellion and started expanding the army. And they really had to wait for the situation to turn that bad to be able to do that.

People in general don't see stuff like that in objective terms. What people see is that suddenly the government made it more expensive or difficult for them to conduct the usual business of life (which was the effect of all the legislation regarding the colonies from 1763 on) and of course they will complain about it, regardless of how good they have it on a cosmic scale. You might as well tell workers in a first world country that they shouldn't go on strike because slavery is still practiced in certain places. That's a very bad idea, because, you know, there are still hostile natives in the borders . In order to not to lose the territory to them, they'd have to station a permanent army all over the border, and that most likely would end up being more expensive than just let the settlers take care of their own defense. And that's not even going into the possibility of slave rebellions in the places where slavery is still legal...
items.original_question: What if Britain pursued a more hostile stance against the American Colonies following the Boston Tea Party, going on the offensive in 1774? As the title suggests, I've been trying to figure out what an earlier beginning to the American Revolutionary War might entail. As to how this happens specifically, military action was advocated as soon as news of the tea party reached London by some hard-line MPs such as Germain OTL. Some thoughts: - This happens before the Continental Congress even assembles, so everything might happen much more hastily. There probably is much less wrangling over things like sending an olive branch to the King and instead a more decisive stance taken on independence. - With the states forced to pick sides immediately, I think it's highly likely that Georgia remains decidedly loyalist, which has very interesting implications for the US post-independence Other than that, my knowledge on the American Revolutionary War is very much limited and it'd be great to have some input on this scenario. Cheers!
items.model_answer:
If Britain had responded to the Boston Tea Party with a much more openly military and offensive strategy in 1774, rather than primarily coercive punishment and political pressure, the most likely result is that the American Revolution would have started earlier, spread faster, and unified the colonies more completely.

In actual history, Britain’s Coercive Acts already pushed many colonists toward resistance, but there was still division in 1774. Many Americans were angry at Parliament yet not ready for independence. If Britain had gone further—sending larger forces, occupying more towns, arresting leading Patriot figures more aggressively, seizing colonial arms, or attempting to crush resistance in Massachusetts before it spread—London would probably have eliminated some ambiguity. Colonists who still hoped for reconciliation might have concluded sooner that Britain meant to rule by force.

That would likely have strengthened colonial unity. One of Britain’s recurring problems was that many colonists remained neutral or hesitant for a long time. An offensive campaign in 1774 could have made British intentions appear unmistakably tyrannical in Patriot propaganda, making it easier for colonial leaders to rally support not just in New England but in the middle and southern colonies as well. The First Continental Congress might have become more radical more quickly, perhaps moving beyond economic resistance toward military coordination earlier than it did.

At the same time, Britain might initially have enjoyed some military advantages. In 1774 the colonies were less organized militarily than they became by 1775–76. Continental institutions were weaker, militia coordination was less developed, and there was no formal Continental Army yet. A rapid British strike could therefore have disrupted Patriot leadership, captured arms stores, and temporarily intimidated opposition. If executed decisively, this might have delayed the colonies’ ability to resist effectively in the short term.

But that short-term advantage would probably have come at a strategic cost. Britain’s central problem in North America was never simply winning battles; it was imposing lasting political obedience over a large, hostile population across great distances. A harsher offensive in 1774 would likely have deepened that hostility. Instead of isolating Massachusetts, Britain might have turned it into a symbol of shared American victimhood even sooner. More colonial assemblies might have openly defied royal authority, and local militia mobilization could have accelerated.

There is also the question of independence itself. A more hostile British stance in 1774 might actually have moved colonial opinion toward independence earlier, perhaps by 1775 rather than 1776. In real history, many colonists took time to abandon loyalty to the Crown. Direct offensive action could have discredited moderate voices sooner. Thomas Paine’s arguments later became powerful partly because events convinced people reconciliation was impossible; more aggressive British action might have created that same conclusion earlier.

Internationally, an earlier and more brutal conflict could have had mixed effects. France and Spain would still have watched carefully. If Britain seemed likely to crush the rebellion quickly, foreign powers might hesitate. But if British offensiveness produced colonial resistance without a decisive victory, France in particular might see an opportunity sooner to weaken Britain. Even without immediate alliance, earlier conflict could have accelerated covert foreign assistance.

So the overall counterfactual is this: Britain going on the offensive in 1774 might have produced some early tactical successes, but it would probably have worsened Britain’s long-term position. The most plausible outcome is an earlier, more unified, and more openly revolutionary colonial resistance, making war begin sooner and making reconciliation even less likely than it was in actual history. In trying to overawe the colonies, Britain would probably have helped create a broader American rebellion faster.

items.original_question: If not Russia, which country could have become the Soviet Union? In OTL, the Soviet Union was essentially the leader of communism, the state that embodied and exported the ideology. In France, after the birth of the “first republic in Europe,” the country faced massive wars against the old Western monarchies. As a result, although Napoleon, an extraordinary hero, almost succeeded in conquering Europe, France ultimately fell. Soviet Russia also faced a similar crisis. After the October Revolution, the first communist state was born, and the great powers, much like the monarchies a century before, sought to destroy Soviet Russia. However, unlike France, Soviet Russia survived the Russian Civil War. Afterward, the Soviet Union was no longer simply "Communist State A." They developed the potential of the land that was Russia. They transformed the underdeveloped economy of the Russian Empire into one of growth. Using that newfound capability, they exported revolution to various countries around the world. From Eastern Europe to Asia, the surrounding countries of Russia were all affected by communism. Furthermore, after 1945, they became a superpower alongside the United States, exporting revolution globally. Let’s consider a historical counterfactual. After Alexander II, the imperial succession changed. Unlike in OTL, Tsarevich Nicholas survived, and instead of the reactionary Alexander III, he ascended the throne. This alternate Nicholas II continued the reforms initiated by Alexander II, complementing, improving, and strengthening them. Unlike in OTL, Russia underwent a different trajectory. The Russian Empire was preserved, and Soviet Russia never came into being. In this scenario, which country could have replaced the Soviet Union? Which nation would need to become communist in order to "survive against surrounding capitalist powers" and "become a great power capable of exporting revolution?" Sometimes, in alternate history works (especially in game mods by Paradox Interactive), there are many timelines where a socialist revolution occurs in a country other than Russia. However, in my view, it’s questionable how many countries could do what the Soviet Union did. France? Germany? They have many geopolitical enemies. Even if they were to become communist after World War I, could they, like the Soviet Union, export revolution worldwide and become a superpower? It seems more likely that they would struggle just to survive. Britain, the United States? In OTL, Marx argued that a sufficiently developed capitalist system was necessary for a communist revolution to occur, with Britain being his example. Britain was also the world’s leading superpower at the time. However, a communist revolution did not occur in Britain. Because capitalism was so advanced, ironically, the entrenched privileges of the system were also too strong. British socialists who advocated for a revolutionary overthrow of the system did not have the power to challenge the entrenched elites, while others accepted the system and sought reforms within it. Ultimately, the conditions I believe are necessary for a "Soviet candidate" are as follows: 1. Geopolitically, it must be easy to defend. The country should be able to secure its borders and have a strategic position that allows for long-term survival and expansion. 2. It must have the potential to become a great power. The country needs the necessary resources, population, and industrial capacity to rise as a major global player. 3. Capitalism cannot be overly developed, and the elites must be driven toward 'system overthrow' rather than 'system compliance.' There must be enough dissatisfaction with the existing system to foster a desire for revolution, not merely reforms within the system. These are the core elements for a country to replicate the role of the Soviet Union. Where, besides Russia, could there be a land or country that fits these conditions? As a side note, it doesn’t necessarily have to be pure communism in this alternative Soviet ideology. It could be something like Maoism, syndicalism, or a unique form of socialism tailored to the needs of that country.
items.model_answer:
If the question means “which other country was most plausible as the core of a Soviet-style multinational communist superstate,” the strongest answer is probably Germany, though in a very different form from the historical USSR.

The Soviet Union emerged from a rare combination of conditions: a huge empire, state collapse during war, revolutionary movements, weak democratic institutions, and a political center capable of holding many nationalities together by force and ideology. Very few countries had all of those features. Russia did because the Russian Empire was already vast, multinational, unevenly industrialized, and politically brittle.

Germany is the best alternative because after World War I it had revolutionary upheaval, a powerful socialist tradition, a large industrial base, and the capacity to dominate neighboring regions if a communist revolution had succeeded there. A communist Germany might not have been called the “Soviet Union,” but it could have led a federation or bloc of socialist republics across Central Europe. In terms of global power, industrial capacity, and ideological influence, it is the closest counterfactual rival to Russia.

If the question is instead “which country could have produced something most structurally similar to the USSR,” then Austria-Hungary is another good candidate. It was already a multinational empire containing many ethnic groups under one state. If it had undergone a socialist revolution rather than dissolution after World War I, it might have been reorganized into a federation of socialist republics resembling the USSR’s formal structure more closely than Germany would have.

China is also a contender, especially because it did later become a huge communist state ruling a vast population. But it is less convincing as a substitute for the Soviet Union in the early twentieth-century sense, because it was more fragmented, more colonially pressured, and not the center of the Marxist movement in the way Germany or Russia could have been.

So the best single answer is Germany if you mean a plausible alternative communist great power, and Austria-Hungary if you mean a state that could most closely have resembled the USSR’s multinational imperial-federal form.
