items.model_answer:
If the Alans had formed a lasting kingdom in Europe, the most likely result would have been a more visibly Iranian, steppe-derived element in medieval European politics and culture, especially in the western Mediterranean or in Gaul where they briefly appeared during the late Roman collapse. The Alans were a Sarmatian-Iranian nomadic people who moved westward under pressure from the Huns, and in actual history they were absorbed into larger successor states such as those of the Visigoths and Vandals. If instead they had created a durable kingdom, Europe would probably have gained one more major post-Roman successor state with a distinctive identity rather than seeing the Alans disappear into other peoples.

Politically, this kingdom could have altered the balance among the early barbarian realms that emerged from the Western Roman Empire. A stable Alan state in Gaul, Hispania, or even alongside the Vandals in North Africa might have blocked or redirected the expansion of the Visigoths, Franks, or Suebi. That would have changed the map of western Europe in late antiquity and perhaps delayed the dominance of the Franks in Gaul. If the Alans had held a strategic corridor, they might have served as a military intermediary between settled Roman populations and steppe-style cavalry warfare, giving their kingdom unusual military strengths compared with neighboring Germanic states.

Culturally, a lasting Alan kingdom would likely have preserved more Iranian linguistic and aristocratic traditions in Europe. Instead of vanishing into Latin- and Germanic-speaking societies, Alan elites might have maintained a court culture that blended steppe, Roman, and Christian influences. Over time this could have produced a hybrid kingdom similar to other post-Roman states, but with stronger cavalry traditions, different noble lineages, and perhaps some survival of Iranian names, legal customs, and religious practices before Christianization fully took hold. There might even have been a clearer ancestral link between medieval western Europeans and the Ossetians of the Caucasus, who are the modern descendants of the Alans.

Religiously, the Alans would probably still have become Christian if their kingdom endured inside the former Roman world, but the timing and form could have mattered. If they converted through Arian Gothic networks, they might initially have joined the religious divisions common among post-Roman elites. If they converted through Roman channels, they could have integrated more quickly with local populations and the Latin Church. In either case, religion would have been crucial to whether they remained a separate ruling people or fused rapidly with their subjects.

In the longer run, the most probable outcome is that even a durable Alan kingdom would eventually have become linguistically and culturally assimilated, much as other conquering groups in the West did. But before that happened, it could have left a stronger mark on European nobility, warfare, and regional identity. We might today remember the Alans not as a vanished migratory people but as founders of a medieval kingdom, with traces in place names, aristocratic genealogies, and perhaps even a surviving regional language. So the biggest difference would not necessarily be a completely different Europe, but a Europe with one more important post-Roman people shaping its early medieval foundations.

items.original_question: What if Partition of the Austrian Netherlands in the 18th Century? Hi, everyone. This is my second post sharing some lesser-known yet fascinating PoDs in European history. I stumbled upon a historical academic journal written by Frederik Dhondt, a history professor from the Ghent University in Belgium titled " So Great a Revolution’: Charles Townshend and the Partition of the Austrian Netherlands, September 1725 " (2012, Journal of Low Countries Studies). According to the article, Charles Townshend, the British Northern Secretary (equivalent to the Foreign Minister) and his predecessor James Stanhope (†. 1721) had proposed a partition of the Austrian Netherlands. The plan would see Austria surrendering its holdings in the Low Countries. The article summarised three possibilities. Some background before moving on. In the Nine Years' Year and the War of the Spanish Succession, Austria had allied with the Dutch Republic and Great Britain (or England-Scotland before 1707) to counter French ambitions in the Low Countries and the Rhineland. Towards the end of the Spanish Succession War, Britain became weary of increasing Austrian power. In 1716, it allied with France. The Austro-Spanish alliance confirmed by the Treaty of Vienna rang alarm bells in London. Not only did it reconcile the enmity between Emperor Charles XI and King Philip V, the combined power of Spain and Austria threatened the established balance of power. There were even talks to marry Maria Theresa to Don Carlos (future Charles III). Prime Minister Walpole and Townshend, therefore, desired to weaken the power of Austria. These plans were never made public, Townshend only discussed them with the ambassador in Paris, Horace Walpole. On page 56, Townshend suggested the partition plan could be implemented if the marriage between Maria Theresa and Don Carlos took place. James Stanhope first suggested that the Duke of Lorraine could receive Austria Netherlands. Alternatively, Stanhope suggested awarding it either to the Elector of Cologne or the Elector of Trier. The Electorate would be secularised. Townshend outright dismissed these ridiculous ideas, and offered his own solution. The Dutch will annex some territories including Antwerp. Ypres, Bruges, and Ostend would fall under joint Dutch-British control while the inland and southern portions of the Austrian Netherlands will go to France. What will be the geopolitical and diplomatic consequences of one of these plans was realised? Although I personally doubt the likelihood of this happening, nevertheless the ramifications will be interesting. You can access the article here through your university: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1179/0309656411Z.0000000002 .
items.model_answer:
If the Austrian Netherlands had been partitioned in the 18th century, the consequences would likely have been significant for the balance of power in western Europe, for the later history of Belgium, and for the rivalry among Austria, France, Prussia, and the Dutch Republic.

The Austrian Netherlands roughly corresponded to most of present-day Belgium and Luxembourg. In the 18th century, it was a strategic buffer zone between France and the Dutch Republic and also an important outpost of Habsburg influence far from Vienna. A partition would most plausibly have happened during one of the major continental settlements, especially after the War of the Austrian Succession or during the diplomatic reshuffling associated with the French Revolutionary era. The exact outcome would depend on who divided it, but the most likely beneficiaries would have been France, the Dutch Republic, and perhaps Prussia or a German prince backed by Austria.

If France had annexed the western and more economically valuable provinces earlier in the century, it would have pushed its frontier northeastward and strengthened its position along the Scheldt and Meuse. That would have alarmed both Britain and the Dutch Republic, because one of their long-term strategic goals was to prevent France from controlling the Low Countries. A French gain there would probably have triggered stronger coalition politics against France and could even have accelerated British military involvement on the continent.

If the Dutch Republic had taken some northern portions or fortified lines, the main effect would have been defensive rather than expansionist. The Dutch wanted security more than territory. A partition favoring them might have created a broader Dutch barrier against France, but it would also have increased the Republic’s administrative and military burdens at a time when Dutch power was already in relative decline. So even if the Dutch gained territory, it might not have translated into long-term strength.

For Austria, losing the Austrian Netherlands in a partition would probably have been accepted only in exchange for compensation elsewhere, most likely in Germany or Italy. Vienna often regarded the territory as difficult to defend and geographically detached from its core lands. In that sense, partition might actually have fit Austrian strategic logic if it were compensated adequately. Austria might then have focused even more heavily on central and eastern Europe, reducing its involvement in the far west.

The most important long-term effect is that a partition would likely have prevented the later emergence of Belgium in the form it took in 1830. Belgian identity in the modern political sense was already complex and regionally divided; if the territory had been split among neighboring powers before the revolutionary era, there may never have been a single Belgian state created after the Napoleonic period. Instead, the region could have resembled Poland’s fate in another form: its provinces absorbed into larger states, with local identities surviving but without sovereign unity.

Economically, partition would have disrupted one of Europe’s most urbanized and commercially active regions. Different provinces had different legal traditions, fiscal systems, and trading links. Incorporation into France might have modernized administration in some areas, while attachment to the Dutch or German states might have preserved more local autonomy. The Scheldt question would have become even more politically sensitive, especially for Antwerp. If France controlled Antwerp, it could have developed into an even earlier strategic port against Britain. If the Dutch kept influence over access to the Scheldt, Antwerp’s revival might have remained blocked longer.

There would also have been cultural and political consequences. The Austrian Netherlands contained Dutch-speaking and French-speaking areas, along with strong provincial identities such as Brabant and Flanders. Partition could have hardened linguistic and political frontiers earlier than actually happened. Some Flemish areas might have been drawn more closely into a Dutch orbit, while Walloon areas might have been drawn more tightly into France. That, in turn, could have reduced the later tension inside a unified Belgian state simply because such a state might never have existed.

In a broad historical sense, an 18th-century partition of the Austrian Netherlands would probably have made western Europe less buffered and more polarized. The territory’s historical role was to sit between major powers. Once divided, that mediating space would disappear. France might become stronger and more threatening, Austria less western, and the Dutch more exposed or overextended. The Congress of Vienna in 1815 would then have had a very different problem to solve, and the Kingdom of the Netherlands or Belgium as later created might not have emerged at all.

So the short answer is that partition would likely have reshaped the western European state system: strengthening some neighbors in the short term, weakening Austria’s role in the Low Countries, and making the eventual creation of Belgium much less likely.

items.original_question: My Alternative History Scenario: What if Napoleon couldn't make it to France at 1799? EPISODE THREE​ German Pact ​ ​ A sudden storm breaking out across Europe had created a massive shockwave. Austria, still struggling to recover from the economic and military wounds of the War of the Second Coalition, was deeply displeased by France’s abrupt rekindling of hostilities. Emperor Francis II had been expecting a long period of peace, one he intended to devote to revitalizing Germany. Unfortunately, history had once again disappointed him. His federalist ambitions had not yet completely faded, but this meant confronting French republicanism earlier than anticipated. Moreover, following the referendum held on 18 February 1803 and the subsequent election, the country transitioned into what was called a presidential system. As a result, Fourier—who came to power and was a prominent representative of socialist thought—began spreading his ideas more widely across Europe. This signified a gradual shift of the German peoples toward republicanism. Although the Kingdom of Prussia and the Habsburg Monarchy did not hold each other in high regard, they shared a common enemy: France and republicanism. Approximately one week had passed since the outbreak of the Franco-Spanish War. French armies advanced rapidly, exploiting the dire condition of the Spanish forces to seize Catalonia and push toward Eastern Aragon. The Basque region had also fallen. Emperor Francis convened his cabinet, and they debated at length what course of action should be taken. Johann Amadeus Franz, the Minister of Finance of the era, was firmly opposed to breaking the peace with France, as any potential war would further devastate Austria’s already fragile economy. József Alvinczi, the Chief of the General Staff, argued that this war represented an opportunity to eliminate both France and the spread of republican ideas on the European continent. He maintained that, as demonstrated in the previous conflict, the Austrian army was not in as poor a condition as believed and demanded that an open ultimatum be issued to France. However, the Emperor had a different plan in mind. Although there was no certainty it would succeed, he deemed it worth attempting. For this reason, he decided to send a delegate to the Kingdom of Prussia, carrying a note requesting a private meeting with the King. The delegation set out on 15 March 1803. Meanwhile, across Europe, no clear decision had yet emerged from the British Isles. Prime Minister Henry Addington had no desire to see Spain under French control, but he also believed that the British Army was not yet prepared. After lengthy discussions with other statesmen, he sent an envoy to the Kingdom of Portugal to further expand the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance and present several proposals. In the meantime, the delegation sent by Austria to Prussia returned two weeks later. The Emperor’s proposal to the King of Prussia was to intervene in the Franco-Spanish War by forming a German coalition. The Prussian King, eager to enhance his prestige among the German states, responded favorably and announced his acceptance. Thus, the German Pact was formed. Both sides began final preparations for their already mobilized armies, and within approximately two weeks, everything was ready. A note bearing the personal signatures of both the Emperor and the King was delivered to the French delegates by a joint Austro-Prussian mission. The note demanded that France sever its alliance with the United States, withdraw from Spain, and agree to certain trade arrangements. French President Charles Fourier tore the original document to pieces in parliament. This act provided the Habsburg Monarchy and the Kingdom of Prussia with sufficient legitimacy to launch a military intervention against France. Emperor Francis II was deeply uneasy about Russia’s ambiguous stance. He neither wanted Russia to emerge excessively strong nor excessively weak. Poland could be the first step, and the Russian flag might one day fly over Hungary or the borders of the Holy Roman Empire. Taking such a risk seemed irrational. Therefore, depending on the course of the war, he considered enticing Russia into joining their side by offering the Balkan territories of the already weakened Ottoman Empire—despite his preference for preserving the balance of power in the Balkans and Eastern Europe. The French threat, however, took precedence. Although the United States did not yet pose a direct threat to Europe, it continued to threaten the colonial powers in the Americas. While it had not yet entered the conflict, such an involvement was not impossible. On the other hand, the Emperor foresaw that the French government’s aggressive and overly idealistic actions would ultimately lead to its downfall. By initiating this war, France had effectively shot itself in the foot, and these events would pave the way for a rise in anti-French sentiment throughout Europe.
items.model_answer:
If Napoleon could not return to France in 1799, the most likely outcome is that there would be no Coup of 18 Brumaire, no Consulate under Napoleon, and probably no Napoleonic Empire in the form we know. France would still likely move away from unstable revolutionary republicanism, but through a different strongman or military-political coalition. The broader result would be a weaker, less centralized France, a different balance of power in Europe, and a much less sweeping spread of Napoleonic legal and political reforms.

In the short term, the key issue is the condition of France in 1799. The Directory was unpopular, corrupt, and militarily strained. It was vulnerable to collapse even without Napoleon. His importance was that he provided a uniquely prestigious, politically useful, and publicly admired figure around whom plotters such as Sieyès could build a new regime. If Napoleon was stuck in Egypt, captured at sea, killed, or simply delayed too long, Sieyès would still probably seek a coup, but he would need another general. Jean Moreau would be an obvious candidate, and Jourdan or Bernadotte might also matter, though each had different political instincts and less personal magnetism. A coup could still happen, but it would probably be messier and less decisive.

That matters because Napoleon was not just a general available for use; he was unusually good at dominating allies, outmaneuvering rivals, and converting a provisional seizure of power into a durable personal regime. Without him, a post-Directory government might be more collective and more fragile. A revised constitution could emerge, perhaps creating a stronger executive and limiting democratic participation, but it might not so quickly become a personal dictatorship. France would likely still centralize state power, because the revolutionary decade had already pushed politics in that direction, yet the specific Napoleonic blend of authoritarianism, plebiscitary legitimacy, administrative efficiency, and military glory would be hard to replicate.

Militarily, the consequences could be enormous. In actual history Napoleon’s campaigns of 1800, especially Marengo, stabilized the new regime and restored French dominance over Austria. Without him, France would still have strong armies and capable generals, but victory would be less assured and less theatrically tied to one man. Moreau was a competent commander and might still win important battles, but he was not likely to found an empire from them. This means France might negotiate from a less dominant position. The War of the Second Coalition could end in compromise rather than in the unmistakable reassertion of French supremacy associated with Napoleon’s rise.

If France remains under a more collective authoritarian republic, peace with Britain might also look different. Napoleon’s personal ambition and strategic vision helped drive the renewed cycle of continental war after the brief Peace of Amiens. Another regime might be more cautious, more interested in consolidating the gains of the Revolution inside France and its satellite republics than in seeking continental hegemony. There would still be deep Anglo-French rivalry, so conflict would not disappear, but the scale and intensity of the Napoleonic Wars might never develop in the same way.

The internal development of France would also diverge. Some changes often associated with Napoleon were already broadly desired: administrative rationalization, reconciliation with parts of the old elite, financial stabilization, and an end to revolutionary chaos. So a non-Napoleonic government might still create a stronger bureaucracy, a national bank, and a more orderly tax system. But the Civil Code, the Concordat with the Church, the lycée system, and the prefectural structure might emerge more slowly, in altered form, or under different names. The legal unification of France and its export across Europe would be much less dramatic. The same is true of careers open to talent: some meritocratic features of the Revolution would survive, but they might be less consistently institutionalized.

For Europe as a whole, the biggest difference is that there may be no vast Napoleonic imperial expansion. Without Austerlitz, Jena, Wagram, the Continental System, the Peninsular War, and the invasion of Russia, the old monarchies would face less existential shock. The Holy Roman Empire might survive longer, perhaps in weakened reforming form rather than being swept away in 1806. German and Italian nationalism would probably develop more slowly, because Napoleon both destroyed old structures and unintentionally stimulated national reaction against French domination. Prussia might reform less quickly without the humiliations of 1806. Russia would remain important, but without the patriotic myth of 1812 as we know it. Britain would still expand commercially and overseas, but in a Europe not dominated by one continental super-rival.

This also affects colonial history. Napoleon’s role in the Haitian Revolution and the sale of Louisiana were highly consequential. If he never returns to power, France might not mount the same large expedition to Saint-Domingue, or at least not under the same assumptions. Haitian independence might come earlier, or through a different diplomatic path. Louisiana might remain French somewhat longer, or be sold later under different conditions. That in turn could affect U.S. westward expansion, though the United States would still likely grow. A weaker or more cautious French regime might focus less on grand imperial restoration and more on European survival.

One should be careful, though, not to imagine that Napoleon alone created modern Europe. Many of the forces that empowered him were already present: state centralization, mass conscription, revolutionary ideology, and the collapse of old-regime legitimacy in France. If he does not return in 1799, France does not simply become peaceful and stable. It still faces factionalism, war, and pressure for a stronger executive. So the most plausible alternative is not “no authoritarian turn,” but “a different authoritarian turn.” France likely ends the Directory anyway, but under a less brilliant and less domineering ruler.

So the best concise answer is this: if Napoleon could not make it back to France in 1799, the Directory would probably still fall, but Napoleon’s specific seizure of power would not happen. France might be taken over by another general-backed regime, perhaps with Sieyès playing a larger role, yet it would likely be less stable, less militarily spectacular, and less personally dictatorial. Europe would probably avoid the full Napoleonic cycle of empire and total continental war. Revolutionary France would still matter greatly, but the map, laws, and political development of nineteenth-century Europe would be transformed more gradually and less violently.

items.question: What If the Greek 'Great Plan' had succeeded and the Greek War of Independence had triggered an early collapse of the Ottoman Empire?
human_answers: A more decisive Ottoman defeat against Greece can give birth to the "Megali Idea" before 1844. In such a scenario, a larger independent Greek state can invited Louis-Philippe d’Orléans to become its king, before 1830 of course. This arrangement can be supported by both France and its Bourbon king, who might want to sideline a troublesome cousin, and by the United Kingdom. For the British, the presence of a Great European power south of the Straits, one aligned with neither Austria nor Russia can further divide the continental great powers and serve British strategic interests. With France satisfied in Greece and Austria compensated with territories along the Adriatic coast, Britain can focus on securing Egypt for itself. Even if the Suez Canal is not even a dream, control of Egypt is already strategically valuable for strengthening connections with India. By 1829, railway projects are already under consideration, making overland transit increasingly plausible and reinforcing Egypt’s geopolitical importance. And if its happen after 1830, Louis-Philippe has enough sons (6 minus one who died in 1828) to send one to Greece.

Considering their interest is not even religious (GB: Protestant, France: Catholic, Russia: Orthodox) and that really none of these Great Powers saw the Greek War of Independence with positive eyes (to them it was no different than the revolutions in Spain, Portugal and Naples; which, btw, they sent huge armies to crush). There was later a British change, but even the Metternich, Alexander and so on weren't super happy about it. Remember: at this point, the memory of Napoleon is far fresher than that of the Ottoman invasions into the Balkans, so the concern, far above Islam, is revolutionary sentiment. What I do see happening is them deliberating and taking too long to make a decision that the situation ends up devolving on its own (it took them like 3 years to agree to send an invasion to Spain). Then again, the French were sympathetic to Muhammad Ali while the British aided Ali Pasha plenty of times (through Maitland, specifically). They will always prefer a rotting corpse of the Ottoman empire maintaining power over the ambitious and reformist Albanian Pashas in power, this is why they went out of their way to put them out IRL, but when shit hits the fan, they have to re-examine their approach of course.

Agreed that the Great Powers, including even Russia under Alexander, don't want a full Ottoman collapse. That's not the same as saying they would intervene to stop it. It's hard to conceive of a situation in which Great Britain, France, or Russia would go to war to suppress Christian rebels fighting against the Sultan, particularly after the various atrocities committed at Chios and other places. There were also similar atrocities committed by the Greeks against Muslims, but this did not register in the European consciousness of the time and would not be a factor. It's also not a given that any intervention would be successful at stopping chaos and preserving the Empire, even if it did somehow occur. This would be a formidable job if the situation became so extreme that the Ottomans asked for such support. More likely the intervention would be directed towards managing the collapse and achieving a partition either formally or in terms of spheres of influence.

items.model_answer:
If the Greek “Great Plan” had succeeded early—meaning the Greek War of Independence not only created an independent Greece but also triggered a much broader and premature collapse of the Ottoman Empire in the 1820s or 1830s—the political map of southeastern Europe and the eastern Mediterranean would likely have changed dramatically, and much earlier than it did in real history.

The most immediate result would probably have been the creation of a much larger Greek state, likely centered not just on the Peloponnese and central Greece but also claiming Constantinople, western Anatolia’s Greek-populated coast, many Aegean islands, and perhaps parts of Thrace. Whether Greece could actually have controlled all of this territory is another matter, but the “Great Idea” would have become the founding principle of the new order rather than a later irredentist dream. Constantinople might have become either a Greek capital, an international city, or the main object of rivalry among the great powers.

An early Ottoman collapse would also have opened space for other Balkan national movements much sooner. Serbia, Bulgaria, Romania, and possibly Albania would likely have sought independent or semi-independent states decades earlier. But this would not necessarily have meant a peaceful liberation. The Ottoman Empire had held together a vast multiethnic region, and its sudden disappearance would have produced a scramble over borders, populations, ports, and holy cities. In that sense, the Balkans might have entered their age of nationalist conflict much earlier, perhaps in the mid-19th rather than the early 20th century.

The great powers would have been decisive. Russia would likely have tried to present itself as protector of Orthodox Christians and push toward the Straits. Britain would have feared Russian access to the Mediterranean and probably opposed any settlement that made Greece too large or too dependent on Russia. France might have supported intervention for prestige and influence. Austria, deeply worried about nationalism and instability in the Balkans, would probably have resisted revolutionary fragmentation. So a successful Greek-led collapse of the Ottoman Empire could easily have triggered not just local wars but a major European diplomatic crisis, possibly even a continent-wide war well before the Crimean War.

There would also have been major consequences for Muslim populations. If Ottoman authority had broken suddenly in Europe and the Aegean, many Muslim communities would likely have fled, been expelled, or faced reprisals, just as Christians in contested areas might have suffered in return during the struggle. The region’s demographic reshaping—population flight, ethnic cleansing, refugee movements—could have begun a century earlier. The pattern seen later in the Balkans and after the Greco-Turkish War might have been compressed into an earlier and more chaotic phase.

In the Arab provinces, the effects are less certain. A Greek success in the Balkans would not automatically destroy Ottoman power in Syria, Iraq, or Arabia, but it could have accelerated the rise of semi-independent rulers such as Muhammad Ali in Egypt. In fact, Egypt might have emerged as the real successor power in much of the former Ottoman Middle East. Instead of a long Ottoman 19th century followed by gradual European penetration, the eastern Mediterranean might have been divided earlier between local successor states and direct great-power influence.

Economically and culturally, an enlarged Greek state controlling major ports and trade routes could have become a powerful maritime kingdom, especially if it incorporated Constantinople and the Aegean coast. Greek merchant networks were already strong; with state backing, they might have dominated eastern Mediterranean commerce. On the other hand, trying to rule over huge mixed populations with limited institutions might have overstretched the new state from the start.

The biggest long-term question is whether this would have prevented later disasters or merely moved them earlier. It might have prevented the exact sequence of the late Ottoman decline, the Balkan Wars, and the First World War’s Near Eastern front. But it probably would not have removed the underlying tensions of nationalism, imperial rivalry, and ethnic competition. More likely, it would have shifted the “Eastern Question” forward by several decades. Instead of asking how to manage a weakening Ottoman Empire in the late 19th century, Europe would have faced the same question in the 1820s or 1830s, under even less stable conditions.

So the most plausible answer is that an early success of the Greek Great Plan would have produced a larger and more ambitious Greece and a much earlier end to Ottoman dominance in Europe, but at the cost of intense great-power competition, unstable successor states, and earlier nationalist wars across the Balkans and eastern Mediterranean. It would have been a revolutionary transformation, but probably not a peaceful one.

items.question: What If the French become one of the largest communities in the US
human_answers: Hordes of Catholics, even if not all that devout, descending on the US will cause some tension. On the flip side, though, France is one of the civilized nations, and they're seen as more desirable shade of white. Timing matters, too. Napoleonic era, when immigration is still low, is a whole lot different than the final decades of the 19th century, when millions is a drop in the bucket. Location matters, too. Are the French hordes joining into the crowded East, where they likely assimilate? Or are they carving out a big chunk of the midwest/west as largely French? Reason for the diaspora might matter. If we mess with the Napoleonic era, especially if we butterfly it (not killing off a generation or two of males would be a good start in having excess population to export), the state of the world could affect the state of the USA (maybe even the size if no Mex-Am War/Texas). If we stipulate a recognizable world, more or less the same, except a massive French diaspora for some reason that hasn't caused OTL to derail.... I would guess the French would be like any other large group. There'll be tension, but everyone will adapt. It's an age of racism, and French are in the top class, so I suspect they'll have an easier time of it. (caveat edit: In no way am I saying French are better than any other nation, but reality is that skin color mattered. My understanding is that not all whites were considered equal)

I would assume rather than staying in the east, the French would largely settle in former Louisiana- centring probably on New Orleans. Texas and Florida as well are likely spots for French settlement. It’s difficult as well to say what the economic impact of French settlement would be- I’d say as a community they’d probably be more educated and thus better off than the Irish or Italians, perhaps more comparable to German or Swedish immigrants. items.original_question: What if the French become one of the largest communities in the US Let’s suppose that millions of French flocked to the US in the 19th century for one reason or another—for example, because harsher Napoleonic Wars and a more severe Congress of Vienna plunged France into a deep economic crisis, while the Irish and Italians would be less numerous in the US, for example because the Irish Great Famine never happened and the Italian peninsula unified and modernized earlier. No PoD before 1780. How would the French be treated in the US? Would they face xenophobia and form a distinct community like the Irish and Italians, or would they be assimilated among the WASPs within one or two generations like the Germans did IOTL? French culture was admired, but I’m not sure that the arrival of millions of French people (with a Latin culture and Catholic religion) would be particularly well received.
items.model_answer:
If the French became one of the largest communities in the United States, the country would likely still remain recognizably American, but its culture, politics, language, and international orientation would be noticeably different.

The biggest change would be cultural. French language and customs would probably have a much stronger public presence, especially in major cities and in regions where French settlement was dense. Bilingualism in English and French might become common in schools, government services, media, and business, much as Spanish has a major presence today. American food culture would also shift: French culinary traditions, café culture, bread, cheese, wine, and regional cooking styles could become more mainstream parts of everyday life rather than markers of elite taste.

Politically, a very large French-origin population might strengthen support for a more centralized state in some areas, depending on when and how that population arrived. French political traditions have often placed greater trust in public administration, secular education, and national cultural policy than the classic American preference for localism and limited government. That would not automatically make the US “more French,” but it could push debates over welfare, education, religion in public life, and labor protections in a different direction.

Religion and secularism could also develop differently. If many of these French Americans came from historically Catholic backgrounds, Catholic institutions might become even more influential than they already were. But if they carried modern French republican ideas, the US might also adopt a stronger form of secular public culture, with sharper boundaries between religion and state.

Regionally, places with French roots such as Louisiana would likely hold much greater national influence. French-derived legal traditions, architecture, music, and local identities might spread beyond isolated pockets and become part of the national mainstream. The symbolic story Americans tell about themselves might also change: instead of being framed mainly as an Anglo-Protestant society later diversified by immigration, the US might be understood from the beginning as a dual Anglo-French or even broader multilingual republic.

Foreign policy could be affected too. A large French-American community might make the US somewhat more attentive to France, Quebec, the Caribbean, and parts of Africa where French influence was strong. Diplomatic and commercial ties with the Francophone world would probably deepen.

That said, the exact outcome would depend on timing. If the French became one of the largest communities through colonial settlement early in US history, the entire national identity could be fundamentally reshaped. If it happened later through immigration, the French would more likely become a major ethnic bloc within an already English-dominant system. In either case, the most likely result is not that America becomes “French,” but that it becomes more bilingual, more culturally continental, and more shaped by French traditions than in our timeline.

The year 1502 starts very rough for Catalina of Aragon. She and her husband, Arthur , Prince of Wales had both fallen ill at the end of March and when she recovered, she discovered that her husband had died. She could not believe it. She was a widow after only five months of marriage. She knew that she was not pregnant, as her marriage was unconsummated. One month after she was made a widow, Catalina was moved to Durham House in London and was visited by King Henry VII and his wife, Queen Elizabeth of York. Catalina told them that she had bled already and there was no hope for an heir from their late son, so his younger brother, Prince Henry, Duke of York, was officially declared as the heir. When the news to Catalina's parents, King Fernando II of Aragon and Queen Isabella I of Castile, they were disappointed that the alliance seemed to have fallen through and that their daughter was widowed at only sixteen years old. This began a struggle over Catalina. Queen Isabella was adamant that her youngest child be returned to her, since there was not a hope of an English grandchild to seal the alliance with Spain and England. King Henry VII, however, did not want to lose her or her dowry. He offered to marry her to his younger son and she could still be Queen of England one day. Queen Isabella made up her mind and told her husband that she wanted their daughter to be returned home. King Ferdinand sent an ambassador to tell King Henry that the Princess would be returned to Spain, either with her entourage or by force. When King Henry VII heard this, he was furious, but also terrified. He needed this alliance with Spain and he did not want to let his daughter-in-law go. Finally, an agreement was finally reached. The Infanta would return to her parents and half her dowry would be returned with her and she would retain her status of Dowager Princess of Wales and would still receive her marriage jointure for the remainder of her life. Her English attendants, like Margaret Pole, would remain in England. When she was told Princess Catalina had a mix of grief and relief. She was happy to return home to her parents, especially since her older sister, Juana, who was now Princess of Asturias, was back home as well. On August 1, 1502, Princess Catalina and her entourage arrived at Dover, preparing to board the ship that will cross the sea once again. Prince Henry, the young Prince of Wales accompanied her, just like he escorted her down the aisle to marry his late older brother. The eleven year old, who was talkative and social, was unusually quiet through the journey. Princess Catalina gave him a little kiss on his forehead and told him that she will never forget him or her time in England and she knew that one day, he will be the greatest King that England ever had, before she boarded the ship. Thankfully, this journey was much easier than her original one taking her to England. She and her entourage arrived in Laredo on the 15th of August. Princess Catalina found herself smiling, as she saw the familiar Castilian villages and knew she was home. However, she then was wondering what would happen to her and her future. Due to the deaths of her older brother, sister and nephew, she knew that taking holy vows was not an option, as he parents only had three surviving daughters. Would she just remain a spinster? items.original_question: Independent Naples: What if Catherine of Aragon marries Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505? Hey all! This question has been on my mind a little too. What if instead of the long seven years in England in virtual poverty, Catherine of Aragon returns to her parents in the summer of 1502 and they arrange a marriage for the young King of Naples, which is still an independent Kingdom in this timeline? In this timeline, Henry VIII will instead marry Eleanor of Austria instead.
items.model_answer:
If Catherine of Aragon had married Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, in 1505, the most likely result is not a permanently independent Naples, but a stronger short-term Aragonese-Neapolitan bloc in Italy and a very different dynastic future for England. The key consequence is that Catherine would leave the Anglo-Spanish marriage market after Arthur’s death and be redirected into Mediterranean dynastic politics. That would shift her from being the future queen of England to being a queenly figure in the orbit of Naples, Valencia, and the wider Crown of Aragon.

The first and biggest immediate effect would be on English history. Henry VIII would almost certainly never marry Catherine. Without that marriage, there is no Princess Mary in the same form, no “King’s Great Matter” over annulment from Catherine, and therefore no Reformation in England triggered in the same way or at the same moment. England might still eventually break with Rome for other reasons, but the specific chain of events that produced the English Reformation would be broken. Henry would need a different foreign bride, probably from France, Burgundy-Habsburg circles, or a lesser Iberian line. That alone makes this a major European divergence.

For Naples, the marriage would matter because Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, was heir to the dispossessed Neapolitan Trastámara line. Catherine herself was the daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella, whose policies had brought Naples under Spanish-Aragonese control. A marriage between Catherine and Ferdinand would symbolically reconcile two branches of the wider Aragonese world: the ruling Spanish monarchy and the old Neapolitan royal house. It could be used to strengthen legitimacy in southern Italy, especially among elites who still remembered the old Neapolitan dynasty. In that sense, the marriage could have given Naples a more distinct court identity within the Spanish system.

But “independent Naples” is the harder part. In 1505, Naples was strategically too important for Ferdinand the Catholic to let go easily. It was a core Mediterranean possession, essential for projecting power into Italy and checking France. Even if Catherine and Ferdinand were installed in Naples, they would probably rule as dependents or viceroyal royals under Spanish supremacy, not as fully sovereign monarchs. Ferdinand the Catholic was not in the habit of creating genuinely independent cadet kingdoms when direct control served his interests better. So the realistic outcome is a semi-autonomous Naples, perhaps with more local prestige and dynastic coloration, rather than complete independence.

Still, over time, a Catherine-Ferdinand marriage could create conditions for partial separation. If they had sons, those children might become the nucleus of a junior Aragonese-Neapolitan branch. In a succession crisis, especially after the deaths of Isabella of Castile and then Ferdinand the Catholic, Naples could become attached to this cadet line instead of being absorbed so tightly into the emerging Habsburg monarchy under Charles. That would be the best path toward “independent Naples”: not immediate separation in 1505, but gradual dynastic differentiation aided by Italian politics and Habsburg overstretch.

This matters because the Habsburg inheritance was about to transform Europe. Historically, Naples became part of the massive Habsburg system under Charles V. If Catherine were in Naples and her husband’s line were politically useful, some anti-Habsburg forces—French, papal, Venetian, or local baronial—might support a distinct Neapolitan monarchy as a buffer state. Catherine’s royal status as daughter of the Catholic Monarchs would enhance that claim. Naples could then resemble a satellite kingdom with its own court, diplomacy, and succession, though still under strong Spanish influence.

However, several constraints make full success unlikely. France would oppose any settlement that strengthened an Aragonese cadet branch in Italy. Spanish rulers would fear that autonomy in Naples could invite renewed French intervention. Neapolitan barons were often divided and could be unreliable partners in state-building. And Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, though dynastically significant, was not in a strong independent power position. So unless the Spanish monarchy itself fragmented more than it historically did, Naples would probably remain tied to the larger Spanish imperial framework.

The most plausible long-run counterfactual, then, is this: Catherine’s marriage to Ferdinand of Calabria produces a more locally rooted and ceremonially royal Naples, perhaps one with intermittent claims to separate status, but not a cleanly independent kingdom right away. The larger historical transformation happens elsewhere. England loses Catherine, so the Tudor succession and the English Reformation are radically altered. Italy gains a potentially stronger Aragonese-Neapolitan dynastic center, but one that would still struggle to escape Spanish control unless broader Habsburg politics gave it an opening.

So if Catherine marries Ferdinand in 1505, “independent Naples” becomes more thinkable, but only as a contingent later development. The immediate and certain result is not Neapolitan independence; it is the removal of Catherine from English history and the creation of a more dynastically coherent southern Italian branch of the Aragonese world.

items.question: What If Curb Global Warming after 1980
human_answers: India has only recently emerged as one of the world’s chief polluters; some two decades ago, Russia and Japan had a bigger mark, and in 1980 Canada was the bigger polluter. Depending on how decarbonized the economies of the First World are by 2000, India’s subsequent economic growth could be magnitudes cleaner than it was OTL. China you have a better point about, though first, their massive economic rise in the three decades after Mao’s death or so is pretty contingent, and second, they still only caught up to the already carbon stagnant EU in 2002. Imagine if the US was still comparable, as they were OTL until the mid 1980’s; now imagine, as China is getting ready to join the WTO in the late 90’s and early 2000’s, the west is also pushing a world climate treaty that (among other things) pushed these three major blocs (the US, Europe, and China) to curb their emissions going into the future. Even if India still sees their emissions rise, wouldn’t the fact that by far the largest producers are simultaneously cutting emissions lead to net reduction?

Well, is the point of your question, can we limit temperature rise by today , or in perpetuity? If the former, then greater adoption of nuclear energy in the West is probably a good enough answer; by the time Chinese and Indian energy use spikes, the resultant temperature spike won't come until after today. Maybe. But that seems like the wrong question, I interpret it as how to prevent such a spike from EVER occurring, rather than just occurring 10 years late. And for that, there's a big challenge. How do developing countries get off the ground? Hydrocarbons are great for that. If the big emitters of the 60s all switched to nuclear, that's fantastic--but China and India can't afford to START with nuclear, nobody can, which means a huge amount of hydrocarbons being burned when they start heavily industrializing. As a solution, perhaps their rise as industrial powers can be delayed a few decades? If they started industrializing in 2025 instead, they might use shale gas or solar, which are now the cheapest sources of power. But the production of those isn't domestic to China, which is a huge part of their use of coal--they don't have to import it. Tentatively, maybe the Soviet Union needs to have greater economic development and a softer landing when it falls? If they can be an industrial exporter while powered off domestic nuclear and natural gas, and remain so in the 1990s, then Chinese growth will be very different, and overall emissions will be lower. Cars and planes are obvious problems. I would also posit beef as a problem--methane is significantly more powerful than carbon in greenhouse effect, and is estimated as responsible for 20 to 30 percent of human-origin warming. Sixty percent of methane emissions are estimated as human-caused, with a big one being agriculture, and beef is responsible for a LOT of agriculture. So a poorer world, that eats less meat, would have lower methane emissions. So too would a world with fewer wetlands, so perhaps a little more paving of swamps would be good from the perspective of this question. Just thoughts. I'll be back for more, probably.

No, because they're already too anti-nuclear. The R&D and thus cost curves on silicon-based solar cell production, and on improved battery capacity, are both pushed pretty hard historically by electronics industry spinoffs. It's hard to see any sort of policy pushes for renewables accelerating those more than marginally, and dramatic acceleration is what you need to make them cost-viable decades ahead of schedule. On the other hand, nuclear was deliberately hobbled by US policy in the 1970s. People like to blame 1979's Three Mile Island, but (for a couple examples) the AEC to NRC switchover was passed by Congress and signed by Ford in 1974, while Carter's anti-reprocessing moratorium was in 1977. If you instead have the US adopt its own version of France's Messmer Plan in 1974 (which is tricky, because Messmer was able to simply ignore anti-nuclear sentiments due to government and economy structure in ways the US government couldn't), you get nuclear power economies of scale driven by the joint US-French demand that make it a more-attractive alternative throughout the rest of the industrialized world. Imagine Thatcher's government nuclearizing Britain in part to undercut the coal unions, for example. Then, if US electricity is something like 75% nuclear in 1990 (like France in 1990, instead of the historical 20%), with the UK fast-following? Now you have the necessary condition (it not hobbling the US) for international trade treaties and the like based on carbon emissions, after a decade of greenhouse effect publicity (since the 1979 NAS report), with the first IPCC report coming out. (Yes, sure, butterflies will scramble the details, but "coal is bad" science, if anything, will be better-funded if the US is transitioning from coal.) If Japan has (as is likely) lagged the US/France/UK in adoption of nuclear, this will be a particularly easy sell, since everybody in the West in 1990 is looking for an excuse to be protectionist against "Japan, Inc." And with that set up, you have the trick for going forward. If China (etc.) has to avoid coal power to export to Western markets, China either will figure out how to avoid coal, or it won't develop because it won't have markets to sell into.

I can give you two, PODs, One being no 3 Mile Island and the other being no John Sununu. So the real easy way to cut down on CO2 emissions is to cut down on coal use, and both PODs give easy ways to do just that. After the banning of CFCs in the late 80s, momentum existed for much harder caps on carbon than were discussed later. In particular, serious curtailment of coal as an energy source in the developed world was mooted. However, this momentum was handicapped with a lack of US Presidential support, with Bush Sr being advised against supporting these efforts by his Chief of Staff, John Sununu. Remove Sununu, and US support for carbon caps become more likely earlier. In addition with no 3MI incident, nuclear technology in the west could become less taboo, giving a viable alternative to coal fired power earlier. I could see a scenario where industry, much like CFCs, sees the financial opportunities in replacing coal with a nuclear/gas mix, and does not get in the way of any cuts to carbon emissions. A good book on the subject in your timeframe is Loosing Earth, by Nathanial Rich, which goes into detail about the drive to curtail emissions in the late 80s. would highly recommend giving it a read.
items.original_question:
AHC: Curb Global Warming after 1980

So you know how Global Surface Temperatures have increased 1.3°C over pre-industrial levels at present, and how a big part of the current Climate Movement is trying to limit further change as much as possible, 1.5°C being the best known* goal? Well, as recently as circa 1980, GST above PIL was only about 0.3°C, and had been hovering just below those levels for decades since the aftermath of WWII; in other words, a full degrees celsius of global warming only happened in the past 45 years alone. This is actually pretty astonishing when you realize how much of a turning point circa 1980 was to global carbon emissions -- both the biggest producers world-wide at the time, the US and Europe, initially saw their emissions peak, with Europe remaining controlled even as the US reversed course after a few years; Japan and Canada have a similar "false peaks" around the same time as the US; the USSR, of course, collapse circa 1990 and saw their emissions collapse thereafter, never to recover; and China was about to undergo a massive economic expansion that would see them become the world's largest emitters. So what I want to determine here is -- what is the latest PoD for avoiding this massive escalation of climate change, or of making it as small as possible? Could a PoD in the late 1970's (eg a continuation of Carter's energy policies in the US) have done the trick? If avoiding a full degrees celsius of warming wasn't seriously avertable by, say, 1975, how early do we need to go? 1960? The aftermath of WWII? In the event we can come to a consensus on the latest possible PoD and what would do the trick, we might also discuss how those changes to said countries' energy polices and to the global economy as a whole would have changed things overall. Thanks. *I'm really trying to avoid getting sidetracked in this discussion for the thread, so for anyone wanting to weigh in on whether its still feasible or how big of a deal missing that goal is, please take that to one of the Chat discussions -- much thanks!
items.model_answer:
If the world had seriously moved to curb global warming after 1980, the most likely result is that climate change would still exist, but it would be much milder, slower, and easier to manage than it is today.

By 1980, scientists already understood the basic greenhouse effect and were becoming increasingly confident that rising carbon dioxide from fossil fuels would warm the planet. If governments had acted then with strong policies—such as limiting coal use, improving energy efficiency, investing early in solar, wind, nuclear power, public transit, and protecting forests—global emissions could have peaked much earlier. That would have meant lower atmospheric CO2 concentrations, less total warming, and fewer extreme climate impacts by the 2000s and 2020s.

In practical terms, the world might now have lower average temperatures, slower sea-level rise, less glacier melt, and reduced risks of heat waves, droughts, floods, and intense storms. Some damage would still occur because the climate system responds slowly and because industrial emissions had already built up before 1980. But many of today’s most dangerous trends would likely be less severe. Coral reefs, Arctic sea ice, and vulnerable ecosystems would probably be in better condition. Food and water stress in some regions would also likely be less intense.

Economically, early action would probably have been cheaper overall than delayed action. The transition away from fossil fuels would have been gradual rather than rushed, allowing infrastructure to be replaced over time. Cities, industries, and transport systems could have adapted earlier. While some sectors—especially coal, oil, and gas—would have faced disruption, new industries in clean energy and efficiency would likely have grown sooner. Many economists argue that acting early reduces both future climate damages and the cost of emergency adaptation.

Politically, an early response after 1980 might also have changed international relations. Climate cooperation could have become a major global project before emissions grew rapidly in emerging economies. Rich countries, which were then responsible for most historical emissions, would have had more opportunity to lead and finance cleaner development elsewhere. That might have reduced some of the fairness disputes that later complicated climate negotiations.

However, this outcome would have depended on how strong the response was. Small symbolic steps after 1980 would not have been enough. To truly curb global warming, countries would have needed sustained international cooperation, carbon regulation, technological innovation, and public support over decades. That would have been politically difficult, especially because fossil fuels were deeply tied to economic growth and geopolitical power.

So the best short answer is this: if the world had moved decisively after 1980 to curb global warming, we would probably still face climate change today, but it would likely be significantly less dangerous, less costly, and less destabilizing than the version we are now experiencing.
