So much so it caused quite a stir in Francia. His sons were scared of him at certain points and expected to be blinded at his hands for some of the actions they'd done. Instead of blinding, a firm punishment such as tonsuring his most rebellious sons for their pride (long hair was a cultural hallmark of the Franks) would have probably done the job. These rebellious sons being sent to a monastery close under his own influence and watch would have set a decent enough example for those who defied his will. As for the division of the Empire, if it were subdivided along reasonable lines it might have actually worked to some degree, as it would have accounted for the natural fragmentation of power and regionalism that would develop in a state like this without any sense of overarching national identity or even political capital. The fragmentation of these Kingdoms within the Empire would have unironically helped the Emperor maintain power over his kin who'd reign as subkings under his authority.
items.original_question: What if Louis the Pious was able to successfully pass his reforms? Louis the Pious had conceived the empire to never be divided. It was through this conception that he decided that power would only be relegated to his eldest son while to compensate for the lack of power, the younger sons would be gifted smaller kingdoms (like, for example, the kingdom of Italy). Nevertheless these smaller kings would still declare loyalty towards the emperor. He had also believed that imperial power came from the pope, hosting his coronation in Reims with the pope. These reforms were never truly put in place however, as the Frankish court had viewed them negatively as they did not follow Frankish tradition. In tandem, the younger brothers of Lothaire (who was meant to have the throne) played against their father. Coupled with Judith of Bavaria attempting to give her son, Charles the (eventual) Bald as much heritage as he could possibly get. Thus, progressively, until the day of Louis the Pious’ death his power was more and more fractured. Therefore, what would happen if he was more politically competent, if he was able to somehow circumvent of push back against the court politics that brought about his downfall and the division of the empire?
items.model_answer:
If Louis the Pious had successfully passed and entrenched his reforms, the Carolingian Empire likely would have remained more unified for longer, and the political fragmentation that followed his reign would have been delayed or reduced. The key issue in his reign was succession: Louis tried to impose an orderly inheritance through measures like the Ordinatio Imperii, which aimed to preserve imperial unity while assigning subordinate roles to his sons. In reality, repeated rebellions, family rivalry, and aristocratic opportunism undermined that plan. If he had succeeded, the empire might have developed a more stable principle of imperial succession instead of breaking into competing kingdoms.

A successful reform program would probably have strengthened central authority over the nobility and the church. Louis was deeply concerned with moral order, ecclesiastical reform, and imperial governance. If those reforms had taken hold, bishops and abbots might have remained more closely tied to a functioning imperial center, and regional magnates would have had less room to turn their offices into semi-independent power bases. That could have produced a stronger administrative structure across Francia, making it harder for local dynasties to dominate politics after his death.

One major consequence would be on the Treaty of Verdun in 843, which divided the empire into western, middle, and eastern realms. If Louis had secured acceptance of a unified imperial order, Verdun might never have happened, or it might have taken a much milder form. Without that division, the later emergence of distinct political cores that became France and Germany may have been slower, less sharp, or taken very different forms. Europe might have seen a more durable trans-regional empire centered on the old Carolingian lands.

This would also have affected military defense. A more coherent empire could have responded more effectively to Viking, Magyar, and Saracen raids, which in reality exposed the weakness of divided rule. Coordinated frontier defense, shared military resources, and stronger royal authority might have reduced the scale of devastation and lessened the need for local lords to assume military powers for themselves. That, in turn, could have slowed the growth of feudal decentralization.

Still, even if Louis had succeeded, long-term unity was not guaranteed. The empire was very large, culturally diverse, and difficult to govern with ninth-century communications and institutions. Regional identities and aristocratic ambitions would still have posed problems. So the most plausible outcome is not a permanent united Europe, but a Carolingian Empire that stayed intact for a longer period, with stronger central institutions and a delayed transition into the separate medieval kingdoms that later dominated western Europe.

items.question: What If Japan had pursued a navy-centered national strategy?
human_answers: Your argument is intriguing. I wrote a post last year that made a similar argument to yours. Post in thread 'If Japan had not taken over Korea, where would they have expanded instead?' Feb 8, 2025 I feel like Korea keeping Japan from being too aggressive gives china a lot more breathing room to consolidate its own development- Seeing the modernisation happening in Korea probably strengthens reform factions in china- although if it means the Qing feel the need to reestablish control over this unpredictable vassal, could potentially lead to the sino Japanese war being replaced by a sino Korean War that also humiliates china and exposed its failure. Madhukar_Shah However, even back then, there were comments on that post saying that “even if Korea were to modernize, Japan would not abandon its ambitions toward Korea and the continent. One of the reasons for that is precisely the topic of this post. I once read a Korean alternate-history novel in which the Japanese Army and its internal factions acted as obstacles to cooperation between Korea and Japan. In the end, meaningful Korea–Japan cooperation only began to make real progress after Yamagata Aritomo fell from power following the Ōtsu Incident and was even subjected to an assassination attempt.

Huh? After the Sengoku Period Japan experienced one of the most peaceful and stable periods in its history under the Tokugawa Shogunate, which lasted lasted 250+ years. The only period in Japanese history that lasted longer was the Heian period. But that was hardly a stable regime, with regular infighting between retired emperors, the Fujiwara, and ultimately the Taira and Minamoto clans. And after the failed invasion of Korea at the end of the Azuchi-Momoyama period there were no serious Japanese attack against the mainland until the Meiji Period. ​ I am not sure why you think it was the army that uniquely pushed Japan to pursue expansionist policies? The navy was fully complicit in this as well, in fact the navy is the enabling factor in this because it's the only way for Japan to actually attack anybody outside the home islands in the first place. You use Britain and Venice as examples but how did these two powers not also use their navies for aggressive expansionism overseas? The bushi never rising in the first place, which takes you all the way back to the aforementioned Heian period. The utter failure of e.g. the Jokyu War or the Kenmu Restoration shows how powerless the court nobility became once the bakufu was established. Not to mention that the ultimate restoration of imperial power itself was enabled by the military power of the bushi, just the ones that opposed to bakufu.

I think the most interesting POD would be in the early 17th century during the first decades of the Togugawa shogunate. During the Senkaku period Japan had been relatively open to foreign trade due to the lack of central authority and when they first came to power the Togugawa tried to regulate but not stop this exchanges, including provisions such as the "Ted Seals" that allowed large Japanese merchantmen of the same name reach all the way down to Indonesia if not further. The shogunate and their allies also possessed a few European style galleons, most famously the San Juan Bautista . Now OTL the shogunate would end up halting this trade and impose the Sakoku policy which closed off Japan from almost all foreign trade, as well as starting the persecution of Christians. While the reasons behind this are still debated two of the primary reasons stated is that the Shogunate was increasingly worried about the threat that colonial European powers presented to Japan as well as the fact that a lot of this trade (including many of the Read Seal Ships) were controlled by southern houses that were not seen as loyal to the Togugawa. Now ponder a reality where the Shogunate decides a forward defense policy is better as an answer to European encroachment and that rather than cut off trade its better to let its own vassals control the Red Seals. Such a Japan would eventually have to develop the centralized naval infrastructure to protect that trade and fend of Europeans, resulting in a state for whom the navy is the central military concern (much like Britain). Edo era Japan was no economic slouch and could probably sustain a trade/semicolonial empire. Places like the Ryukyus and Hokkaido would fall under central Japanese control much earlier and sino-japanese relations would be very different. A Japanese naval empire could lead to similar responses from the Qing and the Joseon as well. Of course this would have big social ramifications within Japan: we probably wouldn't' see the same system for controlling samurai as OTL and merchants would end up much more influential much quicker. The rigid social hierarchy that the Togugawa tried to impose would fall apart before it was even properly enforced. Christianity might be more accepted but its equally possible that anti-Christianity could form the roots of an early form of Pan-Asianism.

Due to the influence of typhoons and unstable wind patterns in the East Asian seas, the region's "most strategic commercial sea lane" has historically been the trade route along the coastline, while the distant island chains have traditionally been uninhabited. Regarding the so-called "central place in trade," there were four key players in East Asian trade: mainland Japan, which produced precious metals; mainland China, which produced handicrafts (I don't believe that naval power alone could completely control trade along the Chinese coast, especially since excessive trade with China would only lead to all the precious metals flowing into China, destroying Japan's domestic industries); the Europeans; and the Spice Islands (which were within the Dutch sphere of influence, and required passing through the Philippines to reach Japan). It is clear that Japan could only control valuable trade centers if its navy surpassed the combined strength of Spain and the Netherlands; any navy less powerful than that would be meaningless. However, without any positive feedback or incentives, I don't believe it would be possible to build a navy in mainland Japan that could surpass the combined naval power of these two countries.
items.original_question: What if Japan had pursued a navy-centered national strategy? Unlike most island nations, Japan historically possessed an army with substantial political and social influence. With the emergence of the samurai class, Japan experienced prolonged periods of civil war and state formation led primarily by warrior elites. Particularly after the Sengoku period, cycles of civil war, the birth of new regimes, and expansion toward the continent were repeatedly observed. After the Toyotomi Hideyoshi regime emerged from the outcome of internal conflict, Hideyoshi employed the greatly expanded army to pursue continental ambitions, leading to the invasion of the Korean Peninsula. Following the fall of the Tokugawa shogunate and the wars that accompanied it, the Meiji government was established and Japan embarked on a program of modernization. However, unlike Britain and other island nations, Japan maintained an army with considerable autonomy and political influence despite its insular geography. Consequently, Japan’s expansionist trajectory once again focused on the Korean Peninsula, Manchuria, and the Asian continent. What I am curious about is the following. If Japan were to become a country in which the navy held complete primacy over the army, how would its history have needed to unfold differently? In this scenario, the army would be limited to roles such as suppression of internal rebellions, defense of the home islands, and naval infantry (marines), possessing only minimal status and political influence. The navy would constitute the principal military force, and national defense strategy and institutional design would likewise be shaped under naval leadership. Furthermore, the direction of external expansion would be determined from the perspective of a maritime power, rather than that of a continental state. If Japan had chosen the route of a maritime power like Britain or the Venetian Republic, or if its modernization had been deliberately oriented toward a completely navy-led military structure, how would Japanese history have unfolded differently? The Japan I'm referring to includes not only the Empire of Japan but also earlier periods of Japanese history. POD is not just in 1868 but extends to several centuries earlier.
items.model_answer:
If Japan had pursued a more consistently navy-centered national strategy, its modern history would likely have looked more maritime, more commercially oriented, and somewhat less dominated by the army and continental expansion—though not necessarily more peaceful.

In actual history, Japan developed both a strong army and a strong navy, but the balance of power often shifted. The army was especially tied to intervention on the Asian mainland, above all in Manchuria and China. A truly navy-centered strategy would probably have pushed Japan to think of itself primarily as a sea power rather than a continental empire. That would have encouraged greater emphasis on securing shipping lanes, ports, island bases, and overseas trade instead of conquering and occupying large stretches of mainland territory.

Politically, this might have weakened the influence of the army, especially the officers and factions that favored expansion into Korea, Manchuria, and North China. The navy tended to be more internationally minded, partly because naval power depended on technology, shipbuilding, fuel supplies, and diplomacy with other maritime powers. A navy-led Japan might therefore have invested even more heavily in industry, merchant shipping, naval aviation, and alliances, while avoiding deep military entanglement in China. That could have reduced the chance of a drawn-out land war like the Second Sino-Japanese War, which was enormously costly and helped trap Japan in a cycle of escalation.

Economically, a navy-centered strategy might have made Japan more dependent on trade and access to raw materials through markets and protected sea routes rather than territorial conquest. This could have encouraged a stronger focus on commercial empire—informal influence, privileged access, naval bases, and colonial outposts—rather than direct annexation of vast inland territories. Japan might have resembled a more Asian version of a classic maritime imperial power, seeking dominance through fleets, finance, and chokepoints. However, this also would have created vulnerabilities, because Japan lacked many key resources, especially oil. A navy-first strategy would have made secure access to imported fuel and materials even more essential.

That dependence cuts both ways. On one hand, it might have made Japanese leaders more cautious about provoking the United States and Britain, since conflict with the major naval powers threatened the very trade routes Japan needed. On the other hand, if Japanese policymakers still aimed at great-power status and regional hegemony, a navy-centered strategy could have led even more directly to confrontation in Southeast Asia and the Pacific, where oil, rubber, and strategic sea lanes were concentrated. In that case, Japan might have avoided a massive land war in China only to pursue a sharper maritime contest against Western colonial empires.

In military terms, Japan would likely have devoted more resources earlier to battleships, carriers, submarines, naval aviation, amphibious forces, and merchant marine protection. It may also have developed stronger doctrines for blockade, commerce protection, and limited maritime war. If paired with restraint on the mainland, that might have produced a more sustainable grand strategy. Japan’s actual wartime position was badly undermined by trying to fight simultaneously in China, the Pacific, and across a vast empire with insufficient industrial depth. A navy-centered strategy that avoided overextension on the continent could have been strategically smarter.

Still, it is important not to romanticize the navy. The Imperial Japanese Navy was not inherently moderate or anti-imperial. It could be aggressive, expansionist, and committed to decisive war. Naval leaders also supported southern expansion and ultimately backed war with the United States. So the main counterfactual is not simply “navy equals peace.” It is more that Japanese expansion might have been channeled differently: less into continental occupation, more into maritime competition and imperial influence.

The most plausible overall result is that Japan becomes a more trade-focused, industrial, and maritime empire, perhaps less bogged down in China and better positioned economically in the short term. If this strategy were combined with diplomatic restraint, Japan might have avoided the catastrophic wars of attrition that destroyed it by 1945. But if maritime strategy still served an ambition for regional domination, then conflict with the United States, Britain, and the Netherlands might still have come—just in a form even more centered on fleets, bases, and sea lanes rather than huge campaigns on the Asian mainland.

items.question: What If Joseph Bonaparte became a US Senator in 1829?
human_answers: The Know-Nothings don't exist yet in the 1820s. That said, there is something that might alienate him from the nascent Whigs - he's a Freemason, and a pretty involved one - he was Grand Master of the Grand Orient of France during Napoleon's entire reign as emperor, founded the National Lodge of Spain, and that aspect in particular helped hurt his legitimacy among the Spanish when he was made king there. Now, the period where Joseph would enter American politics in your scenario largely coincides with the spread of the Anti-Masonic movement in New York, and their members would largely go on to integrate the Whig party later down the line. In the other hand, as time passed, the Anti-Masonic aspect was diluted so much that they ended up running a Mason as their 1832 presidential candidate, who even defended the Order in a speech before the convention that nominated him, so he might go either way.

In 1908? Highly doubtful, given Bonaparte's Catholic faith. That wouldn't have played at all in much of the South (not that it would have mattered much in terms of getting votes for the GOP there), and might have been a hindrance elsewhere. If he had somehow gotten the nomination, his running mate would certainly have been a Protestant from (likely) the midwest (Albert Beveridge?); TR would have had to do some strenuous campaigning on his behalf especially if Bryan (often referred to as "the Protestant pope") had been his opponent. The result would have been close if Bonaparte had won, and he'd have had to go to great lengths to demonstrate his independence from the Vatican. Still, the idea is intriguing: imagine the polling place schizophrenia of the Irish community in Boston, for example, given how accustomed that segment was to voting a straight Democrat ticket at the time. Also fascinating: Bonaparte was a strong advocate for civil rights for African-Americans. Had he somehow been elected, perhaps the entire cause of civil rights might have been advanced five years or so.
items.original_question: What if Joseph Bonaparte became a US Senator in 1829? Joseph Bonaparte in the early 1830s. ​ Yes, this is completely unrealistic, but it's not quite as outlandish as an actual ASB (hence why I'm posting it on here), as it was theoretically something that could have happened. Joseph Bonaparte had lived in the US since 1817, seemed to have been relatively well-liked during his time in America, and to be a senator you need to be a US citizen for at least nine years. Theoretically, had the former king of Naples and then Spain had desired it, he could have very well becoming a senator by the beginning of the Jacksonian period, when both of New Jersey's seats in the US senate were up for grabs in the 1828-29 senate elections. For this scenario, Joseph Bonaparte comes to decide he wants to integrate himself in the United States. After becoming a US citizen in 1819, Joseph manages to be elected to the US Senate representing New Jersey in the 1828-29. replacing Theodore Frelinghuysen from our own timeline. What exactly happens, domestically, and in terms of the US' relationships with foreign countries, and in any other conceivable aspect, in this timeline where a former monarch manages to become a US Senator at the beginning of the Jackson administration.
items.model_answer:
If Joseph Bonaparte had become a U.S. senator in 1829, the most likely result is not a dramatic transformation of American politics, but a strange, symbolically powerful episode with modest practical effects and some interesting ripple effects in diplomacy, immigration, and partisan culture.

The first thing to note is that this would have been constitutionally and politically extraordinary. Joseph Bonaparte, Napoleon’s elder brother and former king of Spain and Naples, lived in the United States after Napoleon’s fall and became a well-known exile figure in New Jersey. For him to become a senator in 1829, he would have needed to be a U.S. citizen for nine years, which means he would have had to naturalize by about 1820. If we assume that happened and that New Jersey’s political elite accepted him, his election would have made him one of the most famous and controversial members of the Senate overnight.

Domestically, his presence would probably have been more theatrical than decisive. In 1829, the United States was entering the Jacksonian era. The great political struggles centered on Andrew Jackson, executive power, banking, tariffs, internal improvements, and the reorganization of party politics. Joseph Bonaparte, despite his royal background, had actually shown relatively moderate and pragmatic tendencies in Europe, so in America he likely would not have become a champion of monarchy or anti-republican politics. He would almost certainly have adapted himself to the American constitutional system and presented himself as proof that even a former king could prefer republican liberty to European reaction.

Still, his election would have been used by opponents in vivid ways. Jacksonian populists might have attacked him as an aristocratic foreigner, a relic of European dynastic politics trying to enter the councils of the republic. National Republicans, or later Whigs, might have found him socially useful and intellectually interesting, especially if he aligned with commercial and developmental interests in New Jersey. He likely would have been treated less as a party builder than as a celebrity statesman, someone whose speeches drew attention because of who he had been rather than because he could command blocs of votes.

In foreign policy, his presence could have mattered more. A Bonaparte in the Senate would have been watched very closely by France, Britain, Spain, and the restored Bourbon regimes. European conservatives would see it as yet another sign that the United States was a haven for politically dangerous exiles. At the same time, Joseph himself was not Napoleon, and by 1829 he was more an aging notable than a revolutionary threat. So his office would probably not trigger a crisis, but it might slightly sharpen European suspicion of the United States as a republic willing to elevate displaced continental elites who had fallen afoul of the Restoration order.

With France, the effect is especially interesting. During the late 1820s and early 1830s, U.S.-French relations involved unresolved claims from the Napoleonic era and compensation disputes. Joseph Bonaparte’s Senate role might have given him informal value as an interpreter of French political culture, but he also could have complicated matters by becoming a symbolic irritant. French governments after Napoleon might not want an imperial Bonaparte publicly participating in American statecraft. Still, because Joseph was not an active conspirator, practical diplomacy would likely continue.

On questions of immigration and citizenship, his election might have had a broader cultural effect. Americans would be forced to confront whether the republic was merely a refuge for immigrants or whether even the highest offices, short of the presidency, could be open to a naturalized foreign-born exile of immense former rank. A Joseph Bonaparte senatorship would have dramatized the openness of American political society. Supporters would celebrate it as evidence that republican institutions domesticate ambition and absorb talent. Critics would say it proved that fame and title could still distort republican equality. This could have fueled stronger nativist rhetoric somewhat earlier, especially among people already uneasy about foreign influence.

In the Senate itself, he might have been most effective on committees related to foreign affairs, commerce, or perhaps military matters, where his European experience gave him unusual credibility. He probably would not have become a mass democratic figure; his temperament, background, accent, and elite associations all make that unlikely. But he could have become a respected salon politician in Washington, someone known for cultivated conversation, international contacts, and occasional eloquent interventions on liberty, war, and Europe.

The larger long-term effect would probably be symbolic rather than structural. American memory would preserve him as an emblem of the republic’s absorptive power: a former king turned American senator. That image could strengthen a national self-conception in which the United States stands as the political asylum and eventual political home of the world’s displaced elites and dissidents. It might also encourage more European émigrés to imagine not just refuge in America, but full political integration.

So if Joseph Bonaparte became a U.S. senator in 1829, the United States would not become Bonapartist, and the Senate would not suddenly be ruled by European intrigue. But his election would have been sensational, would have sharpened debates over citizenship and republican identity, and would have made the early Jacksonian republic look even more self-consciously like a nation capable of converting the remnants of the Old World into servants of the New.

items.question: What If Empress Elizabeth of Russia lives longer, long term trajectory of Germany without the Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg?
human_answers: I mean, that was more or less the agreement. The Prussians, or more likely Brandenburgers, most likely considered that they would not control Prussia, would be a power on the level of Saxony or Bavaria. Prussia would be divided between Austria (Silesia + border areas), Saxony (Magdeburg/Halberstadt), Sweden (Pomerania), Russia (East Prussia), and possibly others for the Rhineland territories. The kingdom would be drastically reduced, possibly returning to approximately the size of the central Electorate of Brandenburg, destroying its status as a great power. France would likely gain the Austrian Netherlands unless Austria withdrew from the deal. However, I'm not sure if they would do that. What, Germany? The kingdom that united the German kingdoms is no longer a great power. France, which became a republic in OTL, may very well not experience total collapse, instead becoming a constitutional monarchy. Eliminating the entire process of potentially creating Germany. Honestly, the idea of Germany may very well never leave the drawing board. Austria didn't really want to unify the German kingdoms; it was quite happy with the kingdoms being linked to it but not absorbed. Perhaps some form of federation of northern Germany will occur, but that's not a certainty.

I think it depends on the exact settlement. What are the full concessions Prussia is forced to make? Does Frederick II remain in power or does he abdicate or just maybe try in die on the battlefield if it seems like all is lost? Are events in the west impacted, the Franco-British peace settlement? And how is the domestic situation in Russia impacted with Elizbeth living longer? And do changes in Russia spill over into Poland ie with the election for the successor to Augustus III? Then I think you really have to run through the events of the 1770-80s to figure out what the international scene looks like by the 1790s which in tern dictates how much room to maneuver Austria has in Germany as the subject of Imperial reform becomes a pressing issue. If we go with a healthy butterfly net and assume the war mostly ends as IOTL but with Austria regaining Silesia then yes, Austria retains preeminence in Germany and Prussia is knocked down a peg to the level of the other Electors. That certainly changes Austria's strategic outlook. I think there would be less pressure to secure Bavaria on the death of Max III. Since the claims were mostly fabricated Joseph may just let it pass to Charles Theodore without incident. The Balkans are probably where you would first see the new strategic situation begin to change things. To some extent that depends on the fate of Russia. Again, assuming a butterfly net that still places Catherine on the throne with a similar eye cast towards the south and things get interesting. Without the threat of Prussia to the north Austria is better positioned to make gains in the Balkans. IOTL the Prussians were fairly obsessed with blocking any Austrian gains to the south which would strengthen Austria and upset the relative balance of power between the two. I still think the Greek Plan is a fantasy but its entirely possible that Austria recovers something along the lines of the Passarowitz borders, perhaps incrementally over the course or the rest of the century. IOTL Austria almost took Oltenia but instead opted for Bukovina when Prussia redirected everyone towards a partition of Poland. ITTL attention Austria will be focused squarely to the south and the Danube so gains in Serbia, Bosnia and Wallachia are likely but Moldavia less so. Poland meanwhile probably does not undergo partition and remains a Russian client state in the near term. Although its also possible in a different context post ATL Seven Years War that the Polish Royal election in 1764 leads to a falling out between Russia and Austria. Then the next big question is whether the French revolution still breaks out and still proceeds as IOTL and what kind of state Austria is in internally at the end of Joseph II's reign. Presumably even if the Josephine reforms spark a backlash Austria is much better positioned to ride them out with the southern border secure and gains already made from the Ottomans and with no Prussia threat in the north. So even if the Austrian Netherlands break out in rebellion Joseph or Leopold would be able to put down the revolt more easily without it posing any kind of existential threat.

Considering that theoretically the agreement signed between Russia, Austria and Saxony, envisaged a territorial exchange between Royal Prussia and Courland ( with the recognition that the Wettins would retain the throne of the PLC ) while the Habsburgs would recover Silesia or parts of it, that said, the internal balance of the HRE, would be brought back to the previous Leopoldine period, with Vienna as the undisputed leader, and therefore there would be more room for maneuver to try to pass a new package of imperial reforms, certainly France gaining control of the Austrian Netherlands, would not let the imperial princes of the Rhineland and the Hanoverians sleep peacefully, but unfortunately the latter pay the price of having sided with Prussia or of wanting to remain neutral, regarding the possible idea of German unification, it is difficult for the Habsburgs to show a real interest, when they would prefer to maintain the Status Quo or at most consolidate their position in Swabia / Bavaria ( I could see the Bavarian crisis being easily resolved through an agreement, with Charles Theodore inheriting a good part of the duchy, while Vienna annexes small border areas ) finally I am of the opinion that in this scenario, the role of leadership of the Protestant front ( in Otl led by Berlin ) will be taken by the Hanover, who paradoxically will have to review their political priorities ( especially from the London point of view ), because with their choices they will find themselves diplomatically isolated, therefore they will necessarily have to be more active on the continent

It was already happening: Elizabeth could not force Buturlin to get out of his bases and start acting against Prussia. The only meaningful operation was capture of Kolberg and even it was to provide a secure supply line because the Austrians were refusing to do so and getting supplies from the PLC was extremely problematic. Among the Russian military (except those safely away from the front) there was not too much of an appetite for the further fighting and definitely no serious anymosity toward Fritz. Rumyantsev in OTL was quite happy when PIII made peace and Russian #2 general was Fritz’s admirer. It would take very little time for Russia, no matter who was in charge, to figure out that Prussia is more convenient ally than the Hapsburgs. Even under Elizabeth, no matter what the politicians in St.Petersburg were deciding, relations between the Russian and Austrian commanders hd been steadily deteriorating since Kolberg. The Austrians could not reconquer Silesia on their own and the Russian commanders were not willing to keep doing the Austrian job, especially after Doun failed in obligations to provide them with the food and was very cautious in risking the Austrian troops. Anyway, even in OTL, Fritz was playing a second fiddle to CII until she managed to screw up her foreign policy to a degree which gave Fritz “an opening”.
items.original_question: What if Empress Elizabeth of Russia lives longer, long term trajectory of Germany without the Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg? She lives between a few months to a few years longer in this scenario. Peter III does not withdraw Russian troops from the Seven Years War, the Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg does not materialize. Now, nobody was interested in total defeat of Prussia, it would remain a viable country but remains a second rate power in Europe, Silesia would go back to Austria, there would be possibly other territorial concessions as well. What happens to Germany long term in this timeline? Austria obviously becomes the natural candidate for unification of the country but the timeline will likely change.
items.model_answer:
If Empress Elizabeth of Russia had lived longer, the most likely immediate consequence is that Frederick II of Prussia loses the Seven Years’ War, or at minimum emerges so weakened and territorially reduced that the “Second Miracle of the House of Brandenburg” never happens. That miracle was Russia’s sudden withdrawal from the anti-Prussian coalition after Elizabeth’s death in 1762, when her successor Peter III admired Frederick and reversed Russian policy. Without that reversal, Prussia probably cannot continue resisting Austria, Russia, and their allies indefinitely.

That matters enormously for the long-term trajectory of Germany because the rise of Prussia as a great power was the central precondition for the later unification of Germany under Prussian leadership. If Frederick is defeated decisively in the 1760s, Germany’s future likely becomes much less Prussian, much more Austrian, and much less likely to culminate in the kind of German Empire created in 1871.

In the short term, the most plausible outcome is that Prussia loses Silesia back to Austria, which had been Maria Theresa’s main war aim. Depending on how complete the collapse is, Prussia might also lose territory or at least suffer military and financial exhaustion that strips it of great-power status. It would probably remain an important north German state, but no longer the state capable of challenging Habsburg Austria for leadership in the German world. Once Silesia is lost, the economic and strategic base that made Prussia formidable is badly damaged. Frederick’s prestige would also be shattered. Instead of becoming the symbol of disciplined military monarchy and enlightened great-power resilience, Prussia might be remembered as an overextended state brought back into line by a coalition.

From there, the long-term German trajectory changes in several connected ways.

First, the Austro-Prussian dualism that defined German politics in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries is either greatly weakened or effectively resolved in Austria’s favor. In real history, there were two plausible candidates to dominate Germany: Austria and Prussia. If Prussia is crippled in the 1760s, Austria becomes the overwhelmingly stronger German power. That does not mean immediate unification under Austria, because the Holy Roman Empire was still a highly decentralized structure and the Habsburg monarchy had many non-German interests. But it does mean that any future reorganization of Germany is likely to occur under Austrian hegemony, not Prussian rivalry.

Second, the Napoleonic era would probably still transform Germany, but the state best positioned to shape the aftermath would be Austria, not Prussia. The Holy Roman Empire would still be vulnerable to French pressure and likely still collapse in some form under Napoleon. German mediatisation and the reduction in the number of small states would probably still happen, because those changes were driven largely by French conquest and administrative rationalization. But after Napoleon’s fall, there would be no comparably strong Prussia to demand an equal role in redesigning Germany. The German Confederation created after 1815 would likely be even more clearly an Austrian sphere. In real history, Prussia’s survival and later recovery allowed the “German question” to remain open. In this counterfactual, it is much easier for Austria to keep that question closed.

Third, nineteenth-century German nationalism would still emerge, but its political resolution would likely be delayed, softer, or diverted. Nationalism was not simply a Prussian creation; it grew out of Romanticism, anti-French sentiment, modernization, and the spread of mass politics. So some desire for a German nation-state still appears. But without a powerful Prussian state to turn nationalism into war and state-building, German nationalism may remain fragmented between liberals who want a constitutional Germany and conservatives who prefer dynastic federalism. The Frankfurt Parliament of 1848 might still try to create a united Germany, but the basic dilemma would look different. In real history, the choice was often framed as Greater Germany under Austria or Lesser Germany without Austria under Prussia. If Prussia is too weak, only some variant of Greater Germany or a looser confederation is politically realistic.

That in turn makes a 1871-style unification much less likely. Bismarck’s path depended on a strong Prussian army, efficient bureaucracy, a large north German base, and Austria’s exclusion after the war of 1866. All of that presupposed that Prussia had remained a first-rank power since Frederick’s era. Without the Second Miracle, there may be no Bismarckian Germany at all. Instead, central Europe may continue as a patchwork of German states under Austrian diplomatic leadership, perhaps gradually federalized, perhaps not. If a German nation-state does eventually appear, it is more likely to be looser, more multinational, and more constrained by Habsburg structures than the centralized, militarized empire founded in Versailles.

The wider European balance also changes. A weaker Prussia means less pressure on Austria from within Germany, which may allow the Habsburg monarchy to devote more attention to its other frontiers and internal reforms. It could strengthen Austria’s position in Italy and the Balkans for a time. Russia, having helped crush Prussia, might enjoy greater influence in central Europe as well, though Austria and Russia would still have conflicting interests in southeastern Europe. France benefits in one sense from the absence of a future powerful unified Germany on its eastern border, though in the short term it may worry about excessive Austrian influence in Germany.

One important implication is that the specific chain leading to the world wars becomes less likely. No strong Prussia probably means no Prussian-led German Empire in 1871, no sharply altered continental balance after France’s defeat, and no Wilhelmine Germany in the form we know. That does not mean Europe becomes peaceful; an Austrian-dominated central Europe would have its own tensions, especially because the Habsburg monarchy was ethnically diverse and structurally fragile. But the particularly powerful, industrial, and militarized German nation-state that emerged in the late nineteenth century is much less likely to arise on the same timetable or in the same form.

So the best concise answer is this: if Elizabeth lives longer and Russia does not switch sides, Prussia probably loses the Seven Years’ War decisively enough to prevent its rise as the engine of German unification. Germany then likely develops either as a looser Austrian-led confederative space or, at most, as a delayed and different “Greater German” political structure. The long-term trajectory is therefore less toward a Prussian-national empire and more toward prolonged fragmentation under Habsburg predominance, with major consequences for all of European history.

items.original_question: What if New Spain kept appointing a tlatoani? When we think of the Fall of the Aztec Empire, we think of the Spanish coming in and overthrowing the existing order and building New Spain upon the ashes of the Aztec Empire. Well, the answer is a lot more complicated than that thought. One aspect from the Aztec Empire Spain kept was the position of a Tlatoani. Initially, the last sovereign of the Aztec Empire, Cuauhtémoc, was kept alive until Hernan Cortes killed him while bringing along to Honduras. However, Hernan then appointed a person named Tlacotzin (A former advisor of Cuauhtémoc) as tlatoani, (Though he was titled Cuauhtlatoani) but he died the next year before he could return to Tenochtitlan. So, Cortes then appointed a commoner named Motelchiuhtzin net, then he died fighting the Chichimeca up north. Then a man named Xochiquentzin ruled until he died of natural causes. So after that stint, the Spanish appointed Tlatoanis from the previous Aztec dynasty, who were both Tlatoani and Governor of Tenochtitlan (By this point Mexico City) under the Spanish colonial government of New Spain. It started with Panitzin and ended with Cipac. The last one got into frequent disputes over legal issues and disagreements on taxes with the colonial authorities. Afterwards, in just 1565, the Spanish ceased appointing a member of the former dynasty of Tlatoani. But they did continue to appoint a native Judge-governor until Mexican independence in 1821, who were either indigenous or mixed descent and many were descendants of Aztec nobility, though not of the royal dynasty. What if the Spanish continued to appoint continued a blood member of the previous Aztec Empire as "Tlatoani," and continues this until Mexican independence? How would a direct descendent of the Aztec emperors affect the search for a Mexican monarch? Could we see a movement similar to the "Inca Plan" where the Mexicans elect a native Nahuatl as Emperor instead of a European Prince or later Iturbide?
items.model_answer:
If New Spain had continued appointing a tlatoani after the Spanish conquest, the colony likely would have developed a more visibly hybrid political order, blending Spanish imperial rule with surviving Nahua ideas of legitimate kingship. The tlatoani had been the ruler of Tenochtitlan and, more broadly, a central symbol of Mexica sovereignty. Keeping that office alive under colonial supervision would not have restored the Aztec Empire, but it could have given indigenous elites a stronger, more institutionalized place inside the new regime.

In the short term, this probably would have helped the Spanish govern central Mexico. The Spanish often ruled through existing native nobility anyway, using local rulers to collect tribute, organize labor, and maintain order. An officially recognized tlatoani in Mexico-Tenochtitlan could have served as a symbolic intermediary between the viceroy and indigenous communities, making Spanish rule appear less like total rupture and more like succession. That might have reduced some early resistance and preserved more continuity in law, ceremony, and urban identity.

Over time, though, the arrangement could have cut in two different directions. On one hand, the tlatoani might have become mostly ceremonial, much like many indigenous offices under colonialism: useful for tribute collection, local legitimacy, and pageantry, but stripped of real military and sovereign authority. In that case, New Spain would still remain a Spanish colony, but one with a stronger recognized indigenous aristocratic layer and a more publicly acknowledged Nahua political legacy.

On the other hand, the office could have become a rallying point for broader indigenous claims. Even if tightly controlled, a tlatoani would embody the memory of preconquest rulership. In times of crisis—famine, taxation disputes, caste tensions, Bourbon centralization, or later independence struggles—that office might have offered a ready-made symbol for resistance, reform, or autonomy. Instead of indigenous politics being dispersed across many local communities, some grievances might have been concentrated around a central native institution in Mexico City.

Culturally, the consequences could have been important. The survival of a tlatoani would likely have preserved more court ritual, Nahuatl prestige, noble genealogies, and public recognition of Mexica history. Colonial identity in central Mexico might have become more explicitly mestizo in political symbolism, not just socially mixed. New Spain may have looked a bit more like a composite monarchy, where different peoples kept distinct political traditions under one crown, rather than a colony that formally replaced native sovereignty.

Still, there are clear limits. Spanish authorities, especially after the sixteenth century, were generally suspicious of concentrated indigenous power. They preferred fragmented local rule to any revived native monarchy that could challenge royal authority. So if a tlatoani had continued to be appointed, the office likely would have survived only by becoming dependent on the Spanish crown, Christianized, and carefully managed. It would not have meant an independent Aztec state inside New Spain, but rather a colonialized indigenous kingship.

So the most likely outcome is not “the Aztec Empire survives,” but “New Spain becomes a more openly dual political system,” with stronger indigenous elite continuity, richer Nahua ceremonial life, and a potentially more powerful symbol around which indigenous identity and resistance could later gather.

items.original_question: What if No Almanzor Ibn Abi Amir ‘al-Mansur’, better known Latinized as Almanzor, was the Hajib (chamberlain) and de facto ruler of the Caliphate of Qurtubah (Córdoba) from 978 to 1002 AD. A highly ambitious man, ibn Abi Amir would rise through the collection of various powerful offices over the course of the 960s and 970s as an administrator. Through this and his alliance with Subh, mother of the Umayyad boy-caliph Hisham II, ibn Abi Amir would become the most powerful man in al-Andalus by 980. Except, he wasn’t alone. He shared this spotlight with Ghalib ibn Abd al-Rahman ‘al-Siqlabi’ (the Slav), a widely-respected octogenarian general who had served both of Hisham’s predecessors. The two men formed an alliance with one another following the death of Caliph al-Hakam II in 976, allowing for them to rise the ranks of the Caliphate. However by 980 the two men had fallen out, and were increasingly at odds. That year, while together on campaign against the Christians, Ghalib attempted to murder ibn Abi Amir during a feast. The injured ibn Abi Amir would escape with his life and then proceed to capture Ghalib’s fortress in Madinat Salim (Medinaceli). This would lead to a brief civil war between the two, culminating in 981 with the Battle of Torrevicente. There, Ghalib’s army of Andalusi soldiers and his Christian allies would initially rout the Berber troops of ibn Abi Amir. However, Ghalib would unexpectedly die of seemingly natural causes in the middle of the battle, allowing for ibn Abi Amir to claim victory and the mantle of ‘al-Mansur’. Al-Mansur would go on to rule al-Andalus with an iron fist for the next two decades, sidelining the Umayyads, Arab nobility, and Muwalladi (native Iberian Muslims) alike while utilizing increasing numbers of Berber troops to repeatedly devastate the Christian north. While al-Mansur would lead al-Andalus to its peak of dominance over the whole of Iberia, he would also destroy its literal and cultural wealth while gutting its institutions. Upon his death in 1002 the Caliphate was a house of cards waiting to collapse, which it did after Abd al-Rahman ‘Sanchol’, better known as Sanchuelo, attempted to directly usurp the Umayyads as Caliph himself in 1009. This led to the 22-year-long Fitna (unrest) of al-Andalus, ending with Córdoba in ruins and the Caliphate shattered into 30+ petty kingdoms known as Taifas . A situation that would enable the Reconquista to gain steam, culminating in the capture of Tulaytulah (Toledo) by the Christians in 1085. Had Ghalib succeeded in the attempt on his life, ibn Abi Amir would have never become al-Mansur. The Umayyads would have maintained control over their Caliphate. Al-Andalus wouldn’t come to be dominated by a single dictatorial ruler. And the seeds of the Fitna wouldn’t be planted. The Reconquista will unfold differently, or even not at all. What are your thoughts on this scenario? I’ve come to believe that it represents the best chance the Caliphate of Córdoba had at ensuring long-term survival. Averting Almanzor and his excesses would blunt the height of Andalusi authority, but paradoxically preserve the state itself. Of course, stability following his death wouldn’t be ensured, and Ghalib wouldn’t have much longer to live anyway. However, the two had taken care of most rivals, and Ghalib was in good standing with the old guard of al-Andalus. Caliph Hisham II can actually grow up and become a proper ruler, preserving the legitimacy of the Caliphate itself. And without Almanzor, you don’t see increasing numbers of Berber tribesmen relocated to Iberia, provoking ethnic strife.
items.model_answer:
If Almanzor had never risen to power in al-Andalus, the late Umayyad caliphate of Córdoba would probably have remained more stable in the short term, but it would still have faced serious structural problems. His rise concentrated power in his own hands, sidelined the caliph, strengthened the military at the expense of the old elite, and helped create the conditions that led to the caliphate’s collapse soon after his death. Without him, al-Andalus might have avoided that particularly destructive path.

Politically, the caliph Hisham II might have remained under the influence of a broader court elite rather than one dominant strongman. That could have preserved the authority and prestige of the caliphal institution for longer. Almanzor’s regime effectively hollowed out the caliphate by reducing the caliph to a figurehead while he ruled through patronage, intimidation, and military success. Without that precedent, the state may have retained more legitimacy and continuity.

Militarily, there would likely have been fewer spectacular raids against the northern Christian kingdoms. Almanzor’s campaigns brought him prestige and temporarily checked León, Castile, and other rivals, but they also tied the regime’s legitimacy to constant warfare and required heavy military mobilization. Without him, the frontier might have been less dramatic and perhaps more diplomatic, with truces, tribute, and limited warfare continuing rather than relentless major expeditions. The Christian kingdoms in the north may have had more room to consolidate earlier, though they would also have lacked the unifying effect of resisting Almanzor’s attacks.

Internally, one of the biggest differences would have been in the balance of power within al-Andalus. Almanzor relied heavily on Berber and Slav military elements and weakened traditional Arab-Andalusi elites. That intensified rivalries that later exploded into civil war, the fitna, after his family lost control. Without his personal dictatorship and reshaping of the army and administration, those tensions might have been less severe, making the breakup of the caliphate into taifa kingdoms less sudden or less complete.

Even so, it is unlikely that al-Andalus would have remained permanently strong just by removing Almanzor. The Umayyad state already faced deep issues: factionalism at court, ethnic and military divisions, succession weakness, and the difficulty of ruling a rich but politically fragmented realm. So the caliphate might still have declined, but perhaps more gradually and with less catastrophic internal violence.

In the longer term, that could have changed Iberian history in two opposite ways. A more stable Córdoba might have slowed the political fragmentation that benefited the Christian kingdoms, potentially delaying the taifa period and altering the pace of the Reconquista. On the other hand, without Almanzor’s devastating raids, the northern kingdoms might have strengthened earlier and with less disruption. The most plausible outcome is that al-Andalus would have been less militarily aggressive, more institutionally coherent for a time, and less likely to collapse so abruptly in the early eleventh century.

items.model_answer:
If Nixon had managed in 1972 to make the United States look like the definitive winner in Vietnam before his reelection, the biggest immediate effect would have been political: he would have entered his second term not just as the incumbent who won a landslide, but as the president who ended America’s most divisive war on favorable terms. That would have strengthened his authority at home, reduced some of the bitterness surrounding Vietnam, and likely reshaped both US politics and Cold War strategy for years.

To make this plausible, “definitive winner” would have to mean more than the Paris Peace Accords. It would likely mean that South Vietnam was clearly stabilized, North Vietnam had been forced to halt major offensives, American POWs were returned, and Washington could plausibly claim that Saigon would survive without renewed large-scale US intervention. If that had happened by late 1972, Nixon and Kissinger could have presented Vietnamization as a genuine success rather than a face-saving exit.

Domestically, Nixon’s reelection margin might not have been dramatically larger, since he already crushed McGovern, but his mandate would have looked even stronger and more substantive. The antiwar movement would have lost much of its force almost overnight. Many Americans who opposed the war did so because it seemed endless, unwinnable, and costly; a visible success would not have converted everyone, but it would have undercut the belief that the war had been a humiliating failure. Conservatives, Cold War hawks, and much of the political center would have argued that persistence had worked. That would have had major consequences for the national mood. The “Vietnam syndrome” that made later US interventions politically difficult might have been much weaker or delayed.

For Nixon personally, this could have had an important indirect effect on Watergate. A stronger, triumphant Nixon might have felt less paranoid and less obsessed with enemies, though his personality and governing style would still have made abuse of power likely. Watergate itself began before the 1972 election, so a Vietnam victory would not automatically prevent it. But the political fallout might have been different. A president seen as the man who won the Cold War’s hardest active conflict might have retained more elite and public support for longer. He still could have fallen if the evidence remained overwhelming, but the path to resignation might have been slower and more contested.

In Vietnam itself, the key question is whether the “victory” was real or only temporary. If South Vietnam had genuinely been made durable through larger military aid, harsher bombing, mining, destruction of North Vietnamese logistics, and stronger South Vietnamese governance, then the Republic of Vietnam might have survived for years, possibly indefinitely in something like a divided-Korea scenario. In that case Southeast Asia would have looked very different. Cambodia and Laos might still have remained unstable, but the symbolic communist sweep of Indochina in 1975 would not have happened in the same way. Refugee flows, reeducation camps, and the post-1975 trauma in Vietnam would have been reduced or postponed.

If, however, Nixon merely created the appearance of victory in 1972 while leaving South Vietnam fundamentally dependent and fragile, then the US would have claimed victory, withdrawn, and then faced a later collapse anyway. In that case the short-term political gain would have been real, but the long-term result might have been even more corrosive: Americans would feel they had been told they won, only to see Saigon fall later. That could have deepened distrust in government beyond what actually happened.

Internationally, a clear US success in Vietnam would have strengthened American credibility with allies. NATO governments, Asian allies like Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, and the Philippines, and anticommunist governments elsewhere would have taken from it the lesson that the US could bear costs and prevail. The Soviet Union and China would have had to reassess American resolve. This would not necessarily transform the overall Cold War balance, since détente, the Sino-Soviet split, and nuclear parity were shaped by larger forces, but it would have given Washington a stronger hand. US diplomacy with Moscow and Beijing might have proceeded from a position of greater confidence rather than from a desire to escape Vietnam.

A US “win” in Vietnam could also have changed later intervention debates. The reluctance to commit ground troops abroad in the late 1970s and early 1980s might have been weaker. American policymakers might have been more open to using force in the Third World, believing that counterinsurgency and limited war could succeed. That could have meant a more assertive US role in places like Angola, Central America, or even the Middle East. Whether that would be beneficial is less clear; success in Vietnam might have encouraged overconfidence and more interventions.

There would also be major historical and cultural consequences. Vietnam became in American memory the emblem of strategic failure, official deception, and the limits of US power. If Nixon had turned it into a recognizable success, the entire language of postwar American politics would shift. There might be no “lost in Vietnam” lesson in the same form, fewer films and books centered on defeat and moral breakdown, and less of the sharp divide between military service and public opinion that developed afterward.

So the most likely broad answer is this: if Nixon had made America the unmistakable winner in Vietnam before the 1972 election, he would have gained enormous prestige, the antiwar era would have ended differently, US global credibility would have risen, and the post-1975 sense of Vietnam as a national humiliation might never have fully formed. But everything would depend on whether the victory was structurally real. If South Vietnam endured, it would be one of the biggest Cold War turning points of the 1970s. If it was only a temporary illusion, then the later backlash could have been even harsher than in actual history.

items.question: What If NACA had significantly improved the P-38 early in World War II?
human_answers: "All told, these NACA modifications solve three of the biggest issues with the early combat performance of the P-38 with the 8th Air Force: Limited Dive, Engine Cooling/Reliability, and Cockpit heating. In addition, the lack of the radiator ducts in the booms reduces drag and would likely result in a better level-flight top-speed (I would expect a gain of 10-20 mph from this) and improved/decreased fuel consumption. This leaves only two big problems to solve with later models. The first of these remaining problems was that the Fuel Mixture, Propeller RPM, and Throttle controls were independent and never had an implemented solution in OTL. For those not familiar with what those are, it means that to change from a “Cruising” condition to a “Combat” condition, the pilot needed to adjust three different levers for each engine (a total of six adjustments): Move Fuel Mixture from Auto-Lean to Auto-Rich; Increase Propeller RPMs; Increase manifold pressure (throttle). I have read some anecdotal evidence* that Lockheed had developed an “automatic manifold pressure regulator” which automated all of these adjustments into a single lever per engine but that the Air Force deemed it “unnecessary” and never authorized its implementation (Allison, the engine manufacturer, implemented this system on the post-war “G” series V-1710 engines). Supposing, with the “big three” problems solved due to the NACA redesign early in the combat life of the airplane the 8th AF decided to keep the P-38’s in primary service longer it is reasonable, I think, to assume this modification would become “necessary” and it could be implemented by late 1943/early 1944 models of the airplane (OTL P-38J, but in ATL, probably be considered second or third block P-38H). The second remaining issue was that the ailerons became heavy at high speeds and the so the airplane’s roll rate was quite slow, limiting its use as a dog-fighter. In OTL this was fixed in June 1944 with the P-38J-25-LO which introduced hydraulically boosted ailerons. These exponentially increased the force on the ailerons when turning the yoke and allowed the P-38 to flick-roll faster than most other fighters of the time. I am not certain how much more quickly these would be introduced in ATL vs. OTL as the slow-roll performance wouldn’t be altered by the NACA modifications nor was its solution delayed or prevented by AF brass. So, let’s say that this modification is introduced as it was in OTL, i.e. June 1944. Finally, with the 8th AF decision to keep the P-38 as the primary long-range escort fighter I believe it is reasonable to presume that they would have dedicated more time and resources to addressing the basic and tactical training for the pilots that was largely ignored in OTL, possibly even to the extant to sharing information with the P-38 FGs in the PTO—although that is uncertain. The result is, that when the 55th FG is transferred to the 8th AF with P-38H’s in September 1943 they have an aircraft capable of escorting bombers, at high-altitude, comfortably, reliably, and with significantly improved performance over most Axis fighters. This would reduce the demand for P-51’s and while I still expect them to come in theatre I would expect the P-38 Fighter Groups to keep the P-38’s rather than switching to P-47’s and P-51’s resulting in a near even three-way split between the fighter types by war’s end. I don’t know that this would have any significant impact on the eventual course or outcome of the war but improved long-range escort earlier in the war could have had a large positive impact on bomber-loss rates and morale. The reduction in bomber-losses in turn could mean a faster buildup of US Bomber forces and an earlier launch of major 1000+ raids perhaps even increasing the time-table for the Normandy Invasion, although other logistical problems likely lock that in no earlier than May ’44. The biggest difference would be in the reception and memory of the P-38 and its potential for a continued career post-war, similar to the P-51. The possibility of keeping them in service longer could also lead to the late-war approval for the adoption of the P-38K-1 with the F15 (Allison V-1710-75/77) engines and Hamilton-Standard Hydromatic high-activity propellers. In OTL only one of these was made using the large P-38J style chin and retaining the high-drag boom radiators. Even with all that drag it was able to achieve 432mph in level flight using Military Power and was expected to make 450mph with War Emergency Power with matching improvements in range and fuel consumption (about 10%). It also had a ceiling of 46,000 feet, a max climb of 4,800 ft/minute and could make it to 20,000 feet in only five minutes. Without the full coat of pain and with the reduced drag of the NACA design modification I can only image what its performance could be. In this case the P-38K would likely replace the F/P-82 Twin-Mustang of OTL and see continued service into the early 1950’s including limited combat in Korea as bomber-escorts and Close Air Support. So, any thoughts on this, its feasibility, and any effects I may have missed?" ----------------------- * http://www.ausairpower.net/P-38-Analysis.html (Pertinent section about 45% down in the italicized letter from Col. Harold J. Rau to “Commanding General, VIII Fighter Command, APO 637, U.S. Army”)[/QUOTE] Thank-you, I wasn't aware that this investigation into the P-38 compressibility problem had been conducted. It would have been a very productive and effective modification and I'm inclined to agree if the NACA mod had been developed earlier then it would have made it into production. After Pearl Harbor the pressure to produce what ever was available delayed OTL improvements to the P-38 like for example the high-activity propellers as you mentioned. I haven't finished reading the 1942 document yet so I have some questions for you. After the NACA mod had been developed the engineers still thought that dive recovery flaps would be required? Also with the relocation of the Prestone radiators and oil coolers to the new leading edge did the designers consider the Meredith effect when designing the new installation? Making the assumption they were aware of it at the time. The P-38's OTL canopy was one of its' poorer features. If they were redesigning the canopy contours could that also mean replacing it with a bubble type sliding canopy?

1) There is no explicit mention of the Dive Recovery Flaps in the NACA report, however the information about the airflow under the wing at different flap possitions is what ultimately led to their development so it is possible that they could have still been developed although they would have been by no means neccesary (assuming the NACA estimates are accurate). 2) I haven't read any specific refereces to it but it is possible they were aware of the Meredith effect. However, if memory serves, the radiator installations in the P-38 were not well suited or designed for it producing more drag than thrust. The NACA installation would likely also be poor canidatea for Meredith thrust so it is likely a dead end for the sake of this exploration. 3) Indeed the canopy was junk. While it never happened OTL I may explore better canopy options in the ATL. I think this is likely the direction I would go anyway. Some narrative, some ATL technical evaluation reports, maybe even some Encounter Reports when the shooting starts. Yeah, several of the British twin wing designs could be good but are beyond the scope of the PoD and this ATL. The issue with the dive flaps was that the first shipment in a C-54 was shot down by the British and they never bothered sending replacements. Then they didn't want to slow down production to integrate them into the line until all the planned blocks werw complete which meant they weren't factory installed until the P-38J-25 starting June 6, 1944...what a day! And yes, the treatment of the P-38 in the 8th AF was criminal because their disdain led directly to lost aircrew. Edit: sorry for all the typoes...I am on my phone instead computer at the moment.

As a lover of the P-38, a believer in its unrealized superior potential, a person saddened that it was not properly appreciated and thus its potential to escort early US bomber raids and save the lives of countless bomber crew members (not to mention recovering and reusing their OTL shot-down planes)--let me play a bit of Devil's Advocate here. I've seen some of the online wars between P-38 fans and their detractors, and come away more convinced by the former, especially after this most informative OP! But one simple point the naysayers have is clearly true...P-38 was a two-engine plane, while its eventual successor (if we assume the -38 were improved and permitted to do the escort mission) the P-51 was single engine. Thus Lightnings were inherently more costly than any single engine plane, good, bad or mediocre. If the choice was between an excellent two engine job and terrible to mediocre single engine, we just pay the higher price as part of the necessary cost of doing business with the best--except that in Jan 1942, the USAAF needed aircraft in numbers, and soon. If single engine alternatives existed that would be cost-effective, then clearly the Army would prefer that. I don't mean to mention this as some sort of trump card killing the -38's prospects, just as pointing out a factor that was relevant in decision making. The fact is I believe the P-38 was originally authorized under the impression it would be a superstar, just as the B-17 was hoped to be a super bomber the P-38 was to be the star fighter. But that was when war was hypothetical; once it started a panic for sheer numbers set in, and the question of whether one P-38 was worth 2 of another type--or less than 2, or more--was not transparent. One big advantage the P-38 offered, especially if it had indeed been modified to remove its worst drawbacks, and more appreciated hence ordered in more numbers, is that though it used twin engines, those engines were not Merlins! Not to say anything was wrong with Merlins, quite the contrary--though I do seem to recall some comparisons over ranges of altitude wherein the Allison engines, due to being turbosupercharged, had superior perfomance, while the Merlins had a mechanical supercharger. But the point here is, Merlins were good--but in severe demand therefore, so it was most excellent that the Lightning did not require them. I particularly like the way the twin engine layout leaves the central command nacelle to be loaded with heavy and reconfigurable arms.

TTL, it seems likely the dive-recovery spoiler (even assuming it takes OTL's duration to find the answer, which seems less probable; IMO, it'd be quicker TTL) would be on a different C-54, so not shot down. (Might be soon enough to get to production directly, in the *P-38E or -F TTL.) Other improvements? Turbos are hard, but without new materials, there's still reducing the rotating mass (drill the blades, so they look a bit like Swiss cheese), & (possibly) sizing issues (boost lag). Direct improvements to the aircraft itself? Cockpit heat is a must. Adding the wing leading-edge fuel tanks sooner would be good, but TTL, better fuel economy might butterfly them away... Flipside, tho: more P-38s means more headaches, with pilots who don't like twins & aren't trained in them correctly getting themselves in trouble. There was a myth going around England: if a P-38 lost an engine on takeoff, it'd kill you. It would--because the pilots weren't trained how to recover. Tony LeVier showed 'em: kill one engine, boot the rudder hard over against the dead one, crank on full power to the other & climb out to go around...

The 1944 Report clarifies some things I'd heard elsewhere. Thanks for that. All I have for the 1940-41 period is Dolittles commentary, but since he had worked some years as a aircraft engineer for a fuel manufactor his account has some small weight. The short version is through the 1930s commercially available gasoline fuels had a very low octane rating by post WWII standards. 65 Octane is the number I recall. Dolittle & his peers were trying to persuade the corporate suits to develop and market higher octane fuels, up into the 80 & possiblly 90 octane range. The refusal was based on the lack of market since the engine manufactors provided nothing that could use such fuels. To complete the circle the motors that could use high octane fuel were not built because the fuels were not being made. Dolittle did make clear that custom built engines were common for fuels in the 70 to 90 and higher octane ranges. Additives and custom fuel mixes were available in small batches to those who could pay. Dolittle like other knowledgeable pilots carried a witches brew of additives in his aircraft for boosting the commercial fuels of the aircraft he used. Later in 1940-41 Dolittle observed the same problem in plotting the development of the Army Air Corps engines beyond 41. At one point the head of the Quartermasters Corps informed the Air Corps that only 65 octane fuel would be provided across the board to simplify logisitcs. Fortunately the reorganization of early 1942 gave the Army Air force control of its own material supply & development went ahead.
