I know there have been several discussions over the years surrounding the Lockheed P-38 American Twin-Engine fighter/interceptor of WWII but one part of the equation that I have never heard discussed is the “What If…” the NACA recommended modifications to the airplane had been implemented, especially at or near the beginning of P-38 operations. OTL Background : Without re-hashing the origin and initial development history of the Lockheed Model 22 / P-38 (all of that information is readily available on numerous on-line sources) I will focus on what led to the NACA studies of the airframe, their proposed solution to the problems encountered, and why these solutions weren’t put in place. A record-breaking cross-country flight in early 1939 (which resulted in the loss of the only XP-38) garnered enough attention and excitement that the US Army Air Corp (USAAC) placed orders for pre-production (YP-38) and production (P-38) aircraft in numbers greater than Lockheed had anticipated for the entire Model 22 life. This necessitated a rushed production development and major reconfiguration to accommodate the unintended mass-production. Tests in early 1941 of the first pre-production YP-38’s quickly ran into issues when at high speed (around Mach 0.68), especially in dive, where the nose of the aircraft would drop--locking into an often un-recoverable dive accompanied by “buffeting.” The problems getting the production line up and fully operational prevented Lockheed from directing any engineering resources to these problems until November 1941, but they were unable to identify the cause or provide any solutions until Gen. Hap Arnold, head of the by then renamed Army Air Forces (USAAF), ordered the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA—predecessor of NASA) to analyze the YP-38 in their full-scale wind-tunnel in December 1941 – January 1942 which resulted in the report “ Full-Scale Wind-Tunnel Investigation of Buffeting and Diving Tendencies of the YP-38 Airplane .” [EDIT: NASA reorganized its online archives in 2020 so this link is no longer functioning. The upload size limitations on this site prevent me from dropping the file here, but you can find a copy I uploaded at another site, Here ] This report was finally able to identify that the control lock and diving difficulties were the result of a high-speed pressure wake developing over the wing and fuselage resulting is loss of lift to the central wing and buffeting of the tail as the turbulent wake passes over it, a phenomenon just recently discovered at the time which led the idea of the “sound barrier.” This is often referred to a “Compressibility” problem as it related the change of aerodynamics at high speed from a traditional non-compressible fluid to a compressible one. The specific behavior of the P-38 is now better known as “Mach Tuck.” NACA tested several solutions to the problem including wing filleting, partial flap deployment, three different inboard (between the engine booms and the center gondola) wing designs, two revised canopy designs, and an extension to the trailing edge of the gondola. They found the best performance gain (delay of up to 64 mph in the formation of the shock-wave) resulted from a simple 0.2c (20% of chord) leading edge extension to the center wing section and using their second canopy revision. They also noted that although the gondola extension did not increase the Critical Mach number, it did reduce the turbulence of the wake re-joining the airstream and smoothed out the air flow over the tail surfaces. One aspect which I find very interesting with these design modifications was that the extended leading edge moved the center of lift forward causing the plane to become unbalanced. They recommended moving the coolant radiators from the mid-boom into the extended leading edge of the wing to rebalance the aircraft with the added benefit of reducing drag and further streamlining the aircraft. I will address this again in the ATL discussion to follow. The problem is that the report wasn’t completed until March 31, 1942, by which time the US was at war and Lockheed was ramping up to start production on the combat-ready P-38F (beginning in April 1942) at war-time production rates. With the P-38 the most capable fighter then in inventory there simply was not the opportunity to re-design and re-tool for the modifications NACA recommended and the P-38 was sent into combat while still suffering numerous problems, not least of which was the issues with compressibility. The results are well known and documented: the P-38 in the ETO struggled the first 18 months of combat prompting 8th Fighter Command to pre-emptively phase them out in favor of the new P-51 as they became available at the end of 1943 and through the first half of 1944 which prevented Lockheed and the USAAF from implementing a number of fixes for the problems and delayed others until it was too late to have much impact in the reputation of the P-38 in Europe. It was not until the P-38J-25-LO and P-38L-5-LO/VN the airplane really came into its own and that was realized almost entirely in the Pacific. Arnold did not wait for Lockheed to tackle the dive issues first and instead ordered the NACA study to take place in June-July of 1941 with the final report completed September 30, 1941 (six months earlier than OTL). This updated timeline would allow Lockheed engineers to immediately go to work implementing the NACA design changes in fall 1941 prior to US entry into the War and the corresponding production pressures which prevented it from happening in OTL. The first production P-38’s with the NACA modifications would then roll out either as late block P-38E’s in early ’42 or, more likely, as the finalized P-38F in April 1942. OTL, the P-38F/G/H continued to use the enclosed intercooler in the leading edge of the outboard wings, which provided adequate cooling for the early model engines and low-boost ratings but which, by the P-38G and even more so the P-38H, limited engine power to lower settings due to in-adequate cooling. This was a problem that was not anticipated so it wasn’t until the P-38J in August 1943 that the intercoolers were switched to the core-type, chin-mounted position—squeezed between and behind the oil radiators. However, in my ATL, with the oil radiators moved adjacent the coolant radiators in the leading edge extension the space in the chin of the nacelles is completely freed up which allows the core-type intercoolers to be installed in the space previously occupied by the oil radiators as soon as it becomes apparent it is needed without re-designing the nacelles themselves. This means that the engine power limitations of the G either never occurs (because the intercoolers have already been moved) or are quickly overcome by sending field modification kits in early 1943 with full integration on the assembly line taking place with the P-38H in the spring of 1943. Additionally, moving the intercoolers in these earlier models (G or H) would allow a matching earlier installation of the leading edge fuel tanks in the outer wings, increasing the range and combat radius in 1943 sufficient to provide full escort coverage to 8th AF Bombers even to deep penetration targets. Another advantage of moving the Prestone (engine coolant) radiators to the inboard position in the extended leading edge is that the heated coolant can be run through a heater core close to the cockpit cupola, increasing available cockpit heat as soon as it becomes apparent the existing heat is insufficient for high-altitude or cold weather operations. Again, this is something I expect would be utilized no later than early-mid 1943. One final advantage of this layout is that frees up a large amount of space in the tail booms which could be utilized in later production models. With engine weight increases in the F/G and again in the H/J models the Center of Gravity could potentially have been moved forward enough to justify installation of either additional small fuel tanks in the booms where the radiators used to be, or—perhaps a better option—small water/alcohol tanks which would permit the use the Water Injection under War Emergency Power, further increasing performances and reducing the risks of detonation under high manifold pressure (> 60 in/Hg). Even if pushing the ’51 to Mach 0.8 or beyond is considered acceptable these NACA estimates for the modified ’38 show a similar diving capability considering a margin for error of the conservative estimate, especially if using Dive Recovery Flaps in addition to the NACA modifications. In these cases the P-38 would be favorable because it can accelerate to max speed faster than the P-51 allowing to either pull-away faster or to gain faster on a diving E/A. Combine that with the faster climb of the P-38, higher peak turning rate, and—in later airplanes—faster roll, there would be nothing that the P-51 could do that the P-38 couldn’t do better. items.model_answer:
If NACA had significantly improved the P-38 early in World War II, the biggest likely effect is that the aircraft would have become a far more consistently successful long-range fighter much earlier, especially in Europe. The P-38 was already fast, heavily armed, and had excellent range, but it suffered from important problems in compressibility dives, high-altitude handling, cockpit heating, engine management complexity, and reliability in cold European conditions. If NACA had solved a substantial share of those issues early, the aircraft’s combat record and strategic role could have changed a lot.

In the short term, the USAAF would probably have had a better escort fighter before the P-51 fully matured into that role. That matters because one of the central air-war problems in 1943 was getting bombers deep into enemy territory with fighter protection. A better early-war P-38 would likely have reduced bomber losses on some long-range missions and improved the performance of escort units over Western Europe. It would not automatically replace the P-51, since the Mustang still had major advantages in simplicity, cost-effectiveness, and high-altitude efficiency, but it could have narrowed the gap enough that the P-38 remained a first-rank escort fighter in Europe rather than becoming more marginal there.

In the Mediterranean and Pacific, the effects might have been even stronger. The P-38 was already highly valuable in those theaters because its range was crucial. A significantly improved version entering service earlier would likely have increased Allied air superiority sooner, improved interception capability over long distances, and made reconnaissance, ground attack, and anti-shipping missions more effective. In the Pacific especially, where distances were enormous and twin-engine range mattered greatly, an earlier-optimized P-38 could have increased pressure on Japanese air and naval operations and perhaps accelerated Allied control of key areas. American aces and long-range units there might have become even more effective.

There could also have been industrial and doctrinal consequences. If the P-38 had performed better earlier, the USAAF might have invested more heavily in refining and producing it rather than shifting emphasis so decisively toward the P-51 for European escort work. Training pipelines would also have adapted: pilots and mechanics might have become more proficient with twin-engine fighter operations sooner, reducing operational losses caused by complexity. The aircraft’s reputation, which was mixed in Europe and much better elsewhere, would likely have improved across the board.

Still, the change should not be exaggerated. Even a much-improved P-38 would not by itself transform the war. Allied victory depended on production scale, pilot training, radar, logistics, intelligence, and overwhelming industrial power. The P-51, P-47, and other aircraft would still matter enormously. Also, “significantly improved” could mean different things: if NACA only fixed aerodynamic issues like compressibility, the impact would be meaningful but limited; if it also solved engine reliability, cockpit environment, and maintenance complexity, then the effect could be substantially larger.

So the most plausible answer is that an early, significantly improved P-38 would have given the Allies a better long-range fighter sooner, especially improving bomber escort in Europe and strengthening already successful operations in the Mediterranean and Pacific. It probably would have raised Allied effectiveness and reduced some losses, but it would not have radically changed the ultimate outcome of the war.

items.question: What If The Enterprise completes its five year mission (Star Trek survives for 5 seasons)
human_answers: The problem with keeping "TOS" on the air is its consistently poor ratings. In third season, it never got out of the bottom 50 (&, IIRC, was #52 when cancelled). NBC recognizing the better demos early enough might save it in spite of that, much the same way golf gets broadcast despite poor numbers: it attracts a desirable audience. They had two great opportunities to set up a continuing villain, undermined (I suspect) by inability to cast the same actor each time: "Tribbles" & "Day of the Dove". It would have taken more forethought about what Klingons would be like to achieve it, but I'd have loved "DotD" to end with Kirk saying, "Die well, Kang.", & a surprised Kang to say, "Die well, Kirk."--in essence, to be forced to acknowledge UFP as peers. (I know, I know, they didn't even have the concept for the bat'leth , yet...) Depressingly, the writing would have to get a lot better. Even if you take out "Spock's Brain", you've already been saddled with "Errand of Mercy" (the Organian Treaty) in S.1 & "Omega Glory" in S.2. About half of S.3 is pretty awful. Even Dorothy's "Enterprise Incident" has a major flaw, one that would recur for the rest of the franchise: doesn't Starfleet Intelligence have it's own f*ng operatives? You've also got two big issues: personality conflict between Shat's ego & just about everybody, & Leonard being really sick of playing Spock. That said, I'll be watching to see how you save the show, & what butterflies that has down the road.

NBC CONDUCTS STUDY ON TREK: NIELSEN RATINGS NOT FULLY ACCURATE? NBC is unsure of how to handle Star Trek, the big hit with younger American television viewers but a ratings laggard with the general public. The network conducted a study to determine exactly what it has with the science fiction series and its findings were surprising. They determined that younger Americans often watched Star Trek in groups, and it was one of the most popular shows among the age 20-30 and age 30-40 brackets. They also determined that Captain Kirk, Mr. Spock, and the rest of the characters were extremely popular with young kids, who often wanted to stay up past their bedtimes on Friday night to see where they and the Enterprise would go next. However, NBC found a significant decline in popularity among viewers older than 50. NBC contacted Gene Roddenberry, the show's creator, Herb Solow, the showrunner at Paramount, who recently acquired Desilu Studios, and Robert Justman, one of the show's producers, for a planning session to widen the show's popularity for a general audience. Roddenberry objected to NBC's proposal to make Star Trek a show with a more pragmatic, less optimistic future. He also objected to the idea that the show had to appeal to older audiences, arguing that the strength of the show was rooted in the creative storytelling that attracted younger adults and children. Solow and Justman also disagreed to an extent but determined that parts of the show had to be remodeled in order to make it a wider hit. Ideas for the third season were pitched to the network; one was rumored to involve Mr. Spock's brain being removed from his body, while another was rumored to have the Enterprise enter Romulan space unprovoked in order to spy on them, a major diversion from the normal behavior of the Enterprise crew.

If Star Trek: The Original Series had survived long enough for the Enterprise to actually complete its five-year mission on television, the most important change is that Star Trek probably would have become a mainstream success much earlier, and the whole franchise would have developed in a smoother, less improvised way.

In the real timeline, the original series was cancelled after three seasons, and a lot of what made Star Trek into a giant cultural force came later through syndication, fan activism, the animated series, and then the films. If it had run for five full seasons, NBC and the studio would have had much stronger proof that the show could sustain an audience. That likely means Star Trek would not have been remembered first as a “cancelled cult classic,” but as a successful network science-fiction drama that completed its intended arc.

Creatively, two extra seasons would probably have changed the internal identity of Star Trek. The show would have had more time to deepen Kirk, Spock, McCoy, and the broader crew, and to revisit worlds, enemies, and political ideas that in reality were left underdeveloped. The Federation, Starfleet, and the Klingons in particular might have been defined more clearly much earlier. The sense of a genuine long voyage through space would also have landed more fully; as aired, the “five-year mission” is iconic, but it was never actually completed on screen. Finishing it would have given the series a stronger narrative closure.

That said, there is an important complication: by the third season the budget was strained, morale was down, and network support had weakened. So a fourth and fifth season are not automatically better seasons. If the show simply limped on under the same conditions, it could have produced more uneven episodes and damaged its reputation. For this counterfactual to really matter, the show would need either better scheduling, better funding, or at least more stable production. If that happened, the extra years could have been some of the most important in establishing the franchise’s canon and tone.

The later history of Star Trek would likely change a lot. The animated series might never happen, or would happen differently, because there would be less need to “revive” a recently cancelled property. The first wave of fandom might still grow, but it would be less centered on saving a lost show and more around extending a successful one. Star Trek conventions and fan culture would still exist, but perhaps with a slightly less oppositional, grassroots identity. The famous story of fans rescuing Star Trek from cancellation is one of the foundations of modern fandom; if the show lasts five seasons, that myth is weaker.

The movies would also probably be different. In our timeline, Star Trek: Phase II was conceived in the 1970s as a return to television, then became Star Trek: The Motion Picture after Star Wars changed Hollywood’s view of science fiction. If TOS had already completed a respected five-season run, Paramount might have moved earlier either toward a sequel series or toward feature films with more confidence. The franchise might have reached the big screen sooner, or with a different cast balance and tone. It is even possible that some ideas later used in The Next Generation or the films would have been used up in seasons four and five of the original show.

There is also a broader television-history effect. A five-season Star Trek would likely have strengthened the position of serious science fiction on American television in the early 1970s. Networks might have been a little more willing to back ambitious speculative shows, especially ones mixing adventure with social commentary. Star Trek was already influential, but a longer original run would have made that influence more immediate and institutional rather than delayed and retrospective.

At the level of franchise mythology, completing the mission would have changed how people think about the Enterprise crew. Kirk’s era might feel more complete and self-contained, more like a finished chapter than a brilliant fragment that later generations kept expanding. The original cast might become even more dominant in the public imagination, which could have made it slightly harder for later incarnations like The Next Generation to step out from their shadow. In our timeline, TNG benefited from there being a gap and a sense that Star Trek was bigger than one cancelled 1960s show. A fuller, more definitive five-season TOS might have made succession trickier.

So the short answer is: if the Enterprise had completed its five-year mission on TV, Star Trek probably becomes more successful sooner, more narratively complete, and more clearly defined in its original form. But it might also lose some of the underdog, fan-saved quality that became central to its legend. Ironically, part of Star Trek’s power in real history came from the fact that it did not finish cleanly; it had to be rediscovered, defended, and rebuilt. A five-season run would likely make it stronger as a 1960s-70s television success, but possibly a little less mythic as a cultural comeback story.

AHC: Complicate the US Civil War

Some time ago, somewhere, I stumbled upon some talk about the US Civil War - and of course, the good ol' debate what it was all about appeared - states rights, whatnot; but then, a single person rugged the whole debate with an argument that went something along these lines: The American Civil War was about states' rights, but not their rights to slavery - instead, it was about the states' rights to secede. This I found to be, pretty much, the final word on that whole argument - sure, slavery was the cause of the Civil War - but in the same manner tensions between Great Powers were the cause of WW1. Whereas the World War was triggered by the assassination of Franz Ferdinand, essentially making the war about it in the first place - the Civil War wasn't started by slavery merely existing or not existing, but instead by the Southern states seceding, making the entire war about secession in the first place. This also tracks with the fact that several states only seceded after the start of the war (such as Arkansas), after President Lincoln ordered all states to mobilize troops. Now, with that in mind, I have a challenge for the esteemed posters of this venerable Forum: without changing the cause, nor the trigger for the war (it has to be over slavery, and it must be triggered by secession), complicate the sides of the war. For example, a free state siding with the Confederacy counts as a complication, and so does a slave state siding with the Union. Note that the latter already happened, in the form of Delaware and Maryland - now let's be clear, I'm not talking about this being a "make Maryland secede" challenge: the weirder the pick, the better - I'm talking Confederate Michigan and Union Mississippi tier. You may, however, shift when the war occurs. Good luck, and happy imagining!
items.model_answer:
If the U.S. Civil War had been “complicated” further, the most important question is: complicated in what way? The war was already driven by slavery, secession, constitutional conflict, economics, regional identity, and military strategy. But several additional factors could have made it much longer, bloodier, and more politically unstable.

The biggest complication would have been foreign intervention. If Britain or France had formally recognized the Confederacy, or even pressured the Union strongly enough, the South might have gained diplomatic legitimacy, loans, naval assistance, or trade protection. That would not necessarily have guaranteed Confederate independence, but it could have prolonged the war and made Union victory much harder. European powers were cautious, though, especially after the Emancipation Proclamation turned the conflict more clearly into a war against slavery, which made open support for the Confederacy politically dangerous.

Another major complication would have been broader internal division within the North. The Union was not politically unified. There were Democrats who opposed the war, feared federal power, or resisted emancipation. If antiwar sentiment had grown stronger—because of casualties, economic strain, or military defeats—Lincoln might have faced overwhelming pressure to negotiate peace. In that case, the Union could have fractured politically even if it remained stronger militarily.

The border states were also crucial. If states like Kentucky or Missouri had fully joined the Confederacy, the strategic map would have changed dramatically. These states were important for rivers, railroads, manpower, and geography. Their loss would have made it harder for the Union to invade the South and easier for the Confederacy to defend itself. Likewise, if Maryland had seceded, Washington, D.C. would have been nearly surrounded, creating a severe political and military crisis.

Complication could also have come from slave uprisings or larger-scale guerrilla warfare. Enslaved people already resisted in many ways and fled to Union lines, undermining the Southern economy and war effort. If resistance had become more coordinated and violent on a large scale, the Confederacy would have been forced to divert more manpower internally. On the other hand, irregular warfare across the border regions—as happened in places like Missouri—could have spread more widely and made the war even more chaotic and harder to end.

A weaker Union military leadership early in the war could have complicated things too. The North had more resources, but poor coordination and hesitant generals repeatedly delayed victory. If the Union had suffered more major defeats, or if Confederate leaders had translated battlefield success into diplomatic recognition or Northern political collapse, the outcome could have become uncertain. The Civil War was not inevitable in its exact result; Union victory depended on sustaining military pressure and political will over time.

Finally, Reconstruction shows how the war remained complicated even after the battlefield conflict ended. Even with Union victory, the country did not smoothly resolve the issues beneath the war. Racial inequality, white supremacist violence, sectional resentment, and disputes over federal authority continued for decades. So if the war itself had been further complicated—through foreign intervention, deeper Northern division, border-state secession, or prolonged guerrilla conflict—the aftermath would likely have been even more unstable, perhaps leaving the United States permanently divided or producing a much weaker postwar union.

So the short answer is that additional complications would likely have made the Civil War longer, more international, more politically fragile, and potentially less likely to end in a clear Union victory.

If the British–Russian alliance were broken, the effects would depend on which historical moment you mean, but in general it would have destabilized the balance of power in Europe and Asia and likely changed both diplomacy and war planning in major ways.

If we are thinking about the early 20th century, especially the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 and the broader alignment that fed into the Triple Entente, breaking that relationship would have weakened the anti-German bloc. Britain, France, and Russia were not a formal single alliance in the same way as the Triple Alliance, but their cooperation mattered enormously. Without British–Russian understanding, Germany and Austria-Hungary would have faced a less coordinated opposition. Russia might have been more isolated diplomatically, Britain might have hesitated to support continental commitments, and France would have lost part of the strategic advantage of encircling Germany with allies on both east and west.

That could have altered the path to World War I in several ways. It might have reduced immediate tensions in some imperial regions, since Britain and Russia had long competed in Central Asia and Persia. But it also could have made crises in Europe more dangerous by increasing uncertainty. Germany might have felt freer to pressure France or Russia if it believed Britain and Russia were divided. Alternatively, Britain, fearing Russian expansion without any agreement in place, might have focused more on imperial defense than on European commitments. In that case, the formation of the wartime coalition against the Central Powers would have been slower, weaker, or less certain.

In Asia and the Middle East, a broken British–Russian relationship would likely have revived the “Great Game.” Competition over Afghanistan, Persia, Tibet, and routes toward India would have intensified. Britain’s main fear was Russian movement toward India; Russia’s goal was influence and security along its southern frontier. Without cooperation, both empires would probably have increased military and diplomatic rivalry in those buffer zones. That could have led to proxy conflicts, stronger local resistance movements being courted by one side or the other, and greater instability in Persia and Afghanistan.

Economically and politically, a break would also have encouraged each side to seek new partners. Britain might have leaned more heavily on Japan, the Ottoman Empire, or even sought some accommodation with Germany under certain conditions. Russia might have moved closer to France alone, or tried to repair ties with Germany if possible. Such a realignment could have reshaped alliance systems across Eurasia.

If the alliance broke during World War I itself, the consequences would have been even more dramatic. Britain depended on Russia to tie down German and Austro-Hungarian forces in the east, while Russia benefited from British finance, supplies, and naval pressure on Germany. A rupture would have relieved pressure on Germany, potentially allowed greater concentration of German force on the Western Front, and weakened the Allies’ overall strategic position. It might have shortened the war or changed its outcome.

So, in the broadest sense, breaking the British–Russian alliance would probably have produced more rivalry in Asia, more uncertainty in Europe, and a weaker counterweight to Germany and Austria-Hungary. Rather than creating a stable peace, it would most likely have made the international system less predictable and more dangerous.

Most likely, the Dutch army will retreat behind the New Dutch Waterline ( Nieuwe Hollandse Waterlinie ). The fortresses are already obsolete, AFAIK. However, the inundation zones may still be an impassable obstacle.... Most obvious POD is that Molkte decides against a coup de main on Liege, but instead decides to bypass Liege to the north. This is consistent with Schlieffen's original "Schlieffen plan". The German army moves roughly between Maastricht and Roermond on its way to northern France.... Assuming that France is not defeated in this ATL either, will attention shift north? Will Germany want to occupy all of the Netherlands? Will the waterline hold? What does it mean for Germany's chances in WW1? It is also fine to discuss other POD's in which the Netherlands is invaded. The Dutch defenses are shown on this map I made:
items.model_answer:
If Germany had invaded the Netherlands in World War I, the effects would likely have been significant both militarily and politically, though probably not enough by themselves to change the ultimate outcome of the war in Germany’s favor.

The most immediate reason Germany might have invaded would have been strategic convenience. In 1914, the Schlieffen-style war planning depended on sweeping through Belgium to outflank French defenses. The Netherlands, especially the southern region around Maastricht and the lower Rhine, could have offered additional routes for troop movement and logistics. Invading it might have made German operations in the west somewhat easier in the opening weeks, at least on paper.

But the costs would have been serious. Dutch neutrality had important value to Germany. As long as the Netherlands stayed neutral, it remained a channel for trade, finance, intelligence, and access to overseas goods despite the British blockade. Rotterdam in particular functioned as a vital economic gateway. If Germany invaded, that neutral outlet would disappear. Britain would almost certainly have tightened its naval and economic pressure even further, and the Dutch colonial empire, especially the Dutch East Indies, would be exposed to Allied seizure or isolation. Germany would gain territory in Europe but lose an important indirect economic lifeline.

An invasion would also have widened the diplomatic shock caused by the attack on Belgium. Britain had already entered the war over Belgium’s neutrality and the broader balance of power. Violating Dutch neutrality too would reinforce the image of Germany as openly disregarding international law. That would strengthen Allied propaganda, make neutral opinion more hostile to Germany, and possibly push fence-sitting countries further toward the Entente sooner.

Militarily, the Dutch army was smaller than the Belgian one and the country might have been overrun relatively quickly in many areas. However, the Netherlands was not easy terrain for large-scale operations. Waterlines, rivers, dikes, and the possibility of deliberate flooding made parts of the country defensible. Even if Germany occupied much of it, that would require troops, occupation forces, and supply commitments at a moment when speed was essential. Any delay in the opening campaign could undermine the very advantage Germany hoped to gain.

There is also the British angle. A German presence on the Dutch coast would alarm Britain greatly. Control, or attempted control, of ports facing the North Sea could be seen as an even greater threat to British security than Germany’s move through Belgium alone. Britain would almost certainly commit to preventing Germany from benefiting from Dutch ports and coastline. The Royal Navy could blockade and attack aggressively, and Britain might support Dutch resistance or seize Dutch colonial possessions.

For the Netherlands itself, the consequences would be severe. Instead of remaining outside the direct fighting while mobilized and economically strained, it would become a battlefield and occupied zone. Civilian hardship, destruction of infrastructure, refugee movements, food shortages, and possibly flooding from defensive measures would all become much worse. Dutch politics after the war would also be transformed, likely with stronger anti-German feeling and deeper domestic trauma.

In terms of the larger war, the most plausible outcome is that Germany gains some short-term operational flexibility in 1914 but pays a larger long-term strategic price. It would lose the benefits of Dutch neutrality, intensify British hostility, and burden itself with another occupied country. So the likely result is not a German victory, but a slightly broader and even more economically damaging war for Germany, while making the Netherlands suffer far more than it did historically.

items.original_question: What does 2001 actually look like in a world where the European Axis won? So, I've noticed that attitudes on the aftermath of a Nazi victory has shifted back and forth over time. Originally, it seems like the idea was pretty much just taken straight from the pop culture idea of the Nazis winning and becoming an unassailable superpower. Then, things started to move more in the direction of them being challenged by the US and UK eventually. Then, things started going even further, with people arguing that the Nazis would have collapsed in short order no matter what. Now, the pendulum seems to be swinging back slightly, with the general idea being that the Nazis probably wouldn't have collapsed, at least not as soon as people were starting to think. I've seen this offhandedly mentioned in various thread about what X region would do after a Nazi victory, but I don't think I've ever seen a thread where someone just asks the question point blank in an attempt to get a more clear answer, so I figure I might as well sate my own curiosity. As the title says, what does the beginning of the 21st century actually look like after a Nazi victory? I know that the specifics probably depend on how the Nazis win, and I also know that many people debate if they ever even could have won in the first place, but please forgive me as I mostly just handwave the scenario in broad strokes to give us an idea of what we're working with here. Basically, by 1950: 1. The Germans and Italians are completely victorious in Europe. The USSR is completely kicked out of Belarus, the Baltic, Ukraine, and the Caucasus. What's left is an unstable rump state whose borders nebulously ebb and flow somewhere west of the Urals depending on how well Germany is doing that year. 2. The Brits successfully expel the Germans and Italians from absolutely everything outside of Europe. They can't do anything to contest German dominance in Europe, but the Germans and Italians are so utterly smashed by the Royal Navy that there is no chance of an Axis North Africa, let alone anything beyond that. Likewise, the Middle East is Axis-free 3. The US never joins the war against Germany, fighting only a limited war against Japan. Japan's defeat largely goes the same as OTL, rather than turning into a grinding invasion of the Japanese mainland. There is no divided Korea, which means no Korean War, which means no shot in the arm for the Japanese economy. Still, Japan's overall economic future looks quite bright nonetheless. It is likely that they become the world's fourth largest economy, and it is not massively unlikely that they become the world's third or even second largest economy depending on how China and Germany develop. 4. Again, Korea is united under a single capitalist state. It's corrupt and authoritarian, but generally not so much so as KMT China. The lack of devastation from the Korean War helps immensely. Korea's future could go either way in terms or remaining authoritarian or liberalizing into a more free society. 5. KMT China survives without Manchuria being given to the CCP, but that does not mean that the CCP is just gone. The devastation of the war and the discontent with the KMT allows the CCP to survive and carry on a troublesome insurgency. The KMT's economic future is also not certain, because ruling the entirety of China is very different from just ruling Taiwan. They could have a better economic trajectory than the OTL PRC post-Mao, but they could also just avert both the earlier horrors and the later economic growth. 6. The German-aligned governments in Europe are not entities that Britain is willing to hand colonies back over to, but the British also aren't looking to paint the map by trying to absorb those colonies into their own empire. Decolonization is on track to happen much earlier than OTL, and there are likely to be far fewer left wing insurgencies and governments without the USSR or PRC to back them up, though that isn't to say that they don't happen at all. 7. The US absolutely does not want global German dominance. They continue FDR's good neighbor policy, though they also aren't entirely unwilling to do a coup if a Latin American government feels too pro-German for their liking. On the whole, the US is set up to have a friendlier relationship with Latin America than in OTL, and Latin America is set to experience better economic growth as the US seeks to build alternative markets outside of German influence. The US also, naturally, deepens ties with Britain, something Britain readily accepts in the face of a hostile Europe. 8. Turkey is vaguely pro-German, if only out of pragmatism. Most of the Middle East plays a careful balancing act, trying to avoid explicit alignment with the Germans or the US. Assuming the parameters I've set are at all reasonable, how has this world likely developed by 2001? Is Germany still around as a pariah? Has Germany surpassed the US and become the foremost global power? Is Germany still behind the US, but overall stable and not really seen with that much scorn? Has Germany collapsed already? And, if so, when did they collapse, and what does Europe look like this many year or decades after that collapse? Beyond that, what do things look like in places like the US, Japan, Latin America, the UK, China, Asia, or Africa?
items.model_answer:
In a world where the European Axis actually won the Second World War, “2001” would likely not look like a futuristic extension of our liberal, American-led global order. It would look like a modernized authoritarian world: technologically advanced in some areas, socially rigid, politically brutal, and culturally organized around empire, hierarchy, and permanent militarization.

The first thing to clarify is that an “Axis victory” could mean different things. The most plausible version is not a perfectly unified Nazi planet, but a Europe dominated by Germany, a large East Asian sphere dominated by Japan, and either a weakened, isolated United States or a cold-war-like standoff among victorious authoritarian empires. Even in victory, the Axis powers had competing interests, weak long-term coordination, and different ideological goals. So 2001 would probably be divided into blocs, not peacefully unified.

In Europe, Germany would likely sit at the center of a continental empire stretching from France deep into Eastern Europe. But this would not be a stable or humane “European Union under Berlin.” Nazi rule was based on racial hierarchy, colonization, forced labor, and extermination. If that system had survived and consolidated, by 2001 much of Eastern Europe would have been radically transformed through settlement, mass deportation, demographic engineering, and the destruction of local elites and cultures. Some regions would be heavily Germanized; others would function as permanent internal colonies. The visible surface in 2001 might include efficient transport, monumental architecture, and a high-capacity surveillance state, but underneath it would be built on generations of terror and coerced labor.

Politically, everyday life in the European Axis sphere would be defined by one-party dictatorship, secret police, censorship, and highly unequal citizenship. The regime would likely become more bureaucratically routinized over time. Instead of constant revolutionary fervor, it might resemble a hardened imperial order in which ideology is embedded in schools, media, law, and urban planning. There would be elections only as ritual, if at all. Independent unions, free universities, oppositional churches, and a free press would not meaningfully exist. People might still have consumer goods, vacations, films, and sports, but all within a heavily controlled public culture.

By 2001, the Nazi state itself would probably have changed form from Hitler’s personal rule. Hitler would almost certainly be dead, so the system would either pass into a collective party-security apparatus, military-backed leadership, or periodic succession struggles. If it survived that long, it would probably do so by becoming less chaotic administratively, not less oppressive. Many successful dictatorships outlive their founders by institutionalizing repression. So the Germany of 2001 might look less like a nonstop rally and more like a fusion of technocratic bureaucracy and racial oligarchy.

Economically, this world could be advanced but uneven. There is a temptation to imagine Axis victory producing a sleek super-scientific order, but Nazi governance was often corrupt, ideologically distorted, and strategically self-destructive. A victorious Reich might still achieve major industrial and military development, especially if it controlled the resources of Europe and western Russia. But innovation would be shaped by regime priorities: weapons, aerospace, infrastructure, medicine for preferred populations, surveillance, and prestige engineering. Scientific research considered “degenerate” or associated with persecuted groups would have been crippled. The expulsion and murder of intellectuals, combined with political control over science, could slow progress in key fields even if military technology remained impressive.

So 2001 in an Axis Europe might have very advanced rockets, jet travel, cryptography, chemical engineering, broadcasting, and internal security systems, while lagging in open scientific collaboration, computing culture, and consumer-oriented digital innovation compared with our world. Or, if the regime managed to harness continental resources effectively, it might also have strong computing and telecommunications sectors—but these would likely be designed first for administration, policing, and command rather than individual freedom. Think less “internet as open network” and more tightly monitored state datanets.

The Holocaust and related genocides are central to any realistic answer. If the Axis truly won and stayed in power, Jewish life in much of Europe would have been nearly annihilated. Roma communities would be devastated. Disabled people, many Slavic populations, queer people, political dissidents, and many others targeted by Nazi rule would have been exterminated, enslaved, sterilized, deported, or permanently marginalized. By 2001, this would not just be a political fact but a civilizational one. Entire intellectual traditions, neighborhoods, languages, and family lineages would be missing. Europe would be culturally poorer, more homogenized in some places, and haunted by enforced silence where memory itself had been repressed.

Culture in this 2001 would likely be superficially grand but deeply constrained. Architecture might favor neoclassical monumentality, imperial boulevards, and staged historical symbolism. Film, radio, television, and later digital media would glorify state power, military sacrifice, fertility, racial destiny, and orderly family life. Avant-garde art, much critical theory, jazz cultures, and many forms of modernist experimentation might survive only underground, in exile, or in tolerated apolitical forms. Popular culture would still exist—people always create it—but under censorship and ideological pressure.

The status of women would also be shaped by contradiction. Total war and industrial empire tend to pull women into work, administration, science, and logistics, but fascist ideology pushes toward patriarchy, motherhood, and demographic policy. So by 2001, women in Axis Europe might be visibly present in some professions while still legally and culturally subordinated, especially in elite political life. Reproductive policy would likely be highly intrusive: encouraging births among favored populations, restricting autonomy, and regulating marriage and family according to racial doctrine.

As for the wider world, the United States matters enormously. If the European Axis won without conquering America, then 2001 might resemble a long three-way or two-way global rivalry: German Europe, Japanese East Asia, and an embittered or heavily militarized U.S. Such a world could produce an authoritarian version of the Cold War, with proxy conflicts in Latin America, Africa, the Middle East, and remaining independent states. Nuclear weapons would almost certainly exist. By 2001, the planet could be locked in a balance of terror among regimes even less constrained by public opinion than those in our history.

If, on the other hand, Britain made peace early and the U.S. withdrew into hemispheric defense, then much of Eurasia and Africa might be partitioned into imperial spheres. Decolonization would likely be delayed or reshaped. African and Arab independence movements might face not postwar European exhaustion, but harsher imperial repression backed by stronger metropolitan states. That said, empire would still generate rebellion. So 2001 would probably feature constant insurgency, resistance networks, partisan memory, and brutal counterinsurgency across colonial zones.

Japan’s side of the Axis would produce its own version of 2001: an imperial East Asian order centered on Tokyo, exploitative, militarized, and racially stratified, though not identical to Nazism. China would be the crucial question. If Japan had subdued large parts of China, East Asia by 2001 would be economically important but politically violent, with puppet regimes, extraction, and assimilation pressures. If Chinese resistance persisted successfully, then one of the world’s major fault lines would be the long struggle between Japanese imperial power and Chinese nationalism or communism.

Technologically, spaceflight is an interesting case. A victorious Axis world might well reach space early, perhaps even earlier in rocketry, because Germany already invested heavily in missiles. But the symbolism would differ sharply. Space would not primarily be framed as universal human achievement; it would be a theater of prestige, military high ground, and civilizational competition among empires. A “2001” with orbital stations and lunar missions is conceivable, but the flags planted there would represent regimes built on exclusion rather than democratic idealism.

Would daily life feel “normal” to many people living in it? For those inside the favored ethnic core and not politically suspect, probably yes in a limited sense. Authoritarian societies often normalize themselves. People go to school, work, marry, complain privately, watch entertainment, and adapt. By 2001, younger generations might know no other system. The horror would be structural and selective as well as overt: embedded in who disappeared decades earlier, who cannot travel, who is watched, who can marry, who can own property, which history is taught, which language is honored, and which lives count.

So the short answer is that 2001 in a world where the European Axis won would probably look modern but morally ruined: a developed authoritarian empire or set of empires, with impressive infrastructure and military technology, deeply censored culture, delayed or distorted decolonization, institutionalized racial hierarchy, and whole peoples erased or permanently subordinated. Not a shiny alternate future, but a technologically capable civilization built on victory in genocide and empire.

Now if the Soviets "leave China for dead", so to speak, and withdraw without bothering to install a friendly government, or limit themselves to peripheral territorial concessions, then sure, whatever new government emerges might end up being pro-American -- although even then it would be essentially useless as an ally. (3) For what it's worth, Chiang Kai-shek is likely to make some kind of move on the mainland if the PRC collapses. items.model_answer:
If a full-scale Sino-Soviet nuclear war had broken out during the 1969 border conflict, the result would almost certainly have been one of the greatest human catastrophes in history, with consequences far beyond China and the Soviet Union. The most likely outcome is not a neat military “victory” by either side, but the devastation of both states, the destabilization of the Cold War balance, and a radically different late twentieth century.

In 1969, the Soviet Union had a far larger and more advanced nuclear arsenal than China. China had only a small and relatively primitive nuclear force, with limited delivery capability. That means the Soviet Union would probably have had the ability to inflict much greater immediate destruction. If Moscow chose a full-scale nuclear campaign, it could likely have destroyed many Chinese military, industrial, and political centers. China, however, would still have retained some capacity to retaliate, especially against Soviet cities and military targets in Asia, and possibly parts of European Russia depending on what survived and what could be launched. Even a weak Chinese retaliatory strike would have been enough to make the war catastrophic for the USSR as well.

The first phase would probably have involved Soviet strikes against Chinese nuclear facilities, air bases, command centers, major cities, and troop concentrations near the border. China, fearing disarmament, would have had every incentive to use whatever nuclear capability it had before losing it. So instead of a clean Soviet first strike that “solves” the problem, the likely pattern is rapid escalation: Soviet attacks, Chinese retaliation, further Soviet strikes, and then massive conventional collapse across parts of Inner Asia. Border regions, major urban centers, and industrial zones would have been hit especially hard.

Human losses would have been enormous. Millions, and probably tens of millions, could have died in the short term from blast, fire, and radiation, especially in densely populated Chinese cities. The Soviet Union would also suffer heavily, though probably on a smaller demographic scale at first because China had fewer warheads. But once infrastructure collapsed, famine, disease, refugee flows, and radiation contamination could push the toll far higher over subsequent months and years. China in 1969 was already dealing with the political chaos of the Cultural Revolution, which would have made organized recovery far more difficult. State authority might have splintered in some regions.

Politically, the Chinese Communist regime might not have survived in recognizable form. A full nuclear assault during the Cultural Revolution could have shattered central command, killed top leaders, and triggered local military rule, regional fragmentation, or prolonged civil conflict among surviving factions. Mao might have died in the strikes or shortly thereafter. Even if the regime survived formally, postwar China would likely be far weaker, poorer, and more internally fractured than the historical PRC.

The Soviet Union might initially appear to “win” because of its overwhelming nuclear superiority, but that victory would be deeply poisoned. It would become an international pariah for initiating or participating in the destruction of another socialist great power on such a scale. It would face contamination in Siberia and the Far East, severe economic disruption, military overextension, and long-term strategic uncertainty. If China fragmented, the USSR could be drawn into endless occupation problems, insurgencies, border crises, and humanitarian disaster. So even from a Soviet perspective, a nuclear war would likely be a strategic self-injury, not a meaningful success.

The United States would face an extraordinary dilemma. Washington in 1969 regarded both the USSR and China as adversaries, but it would not have welcomed unrestricted nuclear war in Eurasia. The US might go to the highest nuclear alert, fearing that the Soviet Union, after eliminating China, would gain strategic freedom elsewhere or that general US-Soviet war might follow through misunderstanding or opportunism. American diplomacy would probably focus on preventing the conflict from widening. There is also a serious possibility that the United States would accelerate rapprochement with whatever remained of China, or at least use the crisis to isolate the USSR diplomatically. The triangular diplomacy of the 1970s would still happen, but in a much darker form, and perhaps with a devastated China rather than an emerging one.

Globally, the Cold War would be transformed. The communist world would be shattered beyond repair. Any idea of socialist solidarity would be discredited by an open nuclear war between its two largest states. Nonaligned countries would panic. Japan, India, and Western Europe would likely reconsider their security doctrines immediately. Nuclear proliferation might accelerate, because many governments would conclude that only an independent deterrent could prevent coercion by superpowers. On the other hand, the horror might also produce stronger anti-nuclear movements and arms-control pressure. Both trends could happen at once.

The environmental effects would depend on the scale of the exchange. A limited but still “full-scale” bilateral war by 1969 standards might not produce the most extreme nuclear winter scenarios associated with later US-Soviet arsenals, but it could still inject enough smoke and soot into the atmosphere to damage agriculture regionally or even globally. Large fires in Chinese and Soviet cities, plus radioactive fallout across East and Central Asia, would devastate farmland, rivers, and transport corridors. The effects would likely be especially severe in northern China, Manchuria, Mongolia, Soviet Central Asia, and Siberia. Food shortages could spread well beyond the combatant states.

The long-term world historical consequence is that modern China’s rise would probably never occur in anything like the form we know. No reform era on the same timeline, no rapid industrialization under Deng on the same scale, and no twenty-first-century China as a near-peer to the United States. The Soviet Union, meanwhile, might either harden temporarily under siege conditions or weaken much faster than it did historically. If the war badly strained the Soviet system, it could even bring forward a crisis of legitimacy and economic exhaustion. Alternatively, if China collapsed completely, Moscow might dominate the Eurasian interior for a time, but at immense cost and with little real stability.

So the clearest answer is this: a full-scale Sino-Soviet nuclear war in 1969 would probably have meant Soviet military superiority in the immediate exchange, Chinese devastation on a larger scale, and no true winner. It would likely have killed tens of millions, destabilized both regimes, poisoned much of Asia, transformed the Cold War, and erased the historical path that led to China’s later recovery and rise.

items.original_question:
AHC: Female US Combat Pilots in WWII

USSR famously employed some female combat pilots, but the conditions that made this possible did not exist in the USA (not nearly so desperate a war, and no communist philosophy which held gender equality as an ideal). Of course women flew for the war effort in non-combat capacities (Jackie Cochran’s WASPs, etc.) How far back would a POD have to be to get at least a few American women flying fighters or bombers? Much worse opening to the Pacific War, more carriers sunk and experienced pilots killed, leading to an approval for female volunteers to serve as combat pilots in provisional capacity? A more developed feminist movement through the 20s and 30s, bringing such a possibility just barely into the Overton window?
items.model_answer:
If women had served as U.S. combat pilots in World War II, the biggest immediate effect would probably not have been a dramatic change in the war’s outcome, but a major change in American military culture, gender norms, and the postwar history of the armed forces.

In reality, women did fly military aircraft in the United States during the war through the WASP program, but they were kept out of combat. If the U.S. had instead allowed qualified women to fly fighters, bombers, or attack aircraft in combat zones, they likely would have performed effectively once trained and integrated, because WWII combat aviation depended heavily on skill, discipline, endurance, and decision-making rather than brute strength alone. There would almost certainly have been resistance from male officers, politicians, and the public, but wartime necessity often overrode social prejudice.

Operationally, the United States might have gained a modest manpower advantage. More women in combat cockpits would have freed additional men for other flying roles or for ground combat. In a total war context, even a small expansion of the pilot pool could matter, especially during periods of rapid military growth. However, U.S. industrial capacity, training systems, and overall Allied strength were so large that female combat pilots probably would not by themselves have altered the broad trajectory of victory over Germany and Japan.

The more profound consequences would have been symbolic and institutional. Visible female fighter or bomber aces, decorated veterans, prisoners of war, or casualties would have made it much harder after 1945 to argue that combat was inherently male. That could have accelerated women’s integration into the regular armed forces by decades. Debates over women in military aviation, and later over women in combat generally, might have begun from a very different baseline. Instead of asking in the late twentieth century whether women could handle combat flying, policymakers would have had WWII precedents proving that they already had.

This likely would also have affected American society beyond the military. WWII already helped expand women’s roles in factories and public life. Female combat pilots would have provided one of the strongest possible wartime images of female citizenship: not just supporting the nation, but directly fighting for it. That might have strengthened postwar claims for workplace equality, political authority, and civil rights. It would not necessarily have produced immediate equality—postwar America still pushed many women back into domestic roles—but it would have given feminists and reformers a powerful, patriotic precedent.

There would also have been costs and backlash. Captured or killed women pilots would have provoked intense public emotion. Some Americans would have seen this as intolerable and used it to argue against women in combat. Military cohesion could have suffered in some units if commanders resisted integration. There may also have been pressure to segregate women into special units rather than fully integrate them, limiting the broader effect.

So the most plausible counterfactual is this: female U.S. combat pilots in WWII would probably not have decisively changed battlefield results, but they could have significantly changed the history of gender, military service, and citizenship in the United States. Their legacy would likely have been less about winning the war differently and more about changing what Americans believed women were allowed, expected, and entitled to do.

items.question: What If Tom Daschle wins re-election in 2004
human_answers: Another Daschle term would have been a real step down for Democrats in terms of leadership. Reid and Pelosi were the best Democratic floor leaders in generations and having them commanding the two chambers at the same time is a very big part of why Obama's first two years were so damn productive. Daschle rose through the ranks because he was really good on TV. Reid was terrible on camera, so Daschle is a plus for Democrats here, but I'm not sure it really matters. W was so badly screwing up his second term that Dems didn't really need to convince anyone that things were on the wrong track. The really interesting Qs are what Dems would do with an extra vote's breathing room in the Senate -- is it enough for Daschle to actually get things done even if he's less of a vote-counter than Reid? -- and what impact Daschle's somewhat more expansionist personal opinion on healthcare reform does to Obamacare. Daschle's tax fraud stemmed from income he earned from 2005-2007 -- i.e, after he lost re-election. He won't have that job or that income in ATL, so the whole scandal is butterflied away.

I don't see anyone mentioning the biggest butterfly: Ted Kennedy. Ted Kennedy died in August (I think?) taking Dems down to 59 seats. That's not going to happen if there's an extra seat. They're not going to have to bargain with Ben Nelson to get anything through. Dems are going to be at 60 seats through 2010. Also consequential, they're going to beat 60 seats before March of 2009 because of Al Franken. They had to do a run-off election which meant the Obama administration had to wait an extra 2-3 months to get their super majority. Daschle-Reid were effective. They got Jim Jeffords to switch. They'll be able to get something passed. Daschle wrote a book about how how single-payer is the ideal system but it's problematic in the states. I expect him to push for some Federal Health Board which will only increase death panel comparisons. I'd be interested in what others thing they can get passed through 2009-2010. More stimulus. More infrastructure. I'd love to hear thoughts. There's a small miracle that Daschle can survive in 2010 especially if he's up against a Tea Party lunatic. It's forgotten now but there was some talk after 2012 post-Sandy Hook that Obama might be the rare President who makes gains in the sixth year midterms. I think that's a stretch but it's not inconceivable. If Daschle can convince the retiring Senate Democrats to stay they certainly don't need to lose 9 seats.

Daschle loosing was a real bit of mud in the eye for Democrats in 2004. Him squeaking through would have been a help for sure; anything that gives Democrats an extra vote in the Senate in 2008-2010 will be a big help for Obama's agenda and the ACA. I don't remember how effective he was as a senate leader, Reid wasn't exactly a slouch though. He also had a corruption scandal in 2009 which might become a bigger deal if he's Senate majority leader. Big picture wise, the question is does the extra vote in the Senate and easier passage of a stronger ACA snowball into a more successful presidency for Obama? There's still going to be backlash in 2010, but if more gets done in 2008-2010 thanks to a less intransigent senate, then that momentum could carry forwards. Do they try to do immigration reform, or a stronger recovery package if less of the oxygen is sucked up by healthcare? Big picture the country would have all the same fundamental issues it currently does, but if the vibes are shifted enough in 2016 things could get very different, especially if a certain Orange man decides to stay out of the race.
items.original_question: What if Tom Daschle wins re-election in 2004 Tom Daschle was a Democratic senator from South Dakota who served as the Senate Democratic Caucus leader from 1995 to 2005. In 2004, Daschle was defeated by Republican John Thune by a narrow margin of only 4,508 votes. Daschle would be succeeded as the Senate Democratic leader by Harry Reid of Nevada, who would go on to serve as Senate Majority Leader during the last two years of George W. Bush’s second term and the first two years of Barack Obama’s first term. Democrats would achieve a supermajority during Obama’s first term, enabling the passage of the Affordable Care Act. However, the presence of Senator Joe Lieberman in the Democratic caucus would frustrate Obama’s agenda, axing the public option from the ACA. However, had Tom Daschle won re-election in 2004, perhaps Daschle would have been the 60th vote instead of Joe Lieberman. And unlike Lieberman, Daschle would very likely be for the public option. What would be the impact of a public option being passed as part of ObamaCare? What might change in the 2006, 2008, and 2010 elections if Daschle continued to lead the Democrats rather than Harry Reid? Would Democrats still win all of the seats they would win IOTL?
items.model_answer:
If Tom Daschle had won re-election in South Dakota in 2004, the immediate effect would have been symbolic and institutional at the same time. Daschle was the Senate Democratic leader, and his real-life defeat by John Thune was historically important because it was the first time in decades that a sitting Senate party leader lost re-election. If he survives in this scenario, that shock to Democratic leadership never happens, and the balance of power inside the Senate Democratic caucus changes for years.

In the short term, Daschle almost certainly remains the top Senate Democrat. That means Harry Reid probably does not become Senate Democratic leader in 2005, at least not then. This matters because Reid and Daschle had different styles. Daschle was more associated with negotiation, message discipline, and a somewhat more establishment, institution-minded leadership approach. Reid was tougher, more combative procedurally, and more willing to use Senate rules aggressively. So a Daschle win likely produces a Senate Democratic caucus that is somewhat more centered on bipartisan bargaining and less defined by Reid’s style of trench warfare against Republicans.

On legislative politics under George W. Bush, the broad Republican advantage in 2005 would still exist, so Daschle’s victory would not suddenly stop Bush’s second-term agenda. Republicans still won the presidency and expanded their Senate majority in 2004. But Daschle could have influenced the pace and shape of fights over Social Security privatization, judicial nominations, and the Iraq War. He had more national profile than most Senate Democrats and might have served as a more visible, coordinated opposition figure. Bush’s Social Security push probably still fails, because that failure was driven by underlying political resistance, but Daschle might have framed Democratic opposition in a more unified and leadership-centered way.

The biggest downstream consequence is probably on Democratic leadership after the 2006 midterms. If Democrats still win back the Senate in 2006, Daschle would be the obvious candidate to become majority leader again. In real history that was Reid. A Majority Leader Daschle in 2007–08 could have changed Senate management, relations with moderate Republicans, and perhaps the handling of Iraq oversight and domestic legislative strategy. He was generally seen as more polished and more comfortable as a national spokesman than Reid, though not necessarily more effective in every procedural fight.

This also could affect Barack Obama’s rise, though indirectly. Obama entered the Senate in 2005. In real history, he arrived in a caucus led by Reid, who later played an important role in clearing the field for Obama in 2008 and helping manage Senate Democrats during the transition. Under Daschle, Obama would still likely become a major figure, but the mentoring and coalition-building around him might look different. Daschle, as a fellow Midwesterner with deep party connections, may well have become one of Obama’s key Senate patrons earlier. That might even strengthen Obama’s position with establishment Democrats rather than weaken it.

There is also a direct health-policy angle. In reality, after losing his seat, Daschle moved toward policy work and was later tapped by Obama for a major health-policy role before withdrawing over tax issues. If Daschle remains in the Senate, he is not displaced into that outside-policy world in the same way. During the 2009 health-care reform fight, he might instead play a central legislative role from inside the Senate. Depending on whether he is majority leader or a senior committee-influencer, the drafting and coalition management behind what became the Affordable Care Act could look somewhat different. He had long-standing interest in health reform and might have tried to build a slightly more bipartisan or institutionally brokered approach, though polarization would still sharply limit that.

For South Dakota politics, a Daschle win would likely delay Republican consolidation at the federal level. John Thune’s defeat in 2004 would be a major setback. He might still return later, but his trajectory to becoming a leading Senate Republican would be interrupted or postponed. Since Thune eventually became a central Republican leader, this could have notable long-term effects on the GOP Senate conference as well.

That said, this is not a world where everything changes. Structural forces still matter more than one Senate race in many areas. Republicans would still control Washington in 2005. Bush would still face the same Iraq and second-term problems. Democrats would still benefit from backlash in 2006. Obama would still likely emerge as a national figure. But Daschle’s survival would likely produce three important differences: Senate Democrats would be led by a different kind of leader, Harry Reid’s rise would be delayed or prevented, and the institutional politics of the Senate in the late Bush and early Obama years would be somewhat more negotiation-oriented and less shaped by Reid’s procedural hardball.

So the most plausible answer is that a Daschle re-election would not radically alter national history, but it would meaningfully reshape Senate leadership, Democratic strategy, and possibly the legislative path of health reform and Obama-era governance.
