items.original_question:
AHC: Equip the Best Possible Interwar Army From Scratch

It's 1930, you're put in charge of the military procurement of a smaller developed nation -- a small or middle/regional power: fairly wealthy, fairly industrialized, fairly well-educated workforce, with robust institutions...etc., but not a major power (think Poland, Canada, Australia, the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Czechoslovakia, or Sweden). Despite the global depression, the government has magically found the funds for a major military expansion. The nation has a small military and professional officer corps to expand on, equipped with a smattering of WW1/post-WW1 weapons, but the point is you basically have nothing in large numbers so you essentially get to start from scratch. There's no massive stock of rifle ammunition forcing you to stick with a specific caliber for cost saving reasons, no huge pile of 2pdr shells in a warehouse forcing you to stay with the pom-pom...etc. Money is not the limiting factor (within reason); it's not infinite, but you're going to hit manpower constraints before budget constraints. In addition to the small professional military, the nation has a small armaments industry (e.g., Czech tanks/small arms, Canadian shipbuilding, Dutch aircraft design/manufacture) -- but not enough to design/build everything you need at scale. So you're going to have to buy/import a lot foreign, at least to start. The goal is a primarily defensive military that still has some expeditionary capability (not independent expeditionary operations, but in support of / in concert with great power allies). You're not aligned with a specific bloc so you can buy/import/adopt from wherever you want. Naval needs are more complicated and specific, so ignoring that to start: how do you equip your army and air force?
items.model_answer:
If you are building the best possible interwar army “from scratch,” the answer depends on what “best” means. In the interwar period, no army could maximize everything at once. You had to choose among strategic defense, rapid offensive war, colonial policing, budget limits, industrial capacity, and political constraints. But if the question is: with the benefit of hindsight, what would the strongest all-around army between roughly 1919 and 1939 look like if you could design it from zero, then the ideal answer is a force that combines German-style operational doctrine, French-style artillery seriousness, British attention to professional training and logistics, and the best available communications and mechanization—without repeating the political, doctrinal, and procurement mistakes real states made.

The single biggest point is that the “best” interwar army would not be one centered on any single arm, whether infantry, tanks, cavalry, or static fortifications. It would be a balanced combined-arms army built around mobility, radios, artillery coordination, and logistics. Most real interwar armies failed because they overlearned one lesson from World War I. Some concluded that firepower and fortification had made maneuver obsolete; others became too enamored of armor; others still lacked the industrial and doctrinal base to integrate new technology. The optimal army would avoid these extremes.

Its doctrine would be built around combined-arms maneuver at the operational level. That means infantry, artillery, armor, engineers, reconnaissance, and air support would be trained to work together routinely, not improvised in war. The Germans came closest in doctrine and command culture, especially by the late 1930s, because they emphasized initiative, decentralized leadership, rapid exploitation, and concentration at decisive points. But an ideal army would improve on the Germans by avoiding overreliance on short-war assumptions and by paying far more attention to sustainable logistics, replacement systems, and industrial depth.

Command culture matters as much as equipment. The best interwar army would have a professional officer corps selected for competence rather than aristocratic standing or political loyalty. It would train junior officers and NCOs to act independently within commander’s intent, because modern warfare moves too quickly for rigid top-down control. This is one reason the German army often outperformed numerically comparable opponents early in World War II. So from scratch, you would design a command system closer to Auftragstaktik—mission command—than to highly centralized, methodical battle systems. But unlike the Germans, you would also create strong staff procedures and logistical planning, more like the better British and French traditions, so flexibility did not become chaos.

On force structure, the backbone should still be infantry divisions, because interwar armies needed mass, staying power, and the ability to hold ground in difficult terrain. But these infantry divisions should not be slow, horse-dependent formations with weak communications. The ideal infantry division would be partially motorized, with sufficient organic transport to move artillery, supply, engineers, and key infantry elements rapidly. Full motorization of every soldier was not economically realistic for most states before 1939, but enough trucking to increase operational mobility was both feasible and decisive. Infantry should be supported by plentiful light and medium artillery, modern mortars, anti-tank guns, and engineers.

Artillery remains central. World War I and every serious conflict after it showed that artillery was still the main killer. So the best interwar army would invest heavily in flexible, mobile artillery with excellent fire direction, forward observers, sound communications, and standardized calibers. The French understood artillery better than many of their critics admit, and any ideal army would borrow from that strength. But artillery should not be tied to static battle methods. It must be mobile enough to support maneuver forces and responsive enough to exploit radio-directed fires. A superb interwar army would likely standardize on a few highly effective field and medium guns rather than maintaining a sprawling inventory of legacy pieces.

Tanks should be important, but not treated as independent wonder weapons. The ideal interwar army would field armored divisions built around reliable medium tanks, supported by motorized infantry, self-propelled or rapidly towed artillery, engineers, anti-aircraft units, and reconnaissance. The key lesson is not merely “have tanks,” but “have radios in tanks, mass them, and use them in coherent operational formations.” Early war German panzers were often technically inferior to some French and Soviet tanks, but they were better organized and employed. So the best army from scratch would emphasize reliability, maintainability, crew training, radio communications, and operational doctrine over sheer armor thickness or gun size.

At the same time, this army would avoid one of the great interwar mistakes: splitting tanks into tiny infantry-support packets under foot infantry. There is room for infantry tanks or assault armor in support roles, but the core striking power should be concentrated armored formations. The ideal mix would likely include a standard medium tank for armored divisions, a lighter reconnaissance vehicle family, and perhaps a more heavily armored infantry support vehicle for deliberate attacks. But standardization is vital. Real interwar armies often wasted effort producing too many types.

Motorization and logistics are where many “paper-best” armies collapse. A true best-possible interwar army would put enormous emphasis on trucks, workshops, spare parts, fuel distribution, bridging equipment, and road/rail integration. This may sound less glamorous than tanks, but it was what determined whether breakthroughs could be exploited. The Germans were operationally brilliant in many cases, but they never fully solved the contradiction between their modern fast spearheads and their largely horse-drawn main force. If you are building from scratch, you solve that by investing early in transport, maintenance battalions, standardized vehicle fleets, and railway troops. If the army belongs to an industrial power, this is achievable and transformative.

Communications would be another decisive area. The ideal army would equip not just headquarters but front-line units, artillery observers, and armored vehicles with radios. Many interwar armies had modern weapons on paper but could not coordinate them under combat conditions. Reliable wireless communications let commanders redirect artillery, exploit breakthroughs, call reserves, and adapt to enemy action. In hindsight, this is one of the clearest force multipliers available in the period.

Air-ground cooperation should be institutionalized, though not to the point of making the army dependent on total air superiority. The best interwar army would have doctrine and communications for reconnaissance aircraft, artillery spotting, interdiction, and limited close air support. It would not assume that aircraft alone could replace artillery or break morale strategically. Instead, aviation would serve the land campaign. This is another area where the ideal army blends lessons from several powers: German tactical integration, British professionalism, and French artillery awareness, while rejecting exaggerated theories of independent air power.

Anti-tank and anti-aircraft defense would also have to be stronger than many real interwar armies achieved. By the late 1930s, any serious army needed distributed anti-tank guns in infantry units, doctrinal training for anti-armor defense in depth, mine warfare, and mobile reserves to contain breakthroughs. Similarly, it needed light and medium anti-aircraft assets to protect columns, guns, bridges, and headquarters. The army that best anticipates these needs will be much harder to destroy by mechanized thrust or hostile air attack.

Training and readiness would likely be the real differentiator. The best army is not the one with the most advanced prototypes; it is the one whose ordinary units can execute doctrine under stress. That means large-scale exercises, realistic staff rides, reserve mobilization tests, live-fire combined-arms training, and a reserve system that produces competent formations rather than hollow numbers. One weakness of many interwar forces was that they looked stronger on mobilization tables than they really were in trained manpower and unit cohesion. The ideal army would therefore balance a professional active core with a well-drilled reserve system, probably something between the German and British models: a highly competent cadre with scalable expansion capacity.

In terms of procurement philosophy, the best interwar army would prefer rugged, standardized, mass-producible equipment over fragile technical marvels. This is another hindsight lesson. The ideal medium tank is not the most heavily armed machine theoretically possible in 1938; it is the one you can build in large numbers, train crews on quickly, repair in the field, and keep supplied. The same goes for rifles, machine guns, artillery tractors, radios, and trucks. The more an army standardizes ammunition, parts, and vehicle families, the more operationally effective it becomes.

If we imagine this army belonging to a major industrial state with no political constraints and full hindsight, then by the late 1930s it would probably look like this: a largely motorized army with infantry divisions supported by abundant artillery and anti-tank guns; several concentrated armored corps built around radio-equipped medium tanks and motorized infantry; strong engineer and logistics units; universal mission-oriented leadership; integrated air liaison; and excellent communications. It would likely outperform any actual interwar army because it would combine strengths that in reality were distributed across several states and often undermined by bad assumptions.

If, however, the question is asking which real country gave the best template, the answer is that no single interwar army is sufficient by itself. Germany offered the best operational doctrine and command flexibility; France had serious strengths in artillery, materiel, and some excellent armored ideas but was hobbled by flawed doctrine and command; Britain contributed professionalism, logistics, and mechanization experimentation; the Soviet Union grasped large-scale mechanized warfare early but was crippled by purges and uneven execution. The best “from scratch” army would borrow from all of them.

So the careful direct answer is this: the best possible interwar army from scratch would be a balanced, radio-connected, highly trained combined-arms force built around mobile infantry, concentrated armored formations, responsive artillery, strong logistics, decentralized command, and integrated air support. It would not worship tanks, trenches, or manpower alone. It would be designed to fight both a short mobile campaign and a longer industrial war. And that last point is crucial: with hindsight, the strongest interwar army would be the one that combined German operational excellence with the logistical, industrial, and doctrinal depth to survive beyond the opening victories.

items.question: What If Germany had secured a sustainable wartime supply of food, oil, and rubber despite the Allied blockade in World War II?
human_answers: The RN and other allies can only block the marine trade, so the first thing is to look at who Germany has land borders with. Then, which of those countries might have food or other essentials that Germany needs. If these are willing and able to trade [1], then Germany can maybe get by but if not then they either make do or try to take things by force. Nazi Germany chose force instead of negotiation and trade to try to beak the blockade. Why? because their leaders were mad bastards who were completely untrustworthy to trade with, thought they were better than everyone else, thought that violent conflict was good and who wanted to take over Russian lands for themselves: it ended badly. [1] Italy, for example, might have been willing to trade with Germany, but getting goods into Italy by sea is difficult with the British blocking imports intended for or suspected to be intended for Germany.

Yes its difficult to imagine it now but in 1939 the British had a near monopoly on merchant shipping and many nations merchant ships and their cargos would be 'under written' that is insured by British firms. And much of a nations cargos would likely travel on British ships or ships owned by British firms. In WW1 the blockade of Germany had been part physical i.e. warships stopping ships and inspecting cargos and manifests etc and part commercial pressure. By 1915 this 'loop hole' was effectively stopped using the commercial apparatus to quite simply restrict goods to no more than had been going to those neutral nations before the war meaning that very little would be left to sell on to Germany.
items.original_question: What if what if successful WW2 German breaking of the blockade I'm new here (and I'm a student, so please don't be too harsh, this is my first post), and I had a question, What if the Germans somehow broke the British blockade, or at least got any form of a sustainable food and oil (and rubber, and many other things, though the main question is about food) source that wasn't pillaging and murdering all of Eastern Europe and inspiring massive insurgencies? items.model_answer:
If Germany had somehow secured a sustainable wartime supply of food, oil, and rubber despite the Allied blockade, the war would likely have been longer, deadlier, and much more difficult for the Allies to win, but it would not automatically mean Germany would have won. Those shortages were among the Reich’s most serious structural weaknesses. Removing them would strengthen German military staying power, operational mobility, civilian stability, and diplomatic flexibility. But Germany would still face major obstacles: the industrial scale of the United States, the manpower and depth of the Soviet Union, Allied air power, and Hitler’s own strategic misjudgments.

The biggest immediate effect would be on Germany’s capacity to wage modern war continuously. Oil was crucial above all. German offensives repeatedly ran up against fuel constraints, and by the later war years shortages crippled training, mechanized movement, and air operations. If Germany had reliable oil supplies, the Wehrmacht and Luftwaffe could have kept more tanks, trucks, and aircraft in action for longer. Pilot training would improve, armored reserves could move more freely, and strategic mobility on both the Eastern and Western fronts would increase. This would not just affect spectacular offensives; it would also transform the daily ability to reinforce, retreat, and counterattack.

Rubber mattered because modern armies depended on tires, seals, hoses, vehicle components, and countless industrial uses. A secure rubber supply would improve the reliability and production of trucks, aircraft, and mechanized logistics. Germany’s war effort suffered not only from shortages of weapons but from the difficulty of sustaining transport systems. Better access to rubber would make German logistics less fragile, especially in long continental campaigns like the invasion of the Soviet Union.

Food would matter in a different but equally important way. Germany and occupied Europe were under severe strain, and food scarcity weakened morale, health, labor productivity, and political stability. If Germany had enough food for both the home front and the army, it could reduce internal stress and probably lessen some of the desperate exploitative pressures that drove occupation policy, though not necessarily the brutality of Nazi rule. A better-fed civilian population would be more resilient under bombing and prolonged war, and the military could maintain troop strength and health more effectively.

Together, these changes would likely make Germany much more dangerous between 1941 and 1944. On the Eastern Front, the most important consequence is that German offensives could be sustained longer and defensive operations conducted more effectively. During Operation Barbarossa and later campaigns, logistics and fuel were central constraints. With better supplies, Germany might have advanced farther in 1941, mounted stronger operations in 1942, and avoided some of the catastrophic weakening that came from overextension and shortage. The drive toward the Caucasus, for example, was in part motivated by oil desperation; if that desperation did not exist, German strategy might be less reckless, or alternatively, Germany could support larger and more coherent southern operations. It still would not guarantee victory over the Soviet Union, because the USSR had enormous manpower, industrial relocation east of the Urals, and increasing Allied support. But it could make Soviet survival far more costly and uncertain, especially before the full weight of American production and the Red Army’s operational maturation took effect.

In North Africa and the Mediterranean, secure oil and rubber would have had a dramatic effect. Axis logistics there were chronically constrained. A better-supplied Germany could have supported stronger campaigns in Libya and Egypt, posed a more serious threat to the Suez Canal, and forced Britain to commit even more resources to the theater. That in turn could affect imperial communications, Middle Eastern oil politics, and Allied strategic priorities. Still, naval and air superiority in the Mediterranean would remain contested, and supply over distance would still be difficult unless Germany also solved the shipping and access problem, not just the raw-material problem.

In the air war, reliable oil would help Germany more than any single other commodity. By 1944 the Luftwaffe was collapsing in large part because of fuel shortages and the destruction of synthetic oil production. If those vulnerabilities were removed, Germany could put up stronger air defense, train more pilots, and resist Allied bombing more effectively. That would matter enormously. Allied strategic bombing might become less devastating and less decisive, at least in the short run. But the Allies still had larger productive capacity and could replace losses on a scale Germany could not match indefinitely.

Would this change D-Day and the Western Front? Quite possibly. A Germany with ample fuel and functioning transport could move reserves faster, train armored units better, and respond more effectively to an invasion of France. The Normandy campaign might become much bloodier or even fail in 1944, forcing the Western Allies to delay a successful continental return. If Germany retained stronger air and armored forces, Allied planners would face a much harder problem. That said, the Allies could still choose where and when to invade, and they had overwhelming naval superiority. Germany could make invasion costlier and perhaps postpone defeat, but not necessarily prevent eventual pressure from both west and east.

The political effects would also be significant. One reason Germany pursued extreme territorial conquest was to seize resources and escape strategic encirclement. If food, oil, and rubber were sustainably available from the beginning, German leaders might feel less urgency in some directions, though Nazi ideology would still push expansion and racial empire. More importantly, Germany’s coalition relationships might stabilize. Italy, Romania, Hungary, and others were affected by German weakness and dependence. A more materially secure Reich would be better able to support its allies and maintain a stronger European bloc.

Still, even under this favorable scenario, Germany’s chances of ultimate victory remain uncertain and probably still limited if the United States, Soviet Union, and British Empire remain fully committed. The war was not lost only because of shortages. Germany also suffered from chronic strategic overreach, poor grand strategy, duplication and inefficiency in procurement, interservice rivalry, and Hitler’s increasingly disastrous command decisions. Even a well-fueled Wehrmacht would still have to conquer or force the surrender of enemies with much greater aggregate economic strength. Unless secure access to those supplies also implied a much larger geopolitical shift, such as neutralizing British sea power or preventing American entry, Germany would still be fighting a coalition with superior long-term resources.

So the most defensible conclusion is that secure food, oil, and rubber would not guarantee a German victory, but it would remove some of the key material constraints that made defeat highly likely. The war would probably last longer. German offensives would be stronger, German defense more resilient, and Allied victory more delayed and costly. The Soviet Union might come under even greater strain, the Mediterranean could become more dangerous for Britain, and the 1944–45 collapse of Germany might not occur in the same way or on the same timetable. In short, Germany would become a far more formidable wartime power, but not necessarily an unbeatable one.

items.question: What If nuclear fission had been discovered early enough for a practical reactor to be built around the 1900s?
human_answers: Well, according to Google "Canada's first CANDU prototype, the Nuclear Power Demonstration (NPD) reactor, required a significant amount of heavy water (D2O) for its moderator and coolant, generally around 1 tonne of heavy water per megawatt (MW) of capacity, translating to roughly 20-25 tonnes for its small 20 MWe output..." and "In the 1930's Norwegian company Norsk Hydro began industrial-scale extraction of heavy water (deuterium oxide) at its Vemork plant in Rjukan, using electrolysis as a byproduct of fertilizer production, " Finally from Wikipedia (yes, I know this may well be nonsense) "It was the world's first site to mass-produce heavy water (as a byproduct of nitrogen fixing), with a capacity of 1.2 tonnes per year. " So, by the late 1930's / early 1940's it might well be possible to build a 1 or 2MW CANDU stream generator using just one or two years production from the single Norsk Hydro plant. I assume Canadian hydro plants were built with higher capacity since they (the Canadians) managed to build commercial output (GW) plants requiring 200-300 tones of heavy water in a 'reasonable' timescale (ie. less than 200 years )

Believe it or not, my first engineering degree was in Nuclear Engineering (it was a dead field when I graduated 30 plus years ago, and still is, so I got another degree in Manufacturing Engineering). Yes, you can run reactors with natural enrichment, and the right neutron moderator - heavy water (as in the water molecules have Deuterium instead of your usual one proton no neutrons hydrogen) or graphite come to mind. Both would avoid the need to enrich the fuel (which is a major hassle to do). BUT, that's only part of the story - you need the instrumentation for monitoring the nuclear reactions (to make sure they're occurring, and not getting out of control) which is basically electronic in nature (sorry mechanical won't cut it). In the early 1900s, the field of electronics was embryonic at best. Then there's the material science aspect - you need materials seriously capable of dealing with the high reactor temperatures, and radiation effects (oh yeah, and the material can't interfere excessively with the neutron flux, which would disrupt the reaction) - sorry not happening, material science was in its infancy IMO. There is also the safety aspect - you need shielding for any radiation emitted from the reactor. The health aspects of radiation exposure were basically unknown, resulting in many people getting exposed to and dying of cancer (Marie Curie, early X-Ray technicians, the so called "Radium Girls" who painted the glowing dots on watch faces). In certain cases of extreme exposure (due to reactor surges, etc.), you can die from the radiation days after the exposure. In short, IMO, having a viable nuclear reactor in the early 1900s is a non-starter.

To your first part: Fair enough. It seems like this might require ASB, like just magically gifting people the entire lexicon of nuclear understanding and teaching them how to make purer graphite. I'm not sure I entirely agree with the second part. Were the engineers that built the Chicago Pile doing sophisticated core analysis? Did they know the neutron flux? I feel like you could "fly blind" and just go by heat/steam output, especially since "won't immediately melt down and ruin my investment" is probably considered sufficient by 1900s standards of safety (especially if the health effects of radiation are not yet understood). Granted, it seems very, very likely that the long term effects of this mentality would make for a much more radioactively contaminated world... Ah, but I didn't say for generating electricity, per se. A nuclear boiler just for steam would be useful. And I doubt they'd come up with a design that requires steam generators or controlling boron concentration in the coolant: I wouldn't expect anything like a PWR with its separation between a primary and secondary loop. More like a BWR or RBMK, where the radioactive steam is directly used. If the objective is electricity, it may require a bit longer than early 1900s. But by the time you have coal plants coming online, you have everything you need for the conventional thermal plant.

To elaborate on some things: as far as I can tell, there are possibly 3 historical reactor designs that used unenriched/natural uranium: heavy-water moderated CANDU reactors, graphite-moderated gas-cooled reactors (Magnox and UNGG), and possibly the graphite-moderated Soviet RBMK reactors (although RBMK reactors typically used low-enriched uranium). Heavy water's out of the question; it was only discovered in the 1930s, and even WW2-era methods for extracting heavy water were massively energy-intensive. NPD, the first CANDU reactor producing some 20 MW of electricity, required 28,660kg of heavy water. Using pure electrolysis to extract the heavy water - the initial method used to extract heavy water at Vemork - required about 58,000 kilowatt hours per pound of heavy water, or 3.6 billion kilowatt-hours to produce all the necessary heavy water. As a quick comparison, the US' entire monthly electricity generation in April 1922 was about 3.6 billion kilowatt hours. That means the NPD reactor, if it obtained heavy water using pre-WW2 methods, could run for 20 years straight and not break even on the power needed to create the heavy water necessary to run the plant (not to mention some heavy water will be lost in operation) before the development of postwar heavy water production methods. UNGG and RBMK definitely used zirconium cladding for their fuel elements (necessary because zirconium has a smaller neutron absorption cross-section and is resistant to corrosion); the issue is that metal zirconium wasn't commercially synthesized until 1925, and it wasn't commercially synthesized cheaply until after WW2. The specific zirconium alloys used in the fuel claddings weren't developed until the postwar either. RBMK reactors operate with water at pressures of about 1,000 psi; that wasn't achieved by land-based power generation systems until 1925. Uranium metal used in the gas-cooled reactors is difficult to work with considering it corrodes a lot of metals when molten, thus requiring graphite molds of decently high purity (maybe not as pure as nuclear graphite, but boron has to be minimized). Also the furnaces used to cast the uranium were vacuum induction furnaces, a technology not invented until the 1920s. Turning the uranium metal into fuel rods that can be inserted also required a ton of research and development to the point where it was once considered the most critical job at Hanford for the Manhattan Project.
items.original_question: What if A nuclear reactor, four decades early? I posit that with the technology of the early 1900s, a nuclear reactor could've been theoretically possible had the theory been understood. Uranium enrichment is entirely out of the question, but not all reactor designs require it. The industrialists of the 1900s had access to graphite, yellowcake, and boron, which would allow the creation and control of a graphite-moderated natural uranium reactor, so long as the graphite was pure enough (I am admittedly unsure if that level of purity would be possible, but I am presuming so given what little I know of the process). Is there any plausible scenario where the discovery of nuclear fission is pushed back far enough for our enterprising titans of industry to begin harnessing nuclear steam, short of dropping off a modern nuclear physics textbook in their engineers' laps? If so, what effects would this have on the world?
items.model_answer:
If practical nuclear fission had been discovered early enough for a working reactor to be built around 1900, the twentieth century would likely have been transformed even more dramatically than it already was, but not in a simple “instant futuristic world” way. The biggest change is that a very dense new energy source would enter a world that was still dominated by coal, imperial navies, early electrical grids, and pre-electronics industry. That timing matters: the reactor would appear before radar, before modern control theory, before advanced materials science, before jet aircraft, and before the political lessons of two world wars. So the effects would be enormous, but also uneven, dangerous, and heavily shaped by the institutions of the age.

The first and most immediate effect would probably be on elite state power rather than ordinary life. Around 1900, only a few countries had the industrial base, scientific culture, and capital to exploit such a reactor: Britain, Germany, France, perhaps the United States, and later Russia and Japan. A practical reactor in that era would almost certainly begin as a national prestige project, much like dreadnought battleships or early radio. Governments and major industrial firms would see it as a strategic asset for electricity production, naval propulsion, and possibly industrial heat. Because coal was central to both industry and military logistics, any power source that reduced dependence on coaling stations and rail-based fuel delivery would be geopolitically revolutionary.

The British Empire in particular might have benefited enormously. One of Britain’s great strategic burdens was fueling its navy and sustaining global shipping. If reactors could be made compact enough for marine use even a few decades earlier than in our timeline, Britain could maintain ships with far greater endurance and less need for global coal infrastructure. That might strengthen imperial control, prolong naval supremacy, and intensify rivalry with Germany. On the other hand, if Germany got there first or caught up quickly, the naval arms race before World War I could become even more unstable. Nuclear-powered fleets without nuclear weapons would still be a huge military advantage.

Electricity development would also change. In 1900, electrification was spreading, but many regions still relied on local generation and coal-fired plants. A practical reactor would offer centralized power on a new scale. Industrial centers such as London, Berlin, New York, and Paris might build reactor-backed grids decades earlier than our world developed large-scale nuclear power. That could reduce urban coal smoke, one of the great environmental and public health burdens of the early industrial age. Cities might become cleaner in air quality terms, with fewer soot-filled skies and less respiratory disease from coal burning. But this would be offset by primitive radiation safety practices. Since the culture of industrial safety was often poor even in mines and chemical plants, early nuclear accidents and contamination events would probably be common before the risks were understood.

That point is crucial: a 1900 reactor is not entering a world prepared to handle it. Early twentieth-century engineering was impressive, but metallurgy, instrumentation, and radiation biology were much less mature. Operators would initially know far less about shielding, long-term exposure, contamination pathways, reactor stability, and waste handling. There would likely be serious accidents, possibly catastrophic ones, before a safety culture emerged. Entire districts or industrial sites might be irradiated by ignorance rather than malice. Workers, soldiers, and nearby civilians would often bear the cost. In that sense, early nuclear power could resemble the early chemical industry or early mining: transformative, lucrative, and brutally unsafe.

Would nuclear weapons arrive earlier too? Very likely yes, though not necessarily immediately in 1900. Once fission is understood well enough to build practical reactors, states would also become interested in neutron physics, isotopes, and explosive possibilities. The decisive question would be whether the surrounding scientific and industrial ecosystem could support uranium enrichment or plutonium production. If reactors existed by 1900, then by the 1910s or 1920s, major powers might be investigating atomic bombs. That creates perhaps the most dramatic divergence from real history: World War I or the interwar period could become the nuclear threshold.

If atomic weapons appear before or during World War I, the consequences are hard to overstate. A war already driven by rigid alliances and mass mobilization could become even more destructive. Yet because delivery systems were primitive, early bombs might be used less like strategic missile warheads and more like giant devices delivered by ship, rail, or short-range aircraft. Port cities, fortresses, and troop concentrations could become targets. Even one or two uses in the 1914–1918 period could shock governments into either arms control or even deeper militarization. It is possible that the horror of early atomic use would shorten major wars through terror; it is also possible it would normalize extreme destruction before any anti-nuclear taboo formed.

There is another possibility: earlier nuclear knowledge could deter great-power war before it begins. If states recognize by, say, 1910 that industrial civilization itself is vulnerable to atomic attack, leaders might be more cautious. But this is less certain than it sounds. The leaders of pre-1914 Europe were not especially good at managing risks they only partly understood. They might instead treat nuclear technology as just another prestige weapon, much as they did battleships and heavy artillery. In that case, the prewar arms race becomes even more dangerous, not less.

Economically, early nuclear power could accelerate industrial concentration. Reactors would not be village technologies. They would require state backing, advanced engineering, and centralized infrastructure. That would favor large corporations and national governments over local industry. Countries with reactor capability might industrialize faster and more deeply, widening the gap between the great powers and the colonized world. Colonial empires might become more entrenched, because a handful of powers would gain access to cheap high-density energy while continuing to extract raw materials from abroad. Electrified railways, heavy industry, aluminum production, and chemical manufacturing could all expand sooner in core regions, reinforcing global inequality.

Oil might still rise, but differently. Around 1900, oil was becoming important for lighting, engines, and eventually transport. A practical reactor would compete most directly with coal in electricity and large-scale power, not immediately with petroleum in cars, trucks, and aircraft. So internal combustion might still spread widely. The world might therefore end up with a mixed energy economy: nuclear for grids, industry, and navies; oil for vehicles and aviation; coal declining earlier than in our timeline. That could reduce cumulative greenhouse emissions significantly over the century, especially if nuclear displaced a large share of power generation. But radiation contamination and waste mismanagement could create a different environmental legacy.

Science and technology overall would probably advance faster in some areas and slower in others. Earlier nuclear physics would stimulate materials science, instrumentation, chemistry, and medicine. Radiology and isotope tracing could develop sooner. Universities and military labs would expand. But because so much talent and money might be absorbed into nuclear projects and related strategic competition, some other fields could develop under different pressures. Electronics, rocketry, and aviation might either accelerate through military spillover or become relatively neglected compared with reactor and weapons work, depending on the country.

Socially and culturally, nuclear technology arriving in 1900 would produce a very different modern imagination. Instead of “atomic age” imagery belonging to the post-1945 world of suburbia, television, and rockets, it would belong to the age of empires, steamships, class hierarchy, and faith in grand engineering. Writers like H. G. Wells would seem prophetic almost immediately. Public attitudes might swing between awe and dread much earlier. If accidents or weapons use happened before strong democratic oversight and mass media matured, the technology could become associated with secrecy, aristocratic state power, and industrial sacrifice rather than consumer optimism.

In medicine, some benefits would come early, but also serious harm. Radiation therapies and diagnostics might develop sooner, but in an era with weak regulation and incomplete understanding, dangerous overexposure would be common. The same pattern would likely repeat across mining, factory work, and military experimentation.

The long-run political effect might be a world that is either more centralized or more shattered. One plausible path is that early nuclear technology strengthens big states and empires, making the twentieth century more authoritarian and technocratic. Another is that the sheer destructiveness of early nuclear war breaks confidence in old regimes and produces earlier international control efforts, perhaps something like nuclear treaties or a stronger League-style institution decades sooner. Much would depend on whether the first major public encounter with fission was “cheap electricity” or “a city destroyed.”

So the most careful answer is this: a practical reactor around 1900 would not simply make the world more advanced earlier. It would front-load the atomic age into a much less prepared political and technical environment. That likely means faster electrification, earlier decline of coal, stronger industrial great powers, and possibly cleaner urban air. But it also likely means worse safety failures, harsher imperial power, an intensified pre-1914 arms race, and a serious chance that nuclear weapons appear during or soon after World War I. In short, the world would probably become more powerful, more unequal, and more dangerous much earlier.

items.question: What If Create an exotic party system
human_answers: Led to: Independent Growers Union Party: AKA the Green Farmers Party, Green and Grow Party ... ( In derogatory terms also referred to as the Goatwool Sock Party, the goats ) A split-off from the Farmers Union Party that contends that the latter has become too subservient to the big agricultural businesses, megafarms and meat-packing plants to the detriment of small family farms and independent growers. Quickly gained a following in rural New England, Colorado, New Mexico and parts of California. Also gained support from the microbrewery industry, whole food grocery chains and Willie Nelson... However while promoting small farms and orchards, they quickly adopted ideas of sustainable green farming which lead to talk radio now openly calling them 'that other green lefties'. The fact that they are also heavily promoting the legalization of marijuana does not help and lately their appeal with traditional small family farms - once their core constituents- has waned. Many of hem now lamenting that they "revolted against being pushed out by corporate megafarms, only to now be pushed out by hippie goat farmers". Still their upward trend has slowed but not stopped andbin the last elections they managed to get as many votes as the FUP. Platform : pro small farms, pro sustainable farming, pro farm subsides but vehement watchdog making sure said subsidies are not gobbled up by large agribusiness. Socially conservative to pro-busines, pro-family and pro states rights. However also pro marijuana and against fracking, pesticides and GMO seeds. Although not official, in analogy to the Democrat's mule and the Republican's elephants, political cartoonists have taken to depicting the IGUP as a small goat or a goat Inna farmers outfit. Apparently many IGUP members liked the idea and bumper stickers of goats driving tractors, goats headbutting mules and goats p.... against the leg of an elephant have become quite popular in rural parts of the states. Closely aligned with: Fraternal Order of Local and Small Businesses: Originally an action group turned political party, the FOLSBee is - as the name implies- pro-busines but against 'big business' and megacorporations running roughshod over small neighborhood mon-and-pop stores. Unsurprisingly they have a strong following on the local levels, in several smaller towns being the biggest party in city council. Their reach however declines with each superimposed layer of government and their overall impact in the state elections I negligible. Nationally, so far they have only yielded one senator and four congressmen in their 50 years of existence. The name invokes strong images of early 1900's idyllic New England town streets with lots of stores that are just known by the family name of their owner and it must be said that the FOLSBee is quite successful in playing on the nostalgic feel of that image. Their mythical hero is George Bailey, the community banker protagonist from Frank Capra's ' It's a Wonderful Life'. And like Bailey, their main tenet is that it is a local business' task to help it's community especially when this does not exclude getting ahead themselves as well. Therefore on a national level it should be the government's task to help small businesses helping the community. As a platform, they are rather conservative, pro gun rights, pro law and order and pro-busines. However they are quite effective as a watchdog making sure that every proposed business law is effectively helping ALL businesses an not just the ones big enough to afford their own lobbyists and their idea of 'a level playing field for all' also ties in with support for education and immigrants' rights. However like the IGUP, the FOLSBee also has taken on -critics say:'has been infiltrated by' - some rather leftist and environmentalist views. So they tend to promote public transportation over new highways (there are more clients at bus stops then at parking lots) green energy over fossil fuel (no startup will come to our city thinking 'Hey, let's build a car that runs on coal') public housing, a strong social welfare net and lately even state-run healthcare. So much like conservatives paint the IGUP as the party of goat wool sock wearing weed farmers, they taken to deride the FOLSBee as the party of hippie farmers market organic bath salt sellers. Like the IGUP, this has not really affected their base and although rather small nationally, by coordinating their programs with the IGUP 'goats' they are still on of the more influntial minor pressure parties. In political cartoons to the FOLSBee is usually represented as a Norman Rockwell-esque 1920's drug store owner. Typically he is standing behind a soda fountain doling out fatherly advice to a donkey or elephant sitting at the drug store counter.

Law and Order : Center-right to right-wing, MacArthurism, law and order, strong government, agrarianism (faction) Originally formed during the Dorr Rebellion, however, they soon grew to great lengths due to the Great Rebellion. As of now, they are the party in power and have a strong grasp over the country's House of Burgesses, most likely due to the recent riots in cities such as Cleaveland and St. Elmo. items.original_question:
AHC: Create an exotic party system

So the challenge, inspired by these two excellent examples (all credit to @Wolfram and @TheNixonator , respectively), is to create an alternate political party system for a country using obscure, defunct or marginal political parties or factions that existed in that country historically. Paramilitaries and secret societies pulling a Know-Nothing are allowed. There was some support for Social Credit in the US so I'm counting it as an example. As for the rules: I'm being pretty loose in my definition of party/faction, but please limit it to historical groups that existed in the country you're writing about, or create a scenario where the that country expands if you want to bring in outside groups. Alternate party mergers are acceptable as long as the names of the current major or third parties aren't used. A heterodox blend of political planks makes it more interesting for all involved. I think that about covers it, have at it and try to have a little fun!
items.model_answer:
Imagine a party system built not around ideology, class, or region, but around time. In this exotic system, political parties represent different attitudes toward the past, present, and future.

One party, the Preservation Party, believes society should move very slowly. Its members argue that traditions, inherited institutions, and long-tested customs are humanity’s safest guide. They do not reject change completely, but they insist that nearly every reform must prove itself against the wisdom of previous generations.

A second party, the Immediate Party, focuses almost entirely on present conditions. It does not care much whether a policy is ancient or visionary; it asks only whether it improves life now. Its politicians are practical, short-cycle thinkers, often popular in times of crisis because they promise visible results rather than grand theories.

A third party, the Horizon Party, represents the future. It supports experimental policies, long-term planning, and investment in projects that may not pay off for decades. It might champion radical technologies, environmental transformation, or social redesign. Critics would call it reckless; supporters would call it visionary.

Elections in such a system would not just be about left versus right, but about which time horizon should dominate government. During war or economic collapse, voters might turn to the Immediate Party. In culturally anxious periods, they might favor the Preservation Party. In moments of optimism, they might empower the Horizon Party.

This system would be exotic because it reorganizes politics around a basic human tension: whether legitimacy comes from what has endured, what works now, or what could exist tomorrow. It could produce richer debates than many modern party systems, though it might also create conflict, since each party would accuse the others of blindness—one trapped in nostalgia, one in short-termism, and one in fantasy.

items.question: What If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon for crewed lunar missions?
human_answers: I don't think you understand SpaceX very well. The Starship "failures" are the result of rapid design-test-redesign, pushing the hardware to its limits to find out just what those limits actually are. I think they are up to the third generation design. If putting a Starship into orbit was so important to them, they'd have done by now. Still in test phase. Falcon 9 (and Heavy) is not about putting maximum mass into space, it is about putting payloads into space at minimum cost. So yes, a single type of engine and propellant all the way to orbit: the upper stage is just a cut-down version of the launcher and Merlin Vacuum is a Merlin 1D with a longer nozzle for more efficiency. Reusing a booster cuts payload mass by about 40%, but they break-even on the second or third flight. Falcon 9 is so cost-efficient that SpaceX is eating everyone else's lunch at this point. It's no Saturn V, to be sure, but it isn't meant to be. Saturn V was designed with each stage optimized just for its specific part of the mission... which made it extremely expensive to develop and build and totally uneconomic. A diametrically opposite design approach.

items.model_answer:
If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon specifically for crewed lunar missions, the most likely outcome is that the company could have fielded a limited, commercially driven circumlunar capability earlier than Starship, but a full lunar landing architecture would still have been difficult, expensive, and operationally constrained.

Falcon Heavy plus Dragon was always more plausible for missions around the Moon than for landing on it. A crew-rated Dragon launched by Falcon Heavy could, in principle, support a free-return circumlunar flight if enough performance margin, life support duration, radiation protection, communications, and deep-space reentry capability were added. That kind of mission might have happened in the late 2010s or early 2020s if SpaceX had treated it as a core program rather than a publicity concept. It would probably have resembled an upgraded version of the dearMoon or early tourist circumlunar ideas: a few astronauts or private passengers looping around the Moon and returning to Earth without entering lunar orbit for long or attempting a landing.

Actually landing astronauts on the Moon with Falcon Heavy and Dragon would have been much harder. Dragon was not a lunar lander, and turning it into one would have required major redesign. Even if SpaceX revived a propulsive landing variant, a Moon-capable Dragon would need deep-throttling engines, landing sensors, dust tolerance, surface power, ascent capability, and substantial redundancy for crew safety. Falcon Heavy also would not have been able to send a crewed Dragon and all required lunar landing hardware directly to the Moon in one simple launch. That would have pushed SpaceX toward an architecture involving multiple launches, on-orbit assembly, refueling, or separate transfer and landing stages. At that point, the company would essentially be building a smaller, more complex version of what Starship later aimed to do in a more integrated way.

If SpaceX had committed to this path, NASA’s Artemis era might have looked somewhat different. SpaceX could have offered NASA a commercial circumlunar transport service years before Starship Human Landing System was ready. NASA might have used such missions for crew training, deep-space systems validation, or even as an Orion alternative for some roles, though political and institutional factors would still strongly favor SLS/Orion for flagship government missions. For lunar landings, SpaceX might have competed with a modular architecture: Falcon Heavy launches a crew vehicle, another launch sends a lander, and perhaps a third sends a propulsion stage. That might have made SpaceX a more direct competitor to traditional lunar programs earlier, but probably not a cheaper or faster provider of actual landings than the company hoped.

The tradeoff is that continuing Falcon Heavy/Dragon lunar development would likely have slowed Starship. SpaceX has finite engineering capacity, and a serious crewed lunar adaptation of Dragon would have absorbed money, management attention, test flights, and safety certification effort. In return, SpaceX might have achieved an earlier but narrower milestone: getting people around the Moon before Starship was ready. But the company would probably have delayed the fully reusable super-heavy-lift system that underpins its longer-term Mars and lunar ambitions. In that sense, SpaceX might have gained a near-term lunar presence while sacrificing some progress toward the much larger architecture it actually wanted.

Commercially, there may have been a viable niche. Wealthy private customers, space agencies outside NASA, or prestige missions could have paid for circumlunar flights. A lunar Dragon program might also have strengthened SpaceX’s position in human deep-space transportation and given it more flight heritage beyond low Earth orbit. But it is unlikely that Falcon Heavy and Dragon would have become the dominant long-term system for sustained lunar exploration. They would have been too limited in payload, too operationally complex, and too expendable compared with the kind of reusable high-capacity system SpaceX ultimately pursued.

So the clearest counterfactual is this: SpaceX could probably have delivered a real crewed circumlunar program with Falcon Heavy and Dragon if it had stayed focused on that goal, and it might have done so earlier than any Starship-based human lunar mission. But for actual lunar landings, Falcon Heavy and Dragon would probably have led to a stopgap architecture—impressive, technically possible, but cumbersome and strategically inferior to a purpose-built reusable system.

items.model_answer:
If the British had carried out a second major carrier strike on Taranto soon after the first attack in November 1940, the most likely result is that the Italian battle fleet would have been damaged even more severely and forced to withdraw for a longer period, giving Britain a stronger temporary advantage in the central Mediterranean. But it probably would not have transformed the whole war in the Mediterranean on its own.

The first Taranto raid had already shown that the Italian navy was vulnerable at anchor and that shallow-water torpedo attack was practical. A second strike, especially if launched before the Italians could fully reorganize defenses, might have sunk or crippled additional battleships, damaged cruisers and support ships, and further disrupted repair and fuel arrangements. That would have made the Regia Marina even less willing to risk decisive surface action. In the short term, British convoys to Malta, Egypt, and Greece might have moved with somewhat less fear of interception by heavy Italian units.

This could also have had an important psychological effect. Taranto was already a shock. A second successful blow would have reinforced British naval prestige and deepened Italian caution. Italian commanders, already constrained by fuel shortages, air cover problems, and the need to preserve capital ships, might have become even more defensive. The British might then have enjoyed greater operational freedom in the eastern and central Mediterranean during the following months.

However, there are important limits to the counterfactual. First, the British carrier force was small and fragile. Mounting another attack quickly would have required aircraft, trained crews, good weather, and a carrier kept in action despite substantial risk from submarines, surface forces, and land-based airpower. The Royal Navy could not strike repeatedly without exposing itself. A second raid might also have met stronger defenses, because after the first attack the Italians would likely improve torpedo nets, anti-aircraft guns, smoke screens, barrage balloons, dispersal, and readiness. So the second attack may have been less effective than the first.

Second, the Mediterranean balance was not determined by battleships alone. Airpower, submarines, convoy protection, logistics, and Axis support from Germany mattered enormously. Even with the Italian battle fleet weakened further, the British still faced the Luftwaffe, especially once German air units became more active in the theater, and the constant problem of sustaining Malta and Egypt over long distances. Italian naval losses would not automatically stop Axis supply to North Africa, because merchant shipping, escorts, aircraft, and later German involvement remained crucial factors.

Third, strategic priorities mattered. Around this time Britain was also drawn into Greece and other commitments. Even if Taranto had been followed up more aggressively, British gains at sea could have been diluted by broader strategic overreach. A stronger naval position does not necessarily translate into a decisive strategic outcome if army and air commitments are stretched elsewhere.

So the best answer is: a second attack on Taranto would probably have increased British naval superiority for a time, further weakened Italian willingness and ability to contest the Mediterranean by surface action, and perhaps improved convoy operations and pressure on Axis logistics. But it is unlikely by itself to have knocked Italy out of the naval war or radically changed the final course of the Mediterranean campaign. It would have been an important operational success, not a single war-winning stroke.

items.original_question: Impact of French soldiers in the Atlantic Wall? In that case, would that impact production? And what could be the performance of those soldiers fighting clearly for Germany as late as 1944?
items.model_answer:
If Vichy France had somehow sent 100,000 French troops to help defend the Atlantic Wall in 1944, the overall result of the war in Western Europe probably would not have changed, but the Normandy campaign likely would have been bloodier, slower, and politically more complicated.

The first thing to note is that this scenario requires a major political break from what actually happened. By 1944, Vichy France had very limited real autonomy, much of France was under direct German occupation, and the French armed forces available to Vichy were tightly constrained. So for 100,000 troops to appear on the Atlantic Wall, Germany would have had to rearm, organize, and trust a very large French collaborationist force. That alone would have been difficult, because the Germans were never fully confident in French loyalty, especially by the late war when resistance activity was growing and Germany was clearly under strain.

If we assume those troops do exist and are deployed in a serious way, their military effect would depend on quality more than raw numbers. One hundred thousand additional men spread along the Atlantic Wall could strengthen coastal defenses, man bunkers, guard roads, patrol rear areas, and free some German units for mobile reserve duties. In the best case for Germany, this could make the initial Allied landings in Normandy more costly. More defended strongpoints, more infantry around beach exits, and more manpower to contain airborne drops might delay Allied consolidation. The Americans at Omaha in particular, or the British and Canadians against fortified villages and coastal batteries, might have faced stiffer resistance.

But these troops would not have solved Germany’s main problems. The Atlantic Wall was never going to stop the Allies by itself if they achieved air and naval supremacy, which they did. Allied warships could still bombard fixed positions, Allied aircraft could still isolate the battlefield, and Allied logistics still dwarfed anything Germany and its collaborators could sustain in France. Even if French collaborationist troops added density to the defense, they would remain vulnerable to massive firepower and to disruption once the landings succeeded.

Their reliability would also be a huge issue. Many might fight poorly, desert, surrender quickly, or switch sides once the invasion began, especially if they were defending French soil against forces that included Free French elements and were clearly backed by the likely victors. Others, especially hardened collaborationists, might fight stubbornly. So the effect would probably be uneven: some sectors might hold longer, while in others the presence of French troops might collapse under pressure or create confusion in command and morale.

Politically, the consequences could be significant. If large French forces openly fought for the German side in Normandy, it would deepen the stigma of collaboration after liberation. Postwar France might see even harsher purges, more civil conflict, and a more difficult effort by de Gaulle to rebuild national unity. The narrative that Vichy was an illegitimate aberration, separate from the “real France” of the Resistance and Free French, would be harder to sustain if 100,000 French troops had visibly fought against the liberation. That could leave a more bitter domestic legacy, even if it did not save Germany militarily.

In operational terms, the most plausible outcome is not that D-Day fails outright, but that Allied casualties rise and the breakout from Normandy is delayed. A stronger infantry screen might slow the seizure of beachheads, complicate linkups between beaches, and increase the time needed to capture Cherbourg, Caen, or key road networks. But once the Allies established themselves ashore, Germany’s wider strategic position would still be dire. The Soviet advance in the east, Allied bombing, fuel shortages, and the imbalance in industrial capacity would remain overwhelming.

So the likely answer is that 100,000 Vichy French troops on the Atlantic Wall would make the liberation of France more costly and perhaps somewhat slower, but they would not prevent it. The deeper effect might be less on the military outcome of the war than on the political memory of France, making collaboration far more central, visible, and traumatic in the country’s postwar history.

Germany and its friends would be pleased to hear that. As I understand it, the Haber-Bosch process spread more slowly than people often assume. Fixing nitrogen in a laboratory and mass-producing chemical fertilizer in a factory are entirely different challenges. Building reactors that could withstand pressures of 200 to 300 atmospheres, developing steel alloys that could endure prolonged exposure to high temperature and high pressure, solving catalyst lifespan problems, controlling thermal runaway and explosions, designing continuous processes, and making the system capable of running nonstop for thousands of hours—this was not simply a matter of chemistry, but a comprehensive scientific and engineering project that required physics, materials science, mechanical engineering, and electrical engineering as well. In the 1910s, Germany was the only country in the world capable of doing both. In the OTL, once the Haber process had been developed, the First World War broke out almost immediately. During that period, all resources were directed not toward chemical fertilizer production, but toward the development of explosives. Even afterward, BASF maintained its monopoly over the Haber method.

items.model_answer:
If World War I had happened in 1905 instead of 1914, the war would likely still have been a major European conflict driven by rival alliances, imperial competition, and nationalism, but its course and consequences would probably have been quite different because the political map, military technology, and internal stability of the great powers were all somewhat different.

The most immediate difference is that a 1905 war would probably have emerged out of a different crisis. In 1905 Europe was in the middle of the First Moroccan Crisis, Russo-Japanese War fallout, and continuing instability in the Balkans, but the alliance blocs were not yet as rigidly mobilized around a Sarajevo-style trigger. Germany was already worried about encirclement, France wanted security, Russia was weakened by defeat against Japan and by the 1905 Revolution, and Britain had only recently aligned more closely with France. So a war in 1905 might still have pitted Germany and Austria-Hungary against France and perhaps Russia, but Russia would have been less ready, and Britain’s role might initially have been more hesitant or limited.

Militarily, a 1905 world war would have been less industrially mature than the one that began in 1914. Machine guns, heavy artillery, rail mobilization, and barbed wire already existed, so the war could still have become very deadly. But tanks did not yet exist, military aviation was in its infancy, and some of the massive artillery and logistical systems of 1914–18 were not yet fully developed. That means the war might have begun with more fluid maneuver and less of the fully developed trench deadlock that came to define the Western Front, though stalemate was still possible. Armies would also generally have been smaller and somewhat less prepared for a total war of attrition on the later scale.

Russia is one of the biggest variables. In 1914 Russia was still flawed but stronger than it had been in 1905. If a general war had broken out in 1905, Russia’s recent defeat by Japan and domestic revolution could have made it militarily and politically weaker. That might have benefited Germany and Austria-Hungary early in the conflict and perhaps made a Central Powers victory more plausible than it was in the actual war. On the other hand, Austria-Hungary was already fragile, and an early war could still have exposed its military weakness and internal ethnic tensions.

Germany’s position would also be different. In 1905 Germany faced a France that had not yet completed all the military reforms and a Russia that was temporarily crippled. From Berlin’s perspective, this was in some ways a better moment for war than 1914. The Schlieffen-style logic of defeating France quickly before turning east might therefore have seemed even more attractive. If Britain stayed out at first or intervened late, Germany’s chances of a favorable outcome would rise sharply.

A key global difference concerns the United States. In 1905 the United States was less likely to play the decisive financial and military role it eventually did after 1917. America was important, but not yet positioned psychologically or diplomatically in relation to Europe in the same way. Without later U.S. intervention, a long war might have ended in a negotiated peace rather than a clear Allied victory. That would dramatically change the twentieth century.

If the war ended earlier or more indecisively, many later historical outcomes might not occur in the same form. There might be no Treaty of Versailles as we know it, no “stab-in-the-back” myth in exactly the same way, and possibly no Hitler or Nazi movement emerging from the specific German resentment and post-1918 crisis that actually happened. The Russian Revolution might also look very different. A war in 1905 could either destroy the tsarist regime earlier, because it was already under huge stress, or it might produce a limited constitutional settlement without the exact chain of disasters that led to the Bolshevik seizure of power in 1917. Either way, the Soviet Union might not emerge in the same form, or at least not on the same timetable.

The Ottoman Empire might also fare differently. By 1914 it had already been badly weakened by the Balkan Wars. In 1905 it was still fragile, but somewhat less diminished. Its role in a general European war might therefore be less predictable. The Balkans too would matter differently: nationalism was already dangerous, but the alignment of Serbia, Bulgaria, and the surrounding powers was not yet identical to the pre-1914 situation.

In the colonies, an earlier war would likely weaken European empires, but perhaps not as decisively as the real war did. Since World War I helped accelerate anti-colonial movements by exhausting imperial powers and mobilizing colonial troops, a 1905 version might still push in that direction, but perhaps more slowly if the war were shorter or less total.

So the most plausible broad answer is this: a world war in 1905 would probably still be devastating, but it might be shorter, somewhat less technologically mature, and more favorable to Germany because Russia was weaker and Britain’s commitment was less certain. The biggest historical consequence is that the chain leading from 1914 to Versailles, the Bolshevik Revolution, fascism, and then World War II would be disrupted. Europe might still emerge unstable and violent, but the specific path of the twentieth century could be radically different—possibly with no Nazi Germany, no Soviet Union in its familiar form, and no Second World War as we know it.

items.model_answer:
A 1996 election between Nelson Rockefeller/Cisneros and Dan Quayle/Lamar Alexander would require a very different prior history, since Rockefeller died in 1979, but as a counterfactual it points to a very different ideological and demographic contest than the actual Clinton–Dole race.

The broad shape of the election would likely favor Rockefeller/Cisneros, probably by a clear but not overwhelming margin. Rockefeller represented the old liberal-to-moderate Republican establishment: pro-business, internationalist, socially moderate, comfortable with a strong federal government, and appealing to suburban professionals, Wall Street, much of the Northeast, and moderate independents. Adding Henry Cisneros would strengthen the ticket’s appeal to urban voters, Latinos, and Sun Belt moderates, while also signaling generational and ethnic modernization. In effect, this ticket would try to build a coalition of affluent suburbanites, minorities open to pragmatic centrism, and voters tired of ideological polarization.

Quayle/Alexander would be much more purely conservative, though in somewhat different styles. Quayle would bring cultural conservatism, ties to the Reagan-Bush right, and appeal in the South and parts of the Midwest, while Alexander would project a more competent, technocratic, and less combative image than Quayle alone. Still, the ticket would likely struggle with credibility and gravitas. Quayle’s real-world public image in the 1990s was weak; many voters saw him as inexperienced or unserious. Alexander would help, but probably not enough to fully overcome that liability.

The campaign’s main divide would not be Democrat versus Republican in the normal sense, but moderate establishment pragmatism versus movement conservatism. Rockefeller would probably dominate among Northeastern and West Coast moderates, upscale suburbanites, and many independents. Quayle would do well with evangelical voters, rural conservatives, and the South. The Midwest would be mixed: Alexander could help in border-state and upper-South areas, but Rockefeller’s managerial competence and centrist image would likely appeal in major metropolitan regions.

In electoral-college terms, Rockefeller/Cisneros would probably win states like New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, California, Illinois, and likely much of the industrial Northeast. They would also be competitive in places like Florida, where Cisneros’s Hispanic appeal and Rockefeller’s moderate profile could matter. Quayle/Alexander would likely hold much of the Deep South, the Great Plains, and strongly conservative Mountain West states. Texas would become especially interesting: Cisneros could make it closer than expected, but Quayle’s conservatism would still probably keep it in his column unless Rockefeller’s campaign became a major national wave.

Compared with the real 1996 election, this race would probably be more ideologically clarifying. Clinton in reality occupied much of the center and deprived Republicans of moderate suburban space. In this counterfactual, Rockefeller would be the one monopolizing the center, leaving Quayle with fewer paths beyond energizing the right. That is a harder general-election strategy in the 1990s, when the national mood was relatively prosperous, post–Cold War, and not especially hungry for sharp ideological change.

The result, then, is most likely a Rockefeller/Cisneros victory, perhaps something like a solid popular-vote win and a comfortable electoral-college majority, though not necessarily a landslide. Quayle/Alexander would run strongly in conservative America, but Rockefeller’s stature, moderation, and broader coalition would probably make him the favorite in a 1996 national electorate.

items.question: What If Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest
human_answers: I would think that you would see a Nelsonian style of celebration and loss. Assuming that the weather was clear enough to allow for Odell, who was alone, to witness their summit and subsequent descent and deadly fall, the MAJOR issue is that Odell does not have a camera on him. The one thing that would irrefutably prove that Mallory and Irvine summited the mountain and then died on their decent would be a photograph, even a distant one, of them on or practically at the summit. Now, Irvine or Mallory did have a camera on them, the near legendary Kodak that is still missing to this day and may hold the truth of whether or not they made it. Assuming that Odell witnessed the summit and the subsequent fall, AND he could record where their bodies fell or near where they fell, then it becomes an issue of finding their bodies and the Kodak. Odell was a respected and trusted witness so i do not think that many would dispute his claim, but finding their remains and the camera would be a major point of corroborating his account. If their bodies and the camera were found, with photographic proof that they did make the summit found in it, it would be both widely celebrated and mourned. Mallory and Irvine would be national heroes in Britain and probably recognized across the world for their achievement. They were historically given a memorial service at St Paul's in London, which was widely attended by many people up to an including the then Prince of Wales, the future Edward VIII. Unlike Franklin or Scott, who were either not found or left where they died, Mallory's body at the least was in a location that its recovery was certainly possible, an Irvine's body may have ended up in a similar location if their death was witnessed. If their bodies were recovered, probably with a sponsored expedition, i could easily see a joint funeral for both in St. Paul's, potentially even reaching a State Funeral with full Royal attendance. Then you have the lasting impact that this would have on the psyche of Britain and the world. After the 1924 Expedition there was a major underswell in mountaineering circles, especially British ones, and to a lesser extent in the greater British populace, that Everest was "unfinished business." While there was a drop off in attempts after the 1924 failure, there was a massive resurgence in the 1930s, a pause during the war for obvious reasons, and then a similar surge in the 1950s culminating in the 1953 success. If Mallory and Irvine reached the top in 1924, that would greatly decrease the interest in Everest. Ironically, Mallory's and Irvine's death, and the debate that raged and still rages over whether they made the summit or not, drove the popularity and allure of the mountain far beyond what it would be if they succeeded but died on the way down. There probably would be several more attempts in the aftermath, at least one of which would probably be sponsored by groups like the British Alpine Club or the Royal Geographic Society as a symbolic summit and successful decent in tribute to Mallory and Irvine. I wouldn't be surprised if they hauled a plaque all the way up there to set up a memorial for them. But Everest probably wouldn't have the same level of mystique is has today. By provably succeeding and dying in the aftermath, Mallory and Irvine would probably completely reshape how we see Everest. Edit: Having gone over this again, the nerd in me now wants the Kodak to be a legendary item in a video game OR an SCP entry. would be a fun nod to an event few people would ever know about.

And that infamous camera. What we know for sure: the cylinder, the ice axe and Mallory's body tells us they were roped together at a minimum of 8475 metres, before they fell. Bummers, that's 2133 meters below. Talk about a fall, even if the glacier probably lowered the body on the moutain, along the years.
