So I can tell you that summit fever is very real. I have never climbed anything like Everest obviously but I have scaled (as in hiked) a few 14,000 footers in Colorado and even with that I can state with authority that due to the combination of being tired and euphoric on the way down along with the general feeling that the mission has been accomplished, the brain is not working quite right. That's just reality. Plus, you now have gravity pulling you along. Given that I agree that it is far more likely Mallory and Irvine fell on the descent, either after making the summit or deciding to turn back for whatever reason. While it is unlikely they would have turned back that close to the summit we can't dismiss it either. 400 meters from the summit may not sound like much but at that altitude is actually a very long distance and maybe the combination of bad weather, declining oxygen supplies, or overall uncertainty caused them to turn around. My personal opinion - they made it to the top (it part because I want it to be true) and fell badly on the way down but until we can get actual physical evidence that clearly shows they made the summit that's all it is, an opinion.

Interestingly a lot of practical research has gone into trying to answer the question of whether or not the clothing worn by Mallory and Irvine would have been sufficient to enable them to survive the extreme environment. This has included tests in weather chambers and even a 2006 Everest expedition with climbers wearing exact replicas of Mallory's clothing. The overall conclusion of these tests in generally that the clothing itself was actually quite comfortable and well insulated and that provided Mallory and Irvine kept moving and didn't stop for any length of time or encounter any serious deterioration in weather conditions they could have continued to "operate effectively". Weather chamber tests showed that with the clothing they had Mallory and Irvine could have survived temperatures of −30 °C. Although it was also found that if wind speed picked up the insulation of the clothing would only just be sufficient to −10 °C. While a lot of luck would have been required its not beyond the realms of possibility that Mallory and Irvine could have succeeded in the right conditions. A bigger factor would have probably been whether or not they were carrying sufficient oxygen and if their relatively primitive breathing apparatus could be relied on not to fail (One of the reasons why Mallory chose the relatively inexperienced Irvine to accompany him on his summit attempt was due to the latter's expertise with the breathing apparatus).

They never intended to climb the second step. In fact, no one knew the second step existed in 1924. And Mallory wrote that he considered the NE ridge route impossible. Odell's sighting put them at the base of the summit pyramid, above the third step, anyway. Mallory very clearly explained his intended route in his letters, which was to bypass the steps and either take the zig-zag or the couloir. Anker is ... a controversial source on anything 1924. He has a habit of disregarding any evidence that contradicts his theories on Mallory/Irvine. It's more likely than not that they summited and died on the way down, by virtue of the fact that they died . The vast majority of climbers who've died on Everest got summit fever and died on the descent because they pushed themselves way too hard to reach the peak. Michael Tracy is a grump, but he's done more to shed light on the truth of 1924 Mallory/Irvine than basically anyone else. This video is one of his that cover's their intended routes. We'll never know what actually happened of course – the '99 team utterly botched their investigation upon finding Mallory, and given Irvine's foot was found in the Rongbuk Glacier, his body probably fell clean off the mountain below Mallory in '24 so we're unlikely ever find it. But barring new evidence, the most plausible theory is that they made the summit and died on the descent that evening/night.
items.original_question: What if Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest In 1953 the New Zealand Mountaineer Edmund Hillary and Nepalese Sherpa Tenzing Norgay became the first people to reach the summit of Mount Everest (8.849m). However there remains to this day an enduring question about whether or not Hillary and Norgay actually were the first people to reach the summit of Everest or simply the first to do so and survive the experience. In 1924 during the second British expedition to attempt to conquer Everest British climbers George Mallory and Sandy Irvine set off on the expeditions third attempt to reach the summit. An attempt from which neither man would return. On the morning of the 6th of June Mallory and Irvine had set off for the summit from their final camp (8,138 m on the North Ridge). Their progress was tracked and filmed by expedition leader Noel Oddell who had positioned himself on a ridge further down the mountain to observe and record the expected first summit of the mountain. Mallory and Irvine were last spotted through a gap in the clouds approximately 240 metres from the summit still proceeding onwards. After this the pair simply disappeared. Despite many searches in the days and years following their disappearance the pair would not be seen again for another 75 years when Mallory's remarkably well preserved body would be discovered at an altitude of 8,156m. In the 1933 expedition an ice axe that could only have belonged to Mallory or Irvine was discovered at an altitude of 8,380m proving that the pair had reached at least this altitude. The location and state of Mallory's body (Irvine's partial remains in the form of a detached foot would later emerge from a glacier at a much lower altitude) indicated that he had suffered a fall which had resulted in his death either as a direct result or by later exposure likely during a decent of the mountain. The body revealed circumstantial evidence that suggests Mallory might have successfully reached the summit. Mallory carried a photo of his wife with the intention of leaving it on the summit. No such photo was found on the body. Given the excellent preservation of the body and personal possessions, the absence of the photo suggests he may have reached the summit and deposited it there. Mallory's snow goggles were in his pocket, indicating he may have died at night; that he and Irvine had made a push for the summit and were descending very late in the day. Given their known departure time and movements, had they not made the summit, it is unlikely they would have still been out by nightfall. Perhaps the one artefact that may put the mystery to bed is the Kodak pocket camera that Irvine was known to be carrying and which he presumably would have used to take a photo of the first successful ascent had such a thing occurred and may still contain useable photographs of the attempt. Assuming that Mallory had been successful in reaching the summit and managed to avoid whatever calamity befell on their decent and are able to survive the whole ordeal what would the the effects have been of Mount Everest having been summited for the first time by George Mallory in 1924? How would this have affected the history of Everest and expeditions to climb the mountain after 1924? How would Mallory and Irvine's achievement have been received and remembered?
items.model_answer:
If George Mallory and Andrew “Sandy” Irvine had reached the summit of Everest in 1924 and then survived to tell the story, it would likely have changed both the history of exploration and the cultural meaning of Everest in major ways.

First, the British Empire would have claimed one of the greatest exploration victories of the age. In 1924 Everest was not just a mountain challenge; it was tied to national prestige. Britain had failed to be first to the poles in the most triumphant way and still valued heroic exploration as proof of national character. A successful and surviving Mallory and Irvine would have become instant global celebrities, probably among the most famous men in the English-speaking world. Their ascent would have been framed as a triumph of courage, discipline, and imperial science. That would have mattered especially because Everest was then approached from Tibet, under conditions shaped by diplomacy and empire rather than modern mountaineering tourism.

Second, the mythology of Everest would be very different. In our history, Mallory’s disappearance helped create the mountain’s central legend: the unresolved question of whether they were first. That mystery gave Everest a haunting quality. If they had summited and survived, there would be no great “did they make it?” debate. Instead of being remembered as tragic, semi-mythic figures, they would be remembered as clear victors and pioneers. The mountain’s symbolic history would shift from one of fatal obsession and ambiguity to one of early human conquest through improvisation and boldness.

Third, the 1953 ascent by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay would still have been important, but not as the “first ascent.” It might instead have been celebrated as the first ascent by a new route variation, the first fully documented modern ascent, or the first postwar ascent. Hillary and Tenzing would still likely be famous because of the quality of their climb and the era’s media coverage, but their place in global memory would probably be reduced. Tenzing in particular might not have become quite the same symbol of Himalayan mountaineering achievement, because the defining “first” would already belong to two Britons from the interwar period.

Fourth, mountaineering technique and risk culture might have evolved differently. A successful 1924 oxygen-assisted ascent would have validated high-altitude climbing technology much earlier. It might have encouraged faster acceptance of supplemental oxygen, clothing systems, and siege-style expedition planning. At the same time, because Mallory and Irvine would have succeeded with equipment far cruder than later climbers used, their climb might have reinforced a heroic ideal that boldness and endurance mattered more than technical refinement. Future expeditions may have felt both inspired and pressured to emulate them, possibly leading to more attempts in the 1920s and 1930s if political access to Tibet had allowed it.

Fifth, their survival would have had a large effect on how the story was told because they could explain what actually happened near the top. Historians and climbers would know whether the Second Step was climbed, how effective their oxygen gear was, what route choices they made, and what conditions they faced. That knowledge could have advanced Himalayan climbing earlier by replacing speculation with practical experience. Their testimony would also have shaped debates about human limits at extreme altitude.

There would also be consequences for the culture of heroism. Mallory’s famous reply, “Because it’s there,” became iconic partly because he died and was turned into a symbol of pure, fatal aspiration. A living Mallory might have become not just a legend but a public intellectual of climbing—lecturing, writing, advising expeditions, perhaps influencing generations of mountaineers directly. Irvine, who was young and technically gifted, might have gained recognition as more than Mallory’s junior partner; he could have become an important figure in expedition engineering or oxygen-system design.

Politically and culturally, Britain might have woven the ascent into a broader story of imperial endurance during a period of weakening global dominance. It would not have reversed imperial decline, but it would have offered a potent symbolic victory. Schoolbooks, newspapers, and public ceremonies would likely have enshrined the ascent as a quintessential British achievement. The fact that Everest was later first climbed in the age of decolonization gave the 1953 ascent a different tone; a 1924 success would have been more straightforwardly imperial in its meaning.

At the same time, some longer-term effects would be surprisingly limited. Everest would still eventually become a global obsession. Nepal’s later opening, advances in aviation, postwar media, and commercial expedition culture would still transform the mountain. Mallory and Irvine’s success would not stop Everest from becoming crowded in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries. But the origin story of that obsession would be different: Everest would have been “won” much earlier, and perhaps seen less as the final unconquered summit of the modern world than as an interwar masterpiece of exploration.

So the biggest change is this: Everest would lose one of history’s greatest mysteries and gain one of history’s clearest heroic victories. Britain would likely have owned the symbolic first ascent, Mallory and Irvine would stand beside the greatest explorers of any age, and the later history of mountaineering would unfold under the shadow not of their disappearance, but of their success.

items.model_answer:
If film, comics, and broadcasting in the United States had gained strong First Amendment protection and stable union protection much earlier in the twentieth century, American mass culture would likely have developed into a more openly political, more artistically diverse, and more labor-stable system much sooner. The biggest effects would probably appear in censorship, labor relations, representation, and the political role of media.

In actual history, each of these media developed under constraints that limited both content and working conditions. Film faced censorship and the Production Code; comics were shaken by moral panic and the Comics Code; broadcasting operated under heavy political scrutiny and the logic of licensing, which encouraged caution. At the same time, labor protections in these industries were uneven, delayed, or contested, leaving writers, actors, animators, technicians, and later broadcasters vulnerable to studio control and blacklisting. If constitutional and union protections had arrived earlier and been more secure, media industries would likely have matured differently.

In film, earlier First Amendment protection would probably have weakened the legitimacy of state and local censorship boards and reduced the power of the Hays Code. Hollywood films in the 1920s, 1930s, and 1940s might have addressed sexuality, race, labor conflict, poverty, fascism, and political corruption more directly. The sharp boundary between “respectable” studio entertainment and more daring independent or foreign work might have been less pronounced. American cinema could have resembled postwar European film earlier in its willingness to treat controversial themes as normal subjects rather than dangerous exceptions.

In comics, earlier legal and cultural protection would have mattered enormously. Comics were treated as low-status and suspect, especially by midcentury critics who blamed them for juvenile delinquency. If they had enjoyed robust First Amendment protection earlier, the anti-comics panic of the 1950s might have had far less power. The Comics Code Authority may never have become as dominant, or it might have emerged in a much weaker form. That would likely have allowed horror, crime, political satire, adult drama, and autobiographical comics to flourish decades earlier. The idea of comics as a medium for all ages, rather than primarily for children, might have become mainstream by the mid-twentieth century instead of much later.

Broadcasting is a more complicated case because it was tied to public spectrum regulation. Even with stronger First Amendment protection, radio and television would still likely have remained subject to some licensing rules. But earlier constitutional protection could have reduced the climate of caution that made networks vulnerable to advertiser pressure, anti-radical campaigns, and government intimidation. News and public affairs programming might have become more adversarial earlier. There may have been more room for dissenting political viewpoints, stronger investigative journalism, and less fear-driven self-censorship during periods such as the Red Scare and McCarthy era.

The labor side is equally important. Earlier and stronger union protections in film, comics, and broadcasting would likely have shifted power away from studio heads, publishers, and network executives. Writers, performers, animators, camera crews, radio workers, and comic artists could have secured better pay, credit, residuals, job security, and control over working conditions much earlier. In comics especially, where creators often lost ownership of characters and received little compensation, stronger unions might have transformed the economics of the field. Creator rights and royalties might have become standard long before the late twentieth century, changing not only artists’ livelihoods but also the kinds of works they were willing to produce.

This would also likely have reduced the effectiveness of blacklisting. If media workers had both stronger labor institutions and stronger speech protections, anti-communist purges in Hollywood and broadcasting might still have occurred, but they would have been harder to enforce and easier to challenge. Careers destroyed by political suspicion might have survived. As a result, American media culture in the 1940s and 1950s might have contained more openly left-liberal, labor-oriented, and anti-racist perspectives.

Representation would probably have changed as well. Earlier freedom from censorship and stronger collective organization could have opened more space for women, racial minorities, immigrants, and queer creators and characters. This would not automatically eliminate prejudice, since industries and audiences still reflected broader social inequalities. But institutional barriers would have been lower. More creators from marginalized groups might have found sustainable careers, and more stories about minority experiences might have reached mass audiences earlier.

There would also be economic consequences. Stronger unions often raise labor costs, so the big studios, publishers, and networks might have produced fewer works at certain points or resisted innovation more aggressively. Some executives would likely have argued that heavy labor protections reduced flexibility. At the same time, more secure workers and freer creators often produce more durable and ambitious cultural products. So the result might not have been less media, but a different mix: fewer disposable, tightly controlled products and more works with distinctive authorial voices.

Politically, earlier constitutional and labor protection for these media could have made the United States more accustomed to mass media as a site of democratic contest rather than moral regulation. Public debates over media harm would not disappear, but the presumption might shift from “control dangerous media” to “protect expressive freedom unless there is clear harm.” That would have broader implications for American political culture, making it harder to suppress controversial ideas simply because they were popular, visual, or aimed at mass audiences.

Overall, if film, comics, and broadcasting had gained First Amendment and union protections much earlier, twentieth-century American culture would likely have been less censored, less hierarchical, and more politically and artistically pluralistic. The United States probably would have seen earlier development of adult comics, more daring studio films, more independent broadcasting, stronger creator rights, and weaker blacklists. The central tradeoff would have been greater conflict between labor and management and fewer mechanisms for elite control, but the likely long-term result would have been a richer and more democratic media landscape.

Luigi Casale develops the Casale process after WWI. Italy had a deficit of fertilizers pre-war; it didn't have the trade networks or finances of other nations to purchase Chilean saltpeter in large amounts, and they invested heavily in nitrogen fixation as a result. WWI worsened that deficit, compounded by the loss of wheat imports from Russia, so Casale started work in 1917 on a more efficient method of nitrogen fixation. Said research continued in the postwar, because BASF refused to license the Haber-Bosch process elsewhere, and the Haber-Bosch process would have required modification anyways because Italy didn't have sufficient coal to use it to produce hydrogen gas in the original Haber-Bosch process. So Italy has the incentive to develop efficient nitrogen fixation processes for strategic autonomy, and Casale has the means to do so. Casale did postgraduate research in Berlin under Walter Nernst, whose research into physical chemistry mirrored that of Haber's, before returning to Italy. Casale then works near the Terni steelworks, which provided the steel to build pressure reactors able to stand pressures more than 3 times that of the Haber-Bosch process (notably by providing an unused battleship gun barrel). Even if we assume some sort of inexplicable theft or espionage on the part of Casale not mentioned in these histories and somehow nobody else thinks to apply Le Chatelier's Principle or try different catalysts, that just means the Frank-Caro process dominates. Sure, the 3x difference in energy usage is going to be difficult to bear, but between that and losing a total war/starving, people will just build more power plants and mine more fossil fuels or mineral nitrates/phosphates. Central to the mass production of fertilizer and explosives. It has been billed as the most consequential scientific breakthrough of the twentieth century. Historical perspectives on ammonia range from technological development to natural resource use, geopolitics, wartime... www.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de

Arguably the only hard bit of the Haber process is the need for pressurisation to encourage the reaction to react in the right direction. The rest is more or less basic chemistry. So initially the other less efficient methods get adopted (because the nitrates are useful and profitable) and when suitable pressure vessels become available someone discovers the alt-Haber process. Unlike OTL, there will be more opportunity to refine and improve the other less efficient methods of manufacture. Pressure vessels themselves are relatively easy once you have late 19th century naval guns to adapt or inspire: durable pressure vessels are a bit harder [1], but any ferrous vessel will tend to provide iron catalyst even if nobody thought of using it beforehand. items.original_question: What if the Haber process is never invented? Let's say that Haber fails to impress Bosch and the BASF in July 1909 due to a failed demonstration of ammonia synthesis. What happens next? Would Haber go elsewhere to find a sponsor, or move on to something else? Cause this would mean that the entire discipline of industrial chemistry is stunted, and high pressure chemistry doesn't exist. Would WW1 even start?
items.model_answer:
If the Haber process is never invented, the modern world is much poorer, smaller, and more politically unstable.

The core reason is nitrogen. Plants need usable nitrogen to grow, but most of the nitrogen in the air is chemically inaccessible to them. Before Haber-Bosch, agriculture depended on natural nitrogen sources like manure, crop rotation with legumes, compost, and mined nitrate deposits such as Chilean saltpeter and guano. Those sources are limited. Without industrial nitrogen fixation, global food production would hit a hard ceiling much earlier.

The biggest consequence is population. In real history, synthetic fertilizer supported the huge agricultural gains of the twentieth century. Without it, yields would be much lower almost everywhere, especially for cereal crops like wheat, rice, and maize. The world population would almost certainly be far smaller than today, perhaps by billions. Many countries that in reality underwent rapid population growth would instead face chronic food scarcity, stronger pressure to limit family size, or repeated famine.

Agriculture would look different. Farmers would devote much more land to maintaining soil fertility, especially through legume rotations and livestock manure. More people would have to work in farming because productivity per worker would be lower. Meat production would also be constrained, since livestock both consume grain and produce manure, creating a tighter agricultural balance. Forests and grasslands would likely be converted to cropland more aggressively in some regions to compensate for lower yields, though in other regions population limits might reduce total pressure on land. So the environmental outcome is mixed: less synthetic fertilizer pollution, but potentially more deforestation and habitat loss per unit of food.

Economically, industrialization would still happen, but with a lower ceiling on urbanization and growth. Modern economies rely on a small farming sector feeding a huge non-farming population. Without synthetic fertilizer, many more workers stay tied to the land, slowing the expansion of cities, education, heavy industry, and service economies. Standards of living rise more slowly, especially in densely populated countries with poor soils or limited access to natural nitrates.

Geopolitically, the world changes sharply. Access to natural nitrate deposits becomes strategically crucial. Countries with nitrate resources, especially Chile, become much more important. Major powers would compete intensely over fertilizer and explosives precursors, because fixed nitrogen matters not just for farming but also for munitions. Germany’s situation in World War I is a classic example: the Haber-Bosch process helped it keep producing explosives despite blockade. Without it, Germany would likely run short sooner, which could shorten the war or alter its course. More broadly, states would be more vulnerable to blockades and resource chokepoints.

There is also a dark military tradeoff. No Haber process means less large-scale domestic production of nitrates for explosives, which could reduce the intensity or duration of some wars. But it would not eliminate industrial warfare, and it would increase competition for natural nitrate supplies. So military effects would be significant but not straightforwardly peaceful.

Public health and society would also be different. Chronic malnutrition would be more common. Political systems would face repeated crises over bread prices and harvest failures. Governments might invest much earlier in birth control, land reform, rationing systems, agricultural science, and alternative nitrogen-fixation methods. In fact, strong pressure would exist to develop some substitute process sooner or later, because the demand is so overwhelming. If Haber specifically never invents his process, someone else might eventually discover another scalable route to synthetic ammonia, though perhaps later, more expensively, or less efficiently. If we assume no equivalent process emerges at all, then the long-run constraint on human society is severe.

So the simplest answer is this: without the Haber process, there is no Green Revolution in anything like the form we know, global population stays much lower, famines are more frequent, economic development is slower, and international politics revolve more heavily around scarce natural nitrogen. The world is less chemically intensive, but also less prosperous and less capable of feeding itself.

items.original_question:
AHC: one people, two nation-states

There have been plenty of cases where one people with a common language and ancestry are separated into two nation-states. I'm not talking about ideological reasons like in the case of Germany and Korea, but in terms of centuries-long division of religion (Catholic Croats and Orthodox Serbs or Catholic Austrians and Protestant Germans) or geopolitics (Montenegro and Ottoman-dominated Serbia, Russia-dominated Moldova and Romania, Bulgaria and North Macedonia). And this explains why I specifically use the term "nation-state", as one people separated for long enough by the aforementioned factors would eventually evolve into different nation-states with their own ethnic identities. Is there any other scenario where this can happen?
items.model_answer:
If one people are divided between two nation-states, the result is usually a tension between shared identity and separate political loyalty. A single people may still have the same language, history, religion, ethnicity, or collective memory, but once they live under two different states, each state begins shaping them through its own laws, institutions, education system, economy, and foreign policy.

Over time, several outcomes are possible. The two states may remain closely connected, treating themselves as parts of a broader national community despite political separation. This can produce cooperation, cross-border solidarity, and even movements for reunification or confederation. But separation can also harden. Each state may cultivate its own version of history and patriotism, so that the one people gradually become two politically distinct nations in practice, even if they still claim common origins.

This situation can also create conflict. If both states claim to represent the same people, they may compete for legitimacy. Minorities on each side of the border may face pressure to prove loyalty. Questions of citizenship, migration, military service, and sovereignty become sensitive. In extreme cases, one state may seek unification by force, or outside powers may exploit the division.

So “one people, two nation-states” generally means that cultural nationhood and political statehood do not perfectly match. It does not automatically lead to war or unity, but it almost always creates an unstable relationship in which identity, sovereignty, and belonging are continuously negotiated.

AHC: Reverse Cuba and the Philippines

items.model_answer:
If Cuba and the Philippines had been “reversed” in the sense that the United States annexed Cuba as a long-term territory while granting the Philippines rapid independence, the late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century history of U.S. imperialism would likely have looked quite different, though not completely transformed.

Cuba was much closer to the United States, deeply tied to the U.S. economy, and already central to American strategic thinking because of the Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, and the future Panama Canal zone. If the U.S. had kept Cuba outright instead of treating it as a nominally independent protectorate, it probably would have become a much more integrated part of the American sphere, perhaps closer to Puerto Rico in status, though its large population, strong nationalism, and plantation economy would still have made annexation politically contentious. American investors would likely have expanded even faster there, and Washington might have intervened even more directly in Cuban politics rather than relying on devices like the Platt Amendment. Cuban nationalism, in turn, might have become more sharply anti-colonial earlier, because formal annexation would have removed even the symbolic promise of sovereignty.

If, on the other hand, the Philippines had been granted early independence after Spain’s defeat, the United States would have avoided the Philippine-American War or greatly reduced it. That would have meant fewer casualties, less domestic controversy over overseas empire, and a weaker test case for large-scale American colonial rule in Asia. The anti-imperialist movement in the United States might have been stronger politically, because the U.S. would have been able to claim it had liberated rather than conquered a former Spanish colony. At the same time, an independent Philippines in 1898 or shortly after would have faced serious problems: factional conflict, limited state capacity, possible vulnerability to Japan, Germany, or other powers, and heavy continued U.S. economic and naval influence. So independence would not necessarily have meant full autonomy.

Strategically, this reversal would have made U.S. empire look more Caribbean-centered and less Pacific-Asian. The United States still would have pursued Asian trade, but without direct control of the Philippines its military and diplomatic role in East Asia might have been weaker. That could have reduced later American leverage in the western Pacific and slightly altered the buildup to U.S.-Japanese rivalry. Meanwhile, stronger formal control over Cuba would have underscored the Monroe Doctrine style of regional domination in the Americas.

Politically and ideologically, the reversal would have exposed a major contradiction even more clearly. Americans often justified intervention in Cuba in the language of liberation, while rule in the Philippines was defended through “civilizing” arguments. If Cuba had been annexed and the Philippines freed, the U.S. might have appeared more honest in Asia and more blatantly imperial in the Caribbean. Race would have remained central: many U.S. policymakers were more comfortable dominating nearby tropical territories indirectly, and many were uneasy about annexing large nonwhite populations as full parts of the Union. So annexing Cuba might still have stopped short of statehood and produced a colonial arrangement marked by legal inequality.

Overall, reversing Cuba and the Philippines would probably have reduced the scale of U.S. imperial war in Asia, intensified formal American domination in the Caribbean, and shifted the symbolism of 1898. The United States would still have emerged as an imperial power, but one more focused on nearby hemispheric control than on transpacific colonial expansion.

items.original_question: What if Both Germany and Italy don't join PANAVIA Tornado program? What if both Germany and Italy for some reason both bail or don't join the PANAVIA Tornado program at it's inception? What are the options regarding this? What does Germany, Italy and the UK do? Could the UK carry on alone? What aircraft could replace the Tornado and fill in this role? Could a two seat, big wing SEPECAT Jaguar work? Would an advanced Buccaneer work with a modern avionics upgrade? Regards
items.model_answer:
If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado program at the outset, the most likely result is that the whole project would either have been radically scaled down into a mostly British aircraft or collapsed entirely and been replaced by separate national programs.

The Tornado was not just a technical collaboration; it was an economic and political arrangement built around sharing enormous development costs and guaranteeing a large production run. Britain alone might still have wanted a low-level strike aircraft to replace the Canberra and Buccaneer in some roles, but without German and Italian money, orders, and industrial participation, the aircraft would have become much more expensive per unit. That would have put severe pressure on the UK to simplify the design, buy something off the shelf, or pursue a smaller national project. A purely British Tornado-like aircraft might have existed, but it probably would have been less ambitious, produced in lower numbers, and entered service later.

For West Germany and Italy, withdrawing early would probably have pushed them toward other options. West Germany still needed a strike and interdiction aircraft to replace the F-104 and complement the F-4. It might have bought more American aircraft, especially advanced F-4 variants or later the F-15E/F-16 class of multirole designs as they emerged, though timing matters because in the early 1970s many of those were not yet available. Italy, with a smaller budget and a long history of operating US aircraft, would very likely have leaned even more heavily toward American solutions. In practice, both countries might have ended up buying upgraded US types rather than developing a new European combat aircraft.

That in turn would have had major effects on the European aerospace industry. PANAVIA and the multinational industrial structures around the Tornado helped preserve advanced combat-aircraft design and manufacturing capacity in Britain, West Germany, and Italy. Without the shared Tornado experience, European defense-industrial integration would have been weaker. The path to later programs, especially Eurofighter Typhoon, would likely have been rougher, slower, or politically harder to organize, because Tornado created habits of cooperation, production-sharing formulas, and trust among the main partners. A failed or abandoned Tornado collaboration could have made governments more skeptical of future joint aircraft projects.

Operationally, NATO would probably have lost, or at least delayed, a highly specialized European low-level strike aircraft optimized for the Central Front. The Tornado IDS was designed for exactly the sort of interdiction and deep-strike mission NATO expected in a Warsaw Pact conflict. If the partners had instead bought different US aircraft, NATO might still have filled the capability, but less uniformly and with less emphasis on that specific mission profile. Britain in particular might have had a more fragmented force structure, relying longer on older aircraft or purchasing an American design it had not originally preferred.

There are also second-order effects. Without German and Italian participation, the ADV interceptor variant might never have been built, or would have been even harder to justify. The industrial fortunes of companies that later became part of BAE Systems, Airbus, and Leonardo would have shifted. Fewer common aircraft across European air forces would have meant less shared training, logistics, and political symbolism.

So the short answer is this: if West Germany and Italy had withdrawn at the outset, the Tornado as we know it probably would not have emerged. Britain might have attempted a reduced national substitute, but the more likely broader outcome is that all three countries would have moved toward a mix of national stopgaps and American aircraft, while European aerospace cooperation and the later development of projects like Eurofighter would have been significantly weakened or delayed.

items.model_answer:
If nuclear weapons had never been invented, the world would probably still be violent and dangerous, but in a different way. Nuclear weapons did not create war, rivalry, or imperial ambition; they changed the scale of destruction and the way major powers calculate risk. Without them, history after 1945 likely would have seen more conventional great-power wars, less fear of instant global annihilation, and a different balance of power among states.

One likely effect is that the Cold War would have been hotter. Nuclear deterrence helped prevent the United States and the Soviet Union from fighting each other directly, because both knew a full war could become suicidal. Without nuclear weapons, that caution would be weaker. Crises like Berlin, Korea, or even Cuba might have escalated into direct conventional war between superpowers. Such wars would still have been catastrophic, with millions dead, but they would not carry the same immediate threat of ending civilization.

A second major difference is that military spending and strategy would probably shift toward very large conventional forces. Instead of relying partly on nuclear deterrence, states would invest even more in armies, air forces, navies, missile defenses, chemical weapons, biological weapons, and fortified alliances. Europe in particular might have remained even more heavily militarized throughout the second half of the twentieth century. Some countries may also have pursued alternative “ultimate weapons,” especially chemical and biological arsenals, if nuclear arms were unavailable.

Decolonization and regional conflict might also look different. Smaller states without nuclear powers looming over them might have had more room to maneuver, but great powers might also have intervened more freely if they did not fear escalation to nuclear war. Proxy wars could become direct wars more often. In South Asia, the Middle East, and East Asia, rival states might fight larger conventional conflicts than they did in reality.

At the same time, some positive outcomes are easy to imagine. There would be no Hiroshima or Nagasaki, no arms race measured in megatons, no nuclear accidents like Chernobyl’s military-adjacent anxieties or fears of accidental launch, no doctrine of mutually assured destruction, and no permanent possibility that a political or technical mistake could destroy hundreds of millions of people in hours. Global politics might feel less existentially fragile.

But it would not necessarily be a more peaceful world. Nuclear weapons are morally horrifying, yet many historians argue they helped stabilize relations among the strongest states by raising the cost of total war beyond any acceptable level. Without them, war might be more thinkable. The world could be less apocalyptic but more frequently bloody.

So the best short answer is this: if there were no nuclear weapons, humanity might face fewer risks of sudden global catastrophe, but probably more large-scale conventional wars between major powers. The world would likely be less capable of ending itself in a day, yet not clearly safer overall.

If yes then 2.1)Would this be enough to win the war for Germany? 2.2)Would the US use nukes to deter Germany from winning if they reach close enough to Moscow and assuming Hitler has still declared war on the USA?
items.model_answer:
If the USSR had received a credible leak about Operation Barbarossa shortly before it began, and if Stalin and the Red Army leadership actually acted on it effectively without launching a preemptive strike, the most likely result is not a Soviet prevention of the invasion, but a much less catastrophic summer for the USSR in 1941. Barbarossa would still be a huge German offensive, and the Wehrmacht would still have major qualitative advantages in command, coordination, and operational experience. But the scale of Soviet collapse in the opening weeks would probably be reduced substantially.

The biggest immediate change would be readiness. Historically, Soviet forces near the frontier were caught in a confused and vulnerable posture: aircraft crowded on exposed airfields, units not fully mobilized, ammunition and fuel poorly distributed, command arrangements disrupted, and many formations unable to react coherently. If Soviet leaders had warning and were competent enough to use it, they would disperse aircraft, camouflage depots, bring formations to alert, improve communications, lay mines, prepare demolitions, and move some vulnerable stocks and headquarters farther east. Border units would still be hit hard, but they would not be paralyzed to the same extent. The Luftwaffe would destroy fewer planes on the ground, and the initial German breakthroughs would face more organized resistance.

The second major effect would be on encirclements. In 1941 the Germans destroyed enormous Soviet forces in border battles at Bialystok-Minsk, Smolensk, Uman, and Kiev largely because Soviet command either failed to authorize timely withdrawals or ordered counterattacks under hopeless conditions. A better-prepared and more competent Soviet command would probably trade space for time sooner. That means fewer giant pockets, more troops escaping eastward, and more heavy equipment saved. The Red Army would still lose ground fast, but instead of repeated annihilations it might suffer something closer to severe defeats followed by partial retreats. This matters because the Soviet Union’s real strength was depth: manpower, industry, and the ability to rebuild. Preserving even a fraction more of the 1941 field army could have major downstream effects.

A more orderly Soviet response would also help the evacuation of industry and administration. Historically, the USSR did succeed in moving a remarkable amount of industry eastward, but under desperate conditions. If the front collapsed less dramatically, evacuation could begin earlier and with less chaos. Railways would still be overloaded, but key factories, machine tools, and specialists might be transferred more efficiently. That would improve Soviet production in 1942, especially in vehicles, artillery, ammunition, and communications gear.

On the operational level, the Germans would probably still advance deep into Soviet territory in 1941, but more slowly and at higher cost. They would still win many battles, yet their timetable would erode faster. One of Barbarossa’s core assumptions was that the USSR would disintegrate after a few massive frontier encirclements. If those encirclements are smaller and Soviet resistance stiffens sooner, German logistics become an even larger problem. The Wehrmacht was already operating at the edge of what its transport system could support. A few weeks lost here and there, more equipment wear, more resistance on key river lines, and more surviving Soviet reserves could make the drive on Leningrad, Moscow, and Ukraine less effective.

The Battle for Moscow is where this counterfactual becomes especially important. Historically, the Germans reached the approaches to Moscow but failed from exhaustion, weather, overextension, and Soviet resistance reinforced by reserves. In this scenario, if the Soviets are less shattered in June and July, then by autumn they may have more intact armies, better logistics, and stronger defensive belts before Moscow. That makes it less likely the Germans get as close as they did historically. Moscow probably still becomes the central objective, but Operation Typhoon would face a Red Army in bad shape rather than near-disintegration. The German offensive might culminate earlier and farther from the city.

The political dimension is important too. A less disastrous opening would strengthen Soviet internal stability and perhaps reduce panic in the regime. Stalin’s authority, oddly enough, might become more functional earlier if he had accepted the warning and avoided some of his worst initial mistakes. The Soviet state was never likely to collapse quickly, but a better first response would reinforce confidence among officials, officers, and civilians. Internationally, Britain would be encouraged, and material support through Lend-Lease might become somewhat easier to organize if Soviet resistance looked more sustainable from the outset.

That said, this would not automatically produce a rapid Soviet victory. The Red Army in 1941 had deep structural problems: poor training, uneven leadership, weak communications, rigid doctrine in practice, and the lingering effects of expansion and purges. A warning leak cannot fix all that overnight. German operational skill, especially in mobile warfare, would still be formidable. Even a competent Soviet defensive posture in June 1941 might still lead to large losses, retreats, and the loss of huge territories including much of Ukraine and Belarus. The Wehrmacht would remain dangerous through 1942.

So the most plausible overall outcome is that Barbarossa fails more clearly and earlier as a war-winning strategy. Instead of nearly destroying the Red Army in the border battles and then trying to exploit the resulting collapse, Germany runs into a Soviet Union that bends but does not break from the first week. The Eastern Front becomes a grinding war of attrition sooner. Germany loses more men and matériel in 1941, gains less strategic momentum, and probably has even less chance of taking Moscow. The USSR, while still suffering terribly, enters 1942 in a stronger position than it did historically.

In the long run, that likely means an earlier shift in the balance of the war in the East. The Soviet winter counteroffensive of 1941–42 might be somewhat stronger, German 1942 options in the south more constrained, and the road to eventual Soviet victory shorter or at least less precarious. The war probably still ends with Germany defeated, but with a less desperate Soviet near-collapse in 1941 and therefore a somewhat faster, more confident Soviet recovery.

I’m not saying that nothing would change. There absolutely would be changes from neither artist existing. It’s just that fundamentally: You still have popular music derived from Black American musical traditions. You still have a push away from large swing-style bands and towards smaller guitar-based bands - especially since before the digital era the guitar is the most accessible music instrument for young people wanting to make music. You still have the Baby Boom yielding a much larger youth cohort than before - thus yielding a significant generational divide by the early to mid 1960s as they’ve grown up having not known the struggles of their parents or older siblings - and have more room tackling lifestyle changes without worry for economic precarity. You still have big labels and radio stations wanting to play “different music” for “different races” so to speak. And with that you still have white singers becoming popular for their heavily sanitized covers of black R&B songs ( looks at Pat Boone ). You still have the post-WWII dominance and saturation of American pop culture - including music - in Europe and across the globe. And since the UK and the Commonwealth have virtually zero language barrier with the US - music that imitates American musical traditions (twice removed from Black American roots) has the potential to take off. You still have the advancements in recording technology that gave artists room to make more experimental and groundbreaking music than before. Plus the steady rise of FM radio later in the 1960s to provide a market for more ambitious music. You still have the Sexual Revolution to loosen norms around sex. On top of the various other drivers of the counterculture. You still have the payola scandal and the burnout of 1950s rock stars causing the 1959-64 dearth in the quality of pop music. But that’s just structurally speaking. Aesthetically speaking, things could be shifted around - with some new genre inspired by surf rock and garage rock (though realistically not actually either one of them) blowing up out of nowhere by 1964-65 - and Pat Boone is the King of Rock ‘n’ Roll all the artists of the 1960s are inspired by in terms of singing style and aura. While British rock bands are basically seen as a store brand that only gains later appreciation in the social media era decades later a la Japanese city pop. But it would still fundamentally fit the bigger variables that had been brewing years or even decades before the mid 1960s.

While the absence of the Beatles (and particularly Lennon and McCartney) would deprive us of some very good songs, there were vast numbers of competent bands in Britain that could have filled the niche if given the opportunity- whether together or singly. The bigger impact would probably have been on the penetration of British artists into the USA [1], but that's quite likely to happen eventually because there's money to be made from big crowds of relatively wealthy teenagers who happen to hit on a good enough band. The other impact might have been on the pressure to become singer-songwriters, rather than just singers/performers. Again, money is a big driver so it's likely to happen sooner or later. Otherwise, US innovation is likely to remain largely unchanged (Iggy and the Stooges will still form, and the drivers for hippy culture and rock bands is still there). Meanwhile, the Rolling Stones would still be experimenting with blues and quality musicians like Buddy Holly, Carl Perkins will be filling the niche that Elvis is no longer dominating. In short, different but still broadly recognisable. [1] The Monkees are unlikely to be formed, but songs like Day Dream Believer are too good not to end up being a success, even if it takes a few cover versions to become a real hit.

No Beatles or Elvis? Hmmm the amateur musicologist in me (that's what happens when you're a musician, who has also played in rock bands) says that rock 'n roll would still exist. The chances are also good that you would still have its superstar in the 50s - I read years ago that there were plans to push Carl Perkins (he of "Blue Suede Shoes" fame) towards superstardom by Sun Records. He might have actually become one if he hadn't suffered a major injury (he was in a car crash that kept him out of commission for a long time). Sam Phillips and even Elvis stated that Carl was doing rockabilly before Elvis, and unlike Elvis, Carl was also a songwriter. Most musicians will tell you that having that skill gives you much more staying power - you're not just a performer, you can make money off or songwriting royalties. By the time Carl recovered from the car crash it was too late, Elvis had overshadowed him. Jerry Lee Lewis, courtesy of his flamboyant personality might have become the 50s rock 'n roll superstar (how long he would have lasted would have depended upon whether or not he was still foolish enough to marry his underage cousin). The 60s? Hmmm that's not so certain - in the early 60s, rock 'n roll seemed to be on it's way out (or at least heading towards just being a niche genre of music). What rock 'n roll there was on Top 40 radio was mostly bland, and barely even qualified as rock 'n roll (Frankie Avalon anybody?). The Beach Boys were making songs with lame-o lyrics ("Be True to Your School", etc.). Even in Europe it was only doing so-so - I remember reading an interview of Jimmy Page (who along with playing guitar in Led Zeppelin, and the Yardbirds, was an in-demand session guitarist in the early and mid 60s), where he stated that in the early 60s, it was hard to even find rock 'n roll recording sessions to play on. Without the Beatles, rock'n roll might have just kept on being 50s-style teen hearthrob music performed by Cliff Richard, instrumental music played by bands like The Shadows (who also happened to be Cliff Richard's backing band), and possibly music played by 50s American rock 'n roll musicians, who were going nowhere in the USA with their careers (Bo Diddly, Eddie Cochran, etc. performed extensively in Europe in the early 60s when their careers fizzled out in the US). One of the big elements of the Beatles that helped to propel them to stardom IMO, was that for its time (the early 60s), the Beatles' music was considered HARD ROCK. As a result, it had more energy to it than your typical music of the period, and people liked it. The Stones? They were in their infancy, playing what is to me, watered down blues, that sounded nowhere near as intense. That hard rock edge the Beatles had is what kick started rock 'n roll again, and resulted in a million bands wanting to sound like them (even in the US, after they were on the Ed Sullivan Show). No Beatles and IMO, rock 'n roll continues its decline into a niche music genre, with the occasional Top 40 hit by bland groups like Gary Pucket and The Union Gap, Gary Lewis and The Playboys, etc. Not much in the way of edgy, interesting music. In the US, Link Wray never charts as high as he did with "Rumble" (which was actually banned by radio stations because it was "too threatening - it'll incite people to riot"), and Lonnie Mack at most has a few very modest hits like he had with "Wham".

Oh, for the love of Pete, not THIS again.... I just don't understand how some on this board can analyze military events down to the level of minutiae where they can argue that if a particular German general farted at a given moment in 1940, the entirety of World War II would come out differently, and yet at the same time assume that popular culture would remain essentially unaltered without the presence of two of its most important figures. Just as one example: before the Beatles, there was no such thing as a "British rock and roll group" in the eyes of Americans, and particularly American record companies, radio programmers, and concert promoters. Cliff Richard, who was Britain's biggest rock and roll superstar prior to the Beatles, went absolutely nowhere in America. Americans knew that rock and roll had originated in the U.S., and they were very parochial about it - the assumption, and it was not often wrong, before the Beatles was that anything coming from Britain would be a poor copy of records American teenagers already owned. (And it WAS teenagers almost exclusively who listened to rock and roll in 1963; projecting one's own current cultural dynamics into the past is part of the reason one gets lost). No British rock group - not one - had broken in the U.S. before 1964. The Beatles themselves at first were turned down by Capitol, the American division of EMI, who held their recording contract in the UK; Capitol refused to issue their first four singles in the U.S. It took the "Beatlemania" phenomenon to convince Capitol that it was worth giving the Beatles a shot, which enabled Beatlemania to cross the Atlantic. I'm sorry, but it's not as if "Holliemania" or "Dave Clark Fivemania" simply takes the place of that. There's a whole set of intangibles here. You can't just assume that you like the Rolling Stones better, so they automatically take the place of the Beatles. It would never have worked like that. What happens to the Rolling Stones becomes essentially undefinable. And that's just one example. I didn't even address the fact of no Elvis - which probably would have meant no Beatles AND virtually none of the other British Invasion acts either. Removing Elvis from the picture (which automatically would remove the Beatles as we know them) changes the ENTIRE trajectory of popular music from that day to this, in well-nigh unpredictable ways. Period.
items.original_question: What if Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley. American Singer and Actor Elvis Presley and British Rock Band The Beatles are the most Influential musicians in existence. With the former codifying Rockabilly and is credited for advancing the Feminist movement in America, and the Latter spearheaded the British Invasion, increased public interest in Psychedelic Drugs, Asian Spirituality and heralded the Album Era. Let's say both the musician and the Band never had any interest in music, preventing the codifying of Rockabilly and The British Invasion. How would this influence modern music?
items.model_answer:
If modern music had developed without Elvis Presley and The Beatles, it would still exist, but it would likely look and sound very different in pace, style, and cultural reach.

Elvis mattered because he helped bring together rhythm and blues, country, gospel, and pop into a form that became early rock and roll for mainstream white America. Without him, that crossover still probably happens, because the musical forces behind it were already there in Black American music, Southern radio, independent labels, and youth culture. But it likely happens more slowly and through a wider group of performers rather than one giant symbol. Artists like Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Fats Domino, Buddy Holly, Jerry Lee Lewis, and others might have had even greater historical weight. The social shock of rock and roll would still come, but perhaps with less of a single face attached to it.

The Beatles mattered in a different way. They did not invent rock, pop songwriting, studio experimentation, youth fandom, or the album as an artistic statement by themselves, but they accelerated all of those. Without them, the 1960s music scene would probably be more fragmented. The British Invasion might still occur through bands like The Rolling Stones, The Kinks, The Who, and The Animals, but perhaps not as explosively or globally. American pop and rock might remain more dominant in the early 1960s, and British bands might have broken through more gradually.

Songwriting and recording would likely evolve differently too. The Beatles helped normalize the idea that a pop group could write its own material, reinvent its sound repeatedly, and use the studio as a creative instrument. Without that model, the separation between songwriters, performers, and producers might have lasted longer in mainstream pop. The shift from singles toward albums as major artistic and commercial units might also have been delayed. Psychedelic pop, baroque pop, and experimental studio rock would still emerge, but perhaps less quickly or under different leaders, such as Brian Wilson, Phil Spector, Frank Zappa, or later progressive rock musicians.

Culturally, both Elvis and The Beatles were symbols as much as musicians. Elvis represented generational rebellion, sexuality, and the mainstreaming of sounds rooted in Black music, though often in unequal ways. The Beatles represented modern youth culture becoming international, self-conscious, and artistically ambitious. Without them, music would likely remain important, but it might have had a weaker role as a single global language for youth identity in the 1950s and 1960s.

One of the biggest changes would be in influence chains. Countless later artists were shaped directly by Elvis or The Beatles. Without them, the paths leading to classic rock, power pop, folk rock, psychedelic rock, Britpop, singer-songwriter pop, and even some strands of heavy metal and indie music would shift. Bob Dylan’s turn toward rock might happen differently. The Byrds, Beach Boys, David Bowie, Oasis, ELO, and many others might sound different or perhaps not emerge in the same form at all.

Still, modern music would not disappear. The deeper engines of change—Black American innovation, recording technology, postwar prosperity, radio, television, teenage consumer culture, and transatlantic exchange—would still be there. So the most likely outcome is not a world without modern popular music, but a world where it becomes less centralized around a few icons, develops more unevenly, and perhaps gives greater credit to a broader range of artists who were overshadowed by Elvis and The Beatles.

In short, without Elvis and The Beatles, modern music would probably be less unified, less quickly transformed, and less centered on a few legendary figures. It would still become modern music, but through a more scattered and slower revolution.

items.original_question: What if Sea Beaufort and Sea Beaufighters used on Royal Navy aircraft carriers? What if the Royal Navy used a possible Bristol Sea variant of both Beauforts and Beaufighters on their carriers starting in 1940 replacing Fairy Swordfish aircraft in the torpedo attack role for example? Would this be possible design wise? Would they be better than the bomb and torpedo attack aircraft available at the time? Would the aircraft actually be able to be used like this or would they be too large? How effective would they be if used on aircraft carriers? Regards
items.model_answer:
If the Royal Navy had fielded genuinely effective carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward, the result would probably have been a noticeable but not war-winning increase in British naval striking power, especially in the Mediterranean and against Axis shipping. It would not have transformed the war at sea overnight, because British carriers, doctrine, radar integration, escort strength, and pilot training still imposed hard limits. But it could have made Fleet Air Arm carriers much more dangerous much earlier.

The key change would be that the Royal Navy would have had a better torpedo and strike capability at sea before aircraft like the Barracuda and before American carrier practices and aircraft began to influence Allied operations. Historically, the Fleet Air Arm relied heavily on the Swordfish and later the Albacore—slow, vulnerable biplanes that were excellent for some niche tasks but increasingly obsolete in daylight against strong opposition. A navalized Beaufort would have offered a faster, more survivable torpedo bomber with greater range and payload. A navalized Beaufighter would have added a powerful long-range strike fighter and anti-shipping aircraft, capable of suppressing flak, escorting strikes, and attacking lighter vessels directly.

In the Mediterranean, this could have mattered a great deal. British carriers often operated within reach of strong Italian and later German air power. A faster strike wing could have improved attacks on Italian convoys to North Africa and perhaps increased the attrition imposed on Axis supply lines to Libya. Even modest improvements here could have had real strategic effects, because Rommel’s forces were chronically supply-constrained. If carrier-based Beauforts had been available in useful numbers in 1941–42, British naval air strikes against merchant shipping, escorts, and port targets might have been more frequent and more lethal. Sea Beaufighters, in particular, could have made British carrier strikes less dependent on surprise and darkness, since they could provide heavy suppressive fire and better self-defense than Swordfish-type aircraft.

The most obvious comparison is Taranto and Bismarck. At Taranto, slower biplanes actually worked well because of surprise, night attack, and weak fighter opposition. Sea Beauforts would not necessarily have made Taranto dramatically better, and they may even have been less suitable for that specific shallow-water, low-speed torpedo role unless properly adapted. Against Bismarck, however, the Royal Navy might have benefited more clearly from faster torpedo bombers. Swordfish succeeded partly because bad weather and low speed disrupted German fire control, but they were also extraordinarily vulnerable. Sea Beauforts could have offered a better chance of repeated attacks with fewer losses, assuming crews were trained for deck operations and torpedo delivery.

In the Atlantic, the impact would have been more limited but still meaningful. Fleet carriers and especially escort carriers were constrained by deck size and aircraft handling. The Beaufort and Beaufighter were relatively large, heavy twin-engined aircraft. Even if navalized successfully, they would have been difficult to operate from many British carriers, particularly the smaller ones. So this counterfactual only works if we assume not just arrestor hooks and folding wings, but a whole set of successful naval adaptations and carrier operating procedures. If that hurdle is fully cleared, then convoy escort carriers might still struggle to use them efficiently, meaning the biggest beneficiaries would be the larger fleet carriers. This limits the scale of the transformation.

Against the Kriegsmarine surface fleet and coastal shipping, Sea Beaufighters could have been valuable. The land-based Beaufighter became an effective strike aircraft in anti-shipping work later in the war. Putting that capability to sea earlier could have improved attacks on German naval units in Norway or on supply traffic in confined waters. But carrier availability was always a bottleneck. The Royal Navy never had enough fleet carriers to maintain constant pressure everywhere. Better aircraft would improve each strike opportunity, but not solve the basic shortage of decks.

There are also real tradeoffs. Twin-engined naval aircraft generally demanded more deck space, more maintenance, and more fuel. British armored carriers had relatively small hangars and air groups compared with American carriers. So a Sea Beaufort or Sea Beaufighter air group might have reduced total aircraft numbers carried. That could produce a paradox: each individual aircraft is more capable, but the carrier’s overall striking cycle may become less flexible. A carrier packed with large twin-engined strike aircraft might have fewer fighters for combat air patrol, reconnaissance planes, or reserve aircraft. In 1940–42 especially, that could be dangerous.

Another major issue is development burden. Making either aircraft carrier-capable from 1940 onward would have required engineering effort, testing, and production capacity that Britain was already stretching to the limit. Strengthened landing gear, naval corrosion protection, arrestor gear compatibility, folding wings or compact stowage arrangements, low-speed handling improvements, torpedo gear, and deck-landing training would all have taken time and resources. If Britain diverts effort into this, something else likely slips. The payoff could be worthwhile, but it would not come for free.

So the most plausible overall outcome is this: the Royal Navy gets an earlier and more modern carrier strike arm, Axis convoys in the Mediterranean suffer more heavily, some major naval operations become less risky and more effective, and British carriers gain a better daylight anti-shipping punch. But there is no clean revolution. The aircraft would be hard to operate, carrier capacity would still be limited, and the Fleet Air Arm’s broader institutional and logistical constraints would remain.

In short, if the Royal Navy had deployed Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward, Britain would likely have fought a sharper, more lethal carrier war at the tactical and operational level, especially in the Mediterranean. The effect could have been significant enough to worsen Axis supply problems and improve British naval striking options, but not so great as to fundamentally overturn the larger balance of naval power by itself.

items.question: What If : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944
human_answers: The only Southerner who got any serious support at the DNC in 1944 was Alabama Senator John H. Bankhead II, who came in a distant third with 98 votes (8.33%) on the first ballot. The only other (non Alben W. Barkley) Southerners who got even one vote were: J. Melville Broughton (Governor of North Carolina), Prentice Cooper (Governor of Tennessee), Robert S. Kerr (Senator from Oklahoma), Herbert O'Conor (Governor of Maryland), Claude Pepper (Senator from Florida), Sam Rayburn (Speaker of the House), and Bascom N. Timmons (D.C. based newspaperman who grew up in Texas). Of these, only Bankhead II, Barkley, Broughton, Cooper, Kerr, and O’Conor got double digits. So your best case scenario is Roosevelt and/or the convention see a need to nominate a Southerner, and go with Bankhead II who IOTL died on June 12, 1946 following a stroke on May 24, 1946, which means you end up with three Presidents in little over a year. Based on the 1886 Succession Act, Bankhead II’s successor would be none other than… James F. Byrnes. IOTL, Truman appointed him in July of 1945, and it’s pretty likely Bankhead II does similarly, wanting to support a follow Southerner. (Prior to the Succession Act of 1947, neither the Speaker of the House nor the President pro tempore of the Senate were in the line of succession.) So in a roundabout way, you do end up with Byrnes as President…

Right. Byrnes thought he was Roosevelt's choice. Truman went to the DNC planning to make a nominating speech for Byrnes. If Byrnes does get the nod... FDR wins in 1944 anyway. But things diverge after that. IMO the Republicans sweep in 1946 as OTL. Byrnes was a very capable man and won't make any big missteps, so IMO he will be renominated in 1948. There may be a feeling that the 1948 nomination is a poisoned chalice, what with the 1946 GOP sweep and general public fatigue with 16 years of Democrat Presidents. The "Humphreyite" liberals may still try to push a civil rights plank at the DNC, but against Byrnes' at least tacit opposition will fail. They won't bolt to support Wallace overtly. Instead they may sit back to watch Byrnes crash and burn in November, while they regroup for 1952. Byrnes will lose a fair number of voters to Wallace outside the South. Also, AIUI, Dewey chose to soft-pedal civil rights OTL in the vain hope of winning some Upper South states with the Democrats divided. TTL that ignis fatuus isn't around, so Dewey probably emphasizes civil rights to draw the increasingly important black vote in the North and also some white liberals. This should be enough for Dewey to win. The next question is whether he has enough "coat tails" for Republicans to hold Congress. Another question is how the civil rights issue shapes across the next decade. OTL, leadership on the issue was taken by liberal non-Southern Democrats, with the low-key support of Republicans. The first cracks in the "Solid South" came in the 1950s, as a few white Southerners who could no longer rely on the national Democratic party to protect Jim Crow found they could vote Republican. If under Dewey, Republicans claim the leading role, that's not going to happen. The "Humphreyites" will gain control of the Democrats by 1952; there may be a Dixiecrat ticket that year. Dewey will be re-elected, barring some debacle in Korea or whatever. Warren won't be Chief Justice, but the Court will still be making rulings like Brown .
