items.model_answer:
If Franklin Roosevelt had chosen an openly segregationist running mate in 1944, the most important consequence is that the vice presidency would suddenly matter far more than anyone expected, because Roosevelt was visibly frail and likely to die in office. In real history, that is exactly what happened with Harry Truman’s succession in 1945. So in this scenario, the central question is not just campaign optics, but who becomes president after Roosevelt’s death and what that does to the end of World War II and the opening phase of postwar America.

Politically, Roosevelt might have had some short-term reasons to do it. The Democratic coalition still depended heavily on the white South, and by 1944 there was growing tension inside the party over race, labor, and federal power. Picking a segregationist could have been an attempt to reassure Southern conservatives who disliked New Deal centralization but remained Democratic out of habit and regional loyalty. It might also have been meant to block the renomination of Henry Wallace, who many party leaders thought too left-wing and eccentric. So as a convention maneuver, a Southern segregationist might have looked like a compromise: anti-Wallace, acceptable to party bosses, and useful for holding the South.

In the election itself, Roosevelt probably still wins. The war was going well by late 1944, Roosevelt remained an immense political figure, and Republican Thomas Dewey was not in a position to easily overturn the Democratic advantage. A segregationist vice-presidential nominee might have alienated Black voters in northern cities, labor liberals, and some urban ethnic Democrats, but many of those groups were still strongly attached to Roosevelt and the New Deal. Since African Americans outside the South had only recently begun shifting into the Democratic column in large numbers, the move would likely slow that realignment rather than immediately reverse it. It could narrow Roosevelt’s margin, but probably not cost him the presidency.

The real divergence begins in April 1945, when Roosevelt dies. A segregationist vice president becomes president in the final months of the war. On foreign policy, there may be less change than people sometimes assume. The basic machinery of wartime policy was institutional by then: the military, the State Department, the Allied agreements, and the Manhattan Project were already in motion. Any Democratic successor would probably still oversee Germany’s defeat, continue war against Japan, and face the atomic bomb decision in a broadly similar framework. There could be differences in style, administrative competence, and relations with advisers, but not necessarily a completely different outcome in the war itself.

Domestic politics, though, could change sharply. Truman, despite all his limitations, eventually desegregated the armed forces and endorsed a modest civil-rights agenda in 1948, helping trigger the Dixiecrat revolt and beginning the Democratic Party’s long break with the white South. A segregationist president in 1945 would likely do the opposite. He would probably resist civil-rights pressure, avoid federal anti-lynching or anti-poll-tax efforts, and try to keep the Democratic coalition anchored in white Southern dominance. That would postpone a major turning point in party history. The federal government’s early postwar signal in favor of civil rights would be delayed, perhaps by years.

That delay matters because the late 1940s were a formative period. Black veterans returned from war expecting greater citizenship. Civil-rights organizations were gaining strength. Northern Black voting power was growing. If the White House were openly hostile rather than cautiously supportive, civil-rights activists would likely redirect more energy toward courts, grassroots organizing, and pressure on Congress rather than expecting executive action. The civil-rights movement would still come, because its underlying forces were powerful, but it might emerge with a more oppositional, less Democratic-party-centered character in the immediate postwar years.

The party system could also shift differently. In real history, Truman’s civil-rights stance fractured the Democratic coalition in 1948, with Strom Thurmond’s Dixiecrat campaign signaling the South’s growing estrangement from the national party. If the president himself were a segregationist, there might be no Dixiecrat revolt at that moment because the South would feel represented inside the administration. Instead, the strain would move northward: liberals, labor, Black voters, and civil-rights advocates might become more restless within the Democratic Party. Some could defect to Henry Wallace’s Progressive campaign in 1948 in larger numbers, or pressure for a convention fight against the incumbent. The party might split, just not along the same line as in actual history.

That creates an opening for Republicans. A Republican Party that sensed Democratic weakness among northern liberals and Black voters might move earlier and more confidently toward a civil-rights posture, not necessarily out of principle alone but out of electoral opportunity. Since the GOP still had a meaningful liberal and moderate wing in the 1940s, especially in the Northeast and Midwest, it could try to reclaim its older image as the party of Lincoln more aggressively. If so, African American partisan realignment might become more competitive and less one-directional than it became in real history.

There is also a constitutional and institutional angle. Truman was inexperienced in foreign affairs, but he was not a regional ideological outlier in the same way an uncompromising segregationist would have been. If Roosevelt knowingly elevated a man unacceptable to large portions of his own coalition, his final political judgment would later be seen as a major blunder. Historians would likely treat the 1944 convention not as a pragmatic compromise that produced an unexpectedly consequential successor, but as the moment when Roosevelt sacrificed the future of postwar liberalism to preserve temporary party unity.

Everything would depend somewhat on which segregationist he chose. Someone like James Byrnes, for example, was deeply conservative on race but also highly experienced and influential in national governance; under him, policy might be more effective administratively even while remaining reactionary on civil rights. A more purely sectional figure, such as a politician in the mold of Theodore Bilbo, would be far more destabilizing and far less acceptable nationally. So the scale of divergence depends on whether Roosevelt picked a “respectable” Southern conservative or an inflammatory racial demagogue. But in either case, the broad effect is the same: the transition from New Deal liberalism to postwar liberalism becomes much less favorable to civil rights.

So the most likely overall answer is this: Roosevelt probably still wins in 1944, the war abroad ends in roughly similar fashion, but Roosevelt’s death in 1945 puts a segregationist in the White House at exactly the moment when the federal government was beginning to define the postwar order. That would likely delay Democratic support for civil rights, postpone the break between the national party and the white South, unsettle Black and liberal loyalty to the Democrats, and potentially give Republicans a bigger opening in northern and Black politics. In short, the immediate military history might not change dramatically, but the racial and partisan history of postwar America could change a great deal.

items.question: What If the Allies lose on the Salonica front?
human_answers: Alan Wakefield (IWM expert on Salonika, among other subjects) commented that most of the Bulgarian forces in September 1918 facing the British were well motivated, apart from the 1st Macedonian Bde that consisted of many men of Serbian origin. It was the collapse further west when the French & Serbian forces broke through three lines of defence, followed by the Greek breakthrough at Petit Couronne and Doiran Hill to the Bulgarian second line that unhinged the Bulgarian defences. Bulgarian C-in-C Todorov met with the German commanders von Steuben (German 11th Army) and von Reuter (Division Reuter) on 18 September, and agreed that Bulgarian 1st Army would be pulled back from positions east of the Vadar River, while the German 11th Army and Bulgarian 3rd Division would maintain contact. However the orders to 1st Army came as a severe blow to morale as the men were celebrating their stalling the British attacks, They started marching to Kosturino Pass but there was a serious shortage of draught animals, and of the survivors: " The majority of horses & oxen were absolutely unfit for work and they had need of at least six months rest in the interior, where they could be well nourished, Others had need of at least 45 days rest" - Major Nedeff, 9th Division, quoted in Under the Devil's Eye (Alan Wakefield & Simon Moody) from which much of the first three paragraphs are sourced. This was when the RAF caught the Bulgarian withdrawal through the passes, causing serious casualties & further delays. With foreign troops now on Bulgarian soil, political opposition to the war in the Sobranie was widespread. The PM, Malinov, was pro-western and had been appointed that June by Tsar Ferdinand with the purpose of proposing an armistice to the Allies, and on 26 September emissaries were sent through the lines to start discussions, although Franchet d'Esperey would only accept an unilateral unconditional armistice, which the Bugarian government then agreed to give, So it looks like the Bulgarian army was in generally good morale status until the final victories sparked by the French, Serbian & Greek forces, when the order of and losses taken on the retreat caused a final decline. But it looks like the home front collapsed first, if the Tsar was considering an armistice in June, so not sure what caused the domestic problems that drove the government to seek peace (I understand that a military rebelliion / mutiny at Radomir formulated by Bulgarian Agrarian National Union attempted to overthrow the government and establish a republic). Wiki suggests the following reasons: - Extreme war weariness, given Bulgaria had been at war since 1912 (short break 1914-15). Exhausted manpower (see #1 above) - I would add this resulted in dissatisfied minority groups supplying more troops, such as Macedonian Serbs & Greeks, diluting the Bulgar core. Both military & civilians suffering extreme food shortages (result of your point regarding harvests?). Troops poorly supplied - not only food but ammunition, clothing, boots, etc. Troops believing profiteers making hay at home at their expense. Feeling of betrayal by their allies, principally Germany, especialy regarding promised levels of supplies not being met, and lack of support for Bulgarian territorial ambitions at expense of Romania. Not sure how far the German troop levels had been reduced as you comment. The impact of the Russian Revolution. The impact of Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points (maybe a surrender would't be as bad as keep fighting) Recommended is 'The Enemy is Behind Us': The Morale Crisis in the Bulgarian Army during the Summer of 1918 - Richard C Hall, War in History Vol. 11 No. 4 which again refers to the collapse in morale starting by June 1918. Bulgarian C-in-C Nikola Zhekov reported to Tsar Ferdinand on 121 June that: "Today it is impossible ton have any illusions that the spirit of the soldiers is the same as at the beginning of the war, or even last year." I can't access as I don't have a school account! It does look like some units, such as the 9th (Pleven) Division, kept their high morale almost to the end. My main comment on demoralised forces would apply further north and primarily to the Austro-Hungarian troops who fell apart in October 1918, when I daresay no one suggests they were of high morale status. Earlier in the war that would not be the case, and I reckon me & a mountain goat could hold the Neretva Valley!

When you mentioned the Allies, I almost thought it was World War II. In reality, due to the division of Greece, neither the Entente nor the Central Powers could make any progress on the Thessaloniki front. Launching a large-scale offensive meant turning Greece into a battlefield, alienating more Greeks, and pushing more Greeks to the other side. The Entente was able to launch its offensive on the Macedonian front in 1917-1918 because the Entente countries had a large surplus of French reserves, willing to do everything except attack the Germans, such as conducting political work with the Greeks (Germany's reserves were smaller but more elite, and needed to do more important things; Bulgaria and the Ottomans were absolutely unacceptable to the Greeks). Ultimately, the deployment of hundreds of thousands of soldiers from the core countries of the Triple Entente only resulted in the defeat of one vassal state. The Central Powers could not accept this waste of reserves (unless Italy joined the Central Powers, providing some low ability soldiers). Even so, the problem of resource shortages must be taken into account.

It's my impression that it's something of a convention on this post 1900 forum to use "Entente" instead of "Allies", presumably to avoid confusion with the Allies of WW2. IMVHO I do prefer "Allies" for the WW1 military coalition because "Entente" is a derivation of the "Triple Entente" which applies to France/Russia/Britain, but by the end of WW1 the key great powers were Britain/France/Italy/America (and Russia was out) and there were multiple smaller allied powers. Why couldn't the Central Powers advance? Like, I thought Gallipoli ultimately failed because it was a trench-warfare stalemate; the Allies couldn't overcome a German client state. IIRC the proximal reason for the Gallipoli evacuation was that Bulgaria had joined the Central Powers, providing a route for German war material (not merely advisor personnel) like heavy siege artillery to be delivered to Turkey, which the Allies thought would be decisive. Was that assessment correct? Are you saying the Ottomans (with German support) could do something (push an Allied army into the sea) the Bulgarians (with their German support) could not? Or do you think that if the Allies had dug in on the Gallipoli peninsula in 1916, they might have obtained a stalemate which lasted until 1917/1918 when further offensives could be launched? I read that because of the potential futility of the front, Britain (and France) contemplated withdrawing their troops from mainland Greece before lines were solidified. Surely the Central Powers could have conquered Greece under those circumstances, no? I suppose in a grand strategy sense I recognize Germany was trying to fight a multi-front conflict against [the entire rest of the world] and was ultimately all but certain to lose the war. But in the narrower sense of "could the Balkan theater have played out differently", isn't it possible that the Central Powers could have achieved more success? Like, what if some resources from a different offensive (which surely would see less success than in OTL) devoted towards breaking through on the Macedonian front?

The allies couldn't overcome a German ally with more than 50 divisions and more than a million men on the field you mean, which in 1915 were about as well armed as their own troops. This is not 1942 in the Eastern front. But to get to the actual question in the fall of 1915 Greece was fully mobilized with 16 divisions and 325,000 troops in Macedonia and the Germans were doing their level best to keep Constantine in control and Greece out of the war. If they invade Greek territory you can kiss that neutrality goodbye and these 16 divisions just come into play added to the British and French divisions already landed in Salonica. And you'd better time it after the Serbs have been pushed into retreating into Albania, if your invasion comes before you just saved the lives of a couple hundred thousand Serbs. No. You essentially suggest Berlin says "to hell with the shenanigans to keep the Greeks neutral, let's invade them too. " So you just about gave numerical parity to the defenders... who don't have to move everything but food and fodder for the Macedonian and Turkish fronts though a single track railway going all the way back to Vienna. Before Dobro Polie and Desperate Frankie advancing all the way to Hungary and Austria putting the final nail in the Austro-Hungarian empire's coffin the actual front looked a pretty good deal to Berlin. Over 400,000 allied troops before the Greeks joined, that could be fighting elsewhere contained through mostly Bulgarian manpower... which could not be used elsewhere. Biggest POW camp in the world jokes and all that.

Well, Alternate History Challenge: An equivalent of Dobro Polie and subsequent desperate Frankie advances happen six months to a year earlier than OTL, *before* the Germans start getting pushed back on the western front, not after, and perhaps as a consequence, we get to see see the desperate Frankie international force *keep advancing* through the territory of capitulated Austria-Hungary, and over onto German territory from its southern and eastern borders (to Munich, Passau, Dresden, Gorlitz, Liegnitz or further to Cottbus or Berlin) before the Germans actually capitulate. Could this have ever happened in the right combination of circumstances? Could an earlier resolution of the Greek political divide in favor of the Venizelist side, committing the full Greek Army to the Entente side earlier, have helped with this? What might it take, faster French seduction? Or, going the opposite direction, more in line with what the OP wants, is there any way the Venizelist side could have been so marginalized that the Royalist side in Greece became willing to openly side with the Central Powers and openly welcomed/sought CP support in expelling Allied forces from Salonica and any other parts of Greece at any point during the war?
items.original_question: What if the Allies lose on the Salonica front? As I loosely understand it, the Salonica front was established after the Serbian army was routed. What if the Central Powers were able to continue advancing into Greece and expelled the Allies from the mainland Balkans? The Salonica front in some ways seems to resemble Gallipoli (an Allied lodgment supplied by sea) and the Central powers were able to prevail at Gallipoli, so it seems possible. The Allies also had to deal with the fact that the Greek government was divided - if the Central powers were more successful it seems possible Greece would have “switched sides”, or at least had a compliant government installed.
items.model_answer:
If the Allies lose on the Salonica front, the most immediate consequence is that Bulgaria and the Central Powers secure the Balkans more firmly, at least for a time. Historically, the Allied offensive from Salonica in September 1918 helped force Bulgaria out of the war, which opened the way for the collapse of the Central Powers in southeastern Europe. If instead the Allied army at Salonica is defeated or fails badly enough to be driven back, that chain of collapse is interrupted.

The first major effect is that Bulgaria probably stays in the war longer. That matters because Bulgaria was the weakest and most exposed of the Central Powers by late 1918. Its surrender historically shattered the strategic position of both the Ottoman Empire and Austria-Hungary. If Bulgaria holds, Germany and Austria-Hungary preserve their land connection to the Ottoman Empire, and the Central Powers avoid a dangerous breach in the Balkans. Serbia is not liberated in 1918, and Allied pressure from the south against Austria-Hungary is reduced or eliminated.

This would also strengthen the Ottoman position temporarily. The Ottoman Empire was already in serious trouble in Palestine and the Middle East, so a Salonica victory would not magically save it, but it would reduce the sense of total encirclement and delay political collapse. Supplies and communications through the Balkans remain more viable. The Ottomans might hold out somewhat longer, and the armistice at Mudros could be delayed.

Austria-Hungary also benefits in the short run. Historically, the Balkan collapse added to the empire’s internal disintegration and military hopelessness. If the Salonica front is secure, Vienna faces one less crisis. That does not solve the empire’s enormous ethnic, economic, and military problems, but it may delay surrender and perhaps delay the final breakup by weeks or months. The empire was probably still doomed by late 1918 because of internal nationalist revolts, hunger, and defeat elsewhere, but the timing could shift.

For Germany, a lost Allied campaign at Salonica would be useful politically and strategically, but probably not war-winning by itself. By late 1918 Germany’s decisive problem was the failure of its spring offensives in France and the overwhelming superiority of the Allies on the Western Front. Even if the Balkans remain intact, Germany is still being pushed back in the west, its population is exhausted, and its allies are weakening. So a defeat at Salonica likely prolongs the war rather than reverses the final outcome. It may encourage Berlin to hope for better armistice terms or to fight on longer, but it does not remove the core reasons Germany lost.

There are two broad plausible versions of this scenario. In the milder version, the Allies simply fail to break through. In that case, Bulgaria survives into late 1918 or even 1919, the Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian collapses are delayed, and the war may last somewhat longer. In the more dramatic version, the Allies are heavily defeated and forced to evacuate Salonica. That would be a major political shock. It would vindicate critics who had long mocked the Salonica expedition as a sideshow, damage Allied prestige in Greece and the Balkans, and possibly strengthen pro-Central or neutralist forces in the region. Even so, unless this defeat frees major Central Power forces to decisively alter the Western Front, it still probably changes the timing and shape of the ending more than the ultimate winner.

The postwar Balkans would also look different. Serbia, having failed to be liberated by Allied action in 1918, emerges in a weaker position. The creation of Yugoslavia might still happen if Austria-Hungary collapses, but Serbian bargaining power would be reduced and local political dynamics could shift. Bulgaria, instead of being a defeated state forced into the Treaty of Neuilly under the same circumstances, might negotiate from a somewhat stronger position if the broader Central Power defeat comes later and under more confused conditions. Greece might experience even harsher political recriminations over the war, since the Salonica front was tied directly to the National Schism and the Venizelist decision to join the Allies.

So the best overall answer is: if the Allies lose on the Salonica front, the Central Powers gain a temporary but meaningful reprieve in southeastern Europe. Bulgaria likely stays in the war longer, the Ottoman Empire and Austria-Hungary may collapse later, Serbia remains occupied longer, and the First World War could be prolonged. But unless this Balkan victory somehow produces a major knock-on effect on the Western Front, it probably does not save Germany or overturn the final Allied victory; it mainly delays and reshapes the end of the war.

items.question: What If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin engine?
human_answers: 1 - as noted by the fellow member, the P-40F and L used the Merlin 2 - it was a pretty simple upgrade 3 - engine itself does not require a laminar flow wing; a laminar flow wing will cut some drag, however, and thus allow for some speed increase 4 - historically, it offered some 30 mph over the P-40E at 18000 ft and above, IOW it was an improvement the P-40 badly needed 5 - P-51s used the better Merlins, these with 2-stage supercharger; a P-40 with such an engine would've probably be as fast as the Spitfire IX, but not as fast as the Merlin Mustang, nor as rangy - and thus the answer is 'no' 6 - as-is, the performance was better on the P-40F than on the ubiquitous P-40E; with 2-stage Merlin, it would've probably been good for 400+ mph, and much better rate of climb (the XP-40Q did 420+ mph with a 2-stage supercharged V-1710)

I'll have to take your word for it as I'm forbidden from your links but that sounds about right. A more advanced Merlin won't really help the P-40 though. There are availability issues with the Merlin, as ever, which historically forced Curtiss to revert to the V-1710-81 for the P-40M, despite more than half the production run going to the RAF. Not even every P-40F/L received a Merlin as some were completed as V-1710-81 engined P-40Rs. More though, there is the tale of the XP-60, which was a P-40D fuselage with a new laminar-flow wing. It was an improvement, with 387mph at 22,000ft. Modified as the XP-60D with an enlarged tail, it may or may not have received the V-1650-3 slated for it by the time of it's destruction in a crash on 6th May 1943. It certainly didn't perform any substantive testing with it. By that time the Merlin Mustang was established as superior in performance and was already entering production. The XP-60A with 1425hp V-1710-75, good for 420mph at 29,000ft, was part-cancelled in January 1942 (with the remainder following in June 1943) in favour of P-40Ks, Ls and P-47Gs. I think that is going to be the fate of any advanced or improved P-40 variant. Cancelled in favour of sustained production of known quantities.
items.original_question: What if Curtiss P-40 used Merlins? What instead of using Allison V-12's the Curtiss P-40 used the Merlin V-12 instead ? Would this be possible or would it need major airframe development? Would it need a redesigned laminar flow wing to really utilise the engine? How successful would this instillation be? Would it allow the P-40 to be more successful than the later P-51? What boost in combat performance would this instillation allow? Regards
items.model_answer:
If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin from the start, it probably would have been a noticeably better fighter, but not a transformational one on the level of the best late-war designs.

Historically, the P-40 began with the Allison V-1710, which was sturdy and worked well at low and medium altitude, but its single-stage supercharging limited high-altitude performance. Later Merlin-powered P-40 variants showed that the airframe benefited from the British engine. If Curtiss had designed the aircraft around the Merlin from the beginning rather than adapting the existing P-36/P-40 line, the gains could have been somewhat larger than what was actually achieved.

The biggest improvement would likely have been in high-altitude performance. A Merlin-based P-40 would have climbed better, held its power better at altitude, and been more competitive in European-style air combat where altitude mattered greatly. That would have made it a stronger interceptor and escort fighter in 1940–42, and perhaps more appealing to the RAF in the Battle of Britain era than the Allison-powered Tomahawk was. It also might have reduced one of the aircraft’s major criticisms: that it was durable and fast in a dive, but simply outclassed higher up.

Designing around the Merlin from the outset could also have improved the aircraft’s overall integration. The nose, cooling system, center of gravity, and drag profile could have been optimized instead of modified later. That might have produced somewhat better speed, handling balance, and reliability than the Merlin P-40s actually achieved. In the best case, you could imagine a cleaner, lighter, more refined P-40 that closed part of the gap with the Spitfire V or early Bf 109F, especially at medium altitude.

But there were real limits. The P-40 airframe was rooted in an older design philosophy than the top European fighters. It was relatively heavy, not especially aerodynamically advanced, and had more drag than the best contemporaries. Even with a Merlin, it likely still would not have matched the Spitfire or Bf 109 in climb, ceiling, or agility. It might have become a very solid second-tier fighter: rugged, fast enough, better at altitude, and more versatile, but still not the premier dogfighter of the war.

There would also have been production and strategic complications. Merlin engines were in intense demand for Spitfires, Hurricanes, and later Mustangs. If the P-40 had depended on Merlins from the beginning, engine supply could have constrained production unless Packard-built Merlins came online quickly. One reason the Allison-powered P-40 mattered was precisely that it used an engine available in large numbers. In wartime, a slightly inferior fighter produced in volume can matter more than a better one bottlenecked by engine supply.

So the most likely counterfactual outcome is that a Merlin-designed P-40 would have been a better and more balanced fighter, especially at altitude, and might have enjoyed a stronger reputation in Europe. It could have been more effective in RAF and perhaps early USAAF service. But it probably still would not have become the dominant Allied fighter. Its improvement would have been meaningful rather than revolutionary, and the engine supply question might have limited how much that better design could actually matter.

items.question: PT-109: What If JFK Died on 7/2/43?
human_answers: It seems plausible to me that if Jack were to die in the Pacific, Sr would use connections to ensure that Jr would come home in one piece so that grooming for public office could begin. That said, I've read several accounts that suggest/indicate Jr was not as approachable/astute/able to think on his feet as well as Jack. That might make a political career more challenging: still feasible, but more challenging and quite possibly more costly (Sr might have had to write more and/or larger checks to make things happen?). I could see Jr with a House, and later a Senate seat. Then the question becomes: could he work his way into such a position that Adlai Stevenson might consider him as a running mate in 1956? Arguably, that propelled Jack into the limelight enough to become a presidential contender in 1960. My sense is that Jr would not get the same consideration ITTL that Jack did IOTL. Rather, he would plausibly have tried a presidential run having something like 8-10 years of Senate experience under his belt in 1960. We're talking a crowded field for the Dems in 1960: Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Jr, and the usual cast of favorite sons. Johnson might be the favorite, but not a prohibitive favorite: coming from Texas would assure that. Too manybut Lodge won northerners would be skeptical. On the other hand, Humphrey would definitely not play well in the south. Could Jr emerge as a compromise candidate? Maybe, but he'd be a tough sell in the south given his Catholic faith. My sense is that a protracted, multiple ballot convention would ultimately result in a Johnson nomination, with a middle of the road midwesterner (I'll yield to someone else here) as a VP candidate. Nixon will still be the GOP nominee, but Lodge won't be his running mate: don't need to counter a Kennedy. I suggest it would be MD governor Theodore McKeldin, a man who knew how to work with both sides (he was the last GOP mayor of Baltimore). McKeldin would bring a great deal more to the ticket than Lodge, but that's a pretty low bar. While we're at it, look for the 1960 campaign to be nasty. Then all Nixon has to do is take the high road and point out how well things have gone during Ike's tenure, and pump up his role (maybe this time Ike wouldn't make his famous "...if you give me a week..." remark?). And I don't see Richard Daley doing much to help Lyndon Johnson in Chicago, so IL might well flip to the GOP. Long story short: Nixon wins in '60. That leaves 1968 as Jr's next shot at the White House: he wouldn't try to unseat Nixon unless something totally unforeseen happened.

items.original_question: PT-109: What if JFK Died on 7/2/43? In 1943, John F Kennedy's patrol boat PT-109 was rammed by the battleship Amagiri. After PT-109 exploded, JFK was able to survive, swimming from the wreck to a nearby island to stay alive while also saving his fellow soldiers. The moment cemented Jack as a war hero, and after his brother Joe died in a special mission, Jack was seen as next in line to join the Senate, before finally becoming President (which we all know how it ended). But what if things went slightly differently? Maybe Jack is closer to the blast and dies in the initial explosion. What next? What would happen to Joe Jr, and by extension, the Kennedy family? In our timeline, Joe Jr was killed in a special mission, but could the death of JFK stopped Joe Jr from going on the mission, and continue to stay alive to be the frontrunner of the family? Joe Jr had approved of Hitler, but his ideals could have easily morphed over time. Could Joe have done what Jack did and become President, and how would his presidency have looked? And if Joe Jr did in fact die anyway, who would replace him? Robert would have been far too young, along with Ted. Would the Kennedy family fade out of the limelight? What would become of the 1960 elections? The more obvious question, with Jack dead, who would be the man to lead the Democrats against Nixon? The most likely options are Hubert Humphrey, Lyndon Baines Johnson, and (although less likely), Adali Stevenson. Who would have been able to win the primaries, and could they have dealt with Nixon? With whoever becomes President, how would their Presidency look, and what could happen to them if they were also assassinated? For me personally, the most likely ticket would have been Johnson, causing him to be President.
items.model_answer:
If John F. Kennedy had died on July 2, 1943, in the PT-109 episode, the most important consequence is that there would have been no President Kennedy in 1961–63, and that would likely have changed the course of Cold War politics, U.S. domestic reform, and the symbolism of American liberalism in the 1960s.

At the most immediate level, Kennedy’s death in wartime would probably have made him a naval hero remembered within his family and in wartime memory, but it would have removed the particular son whom Joseph Kennedy Sr. eventually treated as the family’s political standard-bearer after the death of the older brother, Joseph Jr., in 1944. Without JFK, the Kennedy family might still have remained politically active, but it is much less likely that any other sibling would have assembled the same combination of charisma, ambition, media skill, war-hero status, and electoral appeal. Robert Kennedy might still have had a major political career, but probably not on the same timetable and probably not as the center of a presidential dynasty in the same way.

The 1960 election is the first major turning point. Without JFK, Richard Nixon becomes the strong favorite to win the presidency in 1960, unless another Democrat somehow unites the party and defeats him. Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Adlai Stevenson, or Stuart Symington might have competed for the Democratic nomination, but none had Kennedy’s particular ability to bridge northern liberals, urban Catholics, and parts of the South while also projecting youth and vigor on television. A Nixon presidency beginning in 1961 is therefore a plausible baseline outcome.

That shift alone would matter enormously for the Cold War. Kennedy’s handling of the Bay of Pigs, the Vienna summit, the Berlin crisis, and especially the Cuban Missile Crisis shaped the period. A President Nixon might have been more experienced in foreign affairs but also potentially more hawkish. It is possible that a Nixon administration would have avoided some of Kennedy’s missteps, such as authorizing the Bay of Pigs under inherited CIA assumptions. But it is also possible that in a Cuba or Berlin confrontation Nixon would have been less restrained than Kennedy was in October 1962. Kennedy’s combination of toughness and caution during the missile crisis is one reason the world avoided nuclear war. In this counterfactual, the risk of a more dangerous superpower clash is real.

On the other hand, if a Democrat such as Johnson had somehow won in 1960, some domestic outcomes might actually have come faster. Kennedy’s record on civil rights and social legislation was mixed: rhetorically important, but often cautious and constrained by Congress. Johnson, had he reached the presidency earlier, might have pushed major civil rights and anti-poverty legislation sooner because he understood congressional power better than Kennedy did. But that also depends on timing, party balance, and whether the political shock of Kennedy’s actual assassination in 1963—which helped propel the Civil Rights Act—would still exist. Without that martyrdom effect, even Johnson might have had a harder time moving landmark legislation.

Space policy is another area where Kennedy’s absence matters. The moon commitment was deeply associated with his presidency. A different president might still have expanded the space race, especially after Soviet successes, but the famous decision to land a man on the moon before the decade was out might have been delayed, reframed, or never made in the same dramatic way.

Vietnam would also likely change, though not in a simple direction. Kennedy increased U.S. involvement, so his absence does not automatically mean less intervention. Nixon in 1961 might have escalated differently or earlier; Johnson in 1961 might also have deepened involvement. The common argument that Kennedy would have avoided full-scale war remains speculative. The safer conclusion is that JFK’s death in 1943 would not guarantee a less violent Vietnam, but it would make the path into war different, because the key decisions would have been made by someone else under different political pressures.

Culturally and symbolically, the United States would lose “Camelot” as a defining myth. Kennedy’s presidency, and then his assassination, became central to the way Americans understood generational change, national promise, and political tragedy in the 1960s. Without him, there is no Kennedy assassination in Dallas, no immediate LBJ succession under those circumstances, and no comparable fusion of glamour, reformist language, Cold War brinkmanship, and martyrdom. The emotional landscape of the decade would be noticeably different.

So the best concise answer is this: if JFK had died in the PT-109 incident, he would have been remembered as a wartime hero, but the larger consequence is that he almost certainly would never have become president. That would most likely have opened the way for a different winner in 1960, probably Nixon, and in turn altered the handling of Cuba, Berlin, civil rights, the space race, Vietnam, and the political mythology of the 1960s. Some policies later associated with Kennedy might still have happened under others, but the specific trajectory of modern American history would have been substantially different.

items.question: What If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981?
human_answers: The core problem with these discussions is that you wind up with a lot of people who had personal experience with home computers imagining their home computer was a long-term viable platform particularly killed by the IBM PC. The inherent market dynamic was, instead, that all the home computers were doomed to extinction at the hands of the standard business personal computer platform. It is businesses that care about backward compatibility with their internal installed base, while the home computer user market has an observable willingness to abandon old platforms and adopt new ones. This means home-targeted versions of the business platform can easily be adopted by the home market, while business-targeted versions of home platforms can only get adopted by businesses if they have a specific compelling business advantage. And then, as soon as the business platform clones the advantage, the home platform is again on the defensive. Home platforms are thus in an inherently weak position, and will be smashed flat by the standard business platform. And, well, there was already a standard business personal computer platform in 1980-1981 -- the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. You could buy that platform as an Osborne 1, or as a Xerox 820, or from any of dozens of other of other makers. You even had the Microsoft Softcard (originally, "Z-80 Softcard", but Zilog complained) which used an Apple II as a host for a 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The major problem that the CP/M-80 platform had going forward was that it had run up against the 64k RAM addressing limit of the 8080/8085/Z80, at a time when RAM prices had dropped enough that it was entirely practical to buy more. And since none of the chipmakers had had the sense to make a 8080-compatible processor with wider addressing, the only real way forward was the 8086/8088, since 8080 assembly code could be easily machine-translated into 8086 code. Everybody was just waiting on Digital Research to get CP/M-86 out. The IBM PC then arrived, with an OS that was arguably even more compatible in its system calls with CP/M-80, and the ability to use all the RAM anybody could practically afford. (Even if Gates never said 640K was enough for anybody, in 1981 that was true. Indeed, the first version of the PC's BIOS had a 544K limit.) It was the perfectly natural successor to the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The IBM endorsement made the transition smoother, and did have some secondary consequences (killing the S-100 bus, for example), but the true key to the IBM PC's success is that it was the natural successor-host for a software ecosystem that had grown up on top of the Altair 8800. What happens in the absence of the IBM PC is simple enough. Digital Research will release CP/M-86. At which point the CP/M-86 systems take over the business market, and eventually all the home computer platforms are killed by the multi-manufacturer business standard, just as in the original timeline.

As I understand it, the IBM machine was intended as an 'intelligent terminal' for their mainframes .. Businesses already had mainframes & dumb terminals but because the terminals were dumb the mainframe had to do everything - which led to limits on the numbers - and whilst IBM would be happy to sell (rent) you another mainframe they then run into the problem of getting the mainframes to talk 'seamlessly' to each other ... so IBM work on evermore powerful / more expensive mainframes as the number of users go up .. If, however, you can off-load some of the 'housekeeping' (things like deciding how to repaint the screen as the user edits a file, without the entire screen contents having to be resent from the mainframe, for example) onto the terminal, you can roll out cheap low end mainframes (at the same cost as the high end ones, naturally) able to cope with 100's more users .. Other companies wanted to 'get in on' IBM's business but had difficulties building mainframes as powerful as the IBM ones = thus, sooner or later, some-one else is going to come up with the concept of 'intelligent terminals' .. after which the PC becomes more or less inevitable ..
items.original_question: What if no IBM PC (2026 ed.) In short - the IBM PC (model 5150) was not an inevitable thing, the IBM leadership was highly skeptical of the project and it would not have seen the light of the day had things gone just slightly differently. So, what if that computer had never been created? My take - the personal computer market would look a lot like mobile or console market - a walled garden of 2-3 incompatible standards, probably Apple and Commodore (which, would do better financially without the competition from PC clones). It's interesting what would happen in Japan and (later) China.
items.model_answer:
If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981, personal computing still would have happened, but it likely would have been slower, more fragmented, and organized around different standards.

The biggest effect of the IBM PC was not that it invented the personal computer. Machines like the Apple II, Commodore PET, TRS-80, and later CP/M systems already existed. What IBM did was legitimize the microcomputer for business and create a hardware-software platform that others could copy. Without that machine, there is a good chance the early 1980s PC market would have remained divided among incompatible systems for much longer.

In business, IBM’s brand mattered enormously. Many companies that might have considered microcomputers risky or toy-like were reassured by the IBM name. Without that reassurance, large firms probably would have stuck longer with terminals, minicomputers, and centralized systems, while adopting personal computers more cautiously. Apple, Tandy, Commodore, and various CP/M vendors might have gained more ground, but none had IBM’s authority in corporate procurement. Business standardization around one dominant desktop platform would likely have been delayed.

Microsoft would probably still have become important, but in a different way and perhaps less quickly. The IBM PC helped make MS-DOS the core operating system of business computing. Without IBM, Microsoft may have remained more of a language and software supplier across many hardware platforms, or it might have tied itself more strongly to another manufacturer. Its eventual dominance is less certain, and the path to Windows becoming the default desktop environment would have been much less direct.

Intel also might not have become so dominant as early as it did. The IBM PC and especially the huge clone market reinforced the x86 architecture. Without that platform, competing processors from Motorola, Zilog, or others could have stayed more competitive for longer. The desktop world might have evolved around a more varied set of CPU families instead of coalescing around x86.

A major consequence involves the clone market. Because the IBM PC used relatively open, off-the-shelf components and could be reverse-engineered, it enabled “IBM-compatible” computers from Compaq, Dell, and many others. If IBM had never launched the PC, there might not have been a single dominant clone standard to unify the market. That could have meant less price competition, slower commoditization, and a computer industry shaped more like the early home computer era: many brands, many formats, poor compatibility.

Apple might have been the biggest beneficiary. The Macintosh, released in 1984, could have entered a world with no entrenched IBM-compatible business standard. In that scenario, Apple might have had a better chance of becoming the main integrated personal computing platform for both professionals and homes, especially if it had adjusted pricing and software strategy effectively. Still, Apple’s habit of maintaining tight hardware control means it might not have generated the same broad low-cost ecosystem that PC clones eventually did.

Software development would have looked different too. In our timeline, developers increasingly targeted the IBM PC standard because it offered the largest installed base in business. Without that focal point, software markets might have stayed split across Apple, CP/M descendants, Unix workstations, and other proprietary platforms. That fragmentation would likely have made it harder for spreadsheets, word processors, databases, and games to achieve universal reach quickly. Some applications might have become platform-specific power centers rather than cross-industry standards.

Networking and the internet era might also have changed. By the 1990s, masses of cheap IBM-compatible PCs helped put networked computing on millions of desks. Without that standard, the spread of networked desktops probably still occurs, but perhaps with more influence from workstations, terminals, or alternative personal computer platforms. The web still likely emerges, but the client side of the internet may be more diverse and less centered on Windows PCs.

At the industry level, the absence of the IBM PC could have reduced the “Wintel” era or prevented it from taking the same shape. Instead of Microsoft and Intel becoming the central pair in desktop computing, power might have been distributed among Apple, Motorola-based systems, Unix vendors, and possibly a different mass-market business platform. The center of gravity in computing might have remained less standardized and more vertically integrated.

So the most plausible answer is not “no personal computer revolution,” but “a messier one.” Personal computing would still grow because the underlying technology and demand were real. But without the IBM PC, the industry likely would have lacked the early common business standard that accelerated adoption, lowered prices through cloning, and helped make Microsoft and Intel dominant. The result would probably have been a more diverse but less unified computer world, with different winners and slower convergence.

items.question: What If No P51 Bomber Escort?
human_answers: The P-51B/C/D was clearly a better dogfighter at medium and low altitude, but at 25-30,000ft the R-2800 engine in the P-47 maintained power even better than the Packard Merlin and the DB-605 engine in the Bf-109G. The P-47 was made to rule at 30,000ft. The P-47 shootdown almost the same number of fighters as the P-51, and the highest scoring USAAF groups in the ETO were P-47 units. Yes, the P-51 was shooting down more German fighters from mid-1944 on but that was because the P-51 was given the high-altitude job where they would encounter more enemy fighters while the P-47 was given most of the low altitude work like CAS, and interdiction missions. This is not to take away any credit from the P-51 but in most histories the Mustang gets the glory, and the Thunderbolt is relegated to being a ground support aircraft. The Mustang was clearly given the right name. She was fast and graceful and could dance with the best of them. The Thunderbolt had the right name as well. She was a warhorse that could absorb more punishment and bring her pilot home while raining thunder on the enemy. The P-38 Lightning is another also run for more complicated reasons, but she has her admirers for many reasons. And in 4th place the P-40 Warhawk held the line from 1940-43. Strangely it's the Mustang and the Flying Tigers Warhawk that are remembered best.

Hence my post about Big Week, P-47 provided 80% of the escort fighters during that effort. I doubt very many people realize that. P-38 is an interesting plane, read an interview with a high scoring German ace who said that provided it was being flown by a pilot who knew how to handle it he thought the P-38 was the toughest Allied fighter he faced. It also presented the Japanese with a difficult tactical problem in that it flew higher and faster than both the Zero and the Oscar. General Kenney liked it best because of the two engines. His pilots flew a lot of missions over water and he appreciated what two engines provided in that sense. General Chennault did not like for the same reason. He was at the ass end of a long logistics chain in a lower priority theater. To him two engines just meant twice the engine maintenance. The P-40 deserves much more credit that it gets. Only the P-51 and P-47 were produced in greater numbers (for US fighters), it was used extensively in the MTO, PTO, and CBI theaters well into 1944 and it was used by more Allied air forces than any other fighter. It was not a thoroughbred by it was definitely a work horse and sometimes that is what you need.

Cost to buy and operate the P-47 was not a factor - USA have had the money, material and fuel. They were after all buying and using the P-38, that offered no savings in any category. P-47 was made in more than 15000 copies. The P-47 was turned into a ground attack aircraft after the fact, and fact being that Merlin Mustang was rangier, a bit faster and a better climber. A combination of the P-51 getting the drop tanks earlier, and the better mileage on internal fuel made it the premier LR fighter of the war. Two very common 75 gal drop tanks make the P-51 going much further than if two 75 gal drop tanks are carried by the P-47 or the P-38. Some mix-up happened there. As-is, it could not do the job. With a bit of foresight, it might've come close. People at USAAF will need to request that P-47 is outfitted with wing racks from day one (ie. already in 1942, so it is debugged and ready for 1943), and there should be the drive to increase the internal fuel tankage. In OTL, the 1st increase was achieved by removing the stuff between the main tank and the top of fuselage so the main tank can get bigger, now with 270 instead of 205 US gals. That change upped the internal fuel tankage to 370 gals, that, together with 2x 150 gal drop tanks, enabled the theoretical 600 mile combat radius under the demanding ETO rules (that included cruising at more than 300 mph TAS at 25000 ft). There is also the need for the actual drop tanks to be available in the UK, with clear contracts with the suppliers. The know 'bubbletop' P-47Ds were the 1st with the main tank being at 270 gals. If there was the earlier go with adding some fuel tanks in the wings - even if it is not a 'surgery' as what was done with the P-47N, but perhaps 2x 50 gals? - together with a drop tank under the fuselage, the radius would've been increased even more, equaling the best P-51D values.

The P 47 was an incredible fighter and despite it's sheer size was fairly good in a dogfight. The P-51 Mustang was until the Rolls Royce Merlin was used a low level fighter at best. The V-1710 engine was fine but needed the two stage supercharger and the like which did happen it just took time. Drop Tanks and education on how to achieve maximum range needed to happen in order to make the Mustand what it became. The P-51 B was the start of the Merlin engines and gave it excellent high altitude performance. The P-47 on the other hand did not need an engine swap to be effective. Instead doctrine and production numbers made the difference. The most important use of the daylight bomber offensive, was the decimation of the Luftwaffe and this occurred in measurable ways. The P-38 was suffering from poor pilot training and tactics. THe presence of 3 high performance fighters whose abilities compliment each other is very desirable.
items.original_question: What if No P51 Bomber Escort? From Jan 1944 the Merlin engined P51 could escort the Bombers all the way to Berlin and beyond and destroyed the Luftwaffe in doing so. However, I would argue the P47 could have done the same job but The P47 did not get the escort gig because it was twice the cost and it was a superb ground attack aircraft. twice the cost in construction and fuel consumption. Really the game changer was the drop tank although the P51 was the best host for them by far I think of the P51 as the sleek technical European sports car sipping fuel, with the P47 as a brute, "cubes is everything", American muscle car guzzling gas like there was no tomorrow. The POD would be North American builds P40s instead of creating the new P51 design for the British. The distance the P-47 could cover evolved rapidly as new tanks were engineered: Early 1943 (No tanks): ~175 miles. (Could barely reach the Dutch border). Mid 1943 (75-gal belly tank): ~230 miles. (Reached Antwerp/Ruhr Valley). Late 1943 (108-gal belly tank): ~375 miles. (Reached Frankfurt). Early 1944 (Maximal 3-tank setup): 475–500+ miles. The P47 did not get the escort gig because it was twice the cost and it was a superb ground attack aircraft with its radial engine. OTL the Mustang was a dangerous aircraft to strafe German airfields while a much better dogfighter than the P47 [fixed after tomo mentioned]. I believe more P51s lost to ground fire than air combat. But I would argue that the Mustang was the best solution to the need for an escort, but the P47 could have done the job. Standardising on the P47 would simplify the training and operations of the fighter arm but at double the cost would it have been as effective and escort in numbers? I look forward to your thoughts.
items.model_answer:
If there had been no P-51 Mustang bomber escort, the air war over Europe would likely have gone much worse for the Allies, at least for a significant period.

The core issue is that long-range escort was essential for daylight strategic bombing. Before effective escorts could accompany bombers deep into Germany, US bombers suffered very heavy losses. Unescorted or partially escorted formations were vulnerable to concentrated attacks by German fighters, especially once they passed beyond the range of earlier escorts like the P-47 and Spitfire. The P-51 changed that because it could go all the way to distant targets and back while still performing well in combat.

Without the P-51, several outcomes become more likely. First, the US Eighth Air Force would probably have had to reduce or suspend deep-penetration daylight raids more often, especially after costly missions like Schweinfurt-Regensburg. Second, bombing strategy might have shifted toward more limited targets near the coast, more night bombing, or a greater reliance on the RAF’s area-bombing campaign. Third, the Luftwaffe would have remained stronger for longer, because one of the most important effects of the P-51 was not just protecting bombers but helping destroy German fighters in the air and on the ground. That mattered enormously before D-Day.

This does not mean the Allies would have lost the war. Germany was still being squeezed by the Soviet advance in the east, Allied industrial superiority, naval blockade, fuel shortages, and the cumulative effects of bombing of transport and oil. Other escort solutions might also have expanded eventually, such as longer-range P-47 variants or drop-tank improvements for existing fighters. So the war in Europe probably still ends in Allied victory.

But the likely counterfactual is that victory comes more slowly and at greater cost. Strategic bombing would be less effective in 1943–44, bomber losses would be higher, German aircraft production and air defenses would suffer less disruption for longer, and preparations for the invasion of Western Europe would be riskier because Allied air superiority would arrive later or less completely. In short: no P-51 escort probably does not save Germany, but it likely prolongs the war and increases Allied casualties substantially.

items.question: How would the population of the Falklands have been treated if Argentina had won in 1982?
human_answers: If GB got beat up per the OPs post and had to give up and go home I am not sure why Argentina would care about upsetting BG with the treatment of British Citizens on an “Argentine island”. They didn’t care about upsetting GB when the invaded and that was before the Royal Navy got beet like a stray dog and sent home with its tail between is legs. So why on earth would Argentina worry about what GB would think? I suspect a lot of folks will leave the Island and i expect Argentina would do everything it could to encourage that. Including being a bit heavy handed and sending over a good number of “settlers” and giving control of everything to its citizens and such. And I would not be surprised that Argentina was a bit brutal. Not the point of blatant executions as that would put them over the line internationally and they don’t really want that kind of reputation for no good reason, frankly I doubt the then current government really cares what happens to the locals or on the island its goal was to take it and use that propaganda to shore up the government. So yes it won’t be fun on the island and many will leave but I doubt it gets to bad, I suspect the local economy goes to hell but I don’t trully know enough about that to say.

What seems to have happened is that the Argentinian occupation forces initially expelled a small number of Kelpers, which attracted international criticism, then a further 14 potential 'troublemakers' were sent to Fox Bay East and placed under house arrest. Otherwise, the occupying forces seem to have been generally respectful - the principal exceptions being at Goose Green, where the civilian population was locked up in the social hall, and Patricio Dowling overstepping his authority as chief of police. The latter was apparently sufficiently objectionable that he was removed by the Argentinian forces. If the islands remained under Argentinian control, I would expect that those 14 might get deported, and favourable conditions offered for anyone wishing to leave voluntarily. Argentinian settlers seem like a given, at a bare minimum to replace departed Kelpers and possibly more - probably subsidised to do so, which won't help the condition of the Argentinian public purse. What, exactly, they would do there I don't know. I'd expect a boom in the popularity of mutton in Argentina as a 'patriotic' product of the 'liberated' islands. Over time the administration would surely revert to the mean of whatever was happening in mainland Argentina. It would be interesting to see what happens if/when Argentina undergoes its economic troubles. If the replacement of Kelpers with Argentinians hasn't progressed very far, I could easily see loud voices for ' erm... can we have the British back now?' on the islands.

I've studied this topic quite a bit and can say with confidence that Arg military did not go in with any concrete, long term plans on what to do with the locals. Their initial move was to try and keep a low profile (correctly) fearing that any incidents would only strengthen the UK's position, but this was more of on the spot decision by General Menendez than anything. My best guess is, if the UK fleet is defeated, eventually most of the locals will end up leaving on their own. Argentinean society is very Kafkean, and complex paperwork is needed for the most simple things. Unless islanders try to work with new local authorities, they will soon find themselves without the ability to drive cars (no driving licenses), lack of permits and licenses to practice trades, unable to open bank accounts, and unpaid property taxes piling up. Solving these things would entail applying for Argentinean ID cards, which could be interpreted as accepting Argentinean rule. I figure most people would refuse and just leave (unless the new authorities go out of their way to accommodate them.)

Probably nothing, except perhaps deporting a few troublemakers and using bureaucracy to force them to take Argentine ids. Even if Argentina wins the war, the Latin America debt crisis will be hitting by August '82, so I don't see that dictatorship lasting and, by that time, it wasn't as murderous as it was prior to 1980. The government, either the dictatorship or a new democratic government replacing it later, may enact tax breaks in the islands, like it had been done with Tierra del Fuego, to attempt to populate them. It doesn't need to be very successful, as they only had about 2000 inhabitants and Argentina had a population of about 30 million. As long as 3000 people move in, the locals become a minority. That may lead to ethnic tensions down the line, but they are just too few people in a too isolated place and facing a country that earned a reputation by going against one of the world's leading military powers and winning IITL.

Argentina would have gone as far as She could (and probably beyond) to accommodate them. It is of course possible that someone in the Islands would misbehave. That person would be crushed. The whole Argentina (Anaya) assumption was the Goa* Hypothesis. They are not going to come, there is not going to be a war, AND our US friends** shall help us. They were very, as in very, very, conscious of their international public reputation. Had they won the situation of the Kelpers and what the world was shown would be one of their primary preoccupations. items.original_question: How would the population of the Falklands have been treated if Argentina had won in 1982? Let’s suppose that HMS Hermes and HMS Invincible had been sunk, forcing the British to make peace and accept the loss of the Falklands. Let’s also suppose that this victory gave the Argentine junta a reprieve of 2-3 additional years, but that it still eventually collapsed so that Argentina followed a political path similar as IOTL. What would the Falklands population have faced? It's almost certain that Buenos Aires would have sent thousands of Argentine settlers to Puerto Argentino/Port Stanley in order to, at least, make the Anglo population a numerical minority and to extinguish any secessionist aspirations. But would this Anglo population have been allowed to remain and then obtain full Argentine citizenship, perhaps even some degree of cultural autonomy, or would it have faced a complete ethnic cleansing in order to permanently erase the Anglo identity of the Falklands? There are fewer than 2,000 people, so if Argentina decided to do it, it wouldn’t have any problem doing so.
items.model_answer:
If Argentina had won in 1982, the Falkland Islanders almost certainly would not have been physically exterminated or expelled en masse, but they also would not have been allowed to continue as a self-determining British community in the way they did after the British victory. The most likely outcome is a combination of political subordination, pressure to accept Argentine sovereignty, and gradual demographic and cultural assimilation.

The key point is that Argentina’s claim treated the islands as Argentine territory under illegal British occupation, not as a separate people with a right to decide their future. So if Buenos Aires had consolidated control, it likely would have regarded the existing population as residents to be incorporated, not as a sovereign community whose wishes were decisive. Islanders would probably have been offered Argentine citizenship or residency under Argentine administration, schools and official life would have shifted toward Spanish and Argentine national symbols, and local institutions would have been remade to fit Argentine law and governance.

At the same time, the military regime in 1982 was authoritarian and had a very poor human-rights record. That matters. Even if there were no plan for mass deportation, any islander resistance, pro-British political activity, or refusal to cooperate could have been met with surveillance, intimidation, detention, or restrictions on civil liberties, especially in the short term under military rule. The population was small enough that tight administrative control would have been feasible.

In the longer term, much would have depended on whether Argentine democracy returned quickly and on how secure Argentine control was internationally. Under a post-junta civilian government, treatment might have become less repressive, but the underlying aim would still likely have been integration into Argentina rather than recognition of the islanders’ preference to remain British. Immigration from the mainland might also have been encouraged over time, which could have diluted the existing islander community politically and culturally.

So the best concise answer is: they probably would have been kept on the islands, but as a population expected to become Argentine, with their British identity, political wishes, and local autonomy progressively weakened—and, under the 1982 dictatorship at least, dissent could have faced serious repression.

items.original_question: If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank? If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank in the twentieth century? In other words, it takes all the modernization and technological upgrade steps it can to protect its sovereignty in the late 19th century world, but either is deterred or self-deters from annexing Chinese or Russian territory, or territory possibly in their sphere, like Korea, or if attempting to do so, because such attempts were rather fashionable among *many* (but not all) modern industrial states, they fail, would the same things constraining Japanese aggression or success *also* doom Japan's ability to increase its economic productive capacity and standard of living over most of the decades of the 20th century? Or not? Could Japan do as well, or better, in absolute GDP growth, per capital GDP growth, PPP measured GDP growth, and GDP global rank, by, for instance, 1920, 1940, or 1960 or 1980, without having any expansionary success beyond consolidating control over the Ryukyu Kingdom and diplomatically clarifying its ownership of the Kurile and Bonin Islands and never having won a territory in a foreign war? I think I can illustrate it best using this graphic. This helpfully long term chart of real GDP growth of Japan, Britain and the US shows Japan's growth curve in * red *. Would Japan's line be higher, lower, or about the same, without Japan's early successful wars with China and Russia, annexation of Korea, WWI absorption of Micronesia, 1930s exploitation of Manchuria and then occupied China, followed by the ultimately futile and highly destructive Pacific War, and the Cold War alliance arrangement the US and Japan set up to deal with the Soviet Union and avoid the recurrence of mutual war? Maybe the red line in the alternate history of an alternate Japan would have lower at some points and higher at others, but if so, please specify roughly when, and where do you think things would be stabilizing by the 1960 through present-day era. It may be tempting to call a Meiji (and beyond) Japan, with this type of foreign policy record that lacks success at military-naval territorial expansion as a Japan "pulling a Thailand" or analogous to a Thailand. But I would urge caution in making such an analogy. Sure, Thailand protected its sovereignty uniquely within its Southeast Asian neighborhood, while not being able to clash with colonial powers head on. But that's as far as the analogy would apply. Thailand's technological advancement and industrialization was for long, until the 1960s, pretty weak, and a Japan on Thailand's *economic* trajectory would be *categorically* poorer and less technologically, industrially, scientifically, and financially sophisticated than OTL's Japan. Thailand also only *began* experiments with constitutional government about fifty years later than Japan, even though Japan in the mid-20th century had some spectacular democratic and especially liberal failures and has some democratic deficits to this day. But their internal political cultures and societies are quite different.
items.model_answer:
Yes—quite possibly, but with a different profile and probably on a slower, less dramatic path.

If “still Meiji” means Japan still carries out the core Meiji transformations—centralization of the state, abolition of the old feudal order, land-tax reform, mass education, conscription, legal modernization, infrastructure building, and active industrial policy—then the biggest drivers of long-run economic growth are still there. Those domestic reforms mattered more to eventual great-power status than empire did. Japan’s rise was not created from scratch by conquest; it was built on state capacity, literacy, social discipline, industrial learning, and successful adaptation of Western institutions and technology.

So in principle, a non-expansionist Meiji Japan could still have become a first-rank industrial economy, and eventually something like a G7-level country. In fact, post-1945 Japan is strong evidence for this. The Japan that actually became an economic superpower after World War II did so after losing its empire, under severe constraints on military power, and with growth driven by exports, technology absorption, high savings, industrial coordination, and human capital. That suggests empire was not necessary for becoming rich.

But the counterfactual has to be handled carefully, because imperial expansion did provide some real advantages. Victories over China and Russia raised Japan’s international prestige, improved treaty revision, increased access to Taiwan, Korea, and later Manchuria, and gave strategic depth and some access to resources and captive markets. Expansion also strengthened domestic nationalist coalitions and military influence. Without those gains, Japan might have faced tighter resource constraints, less geopolitical leverage, and perhaps more vulnerability to Western pressure. It might have remained respected but not feared, commercially integrated but diplomatically less equal for longer.

The key question is what “G7 rank” means. If it means military-great-power status by the early twentieth century, then probably no: without defeating China or Russia, Japan likely does not break into the top rank as quickly or as unmistakably. Those wars were crucial signals to the world that Japan had arrived as a great power. If it means becoming one of the world’s leading advanced industrial economies by the later twentieth century, then yes, that seems very plausible. A Japan that stayed focused on domestic industrialization, shipping, textiles, machinery, chemicals, education, and trade could well have become rich without colonial empire—perhaps richer per capita sooner, because it would avoid the enormous fiscal, political, and eventually catastrophic military costs of imperial overstretch.

In some ways, non-expansion might even improve the long-run outcome. Empire drew Japan into increasingly destructive continental commitments, intensified military dominance in politics, worsened relations with major powers, and culminated in a disastrous war that destroyed much of the country. A Japan that remained reformist, commercially ambitious, and strategically cautious might have looked more like a Northeast Asian version of a highly developmental trading state: less glamorous in hard-power terms before 1914, but potentially more stable and more prosperous over the long run.

So the best direct answer is: yes, Meiji Japan could likely still have reached G7-level economic status without expanding at China’s or Russia’s expense, provided its internal modernization remained intact and it retained access to world markets, capital, and technology. It probably would not have become as quickly or as visibly a military great power, but it may have had a better long-term path to wealth precisely because it avoided the burdens and disasters of empire.
