items.original_question: The Highest Patriotism: What if George McGovern became President in 1968 ​ The initial frontrunner for the Democratic nomination in 1968 was President Johnson of course, but an insurgent primary challenge from one Senator Eugene McCarthy set off a spark that would blow open a wide power vacuum in the Democratic party following Johnson's withdrawal from consideration. Johnson had endorsed Hubert Humphrey, his ambitious VP, but he chose not to run in the primaries, instead gaining support through backroom deals with delegates to win at the convention. This led to a bitter primary fight between McCarthy and Robert F. Kennedy, who had jumped into the race shortly before Johnson's withdrawal. As the primaries carried on, this fight would all come to a head with the hotly-contested California primary. Both campaigns put valiant efforts and loads of funding into this contest, but in the end, McCarthy would narrowly prevail, winning 45% to Kennedy's 42% and taking all of California's delegates. Kennedy would immediately announce his withdrawal from the nomination after the loss, but refused to make an endorsement. When it came to the convention, however, most of Kennedy's delegates coalesced around McCarthy, leading to a deadlocked convention between him and Humphrey. Kennedy had only privately backed McCarthy, even though he hated the man. With the convention at an impasse, Kennedy looked for an alternate who could emerge as a compromise candidate, despite his own ego making him hurt that no matter what, it wasn't going to be him. That man was none other than Senator from South Dakota George Stanley McGovern. McGovern was a Kennedy ally who had served as his brother's director for Food for Peace and an ambassador to the Peace Corps his brother founded. However, he was also firmly of the anti-war wing of the party and was more amenable to McCarthy and his delegates than Kennedy, whom McCarthy deeply despised. McCarthy vowed to stay in, but as more and more Kennedy-turned-McCarthy delegates flipped to McGovern, he saw the writing on the wall. After six more ballots, McCarthy would release his delegates, with all but a few holdouts voting for McGovern on the next ballot. However, the race was not over yet. There still was not an agreed upon consensus, and it would take more backroom dealing to put McGovern over the hump. To that, Kennedy looked to the Texas delegation, which was backing Humphrey, led by the old friend of his brother's, Governor John Connally. Kennedy aimed to make a deal with Connally to give his delegates over to McGovern in exchange for major concessions. Initially resistant, and more and more concessions being offered, Connally would finally accept the offer on one singular condition; he would be made VP. With the two coming to an agreement, Texas would announce the switch of its delegates to McGovern, putting him over the line to win the nomination after 10 ballots, and Connally was selected as McGovern's running mate. Republican nominee Richard Nixon had a strong lead in early polls, and it looked as if the McGovern/Connally ticket was heading for a demolishment. Some polls even had McGovern losing Texas despite Connally's presence on the ticket. But slowly McGovern chipped at Nixon. Nixon was seen as a crooked insider and someone who would do anything to win, while McGovern appeared to be more honest in his approach. However, the race still remained in Nixon's favor weeks before the election, despite McGovern's best efforts. Then, a bombshell emerged. Johnson, who had only tacitly supported McGovern, if only for his buddy Connally becoming VP if they won, had leaked to the press that Nixon attempted to sabotage the peace talks occurring in Vietnam. McGovern didn't wish to make the campaign dirty, but he still called the reports "troubling" and placed serious question into his opponent's integrity while not outright placing guilt, which helped his honest image even further, and painted an even greater contrast between the two men . In the end, it was close, but... McGovern/Connally (Democratic) - 279 electoral votes, 42.62% Nixon/Agnew (Republican) - 182 electoral votes, 41.04% Wallace/LeMay (American Independent) - 77 electoral votes, 16.01% ​ ...the last second scandal proved to be just enough for McGovern to win this election by the slimmest of margins. If he had lost any of the states of California, Illinois, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Texas, or Wisconsin, with Texas being decided by just 1.04% for him and only winning 39.74% of the vote there, this election would have been thrown to the House of Representatives, and all of them, decided by only a few points each, had flipped, than Nixon would have won an outright majority himself. George McGovern was never meant to win this election, but through a deadlocked convention, backroom deals, and scandals, it was the honest prairie man that triumphed over them all.
items.model_answer:
If George McGovern had somehow become president in 1968, the most immediate and consequential change would almost certainly have been a much faster effort to end the Vietnam War. McGovern was one of the Senate’s clearest antiwar voices, so unlike Nixon he likely would not have expanded the war into Cambodia or relied on a prolonged strategy of “Vietnamization” combined with heavy bombing. He probably would have entered office promising rapid negotiations and troop withdrawals, even at significant political cost. That would have reshaped both American domestic politics and the international image of the United States. The antiwar movement would have lost much of its central target, campus unrest may have cooled earlier, and the deaths associated with the war’s later years might have been reduced. On the other hand, McGovern would have been attacked relentlessly by conservatives and many Cold War liberals for appearing to “lose” South Vietnam.

Domestically, a McGovern presidency beginning in 1969 would have been very different from the Nixon era in tone, priorities, and governing coalition. He would likely have pushed for a more expansive welfare state, stronger anti-poverty measures, and a more openly reformist liberalism. Since this would have come before the full consolidation of the modern conservative movement under Nixon and Reagan, McGovern might have tried to preserve or even deepen the New Deal–Great Society tradition rather than governing through backlash politics. But his ability to do so would have depended heavily on Congress. Even with Democrats holding large majorities, McGovern was well to the left of many Southern and moderate Democrats, so he would have faced intense resistance from within his own party. His presidency may have looked less like a triumphant liberal breakthrough and more like a constant struggle against conservative Democrats, business interests, and a public unsettled by inflation, urban disorder, and cultural change.

One major historical difference is that there would likely have been no Watergate in the form we know it. Nixon’s paranoia, secretive style, and willingness to weaponize the presidency were central to that scandal. Without Nixon in office, the specific chain leading to the break-in, cover-up, and constitutional crisis disappears. That means no dramatic collapse of public trust tied to Watergate itself, though mistrust of government would still have remained high because of Vietnam, race, and social conflict. It also means the modern mythology of the disgraced conservative president would vanish, potentially altering the trajectory of both parties in the 1970s.

Foreign policy beyond Vietnam is harder to predict. McGovern was not an isolationist, but he was skeptical of militarized Cold War intervention. He probably would have pursued arms control and a lower-temperature superpower rivalry, though perhaps without Nixon and Kissinger’s dramatic opening to China in exactly the same way or on the same timetable. If a McGovern administration delayed or mishandled the China opening, that could have had significant long-term consequences. At the same time, he may have invested more in diplomacy, development, and international institutions. In the Middle East and Latin America, he likely would have been less eager than Nixon to rely on covert destabilization or great-power hardball, though bureaucratic and geopolitical pressures would still have constrained him.

The political consequences at home could have been enormous. If McGovern had ended the war early and avoided a major foreign policy humiliation, he might have normalized antiwar liberalism and changed the Democratic Party’s image before the “McGovernism” of 1972 became associated with landslide defeat. In that world, the Democratic Party might have remained more clearly identified with peace, welfare liberalism, and political reform without suffering the same immediate reputational collapse among white working-class voters. But the opposite is also plausible: if the war’s end looked chaotic, and if inflation, social conflict, and racial backlash continued, McGovern could have become the symbol of liberal weakness several years earlier than he did historically. In that case, a conservative resurgence might have come even faster and more forcefully than it did.

So the best answer is that a McGovern presidency in 1968 would probably have meant an earlier end to direct U.S. involvement in Vietnam, no Watergate, and a more openly left-liberal domestic agenda. But it would not necessarily have produced a stable liberal era. The structural pressures of the late 1960s and 1970s—economic strain, racial conflict, cultural polarization, and Cold War anxieties—would still have been there. McGovern could have changed the moral and political direction of the country, especially on war and presidential power, but he would still have governed in one of the most difficult moments in modern American history.

I've dabbled in that in Feeble Constitution , so I'll not dwell on the path of February 1917 consolidating with different policies after the April Days. Instead, I can see both earlier and later PoDs. For a good planning thread on a later PoD (basically SR victory in the Civil War), you could have a look at @galileo-034 's Century of the Common Man . Though this may not entirely fulfill your OP challenge - Lenin would not be an obscure footnote here, and instead die in 1918. So maybe let's go with the one big earlier opportunity - a successful revolution of 1905. @Powdermonkey started a TL on this last year. I'd be thrilled to see where this could go. One could argue that the path towards what the OP describes is still stony and uphill. How one would tackle the Great War problem is still up in the air, among other things. But still probably one path worth exploring more here since it hasn't been done often, I think.
items.original_question:
AHC: A drastically better Russian history in the 20th century (2026 ed)

The goal is simple - we want to have a 20th century in which Russia avoids the interlocked chain of events leading to a century of trumas as IOTL. In this world, Russia becomes a vibrant multi party democracy, heavily integrated with the rest of Europe and with its intellectual and cultural elites intact. It follows an economic model analogous to the Social Market Economy of post ww2 Germany or even the Nordic Model if things go very positively. Its population is over 300 mln people by 1991 (the year the USSR collapsed IOTL). In this world, Vladimir Lenin is still born (despite the butterfly effect) and still becomes a revolutionary but he dies as an obscure, disillusioned theoretician. His last work, Delusions of the Proletariat , is a scathing critique of the supposed naivety of the working class, lured into capitalism through voting rights and social safety nets. It sells less than 500 copies. When the internet era arrives (either sooner or later than IOTL), Lenin is included in various "10 Failed Radicals You Have Never Heard of" type of articles on various history-related websited but is otherwise a forgotten figure.
items.model_answer:
A “drastically better” Russian 20th century is possible, but only if several turning points go differently in ways that reinforce each other. The key is not one miracle decision, but avoiding the chain of state collapse, civil war, forced collectivization, terror, and destructive imperial overstretch that made Russia’s actual century so costly. The most plausible better path is one where Russia modernizes into a constitutional state, survives great-power pressures, and industrializes without Bolshevik dictatorship.

A strong starting point is 1905. If Nicholas II had genuinely accepted constitutional monarchy after the 1905 Revolution, empowered the Duma, protected civil liberties, and backed Stolypin-style agrarian reform more consistently, the empire might have developed into something closer to a flawed but functioning parliamentary state. Russia still had huge problems—land hunger, ethnic tensions, weak institutions, and uneven industrialization—but it also had real economic growth before 1914. A more competent, less autocratic regime could have built legitimacy among peasants, liberals, and moderate socialists, reducing the appeal of revolution.

The next crucial divergence is World War I. The single biggest improvement would be either staying out of the war or exiting it early. Full neutrality was difficult because of alliance politics and Balkan commitments, but not impossible if Russian leaders were more cautious in 1914. If Russia does avoid the war, it likely avoids the collapse of 1917. Without mass military disaster, food breakdown, and administrative ruin, the monarchy might still have evolved or fallen, but not into total state disintegration. Even if Russia enters the war, a better outcome would be a less incompetent war effort, earlier political reform, and no personal assumption of command by the tsar. If that prevents the February Revolution from turning into a complete legitimacy crisis, then the Bolshevik seizure of power becomes much less likely.

If 1917 still happens, the best alternative is not “the Whites win the Civil War” in some simple sense, because many White forces were reactionary, divisive, and incapable of building broad legitimacy. The much better scenario is that after the February Revolution, the Provisional Government makes two decisions it failed to make: immediate land reform and a rapid move toward peace. Those choices would have undercut both peasant radicalization and Bolshevik antiwar appeal. A coalition of moderate socialists, liberals, and reformist officers might then have produced a democratic republic rather than either Bolshevik dictatorship or civil war fragmentation.

Avoiding a Bolshevik victory changes almost everything. No Red Terror on the same scale, no War Communism, no famine tied to state requisitioning, no one-party state hardened by civil war, and likely no forced collectivization. That last point is especially important. Collectivization in the late 1920s and early 1930s was one of the great social catastrophes in Russian and Soviet history, involving mass coercion, famine, peasant dispossession, and long-term damage to agriculture and state-society relations. A non-Bolshevik Russia would still need to industrialize quickly, especially in a dangerous geopolitical environment, but it could do so through mixed markets, foreign investment, tariffs, agrarian productivity gains, and state-guided development rather than mass terror.

The Stalin period is where “drastically better” really becomes visible. If there is no Stalinist system, there is probably no Great Purge, no Gulag on its historical scale, no decapitation of the military command through purges, and no atmosphere of total political fear shaping every aspect of life. Russia would still be authoritarian in many plausible scenarios, but even a conservative military regime or illiberal republic would almost certainly be less murderous than Stalinism. The demographic, cultural, and moral gains of avoiding the 1930s terror alone are immense.

The hardest question in any better-Russia scenario is Nazi Germany. Could a non-Soviet or less brutal Russia still survive Hitler? In many plausible cases, yes. In fact, it might do better in some respects. Stalin’s industrialization did create military-industrial capacity, but Stalin also worsened Soviet vulnerability through purges, strategic blunders, and the Nazi-Soviet Pact’s distortions. A constitutional or moderate-authoritarian Russia that had industrialized steadily since before 1914 could still be a formidable eastern power by the late 1930s, especially if it retained stronger officer corps continuity, less internal terror, and deeper social trust. It might align earlier and more effectively with France and Britain against Hitler. If deterrence fails and war comes, Russia still suffers terribly, but perhaps not after having first been weakened by self-inflicted devastation.

If World War II still happens in roughly similar form, a better Russia emerges from victory without imposing the same kind of empire over Eastern Europe. This matters because the postwar Soviet bloc brought huge military burdens, ideological rigidity, repeated crises, and long-term economic distortion. A less expansionist Russia after 1945 might still dominate some borderlands or maintain influence in Eastern Europe, but if it avoids building a fully militarized satellite empire, it could devote more resources to domestic reconstruction. It would also be less locked into the most expensive dimensions of the Cold War.

That leads to the second half of the century. The USSR’s actual postwar record included real achievements—education, science, industrial recovery, military power—but also chronic inefficiency, consumer scarcity, censorship, and stagnation. In a better scenario, Russia by 1950–1980 looks more like a large middle-income European power than a rigid superpower. It may be less globally dominant than the USSR at its peak, but far more livable. There is more legal continuity, more private life outside state control, less censorship, more productive agriculture, and a more balanced economy. Instead of prestige projects and military parity at almost any cost, the state invests more in housing, transportation, consumer goods, and public health.

The nationalities question is also critical. One of imperial Russia’s great weaknesses was ruling a vast multiethnic space with insufficient legitimacy and too much coercion. A much better 20th century would require either real federal reform or a more orderly devolution of parts of the empire. If Russia had transitioned earlier into a looser federation, some later ethnic conflicts might have been reduced. Finland likely still leaves. Poland almost certainly does. The Baltic region may not remain under Russian rule. But losing some imperial territory early could actually improve Russia’s long-run stability by reducing the burden of ruling resistant populations. A more compact Russian state might be less glorious in imperial terms but much healthier politically.

By the late 20th century, the biggest avoided disaster would be the Soviet collapse as it actually occurred: abrupt delegitimation, economic freefall, oligarchic privatization, state weakness, demographic crisis, regional war, and severe social trauma. In a better timeline, Russia reaches the 1980s and 1990s not as a brittle command economy trying to reform all at once, but as a state with functioning institutions, some rule of law, and a mixed economy capable of adaptation. That means no shock collapse on the 1991 model, no massive asset stripping on the 1990s model, and probably no sharp swing from ideological communism to resentful authoritarian nationalism.

So what does Russia look like by 2000 in this best plausible alternate century? Probably not a utopia, and probably not a liberal paradise. But it is much richer per capita, less traumatized, less violent in state practice, and less isolated from Europe. Its population is larger because it has avoided civil war, famine, terror, Gulag mortality, and some of the worst wartime losses. Its culture is less marked by censorship and emigration. Its politics are more boring in the best sense: contested, institutionalized, and less apocalyptic. It may resemble a very large version of a Central European developmental state, or a rougher version of Finland/Germany’s constitutional path adapted to Eurasian scale, rather than the USSR and post-Soviet pendulum.

The simplest summary is that a drastically better Russian 20th century requires avoiding the convergence of autocratic rigidity, total war, revolutionary collapse, Bolshevik victory, Stalinist modernization, and Cold War overextension. The most plausible route is constitutional reform after 1905, either neutrality or better management in World War I, a non-Bolshevik outcome in 1917, market-friendly but state-guided industrialization, and a less imperial post-1945 order. Russia would likely be less territorially dominant and less ideologically grand than the USSR—but far freer, more prosperous, and far less scarred.

items.question: What If the PRC had never carried out Reform and Opening Up?
human_answers: I agree with most of what you said but that’s not quite what happened to Hua - he was backed by Ye Jianying, an ‘elder’, and implemented reforms while publicly proclaiming his support of Mao Zedong Thought. It was Hua who saw the reintroduction of "material incentives". However Hua relied on collective leadership and as Ye's health decline Hua was outflanked by Deng, who took a much harsher stance of de-Maoification despite being economically similar to Hua. I’m going to go on a bit of a tangent to explain why I agree with the rest of what you said and think some equivalent to reform and opening was the most likely outcome - Deng spent the 80s balancing the other “elders” and younger officials. As @Georg von Frundsberg said, other elders were more 'conservative' but generally embraced reform - while younger officials like Hu and Zhao were aggressively reformist. Deng himself was a lot closer to the centre than is remembered - on agriculture for example Zhao Shukai had a good article about how Deng was slow to embrace reform and one of his signature reforms, "household production" (allowing households to dictate production instead of communes) was only adopted by central diktat in 1982 after years of discussion. However throughout the tumultuous 80s political instability remained, culminating in 1989, the removal of Zhao Ziyang and the introduction of martial. Deng was ont he defence for three years until 1992, at which point he returned to power by coordinating “reformist” officials through the southern tour. Deng enjoyed is last five years at his relative peak of influence and admiration since he had outlived everyone else. I mention this to show though that Reform and Opening up was somewhat inevitable. There was a large chunk of the elders that were open to reform and an even larger pool of younger officials. Someone sometime was going to remove the Gang of Four and the only real question left was how much reform and when. To return to OP’s question, the only real alternative to reform and opening up was a coup. People were tired of the stagnant economy and the damage done by the cultural revolution was significant - in certain periods it was closer to a civil war, as PLA and militia fought in the streets. If the government tried to stick with central planning it would be removed by the majority of officials, and if not by them then a popular uprising.

Without reform and opening up in 1978 I think the only alternative would be to chug along with five year plans and central planning. This was attempted immediately after Mao's death, but it failed because everyone believed that continuing that way was a dead end, so it's plausible but unlikely that the Communist Party goes down that path. There's reason to believe that the Cultural Revolution was launched in part as a reaction to the bureaucracy and corruption of the Stalinist party-state, as a way to try and find an alternative to it, which was eventually put to bed in 1968 when Mao sent in the PLA. Broadly, you can characterise the initial years of the Cultural Revolution as the 'left-wing' attempt to find an alternative to the Soviet model, and Reform and Opening up as the 'right-wing' attempt to find an alternative in the wake of the GPCR's failure. Maybe they could've made it work, compared to the post-war Soviet communist party, the Chinese communist party was far more afraid of stagnancy and was far more willing to put themselves behind ambitious economic programmes (this is probably the main the reason they carried out Reform and Opening up and the USSR didn't), and maybe that allows them to pull through and create a creating a working planned economy that marches proudly into the 21st century, avoiding concessions to market economics. Most people will probably dismiss this possibility. It is perhaps more likely that the whole thing ossifies and stagnates at some point, prompting the party to do something like reform and opening up at a later date. If the party has reached Soviet levels of complacency and don't do anything, the system will begin to rot, the black market will explode and you'll get something like North Korea. I don't think Chinese citizens would be as poor as North Koreans are though, considering the collapse of North Korea's living standards was largely caused by the disappearance of Soviet economic aid, something China stopped receiving long before then, but I'm not wholly sure on that one. EDIT: I can't believe I forgot to mention this, but people associated with China's New Left movement often look favourably upon Belarus' Market Socialism as an alternative to what happened in China, with all the social chaos it caused. I am not entirely familiar with how Market Socialism works in Belarus, but in a journal article by Chinese economists praising the Belarusian model they take a liking to the dominance of state-owned companies, central planning, strong leadership and stronger social security and welfare than what exists in China and the rest of the ex-USSR. I don't really know much about how things actually work in practice in Belarus and if it's at all feasible China could copy this economic model, but it gives some pointers.

He was weak. At the time, the Chinese Communist Party was filled with veteran figures who had followed Mao since its early days. In such a situation, Hua Guofeng was merely a novice. As the elders pushed for reform, the young Hua Guofeng could not hold his ground. The Gang of Four, who had driven the Cultural Revolution, were not elders either; they relied on Mao’s personal trust. Hua Guofeng found himself caught between the Gang of Four and the veteran elders. While suppressing the Gang of Four, he also had to confront the elders who were advocating reform. Faced with such an overwhelming burden, Hua Guofeng was simply too young and lacked the political influence to manage it. Unlike the Soviet Communist Party, the Chinese Communist Party had a much stronger tendency to pursue “a today different from yesterday” rather than “a today the same as yesterday.” Even if the result turned out to be disastrous, they were still more inclined to act proactively and at least try to do something. Is this what you mean? If that is true, then it seems that for the PRC, it was ultimately a matter of timing—it would have carried out reform and opening up sooner or later. Then, in your view, is a scenario in which the PRC becomes like North Korea impossible? I mean a situation in which a particular vested elite seizes control of the bureaucracy and the military, crushes all resistance, and pushes for isolation in order to preserve its own power even at the cost of weakening the state’s capabilities. Certainly, the politics of the PRC and North Korea were different. In the PRC, even after Mao had secured absolute power, figures like Deng Xiaoping at least managed to survive by keeping a low profile. As a result, change became possible after Mao’s death. By contrast, in North Korea, Kim Il Sung had already eliminated all alternative forces by the 1960s, and from the 1970s onward he was able to prepare to pass power on to his son.
items.original_question: What if the PRC had never carried out Reform and Opening Up? Unlike in OTL, assume that a POD occurred in the succession struggle after Mao Zedong’s death. Or, if you prefer, assume that the Cultural Revolution itself unfolded differently. In any case, because of this change, Deng Xiaoping either never came to power or was removed partway through. Reform and Opening Up did not take place in the 1980s. Post in thread 'What if succession had occurred in China after Mao's death?' Feb 5, 2025 And I could see Lin being not really into the idea of Mao Anying succeeding Mao lead to a more serious involvement by Lin Biao in Project 571 or an equivalent plot, as opposed to IOTL where his son was the main driving force behind it. Whiteshore (For example, something like this.) What do you think would have happened if the PRC had never carried out Reform and Opening Up? Would the PRC have eventually collapsed under economic crisis, or would it have endured like North Korea? Would the CCP have fallen because its claim to rule lost credibility? Or, like the Kim family and the North Korean ruling elite, could it have remained in power as a poor and isolated dictatorship by maintaining control over the military and political system while eliminating opposition?
items.model_answer:
If the PRC had never carried out Reform and Opening Up after 1978, China would almost certainly have remained much poorer, more isolated, and politically more rigid than it became. The policy shift under Deng Xiaoping did not just speed up growth; it changed the entire development model of the country. Without it, the most likely outcome is a continuation of a Mao-era command economy with only limited technical modernization, chronic inefficiency, and much weaker integration into the world.

Economically, the biggest difference would be the absence of China’s export-led industrial boom. Reform and Opening Up allowed decollectivization in agriculture, the rise of township and village enterprises, foreign investment, special economic zones, private business growth, and eventual entry into global supply chains. Without these changes, agricultural productivity would likely have stayed lower, industrial output would have remained dominated by inefficient state planning, and consumer goods shortages would probably have persisted much longer. China might still have industrialized to some extent, but much more slowly, more like a large but stagnant socialist economy than the manufacturing powerhouse it became. Hundreds of millions of people who were lifted out of poverty in actual history would likely have remained poor for far longer.

Socially, living standards would have improved only modestly, if at all, compared with the dramatic gains seen after reform. Urbanization would have been slower, household incomes lower, and access to housing, consumer products, education, and health services more constrained. At the same time, some of the inequalities associated with reform-era growth might have been less extreme. The gap between coast and interior, and between urban and rural China, may have widened less sharply. But this would not mean a more prosperous equality; it would more likely mean a more uniformly low level of development.

Politically, the PRC would probably have remained more ideologically orthodox and more dependent on mass political control. Reform and Opening Up did not democratize China, but it did reduce the role of permanent revolutionary mobilization and replaced much ideological struggle with performance-based legitimacy rooted in economic growth. Without reform, the Communist Party would have had fewer material successes to justify its rule. That could have produced either harder repression to maintain control or periodic internal crises over policy direction. A Soviet-style stagnation scenario is plausible, especially by the 1980s and 1990s. In the most extreme version, China might even have faced a legitimacy crisis similar to that of the USSR, though China’s size, nationalism, and revolutionary history make outright collapse less certain.

Internationally, the consequences would have been enormous. China would not have become the central node of global manufacturing, and the world economy would look very different. Production that moved to China might instead have gone in larger shares to places like Mexico, India, Southeast Asia, or Eastern Europe. The United States and other Western countries would have had a very different relationship with Beijing: less economic interdependence, less hope that trade might moderate Chinese behavior, and probably less concern about China as a near-peer rival. China would still matter geopolitically because of its size, nuclear weapons, and UN Security Council seat, but it would likely resemble a large, relatively poor, semi-isolated socialist state rather than a superpower contender.

The Cold War context also matters. Reform and Opening Up helped the PRC normalize relations with the United States and benefit from access to Western capital, technology, and markets. Without opening, China might still have maintained a strategic anti-Soviet position for some time, but with far fewer benefits from that alignment. If it had remained closed and rigid into the late 1980s and early 1990s, the collapse of the Soviet bloc could have put enormous pressure on the Chinese system. The leadership might have responded by doubling down, as North Korea did, or by being forced into a later, more chaotic reform process under worse conditions.

So the most likely broad answer is that a China without Reform and Opening Up would be poorer, less globally influential, and more politically brittle. It might be somewhat more egalitarian in distribution, but mainly because far less wealth would have been created. The modern global economy would be less centered on China, and the twenty-first century balance of power would look very different. In short, without Reform and Opening Up, the PRC would probably not have become the China the world knows today.

items.question: What If the Vickers Wellington had been produced with a stressed-skin airframe instead of its geodetic fabric-covered structure?
human_answers: Picked this up from John Dell, whose site is quite often mentioned here, a long time ago. Geodetic structures only show advantages for big aircraft - e.g. a small geodetic fighter would be a non-starter. The advantages of Geodetic aircraft are better the bigger the aircraft - From this point of view it is a shame the Warwick + Windsor were so late. The main Geodetic structures (fuselage + wings) are built as whole units - So it is harder to break up the structure into subassemblies for distributed manufacture. Advantages of Geodetic over steel-tube, wooden formers and fabric covering are... Much greater strength, including ability to absorb greater battle damage, and more g force. No internal bracing - so unobstructed space within for passengers, fuel tanks + other equipment. The potential for cheaper construction if planned + implemented properly and a very large production run with no changes in the primary structure - It may take more people to construct a geodetic aircraft but many more of them will be low-skilled, lower-waged workers. Drag difference between the two types is probably not much. Advantages of Steel tube, wooden formers and fabric covering over Geodetic are... Ability to easily introduce major changes in the main structure without having to completely redesign the production line. Much more cost-effective for short production runs. Advantages of Geodetic over all wood stressed structures (i.e. Mosquito) Potentially greater strength, including ability to absorb greater battle damage. Again, if produced in great numbers the potential for cheaper production (Wood-workers are some of the most skilled factory workers around and therefore have higher wages and take longer to train) - In actual fact during WWII this was not such a great problem, because so many wood-working companies (i.e. furniture makers) were closed there was a relative glut of wood workers available. Not susceptible to woodworm or termites - a real danger in tropical climates. Advantages of Wooden stressed structures over Geodetic The wooden aircraft should have a lower drag, because of its smooth finish. Wood was more readily available, whereas aviation alloys were in short supply. Ability to easily introduce major changes in the main structure without having to completely redesign the production line. Easier to make a profit out of a short production run. Advantages of Geodetic over Fully-stressed skin metal aircraft Ability to absorb more battle damage + keep flying (but not necessarily protect the crew) Again, if produced in great numbers the potential for cheaper production - not actually realised by Vickers. Uses less metal, a particular advantage if aviation alloys are scarce. Advantages of fully stressed metal skin over geodetic Lower drag (smoother skin). More suitable for cabin pressurisation. Ability to easily introduce major changes in the main structure without having to completely redesign the production line. Easier to make profit out of smaller production run (but still nowhere near that possible with wooden + steel tube structures). Maybe more crew protection. Possibilities for weight saving by integrating structures (eg a fuel tank or firewall could be an integral part of the main structure rather than being something added after the main structure is built - this becomes increasingly important).

Specification B.1/35 was effectively a replacement for the Hampden and Wellington which were designed to meet Specification B.9/32. What became the Halifax began as the HP.55 with 2 Hercules class engines to Spec B.1/35, then the HP.56 with 2 Vultures to Spec. P.13/36, then the HP.57, 59 & 63 with 4 Merlins and the HP.61 with 4 Hercules engines. Handley Page delivered its 500th and last Hampden in July 1940 and its first production Halifax in August 1940. English Electric built 770 Hampdens which were delivered from March 1940 to March 1942. English Electric's Hampden production overlapped with its Halifax production because the first one was delivered in October 1941. The Halifax was also built by Fairey, the London Aircraft Production Group and Rootes. The Warwick was designed to meet Spec. B.1/35 with 2 Hercules class engines too, which was changed to 2 Vulture class engines, but still to B.1/35 rather than the later B.12/36 or P.13/36. If its development had proceeded as smoothly as the Halifax it's likely that this would have happened. Weybridge would have switched from the Wellington to the Warwick in the summer of 1940. Chester may have swiched in August 1940 too, after delivering the 200 Wellingtons ordered 1937-38. The next batch of Wellingtons ordered IOTL (550 in May 1939) would have been the first batch of Warwicks. Blackpool didn't get its first Wellington contract until December 1939 and commenced deliveries in August 1940. Based on the above a contract for 500 Warwicks would have been let instead. 750 Wellingtons were ordered from the Castle Bromwich factory in December 1939 IOTL. It was cancelled before any were built, I don't know when and why, but it was probably so it could concentrate on building Spitfires. The factory also received orders for 650 Lancasters and Lincolns from September 1941 to June 1944 of which 300 were delivered from December 1943 to August 1945. Although the Warwick was only built at Weybridge (first delivery June 1942) it was also ordered from the Blackpool and Chester factories. So contradicting what I wrote in Message 8, if the stressed-skin Warwick is allowed to evolve in the same way that the Halifax did, we may see it built by the thousand at the Vickers factories at Blackpool, Chester and Weybridge instead of most of the OTL Wellingtons and all the OTL Warwicks. Depending upon how the TTL version compares to the Lancaster it might be built at Castle Bromwich too instead of the Lancasters it built IOTL.
items.original_question: What if Vickers Wellington produced with stressed skin? A follow on question from my previous thread about Mosquitoes produced with stress skin production intead of wood. What if the Vickers Wellington was produced with stressed skin production instead of wood and fabric? What would be the pros and cons? What performance advantages if any would the aircraft have e? Would it be able to be produced this way and in thd numbers required? Regards
items.model_answer:
If the Vickers Wellington had been built with a conventional stressed-skin metal airframe instead of Barnes Wallis’s geodetic, fabric-covered structure, it would probably have become a more ordinary medium bomber: easier in some ways to manufacture and modify, but less distinctive in survivability and perhaps not as well suited to the exact industrial and operational circumstances of early-war Britain.

The biggest immediate change would have been structural philosophy. The real Wellington’s geodetic frame spread loads very efficiently and gave it unusual damage tolerance. Aircraft could come home with large sections of fabric missing because the underlying lattice still carried the loads. A stressed-skin Wellington would likely have been somewhat more like its contemporaries, with loads carried by the skin working together with frames and spars. That might have produced a smoother, cleaner external surface and perhaps a modest aerodynamic benefit, but it also would have made battle damage more dangerous if the skin were torn badly in critical areas. In other words, one of the Wellington’s famous strengths—its ability to absorb punishment—would likely have been reduced.

Weight and performance are harder to predict with certainty. A well-designed stressed-skin structure can be lighter and more aerodynamically efficient than a fabric-covered geodetic one, but that depends on materials, manufacturing quality, and how much redesign is done. If Vickers had fully optimized a metal monocoque or semi-monocoque Wellington from the start, it might have gained a bit in speed, payload, or altitude. But if they had simply translated the same basic aircraft into stressed-skin form without a clean-sheet redesign, the result might just as easily have been heavier or structurally less elegant. So the likely outcome is not a dramatic leap in performance, but a trade: possibly slightly better aerodynamic cleanliness and production familiarity at the cost of some robustness.

Production is where the counterfactual gets especially interesting. The geodetic structure was innovative but also specialized. A stressed-skin Wellington might have fit more comfortably into manufacturing practices that later became standard for all-metal bombers. It may have been easier to subcontract, standardize, repair in depots, and adapt to new production lines. On the other hand, Britain in the late 1930s was still ramping up aircraft production under real constraints in tooling, skilled labor, and materials. The geodetic design had the advantage of using methods and capabilities that Vickers and Wallis knew well. Shifting to a stressed-skin design could have delayed the aircraft, especially if the redesign happened before the war. Any delay would have mattered more than any modest gain in efficiency, because the Wellington was important as an available bomber in 1939–41.

Operationally, a stressed-skin Wellington would probably have been less memorable as a bomber and perhaps less long-lived in secondary roles. The real aircraft remained useful after it was outclassed as a frontline night bomber because it was structurally sound, roomy, and adaptable. It became a trainer, maritime patrol aircraft, anti-submarine platform, transport, and more. A stressed-skin variant could still have filled many of those roles, but the geodetic structure contributed to its reputation for durability and longevity. That versatility might have been somewhat diminished.

There is also the issue of repairability in combat zones. The Wellington’s fabric covering could make some kinds of visible damage look catastrophic even when the structure remained intact, and replacing fabric was different from patching metal skin. A stressed-skin aircraft might have been more straightforward for units used to metal repairs, but severe skin damage would have had greater structural significance. So repairs might have been more conventional, but not necessarily easier in the situations that mattered most.

Strategically, the RAF probably would not have gained a war-winning advantage from a stressed-skin Wellington. By the time heavy bombers like the Lancaster and Halifax dominated, the Wellington was already being overtaken by larger and more capable designs. A more conventional Wellington might have been a bit faster, perhaps cheaper or easier to mass-produce in some scenarios, but it would also have lost part of what made it especially valuable in the dangerous early-war period: resilience.

So the most likely overall answer is that a stressed-skin Wellington would have been slightly more conventional, perhaps a little cleaner aerodynamically and maybe easier to integrate into mainstream all-metal production methods, but probably less damage-tolerant and less distinctive. Unless the redesign had been exceptionally successful, it would not have transformed the bomber war. It would mostly have exchanged the real Wellington’s remarkable toughness for more ordinary aircraft characteristics.

items.question: What If Napoleon Bonaparte had never risen to power? How would the French Revolution and the wars against the coalitions have unfolded?
human_answers: Alternate-history counterfactuals hinge on small changes producing large downstream effects. Removing Napoleon Bonaparte from the post‑Revolutionary scene doesn’t collapse the French Revolution into a single predictable path; it produces several plausible trajectories shaped by institutional weaknesses, military fortunes, political culture, and international reaction. Below are the most likely variants, their mechanics, and consequences for the war with the Coalition. Summary framing The Revolution’s radical phase (1789–1794) already created durable structural changes: the abolition of feudal privileges, administrative centralization, secular legal reform impulse, and mass mobilization through levée en masse. Those foundations would continue to shape France even without Napoleon. The crucial variables that Napoleon exploited were France’s exhausted but vast manpower, a cohort of competent generals, political instability in Paris, and the European monarchies’ inability to coordinate consistently. Removing Napoleon changes leadership quality and political stability more than the Revolution’s underlying transformations. The outcome of the wars and the Revolution’s political evolution become probabilistic. Two broad families of outcomes dominate: (A) a prolonged Revolutionary/Republican instability with periodic military rule; or (B) an eventual conservative reaction producing a restored monarchy or authoritarian regime under different leaders. Which emerges depends on battlefield results, coalition cohesion, and French political resilience. Probable short‑ to medium‑term scenarios (1797–1815) 1) Revolutionary Directory survives longer but weakens (most likely) With no singular strategic and political talent to convert victories into regime consolidation, the Directory (or a Directory‑like government) would probably limp on. It was already corrupt, factionalized, and unpopular. Military successes would be more uneven. Generals like Moreau, Masséna, Hoche, and Augereau were capable but less politically adroit than Napoleon; they could win theaters but lacked Napoleon’s combination of operational audacity and political ambition. France would likely fight the Coalition to a military stalemate in some theaters, win in others. The levée en masse still supplies manpower: the Republic probably avoids complete defeat but also fails to secure sweeping victories that produce durable peace treaties like those Napoleon negotiated (Amiens/Pressburg/Tilsit analogues would be much harder). Domestic politics: repeated coup attempts, revolts, and coups from both Jacobin and Thermidorian factions. A series of short‑lived regimes and military interventions remain likely until a stronger political solution emerges. 2) A different military strongman rises (plausible) Absent Napoleon, another general could emulate his path. Generals such as Moreau, Masséna, or even Murat might build regional power bases and attempt coups. Any successful military politician would face harder constraints: fewer early spectacular victories (no Italian campaign miracle) and less charisma to exploit domestic exhaustion. But given the Directory’s fragility, a coup‑by‑general remains a strong possibility, producing an authoritarian government similar in form but different in policy from Napoleonic France. If such a figure consolidated power, reforms (legal codification, administrative centralization, meritocratic promotion) could still appear, albeit more modest or delayed. 3) Restoration or conservative stabilization (possible) If the Coalition’s coordination improves and France suffers significant strategic defeats (for instance, if Britain finances continental armies more effectively and Austria/Russia coordinate), royalist and moderate elements could reassert themselves. A negotiated restoration of the Bourbon monarchy or a constitutional monarchy under a conservative regime could occur by the early 1800s. That outcome would reverse some revolutionary gains (partial restoration of elite influence, rollback of some laws) but would struggle to erase deep administrative and social changes already entrenched. Popular resistance would be uneven; rural conservatism in some regions might favor restoration while urban and veteran constituencies resist. Would France win the war against the Coalition? Definitive “win” like the Napoleonic domination of Europe is unlikely without Napoleon’s genius for campaign strategy and diplomacy. France would probably avoid outright conquest by the Coalition but also unlikely to subdue Europe. Most likely military outcome: protracted war with shifting front lines, localized French successes, and negotiated settlements that leave France enlarged territorially in some terms (the Republic might keep some Belgian/Northern Italian gains) but not hegemonic across Europe. If the Coalition obtained decisive coordination and a string of victories (e.g., crushing France in the field and occupying Paris), they could force a restoration. Conversely, if French generals achieve enough operational successes, a compromise peace establishing France as a major but not dominant continental power would follow. Long‑term institutional and global consequences Legal and administrative legacies: the drive for rationalized administration, standardized law, and secular meritocracy likely persists. Even a restored monarchy would inherit the Napoleonic (or proto‑Napoleonic) bureaucracy and many reformist laws because they were efficient and staffed by a new elite. Nationalism and conscription: mass armies and national mobilization create durable national identities and military-industrial practices across Europe. Revolutions and reforms elsewhere accelerate without Napoleon, but not necessarily with the same geopolitical footprint. Colonial and global effects: without the Napoleonic reshuffle (e.g., the sale of Louisiana to the U.S.), colonial transfers follow different paths. Britain remains dominant at sea; colonial contests continue but with alternate timings. Legal codification (Civil Code) may emerge differently or later. The idea of a rational civil code was already present among reformers; in one variant it is completed by another jurist or regime, preserving many modern legal foundations of continental law. Concrete examples and plausible anecdotes Example: A Moreau‑led stabilization. Moreau secures victory over Austrian forces in Germany, returns to Paris, negotiates a constitutional settlement limiting radicalism, and avoids imperial pretensions. France keeps the Rhineland and revenues sufficient to sustain influence but not empire. Example: Coalition success and Bourbon restoration. Improved Anglo‑Austrian‑Russian coordination defeats French armies, occupies Paris, restores the Bourbons with constitutional limits. Local reforms (metric system, secular administration) remain because they are functional; émigrés regain some property through compensation rather than wholesale reversal. Net assessment Napoleon’s absence reduces the likelihood of France conquering Europe and exporting Napoleonic institutions by force. It increases the probability of prolonged internal instability, fragmented military outcomes, and either a delayed authoritarian consolidation under another general or a conservative settlement restoring monarchy with revolutionary reforms partially retained. The Revolution’s social, administrative, and legal transformations mostly survive in adapted form; its geopolitical expansion and specific legacy (Napoleonic Code, Europe‑wide redrawing) are weaker or redistributed differently. Time note: analysis reflects scholarship and primary evidence available through May 2024.

If Napoleon Bonaparte had never risen to power, the French Revolution would probably still have survived in some form, but it would have become less centralized, less militarily effective, and less transformative for Europe as a whole. The wars against the coalitions would likely have continued, but without Napoleon’s personal military brilliance and political ambition, France’s victories would have been more limited, and the conflict might have ended earlier in a negotiated settlement rather than in a continent-wide French empire.

By the late 1790s, France had already changed Europe before Napoleon took control. The monarchy had been overthrown, the republic established, mass conscription introduced, and France had shown that it could mobilize resources on a scale older monarchies struggled to match. So Napoleon was not the cause of the Revolution itself, nor of France’s ability to resist foreign invasion. Even without him, revolutionary France had a real chance of avoiding defeat. The First Coalition had already failed, and French armies had already shown they could win major campaigns under several generals.

What Napoleon changed was the direction and scale of events. Without him, the Directory would likely have remained weak, corrupt, and politically unstable. It might have survived for a few more years, but it was deeply unpopular and vulnerable both to royalist reaction and to Jacobin revival. In the absence of Napoleon’s coup of 18 Brumaire, France might have experienced another coup by some other general or politician, but the resulting regime would probably have been less durable and less personally dominant. A military strongman could still have emerged, yet it is unlikely that another figure would have combined battlefield genius, administrative energy, propaganda skill, and personal legitimacy in the same way.

In military terms, the wars against the coalitions would probably have unfolded less dramatically. France still had structural advantages: large armies, revolutionary nationalism, experienced officers promoted by merit, and opponents often divided by conflicting goals. So France might still have beaten some coalition attacks and defended its borders. But the extraordinary campaigns of 1796–97, 1800, 1805, 1806, and 1809 depended heavily on Napoleon’s operational style. Without him, France would have been less likely to destroy enemy armies so decisively or to overawe central Europe. Austria might have recovered more quickly, Prussia might have avoided the catastrophic defeat of 1806, and Britain would have faced a dangerous France but not a hegemonic continental empire.

That means the coalitions might have had more success containing France. Rather than repeated French conquests followed by constant coalition rebuilding, Europe may have seen a more traditional balance-of-power struggle. France could have retained Belgium and the left bank of the Rhine, perhaps also some satellite influence in Italy, but it probably would not have dominated Spain, Germany, Poland, and much of Italy in the way it eventually did. The Holy Roman Empire might have survived longer, because its destruction in 1806 was closely tied to Napoleon’s reorganization of Germany. Many of the dependent kingdoms and client states he created would never have appeared, or would have taken a very different form.

Inside France, some revolutionary reforms would almost certainly have lasted: the abolition of feudal privileges, legal equality for male citizens, the sale of church lands, and the broader destruction of the old aristocratic order. Those changes were too deep to be simply reversed by foreign armies unless France were fully defeated and occupied, which was difficult even without Napoleon. But other specifically Napoleonic legacies would be weaker or absent. There might be no Napoleonic Code in its famous form, no Concordat on the same terms, no highly centralized prefect system, and no imperial dynasty. France might have remained a more unstable republic, or it might eventually have drifted back toward some kind of constitutional monarchy after exhaustion from war and faction.

For Europe, the absence of Napoleon would likely mean less intense but still important diffusion of revolutionary ideas. Nationalism and liberalism would still spread, but more slowly and less through direct French conquest. The dramatic reactions that Napoleon provoked—Spanish guerrilla resistance, Prussian reform, Russian patriotic mobilization, and the Congress of Vienna order—would either not happen in the same way or would emerge later. Britain would still probably end the period stronger at sea and financially dominant, but it would not necessarily face the same existential continental challenge.

So the most plausible outcome is not that the Revolution collapses immediately, nor that Europe returns neatly to the old order. Rather, France remains revolutionary or post-revolutionary, continues fighting the coalitions for some time, but reaches a settlement sooner and from a less dominant position. The Revolution’s social gains likely survive in France, while Europe avoids the full scale of the Napoleonic Wars and the vast French empire that made Napoleon such a singular force in modern history.

If the Byzantine Empire had successfully contained the emerging Turkish state in Anatolia, the most important immediate result is that Byzantium would likely have remained a major eastern Mediterranean power for much longer. Anatolia was the empire’s core military, economic, and demographic base. In actual history, the loss of most of Anatolia after Manzikert and later Turkish expansion weakened Byzantium decisively. If that loss had been prevented or reversed, the empire would have retained tax revenue, manpower, and strategic depth, making it far less vulnerable to internal collapse and foreign attack.

Politically, this would probably have stabilized the Byzantine state, though not guaranteed permanent strength. A stronger Anatolian base would have allowed emperors to field larger armies without relying as heavily on mercenaries, defend the Balkans more effectively, and maintain stronger control over provincial elites. The empire might still have faced civil wars and dynastic struggles, but those crises would have been less likely to become fatal. Constantinople would have remained the center of a more durable imperial system rather than the capital of a shrinking state.

For the Islamic world and the Turks, successful Byzantine containment would have significantly altered the rise of later Turkish powers. The Seljuks, or any successor Turkish polity in Anatolia, might have remained confined to eastern frontier zones, fragmented into small principalities, or redirected expansion southward into Syria, Iraq, or Iran rather than westward into Asia Minor and eventually southeastern Europe. Without a strong Turkish foothold in Anatolia, the later emergence of the Ottomans in their historical form becomes much less likely. That is one of the largest long-term consequences: no Ottoman conquest of the Balkans, no fall of Constantinople in 1453 in the same way, and a very different balance of power between Europe and the Near East.

This would also have affected the Crusades. In reality, Byzantine weakness in Anatolia helped prompt appeals to the West and shaped the First Crusade. If Byzantium had contained the Turks, there may still have been religiously motivated expeditions to the Holy Land, but the political setting would have been different. A stronger Byzantium might have acted more as an equal partner with Latin Christendom rather than as a threatened state seeking aid. That could have reduced some of the mistrust that culminated in the Fourth Crusade, though tensions between the Greek East and Latin West would still have remained. If the sack of Constantinople in 1204 were avoided, Byzantium’s survival chances would improve dramatically.

In southeastern Europe, the consequences would be major. The Balkans might have remained more firmly under Byzantine influence, limiting the rise of independent Serbian and Bulgarian power at certain moments and preventing later Ottoman domination of the region. Orthodox Christianity might have remained politically anchored in a stronger Byzantine commonwealth. The cultural and religious map of the Balkans would likely look quite different, with less Islamization in places such as Bosnia and Albania and no long Ottoman era shaping the region.

For western Europe, the effects are indirect but important. Without the Ottoman Empire as a major power blocking or taxing eastern trade routes, the commercial and geopolitical pressures that encouraged Iberian Atlantic exploration might have developed differently or more slowly. This should not be overstated—European exploration had many causes—but the absence of Ottoman expansion would alter the wider context of late medieval and early modern Europe. Venetian, Genoese, and other maritime states might have operated under a different eastern Mediterranean trade system dominated partly by Byzantium rather than by Turkish powers.

Culturally, a longer-lasting Byzantine Empire would have meant prolonged influence of Greek learning, Orthodox theology, Roman imperial traditions, and Byzantine art across the eastern Mediterranean and the Balkans. The migration of Greek scholars to Italy before and after 1453, often linked to the Renaissance, might have occurred more gradually or in different forms. So the Italian Renaissance would probably still happen, but one of its channels of transmission would be altered.

Overall, if Byzantium had contained the Turkish state in Anatolia, the likely result is not a restored Roman Empire dominating everything, but a much stronger and longer-lived Byzantine state, a diminished or redirected Turkish political future, no Ottoman Empire in its historical role, a different Crusading era, and a substantially altered Balkan and eastern Mediterranean history. The biggest single consequence is that Anatolia would remain the Byzantine heartland, and that would preserve the empire as a central actor in Eurasian politics for centuries longer.

items.question: What If the Byzantine Empire successfully restored the Roman Empire?
human_answers: Scenario overview: a Byzantine restoration of the Roman Empire—meaning the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) state not only survives but reconquers the Western Mediterranean, reclaims Rome and Italy, reunites the Latin West under Constantinople’s rule, and reforms imperial institutions to sustain unity—would reshape geopolitics, religion, culture, economics, technology diffusion, and the timelines of nation-states. Below are the most consequential and plausible ripple effects, organized by theme and time horizon. Immediate (0–75 years after restoration) Political map and administration Reunified imperial bureaucracy centered on Constantinople (or an institutionalized dual-capital system) reasserts provincial governorships in Italy, North Africa, Hispania and possibly parts of Gaul. Roman administrative divisions (themes adapted, praetorian-like prefectures rationalized) combine Eastern fiscal discipline with Western land structures. Local elites in reconquered regions either integrated through pragmatic accommodation—Roman law privileges, land confirmations, local magistracies—or replaced where resistance persists. Latin-speaking elites retain status; Greek becomes an administrative lingua franca alongside Latin. Military and security A larger, more professional imperial army/navy funded by access to Western tax bases. The fleet secures Mediterranean sea lanes, reducing piracy and increasing trade security. Border pressure continues: Lombards in Italy, Visigothic/Frankish polities in Gaul, and rising Islamic powers. Immediate military focus on consolidating reclaimed provinces rather than deep expansion. Religion Imperial policy toward Christianity attempts enforced reconciliation: either a pragmatic tolerance reconciling Chalcedonian and Western rites, or intensified attempts at Byzantine theological leadership. Papal independence is curtailed but papacy remains influential as a regional institution. If imperial policy favors unity through compromise (miaphysite/Catholic balancing or synodal mechanisms), schism is delayed or softened; if it favors central theological control, conflict with the Latin clergy intensifies. Mid-term (75–300 years) Delay or transformation of the East–West Schism A successful restoration likely postpones the formal East–West Schism or transforms it into periodic ecclesiastical tensions rather than permanent rupture. Imperial authority over church councils and bishop appointments reduces papal unilateralism; a Byzantine-style conciliarism could become normative for Western Christianity. Latin liturgical practices persist locally, but doctrinal formulations reflect negotiated compromises. Monastic networks (Benedictine, Eastern counterparts) intermix, accelerating theological exchange. Economic integration and commercial shift Restoration re-links Western agrarian resources, North African grain, Iberian metals and African trade routes into Byzantine commercial networks. Constantinople cements its role as the imperial market hub; Italian port cities (Venice, Amalfi) become institutionalized as imperial trade partners or semi-autonomous city-ports with privileges. Money and taxation: a unified currency standard (solidus or reformed successor) fosters pan-Mediterranean commerce; stronger imperial fiscal capacity funds infrastructure, fortifications and patronage networks. Cultural syncretism and intellectual diffusion Large-scale bilingualism and cross-fertilization: Latin scholarship gains access to Greek philosophy, medicine, mathematics earlier and more systematically; Byzantine administrative literacy spreads to the West. Classical texts survive and circulate under imperial patronage, accelerating renaissance-like revivals centuries earlier. Architecture and urbanism combine Roman, Byzantine and local styles—imperial building programs in Rome and Ravenna revive monumental public works, forums, aqueduct repairs and fortified city grids. Technological and institutional consequences Military technology (Greek fire refinement, combined arms doctrine) and shipbuilding spread faster into the West, altering European warfare and naval power balances. Bureaucratic centralization may slow the feudal fragmentation typical of medieval Western Europe; serfdom and decentralized lordship could be less entrenched where imperial authority asserts land law and centralized justice. Long-term (300+ years) Different map of European states Nation-state formation (France, England, Spain, Germany) follows alternative trajectories. Frankish and Anglo-Saxon polities may evolve as semi-autonomous imperial vassals or rival kingdoms constrained by a powerful Mediterranean empire. The Holy Roman Empire as a separate entity may not arise in the same form; imperial legitimacy flows from Constantinople, undermining later Germanic claims to "Roman" succession. Islamic-Christian dynamics If Byzantium retains North Africa and the Iberian frontier, Islamic expansion into the Mediterranean faces a stronger imperial naval and logistical counterweight. Muslim polities in Iberia and North Africa might remain coastal enclaves or be contained, changing the Reconquista narrative and altering Mediterranean cultural exchanges. Alternatively, protracted conflict with Islamic caliphates diverts imperial resources and could prompt military-technological arms races (fortifications, naval arsenals). Economic modernization and global exploration A Mediterranean-centered, bureaucratically coherent empire with strong maritime tradition could sponsor long-distance exploration earlier or in different directions. Imperial control of Atlantic Iberian ports might either accelerate or redirect overseas expansion; exploration initiatives could be state-led rather than the more independent maritime republic model that produced the Age of Discovery. Global trade networks by 1500s could be dominated by an imperial Constantinople–Lisbon axis rather than a fragmented European set of maritime powers, concentrating profits and scientific exchange in imperial hands. Legal and cultural legacy Roman law, updated and imperialized, becomes the predominant legal framework across a larger Europe, reducing customary law diversity. Civic institutions (municipal councils, codified rights) flourish under imperial patronage, producing urban civil service cultures earlier than in our timeline. Latin and Greek literary canons merge into a pan-Roman heritage that influences education, philosophy and sciences; the Renaissance becomes an imperial cultural policy rather than a localized Italian phenomenon. Possible alternate outcomes and caveats Overextension risk: reconquest without sustainable administrative reforms could produce a brittle empire vulnerable to simultaneous pressures—northern Germanic migrations, Slavic expansions, and Islamic incursions—leading to fragmentation similar to historical patterns but delayed. Hybridization vs. dominance: the long-term outcome depends on imperial governance style. A flexible, federated Roman Empire that grants local autonomy and integrates elites will likely endure and produce a cohesive Mediterranean civilization. A rigidly centralized, Hellenizing approach may provoke persistent rebellions and eventual disintegration. Technology and demographic constraints: plague, climate events, and resource limits still shape outcomes. Unity cannot insulate the empire from pan-Eurasian shocks (pandemics, Little Ice Age-style cooling) that alter population and economic productivity. Unpredictable cultural agency: the resilience of local identities (Latin, Germanic, Celtic) and emergent ideologies (nationalism, papal reform movements) could still carve out autonomy over centuries, producing a world less fragmented but not uniformly imperial. Representative alternative timelines (concise sketches) Optimistic durable restoration: Byzantium reforms administratively, integrates Western elites, keeps the papacy as a respected regional institution, and maintains coastal control—result: a Mediterranean superstate fostering an earlier, centralized Renaissance, slower feudalization, limited Islamic maritime dominance, and different colonial patterns. Fragile restoration and rollback: initial reconquest succeeds but fiscal strain, military overstretch and local resistance allow new regional powers (Franks, Normans, later German princes) to erode imperial control—result: a delayed but partial reunification followed by fragmentation, producing a hybrid medieval map. Imperial cold war: a long-term bipolar Europe with a Byzantine-centered Mediterranean superstate and rising independent northern kingdoms; competition fosters accelerated military, navigational and administrative innovation, and a multipolar colonial era. Concluding synthesis A successful Byzantine restoration of the Roman Empire would shift the center of gravity of medieval Europe toward a literate, centralized, Mediterranean polity that blends Greek and Roman institutions with local Western practices. That consolidation would likely delay the doctrinal East–West split, reduce the extent of feudal fragmentation in reconquered regions, alter the pace and agents of exploration and colonization, and produce earlier and broader diffusion of classical learning. Outcomes vary by governance choices and exogenous shocks, but the decisive effect would be a less fragmented, more bureaucratically coherent Europe oriented around an enduring Roman imperial center.

If the Byzantine Empire had successfully restored the Roman Empire, the consequences would have been enormous for Europe, the Mediterranean, and the Near East. A true restoration would probably mean not just reconquering Italy and North Africa, as Justinian briefly did, but holding them over the long term and reestablishing a durable imperial center that united the eastern and western Mediterranean.

Politically, Europe would likely have remained far more Mediterranean-centered. Instead of the medieval West developing as a patchwork of Germanic kingdoms, feudal lordships, and a separate Latin Christendom, a revived Roman state could have imposed more centralized law, taxation, and administration across much of southern Europe. The papacy would probably have remained more subordinate to imperial authority, limiting the later independence of the Roman Church and perhaps preventing or softening the split between Eastern Orthodoxy and Roman Catholicism. The idea of a separate “Holy Roman Empire” in the West might never have emerged, because there would already have been a real Roman emperor with credible authority.

Culturally, a successful restoration might have preserved more direct continuity with classical Roman institutions. Latin could have remained stronger in administration in the West, even as Greek stayed dominant in the East, producing a more consciously bilingual empire. Urban life in Italy, North Africa, and parts of Spain may have remained stronger, since Byzantine rule depended on cities, taxation, and trade. This could have slowed the ruralization and fragmentation that characterized much of early medieval western Europe.

Religiously, the result could have gone in several directions, but overall Christianity would likely have been more politically unified. Major theological disputes would still exist, especially in the eastern provinces, but a stronger empire might have had more capacity to manage them. If Constantinople controlled Rome securely, the bishop of Rome would have had less room to develop into an independent power. That could have changed everything from church structure to missionary expansion in northern Europe.

Economically, the Mediterranean might have remained the unquestioned center of European commerce for much longer. A durable Roman restoration would connect Egypt, the Levant, Anatolia, Italy, and North Africa into a single fiscal and trading system. That would likely strengthen long-distance trade, coin circulation, and maritime infrastructure. Western Europe north of the Alps might have developed more slowly relative to the Mediterranean core, because the political and economic center of gravity would remain in the south and east rather than shifting toward Francia, Germany, and later the Atlantic powers.

Military consequences would be critical. A restored empire would still face the Persians, later the early Islamic caliphates, Slavic migrations, and steppe invasions. Its long-term success would depend on whether restoration came early enough, and with enough resources, to avoid exhaustion. If it held Italy and North Africa while also resisting Arab expansion in the seventh century, then Islam’s spread across the Mediterranean might have been sharply reduced or redirected. North Africa might have remained Christian and Roman longer, and the conquest of Spain by Muslim forces may never have happened. That, in turn, would reshape the entire history of medieval Europe.

But the empire’s survival would not be guaranteed just by reconquest. One of the main reasons Justinian’s gains did not last was overstretch. For a restoration to succeed, Byzantium would need a more sustainable tax base, better integration of reconquered western elites, and perhaps less destructive warfare during the reconquest itself. If those conditions were met, Europe might have seen a more unified imperial civilization, less feudal fragmentation, and a weaker divide between east and west.

In the very long run, the modern world could look very different. Nation-states like France, Spain, and perhaps even Italy might emerge later or in altered form. The Renaissance might happen differently, because classical heritage would be less “rediscovered” and more continuously present. The Reformation might be less likely, or take a different form, in a world without such a powerful independent papacy and without the same medieval church structure. Even the later rise of Atlantic Europe could be delayed if the Mediterranean remained politically unified and economically dominant.

So if the Byzantine Empire had truly restored the Roman Empire and kept it together, the most likely result is not a simple continuation of ancient Rome, but a different medieval world: more centralized, more Mediterranean, more urban, more religiously integrated, and less divided between “East” and “West.”
