If steam had advanced beyond a novelty into mine pumps, mills, and workshops—especially with coal use—the ancient world might have entered a proto-industrial era centuries or even a millennium earlier, reshaping the timeline of European and Mediterranean history.

items.question: What If a Modern Programmer with a Laptop Entered World War II?
human_answers:
The biggest advantage I see being given here is simply processing power. You have a machine that can run calculations at a speed that would beggar imagination for someone living in that era.

In relation to the Artillery mentioned in another answer. Generally, an artillerist would consult his range tables to determine how to aim his cannon...rather than running all the math on the fly. You could easily generate more granular artillery tables to pass out.

The number crunching part of code breaking would be massively accelerated. Especially if you built an Enigma machine on the computer, gave it access to a German Dictionary (can be installed with many programs), and just told it to brute force code attempts until it started spitting out actual words.

Hell, give the physicists access to the Microsoft Calculator in Scientific mode, and they are likely to name their first born after you. Then write programs to run common mathematical formulas, and the Manhattan project would happen a whole lot faster. Seriously? Something that can calculate the cubic root of a 20 digit number, accurate to a dozen decimal places? In a matter of milliseconds!? GIMME!

All in all, the best thing he could do (sadly, this isn't very exciting) is to go to all the scientists and ask them for any number crunching that they need to do repeatedly...or any complicated calculations they needed to make, and either write programs to do it for them, or just run the numbers in MS Calculator.

Alternately, install a localized version of Candy Crush, lock out all other features of the computer, and give it to the Furher. Then, when he's so addicted to the game that he isn't paying attention anymore...you win! (kidding, of course)

Note to time travelers: Beware of unintended consequences! Here's one rather significant problem that might occur:

Modern cryptography enables the Allies to crush the Germans much more quickly. Suddenly, they have a lot more resources to devote to taking down Japan.

The Japanese Empire crumbles beneath the onslaught. There is no need to use the atomic bomb on them to force them to surrender.

The Manhattan Project was still there, though, and was probably helped along quite a bit by this computing technology. (See other answers to this question.) Now we have atomic bombs, but have never used them on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

The USSR continues to rise. After a while, war breaks out in Korea. General McArthur wants to use the atomic bomb on the North Koreans and/or the Russians and/or the Chinese. (See: actual history.)

Because it never got used (very sparingly) to end a war, after which there was an interim period of a few decades during which we learned about the horrific after-effects of nuclear weapons, President Truman doesn't force him to resign over this, and The Bomb is now used (enthusiastically) at the start of the next war. Great horrors ensue.

At the risk of offending some, I think several of the answers on this thread are overestimating the skills of the average, fresh out of school, programmer. 

Being in the field, and having interviewed more recent graduates than I want to count in the past few years, I would estimate that somewhere over 80% of the people getting software degrees are doing so because they have heard there is high demand, and the money is good (both statements are true btw). The result is that many of them do not have the natural aptitude and personality traits that make one a good programmer. They got through school, and can be helpful in an established team with experienced people to coach them along, but they can't produce effectively if thrown out on their own with only vague directions from people that don't understand the code any better than they do.

If our time traveler is such a person, then the laptop is primarily going to be useful as a calculator. The programmer just doesn't have enough experience or understanding to do anything else effectively. At best the programmer will be able to implement the algorithms designed by the mathematicians of the era once they gain an understanding of the computer's strengths and weaknesses.

However, if the programmer falls into the group that does have some level of aptitude, then there are numerous possibilities. Stick them in a room with some theoretical scientist and they will be able to generate the algorithms that help to test their theories. Give them a dataset (and people to do the data entry for it), and they will be able to design a database and pattern analysis algorithms to predict future probabilities. Basic cypher algorithms are definitely possible without any deep knowledge of cryptography, but you need a computer on the other end to decrypt them if it is anything more complicated than you could already do by hand. Brute forcing existing cyphers and generating one time pads are probably among the most useful tasks they could do in the realm of cryptography. Creating drafting and 3D modeling tools would help speed the process developing useful prototypes. 

The catch is that the average laptop is still relatively limited in terms of space and processing power. While several orders of magnitude greater than what was available at the time, it will only be able to do a finite number of things before you have to start getting rid of the old stuff to make room for new items. As someone else noted, the only functioning interfaces are the built in ones that people interact with directly (screen, keyboard, speakers, etc.). There is no way to batch information in or out of it, no printers, & no storage media. If you delete something it is gone. The laptop also becomes a single point of failure. If too much relies on what it can do then what happens when it crashes? Eventually something in there is going to fail, and there is no way to recover it.

Others have discussed code-breaking or code-making, which would certainly be useful, but my first thought was more direct:

Artillery

One of the early projects in computing had a goal of pre-calculating shell trajectories to support targeting in the field. This is the ENIAC project. 
I expect a modern laptop could generate the firing tables needed by artillery operators in a fairly short period, giving our side a massive advantage in being able to target artillery quickly in the field.
Even if our protagonist knows nothing but basic programming, he should be able to go to the mathematicians working on these tables and coordinate to crunch all the numbers at a speed that would seem like magic to them.

Your every-man wouldn't have to do it all himself. I mean, if he had a interest in WW2 cryptography then he probably could do it all himself. Here's an enigma machine made with Javascript . Likewise, he could know German. But he doesn't need to do either of those things. 

I think that a modern laptop in WW2 would be the most useful if you got it to the people who ended up breaking enigma. If you showed up at Bletchley Park and said "I have a computer and the knowledge of how to program it, help me with the math" You'd speed up the cracking speed exponentially, which would probably have shortened WW2 by a lot, having that knowledge earlier than they did.

Other effects

Breaking enigma is great, but he could also help develop better ciphers for the allies that would have stumped the Germans. 

Having a little foreknowledge of WW2 events would have helped the allies too. To say "the Germans are going to go around the French Maginot Line though Belgium, attacking from the low countries and forests. Please warn them."

Without France surrendering Germany would have been weakened. 

You wouldn't have even needed to know that much history. Just saying "yeah, that plan to assassinate Hitler in his bunker that you're working on, it fails. try something else."

With some science and physics background, he probably could help give a boost to a lot of the science with better gun design. Jet turbine theory, etc.

Even without knowing exactly how to do something, just giving the raw ideas would do a lot. "I see you are doing it that way. Have you ever though about switching it around?"

A lot of our ideas seem obvious, but they weren't until they were.
items.original_question: 现代程序员和笔记本电脑被投入第二次世界大战，可能会破解恩尼格玛密码机，会产生什么影响？
items.model_answer:
A modern programmer with a laptop entering World War II would matter a lot less than people usually imagine at first, but in the right conditions they could still have a significant impact. The key issue is that a laptop is not a magic industrial machine. It is mostly a container for knowledge, calculation, communication tools, and software. In a war defined by mass production, fuel, metallurgy, logistics, radio, artillery, and codebreaking, one person with one advanced device could not single-handedly transform the conflict. But they could become an unusually valuable specialist if they survived, found the right patrons, and used their knowledge strategically.

The first problem would be survival and credibility. Dropping into the 1940s with a laptop would not automatically make the programmer influential. They would need food, shelter, language ability, and protection from being arrested as a spy or dismissed as a crank. If they appeared in Allied territory and managed to convince military or scientific authorities that they possessed unusual technical knowledge, their chances would be much better. If they appeared in Axis territory, they might still be useful, but the political dangers would be greater and their freedom much smaller. In either case, the programmer’s biggest initial advantage would not be coding skill by itself but broad modern technical literacy. Even a competent present-day software engineer knows ideas about computing, networking, cryptography, optimization, systems design, information theory, software engineering, and often some modern electronics that were decades ahead of the time.

The laptop itself would be extraordinary evidence. Even if nobody could reproduce it, scientists would immediately recognize that it was an advanced computing machine. Its integrated circuits, battery, storage, display, and miniaturization would be far beyond 1940s capabilities. That said, the machine would be fragile and finite. Once its battery ran down, keeping it powered would become a challenge, though not impossible if the programmer could improvise power conversion and had technical support. Replacement parts would be basically unavailable. So the laptop’s long-term value would be less as a permanent tool and more as a demonstration object and temporary reference library. If it contained textbooks, Wikipedia dumps, engineering manuals, scientific papers, programming environments, and historical knowledge, it could be immensely valuable. If it were just an ordinary work laptop with little offline data, its practical effect would shrink a lot.

In military terms, the programmer’s most realistic impact would be in computation, cryptanalysis, logistics, and systems organization rather than in inventing futuristic weapons overnight. They could explain more advanced approaches to radar signal processing, operations research, statistical quality control, inventory management, scheduling, and secure communications. They might help improve artillery tables, convoy routing, aircraft maintenance planning, submarine detection analysis, and industrial production tracking. These areas sound less dramatic than a wonder weapon, but wars are often won by exactly such improvements. A small increase in shipping efficiency, aircraft readiness, or codebreaking throughput could save thousands of lives and meaningfully alter campaigns.

Cryptography is one of the clearest areas where a modern programmer could matter. Even without giving the Allies magical access to every Axis code, they would understand the weaknesses of many classical and electromechanical cipher practices. They could strongly advocate one-time pads used correctly, warn against key reuse, promote better traffic analysis methods, and help design more rigorous cryptanalytic workflows. If they knew the historical facts of the war, they might point intelligence agencies toward particular systems, mistakes, or priorities. If they arrived early enough and reached Britain or the United States, they might accelerate codebreaking efforts around Enigma, Lorenz, or Japanese naval ciphers. Even a modest acceleration in these areas could have major strategic consequences.

Computing history could also shift. A modern programmer could describe the general architecture of digital computers much more clearly than many wartime engineers then understood it. The concepts of stored-program computing, high-level languages, compilers, structured programming, modular design, error detection, version control in principle, databases, and interactive debugging would be revolutionary. Of course, describing them is easier than implementing them with vacuum tubes, relays, and paper tape. The industrial base of the 1940s would still impose severe limits. But ideas can arrive before hardware catches up. The programmer might help wartime teams avoid dead ends, formalize software earlier, and build better programming practices around early computers. This could accelerate postwar computing by years, perhaps even more if the person became attached to a major project like Colossus, ENIAC, Bell Labs, or MIT radiation labs.

Could they help build advanced weapons? To a degree, but much less than science fiction suggests. If the programmer also had strong knowledge of physics, chemistry, aeronautics, or electrical engineering, they might contribute to radar, fuzes, fire-control systems, jet control systems, or even nuclear project organization. But “I know modern technology exists” does not automatically mean “I can build a transistor” or “I can produce a GPS-guided missile in 1943.” The bottleneck would be materials science, manufacturing precision, supply chains, and the huge teams required to turn concepts into weapons. The programmer could point in promising directions, maybe encouraging digital control systems, better feedback engineering, or improved computing support for bomb design and ballistics. But they would not conjure modern electronics from scratch.

If they had accurate historical knowledge, that could be even more important than the laptop. Knowing when and where major battles, invasions, offensives, and political decisions happened could be game-changing if delivered to trusted leaders early enough. Warning about Pearl Harbor, Barbarossa, Midway, the Ardennes offensive, or the vulnerability of supply lines could alter operational decisions. But this also gets complicated. Governments would be skeptical of extraordinary predictions. Even if believed, acting on such knowledge could change the timeline enough to invalidate later predictions. There is also the problem that broad historical outcomes are easier to know than precise tactical details. A modern programmer is unlikely to know exact convoy routes, codebooks, or battle orders from memory. Still, even high-level foreknowledge could help if presented credibly.

The side they joined would matter enormously. If they aided the Allies and were trusted, they could potentially shorten the war somewhat by improving intelligence, operations research, and computing. If they aided the Axis, they might improve efficiency there too, but the Axis had deeper structural problems: weaker industrial depth, strategic overreach, and resource shortages. A single technical expert would probably not reverse those fundamentals. They might make the war longer or deadlier, perhaps improving air defense coordination, cryptography, or logistics, but probably not enough to guarantee Axis victory unless paired with very strong historical foreknowledge used at pivotal moments.

There is also a cultural factor. A modern programmer dropped into the 1940s might struggle badly outside their narrow expertise. Many software professionals today depend on vast invisible infrastructure: modern components, libraries, internet access, cloud systems, stable power, and global manufacturing. Without that ecosystem, they might be far less effective than a contemporary electrical engineer, radio specialist, or mathematician. If the programmer were unusually hands-on, mathematically strong, and knowledgeable about low-level computing and electronics, they could become exceptional. If they were an average web developer with no offline resources and little hardware knowledge, their impact would be much smaller than the thought experiment implies.

So the most likely answer is this: a modern programmer with a laptop would not single-handedly win World War II, but under favorable conditions they could become a highly influential technical adviser. Their greatest contributions would probably come from accelerating computing, improving cryptography and analysis, optimizing logistics and operations, and possibly using historical foreknowledge to influence key decisions. The laptop would impress people and provide a temporary treasure trove of information, but the real power would be the person’s knowledge and their ability to translate advanced ideas into forms the 1940s could actually use. If they reached the right institutions early, they might shorten the war and speed up the computer age. If not, they might simply become a historical curiosity with a dead battery.

items.question: What If My Printer Could Really Print Money?
human_answers: In today’s article, I give shorter answers to several reader questions. (Previous installment here (http://what-if.xkcd.com/14/).) You can fit four bills on an 8.5”x11” sheet of paper: [Image: image] If your printer can manage one page (front and back) of full-color high-quality printing per minute, that’s $200 million dollars a year. [Image: image] This is enough to make you very rich, but not enough to put any kind of dent in the world economy. Since there are 7.8 billion (http://www.federalreserve.gov/paymentsystems/coin_currcircvolume.htm) \$100 bills in circulation, and the lifetime of a \$100 bill is about 90 months, that means there are about a billion produced each year. Your extra two million bills a year would barely be enough to notice. This question gets submitted a lot. It turns out the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration—the agency which runs the National Hurricane Center—gets it a lot, too. In fact, they’re asked about it so often that they’ve published a response (http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/tcfaq/C5c.html). I recommend you read the whole thing, but I think the last sentence of the first paragraph says it all: “Needless to say, this is not a good idea.” It makes me happy that an arm of the US government has, in some official capacity, issued an opinion on the subject of firing nuclear missiles into hurricanes. [Image: image] A house in a very rainy place, like the Alaska panhandle, might receive close to four meters of rain per year. Water turbines can be pretty efficient. If the house has a footprint of 1,500 square feet and gutters five meters off the ground, it would generate an average of less than a watt of power from rainfall, and the maximum electricity savings would be: \[1500\text{ft}^2 \times 4\tfrac{\text{ meters}}{\text{year}}\times1\tfrac{\text{kg}}{\text{liter}} \times9.81\tfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2}\times5\text{ meters}\times15\tfrac{\text{cents}}{\text{kWh}}=\frac{$1.14}{\text{year}}\] The rainiest hour on record occurred in 1947 in Holt, Missouri, where about 30 centimeters of rain fell in 42 minutes. For those 42 minutes, our hypothetical house could generate up to 800 watts of electricity, which might be enough to power everything inside it. For the rest of the year, it wouldn’t come close. If the generator rig cost $100, residents of the rainiest place in the US—Ketchikan, Alaska—could potentially offset the cost in under a century. There are about 300,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 stars in the universe. If you make a word pronounceable by alternating vowels and consonants (there are better ways to make pronounceable words, but this will do for an approximation), then every pair of letters you add lets you name 105 times as many stars (21 consonants times 5 vowels). 105 possibilities per two characters is about the same information density that numbers have, which suggests the name will end up being about as long as the total number of stars written out: [Image: image] I like doing math that involves measuring the lengths of numbers written out on the page—which is really just a way of loosely estimating log~10~x. It works, but it feels so wrong. Reentering spacecraft heat up because they’re compressing the air in front of them (not, as is commonly believed, because of air friction). According to this calculator (http://www.grc.nasa.gov/WWW/BGH/stagtmp.html), to increase the temperature of the air layer in front of your body by twenty degrees Celsius (enough to go from freezing to room temperature), you would need to be biking at 200 m/s. The fastest human-powered vehicles at sea levels are recumbent bicycles enclosed in streamlined aerodynamic shells. These vehicles have an upper speed limit near 40 m/s. This is the speed at which the human can just barely produce enough thrust to balance the drag force from the air. Since drag increases with the square of the speed, this limit would be pretty hard to push any further. Biking at 200 m/s would require at least 25 times the power output needed to go 40 m/s. At those speeds, you don’t really have to worry about the heating from the air—a quick back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that if your body were doing that much work, your core temperature would reach fatal levels in a matter of seconds. There are a lot of ways to estimate the amount of information stored on the internet, but we can put an interesting upper bound on the number just by looking at how much storage space we (as a species) have purchased. The storage industry produces in the neighborhood of 650 million hard drives per year. If most of them are 3.5” drives, then that’s eight liters (two gallons) of hard drive per second. This means the last few years of hard drive production—which, thanks to increasing size, represent a large chunk of global storage capacity—would just about fill an oil tanker. So, by that measure, the internet is smaller than an oil tanker. [Image: image] Aerodynamics aside, I’m curious what tactical advantage you’re expecting to gain by having the high explosive fly back at you if it misses the target.
items.original_question: 如果我的打印机真的可以打印钞票，它会对世界产生那么大的影响吗？
items.model_answer:
If your printer could really print money that was accepted as real currency, the immediate effect for you would seem great: you could buy things without working for the money first. But at the level of the whole economy, it would be a disaster unless the money supply were controlled very carefully.

Money works because it is scarce enough that people trust its value. If anyone could print unlimited valid money at home, then the amount of money in circulation would explode. But the number of cars, houses, groceries, and services would not instantly increase. That means more money would be chasing the same amount of goods, so prices would rise. This is inflation. If it kept going, it could become extreme inflation, where money rapidly loses value because everyone knows more can be created at any time.

In that world, your first few printed bills might buy a lot, but as more money entered circulation, each bill would buy less and less. Stores would raise prices, workers would demand higher wages, and savings held in cash would lose purchasing power. Eventually, “printing money” would no longer make you rich in any meaningful sense, because the value of the currency itself would collapse.

There is also an important distinction between physically printing bills and creating real wealth. Real wealth comes from producing useful things: food, energy, machines, medicine, software, labor, and knowledge. A machine that only creates more money does not by itself create more real goods or services. So it changes claims on wealth, not wealth itself.

If only you had such a printer and no one else did, and if the bills were indistinguishable from legal currency, then you could personally benefit for a while by effectively counterfeiting money. But even then, if you used it on a large scale, it would distort the economy and likely be noticed. Governments tightly control currency creation for exactly this reason.

So the short answer is: if your printer could really print money, you would not create unlimited prosperity. You would mostly create inflation, undermine trust in the currency, and eventually make the money worth much less.

items.question: What If You Tried to Launch a Real Rocket Using Only Model Rocket Engines?
human_answers: About 65,000, give or take a few. You’d have to arrange them like this: [Image: image] The rocket would weigh about as much as a tow truck. There wouldn’t be room for anything except the engines, aerodynamic shell, and minimal staging equipment. Each rocket motor would burn for about three seconds. The layer cake arrangement means that every three seconds, the bottom layer of spent rockets would detaches and the next stage would kick in. It would go through between 25 and 30 of these stages, burning for a total of a minute and a half, after which it would coast upward and just barely brush the edge of space. (For this design, I’m assuming something akin to Estes E9-4 engines, which are on the large end of the common model rocket engines. There are larger ones—the classes go all the way up to O and beyond—but at a certain point, they stop being model rocket engines, and just become rocket engines.) A 30-stage rocket is, to put it lightly, an engineering nightmare. This design assumes the non-engine portion of the vehicle is limited to the weight of a person (60 kg). In effect, the spaceship would be a solid block of rocket engines. They’d need to be insulated from each other so the upper stages didn’t ignite prematurely, and the staging and aerodynamics would both be a challenge. The stack of engines narrows as you go from bottom to top. By the time the top stages are firing, the rocket will have shed most of its mass, so it won’t need as much thrust to get the same acceleration. The reason the engine stack bulges in the middle is so that the acceleration profile will look like this: [Image: image] Rockets work best when their thrust is several times greater than the force of gravity. But you don’t want to accelerate too quickly while you’re low down. Air drag increases with the square of your speed, and if you accelerate too quickly, you’ll find yourself wasting all your fuel just to maintain your speed. You want to accelerate slowly at first, then ramp it up as the air starts getting thinner. [Image: image] Now, as you may have noticed, this rocket will get you into space (for a few seconds, at least), but not orbit. Can you use model rocket engines to dock with the ISS? No. Taking into account atmospheric drag, to get into space, you need a rocket capable of accelerating (in a vacuum) to about 2 kilometers per second. To get to orbit, you need a rocket capable of accelerating to about 10 kilometers per second. If you try to produce an orbital rocket using the same design math we used for the suborbital rocket, it spits out a description of a pancake-shaped mountain of model rocket engines over a mile wide. It would taper to a 10-meter-high spire in the center and would weigh about as much as the Great Pyramid. [Image: image] Not only would this vehicle never get out of the atmosphere, it would probably not stand up under its own weight. Frankly, the word “vehicle” is a bit misleading. Essentially, what you’ve created is an unstable pile of gunpowder the size of Central Park. If it went up in flames—which it would—it would break the record for the largest manmade non-nuclear explosion in history. (Interestingly, the current holder of that dubious record is also a rocket that exploded during launch (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m79UO4HOQmc).) The bottom line is that it would be very difficult, but perhaps not impossible, to launch something up to the edge of space using model rocket engines. However, if you try to build a ship capable of getting to orbit, you will not go to space today.
items.original_question: 将真正的火箭发射到太空需要多少个模型火箭发动机？
items.model_answer:
If you tried to launch a real, crew-scale or even “serious” vehicle using only model rocket engines, it would almost certainly fail unless the vehicle were kept extremely small and lightweight. The core issue is that model rocket engines have very low total impulse compared with what a real rocket needs.

A rocket has to do two things: produce enough thrust to lift off, and keep burning long enough to build up speed and altitude. Model rocket motors can do this for hobby rockets because those rockets weigh very little, often only tens or hundreds of grams. But a “real” rocket, even a very small one carrying useful equipment, quickly becomes too heavy. You would need a huge number of model motors just to match the thrust of one larger professional motor, and then you run into mass, drag, ignition timing, structural complexity, and stability problems.

Even if you clustered many model engines together, several practical problems appear. First, all or nearly all of them must ignite properly at once. If some ignite late or fail, the rocket can tip, spin, or crash. Second, the structure needed to hold many small motors adds weight, which makes the thrust problem worse. Third, model engines are not designed for scaling up to large launch systems; they are made for safe hobby use, not for lifting payloads of significant mass. Fourth, the total amount of propellant you can legally and physically pack into model motors is small, so the burn ends quickly and the rocket runs out of acceleration.

There is also the question of efficiency. Using many tiny engines is generally less efficient than using a properly designed larger motor. The plumbing may be simpler with solid model motors, but the packaging and staging become awkward, and performance losses add up. The rocket equation is unforgiving: as mass grows, the amount of propellant and engine performance required rises rapidly.

So the realistic outcome is this: if the vehicle is basically still a model rocket, then yes, model rocket engines work fine. If by “real rocket” you mean something carrying substantial instrumentation, heavy payloads, or people, then no—model rocket engines are far too weak and impractical. You might be able to make a larger unmanned experimental rocket by clustering many small motors, but it would still be much closer to a hobby or amateur rocket than a true launch vehicle.

In short, trying to launch a real rocket using only model rocket engines would mostly teach you why rockets need high-thrust, high-impulse propulsion systems: model engines scale badly for anything beyond very small rockets.

items.question: What If Humanity Sped Up Earth's Rotation to Eliminate Leap Seconds?
human_answers: The Earth’s spin is slowing down. This is annoying. One reason that it’s annoying is that it makes time standards more difficult. We already have way too many time standards (http://tycho.usno.navy.mil/systime.html), including: TAI, time based on an atomic clock, which ignores all motion of the Earth UT0 and UT1, time based on precise measurement of the Earth’s rotation GPS, the time standard used by GPS satellites UTC, the standard used in computing, which is like TAI but with leap seconds to keep it in sync with Earth TDT, TBT, TCB, and TCG, which are all even worse This leads to all kinds of little headaches, particularly for programmers. For example, the clock in your smartphone’s GPS is 16 seconds out of sync with the phone’s system clock. This is because the system clock uses Coordinated Universal Time (which has leap seconds), but GPS time doesn’t. They were in sync in January of 1980 and probably never will be again. Half a billion years ago (when the Earth was 4 billion years old, instead of 4.5), each day was 22 hours long instead of 24. The day has gotten longer because of tidal forces from the Moon. Loosely speaking, here’s how tidal drag works: The Moon’s tides raise bulges in the Earth, but the Earth’s rotation moves those bulges out of line with the Moon. The Moon’s gravity tries to tug the bulges back into line, which exerts a twisting force on the Earth, slowing it down: [Image: image] Strangely, the Earth is actually not slowing down as much as you’d expect from tidal drag. The biggest reason for the discrepancy is that during the last ice age, the continents were pushed down by the weight of the glaciers, and they’re still springing back into place. This has the effect of shifting mass toward the poles, closer to the axis of rotation: [Image: image] This makes us spin faster—or, at least, keeps us from slowing down as quickly. At the moment, each day is about 0.8 milliseconds longer than the 86,400 seconds it needs to be to avoid adding leap seconds. [Image: image] This difference fluctuates over time based on weather and other effects (it’s actually shortened a bit since the early 1990s), although in the long run, it will definitely get larger as the Earth slows. If we wanted to get rid of leap seconds, we’d need to keep the Earth spinning at a more constant rate. This means speeding up the Earth and shortening each day by about 0.8 milliseconds. This is a tough problem. Here are a few things that won’t work: Spinning counterclockwise (http://xkcd.com/162/) in a chair. It temporarily alters the Earth’s rate of rotation, but not enough to matter. Putting rocket engines on the Equator. This won’t work because the exhaust would go into the atmosphere, which transmits the force back to the ground as wind drag—it’d be like making a bike go forward by pushing on the handlebars. If the engines were somehow mounted above the atmosphere, they’d be able to slow the Earth, but not by enough to accomplish our goal. Triggering big earthquakes. This can alter the length of the day (http://www.nasa.gov/topics/earth/features/japanquake/earth20110314.html), but even those aren’t big enough to make a difference. In the end, there’s only one solution: Hitting the Earth with asteroids. Given enough time, we could send a spaceship (captained by an anti-Bruce Willis) to perform repeated flybys of a comet. Over time, the gravitational perturbation could steer the comet into a collision course with Earth. By hitting the Earth at the right angle, we would give it a push: [Image: image] Even if the comet burns up in the atmosphere, its momentum is transmitted to the surface by wind drag (taking a matter of days). It takes about a decade (http://www.researchgate.net/publication/227650235_Topographic_CoreMantle_Coupling_and_Polar_Motion_On_Decadal_TimeScales) for the core to sync up with the crust, so we’d have to plan the impact schedule carefully to avoid overshooting. Here’s the bad news: To get enough spin, we have to hit the Earth with on the order of a billion liters of rock per second (several times the volumetric discharge rate of the Amazon). This adds up to about one six-mile dinosaur-killing asteroid every couple days. Humanity—and life—wouldn’t survive the bombardment long. What about a steady stream of smaller asteroids? [Image: image] If asteroid B-612 in The Little Prince is four meters across and made of rock, we’d need an average of around fifty thousand of them to enter the atmosphere each second to keep up the pressure. [Image: image] Unfortunately, the steady high-altitude meteor shower would deliver just as much energy to the atmosphere that daily giant impacts would, and the eventual death toll would be the same: Seven billion humans, plus four billion Little Princes per day. But at least we could stop worrying about leap seconds.
items.original_question: 由于地球自转正在减慢，我们时不时地必须插入闰秒。我们能否加快地球自转，这样就不需要闰秒了？
items.model_answer:
If humanity somehow sped up Earth’s rotation just enough to keep solar time aligned with atomic time, we could in principle eliminate leap seconds—but the side effects would be far larger and stranger than the problem they solve.

Leap seconds exist because Earth’s rotation is irregular and, on average, slowly getting slower, while atomic clocks are extremely stable. Coordinated Universal Time is kept close to Earth’s actual day by occasionally inserting a leap second. To “solve” this by speeding up Earth, you would need to make the planet spin slightly faster so that one mean solar day matched exactly 86,400 SI seconds again.

That sounds like a tiny change, and in one sense it is. The mismatch that causes leap seconds is only on the order of milliseconds per day. But Earth is enormous, so even a tiny increase in rotation requires an enormous change in angular momentum and energy. The engineering needed would be beyond anything humanity could plausibly do. You would have to either apply vast torques to the whole planet or rearrange planetary mass on a colossal scale.

If it were done, the immediate physical effects would not be catastrophic if the speedup were truly very small. Day length would shorten by a tiny amount, probably too little for people to notice directly. But changing Earth’s rotation changes more than clocks. It slightly alters the balance of centrifugal effects, making the equator bulge a bit more and shifting sea level and atmospheric circulation patterns. Winds, ocean currents, and long-term climate behavior could all be perturbed. Even small changes in rotation affect the dynamics of the atmosphere and oceans.

It would also affect satellites and space operations indirectly. Earth orientation parameters are used in navigation, astronomy, and tracking. A deliberate change in rotation would require recalibrating many systems. The geoid and reference frames tied to Earth rotation would need updating. Not impossible, but globally disruptive.

There is also a conceptual problem: leap seconds are not caused only by a steady slowdown. Earth’s rotation varies unpredictably because of interactions among the core, mantle, oceans, atmosphere, and even earthquakes. So even if humanity sped Earth up to eliminate the current accumulated difference, irregularities would continue. You would still need future adjustments unless you kept actively controlling Earth’s spin all the time. In other words, you would be replacing occasional leap seconds with ongoing planetary rotation management.

And from a practical standpoint, this would be absurd overkill. The world is already moving away from leap seconds as a civil timekeeping issue because they are inconvenient for software and communications systems. It is vastly easier to redefine timekeeping conventions than to modify the spin of a planet.

So the short answer is: if humanity sped up Earth’s rotation enough to eliminate leap seconds, clocks could be made to stay aligned without leap-second insertions, but the required energy and control would be unimaginably large, the geophysical side effects would be real, and the fix would not even be permanent unless Earth’s rotation were continuously managed. It is a physically meaningful idea, but an engineering and planetary-management nightmare compared with simply changing how we define civil time.

items.question: What If One Extra Person Died Randomly Every Second?
human_answers: Every second, 1.8 humans die and 4.2 humans are born. Under Mr. Petzall’s plan, the number of deaths would increase to 2.8. This randomized culling would obviously be a big deal—it would be responsible for over a third of all deaths—but, at least for a while, our population would continue to grow. At one death per second, any given person currently has a 0.464% chance of being chosen each year. Put another way, the scenario would result in 4.64 deaths per 1,000 people (or 464 per 100,000). [Image: image] There are about twenty countries with death rates below 4.64 per 1,000. It’s an odd bunch (https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook/rankorder/2066rank.html), including the Dominican Republic, Brunei, Singapore, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the Maldives, and Paraguay. These are the countries where Guy’s program would be responsible for the majority of all deaths. The death rate in all of these countries is going to go up. It has to, because of math. It seems intuitively obvious that death rates below 10 per 1,000 are unsustainable. If fewer than one person out of every hundred dies each year (and enough are born to sustain the population) then the average person must have to wait over a hundred years to die—which is clearly not compatible with our current lifespans. In those countries with low single-digit death rates, the rates are guaranteed to rise in the future. This includes the United States, whose death rate is 8.40 per 1,000—a number which will go up substantially as the Baby Boomers age. A rate of one death per second isn’t enough to reverse population growth at present, but it would have been until recently. In 1950, the world’s population was only 2.52 billion. One death per second would mean 12.5 annual deaths per 1,000 people, almost triple the number in 2013. At the start of the early 20th century, this would have been enough to reverse population growth, and within a handful of decades—as population levels off—it will be again. Of course, if people die faster, this in turn has an effect on birth rates—as people change their behavior in response to the change in mortality—so the actual result would be more complicated. [Image: image] In the United States, Guy Petzall would be the leading cause of death for females between the ages of 1 and 55 and for males between the ages of 1 and 48. Currently, about 96% of infants survive to age 40, but in Guy’s scenario, only 80% would. When would these deaths happen? Given the numbers of aircraft in the air at any given time, it’s certain that some pilots would die while flying. This wouldn’t be a disaster, though, since large commercial airliners have multiple crew members who can take over. Cars would be a different story. Since about 10 million Americans are driving (http://what-if.xkcd.com/5/) at any given time, 127 will die behind the wheel each day (plus a smaller but still significant number of passengers, pedestrians, and other drivers). Interestingly, this is only a little larger than the number of Americans who die in car accidents every day already. (This number has been declining, as a percentage of population, since the 1960s, and as a percentage of miles traveled since at at least the 1920s (http://www.saferoads.org/federal/2004/TrafficFatalities1899-2003.pdf).) About 50 million (http://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nhsr/nhsr011.pdf) outpatient surgery procedures are performed each year. If they’re primarily performed by one surgeon and each last an average of half an hour, then about 13 surgeons per year will unexpectedly die mid-surgery (as will 13 extra patients). This is a scary thought. But to put it in perspective, that’s about the number of surgeons who will operate on the wrong body part or wrong patient every two days (http://www.cnn.com/2011/HEALTH/04/28/ep.wrong.side.surgery/index.html). It’s not that the scenario isn’t scary. It’s just that reality is far more terrifying. Lastly, what about our leaders? Members of Congress die in office at a rate of two or three per year, or about five per Congress. This used to be much higher, as explained in this strangely florid paper (http://home.gwu.edu/~forrest/fmdeathincongressps.pdf). 29 members of Congress died during 1939 and 1940, the two years the 76th Congress was in session. In Guy’s scenario, the current rate would double, leading to a loss of 10 per Congress. This would certainly be tragic, but it would be no higher than the levels seen as recently as the 1960s. All in all, the losses would be dramatic, but not devastating to our species as a whole. And really, in the end, the global death rate is 100%—everyone dies. [Image: image] … or do they? Strictly speaking, the observed death rate for the human condition is something like 93%—that is, around 93% of all humans have died. This means the death rate among humans who were not members of The Beatles is significantly higher than the 50% death rate among humans who were. [Image: image] I expect this significant[dubious–discuss] fact[citation needed] will pave the way[citation needed] for a great deal[dubious–discuss] of important[citation needed][dubious–discuss] research.
items.original_question: 如果在地球上的某个地方每秒随机选择一个额外的人死亡，这会对世界人口产生什么影响？
items.model_answer:
If one extra person died at random every second, that would mean 86,400 additional deaths per day, about 31.5 million per year.

That is an enormous number. For comparison, total global deaths from all normal causes are on the order of 60–70 million per year, so this would raise worldwide mortality by roughly 45–50%. The global population would still probably continue growing for a while, because births are currently around 130 million per year, but growth would slow dramatically. Instead of increasing by tens of millions per year, humanity might grow only slightly, or in some years nearly stall depending on birth rates and existing mortality trends.

Because the deaths are random, the effect would be especially disturbing socially and scientifically. They would not cluster by age, health, geography, or behavior in any predictable way. Infants, healthy adults, surgeons in the middle of an operation, pilots in flight, political leaders, and farmers could all be struck with equal probability if “random” truly meant uniform over the whole population. That randomness would create fear far beyond the raw numbers, because there would be no reliable way to reduce risk.

The direct demographic effect on any one individual would still be small on short timescales. With a world population of about 8 billion, the chance that a specific person is the randomly selected victim in a given second would be about 1 in 8 billion. Over a year, that adds up to roughly a 0.39% annual chance of dying from this new cause, or about 1 in 255 per year, assuming the selection remains uniform and independent. Over an average lifetime, that becomes a substantial added mortality risk.

The indirect effects might be even larger than the direct ones. If deaths happened literally anywhere and anytime, society would have to redesign critical systems for sudden human disappearance or collapse. Transportation would need more automation and fail-safes. Hospitals, power plants, military systems, and financial markets would require stronger redundancy. Jobs that depend on one person staying continuously conscious and alive would become much riskier. Insurance markets would be disrupted, and many people would demand explanations, protections, or rituals even if no protection actually existed.

Economically, losing 31.5 million people per year at random would reduce productivity, experience, and institutional stability. But civilization would probably not collapse solely from that number. Humanity already absorbs large annual death totals. What makes this scenario uniquely destabilizing is not just the scale, but the unpredictability. Random deaths among highly specialized workers and leaders would create recurring shocks out of proportion to the average death rate.

So the short answer is: the world would not instantly end, but it would become much more fearful, less stable, and much more mortality-heavy. Population growth would slow sharply, life expectancy would drop, and modern society would adapt by building redundancy everywhere—while living under the constant knowledge that every second, somewhere, one person is dying for no reason anyone can control.

items.question: How Far Would You Have to Drop a Steak to Cook It?
human_answers: I hope you like your steaks Pittsburgh Rare. And you may need to defrost it after you pick it up. Things get really hot when they come back from space. This isn’t because of air friction, strictly speaking—it’s because of air compression. The air can’t move out of the way fast enough, and gets squished in front of the spaceship/meteor/steak. Compressing air heats it up. As a rule of thumb, you start to notice compressive heating above about Mach 2 (which is why the Concorde had heat-resistant material on the leading edge of its wings). A few months ago, skydiver Felix Baumgartner jumped from 39 kilometers, and hit Mach 1 around 30 kilometers. This was enough to heat the air by a few degrees, but the air was so far below freezing that it didn’t make a difference. (Early in his jump, it was about minus 40 degrees, which is that magical point where you don’t have to clarify whether you mean Fahrenheit or Celsius—it’s the same in both.) As far as I know, this steak question originally came up in a lengthy 4chan thread (http://m.chanarchive.org/4chan/sci/63224/5209640#p5209833), which quickly disintegrated into poorly-informed physics tirades intermixed with homophobic slurs. There was no clear conclusion. To try to get a better answer, I decided to run a series of simulations of a steak falling from various heights. This involved a lot of research. I used Mathematica models of atmospheric density to generate a set of descent profiles for the plummeting steak. For a nice tutorial on how to do this, see the Wolfram Blog’s analysis of Felix Baumgartner’s jump (http://blog.wolfram.com/2012/10/24/falling-faster-than-the-speed-of-sound/). An 8 oz. steak is about the size and shape of a hockey puck, so I based my steak’s drag coefficients on those given on page 74 of The Physics of Hockey (which author Alain Haché actually measured personally using some lab equipment). A steak isn’t a hockey puck, but the precise drag coefficient turned out not to make a big difference in the result. I used a handy NASA compressive heating calculator (http://www.grc.nasa.gov/WWW/BGH/stagtmp.html) to determine the temperature of the shock layer in front of the steak. Since this blog tends to wind up looking at unusual objects in extreme physical circumstances, often the only relevant research I can find is US military studies from the Cold War era. (Apparently, the US government was shoveling tons of money at anything even loosely related to weapons research.) To get an idea of how the air would heat the steak, I looked at research papers on the heating of ICBM nose cones as they reenter the atmosphere. Two of the most useful were Predictions of Aerodynamic Heating on Tactical Missile Domes (http://www.dtic.mil/cgi-bin/GetTRDoc?AD=ADA073217) and Calculation of Reentry-Vehicle Temperature History (http://www.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a231552.pdf). Lastly, I had to figure out exactly how quickly heat spreads through a steak. I started by looking at some papers from industrial food production which simulated heat flow through various pieces of meat. It took me a while to realize there was a much easier way to learn what combinations of time and temperature will effectively heat the various layers of a steak: Check a cookbook. Jeff Potter’s excellent book Cooking for Geeks (http://www.amazon.com/Cooking-Geeks-Science-Great-Hacks/dp/0596805888) provides a great introduction to the science of cooking meat, and explains what ranges of heat produce what effects in steak and why. Cook’s The Science of Good Cooking (http://www.amazon.com/Science-Cooking-Cooks-Illustrated-Cookbooks/dp/1933615982) was also helpful. Putting it all together, I found that the steak will accelerate quickly until it reaches about an altitude of about 30-50 kilometers, at which point the air gets thick enough to start slowing it back down. The falling steak’s speed drops steadily as the air gets thicker. No matter how fast it’s going when it reaches the lower layers of the atmosphere, it quickly slows down to terminal velocity. It always takes six or seven minutes to drop from 25 kilometers to the ground. For much of those 25 kilometers, the air temperature is below freezing—which means the steak will spend six or seven minutes subjected to a relentless blast of subzero, hurricane-force winds. Even if it is cooked by the fall, you’ll probably have to defrost it when it lands. When the steak does finally hit the ground, no matter the initial height, it will be traveling at about 30 meters per second. To get an idea of what this means, imagine a steak flung at the ground by a major-league pitcher. If the steak is even partially frozen, it could easily shatter. However, if it lands in the water, mud, or leaves, it will probably be fine. (Not clean, but intact.) A steak dropped from 39 kilometers will, unlike Felix, probably not break the sound barrier. It also won’t be appreciably heated. This makes sense—after all, Felix’s suit wasn’t scorched when he landed. [Image: image] Steaks can probably survive breaking the sound barrier. In addition to Felix, pilots have ejected at supersonic speeds (http://www.ejectionsite.com/insaddle/insaddle.htm) and lived to tell about it. To break the sound barrier, you’ll need to drop the steak from about 50 kilometers. But this isn’t enough to cook it. We need to go higher. If dropped from 70 kilometers, the steak will go fast enough to be briefly blasted by 350°F air. Unfortunately, this blast of thin, wispy air barely lasts a minute—and anyone with some basic kitchen experience can tell you that a steak placed in the oven at 350 for 60 seconds isn’t going to be cooked. From 100 kilometers—the formally defined edge of space—the picture’s not much better. The steak spends a minute and a half over Mach 2, and the outer surface will likely be singed, but the heat is too quickly replaced by the icy stratospheric blast for it to actually be cooked. [Image: image] At supersonic and hypersonic speeds, a shockwave forms around the steak which helps protect it from the faster and faster winds. The exact characteristics of this shock front—and thus the mechanical stress on the steak—depend on how an uncooked 8 oz. filet tumbles at hypersonic speeds. I searched the literature, but was unable to find anything to help me estimate this. For the sake of this simulation, I assume that at lower speeds some type of vortex shedding creates a flipping tumble, while at hypersonic speeds it’s squished into a semi-stable spheroid shape. However, this is little more than a wild guess. If anyone puts a steak in a hypersonic wind tunnel to get better data on this, please, send me the video. If you drop the steak from 250 kilometers, things start to heat up. 250 kilometers puts us in the range of low earth orbit. However, the steak, since it’s dropped from a standstill, isn’t moving nearly as fast as an object re-entering from orbit. [Image: image] The steak reaches a top speed of Mach 6, and the outer surface may even get pleasantly seared. The inside, unfortunately, is still uncooked. Unless, that is, it goes into a hypersonic tumble and explodes into chunks. From higher altitudes, the heat starts to get really substantial. The shockwave in front of the steak reaches thousands of degrees (Fahrenheit or Celsius; it’s true in both). The problem with these levels of heat is that it burns the surface layer completely, converting it to little more than carbon. That is, it becomes charred. Charring is a normal consequence of dropping meat in the fire. The problem with charring meat at hypersonic speeds is that the charred layer doesn’t have much structural integrity, and is blasted off by the wind—exposing a new layer to be charred. (If the heat is high enough, it will simply blast the surface layer off as it flash-cooks it. This is referred to in the ICBM papers as the “ablation zone”) Even from those heights, the steak stilldoesn’t spend enough time in the heat to get cooked all the way through. (I know what some of you are probably thinking, and the answer is no—it doesn’t spend enough time in the Van Allen belts to be sterilized by radiation). We can try higher and higher speeds, and we might lengthen the exposure time via dropping it at an angle, from orbit. But if the temperature is high enough or the burn time long enough, the steak will slowly disintegrate as the outer layer is repeatedly charred and blasted off. If most of the steak makes it to the ground, the inside will still be raw. Which is why we should drop the steak over Pittsburgh. As the probably-apocryphal story goes, steel workers in Pittsburgh would cook steaks by slapping them on the glowing metal surfaces coming out of the foundry, searing the outside while leaving the inside raw. This is, supposedly, the origin of the term Pittsburgh Rare (http://www.livestrong.com/article/436635-how-to-cook-pittsburgh-style-steaks/). So drop your steak from a suborbital rocket, send out a collection team to recover it, brush it off, reheat it, cut away any badly charred sections, and dig in. Just watch out for salmonella. And the Andromeda Strain. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 当牛排落地时，你需要从多高的地方扔下牛排才能将其煮熟？
items.model_answer:
If you mean “could a steak be cooked just by dropping it from a great height,” the basic answer is: in principle, yes, but only from an absurdly large drop, and in practice it would burn on the outside, stay undercooked inside, and probably be ruined.

The key idea is that falling converts gravitational potential energy into heat, but only if that energy is actually dissipated into the steak, mainly through air resistance or impact. To estimate the minimum height, suppose you want to raise a steak to a cooked temperature.

Take a roughly 0.3 kg steak. Meat is mostly water, so a reasonable specific heat is about 3500 J/kg·K. If it starts at refrigerator temperature, say 5°C, and you want the center around 60°C, that is a temperature rise of about 55 K. The thermal energy needed is roughly

Q ≈ mcΔT ≈ (0.3)(3500)(55) ≈ 58,000 joules.

The gravitational potential energy from a drop height h is

E = mgh.

Setting mgh equal to 58,000 J gives

h ≈ 58,000 / (0.3 × 9.8) ≈ 20,000 meters,

so about 20 km.

Interestingly, the mass cancels if all the gravitational energy heats the steak, so the estimate is of the same order for different steak sizes. More generally,

h ≈ cΔT / g ≈ (3500 × 55) / 9.8 ≈ 20,000 m.

That is already extremely high, but this is an unrealistically optimistic lower bound. In reality, not all the lost gravitational energy goes into heating the steak. Most of it goes into heating the surrounding air, generating turbulence, sound, and possibly heating only the surface. If the steak reaches terminal velocity, then extra height no longer increases impact speed; instead, the energy is dissipated gradually through drag, mostly into the air. That might char the surface somewhat, like atmospheric reentry, but it would not heat the interior evenly the way cooking does.

If you relied on impact instead, the steak’s kinetic energy at ordinary terminal velocity is far too small. For a steak-sized object, terminal speeds might be on the order of 50–100 m/s. The impact energy of a 0.3 kg steak at 100 m/s is only

½mv² ≈ 0.5 × 0.3 × 100² = 1500 J,

which is nowhere near the roughly 58,000 J needed.

So the careful answer is: the absolute best-case energy estimate says on the order of 20 kilometers, but in the real atmosphere there is no practical drop height that would “cook” a steak properly. A very high fall might heat or damage the outside, but it would not reliably cook the steak through.

items.question: What If You Went Swimming in a Spent Fuel Pool?
human_answers: Assuming you’re a reasonably good swimmer, you could probably survive treading water anywhere from 10 to 40 hours. At that point, you would black out from fatigue and drown. This is also true for a pool without nuclear fuel in the bottom. Spent fuel from nuclear reactors is highly radioactive. Water is good for both radiation shielding and cooling, so fuel is stored at the bottom of pools for a couple decades until it’s inert enough to be moved into dry casks. We haven’t really agreed on where to put those dry casks yet. One of these days we should probably figure that out. Here’s the geometry of a typical fuel storage pool: [Image: image] The heat wouldn't be a big problem. The water temperature in a fuel pool can in theory go as high as 50°C, but in practice they're generally between 25°C and 35°C—warmer than most pools but cooler than a hot tub. For the kinds of radiation coming off spent nuclear fuel, every 7 centimeters of water cuts the amount of radiation in half. The most highly radioactive fuel rods are those recently removed from a reactor. Based on the activity levels provided by Ontario Hydro in this report (http://www.osti.gov/energycitations/servlets/purl/7284014-xaMii9/7284014.pdf), this would be the region of danger for fresh fuel rods: [Image: image] Swimming to the bottom, touching your elbows to a fresh fuel canister, and immediately swimming back up would probably be enough to kill you. Yet outside the outer boundary, you could swim around as long as you wanted—the dose from the core would be less than the normal background dose you get walking around. In fact, as long as you were underwater, you would be shielded from most of that normal background dose. You may actually receive a lower dose of radiation treading water in a spent fuel pool than walking around on the street. [Image: image] That’s if everything goes as planned. If there’s corrosion in the spent fuel rod casings, there may be some fission products in the water. They do a pretty good job of keeping the water clean, and it wouldn’t hurt you to swim in it, but it’s radioactive enough that it wouldn’t be legal to sell it as bottled water. (Which is too bad—it’d make a hell of an energy drink). We know spent fuel pools can be safe to swim in because they’re routinely serviced by human divers. However, these divers have to be careful. On August 31st, 2010 (http://www.isoe-network.net/index.php/publications-mainmenu-88/isoe-news/doc_download/1756-ritter2011ppt.html), a diver was servicing the spent fuel pool at the Leibstadt nuclear reactor in Switzerland. He spotted an unidentified length of tubing on the bottom of the pool and radioed his supervisor to ask what to do. He was told to put it in his tool basket, which he did. Due to bubble noise in the pool, he didn’t hear his radiation alarm. When the tool basket was lifted from the water, the room’s radiation alarms went off. The basket was dropped back in the water and the diver left the pool. The diver’s dosimeter badges showed that he’d received a higher-than-normal whole-body dose, and the dose in his right hand was extremely high. The object turned out to be protective tubing from a radiation monitor in the reactor core, made highly radioactive by neutron flux. It had been accidentally sheared off while a capsule was being closed in 2006. It sank to a remote corner of the pool floor, where it sat unnoticed for four years. The tubing was so radioactive that if he’d tucked it into a tool belt or shoulder bag, where it sat close to his body, he could’ve been killed. As it was, the water protected him, and only his hand—a body part more resistant to radiation than the delicate internal organs—received a heavy dose. [Image: image] So, as far as swimming safety goes, the bottom line is that you’d probably be ok, as long as you didn’t dive to the bottom or pick up anything strange. But just to be sure, I got in touch with a friend of mine who works at a research reactor, and asked him what he thought would happen to you if you tried to swim in their radiation containment pool. “In our reactor?” He thought about it for a moment. “You’d die pretty quickly, before reaching the water, from gunshot wounds.”
items.original_question: 如果我在典型的乏核燃料池里游泳会怎么样？我是否需要潜水才能真正经历致命的辐射量？我能在水面安全停留多久？
items.model_answer:
If you went swimming in a spent fuel pool, the outcome would depend almost entirely on where the fuel was, how much water was above it, and whether the pool was operating normally.

In a normally operating spent fuel pool, the water is doing two jobs: cooling the fuel and shielding radiation. Water is actually very effective at blocking much of the dangerous radiation coming from spent fuel, especially if there are several meters of it above the assemblies. That means the surface of the pool can be safe enough for trained workers to be nearby, and in some cases people have even been in the water for maintenance under tightly controlled conditions. So simply touching the water or being near the top of a properly managed pool would not automatically kill you.

But swimming down toward the fuel would become extremely dangerous. As you got closer, the water shielding between you and the radioactive material would decrease, and the radiation dose rate could rise very quickly. Close to recently discharged fuel, the dose could be lethal in a short time—potentially minutes or less, depending on distance and fuel age. You would not feel radiation itself, so there might be no immediate warning before serious injury occurred.

The water itself is usually very clean, but that does not mean harmless. It is carefully treated and monitored, yet it can contain some radioactive contamination. Swallowing it or getting it into wounds would be a bad idea, though the main danger is usually external radiation from the fuel, not the water acting like acid or poison.

There are also non-radiation hazards. Spent fuel pools are industrial facilities, not swimming pools. The water may be warm, visibility may be odd because of the blue Cherenkov glow, and there are racks, equipment, and operational restrictions. You could interfere with safety systems or expose yourself to contamination and physical danger.

So the short answer is: if the pool is functioning normally and you stayed near the surface far above the fuel, you might survive the swim without immediate harm. If you dove down near the spent fuel, you could receive a massive radiation dose and die.

items.question: What If You Flew an Ordinary Airplane over Other Worlds in the Solar System?
human_answers: Here’s our aircraft: [Image: image] The Cessna 172 Skyhawk, probably the most common plane in the world. Here’s our pilot: [Image: image] Here’s what happens when the aircraft is launched above the surface of the 32 largest Solar System bodies: [Image: image] In most cases, there’s no atmosphere, and the plane falls straight to the ground. (If it’s dropped from one kilometer, in a few cases, the crash will be slow enough that the pilot may survive—although the life-support equipment probably won’t.) There are nine Solar System bodies with atmospheres thick enough to matter: Earth—obviously—Mars, Venus, the four gas giants, Saturn’s moon Titan, and the Sun. Let’s take a closer look at what would happen to a plane on each one. The Sun: This works about as well as you'd imagine. If the plane is released close enough to the Sun to feel its atmosphere at all, it's vaporized in less than a second. Mars: To see what happens to aircraft on Mars, we turn to X-Plane (http://www.x-plane.com/desktop/home/?utm_expid=25103718-8). X-Plane is the most advanced flight simulator in the world. The product of 20 years of obsessive labor by a hardcore aeronautics enthusiast who uses capslock a lot when talking about planes, it actually simulates the flow of air over every piece of an aircraft’s body as it flies. This makes it a valuable research tool, since it can accurately simulate entirely new aircraft designs—and new environments. In particular, if you change the X-Plane config file to reduce gravity, thin the atmosphere, and shrink the radius of the planet it can simulate flight on Mars (http://www.x-plane.com/adventures/mars.html). (Note: Thank you to Tom J and the folks in the X-Plane community for their help with aerodynamic calculations in different atmospheres.) X-Plane tells us that flight on Mars is difficult, but not impossible. NASA knows this, and has considered surveying Mars by airplane (http://marsairplane.larc.nasa.gov/). The tricky thing is that with so little atmosphere, to get any lift, you have to go fast. You need to approach Mach 1 just to get off the ground, and once you get moving, you have so much inertia that it’s hard to change course—if you turn, your plane rotates, but keeps moving in the original direction. The X-Plane author compared piloting Martian aircraft to flying a supersonic ocean liner. Our Cessna 172 isn’t up to the challenge. Launched from 1 km, it doesn’t build up enough speed to pull out of a dive, and plows into the Martian terrain at over 60 m/s (135 mph). If dropped from four or five kilometers, it could gain enough speed to pull up into a glide—at over half the speed of sound. The landing would not be survivable. Venus:Unfortunately, X-Plane is not capable of simulating the hellish environment near the surface of Venus. But physics calculations give us an idea of what flight there would be like. The upshot is: Your plane would fly pretty well, except it would be on fire the whole time, and then it would stop flying, and then stop being a plane. The atmosphere on Venus is over 60 times denser than Earth’s, which is thick enough that a Cessna moving at running speed would rise into the air. Unfortunately, the air it’s rising into is hot enough to melt lead. The paint would start melting off in seconds, the plane’s components would fail rapidly, and the plane would glide gently into the ground as it came apart under the heat stress. A much better bet would be to fly above the clouds. While Venus’s surface is awful, its upper atmosphere is surprisingly Earthlike. 55 kilometers up, a human could survive with an oxygen mask and a protective wetsuit; the air is room temperature and the pressure is similar to that on Earth mountains. You need the wetsuit, though, to protect you from the sulfuric acid. (I’m not selling this well, am I?) The acid's no fun, but it turns out the area right above the clouds is a great environment for an airplane (http://ntrs.nasa.gov/archive/nasa/casi.ntrs.nasa.gov/20030003716_2002108457.pdf), as long as it has no exposed metal to be corroded away by the sulfuric acid. And is capable of flight in constant Category-5-hurricane-level winds, which are another thing I forgot to mention earlier. Venus is a terrible place. Jupiter: Our Cessna can’t fly on Jupiter; the gravity is just too strong. The power needed to maintain level flight is three times greater than that on Earth. Starting from a friendly sea-level pressure, we’d accelerate through the tumbling winds into a 275 m/s (600 mph) downward glide deeper and deeper through the layers of ammonia ice and water ice until we and the aircraft were crushed. There's no surface to hit; Jupiter transitions smoothly from gas to solid as you sink deeper and deeper. Saturn: The picture here is a bit friendlier than on Jupiter. The weaker gravity—close to Earth’s, actually—and slightly denser (but still thin) atmosphere mean that we’d be able to struggle along a bit further before we gave in to either the cold or high winds and descended to the same fate as on Jupiter. Uranus: Uranus is a strange, uniform bluish orb. There are high winds and it’s bitterly cold. It’s the friendliest of the gas giants to our Cessna, and you could probably fly for a little while. But given that it seems to be an almost completely featureless planet, why would you want to? Neptune: If you’re going to fly around one of the ice giants, Neptune (Motto: “The Slightly Bluer One”) is probably a better choice than Uranus. It at least has some clouds to look at before you freeze to death or break apart from the turbulence. Titan: We’ve saved the best for last. When it comes to flying, Titan might be better than Earth. Its atmosphere is thick but its gravity is light, giving it a surface pressure only 50% higher than Earth’s with air four times as dense. Its gravity—lower than that of the Moon—means that flying is easy. Our Cessna could get into the air under pedal power. In fact, humans on Titan could fly by muscle power. A human in a hang glider could comfortably take off and cruise around powered by oversized swim-flipper boots—or even take off by flapping artificial wings. The power requirements are minimal—it would probably take no more effort than walking. The downside (there’s always a downside) is the cold. It’s 72 kelvin on Titan, which is about the temperature of liquid nitrogen. Judging from some numbers on heating requirements for light aircraft, I estimate that the cabin of a Cessna on Titan would probably cool by about two degrees per minute. The batteries would help to keep themselves warm for a little while, but eventually the craft would run out of heat and crash. The Huygens probe, which descended with batteries nearly drained (taking fascinating pictures (http://www.beugungsbild.de/huygens/huygens.html) as it fell), succumbed to the cold after only a few hours on the surface. It had enough time to send back a single photo (http://www.esa.int/Our_Activities/Space_Science/Cassini-Huygens/New_images_from_Titan) after landing—the only one we have from the surface of a body beyond Mars. If humans put on artificial wings to fly, we might become Titan versions of the Icarus story—our wings could freeze, fall apart, and send us tumbling to our deaths. [Image: image] But I've never seen the Icarus story as a lesson about the limitations of humans. I see it as a lesson about the limitations of wax as an adhesive. The cold of Titan is just an engineering problem. With the right refitting, and the right heat sources, a Cessna 172 could fly on Titan—and so could we.
items.original_question: 如果你尝试在不同的太阳系天体上空驾驶一架普通的地球飞机会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
An ordinary airplane would only fly where there is enough atmosphere for wings and engines to work, and where the temperature, pressure, and chemistry do not immediately destroy the aircraft or its occupants. In the Solar System, that means the answer is mostly “no,” but with a few interesting partial exceptions.

On the Moon, Mercury, and Pluto, an ordinary airplane could not fly at all because there is essentially no atmosphere. Wings need air to generate lift, and normal jet or propeller engines also need air. The same basic problem applies to most asteroids.

On Mars, things get more interesting. Mars does have an atmosphere, but it is very thin, less than 1 percent of Earth’s sea-level pressure. An ordinary airplane designed for Earth would not fly there. Its wings would not generate enough lift at normal speeds, and its engines would not perform properly because the air is too thin and has very little oxygen. To fly on Mars, you need something specially designed: very large wings, very low weight, very high speed, or rotorcraft built for the thin air, like NASA’s Ingenuity helicopter.

On Venus, the atmosphere is actually thick enough for aerodynamic flight, especially high in the atmosphere. In principle, wings could work very well there. But an ordinary airplane still would not survive. Near the surface, Venus is hot enough to melt lead and the pressure is crushing, around 90 times Earth’s. The atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide with sulfuric-acid clouds higher up. A normal airplane and its engines would fail quickly. If you had a specially built aircraft operating high in the Venusian atmosphere, flight is actually one of the more plausible possibilities in the Solar System.

On Titan, Saturn’s large moon, flying is surprisingly favorable in aerodynamic terms. Titan has a thick atmosphere and low gravity, which makes it easier for wings or rotors to generate lift. In some ways, Titan is one of the easiest places in the Solar System to fly. But an ordinary airplane still would not work well because the air is mostly nitrogen with almost no oxygen, so normal engines could not burn fuel, and the temperatures are extremely cold. A specially designed aircraft could fly there very effectively.

In the gas giants like Jupiter and Saturn, there is no solid surface to take off from in the usual sense, but there is plenty of atmosphere. If you somehow placed an airplane in the right layer of the atmosphere, wings could generate lift. However, an ordinary airplane would still fail because the atmospheric composition is wrong for normal engines, the winds are extreme, and deeper down the pressure becomes enormous. Uranus and Neptune have similar issues, along with intense cold and violent atmospheric conditions.

So the short version is this: an ordinary Earth airplane would only really fly on Earth. On most other worlds there is either too little atmosphere, the wrong kind of atmosphere, or conditions so extreme that the aircraft would not function. But if you allow specially designed aircraft, Mars, Venus’s upper atmosphere, Titan, and even parts of the giant planets become possible and in some cases very promising places to fly.

items.question: What If Hubble Pointed at Earth Instead of Deep Space?
human_answers: This is a common question. The Hubble operators get it a lot, and their FAQ page answers it (http://hubblesite.org/reference_desk/faq/answer.php.id=78&cat=topten). The problem isn’t—as some people say—that the Earth is too bright. As Phil Plait of Bad Astronomy pointed out (http://www.badastronomy.com/mad/2000/hubbleearth.html), Hubble looks at Earth pretty regularly. The real problem is that Hubble is moving over the surface at over 7 kilometers per second. Even a short exposure would be a blur. That’s no fun. Is there a way we could make it work? I decided to take a closer look. As our picture target, we’ll use this typical desk: [Image: image] The Earth’s atmosphere won’t be a problem. It’s actually much more of a problem for surface-based telescopes looking at space than for space-based telescopes looking at the surface. The reason for this is geometric: [Image: image] Hubble is the best visible-light telescope we have, but its resolution does have limits. Pluto, out in the Kuiper belt, lies right at those limits. The best pictures we have of Pluto (http://hubblesite.org/newscenter/archive/releases/solar-system/pluto/2010/06/) come from Hubble, but the ex-planet is still little more than a mysterious blur. At that resolution (about 0.05 arcseconds, give or take) and Hubble’s distance from the desk (about 570 kilometers) the desk would look like this: [Image: image] But that desk is also zooming by, so even a perfect image will be blurred: [Image: image] Combining the two effects gives us an end result that looks like this: [Image: image] That’s no good. Could we rotate Hubble to track the surface, and eliminate the blur? Hubble swivels to follow targets. Usually, they’re far enough away that we can assume they’re at infinite distance. The automatic on-board parallax algorithms can’t handle targets closer than about ten times the distance to the Moon. When astronomers want to use it to take pictures of the Moon, sometimes they send it commands to rotate manually (http://www.stsci.edu/hst/HST_overview/documents/uir/UIR-2007-01.pdf), then turn on the camera mid-maneuver. It doesn’t work very well. Moving Hubble at those speeds is cumbersome with the current guidance package.
