The resulting photos (http://hubblesite.org/newscenter/archive/releases/1999/14) are better than what you can see with the naked eye, but they’re not very good by Hubble standards. Here’s our desk, with the image degraded by a similar amount that the Moon one was: [Image: image] Fortunately, the Moon is bright enough that if you’ll settle for a short exposure, you can avoid the problem. This photo (http://hubblesite.org/newscenter/archive/releases/2012/22/fastfacts/) was taken with a half-second exposure, short enough that it didn’t have to do much in the way of tracking. Unfortunately, our desk is moving across the telescope’s field of view about 600 times faster than the Moon. Tracking is unavoidable. The strange thing is, the desk really isn’t moving all that fast. Hubble is just really slow. To track the surface, it would need to rotate less than a degree per second at maximum. But Hubble wasn’t built for surface tracking. The telescope’s top rotational (“slew”) speed is only a few degrees per minute (about the speed of a minute hand on a clock) and even those speeds are fast enough that its gyroscopes cause it to vibrate (http://www.pha.jhu.edu/groups/hst10x/pdffiles/HST10X_Technical.pdf), which destroys the image quality. Clearly, we’d need to disable Hubble’s guidance system and bolt on our own control system. Hubble’s rotational moment of inertia (http://www.dept.aoe.vt.edu/~cdhall/courses/aoe5984/bs.pdf) is similar to that of a small carousel; too hard for the existing gyroscopes to move, but not hard in the absolute sense. With our custom control system, it could be made to track the surface, and get photos pretty close to optimal quality: [Image: image] But this isn’t just a hypothetical situation. Much of the technology in military spy satellites is believed to be similar to that of Hubble. So in a sense, pointing a Hubble-type telescope at the surface is not only possible—it’s what the US government actually does (http://www.onorbit.com/node/3850).
items.original_question: 如果哈勃望远镜瞄准地球，图像会有多详细？
items.model_answer:
If Hubble pointed at Earth instead of deep space, the main result is that it would not work the way people might imagine. Hubble was designed to observe extremely faint, distant objects, not a bright, nearby, fast-moving target like Earth.

First, Earth would be overwhelmingly bright compared with the galaxies and nebulae Hubble usually studies. That much reflected sunlight could easily saturate its detectors, washing out images and potentially stressing the instruments if proper precautions were not taken. Hubble’s cameras are built for sensitive astronomy, so looking at a sunlit Earth would be more like shining a flashlight into night-vision goggles than using a normal camera.

Second, tracking would be a serious problem. Hubble orbits Earth at about 7.5 km/s, and the ground below moves rapidly through its field of view. Deep-space targets appear nearly fixed, which is ideal for long exposures. Earth features would sweep by quickly, so Hubble would need very different pointing and exposure strategies. It could in principle image parts of Earth briefly, but it is not optimized for that job.

Third, focus and observing geometry matter. Hubble is focused for astronomical distances, effectively infinity. Earth is still far enough away from Hubble—hundreds to a couple thousand kilometers depending on what it looked at—that this is not the biggest obstacle, but it is another reason the telescope is not ideal for Earth observation compared with satellites specifically designed for that purpose.

There is also an operational issue: Hubble usually avoids pointing too close to Earth’s bright limb because scattered light from the planet degrades observations. Earth is more often something to avoid than something to study.

If engineers deliberately commanded Hubble to observe Earth safely, it could probably take very high-resolution images of clouds, coastlines, and large surface features, potentially with resolution on the order of tens of meters under favorable conditions. But it would still be a poor substitute for reconnaissance or weather satellites, which are built for wide fields, rapid imaging, and repeated passes.

So the short answer is: if Hubble pointed at Earth, it would see a very bright, fast-moving target and would perform awkwardly rather than magically. It could likely capture some detailed images, but it is the wrong tool for the job and could not usefully observe Earth the way it observes deep space.

items.question: What If Every Ship Were Removed from Earth's Waters at Once?
human_answers: About six microns—slightly more than the diameter of a strand of spider silk. [Image: image] Archimedes’ principle tells us that the water displaced by a ship weighs as much as the ship itself. If we can figure out the total weight of all the world’s ships, we can figure out how much water they’re displacing, then divide that volume by the surface area of the ocean to figure out how much the water level would drop. Weighing ships is confusing (http://www.pomorci.com/Zanimljivosti/TONNAGE%20MEASUREMENT%20OF%20SHIPS.pdf). There are a bunch of different measurements of the size of a ship, and many of them, like gross tonnage, are actually measures of the volume of the ship’s rooms and other internal spaces, not its weight. The UN Conference on Trade and Development publishes estimates (http://unctad.org/en/Docs/rmt2011ch2_en.pdf) of the size of the world shipping fleet. What the UNCTD publishes is “deadweight tonnage”, which is the maximum weight of the ship’s fuel, cargo, and crew. What we want is “displacement”. Unfortunately, comprehensive numbers for displacement are harder to find. Fortunately, we can estimate it. Brian Barrass’s book Ship Design and Performance for Masters and Mates gives a table of ratios of deadweight tonnage to displacement for different types of ships. Extrapolating from the last few years of UNCTD data, and using the coefficients from the book, suggests that the world fleet weighs about 2.15 billion tons when fully loaded. The main component of the fleet by weight is oil tankers and bulk ore-carrying ships, which make up over two-thirds of the total. (The UNCTD data doesn’t include small recreational boats or naval fleets. However, based on some numbers for naval fleets (http://www.csbaonline.org/4Publications/PubLibrary/R.20090217.The_US_Navy_Charti/R.20090217.The_US_Navy_Charti.pdf) and recreational boats (http://nmma.net/assets/cabinets/Cabinet445/2011_abstract_preview.pdf), neither one contributes much to the total.) A ton of water is about a cubic meter. 2.15 billion cubic meters divided by the surface area of the oceans equals about 6 microns (0.006 mm). But you don’t have to worry about that six-micron sea level drop. The oceans are currently rising at about 3.3 millimeters per year due to global warming (through both glacial melting and thermal expansion of seawater). At that rate (normalized for seasonal variation and short-term fluctations), if you removed every ship from the ocean, the water would be back up to its original average level in 16 hours. [Image: image] Sea levels will likely rise a few feet by the year 2100 (https://what-if.xkcd.com/33). Current fish wet biomass is about 2 billion tons (http://phys.org/news151251277.html), so removing them won’t make a dent either. (Marine fish biomass dropped by 80% over the last century (http://news.aaas.org/2011_annual_meeting/0228declining-fisheries.shtml), which—taking into consideration the growth rate of the world’s shipping fleet—leads to an odd conclusion: Sometime in the last few years, we reached a point where there are, by weight, more ships in the ocean than fish.) And what about the old joke about how much deeper the ocean would be without sponges? While estimates of sponge biomass are hard to come by, the answer is probably that if you removed all the sponges, sea level would drop by no more than a few microns ... and much less if you squeezed them out first. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果每艘船同时从地球水域移走，海平面会下降多少？
items.model_answer:
If every ship on Earth vanished from the oceans, seas, rivers, and lakes all at once, the immediate physical effect on the water itself would be surprisingly small, but the human consequences would be enormous.

Physically, sea level would fall by a tiny amount because ships displace water. All the world’s ships together have a total mass on the order of a few billion tonnes, which means they displace a similar volume of water, only a few cubic kilometers in total. Spread over the surface of the global ocean, that corresponds to only a few micrometers to perhaps around ten micrometers of sea-level change, far too small for people to notice. You would not get giant waves just from the disappearance itself, except possibly very local disturbances where large vessels had been sitting, especially in harbors or narrow channels. Those disturbances would behave more like localized sloshing than a planet-scale tsunami.

The real effects would be economic and logistical. Modern civilization depends heavily on shipping. Most international trade by mass moves by sea, including oil, liquefied natural gas, coal, iron ore, grain, fertilizers, containers full of manufactured goods, and many industrial chemicals. If all ships were removed instantly, global supply chains would begin failing within days. Ports would become useless, factories would run out of parts, supermarkets in import-dependent regions would see shortages, and energy markets would be hit hard. Island nations and remote coastal communities would be especially vulnerable because they rely on ships for food, fuel, medicine, and construction materials.

Oil and fuel distribution would be one of the first major crises. A large fraction of crude oil and petroleum products is transported by tanker. Countries that depend on imported fuel would face shortages quickly, affecting electricity generation, transportation, agriculture, and emergency services. Natural gas markets would also be disrupted because LNG shipping would stop completely. Some regions could compensate partly with pipelines or local production, but many could not.

Food systems would also be stressed. Bulk carriers move huge amounts of grain, soybeans, and fertilizers. Countries that import staple foods would face rising prices and shortages. Fishing fleets disappearing would also abruptly remove a major food source and livelihood for millions of people. In the longer term, some fish stocks might recover because industrial fishing pressure would suddenly drop, but that ecological benefit would come with severe short-term human cost.

Navies, coast guards, ferries, tugboats, research vessels, dredgers, and rescue craft would all be gone too. That would mean immediate losses in maritime security, search and rescue capability, scientific monitoring, offshore maintenance, and passenger transport. Many bridges and tunnels would see increased pressure as people shifted to land routes where possible, but many routes simply cannot be replaced on short timescales.

Environmental effects would be mixed. There would be an immediate drop in ship emissions, underwater noise, ballast-water transport of invasive species, and oil-spill risk from vessels. Marine mammals in some regions might benefit from quieter oceans and fewer ship strikes. But there could also be negative consequences: offshore platforms and coastal infrastructure often depend on ships for maintenance and supply, so failures there could create new hazards. Also, if maritime trade stopped, countries might turn more heavily to trucks, planes, and rail where possible, often increasing emissions per unit cargo.

Rivers and lakes would also be affected. Inland shipping carries large amounts of bulk goods efficiently. Removing barges and ferries would strain roads and rail systems and isolate some communities.

So the best short answer is this: Earth’s waters would barely change physically, aside from a minuscule drop in sea level and some local water disturbances, but human civilization would experience a massive global trade, energy, food, and transportation crisis almost immediately.

items.question: What If You Put a Running Hair Dryer in a Sealed 1x1x1 Meter Box?
human_answers: A typical hair dryer draws 1875 watts of power. All 1875 watts have to go somewhere. No matter what happens inside the box, if there’s 1875 watts of power being used, eventually there will be 1875 watts of heat flowing out. This is true of any device that uses power, which is a handy thing to know. For example, people worry about leaving disconnected chargers plugged into the wall for fear that they’re draining power. Are they right? You can use heat flow to come up with simple rule of thumb: If an unused charger isn’t warm to the touch, it’s using less than a penny of electricity a day. For a small smartphone charger, if it’s not warm to the touch, it’s using less than a penny a year. This is true of almost any powered device (though not necessarily those plugged into a second device. If a charger is connected to something, like a smartphone or laptop, power can be flowing from the wall through the charger into the device.) But back to the box. Heat will flow from the hair dryer out into the box. If we assume the dryer is indestructible, the interior of the box will keep getting hotter until the outer surface reaches about 60°C (140°F). At that temperature, the box will be losing heat to the outside as fast as the hair dryer is adding it inside, and the system will be in equilibrium. [Image: image] The equilibrium temperature will be a bit cooler if there’s a breeze, or if the box is sitting on a wet or metallic surface that conducts away heat quickly. If the box is made of metal, 60°C is hot enough to burn your hand if you touch it (http://www.mascoat.com/assets/files/Insulative_Coating_Evaluation_NACE.pdf) for more than five seconds. If it’s wood, you can probably touch it for a while, but there’s a danger that parts of the box in contact with the mouth of the hair dryer will catch fire. The inside of a box will be like an oven. The temperature it reaches will depend on the thickness of the box wall; the thicker and more insulating the wall, the higher the temperature. It wouldn’t take a very thick box to create temperatures high enough to burn out the hair dryer. But let’s assume an indestructible hair dryer. And if we have something as cool as an indestructible hair dryer, it seems like a shame to limit it. [Image: image] With 18,750 watts flowing out of the hair dryer, the surface of the box reaches over 200°C (475°F), as hot as a skillet on low-medium. [Image: image] I wonder how high this dial goes. [Image: image] The surface of the box is now 600°C, hot enough to glow a dim red. [Image: image] If it’s made of aluminium, the inside is starting to melt. If it’s made of lead, the outside is starting to melt. If it’s on a wood floor, the house is on fire. But it doesn't matter what's happening around it; the hair dryer is indestructible. [Image: image] Two megawatts pumped into a laser (http://what-if.xkcd.com/13/) is enough to destroy missiles. At 1300°C, the box is now about the temperature of lava. [Image: image] One more notch. [Image: image] 18 megawatts are flowing into the box. [Image: image] The surface of the box reaches 2400°C. If it were steel, it would have melted by now. If it’s made of something like tungsten, it might conceivably last a little longer. Just one more, then we'll stop. [Image: image] 187 megawatts is enough to make the box glow white. Not a lot of box materials can survive these conditions, so we’ll have to assume the box is indestructible. [Image: image] Unfortunately, the floor isn’t. Before it can burn its way through the floor, someone throws a water balloon under it. The burst of steam launches the box out the front door and onto the sidewalk. (Note: If you’re ever trapped with me in a burning building, and I suggest an idea for how we could escape the situation, it’s probably best to ignore me.) [Image: image] 1.875 gigawatts (I lied about stopping). According to Back to the Future, the hair dryer is now drawing enough power to travel back in time. [Image: image] The box is blindingly bright, and you can’t get closer than a few hundred meters due to the intense heat. It sits in the middle of a growing pool of lava. Anything within 50-100 meters bursts into flame. A column of heat and smoke rise high into the air. Periodic explosions of gas beneath the box launch it into the air, and it starts fires and forms a new lava pool where it lands. [Image: image] 18.7 gigawatts. The conditions around the box are similar to those on the pad during a Space Shuttle launch. The box begins to be tossed around by the powerful updrafts it’s creating. In 1914, H.G. Wells imagined devices like this in his book The World Set Free (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_World_Set_Free). He wrote of a type of bomb that, instead of exploding once, exploded continuously, a slow-burn inferno that started inextinguishable fires in the hearts of cities. The story eerily foreshadowed the development, 30 years later, of nuclear weapons. [Image: image] The box is now soaring through the air. Each time it nears the ground, it superheats the surface, and the plume of expanding air hurls it back into the sky. [Image: image] 1.875 terawatts is like a house-sized stack of TNT going off every second. [Image: image] A trail of firestorms—massive conflagrations which sustain themselves by creating their own wind systems—winds its way across the landscape. A new milestone: The hair dryer is now, impossibly, consuming more power than every other electrical device on the planet combined. [Image: image] The box, soaring high above the surface, is putting out energy equivalent to three Trinity tests every second. At this point, the pattern is obvious. This thing is going to skip around the atmosphere until it destroys the planet. Let's try something different. [Image: image] We turn the dial to zero as the box is passing over northern Canada. Rapidly cooling, it plummets to Earth, landing in Great Bear Lake with a plume of steam. And then … [Image: image] This one goes to 11. Petawatts, in this case. A brief story: The official record for fastest manmade object is the Helios 2 probe, which reached about 70 km/s in a close swing around the Sun. But it’s possible the actual holder of that title is a two-ton metal manhole cover. The cover sat atop a shaft at an underground nuclear test site operated by Los Alamos as part of Operation Plumbbob. When the one-kiloton nuke went off below, the facility effectively became a nuclear potato cannon (http://nfttu.blogspot.com/2006/01/nuclear-potato-cannon-part-2.html), giving the cap a gigantic kick. A high-speed camera trained on the lid caught only one frame of it moving upward before it vanished—which means it was moving at a minimum of 66 km/s. The cap was never found. 66 km/s is about six times escape velocity, but contrary to the linked blog’s speculation, it’s unlikely the cap ever reached space. Newton’s impact depth approximation (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_depth) suggests that it was either destroyed completely by impact with the air or slowed and fell back to Earth. Our suddenly-activated hair dryer box, bobbing in lake water, undergoes a similar process. The heated steam below it expands outward, and as the box rises into the air, the entire surface of the lake turns to steam. The steam, heated to a plasma by the flood of radiation, accelerates the box faster and faster. [Image: image] Rather than slam into the atmosphere like the manhole cover, the flood of radiation heats the air around it, creating a bubble of expanding plasma which offers little resistance. The box exits the atmosphere and continues away, slowly fading from second sun to dim star. Much of the Northwest Territories is burning, but the Earth has survived. Although we may wish we hadn't. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果打开连续功率的吹风机并将其放入密闭的 1x1x1 米盒子中会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If you put a running hair dryer in a sealed 1×1×1 meter box, the box would heat up quickly, the air pressure inside would rise somewhat, and the hair dryer would soon stop working normally or fail from overheating.

Here’s the basic physics.

A 1×1×1 meter box holds 1 cubic meter of air, which is about 1.2 kg of air at room conditions. A typical hair dryer uses around 1000–1800 watts. In a sealed box, essentially all of that electrical power ends up as heat inside the box. So the dryer is not “making wind” in any useful external sense; it is just converting electrical energy into thermal energy and stirring the air around.

Air heats fast in that small volume. The heat capacity of 1.2 kg of air is roughly 1200 J/K, so a 1200 W hair dryer could raise the air temperature by about 1 °C per second at first, if you ignore heat loss to the walls. In reality, the walls also absorb heat, so the temperature rise slows, but the box still gets hot very quickly.

The pressure behavior depends on whether the box is truly rigid. In a rigid sealed box, heating the air raises pressure roughly in proportion to absolute temperature. For example, going from 20 °C to 120 °C means going from about 293 K to 393 K, so pressure would rise by about 34%. That is significant, but usually not enough by itself to make a strong box explode. In a flexible box, it would expand instead.

What happens to the hair dryer itself is more important. A hair dryer relies on room-temperature intake air to cool its heating element and motor. In the sealed box, it keeps sucking in hotter and hotter air. That means the element, motor, plastic housing, and thermal cutoff all run under worse conditions. Most likely outcomes are that its thermal protection trips, it shuts off, or it burns out. If the box is very well insulated, this happens sooner.

The fan does not create a lasting pressure difference inside the box. It only circulates the air. In a sealed box, there is nowhere for air to go overall, so after transient local motion, the net effect is just turbulent recirculation and heating.

If the box is perfectly sealed and airtight, oxygen is not replenished, but a hair dryer does not burn fuel, so oxygen depletion is not the main issue. The main issue is electrical heating and lack of cooling. If there are flammable materials in the box, the rising temperature could become a fire hazard, especially if the dryer malfunctions.

So the short answer is: the inside of the box gets hot fast, the pressure rises moderately, the air churns around, and the hair dryer will probably overheat and shut off or fail before anything more dramatic happens.

items.question: How Much Cornstarch Can You Pour down a Drain before Bad Things Happen?
human_answers: It depends what you consider unpleasant. If you watered down the cornstarch enough, you could likely pour it down the drain for years without any ill effects. If it didn’t clog the sink, the rest of the pipes could probably handle it. It might provoke some confusion among the sewage treatment people, but it wouldn’t break anything. But it’d be terrifically boring (and thus unpleasant) to pour cornstarch down a sink all day, so I guess that’s— [Image: image] … Oh. Huh. Well, let’s thicken the cornstarch. When you mix cornstarch and water in a bit under a 2:1 ratio, you get oobleck, a substance with some odd physical properties. This is a great kitchen science experiment everyone should try at least once. At low speeds, oobleck behaves like a liquid. If you gently swish your fingers in a bowl of it, it feels like milk or heavy cream. However, if you make a fist and punch the surface, your hand bounces off with a thud—it’s like hitting a slab of raw meat. If you vibrate oobleck, even stranger things happen (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3zoTKXXNQIU). It wouldn’t take much of the mixture to clog a drain. It depends on your plumbing, but you could probably stop up your sink with a small bowl of it. Since your drain is clogged, I guess that’s the answer to your question. [Image: image] Well, ok. I guess some people don’t mind clogged drains. If you keep at it, after a few minutes, your sink will overflow, spilling goop onto your floor. [Image: image] Financially, this will be hard to keep up. If you’re mixing as fast as the water will come out of the sink, this project may cost you in the neighborhood of $5,000 per day if you can’t find a good bulk distributor. [Image: image] At this rate, it should build up on the floor at a rate of an inch or two per day. [Image: image] If your doors are sealed well, it will continue to build up. Once it reaches knee height (a week or two after you started), you may be able to hold the rising tide at bay for a little bit—at least in one room—by getting someone to flush the toilet repeatedly. The pipes there are larger and harder to clog; the limiting factor would probably be how fast the tank filled with water. [Image: image] Eventually, after a month or two, the oobleck would reach the living room window. The pressure would quickly rise, and sooner or later the window would burst. As the deadly Boston Molasses Flood (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Molasses_Disaster) proved, even thick, viscous fluids can flow quickly when in large enough quantities. The oobleck would pour rapidly out onto the lawn, carrying you with it. At this point, the local officials would probably notice and, at the very least, shut off your water. [Image: image] But I guess if you really like cornstarch that much, nothing unpleasant has happened.
items.original_question: 在不愉快的事情开始发生之前，我可以将多少玉米淀粉冲入下水道？
items.model_answer:
Very little. As a practical rule, you should treat the safe amount as essentially none.

Cornstarch is tricky because when it is mixed with water it does not behave like something that simply dissolves and washes away. It forms a suspension and then can settle, clump, and make a paste, especially in slower-moving parts of plumbing like the trap or in partially blocked pipes. If enough accumulates, it can contribute to a clog. In a wider sewer system, small amounts are unlikely to matter, but inside household plumbing repeated “small” disposals can add up.

So the direct answer is: there is no reliable threshold like “half a cup is fine” or “one tablespoon is dangerous.” The amount before “bad things happen” depends on pipe diameter, water flow, existing grease or debris, and whether the starch is dry, slurried, or mixed with other waste. In a typical home drain, even a few tablespoons dumped repeatedly is unwise; a large dump such as a cup or more could plausibly create a blockage, especially if it thickens in the trap or sticks to residue already in the pipe.

If you only sent a tiny accidental amount down with lots of running water, it will probably be fine. But if you have leftover cornstarch or a cornstarch slurry, the best practice is not to pour it down the drain at all. Let it dry and throw it in the trash, or wipe it out with paper towels first.

items.question: What If a Stereo Flew Past at Twice the Speed of Sound?
human_answers: Yes. Technically, anyway. It would be pretty hard to hear. The basic idea is pretty straightforward. The stereo is going faster than its own sound, so it will reach you first, followed by the sound it emitted one second ago, followed by the sound it emitted two seconds ago, and so forth. [Image: image] The problem is that the stereo is moving at Mach 2, which means that two seconds ago, it was over a kilometer away. It’s hard to hear music from that distance, particularly when your ears were just hit by (a) a sonic boom, and (b) pieces of a rapidly disintegrating stereo. Wind speeds of Mach 2 would messily disassemble most consumer electronics. The force of the wind on the body of the stereo is roughly comparable to that of a dozen people standing on it: [Image: image] An ordinary stereo wouldn’t make it, but one with some kind of ruggedized high-strength casing might be able to survive. If we put together a durable, heavy-duty stereo and launch it on a ballistic trajectory, it will only be traveling at supersonic speeds for the first 150 meters or so. This means that the target will hear a maximum of about a third of a second of reversed music. This phenomenon is actually confirmed in the 2008 paper Reproduction of Virtual Sound Sources Moving at Supersonic Speeds in Wave Field Synthesis (http://www.researchgate.net/publication/230702229_Reproduction_of_Virtual_Sound_Sources_Moving_at_Supersonic_Speeds_in_Wave_Field_Synthesis), which says that the sound wave field “contains a component carrying a time-reversed version of the source’s input signal”. The sonic boom would be the first thing the target would hear. It would be followed by several sounds played over one another, including both reversed music (rising slightly in pitch as it fades out) and forward-playing music (which would play at half speed and an octave too low), followed by the crash of a stereo demolishing your neighbor’s shed. Which means that if you’re playing one of those albums containing secret demonic messages, the result will be the strangest listening experience of your life: [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果你设法让立体声以两倍音速传播，当它飞过时，对于一个只是随意坐在某处的人来说，它听起来会是倒退的吗？
items.model_answer:
If a stereo flew past you at twice the speed of sound, you would not hear it approaching in the normal way. Since the stereo is moving faster than the sound waves it emits, those waves cannot get ahead of it. The sound piles up into a shock wave, much like the sonic boom from a supersonic jet.

So the main effect would be this: you would likely hear nothing from it until the moment the shock wave reached you, and then you would hear a sudden loud boom. After that, as the stereo had already passed, you could begin to hear the music trailing behind it. But the music would be highly distorted.

There are two reasons for the distortion. First, the Doppler effect would be extreme, shifting frequencies strongly. Second, at Mach 2 the stereo is outrunning its own sound, so the sound reaching you after the pass would be compressed into the shock structure and turbulent wake rather than arriving as clean, continuous audio. The result would not sound like normal music; it would be more like a burst of noise and scrambled, rapidly changing fragments.

Also, in reality, a stereo moving through air at Mach 2 would face enormous aerodynamic forces, heating, and vibration, so it probably would not function well as a speaker. But in the idealized physics picture, the key answer is: no gradual approach sound, then a sonic boom, then badly distorted sound after it passes.

items.question: What If We Launched a One-Way Mission to Voyager 1 Today?
human_answers: Voyager I is farther from Earth than any other manmade object. After getting a pair of gravitational kicks from Jupiter and Saturn, it’s headed out of the Solar System at a pretty high speed, and nothing else we’ve built is on track to pass it. Strangely, as of the day I’m writing this, Voyager is actually getting closer (http://voyager.jpl.nasa.gov/where/) to us, because Earth is in a part of its orbit where it’s approaching Voyager faster than Voyager is fleeing. But in a few months, we’ll swing around the Sun and Voyager will again be getting farther away. [Image: image] It has a 35-year head start, so it would be hard to catch. But catching up isn’t the problem. New Horizons, the spacecraft currently headed out of the Solar System by way of Pluto, is never going to catch up to Voyager—it’s not moving fast enough and it’s headed in the wrong direction. But it could have. The reason Voyager is moving so fast is that it got gravitational assists from Jupiter and Saturn, while New Horizons only got one from Jupiter. [Image: image] Gravity assists aren’t paradoxical magic. It’s just like bouncing a tennis ball off a passing truck. Gyroscopes, on the other hand, ARE magic. If New Horizons had ditched the Pluto objective and waited for the right planetary alignment (the 2030s look promising), it could have swung by Jupiter and Saturn, then caught up to Voyager in as little as a century or two! (Assuming we could manage to hit Voyager from that far away. But I bet we could; our rocket scientists are pretty good at rocket science.) Of course, getting there’s the easy part. The hard part is getting back. Voyager weighs a little less than a ton and is moving away at 17 kilometers per second (if it were in the atmosphere, that would be Mach 50). And since it’s out in interstellar space, there are no speeding Jupiters to grab on to. Stopping Voyager is going to take a lot of fuel. It’s what engineers call the tyranny of the rocket equation (http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/expeditions/expedition30/tryanny.html): As the amount that you want to change your speed (“delta-v”) goes up, the fuel required increases exponentially. The equation tells us that to turn the 720-kilogram Voyager around, we’re going to need at least 30 tons of fuel. But to get that fuel out there, we need even more fuel. And to get that fuel, we need even more fuel. (This is where the tyrannical rocket equation gets its exponential term.) In fact, to rescue Voyager, we’d have to launch a fleet of—at minimum—60 New Horizons-sized spacecraft loaded with nothing but fuel. Could we do it? Sure. There are a couple plausible ways. Instead of building five to ten dozen fuel-laden Titan IIIEs, we could just build a fleet of ten or fifteen Saturn Vs, and do the whole thing with fewer launches. But however we did it, it would be a massive and expensive operation similar in scale to the Apollo program. The difference between the launch vehicle we’d used to get Voyager out of the Solar System and the fleet we’d need for a round trip is striking: [Image: image] Fortunately, there’s one way around the tyranny of the rocket equation: Ditch the rockets. Ion engines—which use electric fields to accelerate exhaust gas to high speeds—are far more efficient than chemical rockets, and they make accelerating to high speeds much more plausible. The reason we’re not using them for everything is that they produce very little thrust, so it takes a long time to get up to speed. It’s like if you had a car that gets amazing mileage but has a one-horsepower engine. (Actually, are you sure that’s not just a horse?) Ion engines are great; the current ones just take forever to get you moving. But since catching Voyager is going to take a long time anyway, ion engines are fine. We could launch a probe (like this one (https://web.archive.org/web/20150910020454/http://trs-new.jpl.nasa.gov/dspace/bitstream/2014/13644/1/00-0010.pdf)), send it out to Voyager, latch on, turn everything around, and let it spend a few decades slowing Voyager down. Once Voyager had lost nearly all its speed, the Sun’s gravity would take over, and the probe would begin a long slow slide toward the inner Solar System. This would take about 200 years, and with some extremely careful nudges, we could make sure it falls in an Earth-crossing orbit. Two centuries later, Voyager would reach Earth and, with no way to slow down, burn up in our atmosphere, because we didn’t think to send out an aerobraking shell with the rescue craft. So that was a waste of a few centuries of work and billions upon billions of dollars. [Image: image] Maybe a better idea would be to borrow a salvage vessel and set sail for the coast of New South Wales, Australia. There, in the waters off Jervis Bay, the Australian Royal Navy ship Voyager sank in 1964 after an accidental collision. That one’s probably easier to retrieve. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 以今天的技术，是否有可能发起无人回收航行者一号任务？
items.model_answer:
If we launched a one-way mission to Voyager 1 today, the main result is that it would be extraordinarily hard, very expensive, and would take a long time—but it is not forbidden by physics.

Voyager 1 is currently over 24 billion kilometers from Earth and moving away at about 17 kilometers per second relative to the Sun. A spacecraft launched today would not just need to travel an enormous distance, it would also need to catch a target that is still receding. So the mission is really a deep-space chase.

With current or near-current technology, a direct rendezvous would likely take decades. If you launched a conventional chemical rocket mission, even with gravity assists, you would probably be looking at something like 30 to 50 years, depending on the trajectory and how much mass you were willing to launch. A very fast flyby mission could perhaps do better, but matching Voyager 1’s path and speed closely enough to actually meet it is much harder than merely crossing its distance from the Sun.

The biggest challenge is not distance alone but velocity. To rendezvous, the new spacecraft must end up at the same place at the same time and with nearly the same velocity as Voyager 1. That means building up a very large heliocentric speed in roughly the same outward direction. Missions like New Horizons reached high solar-system escape speeds using powerful launch vehicles plus Jupiter gravity assist, and something similar would likely be required. More advanced concepts—solar Oberth maneuvers, solar sails, nuclear electric propulsion, or even nuclear thermal propulsion—could shorten the trip substantially, but these are either not operational at the needed scale or would be technologically and politically difficult.

Communication would also be a major issue. At Voyager 1’s distance, signals take roughly a full day each way. Data rates would be very low unless the new spacecraft carried a large antenna and substantial power. Power itself is a problem: solar panels are ineffective that far from the Sun, so the mission would almost certainly need radioisotope power systems, just as Voyager does.

If the goal were to study Voyager 1 up close, the mission would need guidance and navigation precise enough to find and approach a small, faint, aging spacecraft in interstellar space. That is much harder than navigating to a planet, because Voyager 1 is tiny, dim, and not actively designed to help another spacecraft dock or inspect it. A flyby would be much easier than a rendezvous. A true docking or repair mission would be essentially unrealistic with present-day technology.

Scientifically, such a mission could be interesting. It could inspect Voyager 1’s condition after nearly half a century in space, compare onboard measurements with modern instruments, and continue sampling the local interstellar medium. But from a cost-benefit perspective, it would usually make more sense to build a new interstellar probe rather than chase Voyager 1 specifically. A new probe could be optimized for modern science instead of spending much of its mission budget just catching up to an old spacecraft.

So the careful answer is: if we launched a one-way mission to Voyager 1 today, we could in principle send a spacecraft that eventually reaches it, probably after several decades, but it would be a difficult deep-space interception mission rather than anything like a practical rescue. The mission is possible in principle, marginal with current technology for a flyby or intercept, and far less practical than simply launching a new interstellar probe.

items.question: What If Everyone in America Drove West?
human_answers: [Image: image] Thanks to plate tectonics, the United States is drifting west at about (http://hypertextbook.com/facts/ZhenHuang.shtml) a centimeter per year. (The people who live there, on the other hand, are on average drifting west at about a centimeter per minute (http://www.census.gov/newsroom/releases/archives/facts_for_features_special_editions/cb11ff10.html).) There are 212,309,000 (http://nhts.ornl.gov/tables09/FatCat.aspx) licensed drivers in the US, and since we have more cars than drivers, we can in theory get them all behind the wheel at once. The average car on the road weighs a hair over 4,000 lbs (http://www.nytimes.com/2004/05/05/business/05weight.html), so we have 850 billion pounds of car (plus around 30 billion pounds of driver) to throw around. The North American plate, by comparison, is about 25 million square kilometers in area and probably averages around 35 kilometers thick. Given a density of about 2.7 kg/Liter, its mass is probably in the neighborhood of \(2.3 \times 10^{21}\)kg, so it outweighs our fleet by a factor of about six trillion. [Image: image] But let's say we give it a shot anyway, and all 212 million of us point our vehicles due west and then floor it. For the dozen or so seconds we’d spend accelerating to freeway speed, our cars would exert very close to a trillion newtons of eastward force on the ground. In the absence of other forces, conservation of momentum tells us it would accelerate the plate up to a blistering 18 cm/year, more than enough to reverse the current motion. \[\frac{210,000,000 \text{ cars} \times 4100 \frac{\text{lbs}}{\text{car}} \times 75\text{mph}}{2.3 \times 10^{21}\text{kg}} \approx 18 \frac{\text{cm}}{\text{year}} \gg 0.69 \frac{\text{cm}}{\text{year}}\] But wait. The plates are moving so slowly that their motion isn’t dominated by momentum. They’re held where they are by a balance of forces—the complicated and boring ones from the beginning—and if we’re going to stop them, we probably have to try to figure out what they are. If the plates were drifting along as if they were sliding on ice, then we could push them easily. But it’s possible they’re locked on a slow-but-steady magma conveyer belt, and we can’t move them back without also shifting the flow beneath them. It was only recently—in the mid-20th century—that we discovered that continents move at all, and we’re still getting a handle on the complex forces between the plates and currents in the mantle that control continental motion. But they sound pretty complicated so let’s try to ignore them. We don’t care how it works—we just want to know if we can break it. These forces are hard to measure, so we’re not sure how they all work. There’s some evidence (http://www.umich.edu/~gs265/tecpaper.htm) that the flow of the mantle along the bottom of the plates isn’t as important as the weight of the edges of the crust as it sinks into the mantle, and the forces in the mantle pushing back against it. The geology literature gives us some loose estimates to work with. The drag from the mantle, resisting forward motion, is typically in the neighborhood of \(10^5\) to \(10^7\) newtons per square meter, meaning the existing eastward drag force on the North American plate is on the order of \(10^{19}\) newtons. That’s millions of times more than our fleet. The other forces are greater still. The fact that plates move steadily along in the face of drag that powerful suggests to me that the equilibrium of forces guiding them is probably fairly stable and unlikely to be responsive by our little shove. But conservation of momentum still works—so something has to move, and that something is the entire Earth, whose rotation would be sped up slightly. If our fleet were centered at around 39º N, the day would be shortened by only about 200 attoseconds—about a trillionth of a percent of the time it took you to read the word “attosecond.” If we drove east instead, the day would be lengthened by a similar amount. But considering the gasoline required, those 200 attoseconds would cost at least $50 billion. At 100 octillion times minimum wage, that’s a pretty bad hourly rate. All things considered, it would be a lot easier to just forget to change our clocks next spring and get a whole hour for nothing. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果美国每个人都向西行驶，我们可以暂时停止大陆漂移吗？
items.model_answer:
If “everyone in America drove west” at the same time, the immediate result would be total transportation collapse, not a meaningful migration.

There are roughly hundreds of millions of people in the United States, and well over 200 million licensed drivers. The road system cannot handle anything close to all of them trying to drive in one direction simultaneously. Highways would gridlock almost instantly. Many people would never get far from where they started because exits, intersections, bridges, tunnels, and on-ramps create bottlenecks long before the open road matters.

There is also a geographic limit: America does not extend indefinitely west. People on the West Coast would quickly run out of land and reach the Pacific Ocean. So even in the most literal sense, the process cannot continue very long. The western states and coastal cities would become impossibly overcrowded, while eastern and central areas would be partly emptied only to the extent people could actually leave them—which most could not, because of traffic jams and fuel shortages.

Fuel would become a major constraint almost immediately. Gas stations carry limited supplies and depend on continuous deliveries by truck and pipeline logistics. In a nationwide synchronized westward drive, stations would run dry fast. Electric vehicles would face similar charging bottlenecks. Emergency services, food distribution, freight, and supply chains would break down because roads would be clogged and workers would be displaced.

The economic effects would be severe. Businesses would shut, hospitals would be understaffed, schools and utilities disrupted, and agriculture and manufacturing interrupted. If people abandoned homes and jobs to head west, the result would resemble a self-inflicted national emergency.

If the question is interpreted physically in a simpler way—what happens if every driver just points their car west and starts moving—the answer is that eventually many would stop because of traffic, obstacles, lack of fuel, or the Pacific Ocean. So the practical outcome is not “everyone ends up farther west,” but “the country becomes immobilized.”

In short: if everyone in America drove west, America would mostly come to a standstill.

items.question: What If a High-Speed Train Had to Go through a Vertical Loop?
human_answers: No. Since this is kind of a disappointing answer, I tried relaxing the requirements a little. Could a high-speed train run through a vertical loop, like a rollercoaster, with the passengers staying comfortable surviving? Still no. Could a modified and reinforced high-speed train with a jet engine on top run through a vertical loop, like a rollercoaster, with the passengers staying comfortable surviving? Maybe. The Norwegian aluminium and energy company Norsk Hydro ran a pro-education ad (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hlczxXqez-Y) in which a bunch of kids build a giant roller-coaster loop on a train track as a prank. This is, of course, unrealistic, but not just for the obvious reasons. There are some problems with the whole idea of sending high-speed trains through loops. The first issue is geometry. The biggest vertical loop which a train could conceivably go around has a radius of about 200 meters. If it’s any bigger than that, even the fastest trains will fail to complete the loop. Unfortunately, a 200 meter loop is much too tight. Most high-speed trains are limited (http://khsrcl.com/downloads/Chapter%204.pdf) to vertical curves with radii no shorter than 20 kilometers. [Image: image] The reason for those limits isn't that trains aren't bendy enough. It's how fast they're going. The spec sheet for the Bombardier ZEFIRO (http://www.superscooper.com/en/1_0/pdf/Bombardier_Zefiro_Technical_Description_en.pdf), for example, says it can handle a pretty tight vertical curve radius—just 900 meters. At the train’s top speed, that curve would create about two gees of acceleration. This might be survivable (for the passengers, at least, if not the train), but it would certainly not be comfortable. Yet a 900 meter radius loop is still too big. Even with the engine at full power, the train wouldn’t even be able to get a quarter of the way around the loop before sliding back down. [Image: image] The CGI train in the Norwegian video is an Di 4 (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NSB_Di_4), which is shown moving about twice as fast as it can actually go. Based on its speed and number of cars, the loop appears to have a radius of about 70 meters, which is part of why it’s shown going so fast—the actual Di 4 would be just a little too slow, and would fall off the track at the top. The digital one, however, makes it around the loop in about five seconds, no problem. But the tight loop means the passengers and train are experiencing between 9 and 15 gees. This is at the limit of what fighter pilots can handle in pressure suits. In addition to killing everyone on board, it would certainly destroy the train, to say nothing of the track. 70 meters is much too tight. Clearly, we need a larger loop. 900 meters would be great, but our trains aren’t fast enough for that.\ But maybe we could make the train go faster ... Hmm. [Image: image] Believe it or not, this has been tried before—a number of countries have built jet-engine-powered trains (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turbojet_train). Sadly, they never took off. Fortunately, they never took off. A 747 engine mounted atop a bullet train would probably add about 35% to its speed. Is that enough to do a 900-meter loop? [Image: image] Nope. Ok, putting the jet engine on top didn’t work. Maybe we should try something different. [Image: image] ... why did we think that would work? Forget that idea. Clearly, we need some combination of a fast train and a medium-sized loop. The sweet spot for loop size and shape is probably something like this: [Image: image] Of course, given the height, we’d probably have to build it into a small mountain: [Image: image] The shape of the loop, which is common in roller coasters, would spread out the g-forces more evenly, resulting in a max of only a few gees—totally survivable! Of course, the construction costs would be astronomical, and it goes without saying that no group of kids could pull it off alone without the resources of a major government. To any Norwegian kids reading this who were hoping to build a train loop, don't despair—there may still be a way to make this happen. The US Vice President, Joe Biden, served in the US Senate for 36 years. In all that time, he never moved to Washington, DC. Instead, every night, he took the train home to Delaware to see his family. This is very touching, but after the first few years, I'm sure the commute got a little dull. So, if you’re looking for a high-level backer to help you make someone’s train ride a little more exciting, you might just try talking to Joe. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 高速列车能否像过山车一样在垂直环路中运行，同时让乘客感到舒适？
items.model_answer:
If a high-speed train had to go through a vertical loop, the main issue would be acceleration, not just speed. In principle, a train can go through a loop if it is moving fast enough at the top to stay pressed against the track, but for real passengers the required forces would usually be far too large to be safe or comfortable.

At the top of the loop, the train must have enough speed that gravity plus the track’s inward force can provide the needed centripetal acceleration. The absolute minimum condition for just maintaining contact is

v² / r = g

so the minimum speed at the top is about

v = √(gr).

For example, if the loop radius were 100 m, the minimum top speed would be about 31 m/s, or roughly 110 km/h. But that is only the speed needed to avoid falling off the track at the top. It does not make the ride tolerable.

The bigger problem is what happens at the bottom of the loop. There, the centripetal acceleration points upward, so the track must push on the train much harder than gravity alone. The apparent weight of passengers becomes

N = m(g + v² / r).

That means passengers could feel several times their normal weight. For a high-speed train, especially one entering the loop at very high speed, this would likely create enormous g-forces. If those forces are too high, passengers could be injured, cargo could shift, and the train structure and track would be heavily stressed.

A circular loop would be especially bad because curvature is constant, so the transition into and out of the loop is abrupt. Roller coasters avoid this by using clothoid loops, which have a larger radius at the bottom and a smaller radius near the top. That reduces peak g-forces. Even so, roller coasters are much smaller, lighter, and designed for short-duration thrill loads. A train is long, heavy, and designed for smooth, low-acceleration travel.

There is also a geometric problem: a long train would occupy many parts of the loop at once. The front could be near the top while the rear is still climbing, so different cars would experience different forces and directions at the same time. The couplings between cars would be under unusual tension and compression, and the wheel-rail contact would become much harder to manage. Standard train designs are not built for that.

Aerodynamics and power would matter too. To climb the loop, the train would need enough kinetic energy or propulsion to gain height. Ignoring losses, the train must trade speed for gravitational potential energy, so it would slow as it rises and speed up as it descends. In a full loop of height 2r, the train needs enough initial energy to make that climb while still retaining the minimum top speed.

So the short answer is: a high-speed train could theoretically go through a vertical loop if the loop were extremely large and carefully shaped, and if the train were specially designed for it. But an ordinary high-speed train on an ordinary loop would subject passengers and equipment to unsafe forces, making it impractical. In real rail engineering, tracks are kept smooth and curvature gentle precisely to avoid these problems.

items.question: What If a Bowling Ball Were Enlarged to the Size of Earth?
human_answers: A good, professional-quality bowling ball is smoother than the Earth. Phil Plait, of Bad Astronomy, took a look at the claim that the Earth was smoother than a billiard ball. He concluded that the Earth was smoother but less round (http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/badastronomy/2008/09/08/ten-things-you-dont-know-about-the-earth/#.UZrBpmRAC9a), based on published billiard ball roundness tolerances. However, he couldn’t find any information on the size and shape of a billiard ball’s pits and bumps. Fortunately for us, there are people who digitally scan bowling ball surfaces (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r5V3rFdAIMY). [Image: image] These scans (along with various measurements of ball roughness[1] (http://classic.bowl.com/news/specsandcerts/index.jsp) tell us that a high-end bowling ball is quite smooth. If blown up to the scale of the Earth, the ridges and bumps[2] (http://www.itbca.bowlingknowledge.info/index.php/winter-2013/85-bowling-ball-shell-chemistry-101) would be between 10 and 200 meters high, and the peaks would be between one and three kilometers apart: [Image: image] By Earth standards, this is quite smooth; our highest mountains are 40 times higher. What would this bowling ball world (we’ll call it “Lebowski”) be like? For starters, bowling balls are a lot less dense than rock, so Lebowski’s surface gravity would be a quarter the strength of Earth’s: [Image: image] It would also (at first) have no atmosphere. [Image: image] The finger holes would be about a thousand kilometers across and a few thousand kilometers deep. [Image: image] On Earth, holes this big would expose the molten interior. But Lebowski doesn’t have a molten interior. The Earth’s core is hot for two reasons: It’s still glowing from the heat of all the dust collapsing together when it formed, and it’s full of radioactive metals. Lebowski wouldn’t have either of these, so its core would start out cold. The holes would be far too big to hold themselves open against gravity; On that scale, the polymers in the bowling ball would behave more like a liquid. In the space of about half an hour, the holes would undergo a slow-motion collapse. [Image: image] As they collapsed, the material around the holes would heat to a glow. At the center of the hole, a white-hot jet of charred hydrocarbons would fountain outward into space. When it was over, Lebowski would be left with massive scars, each marking the location where an abyss collapsed to form a molten sea. [Image: image] And now, thanks to this question, whenever I look at the Moon, I’ll notice the Sea of Tranquility, the Sea of Serenity, and the Sea of Crisis (http://www.google.com/url?q=http%3A%2F%2Fen.wikipedia.org%2Fwiki%2FFile%3AMoon_names.svg&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNHIe4YcJnAZYmMY278G3Ko63hJnKQ), and I’ll think: Finger holes. But that’s just, like, my opinion, man.
items.original_question: 有人告诉我，如果地球缩小到保龄球大小，它会比保龄球更光滑。我的问题是，如果保龄球被吹到地球那么大，会是什么样子？
items.model_answer:
If you enlarged a bowling ball to the size of Earth, the result would depend on what exactly you keep the same.

If you mean a real bowling ball made of the same material, just scaled up until its diameter matched Earth’s, then it would be extraordinarily massive—far more massive than Earth. A bowling ball is much denser than Earth on average. Earth’s average density is about 5.5 g/cm³, while a bowling ball is typically around 7 to 8 g/cm³ or so, depending on the material. Since mass scales with volume, an Earth-sized bowling ball would have roughly 1.3 to 1.5 times Earth’s mass.

That would make gravity at the surface stronger too. Surface gravity scales like mass divided by radius squared, and since the radius is the same as Earth’s, the stronger mass directly means stronger gravity. So instead of about 9.8 m/s², surface gravity might be around 13 to 15 m/s². A 70 kg person would feel like they weighed about 90 to 105 kg. Walking would be harder, jumping much harder, and many animals and structures adapted to Earth gravity would struggle.

The pressure inside would also be immense. A bowling ball is a rigid manufactured object on human scales, but at planetary scales, its material would no longer behave like a simple solid sphere. Under its own gravity, it would compress, heat up, and likely differentiate internally if the material allowed it. In other words, it would stop behaving like an ordinary bowling ball and start behaving like a small rocky-metal planet.

If instead you mean “what if Earth itself were replaced by a giant bowling ball-shaped object,” the holes matter only a little unless they were also scaled up. If the finger holes were enlarged proportionally, they would become enormous shafts thousands of kilometers deep. Under planetary gravity, those cavities would not remain empty open holes for long. The surrounding material would deform, collapse inward, and heat up. A planet-sized object cannot preserve neat little bowling-ball finger holes unless made of impossibly strong material.

So the short answer is: an Earth-sized bowling ball would be more massive than Earth, have significantly stronger surface gravity, and would not remain an ordinary bowling ball in structure. It would effectively become a dense planet, and if the finger holes were scaled too, they would collapse under gravity.

items.question: What Would an Alien Civilization on the Nearest Habitable Exoplanet See When Looking at Us?
human_answers: Answer: [Image: image] Let’s try a more complete answer. We’ll start with ... Radio transmissions Contact popularized the idea of aliens listening in on our transmissions. Sadly, the odds are against it. Here’s the problem: Space is big. Really big.[1] (http://www.goodreads.com/book/show/11.The_Hitchhiker_s_Guide_to_the_Galaxy) You can work through the physics of interstellar radio attenuation, but the problem is captured pretty well by considering the economics of the situation: If your TV signals are getting to another star, you’re losing money. Powering a transmitter is expensive, and creatures on other stars aren’t buying the products in the TV commercials that pay your electricity bill. The full picture is more complicated, but the bottom line is that as our technology has advanced, less of our radio traffic has been leaking out into space. We’re closing down the giant transmitting antennas and switching to cable and fiber and tightly-focused cell-tower networks.[2] (http://arxiv.org/PS_cache/arxiv/pdf/1007/1007.0850v1.pdf) While our TV signals may have been detectable—with great effort—for a while,[3] (http://arxiv.org/pdf/astro-ph/0610377v2.pdf) that window is closing. In the late 20th century, when we were using TV and radio to scream into the void at the top of our lungs, the signal probably faded to undetectability after a few light-years.[4] (http://www.worldcat.org/title/earth-as-a-distant-planet-a-rosetta-stone-for-the-search-of-earth-like-worlds/oclc/643269627) The potentially habitable exoplanets we’ve spotted so far are dozens of light-years away, so the odds are they aren’t currently repeating our catchphrases (http://xkcd.com/1212/). But TV and radio transmissions still weren’t Earth’s most powerful radio signal. They were outshone by the beams from early-warning radar.[4] (http://www.worldcat.org/title/earth-as-a-distant-planet-a-rosetta-stone-for-the-search-of-earth-like-worlds/oclc/643269627) Early-warning radar, a product of the Cold War, consisted of a bunch of ground and airborne stations scattered around the Arctic. These stations swept the atmosphere with powerful radar beams 24/7, often bouncing them off the ionosphere, and people obsessively monitored the echos for any hints of enemy movement. (I wasn’t alive during most of this period, but from what I hear, the mood was a little tense.) These radar transmissions leaked into space, and could probably be picked up by nearby exoplanets[5] (http://www.astrobio.net/exclusive/4847/seti-on-the-ska) if they happened to be listening when the beam swept over their part of the sky. But the same march of technological progress that made the TV broadcast towers obsolete has had the same effect on early-warning radar. Today’s systems—where they exist at all—are much quieter, and may eventually be replaced completely by new technology. [Image: image] Earth’s most powerful radio signal is the beam from the Arecibo telescope. This massive dish in Puerto Rico can function as a radar transmitter, bouncing a signal off nearby targets like Mercury and the asteroid belt. It’s essentially a flashlight which we shine on planets to see them better. (This is just as crazy as it sounds.) But it transmits only occasionally, and in a narrow beam. If an exoplanet happened to be caught in the beam, and they were lucky enough to be pointing a receiving antenna at our corner of the sky at the time, all they would pick up would be a brief pulse of radio energy, then silence (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wow!_signal). So hypothetical aliens looking at Earth probably wouldn’t pick us up with radio antennas. But there’s also ... Visible light This is more promising. The Sun is really bright [citation needed (http://www.google.com/search?q=site:craigslist.org+chevrolet+citation)] and its light illuminates the Earth.[citation needed (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation_(horse))] Some of that light is reflected back into space as “Earthshine”. Some of it skims close to our planet and passes through our atmosphere before continuing on to the stars. Both of these effects could potentially be detected from an exoplanet.[4] (http://www.worldcat.org/title/earth-as-a-distant-planet-a-rosetta-stone-for-the-search-of-earth-like-worlds/oclc/6432)[6] (http://planetimager.org/) They wouldn’t tell you anything about humans directly, but if you watched the Earth for long enough, you could figure out a lot about our atmosphere from the reflectivity. You could probably figure out what our water cycle looked like, and our oxygen-rich atmosphere would give you a hint that something weird was going on (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Oxygenation_Event). So in the end, the clearest signal from Earth might not be from us at all. It might be from the algae that have been terraforming the planet—and altering the signals we send into space—for billions of years. [Image: image] Of course, if we wanted to send a clearer signal, we could. A radio transmission has the problem that they have to be paying attention when it arrives. Instead, we could make them pay attention. With ion drives, nuclear pulse propulsion, or just clever use of gravitational slingshots, we could probably send a probe out of the Solar System fast enough to reach a given nearby star in a few dozen millennia. If we can figure out how to make a guidance system that survives the trip (which would be tough) we could use it to steer toward any inhabited planet. To land safely, we’d have to slow down. But slowing down takes even more fuel. And, hey, the whole point of this was for them to notice us, right? So maybe if those aliens looked toward our Solar System, this is what they’d see: [Image: image]
items.original_question: 让我们假设最近的宜居系外行星上有生命，并且他们拥有与我们相当的技术。如果他们现在看着我们的星星，他们会看到什么？
items.model_answer:
If there were an alien civilization on the nearest truly habitable exoplanet and they looked at Earth, what they would see would depend mostly on two things: how far away they are, and how good their technology is.

The nearest potentially habitable exoplanets are a few to several light-years away, such as Proxima Centauri b at about 4.2 light-years or planets in the TRAPPIST-1 system around 40 light-years away. Because light takes time to travel, they would not see Earth as it is now. They would see Earth in the past. From 4.2 light-years away, they would see Earth as it was 4.2 years ago. From 40 light-years away, they would see Earth 40 years ago.

To the naked eye, or with modest telescopes, Earth would just look like a faint pale dot very close to the glare of the Sun. The Sun would dominate the view. Detecting Earth at all would be difficult because Earth is much dimmer than the Sun and very close to it in angular separation. With advanced enough instruments that can block the starlight, they could identify Earth as a small rocky planet in the Sun’s habitable zone.

If their technology were comparable to or somewhat beyond ours, they might be able to determine some basic planetary properties. They could measure Earth’s orbit, estimate its size and mass, and infer that it has liquid-water-compatible temperatures. By analyzing the light reflected from Earth or passing through its atmosphere, they could detect atmospheric gases such as oxygen, water vapor, carbon dioxide, and perhaps methane. The simultaneous presence of oxygen and methane would be especially interesting, because that combination is hard to maintain without ongoing biological activity. So even without “seeing” us directly, they might conclude Earth is very likely inhabited.

They would also notice that Earth’s brightness changes with time because of clouds, oceans, continents, seasons, and rotation. If they observed carefully, they might infer a roughly 24-hour rotation period and possibly even distinguish oceans from land through changes in reflected light and color. They might detect the “red edge” associated with vegetation if their instruments were extremely sensitive, though that would be challenging.

Seeing human beings, cities, or individual structures directly would be vastly harder. At interstellar distances, even Earth itself is barely resolvable with any plausible telescope short of extremely advanced, enormous interferometric systems. So they would not look through a telescope and see continents full of lights or watch airplanes move around, unless they were far more technologically advanced than we are.

However, they might detect technological signatures indirectly. Earth has been leaking radio waves for about a century, so an observer 40 light-years away would only now be receiving our earliest 1980s-era broadcasts; an observer 4.2 light-years away would be receiving signals from about 2021–2022. In practice, ordinary radio leakage becomes weak quickly with distance, so casual detection would be difficult. Stronger signals such as radar would be easier to notice if they were listening carefully. They might also detect atmospheric pollutants that do not occur naturally in large amounts, or nighttime artificial illumination, but those are much harder signals to extract than atmospheric biosignatures.

So the short answer is: they would probably not “see us” as visible individuals or even as obvious cities. They would most likely see Earth as a small, life-friendly planet orbiting the Sun, and with sufficiently advanced instruments they could infer oceans, atmosphere, and probably life. If their technology were good enough and they were specifically searching, they might even suspect a technological civilization—but always as we were years or decades in their past, not as we are right now.

items.question: What If the Sun Suddenly Went Out?
human_answers: This is probably the single most popular question submitted to What If. Part of why I haven’t answered it is that it's been answered already. A Google search for what if the Sun went out (http://www.google.com/search?q=what+if+the+Sun+went+out) turns up a lot of excellent articles thoroughly analyzing the situation. However, since my recent articles on sunsets, the rate of submission of this question has risen even further, so I’ve decided to do my best to answer it. If the Sun went out ... [Image: image] We won’t worry about exactly how it happens. We'll just assume we figured out a way to fast-forward the Sun through its evolution so that it becomes a cold, inert sphere. What would the consequences be for us here on Earth? Let's look at a few: Reduced risk of solar flares: In 1859, a massive solar flare and geomagnetic storm hit the Earth.[1] (http://www.leif.org/research/1859%20Storm%20-%20Extreme%20Space%20Weather.pdf) Magnetic storms induce electric currents in wires. Unfortunately for us, by 1859 we had wrapped the Earth in telegraph wires. The storm caused powerful currents in those wires, knocking out communications and in some cases causing telegraph equipment to catch fire.[2] (http://trs-new.jpl.nasa.gov/dspace/bitstream/2014/8787/1/02-1310.pdf) Since 1859, we've wrapped the Earth in a lot more wires. If the 1859 storm hit us today, the Department of Homeland Security estimates the economic damage to the US alone would be several trillion dollars[3] (http://www.oecd.org/governance/risk/46891645.pdf)—more than every hurricane which has ever hit the US combined.[4] (http://www.google.com/url?q=http%3A%2F%2Fsciencepolicy.colorado.edu%2Fadmin%2Fpublication_files%2Fresource-2476-2008.02.pdf&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNFnOWO7P0PV6qJSPhUUf56glVwZKQ) If the Sun went out, this threat would be eliminated. Improved satellite service: When a communications satellite passes in front of the Sun, the Sun can drown out the satellite's radio signal, causing an interruption in service.[5] (http://www3.alcatel-lucent.com/bstj/vol49-1970/articles/bstj49-8-1943.pdf) Deactivating the Sun would solve this problem. Better astronomy: Without the Sun, ground-based observatories would be able to operate around the clock. The cooler air would create less atmospheric noise, which would reduce the load on adaptive optics systems and allow for sharper images. Stable dust: Without sunlight, there would be no Poynting–Robertson drag (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poynting%E2%80%93Robertson_effect), which means we would finally be able to place dust into a stable orbit around the Sun without the orbits decaying. I’m not sure whether anyone wants to do that, but you never know. Reduced infrastructure costs: The Department of Transportation estimates that it would cost $20 billion per year over the next 20 years to repair and maintain all US bridges.[6] (http://www.fhwa.dot.gov/policy/2010cpr/chap7.htm#9) Most US bridges are over water; without the Sun, we could save money by simply driving on a strip of asphalt laid across the ice. [Image: image] Cheaper trade: Time zones make trade more expensive; it's harder to do business with someone if their office hours don't overlap with yours.[7] (http://eeecon.uibk.ac.at/wopec2/repec/inn/wpaper/2012-14.pdf) If the Sun went out, it would eliminate the need for time zones, allowing us to switch to UTC and give a boost to the global economy. Safer Children: According to the North Dakota Department of Health, babies younger than six months should be kept out of direct sunlight.[8] (http://www.ndhealth.gov/familyhealth/mch/babyfacts/Sunburn.pdf) Without sunlight, our children would be safer. Safer combat pilots: Many people sneeze when exposed to bright sunlight. The reasons for this reflex are unknown, and it may pose a danger to fighter pilots during flight.[9] (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8108024) If the Sun went dark, it would mitigate this danger to our pilots. Safer parsnip: Wild parsnip is a surprisingly nasty plant. Its leaves contain chemicals called furocoumarins, which can be absorbed by human skin without causing symptoms ... at first. However, when the skin is then exposed to sunlight (even days or weeks later), the furocoumarins cause a nasty chemical burn. This is called phytophotodermatitis.[10] (http://dnr.wi.gov/wnrmag/html/stories/1999/jun99/parsnip.htm) A darkened Sun would liberate us from the parsnip threat. [Image: image] In conclusion, if the Sun went out, we would see a variety of benefits across many areas of our lives. Are there any downsides to this scenario? We would all freeze and die. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果太阳突然熄灭，地球会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If the Sun suddenly “went out,” two different things matter: light and gravity.

For about 8 minutes after the event, nothing on Earth would seem different, because sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us. If the Sun also somehow stopped exerting gravity at the same moment, Earth would likewise keep orbiting normally for those same 8 minutes, because changes in gravity would also propagate at the speed of light. After that, the sky would go dark, except for stars, planets, and artificial lights, and Earth would move off in a straight line tangent to its former orbit instead of continuing around the Sun.

The temperature would then begin to fall quickly. Within days, average surface temperatures would drop far below freezing. Within weeks to months, the oceans’ surfaces would freeze, though the deep ocean would remain liquid for a long time because water is a good insulator and Earth has internal geothermal heat. Over longer times, the surface would become extremely cold, roughly tens of kelvins above absolute zero in many places, though not literally zero because geothermal energy and residual heat would still exist.

Photosynthesis would stop almost immediately, so most plants would die, and food chains depending on sunlight would collapse. Humans could survive for a while using stored food, nuclear power, geothermal energy, and underground or insulated habitats, but civilization would be under extreme stress. Some life would likely persist for a very long time around deep-sea hydrothermal vents and underground ecosystems that do not depend directly on sunlight.

If instead the Sun only stopped shining but kept its mass and gravity, Earth would remain in orbit, but the planet would still freeze and the biosphere would still largely collapse.

So, in short: after about 8 minutes, Earth would go dark; without the Sun’s heat, the planet would rapidly become a frozen world; and if the Sun’s gravity also vanished, Earth would drift into space rather than orbiting where it is now.

items.question: What Would It Be Like to Row across Lakes of Mercury, Bromine, Gallium, Tungsten, Liquid Nitrogen, or Liquid Helium?
human_answers: Let's take these one at a time. Bromine and mercury are the only known pure elements that are liquid at room temperature. Rowing a boat on a sea of mercury just might be possible. Mercury is so dense that steel ball bearings float on the surface (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EGv_YVQHu7U). Your boat would be so buoyant that you'd barely make a dent in the mercury, and you'd have to lean your weight into the paddle to get the end of it below the surface. [Image: image] In the end, it certainly wouldn't be easy, and you wouldn't be able to move fast. But you could probably row a little bit. You should probably avoid splash fights. Bromine is about as dense as water, so a standard rowboat could in theory float on it. However, Bromine is awful. For one thing, it smells terrible; the name "bromine" comes from the ancient Greek "brōmos", meaning "stench". If that weren't enough, it violently reacts (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uCwHzTsx5yY) with a lot of materials. Hopefully, you're not in an aluminium rowboat. [Image: image] If that's not incentive enough to avoid it, the Materials Safety Data Sheet on bromine (http://avogadro.chem.iastate.edu/MSDS/Br2.htm) includes the following phrases: "severe burns and ulceration" "perforation of the digestive tract" "permanent corneal opacification" "vertigo, anxiety, depression, muscle incoordination, and emotional instability" "diarrhea, possibly with blood" You should not get in a splash fight on a bromine lake. Liquid gallium is weird stuff. Gallium melts just above room temperature, like butter, so you can't hold it in your hand for too long. It's fairly dense, though not anywhere near as dense as mercury, and would be easier to row a boat on. However, once again, you'd better hope the boat isn't made of aluminium, because aluminium (like many metals) absorbs gallium like a sponge absorbs water. The gallium spreads throughout the aluminium, dramatically changing its chemical properties. The modified aluminium is so weak it can be pulled apart like wet paper (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FaMWxLCGY0U). This is something gallium has in common with mercury—both will destroy aluminium (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z7Ilxsu-JlY). Like my grandma used to say, don't sail an aluminium boat on a gallium lake. (My grandma was a little strange.) Liquid tungsten is really hard to work with. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any element. This means there's a lot we don't know about its properties. The reason for this—and this may sound a little stupid—is that it's hard to study, because we can't find a container to hold it in. For almost any container, the material in the container will melt before the tungsten does. There are a few compounds, like tantalum hafnium carbide, with slightly higher melting points, but no one has been able to make a liquid tungsten container with them. To give you an idea of how hot liquid tungsten is, I could tell you the exact temperature that it melts at (3422°C). But a better point might be this: Liquid tungsten is so hot, if you dropped it into a lava flow, the lava would freeze the tungsten. Needless to say, if you set a boat on a sea of liquid tungsten, both you and the boat would rapidly combust and be incinerated. Liquid nitrogen is very cold. Liquid helium is colder, but they're both closer to absolute zero than to the coldest temperatures in Antarctica, so to someone floating on them in a boat, the temperature difference is not that significant.
