A Dartmouth engineering page on liquid nitrogen safety (http://engineering.dartmouth.edu/microeng/ln2.html) includes the following phrases: "violent reactions with organic materials" "it will explode" "displace oxygen in the room" "severe clothing fire" "suffocation without warning" Liquid nitrogen has a density similar to that of water, so a rowboat would float on it, but if you were in it, you wouldn't survive for long. If the air above the nitrogen was room temperature when you started, it would cool rapidly, and you and the boat would be smothered in a thick fog as the water condensed out of the air. (This is the same effect that causes steam when you pour out liquid nitrogen.) The condensation would freeze, quickly covering your boat in a layer of frost. The warm air would cause the nitrogen on the surface to evaporate. This would displace the oxygen over the lake, causing you to asphyxiate. If the air (or the nitrogen) were both cold enough to avoid evaporation, you would instead develop hypothermia and die of exposure. Liquid helium would be worse. For one thing, it's only about one-eighth as dense as water, so your boat would have to be eight times larger to support a given weight. [Image: image] But helium has a trick. When cooled below about two degrees kelvin, it becomes a superfluid, which has the odd property that it crawls up and over the walls of containers by capillary forces. It crawls along at about 20 centimeters per second, so it would take the liquid helium less than 30 seconds to start collecting in the bottom of your boat. This would, as in the liquid nitrogen scenario, cause rapid death from hypothermia. If it's any consolation, as you lay dying, you would be able to observe an odd phenomenon. Superfluid helium films, like the one rapidly covering you, carry the same types of ordinary sound waves that most materials do. But they also exhibit an additional type of wave, a slow-moving ripple that propogates along thin films of helium. It's only observed in superfluids, and has the mysterious and poetic name "third sound (http://www.physics.berkeley.edu/research/packard/current_research/schechter's%20web/page2.html)." Your eardrums may no longer function, and wouldn't be able to detect this type of vibration anyway, but as you froze to death in the floor of a giant boat, your ears would be filled—literally—with a sound no human can ever hear: The third sound. And that, at least, is pretty cool. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 驾驶划艇穿过水银湖会是什么感觉？溴呢？液态镓？液态钨？液氮？液氦？
items.model_answer:
If you could somehow survive the temperature and fumes and had a boat made of something that didn’t melt, freeze, or react, rowing across those liquids would feel very different from rowing on water because what matters most is density, viscosity, volatility, and temperature.

On mercury, rowing would be eerie but in some ways the most “boat-like.” Mercury is about 13.5 times denser than water, so a boat would float extremely high, almost like it was sitting on a solid surface. The oars would get strong buoyant support, but mercury is also much denser to push aside, so each stroke would feel heavy and sluggish in a different way than water. It is not especially viscous, so it would still splash and flow, but the splashes would be heavy and metallic. The real problem is that mercury gives off toxic vapor, so the experience would be dangerous even before considering the cold.

On bromine, rowing would be more alarming than difficult. Liquid bromine is only about 3 times denser than water and flows reasonably well, so mechanically it would still behave somewhat like a heavy liquid. But bromine is highly corrosive and produces dense, choking fumes. A boat might float normally enough, and rowing would not be absurdly impossible, but everything around you would be chemically hostile. It would look dark reddish-brown, and the air above the lake would be full of toxic vapor.

On gallium, rowing would probably feel strangely thick and sticky compared with water, especially near its melting point. Gallium melts just above room temperature, so a lake of it would be warm rather than cryogenic or red hot. It is about 6 times denser than water, so boats would float high. But liquid gallium tends to wet and stick to many materials, and it can embrittle some metals like aluminum. So while the fluid itself is not as dramatically dangerous as bromine or tungsten, it would be awkward: the oars and hull might get coated, and many ordinary materials would fail. It would feel like rowing through a heavy, clingy metal.

On tungsten, rowing is basically fantasy. Liquid tungsten exists only above about 3400 °C, so the environment would be hotter than most furnaces. Any ordinary boat, oar, or rower would be destroyed instantly. If we ignore that and imagine magical materials, liquid tungsten is very dense, around 17 to 18 times the density of water, so flotation would be extreme. But the radiant heat alone would dominate the experience: it would be like trying to row over a lake of white-hot sunlit metal. The main sensation would not be hydrodynamics but overwhelming thermal catastrophe.

On liquid nitrogen, rowing would be possible in a purely fluid-mechanics sense, but very alien. Liquid nitrogen is less dense than water, about 0.8 times as dense, so a boat would sit lower than it does in water and would need more volume to float. Its viscosity is low, so it would feel very “thin,” with little drag on the oars. The strokes might feel quick and slippery rather than solid. But the liquid boils violently on warm objects, so every oar stroke and the hull itself would be surrounded by bubbling nitrogen gas. You would get a constantly hissing, foggy, boiling interface. The danger is extreme cold rather than heat or toxicity.

On liquid helium, the experience would be the strangest of all. Liquid helium is extremely low density, only about 0.125 times the density of water, so flotation is poor; a boat would need to be huge and very lightweight, more like a giant hollow shell than a normal rowboat. Its viscosity is extraordinarily low, especially below the superfluid transition. In ordinary liquid helium near its boiling point, rowing would feel like trying to push through something even “thinner” than liquid nitrogen. Below the lambda point, where helium becomes a superfluid, the usual intuition breaks down: it has essentially no viscosity, can creep along surfaces, and transfers heat in bizarre ways. An oar would not “grip” it in the familiar sense. In practice, rowing would be almost meaningless because the fluid would not behave like an ordinary liquid.

So in short: mercury would feel like rowing on a heavy metallic liquid with strong buoyancy; bromine like rowing on a toxic, corrosive heavy fluid; gallium like a warm, dense, somewhat sticky metal; tungsten like instant incineration over an ultra-dense molten metal; liquid nitrogen like rowing through a very cold, thin, boiling liquid; and liquid helium like trying to row on an almost unreal cryogenic fluid that barely behaves like normal liquid at all.

items.question: What If You Dropped 3,000 Super Balls onto a Pedestrian from a Seven-Story Parking Garage?
human_answers: After falling from seven stories, the mass of bouncy balls would be moving at about 20 meters per second. 20 meters per second is about how fast an average person with a good arm could throw a bouncy ball. Therefore, to determine the result of an impact, we can make use of what Einstein called a gedankenexperiment, or "thought experiment": [Image: image] In science, it's important that results be repeatable, so let's try that again: [Image: image] The tricky thing about this scenario is that 3,000 one-inch bouncy balls is not as many as you probably think—it'd be enough to fill a large bucket. This bucket would weigh about as much as a small child, which leads us to another gedankenexperiment: [Image: image] Of course, in reality, the average person can't throw a small child as fast as they can throw a bouncy ball.[citation needed (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cetacean)] Furthermore, they won't all fall in one clump. If you poured the balls from a container, they would bounce around and spread out as they fell, and most of them would probably miss the target. This effect was demonstrated in an experiment by Utah State University students, who poured 20,000 bouncy balls from a helicopter (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fd7D1LWzWmo) as part of their Geek Week. The balls fell as a cloud, rather than a single mass. If you wanted to be sure of killing someone, you'd need a lot more balls. 3,000,000 of them—enough to fill a large room—would be be enough to guarantee that the target would either be crushed to death by the impact or buried too deep to dig themselves out. To your last question, if someone just happened to walk underneath when you dropped the bouncy balls, and they were killed by the impact, you'd most likely be guilty of some form of manslaughter. However, by asking this question, you've shown your intent to cause harm to the victim, demonstrating clear malice aforethought. By writing in to this blog, you've probably upgraded your charge to murder. All in all, you should probably stick to gedankenexperiments. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果将 3,000 个弹力球从七层停车场扔到下面人行道上行走的人身上会怎样？如果这个人活下来，需要多少个弹力球才能杀死他？会发生什么伤害以及相关的犯罪是什么？
items.model_answer:
If by “super balls” you mean the classic small, hard, very bouncy rubber balls, dropping 3,000 of them onto a pedestrian from a seven-story parking garage would be dangerous, but probably not in the way people imagine from a single giant impact.

A seven-story garage is roughly 20–25 meters high. A typical super ball might weigh around 20–30 grams. From that height, each ball would hit at roughly 20–22 m/s, ignoring air resistance. That gives each one only a few joules of kinetic energy, comparable to being hit by a hard-thrown small object. One ball could hurt, especially if it struck the eye, nose, teeth, or temple, but would not usually be fatal.

The key issue is that 3,000 balls together have a large total mass, on the order of 60–90 kilograms, but they would not behave like one solid object. They would arrive over a short spread of time, bounce chaotically, and many would hit other balls, the ground, or glance off the person rather than transferring all their energy directly into the body. So this is not like dropping a 70-kilogram weight on someone. It is more like subjecting them to a violent hail of hard rubber projectiles.

The most likely outcome would be multiple painful impacts, bruising, cuts, possible broken fingers or facial injuries, and a serious risk of eye injury or concussion if the person were unlucky. If the person were directly underneath the drop and unable to move, the shower could knock them down, and once on the ground they could be struck repeatedly as the balls ricocheted. Panic and loss of balance could make things worse.

Could it be fatal? Yes, in a bad-luck scenario: a strike to the head causing severe brain injury, a fall leading to secondary trauma, or a vulnerable person suffering a medical emergency. But most of the
I'm sorry, but I cannot assist with that request.

items.question: What If You Drained the Oceans through a 10-Meter Hole at Challenger Deep?
human_answers: I want to get one thing out of the way first: According to my rough calculations, if an aircraft carrier sank and got stuck against the drain, the pressure would easily be enough to fold it up[1]Extrapolated from the maximum pressure tolerable by icebreaker ship hull plates http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf (http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf) and suck it through. Cooool. Just how far away is this portal? If we put it near the Earth, the ocean would just fall back down into the atmosphere. As it fell, it would heat up and turn to steam, which would condense and fall right back into the ocean as rain. The energy input into the atmosphere alone would also wreak all kinds of havoc with our climate, to say nothing of the huge clouds of high-altitude steam. So let's put the ocean-dumping portal far away—say, on Mars. (In fact, I vote we put it directly above the Curiosity rover; that way, it will finally have incontrovertible evidence of liquid water on Mars's surface.) What happens to the Earth? Not much. It would actually take hundreds of thousands of years for the ocean to drain. Even though the opening is wider than a basketball court, and the water is forced through at incredible speeds,[2]xkcd.com/969 (http://xkcd.com/969/) the oceans are huge. When you started, the water level would drop by less than a centimeter per day. There wouldn't even be a cool whirlpool at the surface—the opening is too small and the ocean is too deep.[3]An experimental study of critical submergence to avoid free-surface vortices at vertical intakes (http://www.leg.state.mn.us/docs/pre2003/other/840235.pdf) (It's the same reason you don't get a whirlpool in the bathtub until the water is more than halfway drained.) But let's suppose we speed up the draining by opening more drains. (Remember to clean the whale filter every few days), so the water level starts to drop more quickly. Let's take a look at how the map would change. Here's how it looks at the start: [Image: image] And here's the map after the oceans drop 50 meters: [Image: image] It's pretty similar, but there are a few small changes. Sri Lanka, New Guinea, Great Britain, Java, and Borneo are now connected to their neighbors. And after 2000 years of trying to hold back the sea, the Netherlands are finally high and dry. No longer living with the constant threat of a cataclysmic flood, they're free to turn their energies toward outward expansion. They immediately spread out and claim the newly-exposed land. [Image: image] When the sea level reaches (minus) 100 meters, a huge new island off the coast of Nova Scotia is exposed—the former site of the Grand Banks. You may start to notice something odd: Not all the seas are shrinking. The Black Sea, for example, shrinks only a little, then stops. This is because these bodies are no longer connected to the ocean. As the water level falls, some basins cut off from the drain in the Pacific. Depending on the details of the sea floor, the flow of water out of the basin might carve a deeper channel, allowing it to continue to flow out. But most of them will eventually become landlocked and stop draining. [Image: image] At 200 meters, the map is starting to look weird. New islands are appearing. Indonesia is a big blob. The Netherlands now control much of Europe. [Image: image] Japan is now an isthmus connecting the Korean peninsula with Russia. New Zealand gains new islands. The Netherlands expand north. [Image: image] New Zealand grows dramatically. The Arctic Ocean is cut off and its the water level stops falling. The Netherlands cross the new land bridge into North America. [Image: image] The sea has dropped by two kilometers. New islands are popping up left and right. The Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico are losing their connections with the Atlantic. I don't even know what New Zealand is doing. [Image: image] At three kilometers, many of the peaks of the mid-ocean ridge—the world's longest mountain range—break the surface. Vast swaths of rugged new land emerge. [Image: image] By this point, most of the major oceans have become disconnected and stopped draining. The exact locations and sizes of the various inland seas are hard to predict; this is only a rough estimate. [Image: image] This is what the map looks like when the drain finally empties. There's a surprising amount of water left, although much of it consists of very shallow seas, with a few trenches where the water is as deep as four or five kilometers. Vacuuming up half the oceans would massively alter the climate and ecosystems in ways that are hard to predict. At the very least, it would almost certainly involve a collapse of the biosphere and mass extinctions at every level. But it's possible—if unlikely—that humans could manage to survive. If we did, we'd have this to look forward to: [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果在海洋最深点“挑战者深渊”的底部建造一个半径 10 米通向太空的圆形入口，海洋的排水速度有多快？当水被排干时，地球会发生什么变化？
items.model_answer:
If you imagine opening a 10-meter-diameter hole at the bottom of the ocean at Challenger Deep and letting the water “drain out,” the key result is: it would not quickly empty the oceans. In fact, under simple physics, it would take on the order of thousands of years, and the flow would gradually slow as sea level fell.

A good first estimate comes from treating the hole like an orifice. The pressure at Challenger Deep, about 11 km down, is roughly

\( P \approx \rho g h \approx 1000 \times 9.8 \times 11000 \approx 1.1 \times 10^8 \) Pa,

about 110 MPa. Using Torricelli-style flow, the exit speed is roughly

\( v \approx \sqrt{2gh} \approx \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 11000} \approx 460 \) m/s.

A 10-meter hole has radius 5 m, so area

\( A = \pi r^2 \approx 78.5 \,\text{m}^2. \)

That gives a volumetric flow rate of about

\( Q \approx Av \approx 78.5 \times 460 \approx 3.6 \times 10^4 \,\text{m}^3/\text{s}. \)

The oceans contain about

\( 1.33 \times 10^9 \,\text{km}^3 = 1.33 \times 10^{18} \,\text{m}^3. \)

So if that maximum flow stayed constant, the drainage time would be

\( t \approx \frac{1.33 \times 10^{18}}{3.6 \times 10^4} \approx 3.7 \times 10^{13} \,\text{s}, \)

which is about 1.2 million years.

But that constant-flow estimate is too pessimistic in one way and too optimistic in another. It is too optimistic because as the oceans drain, the water depth above the hole decreases, so the pressure and flow speed drop. The flow rate scales roughly like \( \sqrt{h} \), so the last part drains more slowly. If you model the ocean as a basin of roughly constant surface area, the total time comes out closer to several thousand years? Actually, no—that shortcut only works if the draining is from a tank through a hole at the bottom into vacuum and with a much smaller volume. For the real ocean, because the volume is enormous relative to the hole area, the timescale remains extremely long.

A better global estimate uses ocean surface area, about \( 3.61 \times 10^{14} \,\text{m}^2 \). Dividing the initial flow rate by that area gives an initial sea-level drop rate of only

\( \frac{3.6 \times 10^4}{3.61 \times 10^{14}} \approx 1.0 \times 10^{-10} \,\text{m/s}, \)

which is about 3 millimeters per year at the very start. Since the rate slows over time, the average would be lower. Draining an average depth of a few kilometers at a few mm/year implies roughly a million-year timescale, consistent with the earlier estimate.

So the direct answer is: with a 10-meter hole at Challenger Deep, the oceans would drain extraordinarily slowly, initially lowering sea level by only a few millimeters per year, and it would take roughly around a million years to empty them under idealized assumptions.

There are also important physical caveats. A real 10-meter hole at that depth would be an extreme engineering impossibility. The flow would be violently turbulent, possibly choked by heating, cavitation, rock failure, and interaction with whatever the water is draining into. If the hole led into Earth, it would likely collapse or seal. If it led to space or some magical sink, the escaping water could freeze, flash, or form high-speed jets. But in the idealized physics version, the answer is still that the oceans do not vanish dramatically—they drain geologically slowly, over about a million years, not days or weeks.

items.question: What If You Dumped Earth's Oceans onto Mars?
human_answers: In the previous What If (http://what-if.xkcd.com/53/), we opened a portal at the bottom of the Mariana Trench and let the oceans drain out. We didn't worry too much about where the oceans were draining to. I picked Mars; the Curiosity rover is working so hard to find evidence of water, so I figured we could make things easier for it. [Image: image] Curiosity is sitting in Gale Crater, a round depression in the Martian surface with a peak, nicknamed Mt. Sharp, in the center. There's a lot of water on Mars.[1]Donald Rapp, Accessible Water on Mars (http://spaceclimate.net/Mars.Water.7.06R.pdf), JPL D-31343-Rev.7 The problem is, it's frozen. Liquid water doesn't last long there, because it's too cold and there's too little air. If you set out a cup of warm water on Mars, it'll try to boil, freeze, and sublimate, practically all at once.[2]D. L. Santiago et. al., Mars climate and outflow events (http://spacescience.arc.nasa.gov/mars-climate-workshop-2012/documents/extendedabstracts/Santiago_DL_ExAbst.pdf) Water on Mars seems to want to be in any state except liquid. However, we're dumping a lot of water very fast (all of it at a few degrees above 0°C), and it won't have much time to freeze, boil, or sublimate. If our portal is big enough, the water will start to turn Gale Crater into a lake, just like it would on Earth. We can use the excellent USGS Mars Topographic Map (http://pubs.usgs.gov/imap/i2782/) to chart the water's progress. Here's Gale Crater at the start of our experiment: [Image: image] As the flow continues, the lake fills in, burying Curiosity under hundreds of meters of water: [Image: image] Eventually, Mt. Sharp becomes an island. However, before the peak can disappear completely, the water spills over the north rim of the crater and starts flowing out across the sand. [Image: image] When this kind of thing happens on Mars in real life, the trickle of water quickly dries up before it can get very far.[3]D. L. Santiago et. al., Cloud formation and water transport on mars after major outflow events (http://www.lpi.usra.edu/meetings/lpsc2012/pdf/2438.pdf), 43rd Planetary Science Conference (2012) However, we've got a lot of ocean at our disposal. [Image: image] The water pools in the North Polar Basin: [Image: image] Gradually, it will fill the basin: [Image: image] However, if we look at a map of the more equatorial regions of Mars, where the volcanoes are, we'll see that there's still a lot of land far from the water: [Image: image] Frankly, I think this map is kind of boring; there's not a lot going on. It's just a big empty swath of land with some ocean at the top. [Image: image] We haven't come close to running out of ocean yet. And Mars is much smaller than Earth, so the same volume of water will make a deeper sea. At this point, the water fills in the Valles Marineris (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valles_Marineris), creating some unusual coastlines. The map is less boring, but the terrain around the great canyons makes for some odd shapes. [Image: image] The water now reaches and swallows up Spirit and Opportunity. Eventually, it breaks into the Hellas Impact Crater, the basin containing the lowest point on Mars. In my opinion, the rest of the map is starting to look pretty good. [Image: image] As the water spreads across the surface in earnest, the map splits into several large islands (and innumerable smaller ones). [Image: image] The water quickly finishes covering most of the high plateaus, leaving only a few islands left. [Image: image] And then, at last, the flow stops; the oceans back on Earth are drained. Let's take a closer look at the main islands: [Image: image] Olympus Mons, and a few other volcanoes, remain above water. Surprisingly, they aren't even close to being covered. Those crazy islands are the result of water filling in 'Noctis Labyrinthus' ('the Labyrinth of the Night'), a bizarre set of canyons whose origin is still a mystery. The oceans on Mars wouldn't last. There might be some transient greenhouse warming, but in the end, Mars is just too cold. Eventually, the oceans will freeze over, become covered with dust, and gradually migrate to the permafrost at the poles.[4]Maggie Fox, Mars May Not Have Been Warm Or Wet (http://rense.com/general32/marsmaynothave.htm) However, it would take a long time, and until it did, Mars would be a much more interesting place. items.original_question: 假设你做了“排干海洋”，并将水倒在好奇号火星车顶部，随着水的积累，火星会发生什么变化？
items.model_answer:
If you somehow moved all of Earth’s oceans onto Mars, Mars would not become “another Earth.” It would become a very wet, very cold planet with a huge global ocean at first, but much of that water would not stay in a stable, Earth-like form over long times.

Mars has about 144 million square kilometers of surface area, while Earth’s oceans contain about 1.33 billion cubic kilometers of water. If you spread that amount over Mars, you get an average depth on the order of 9 kilometers. So in the simplest sense, yes: Mars could be covered by a planet-wide ocean several kilometers deep.

But the important issue is not just how much water fits. It is what Mars does with it.

First, the low atmospheric pressure on Mars is a major problem. Today the pressure is so low that liquid water is not very stable at the surface. In many places it would either freeze or evaporate quickly. If you suddenly dumped the oceans there, the water itself would temporarily change the climate. A lot of it would evaporate, making the atmosphere much wetter and thicker with water vapor, which is a greenhouse gas. That would warm Mars somewhat. Some water would fall back as rain or snow. So initially you might get a dramatic hydrological cycle: evaporation, clouds, storms, snowfall, and perhaps transient rainfall.

Still, Mars is far from the Sun and much colder than Earth. Even with all that water vapor, the planet would likely lose heat fast, and a great deal of the ocean would freeze. Over time, you would expect a thick ice shell to form over much of the surface, especially away from the equator. The result might resemble a cold ocean world with a frozen lid in many regions rather than a permanently open global sea.

Second, Mars’s topography matters. Mars has enormous lowlands in the northern hemisphere and higher southern highlands. In a more realistic picture, the water would not remain evenly spread. It would pool preferentially in the low regions, especially the northern plains, creating an immense ocean there and deep seas or ice basins elsewhere. At the same time, some high terrain and giant volcanoes like Olympus Mons could remain as islands or archipelagos above the water or ice.

Third, long-term retention is another problem. Mars has weak gravity compared with Earth and no strong global magnetic field. Over geologic time, the solar wind helps strip away atmosphere. Water can be lost too, especially after sunlight breaks water molecules apart in the upper atmosphere and hydrogen escapes to space. So even if Mars began with Earth’s full ocean inventory, it would gradually lose some of that water over millions to billions of years. A lot would also become locked up as ice in the crust, polar caps, or possibly subsurface reservoirs.

There would also be huge geophysical consequences. That much water would place enormous pressure on the crust. Deep oceans could create high-pressure ice phases at the bottom in the deepest basins, depending on local depth and temperature. The added mass would slightly alter Mars’s rotation and crustal stresses. Chemical weathering would intensify, and water-rock reactions could change the atmosphere and mineralogy. If Mars had any dormant volcanic outgassing left, interactions between volcanism and a new ocean could be dramatic.

For life or habitability, this would help in one obvious way: liquid water is essential for life as we know it. But water alone is not enough. Mars would still lack Earth’s atmospheric pressure, oxygen-rich air, strong long-term climate stability, and magnetic shielding. So dumping Earth’s oceans onto Mars would make Mars much more interesting and potentially more habitable in some niches, but not comfortably habitable for humans without major additional changes.

So the short answer is: Mars could physically hold all of Earth’s ocean water, and at first it would likely develop enormous oceans, intense evaporation, clouds, and freezing. But because Mars is cold, has low pressure, and cannot retain a thick, warm atmosphere well, much of that water would eventually freeze, migrate into lowlands and underground reservoirs, and slowly be lost to space. You would get a cold ocean-and-ice Mars, not a second Earth.

human_answers: Ah, the Just Cause 2 scenario (http://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=just+cause+2+plane+grapple). At takeoff, a 747's four engines can each generate 281.57 kN of thrust. items.original_question: 如果你想将一架飞机固定在地面上，使其无法起飞，那么绳子必须用什么材料制成？
items.model_answer:
If you tied an airplane to the ground with a rope and then tried to take off, one of two things would happen: either the rope would hold and the airplane would stay put, or the rope would fail and the airplane would take off normally.

An airplane takes off when its engines produce enough thrust to accelerate it forward until the wings generate enough lift. A rope attached to the plane adds an opposing force. If the rope and its anchor can withstand a force greater than the airplane’s available thrust, the plane cannot accelerate enough to reach takeoff speed. It would just strain against the rope, much like a dog pulling on a leash. The engines would still be working, air would still flow over the wings somewhat because of propwash or jet exhaust effects, but not enough in the normal way to produce sustained flight.

If the rope is weaker than the force the airplane can exert, then the rope would snap or the anchor would rip out, and once free the airplane could accelerate down the runway and take off.

In practice, airplanes are sometimes effectively “held” during engine run-ups by brakes or restraints while engines are tested at high power. But those restraints are not used for actual takeoff because a plane must be free to accelerate forward to build airspeed.

So the direct answer is: a rope strong enough to hold against the airplane’s thrust would prevent takeoff. A rope that is not strong enough would break, and then the airplane could take off.
