items.question: What If You Dumped All the World's Tea into the Great Lakes?
human_answers: Weak, bordering on homeopathic. The standard cup of tea, as described by the International Organization for Standardization in ISO 3103 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=8250), contains two grams of tea per 100 mL of water.[1]Further ISO standards concerning tea include ISO 3720 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=51541) (black tea), ISO 11287 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=51540) (green tea), and ISO 14502-2 (http://www.iso.org/iso/iso_catalogue/catalogue_tc/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=31357) (the difference between black tea and green tea). The Great Lakes have a volume of about 22,600 cubic kilometers, which means we would need about 450 billion tons of tea to reach proper strength. According to the Tea Board of India, one year's global tea harvest totals only about 4.8 million tons,[2]Using figures from this report (http://www.teaboard.gov.in/pdf/Tea%20Statistics%20Global%20Scenario.pdf) extrapolated forward to 2014. only 1/100,000th of what we'd require to make Great Lake Tea. If we dumped those 4.8 million tons into the lakes, the resulting tea would be about as strong as if we'd dripped two drops of tea in a bathtub.[3]Technically, calling this kind of tea "homeopathic" is an exaggeration, since substances in homeopathy are diluted way more than this. Proper bathtub tea, of course, requires one 3-kg bag. [Image: image] For better lake tea, we should find a lake with a volume of 240 million cubic meters (0.24 cubic kilometers). Wular Lake in Kashmir is one candidate. Its volume varies with the seasons, but during the winter it's just about exactly the right size.[4]Unfortunately, it's shrinking (http://www.ramsar.org/pdf/wurc/wurc_mgtplan_india_wular.pdf). (For winter volume, see the chart on page 18 of that report.) India is the world's second-largest tea producer, so it's also conveniently located. Ullswater, in the UK's Lake District, is another great candidate. With a relatively stable year-round volume of about 0.23 cubic kilometers, it would be an excellent site for brewing a global cup of tea. Of course, while neither Wular Lake or Ullswater has ever been used as a giant teakettle, something like this was—famously—attempted in my own backyard in Boston. In 1773, a group of colonists disguised as American Indians[5]They dressed up as American Indians to align themselves politically with the Americas—against Britain—invoking the popular European stereotype of the free and noble savage. The Mohawk people, the actual Indians who the protesters were mimicking, mistrusted the settlers encroaching on their land, sided with the British during the subsequent war, and afterward were driven from their homes by the Americans and fled to Canada. boarded three British ships and threw the cargo of tea—around 44 tons of it—into Boston Harbor to protest British-run tax policy. Boston Harbor has a volume of about 0.44 cubic kilometers, which means that the "tea" brewed in 1773 would have been even more dilute than our Great Lakes tea. The harbor is also somewhat larger[6]The tidal range in Boston is so large (over three meters) that the harbor's volume at high tide is nearly double what it is at low. than Wular Lake or Ullswater, so all the tea in the world would still make Boston Harbor slightly too weak. [Image: image] There's another problem: Heat. If you wanted to make tea from a lake, such as Ullswater or Wular Lake, you'd have to heat the water up. Is that even possible? There's clearly enough stored energy in the world to do it. After all, we presumably heat that amount of water for tea every year already; we just do it in small batches around the world. To heat up Ullswater to 80°C[7]Lots of people have very strong opinions on what this temperature should be. Please direct any corrections on this matter to What-If Tea-Related Complaints Dep't, c/o Her Majesty The Queen, Buckingham Palace, London SW1A 1AA. would take \(6.6 \times 10^{16}\) joules of energy—about 20 days worth of British electricity consumption. which is roughly what would be released if you dropped a water bottle full of antimatter in the lake. [Image: image] Asking Britain to go without electricity for 20 days just to fill one of their lakes with tea seems like it might be a hard sell. Fortunately, there's an easier solution. Boiling Lake in Dominica is a volcanic lake about 60 meters across. Its temperature varies, but it's often near boiling at the edges and vigorously boiling in the center. Measuring the depth of the lake is difficult, so it's hard to get an estimate of the total volume. [Image: image] Frying Pan Lake in New Zealand, on the other hand, is the largest hot lake in the world. It has a volume of about 200,000 m3, and an average temperature of around 50°C—not quite hot enough for tea, but much closer than Ullswater or Wular Lake. New Zealanders consume about 600 grams of tea per person,[8]Kerryn Pollock. 'Tea, coffee and soft drinks (http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/tea-coffee-and-soft-drinks)', Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand, updated 15-Jul-13 for a total of 2,700 tons of tea. If they waited until Frying Pan Lake got particularly hot, then dunked it all in at once ... [Image: image] ... they could brew a year's worth of tea in minutes.
items.original_question: 如果我们把世界上所有的茶叶都倒进五大湖怎么办？与普通的茶相比，湖茶的浓度如何？
items.model_answer:
If you dumped all the world’s tea into the Great Lakes, the result would be dramatic visually and locally, but it would not literally turn the lakes into “tea” in the everyday sense.

The key issue is scale. The Great Lakes contain about 22,700 cubic kilometers of water, or roughly 2.3 × 10^16 liters. Global annual tea production is on the order of a few million metric tons, say around 6 million tons as a rough figure. Even if every bit of that were dumped in at once, it would still be tiny compared with the lakes’ total mass of water.

If we imagine 6 million metric tons of dry tea leaves spread through the whole Great Lakes system, that is about 6 × 10^12 grams of tea in about 2.3 × 10^16 liters of water, giving an average of roughly 0.00026 grams per liter, or about 0.26 milligrams per liter. That is an extremely weak concentration. A normal cup of tea might use around 2 grams of tea in 250 milliliters, equivalent to about 8 grams per liter before brewing losses. So the lakes-wide average would be tens of thousands of times weaker than a drinkable cup.

In practice, though, the tea would not instantly dissolve. Most of it would be floating or sinking plant matter. Near the dumping sites, the water would become brown, murky, and full of organic debris. There would be a strong local ecological effect: decomposition would consume oxygen, microbes would bloom, and fish and invertebrates could be harmed in affected regions. Nutrients and tannins released from the leaves could alter water chemistry somewhat, especially near shorelines or in enclosed bays.

Over time, currents and mixing would spread the material out. The visual staining would fade as the tea compounds diluted, settled, decomposed, or were flushed downstream through the St. Lawrence system. The lakes would not become a giant potable tea beverage; they are simply far too large. What you would really get is a massive pulse of organic pollution, with local water-quality damage and ecological stress, but only a vanishingly weak “tea concentration” on the scale of the entire Great Lakes.

items.question: What If All the World's Viruses Were Gathered in One Place?
human_answers: It would be a huge pile, but human viruses would make up only a tiny fraction of it. HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, has killed tens of millions of people worldwide, and over 30 million people are currently living with HIV. The number of copies of the virus carried in someone's blood can vary dramatically,[1]Data on viral load—the number of copies of the virus per mL of blood—can be found in this paper (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23196933). but across all the people in the world, there probably exists about a spoonful worth of HIV. [Image: image] The typical healthy human body contains about \(3 \times 10^{12}\) viruses. This is actually not as many as you might expect; by volume, humans are apparently a less friendly environment for viruses than, say, soil.[2]An area of wetlands in Delaware (http://www.rcn.montana.edu/pubs/pdf/2008/Srinivasiah%20Res%20%20Micro%202008.pdf) contains something like four billion viruses per mL of soil, in case you were looking for a fun vacation destination. If you gathered together all the viruses in all the humans in the world, they would fill about ten oil drums: [Image: image] These 10 barrels only represent a tiny portion of the global virus community. Most of the world's viruses aren't found in humans. They're found in the sea. Seawater is full of microorganisms, and we've recently learned that those microorganisms are preyed on by viruses in a big way. Every day, about one in five living cells in the ocean is killed by a virus.[3]Marine viruses—major players in the global ecosystem (https://www.uni-due.de/imperia/md/content/water-science/ws0910/2031b_02z_ws0910_suttle_marine_viruses.pdf) These viruses are found from the surface of the ocean down to the depths.[4]Oddly, as you go further offshore and further down, the concentration of viruses doesn't decrease as much as the concentration of bacteria, so the virus-to-bacteria ratio is higher in the deep oceans than near the shore. Because the sea is so big,[5]Citation: Go and look at the sea. It's big. it contains a staggering number of viruses. If you piled up all these viruses—more than 1030 of them—in one place, they would be the size of a small mountain. [Image: image] It's hard to say exactly what the virus mountain would look like, but it would probably resemble something in between pus and meat slurry.[6]Blame Dave—he's the one who asked. Regardless of its exact appearance, it would almost certainly be disgusting. [Image: image] The pile wouldn't stay mountain-shaped for long, any more than a mountain of any organic secretion would.[7]If you don't believe me, try building a mountain of earwax or snot. You'll find you can't make it higher than a few inches before your friends and family show up and sit you down for a talk. To avoid a gigantic flood, it might be better to collect them into some kind of container. MetLife Stadium, host of Super Bowl XLVIII, has a volume of about 1.5 million cubic meters. Earth's viruses could fill the stadium about 150 times over. So if you watch the Super Bowl, take a moment to picture all the players floating, suspended, in a sea of yellowish-white secretions. [Image: image] Enjoy the game!
items.original_question: 如果世界上的所有病毒都集中到一个区域会怎样？它们会占据多少体积以及它们会是什么样子？
items.model_answer:
If you gathered all the viruses on Earth into one place, the total amount would be astonishingly large in number but surprisingly small in physical size.

A common estimate is that there are about 10^31 viruses on Earth. That is ten nonillion—far more than the number of stars in the observable universe. But viruses are extremely tiny, typically on the order of tens to hundreds of nanometers across.

If you lined up all the viruses end to end, they would stretch an enormous distance—often estimated at around 100 million light-years or more, depending on the assumed average size. That comparison is often used to show just how many there are.

But if instead you physically packed them together into one volume, they would not make something planet-sized. Their total volume would likely be on the order of a few hundred million cubic meters, depending on the average virus size and how tightly they were packed. That corresponds roughly to a large mountain, a small asteroid, or a cube a few hundred meters on a side. If the average virus were larger, the estimate could rise to around a cubic kilometer or more, but still nowhere near the size of a city or planet.

The more important issue is biological, not geometric. Putting all the world’s viruses in one place would create an unimaginably dangerous reservoir of infectious material. Many viruses infect only bacteria, plants, or specific animals, so not all would threaten humans. In fact, most viruses on Earth are probably bacteriophages in the oceans and soils. Still, concentrating all viruses together would massively disrupt ecosystems and create extreme risks of cross-species exposure, recombination, and environmental contamination.

So the short answer is: all the world’s viruses gathered in one place would form a physically modest but biologically extraordinary mass—probably something like a large hill or small mountain of viral particles, containing an incomprehensibly large number of entities and posing immense ecological danger.

items.question: What If You Tried to Catch a Bullet after It Slowed Down?
human_answers: Yes. The "bullet catch" is a common magic trick in which a magician appears to catch a fired bullet in mid-flight—often between their teeth. This an illusion, of course; it's not possible to catch a bullet like that.[1]This was confirmed (http://www.discovery.com/tv-shows/mythbusters/mythbusters-database/catch-bullet-teeth.htm) by Mythbusters in episode 4 of Season 4. But under the right conditions, you could catch a bullet. It would just take a lot of patience.[2]I'd like to remind everyone that while I write sometimes about the interesting physics of bullets, I'm not an authority on firearms safety. I was raised Quaker (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers); I've never held a gun, much less fired one. A bullet fired straight up would eventually reach a maximum height.[3]Don't do this. In neighborhoods where people fire guns upward in celebration, bystanders are routinely killed (http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/PDF/wk/mm5350.pdf) by falling bullets. It probably wouldn't stop completely; more likely, it would be drifting sideways at a couple meters per second. At that speed, as long as you were in the right place at the right time, you could snatch it out of the air. If someone fired a bullet upward ... [Image: image] ... and you were hanging out in a hot-air balloon directly above the firing range ... [Image: image] ... it's possible that you could reach out and snag the bullet at the apex of its flight. If you succeeded, you might notice something odd: In addition to being hot, the bullet would be spinning. It would have lost its upward momentum, but not its rotational momentum; it would still have the spin given to it by the barrel of the gun. [Image: image] This effect can be seen, dramatically, when a bullet is fired at ice.[4]Floor water. As confirmed by dozens of YouTube videos (https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=bullet%20spinning%20ice) (and Mythbusters), bullets fired into ice are often found still spinning rapidly. You'd have to grab the bullet firmly; otherwise, it might jump out of your hand. If you don't have a balloon, you could potentially make this work from a mountain peak. Mount Thor, which you may remember from question #51 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/51/), features a vertical drop of 1,250 meters. According to ballistics lab Close Focus Research, this is almost exactly how high a .22 Long Rifle bullet will fly if fired directly upward.[5]Close Focus Research, Maximum Altitude For Bullets Fired Vertically (http://www.closefocusresearch.com/maximum-altitude-bullets-fired-vertically) [Image: image] If you want to use larger bullets, you'll need a much larger drop; an AK-47's bullet can go over two kilometers upward. There are no purely vertical cliffs that are that tall, so you'd need to fire the bullet at an angle, and it would have significant sideways speed at the top of its arc. However, a suitably tough baseball glove might be able to snag it.[6]In fact, according to Rifle Magazine, a gun writer once claimed (https://www.riflemagazine.com/magazine/article.cfm?magid=78&tocid=1094) that at a thousand yards, he could catch ordinary rifle bullets with a baseball glove. Of course, he was being figurative—you wouldn't see the bullet coming, so you'd be just as likely to catch it with your face as with your glove. In any of these scenarios, you'd have to get extraordinarily lucky. Given the uncertainty in the bullet's exact arc, you'd probably have to fire thousands of shots before catching one at exactly the right spot. And by that point, you may find you've attracted some attention. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 有没有什么方法可以让枪射击后子弹飞到空中，然后可以安全地用手接住？例如射手位于海平面，捕手位于山上，位于枪的最远射程处。
items.model_answer:
If a bullet had really slowed down enough, then yes, in principle you could catch it safely. The key issue is not that it is “a bullet” but how fast it is moving when it reaches your hand.

A normal fired bullet is far too fast to catch. Handgun bullets are often a few hundred meters per second, and rifle bullets can be much faster. At those speeds, the bullet carries enough kinetic energy to tear through skin, bone, and tissue. Your hand would not “grab” it; the bullet would punch into or through it.

But if the bullet were slowed dramatically, the situation changes. Kinetic energy scales with the square of speed, so cutting the speed a lot cuts the danger a lot. If the bullet had slowed to something like the speed of a tossed pebble, then catching it would be more like catching any small metal object. It might still hurt because bullets are dense and often irregularly shaped, but it would not necessarily penetrate your hand.

There is a real-world example behind this idea: bullets fired straight up can lose most of their initial speed on the way up, then fall back down. Even then, they can still be dangerous or deadly, because a falling bullet can still reach speeds high enough to injure. So “slowed down” does not automatically mean “safe.”

Also, trying to catch even a slow bullet is risky because bullets can tumble, be hot, or have sharp deformed edges. And if the bullet is only “somewhat” slowed, your reaction time is another problem: you are not likely to track and grab a small fast object reliably.

So the direct answer is: if the bullet slowed enough, you could catch it, but only once it had become slow enough that it was basically no different from catching any other small thrown object. At ordinary bullet speeds, catching it is impossible and would badly injure you.

items.question: What If Astronauts Tried to Reach the Moon by Hitting Golf Balls in Orbit?
human_answers: It depends how good your swing is. That sounds glib, but it's sort of true. The answer to this question hinges on exactly how fast you can hit a golf ball. Sometimes, exact numbers don't matter that much. If my baseball, car, dog, or Zamboni goes a little faster than yours,[1]$20 says they will! it will go a little farther. But that's not how it works in rocket golf. The design of our spaceship turns out to involve an equation where the speed of the golf ball is in the exponent. That means a small change in speed can make a big difference. The equation in question—which might be my favorite in all of physics—the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation: \[ \Delta v = v_\text{exhaust} \ln \frac{m_\text{initial}}{m_\text{final}} \] This equation comes up a lot in What If calculations. I like it both because it says something fundamental about our ability to explore the universe, and because you can use it to get really good at Kerbal Space Program. With some rearranging, the equation can help us figure out how much of our ship's weight has to be golf balls: \[ \frac{\text{Mass of ship plus golf balls}}{\text{Mass of ship alone}} = e ^ \left ( \frac{\text{Ship's change in speed}}{\text{Speed of golf ball}} \right ) \] Someone who, like me, has never been golfing before, might—after swinging and missing a few times—manage to hit the ball at 120 mph (50 m/s).[2]See Trackman's page on ball speed (http://mytrackman.com/explore/trackman-data/trackman-ball-data/ball-speed) To get to the Moon from low Earth orbit, you would need enough fuel to add 5,300 m/s to your ship's speed. By putting those numbers into the rocket equation, we can find out how large a sack of golf balls would have to be for the average golfer to reach the Moon. If we plug it in to Wolfram|Alpha (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=please+calculate+2*%28%283%2F%284*pi%29%29*%28%28e%5E%285300+m%2Fs+%2F+120mph%29%29*200+kg%29+%2F+%2865%25*1.15+kg%2FL%29%29%5E%281%2F3%29+thank+you) ... [Image: image] ... we find that the bag of golf balls will have to be just about exactly 100 billion miles in diameter. That's much, much bigger than our Solar System.[3]As a Fermi rule of thumb, planets in the inner Solar System are 100 million kilometers away and planets in the outer Solar System are a billion kilometers away. Or miles; either one works. [Image: image] It would also promptly and violently collapse into a black hole. Fortunately, we should be able to avert that disaster by making relatively small changes to the "120" in that equation. If we increase the golf ball's speed from 120 mph to 150, it shrinks the answer dramatically, and the required number of golf balls would fit snugly between the Sun and Mars. Still too big to avoid a catastrophic collapse, but we're getting somewhere. [Image: image] Tiger Woods can hit a golf ball at about 180 mph, which means that if he were powering our spaceship, the bag of golf balls would be only twice the diameter of the Sun! [Image: image] According (http://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/records-10000/fastest-golf-drive/) to the Guinness Book of World Records, the record for fastest golf drive is 211 mph, set by Maurice Allen in 2012. This corresponds to a bag of golf balls only 100,000 kilometers across—smaller than Jupiter, but still (obviously) not practical. However, golfer Ryan Winther claims (http://www.ryanwinther.com/about_records.htm) to have beaten this record, though without Guinness observers there.[4]And, obviously, it doesn't count unless it's overseen by people from a beer company. If you want to set a world record, hit a golf ball at a radar gun and get it certified by the Mike's Hard Lemonade people. His ball speed was measured by something called the "Titleist Performance Institute" to be 226.7 mph, and he claims a personal best of 237 mph. If he could consistently hit 237 mph, we could shrink our fuel container down to the size of Earth[5]Although it would still be large enough to partially collapse under its own gravity, similar to what happened to the mole of moles (http://what-if.xkcd.com/4/). [Image: image] This still wouldn't work; even in a high orbit, the massive tides from your ship—which is much more massive than the Moon—would be highly disruptive. We could probably shrink the fuel tank further by using "illegal" equipment. There are Superball-style balls and "trampoline face" clubs which can hit much farther, and which would not be permitted in tournament play.[6]On the other hand, we're talking about a sport that brought whites-only clubs with it into the 21st century (http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/06/01/AR2010060103918.html), and Agusta, host of the Masters, admitted its first woman in 2012 (http://www.reuters.com/article/2012/08/20/us-golf-augusta-idUSBRE87J0IE20120820). So maybe we shouldn't worry too much about their traditional rules. A hypothetical 270 mph drive would allow a fuel tank the size of the Moon. At this point, why are we even using a club? According (http://arxiv.org/abs/1305.0966) to research from the US Air Force Academy and BTG Research,[7]Oddly, both researchers have the name "Courtney". There are probably about 200,000 people in the US named Courtney (first or last); maybe we should recruit them to all build potato cannons. a potato cannon fueled by acetylene can launch a potato at 140 m/s (310 mph). If it were capable of launching golf balls at that speed,[8]We're not factoring in the weight of the acetylene—but then again, we also weren't factoring in the weight of the hamburgers the golfer would need to eat to keep hitting those drives. our ship would have a diameter of only 150 miles! [Image: image] There's the small problem that manufacturing that many golf balls would cost quintillions of dollars. You could bring the size down further by making the potato cannon more and more powerful and efficient, but at that point you're simply building a rocket. And the potato cannon scenario has an extra perk. If you somehow made the balls durable enough to survive atmospheric entry, and you set up your maneuver so the ejected golf balls covered the middle latitudes evenly, then over the course of this maneuver you would be statistically likely to hit a hole-in-one ... at every golf course in the world. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 假设你有一艘绕地球轨道运行的宇宙飞船，你能通过向另一个方向击打高尔夫球来推动你的飞船达到超过逃逸速度的速度吗？如果是这样，需要多少个高尔夫球才能到达月球？
items.model_answer:
If astronauts in orbit tried to reach the Moon by hitting golf balls, the balls would not make it there in any practical or controlled way.

In low Earth orbit, everything is already moving sideways around Earth at about 7.8 km/s. A golf club can only add maybe tens of meters per second to that speed, which is tiny compared with orbital speed. So hitting the ball would not send it straight toward the Moon the way a golf shot works on Earth. It would just slightly change the ball’s orbit around Earth.

To get from low Earth orbit to the Moon, an object needs a major change in velocity, on the order of several kilometers per second, not a few dozen meters per second. A golf swing is short by roughly two orders of magnitude at least. The ball would most likely end up in a slightly higher orbit, slightly lower orbit, or a different elliptical path, depending on the direction of the hit.

There are also practical problems. A golf ball has very little mass and no guidance or propulsion. Tiny errors in direction matter enormously. Even if an astronaut somehow hit it in exactly the “right” direction, the Moon is moving, the transfer path is precise, and the ball would be affected by Earth’s gravity, the Moon’s gravity, and small perturbations like sunlight pressure. A normal golf shot is nowhere near accurate enough.

If the astronauts were already far from Earth and on a trajectory set up for a lunar transfer, then hitting a golf ball could slightly alter its path. But even then, it would still be an unguided object, so the chance of actually striking the Moon would be extremely small.

So the careful answer is: hitting golf balls in orbit would not be a realistic way to reach the Moon. The balls would just become space debris in altered Earth orbits unless they were already given most of the needed velocity by a spacecraft.

items.question: How Powerful Would Radar Have to Be to Stop a Speeding Car?
human_answers: Radio waves exert force on things. Not a lot of force. The average cell phone transmitter exerts about a billionth of a newton of pressure on its surroundings. That means that it would take several trillion cell phones to collectively levitate a snowflake; the pressure from one phone wouldn't even measurably slow it down. [Image: image] If the phone did put out enough energy to levitate a snowflake by radiation pressure, the power flowing through the snowflake (a few kilowatts) would quickly cause the snowflake to become a raindrop, which would quickly become water vapor, which would quickly become the least of your problems. [Image: image] The fate of the snowflake hints at what kinds of problems our car will encounter. If you want to slow down a one-ton car by radiation pressure, your radar gun would need to deliver about two trillion joules worth of radiation—the energy of a small nuclear weapon.[1]The formula for figuring out that amount out is simple: The energy required is equal to the desired change in speed (say, 20 mph) times the mass of the car times the speed of light. The radar gun would need to emit even more energy than that, since not all of the radiation will be absorbed (or reflected) by the car.[2]The fact that some of it is reflected makes things easier, since that doubles the momentum delivered by the radiation. This is why simple solar sails are white and not black. For more on radar reflectivity of materials, you can check out one of the worst scanned PDFs I've ever seen (http://www.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/601365.pdf). Your radar gun would also vaporize the car. This is a problem, in one sense, but it's also a solution. Even if most of the energy is reflected, the portion that was absorbed would convert the materials in the car into gas or plasma. The expanding cloud would exert a lot more pressure on the car than the radiation itself.[3]This process, called ablation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_ablation), is also what got rid of the Moon in the What If #13 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/13/). This is convenient—it means that we wouldn't need nearly as much energy to stop the car as we would using radiation pressure alone. There are even simpler ways to slow down a car with radiation. For example, you could aim a radiation beam at the tires and melt them, or use the electromagnetic radiation to knock out the car's electrical systems. Or just use a laser pointer to blind the driver and hope they reflexively slow down. Of course, you don't need any of those things. If your goal is to slow down the car—rather than to catch speeders—your radar gun doesn't need any power. You can just stand by the side of the road next to a police car holding a fake radar gun. [Image: image] In the end, a radar gun capable of slowing cars through radiation pressure would be roughly equivalent to a nuclear weapon, and using nuclear strikes in response to traffic violations is probably overkill. It would work, in the literal sense, but it would also destroy the offender, car, police officer, road, and all other traffic for miles around.[4]It would also cause fragments of the driver to violate the speed limit in all directions at once. Of course, maybe using the apocalyptic radar gun wouldn't be necessary; just the threat of a nuclear strike against drivers would probably deter speeding. Come to think of it, maybe that's what those other signs you sometimes see are hinting at. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 我偶尔会在限速标志上看到“雷达强制执行”，我不禁要问：无线电波必须有多强才能阻止汽车超速，如果尝试这样做会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If by “stop” you mean “use radar itself to push backward on the car and bring it to a halt,” the answer is: absurdly powerful—far beyond any practical radar.

Radar uses electromagnetic waves, and electromagnetic waves do carry momentum, so in principle they can exert pressure. But that pressure is tiny. The force from a beam is roughly

\[
F \approx \frac{P}{c}
\]

if the waves are absorbed, or up to about

\[
F \approx \frac{2P}{c}
\]

if perfectly reflected, where \(P\) is beam power and \(c\) is the speed of light.

Take a typical car of mass about \(1500\ \text{kg}\), moving at \(30\ \text{m/s}\) (about 67 mph). If you wanted to stop it in, say, 5 seconds, you’d need a deceleration of

\[
a = \frac{30}{5} = 6\ \text{m/s}^2
\]

so the required force is

\[
F = ma = 1500 \times 6 = 9000\ \text{N}.
\]

To get that much force from radar pressure alone, even in the best-case perfectly reflecting case,

\[
P \approx \frac{Fc}{2}.
\]

Plugging in:

\[
P \approx \frac{9000 \times 3\times10^8}{2} \approx 1.35\times10^{12}\ \text{W}.
\]

That is about 1.3 terawatts.

That is an enormous amount of power—comparable to the electrical generating capacity of a large country, concentrated into one beam. And that’s just to stop one car in 5 seconds. If you wanted to stop it faster, the power requirement goes up proportionally.

Even if you only wanted a gentle braking force, say \(1000\ \text{N}\), you’d still need on the order of

\[
P \sim 10^{11}\ \text{W}
\]

tens to hundreds of gigawatts.

There’s another way to see how extreme this is. The car’s kinetic energy at 30 m/s is

\[
\frac12 mv^2 = \frac12(1500)(30^2) = 675{,}000\ \text{J}.
\]

That energy is not huge by itself, but radar stopping by radiation pressure is inefficient because photons have very little momentum per unit energy. The limiting factor is momentum transfer, not just energy.

So the direct answer is: to stop a speeding car with radar radiation pressure, you’d need roughly hundreds of gigawatts to terawatts of beam power, depending on how quickly you want to stop it. That makes it completely impractical.

If instead you mean “could radar disable the car electronically,” that is a different question. In principle, sufficiently intense microwaves could damage electronics, but that would not be ordinary radar and would be more like a directed-energy weapon than a speed gun.

items.question: What If All the CO2 in Bottled Soda Were Released into the Atmosphere?
human_answers: For most of the history of civilization, there were about 270 parts per million of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. In the last hundred years, industrial activity has pushed that number up (http://www.skepticalscience.com/print.php?r=45) to 400 parts per million. One "part per million" of CO2 weighs about 7.8 billion tons. A can of soda contains in the neighborhood of 2.2 grams of CO2, so you would need about 450 quadrillion cans of soda. That's enough to cover the Earth's land with ten layers of cans. [Image: image] There's clearly not enough room to do this. Even if we stacked the cans up to the edge of space,[1]I don't have any hard numbers, but my guess would be that you could probably stack supermarket soda six-pack crates a few hundred meters high before the bottom layer ruptures. they'd still take up an area the size of Rhode Island.[2]We shouldn't actually try it, given what happened last time (http://what-if.xkcd.com/8/). We'd need to add even more cans to keep up with ongoing emissions. We're currently increasing the atmosphere's CO2 concentration by an average of 2 parts per million each year: [Image: image] At that rate, we'd need to add one can of soda per person every 30 seconds, which is about 10,000 times the current consumption rate.[3]The global average (http://what-if.xkcd.com/74/) is one can per person every 5 days. In the US, the average is one every 18 hours. That would add a new layer of cans to the ground every 6[4]I originally had the wrong number here; thank you to Paulina for catching it! years or so. This layer of cans would get pretty annoying. [Image: image] Are there any ways out of this predicament? In some areas, you can turn in soda cans for recycling and receive a small amount of money; in Massachusetts, where I live, it's 5 cents. If you collected one year's worth of soda cans—instead of layering them across the Earth's surface—and emptied them out, you could redeem them for $372 trillion. With that much money, you could simply buy the world's current reserves[5]Source: xkcd.com/980 (http://xkcd.com/980), bottom right. of coal, oil, and natural gas—the source of the whole problem. Then, you put it all back in the ground and leave it there. [Image: image] Problem solved.
items.original_question: 全球瓶装碳酸饮料库存中含有多少 CO 2？需要多少苏打水才能使大气中的CO 2 恢复到工业化前的水平？
items.model_answer:
If all the CO2 dissolved in bottled soda were released into the atmosphere, the direct effect on Earth’s atmosphere would be tiny.

A typical carbonated soft drink contains on the order of a few grams of dissolved CO2 per liter, roughly about 5–8 g/L depending on the drink and pressure. If you imagine releasing the CO2 from every bottle and can of soda on Earth, the total would sound large in everyday terms, but it would still be extremely small compared with the mass of CO2 already in the atmosphere and especially compared with annual human emissions from fossil fuels.

For scale, the atmosphere contains roughly 3 trillion tons of CO2, and humans add around 35–40 billion tons per year. The CO2 in all bottled soda worldwide at any given moment would likely amount to only a tiny fraction of a millionth to a few millionths of atmospheric CO2, depending on how broadly you count production and inventory. So even if it were all released at once, it would not noticeably change global climate, atmospheric composition, or air quality.

Locally, if you opened a lot of bottles in a small enclosed space, CO2 could briefly build up near the floor because it is denser than air, but under ordinary conditions it would quickly mix into the atmosphere. There would be no dramatic planetary effect.

One subtle point is that the CO2 in soda is usually manufactured from industrial processes, so releasing it is not creating a new kind of carbon source beyond what industry already handles. It is just moving a small amount of CO2 from dissolved form in liquid into the air.

So the answer is: if all the CO2 in bottled soda were released into the atmosphere, you might hear a lot of fizz, but the global atmospheric impact would be essentially negligible.

items.question: What If I Threw a Tungsten Countertop into the Sun?
human_answers: Not very far. With its high melting point, tungsten is a good[1]Except that the word "good" implies that you have some kind of goal you're working toward, which—given how strange the thing you're doing is—I'm not sure about. choice for a sundiving countertop. The first problem would be sunlight. As the countertop approached the Sun, it would heat up. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any element, but the Sun is one of the meltiest things in the Solar System. When the countertop got within a couple of solar radii, it would liquify. [Image: image] If you protected it with a heat shield of some kind, or dropped it from a sundiving spaceship, it could enter the Sun's atmosphere relatively intact. In this case, some interesting physical effects would destroy it.[2]"Some interesting physical effects would destroy it" summarizes the answers to a large percentage of the questions submitted to this blog. Because the Sun is so heavy, anything that falls to its surface will be accelerated to a tremendous speed by its gravity. A falling countertop would reach speeds of over 600 km/s—0.2% of the speed of light. (Our rockets can only accelerate spacecraft to 10-20 km/s.) From the countertop's point of view, particles from the Sun's atmosphere would be slamming into it at 600 km/s. These particles would pack quite a punch.[3]From a particle physics point of view, the individual protons would have energy of about 2 keV. When the countertop got within about a few thousand kilometers[4]I don't want another unit-related word to mentally keep track of, but it's always seemed a little weird that we don't call thousands of kilometers "megameters". of the Sun's surface, these collisions would start delivering more energy to the countertop than the sunlight. The collisions would fling individual tungsten atoms away from the surface—a process called sputtering (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputtering). Between the sputtering and ordinary heating from the impacts, the countertop would start to absorb a lot of energy very quickly. If the countertop were larger, it could penetrate into the Sun's photosphere—the first layer beneath the "surface"—and potentially trigger a solar flare.[5]For a scientific discussion of this, see the article Impacts of comets onto the Sun and coronal mass ejections (http://meetings.copernicus.org/www.cosis.net/abstracts/EGU05/04384/EGU05-J-04384.pdf). For a science fiction discussion of this, see Stephen Baxter and Arthur C. Clarke's 2005 novel Sunstorm. But as it is, it wouldn't even make it through the Sun's atmosphere—it would be vaporized somewhere in the Sun's chromosphere. [Image: image] This brings us around to a key question: Who the hell has tungsten countertops? Sure, it has good heat tolerance. But I'd be nervous about using tungsten as a food-preparation surface. In September of 1994 (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8874460), a French soldier drank wine from a rifle barrel. Fifteen minutes later, he started having seizures. He was rushed to the hospital and treated for "acute tungsten intoxication"—the first known case in medical history. He reportedly made a full recovery, although concentrations of tungsten were present in all his body tissues for weeks. The lesson here is to use normal materials. Michael, just make your countertops out of granite and don't drop them in the Sun. And if you're a French soldier, please just drink wine like a normal person. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果我把钨制台面扔进太阳里，它会下降多远？
items.model_answer:
If you somehow threw a tungsten countertop into the Sun, it would not stay a “countertop” for long. Long before it reached the Sun’s surface, it would be heated so intensely that it would first get red hot, then melt, then boil into tungsten vapor, and eventually become a cloud of ionized atoms mixed into the solar plasma.

Tungsten is famous for having an extremely high melting point, about 3422°C, and a boiling point around 5555°C, so compared with most materials it would survive heating for a long time. But the Sun is far hotter than that. The visible “surface” of the Sun, the photosphere, is about 5500°C, already hot enough to vaporize tungsten. Deeper in, temperatures rise rapidly into the tens of thousands and then millions of degrees, where atoms are stripped of electrons entirely.

There is also the question of whether you could even “throw” it into the Sun in the first place. From Earth, that is surprisingly hard. Earth is already moving around the Sun at about 30 km/s, so to fall straight into the Sun you would need to cancel almost all of that sideways orbital speed. If you just launched the countertop off Earth, it would usually go into some new orbit around the Sun rather than plunging directly in. So in practice, getting it into the Sun is much harder than getting it out of the Solar System.

If it did make it in, the amount of tungsten would be negligible compared with the Sun. Even a very large countertop might weigh a few hundred kilograms. The Sun’s mass is about 2 × 10^30 kg, so adding the countertop would make no meaningful difference at all to the Sun’s brightness, temperature, or behavior. It would just become an utterly insignificant trace impurity.

So the short answer is: it would orbit the Sun unless you removed Earth’s orbital speed; if it really fell in, it would melt, vaporize, ionize, and disappear into the Sun without any noticeable effect.

items.question: What If Earth Spun Fast Enough for a Day to Last One Second?
human_answers: If this is going to happen, I hope it doesn't happen late in the afternoon next Friday. The Earth rotates,[citation needed (https://web.archive.org/web/20151210155028/http://www.timecube.com/)] which means its midsection is being flung outward by centrifugal force.[1]Which is still a real thing (http://xkcd.com/123/). This centrifugal force isn't strong enough to overcome gravity and tear the Earth apart, but it's enough to flatten the Earth slightly and make it so you weigh almost a pound less at the Equator than you do at the poles.[2]This is due to several effects, including centrifugal force, the flattened shape of the Earth, and the fact that if you go far enough toward the pole in North America people start offering you poutine. If the Earth (and everything on it) were suddenly sped up so that a day only lasted one second, the Earth wouldn't even last a single day.[3]Either kind. The Equator would be moving at over 10% of the speed of light. Centrifugal force would become much stronger than gravity, and the material that makes up the Earth would be flung outward. [Image: image] You wouldn't die instantly—you might survive for a few milliseconds or even seconds. That might not seem like much, but compared to the speed at which you'd die in other What If articles (http://what-if.xkcd.com/1/) involving relativistic speeds, it's pretty long. The Earth's crust and mantle would break apart into building-sized chunks. By the time a second[4]I mean, a day. had passed, the atmosphere would have spread out too thin to breathe—although even at the relatively stationary poles, you probably wouldn't survive long enough to asphyxiate. [Image: image] In the first few seconds, the expansion would shatter the crust into spinning fragments and kill just about everyone on the planet, but that's relatively peaceful compared to what would happen next. Everything would be moving at relativistic speeds, but each piece of the crust would be moving at close to the same speed at its neighbors. This means things would be relatively calm ... until the disk hit something. The first obstacle would be the belt of satellites around the Earth. After 40 milliseconds, the ISS would be struck by the edge of the expanding atmosphere and would be vaporized instantly. More satellites would follow. After a second and a half, the disc would reach the belt of geostationary satellites orbiting above the Equator. Each one would release a violent burst of gamma rays as the Earth consumed it. [Image: image] The debris from the Earth would slice outward like an expanding buzzsaw. The disk would take about ten seconds to pass the Moon, another hour to spread past the Sun, and would span the Solar System within a day or two. Each time the disc engulfed an asteroid, it would spray a flood of energy in all directions, eventually sterilizing every surface in the Solar System. Since the Earth is tilted, the Sun and the planets aren't usually lined up with the plane of the Earth's equator. They'd have a good chance of avoiding the buzzsaw[5]I keep reading this as "Buzzfeed". directly. However, Next Friday, April 25th, the Moon will cross the plane of the Earth's equator (as it does every two weeks). If Dylan sped up the Earth at this moment, the Moon would be right in the path of the resulting planetary buzzsaw. The impact would turn the moon into a comet, sending it rocketing from the Solar System in a spray of debris. The flash of light and heat would be so bright that if you were standing at the surface of the Sun, it would be brighter above you than below. Every surface in the Solar System—Europa's ice, Saturn's rings, and Mercury's rocky crust—would be scoured clean ... [Image: image] ... by moonlight.
items.original_question: 如果地球自转加速到一天只持续一秒钟会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If Earth spun so fast that one full rotation took only one second, the planet as we know it would not remain habitable, and probably would not even remain shaped or structured like present-day Earth.

The biggest effect is the enormous rotation speed at the equator. Earth’s circumference is about 40,000 km, so a one-second day means the equator would be moving at about 40,000 km/s, roughly 11% of the speed of light. That is vastly faster than orbital speeds and far beyond anything a rocky planet can tolerate.

The centrifugal effect would completely overwhelm gravity at the equator. Earth’s surface gravity is about 9.8 m/s², but with a one-second rotation period the outward centripetal requirement at the equator would be on the order of 10^9 m/s². In other words, material at the equator would not be held down at all—it would be flung outward violently. The planet could not stay a sphere. It would likely tear itself apart, shedding its crust, oceans, and atmosphere into space, probably forming a disk or ring of debris around what remained.

Even before total breakup, the atmosphere and oceans would be catastrophically affected. Air and water would rush outward and redistribute under the extreme rotational forces. There would be no stable weather, no normal sea level, and no possibility of standing on the surface. The equator would be the worst region, but the whole planet would be under extreme stress.

The shape of Earth would also change drastically. Even much slower rotation makes planets bulge at the equator. At a one-second day, the equatorial bulge would become so extreme that “Earth” would no longer be close to spherical. A stable rocky body rotating that fast is essentially impossible.

There are also relativistic and energy issues. Spinning Earth up to that rate would require an absurd amount of energy, enough to melt, vaporize, and disrupt the planet many times over. The stresses inside the mantle and core would generate immense heating and likely destroy the internal structure.

So the short answer is: if Earth somehow tried to spin fast enough for a day to last one second, it would not simply have very short sunrises and sunsets. It would be ripped apart. There would be no ordinary Earth, no stable surface, no breathable atmosphere, and almost certainly no life.

items.question: What If Rain Broke a Windshield before Speed Did?
human_answers: Fast. [Image: image] Raindrops are tiny. Even in the heaviest rainstorms, the water in the air weighs less than the air itself (which is one of several reasons you can't swim upward in a rainstorm). Even at very high speeds, they can't break a windshield via their momentum alone. Under ordinary circumstances, raindrops don't damage car windshields at all. However, they can destroy the windows of supersonic aircraft. Here's what happens when a raindrop hits a glass surface at high speed: When the droplet makes contact with the surface, a shockwave travels back up through the droplet. [Image: image] Normally, this shockwave would move at the speed of sound within the liquid—about 1300 m/s, four times faster than in air. However, at high impact speeds, this shockwave actually moves substantially faster than the speed of sound in water. The water is squeezed between the incoming drop and the glass surface, which makes it squirt sideways in all directions. These jets of water can move even faster than the original (already supersonic) droplet, and even faster than the shockwaves we mentioned. [Image: image] One paper (http://e-collection.library.ethz.ch/eserv/eth:26251/eth-26251-02.pdf) ran a simulation of water droplets hitting a surface at 500 m/s (about Mach 1.5), and found that the water sprayed out from the point of contact at over 6000 m/s—Mach 18.[1]That's a pretty simple way to expel material at 6 km/s. I wonder if anyone's ever tried to come up with a spacecraft propulsion system using it ... The sharp pulse from the shockwave can crack glass. The highest pressures are found in the ring around the edge of the droplet, and only exist for a tiny fraction of the impact. [Image: image] In addition to the direct downward pressure, the water jetting sideways can cause damage, too. If the material has any microscopic holes, cracks, or bumps, those jets can strike them and create new cracks or widen existing ones. Even at high speeds, a raindrop won't create a bullet hole on its own—but a long series of supersonic droplets would start to eat away at the glass, cracking and pitting it like sand.[2]This type of "erosion" can also cause damage to steam turbine blades (http://www.technicaljournalsonline.com/ijeat/VOL%20II/IJAET%20VOL%20II%20ISSUE%20II%20APRIL%20JUNE%202011/ARTICLE%2014%20IJAET%20VOLII%20ISSUE%20II%20APRIL-%20JUNE%202011.pdf). Eventually, the windshield could fail catastrophically. Luckily, cars can't drive at Mach 1 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/61/) without lifting off, so your windshield is safe from ordinary rain. On the other hand, if you're driving under a thunderstorm with strong updrafts ... [Image: image] ... the precipitation can smash your windshield at any speed.
items.original_question: 如果下雨的话，挡风玻璃会被雨打碎，你需要以多快的速度行驶？
items.model_answer:
If rain could break a windshield before the car’s speed itself became the limiting factor, driving fast in heavy rain would become dangerous in a completely different way.

Normally, a windshield is designed to withstand airflow and ordinary raindrop impacts because raindrops are tiny and deform on impact. Even at highway speeds, they do not act like solid bullets. But in this counterfactual, we are imagining that rain impacts become strong enough to crack or shatter the glass at some speed lower than the speed where engine power, tire grip, aerodynamics, or human control would otherwise limit the car.

That would mean the practical top speed in rain would be set by windshield survivability. Drivers would have to slow down dramatically in storms, not mainly because of visibility or hydroplaning, but because the windshield could fail structurally. Cars might need much thicker or differently shaped front glass, external shields, or even sacrificial transparent layers for wet conditions. Vehicle design standards would include “rain-impact resistance” at speed in the same way they now consider crash safety.

It would also imply that the kinetic energy transfer from raindrops was far larger than in our world, probably because the drops behaved more like rigid pellets than soft liquid masses. If that were true, rain would be hazardous to many exposed surfaces, not just windshields: paint, headlights, aircraft canopies, and even skin at high relative speeds could be damaged.

So the short answer is: if rain could break a windshield before speed itself became the main constraint, then in rainy conditions rain impact would become the true speed limit, and transportation technology would have to be redesigned around surviving precipitation at high speed.

items.question: What If You Drank the Blood of a Drunk Person?
human_answers: You would have to drink a lot of blood. A person contains about 5 liters of blood, or 14 glasses. [Image: image] If your blood is more than about half a percent alcohol, you stand a pretty good chance of dying. There have been a handful of cases of people surviving with a blood alcohol level of above 1%, but the LD50—the level at which 50% of people will die—is 0.40 (http://www.nellis.af.mil/shared/media/document/AFD-110211-015.pdf) (0.4%). If someone had a BAC of 0.40, and you drank all 14 glasses of their blood in a short amount of time,[1]Hey, there's a 50% chance they were going to die anyway. you would throw up: [Image: image] You wouldn't throw up because because of the alcohol; you'd just throw up because you're drinking blood. If you somehow avoided vomiting, you would have ingested a total of 20[2]Thank you to Conor Braman, among others, for correcting a missing zero in the original version of this calculation. grams of ethanol, which is the amount you'd get from a pint of beer. [Image: image] Depending on your weight, drinking that much blood could raise your own blood alcohol level to about 0.05. This is low enough that you could legally drive in many jurisdictions, but high enough to double your risk of an accident if you did. If your BAC is 0.05, it means only 1/8th of the alcohol from the other person's blood made it into yours. Supposing that after you drank all this blood, someone killed you and drank your blood,[3]It's only fair. they would then have a BAC of 0.006. If this process were repeated about 25 times, there would be fewer than 8 molecules of ethanol left in the last person's blood. After a few more cycles, there would likely be none;[4]By homeopathic standards, this is still quite concentrated. they'd just be drinking regular blood.[5]Like a loser. Whether there's any alcohol in it or not, drinking 14 glasses of blood wouldn't be fun. There's not a huge amount of medical literature on the subject, but anecdotal evidence from online forum posts suggests that any normal person who tries to drink more than about a pint of blood will vomit: [Image: image] If you drink blood regularly, over a long period of time the buildup of iron in your system can cause iron overload (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_overload). This syndrome, which sometimes affects people who have repeated blood transfusions, is one of the few conditions for which the correct treatment is bloodletting (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloodletting).[6]Others include PCV (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polycythemia_vera) and PCT (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porphyria_cutanea_tarda). Drinking one person's blood probably wouldn't cause iron overload. What it could give you is a blood-borne disease. Most such diseases are caused by viruses that can't survive in the stomach, but they could easily get into your blood through scratches in your mouth or throat as you drank. Diseases you could get from drinking an infected person's blood include hepatitis B and C, HIV, Hantaviruses, and Ebola. I'm not a doctor, and I try not to give medical advice in these articles. However, I will confidently say that you shouldn't drink the blood of someone with Ebola. That said, drinking or eating blood is not unheard of. It's a taboo in many cultures, but the British eat "black pudding", which is largely blood, and there are similar dishes all around the world. Maasai pastoralists in east Africa once lived mainly on milk, but also sometimes drank blood (http://digitalcommons.calpoly.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1005&context=honors), drawing it from their cattle and mixing it with the milk to form a sort of extreme protein shake. So the bottom line is that drinking enough of someone's blood to get drunk would be very difficult, probably quite unpleasant, and might give you some serious diseases. In the end, the blood itself would do awful things to your body long before the booze ever could. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 喝醉人的血会醉吗？
items.model_answer:
If you drank the blood of a drunk person, you would not get meaningfully drunk.

That’s because the alcohol concentration in blood is quite low, even in someone who is clearly intoxicated. For example, a blood alcohol concentration of 0.08% means there are about 0.08 grams of ethanol per 100 mL of blood. That is a very small amount. To get the alcohol in even one standard drink, you would need to consume a large volume of blood—far more than would be realistic or safe.

Your digestive system would absorb whatever ethanol is present, so in principle a tiny amount of alcohol could enter your body. But the bigger issue would not be intoxication. Drinking blood is dangerous. It can transmit serious infections if the blood is contaminated, including hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV, and it can also cause vomiting, stomach irritation, and other medical problems. Large amounts of blood can also be harmful to digest because of its high iron and protein content.

So the direct answer is: you would absorb a little alcohol, but probably not enough to get drunk; the real risks would be infection and toxicity, not intoxication.

items.question: How Many Birds Would It Take to Collapse into a Giant Bird Ball?
human_answers: The video shows starlings, birds which ... • gather in giant flocks of sometimes more than a million animals • can talk (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VZYG00_qvE) • sound like R2-D2, though not as much as bobolinks (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ABjBldAtPQ#t=9) do The gravitational force between adjacent starlings is small. If two birds were flying half a meter apart and tried to go perfectly straight, they would fly for over a thousand kilometers before the gravitational force between them finally steered them into colliding. [Image: image] Side note: The following is the first sentence from a journal article (http://jeb.biologists.org/content/204/19/3311) on starling metabolism:We trained two starlings (Sturnus vulgaris) to fly in a wind tunnel whilst wearing respirometry masks. I really think the paper should have stopped there; no matter what their results were, they can't possibly improve on the achievement they opened with. [Image: image] Anyway, back to gravity. To calculate the gravitational force from a whole flock of starlings, we need to know the flock's density. Conveniently, a 2008 paper (http://arxiv.org/abs/0802.1667) in Animal Behavior gathered some detailed statistics on starling flocks. The highest density they saw was about half a starling per cubic meter.[1]0.54 (•)>m-3 If the birds weigh about 85 grams each, that means the air in a starling flock weighs 25 times more than the starlings themselves.[2]This makes a certain intuitive sense. If they were that much heavier than the air between them, it's hard to imagine how they'd be able to stay airborne by pushing off of it with their wings. This means that the air's gravity is 25 times stronger than the starling cloud's gravity, and it's the air's gravity that will dominate the collapse. The collapse of giant clouds of gas or birds is governed by the equation for the Jeans instability (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeans_instability). It suggests that in order to undergo collapse, a cloud of uniform room-temperature air full of starlings would have to be much larger than the Earth to collapse. [Image: image] The gas cloud's gravity would be very weak, so the starlings would probably have a hard time flying until they got used to it. (Birds can fly (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w4sZ3qe6PiI&feature=kp) in zero g—or, at least, they flap around in confusion. But, to be fair, that's how I'd react if I were abruptly and without warning yanked from my bed and tossed into the air in a zero g airplane cabin.) Such a cloud wouldn't form in the first place without some extra compression. To collapse naturally under its own gravity, the starling cloud would need to be so large that it would engulf the Solar System. When it did collapse, it would heat up, and the starlings ... [Image: image] ... would become a star.
items.original_question: 我在观看这段视频时想知道：需要多少只鸟才能让重力接管并迫使它们变成一个巨大的鸟球？
items.model_answer:
If you mean “collapse under their own gravity into a single roughly spherical object,” the answer is: an absurdly huge number of birds, far beyond anything biologically plausible.

A quick way to estimate it is to ask when a pile of bird matter becomes self-gravitating strongly enough that its own gravity overcomes the material strength of flesh, bone, and air gaps. For rocky bodies, this transition to a rounded “gravity-dominated” shape happens at roughly a few hundred kilometers in radius. Bird tissue is much weaker and less dense than rock, so the threshold would be somewhat different, but still on the scale of a large asteroid or small moon, not a flock.

Take a typical bird mass of about 0.1 kg. If you compressed many birds together, the average density might be on the order of water, about 1000 kg/m^3. A self-gravitating sphere with radius around 100 km would then have mass

M ≈ (4/3)π(10^5 m)^3(1000 kg/m^3) ≈ 4 × 10^18 kg.

Dividing by 0.1 kg per bird gives about

4 × 10^19 birds,

or tens of quintillions of birds.

That would make a “bird ball” about 200 km across. At that point gravity is strong enough that the mass would no longer behave like a loose heap of separate birds. It would crush, compact, and heat into something more like a grotesque organic moon than a pile of intact animals.

If instead you mean “when does the center get crushed by the weight above it,” the number is still enormous. Pressure in a self-gravitating sphere scales roughly like P ~ Gρ^2R^2. Setting central pressure to around atmospheric-to-megapascal levels, where soft tissue is badly compressed, again gives radii of tens to hundreds of kilometers, corresponding to roughly 10^18–10^20 birds depending on assumptions.

So the direct answer is: on the order of 10^19 birds, give or take a few orders of magnitude. Fewer than that and you mostly just have a giant heap. Around that scale and above, you start getting a true gravity-collapsed giant bird ball.

items.question: What If All the Water on Earth Vanished?
human_answers: As is often the case with these questions, everyone would die. The first people to notice would be swimmers and boaters, for obvious reasons. [Image: image] To avoid a glass half empty (http://what-if.xkcd.com/6/) scenario, we'll assume the water is replaced by air. Most people swim in water which is relatively shallow, so most of them would survive the fall to the bottom, albeit with a few broken bones.[1]Those swimming in quarries and glacial lakes, on the other hand, could easily fall to their deaths a few feet from shore. People out on the ocean, on the other hand, would be in trouble. The ones in shallow water would hit bottom first, since they wouldn't have as far to fall. Within the first second, a large fraction of the boats in lakes, rivers, and harbors would crash into the bottom, and many of those on board would survive. [Image: image] Boats out on the ocean would take longer to fall. Over the next five seconds, a wave of crashes would spread outward from the continents, as boats struck the continental shelf farther and farther from shore. These boats would be smashed to tiny fragments, killing everyone on board. After the first six or seven seconds, there would be a brief lull in the ship destruction rate. Continental shelves drop off steeply, and most of the ships out over the deep sea would take a little longer to fall. The Titanic sank in about two miles of water. After it disappeared beneath the surface, the two halves of the ship took between 5 and 15 minutes to reach the bottom.[2]When the Titanic bow hit the sea floor, it was moving at almost exactly the same speed as when it struck the iceberg three hours earlier. (This is not quite a coincidence.) Without the ocean there, it would have reached the bottom in about 30 seconds, striking it at airliner cruising speed.[3]Although no one has ever dropped a cruise ship from a high altitude,[citation needed] their terminal velocity at the surface is probably a little below the speed of sound. Because the air in the ocean basins would be compressed, the terminal velocity of ships near the bottom would be lower than at the surface. This compression also means that to magically replace the water, you'd need more air than you'd expect from the ocean's volume alone, since it would need a varying density profile. In other words, your water-replacement spells will need to have some calculations behind them. Sufficiently advanced magic is indistinguishable from technology. Within the first minute, just about every large ship would be on the bottom. The final boat to reach the bottom would probably be a small sailboat or life raft that was crossing an ocean trench when the water vanished. Thanks to low weight and/or drag from the sails, one of these vessels could take many minutes to reach the bottom. [Image: image] If there were a seaplane floating on the deep ocean, it could conceivably survive, although it would take some luck and quick thinking by the pilot. The plane would initially drop, but as it gained speed it would tend to pull into a glide. After the initial shock, the pilot would have a reasonable amount of time to try to start the engine. Thanks in part to the thicker air, it's possible a seaplane could successfully land (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YZx6wa6zHAc) on a smooth patch of seabed. If the engine got started, the pilot could also try to fly to shore and land on a runway. Fish, whales, and dolphins, and nearly all marine life would die immediately. Those near the bottom would suffocate or dessicate, while those near the surface in deeper water would suffer the same fate as boats. [Image: image] Then the really weird stuff starts. Without evaporation from lakes and oceans feeding the water cycle, it would stop raining. Without pools of water to drink from, people and most animals would dehydrate and die in a matter of days. Within a few weeks, plants would start withering in the ever-drier air. Within months, mass forest die-offs would begin.[4]Some drought-resistant trees could survive for years, but others wouldn't (http://treephys.oxfordjournals.org/content/33/3/252.full). Huge amounts of dry, dead vegetation lead inevitably to fire, and within a few years, most of the world's forests would have burned. Forests store huge amounts of CO2, and this burning would roughly double the amount of greenhouse gas in the atmosphere, accelerating global warming. All in all, Joanna's scenario would result in virtually all life dying out pretty fast. But then things would get even worse. [Image: image] Without a water cycle to weather rocks, the carbon-silicate feedback system which acts as a long-term thermostat to stabilize climate[5]CO2 is added to the atmosphere by volcanoes (although at the moment, it's being added about ten times faster by people.) When water flows over certain rocks, chemical reactions suck CO2 from the air and eventually bury it in seafloor sediments. With less CO2, the planet gets colder. A colder planet means less evaporation, which means less weathering, which means CO2 removal slows down. This feedback loop—which operates over much longer timescales than human-caused climate change—is probably what's kept the Earth's temperature relatively stable over the last few billion years (give or take a few snowball Earths (http://www.snowballearth.org/overview.html)) even though the Sun has gotten hotter (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faint_young_Sun_paradox). would shut down. Without this feedback, volcanic CO2 would build up in our atmosphere, leading—in the long term—to scorching temperatures similar to what's happened on Venus.[6]Interestingly, because of Venus's lighter color (and thus higher reflectivity), it only absorbs about half the solar radiation that Earth does despite being substantially closer to the Sun. The thick blanket of CO2 in its atmosphere is what keeps it hot (http://www.skepticalscience.com/Venus-runaway-greenhouse-effect.htm). We were going to lose our oceans anyway. As the Sun gets hotter, eventually water will start escaping through evaporation, and—one way or another—the planet will dry out and heat up. However, the loss of the oceans never seemed like something worth worrying too much about, since it's a billion years in the future. The oceans will be here long after our species is gone. [Image: image] Unless Joanna ruins everything.
items.original_question: 如果地球上所有的水体都神奇地消失了，会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If all the water on Earth vanished instantly, Earth would become uninhabitable almost immediately.

First, every ocean, lake, river, groundwater reservoir, glacier, cloud, and all water vapor in the atmosphere would disappear. Since water is essential for all known life, nearly all plants, animals, fungi, and microbes would die very quickly. Humans would not survive for long either, not just because there would be no drinking water, but because food production would collapse at once.

The climate would also change drastically. Oceans currently store and redistribute huge amounts of heat, so without them, temperatures would swing much more violently between day and night and between seasons. Rain would stop entirely, because there would be no water cycle. With no evaporation, clouds, or precipitation, Earth would become a dry, barren world.

The atmosphere would be affected too. Water vapor is a greenhouse gas, so removing it would reduce part of the greenhouse effect, but the larger effect is that the planet would lose the oceans’ thermal buffering and weather system. Also, much of Earth’s oxygen originally came from organisms tied to water, and with ecosystems gone, atmospheric composition would gradually change over time.

Geologically, the empty ocean basins would be exposed, revealing deep seafloor trenches and mid-ocean ridges. Erosion would slow dramatically without rain and rivers. Plate tectonics could also be affected over longer timescales, because water helps rocks melt and influences subduction and volcanism. Without it, Earth’s internal geology might behave differently.

There would also be catastrophic structural effects if water inside living things vanished too. If the question includes all water everywhere, then cells would collapse instantly, and most organisms would die at once. If it includes water bound in rocks and underground minerals, the effects would be even more extreme, potentially destabilizing parts of the crust and mantle.

So in short: if all Earth’s water vanished, life would end, weather would cease, the surface would become a dry rocky wasteland, and the planet would start to resemble a much harsher, more lifeless world than it is now.

items.question: How Long Could Humanity Survive on Cannibalism Alone?
human_answers: There are about 500 trillion calories of human in the world. If it could be frozen or otherwise preserved, that would be enough—at least in terms of raw calories—to keep a tiny breeding population (http://www.newscientist.com/article/dn1936-magic-number-for-space-pioneers-calculated.html#.U8a1mo2gFSE) alive for millions of years. [Image: image] Eating nothing but meat sounds bad, nutritionally, but the lack of vegetables wouldn't necessarily kill you. People can survive on high-meat or all-meat diets, especially if they eat things like organ meat and bone marrow; there are more vitamins and nutrients found in those which are missing from the narrower range of mammal skeletal muscle and fat in the typical western diet. The US experienced meat shortages during World War II because so much food was being diverted to soldiers and allies overseas. In response to this, the US government decided to encourage Americans to eat more organs and other animal body parts. They employed some of the world's best anthropologists, psychologists, social scientists, and food scientists to figure out a way to change American eating habits. One of the ideas the project had was that these foods should be rebranded as variety meats.[1]More on this in the hilarious Mary Roach book Gulp: Adventures on the Alimentary Canal (http://www.amazon.com/Gulp-Adventures-Alimentary-Mary-Roach/dp/0393081575) A Google Books search (https://books.google.com/ngrams/graph?content=variety+meats&year_start=1800&year_end=2008&corpus=17&smoothing=3) shows the phrase appearing suddenly in US books around that time (a pattern not seen in British books (https://books.google.com/ngrams/graph?content=variety+meats&year_start=1800&year_end=2008&corpus=18&smoothing=3).) When the war ended, many of these research efforts were dropped, but this 2002 article (https://books.google.com/ngrams/graph?content=variety+meats&year_start=1800&year_end=2008&corpus=15&smoothing=3) tries to piece together what they learned. There are a lot of things we don't understand (http://www.nature.com/news/nutrition-vitamins-on-trial-1.15459) about nutritional deficiencies, and—to put it mildly—a lot of dispute over what kind of diets are healthy or aren't healthy. But no matter what nutrients we would or wouldn't get in Quinn's scenario, we'd face a bigger problem: contaminated food. Even if you cooked your meat, it would be hard to avoid all kinds of disease exposure as you worked your way through the remains of the human population. [Image: image] In a small enough population, every outbreak is a pandemic; it wouldn't take long for something to wipe you out. There are also some obvious practical problems. Unless you're one of a small handful of people (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_briefcase), you have no way to kill the majority of living humans without some of them killing you first. Let's consider a different scenario, one probably more in line with what Quinn was imagining: What if half the population ate the other half?[2]On second thought, I really have no idea what specific scenario Quinn was imagining, and I'm not sure I want to know. If the average human weighs 50 kilograms and eats a couple thousand calories per day, then—according to Ryan North (http://www.topatoco.com/merchant.mvc?Screen=PROD&Store_Code=TO&Product_Code=QW-PERSON&Category_Code=QW)—then one person contains enough meat to feed another person for about a month. If, every month, half the population eats the other half, we could go for 32 months[3]Which should make sense to the computer science students out there, since "7 billion" is just barely too big to store in a 32-bit integer. of cannibalism before the second-to-last person was eaten by the last. Eating people who have eaten other people is a bad idea. For starters, it's a bad idea because you're eating people. Why are you eating people!? But it's also bad because it's an effective way to transmit prion diseases (https://www.cdc.gov/prions/). On the other hand, most prion diseases have lengthy incubation periods, so it might be a lesser concern in a world where you have a 50% chance of getting eaten every month. Lastly, we'd have to decide who got eaten in which round. We could fight it out, or—to be fair—we could pair off and flip coins. If we did, the result would be, literally, ... [Image: image] ... the tournament bracket (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bracket_(tournament)) to end all tournament brackets.
items.original_question: 人类仅靠同类相食还能生存多久？
items.model_answer:
Not long at all. In a closed human-only population, cannibalism cannot sustain humanity, because it does not create new food energy; it only recycles the calories already stored in human bodies, and with losses at every step.

The key reason is basic ecology and thermodynamics. Humans are consumers, not primary producers. We get energy from plants, animals, and other external food sources that ultimately trace back to sunlight or some other outside energy input. If humans tried to survive on eating only other humans, the total usable energy in the population would steadily shrink. Every living person burns calories just staying alive, moving, keeping warm, and so on. When one person eats another, only part of the victim’s stored energy becomes available to the eater; much is lost through metabolism, digestion inefficiency, waste, and the energy the victim already spent before being eaten.

items.question: What If I Fired an Infinitely Powerful Laser into the Sky?
human_answers: A lot of the time, if a question includes the word "infinity," the answer is "an infinite amount"—when there's an answer at all. An infinitely strong laser pointer would deliver an infinite amount of energy to the air in its path, which would in turn radiate an infinite amount of energy in all directions, which would destroy everything. For more on this, see What If #13 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/13/). Except that's not really the right answer to your question. Most of our equations don't really work when you put "infinity" in them. So the right answer is "an infinitely strong laser beam isn't a real thing." [Image: image] But if you made a laser pointer stronger and stronger, the result would look more and more like what I described. This is sort of like the mathematical idea of taking a limit; you can't say what happens at infinity, but you can see how it acts as you get closer and closer to it. Since we looked at the "destroying the world" consequence in question #13, let's look at the other part of your question: The random aiming. First of all, if you aimed in a truly random direction, you would have an almost 50% chance of hitting the Earth. Almost 50%, but not quite. If we assume you're on a spherical Earth, ignoring hills and trees,[1]And ignoring refraction. you have a slightly better chance of missing the ground than hitting it—because you're holding the laser above the surface, and the Earth curves away from you: [Image: image] If you miss the Earth, 89,999 times out of 90,000, your beam will pass right out of the galaxy without hitting anything. When it does hit something, it will almost always be the Sun or the Moon. The first time I met astronomer Phil Plait (http://www.slate.com/blogs/bad_astronomy.html) in person, he mentioned a clever trick for calculating the "area" of the sky:[2]"Learn This One Weird Trick,"" he said, "Invented By a Local Schoolteacher!"‌[3]He didn't say that.
