The area of a sphere is 4πr2. Ok, great, but what's the "radius" of the sky? Well, if the sky is a sphere around us, the radius is "one radian", because that's the radius of anything. But a radian is also 57.3 degrees, which means the sky is 57.3 degrees "away" from us. 4 times pi times 57.3 = 41,253 square degrees. The Moon and the Sun each take up about 0.2 square degrees, and so the chance of hitting either one of them is about 1 in 180,000. Those aren't great odds, but they're better than the odds of hitting anything else. [Image: image] To calculate the odds of hitting something else, we can use this handy angular size (http://xkcd.com/1276/) reference as a shortcut, dividing the rough angular size of the object in the chart by the Earth's total area to see how much of the sky it covers. The odds of hitting one of Jupiter's moons, for example, are on the order of one in a trillion. Stars are even worse. Your odds of hitting any star at all on your way out of the galaxy are almost zero, even if you aim for the core. This is good, though! If your odds of hitting a star were high, it would mean the galaxy would be opaque. Since most "lines of sight" would terminate on a star, it would be very hard or impossible to see past our galaxy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Ultra-Deep_Field).[4]There are only a few stars in our galaxy in the Hubble Ultra-Deep Field image. The fact that the night sky is dark is at the core of Olbers' Paradox (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olbers'_paradox).[5]I was so tempted to vandalize this article to put a [citation needed] after every claim that the night sky was dark. If you kept shooting long enough, eventually you'd hit a planet. Neptune would be the hardest to hit, followed by Uranus and Mercury. Pluto would be the hardest, but it might be worth it. An impossibly powerful laser would at least settle that debate. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 如果我向天空中的任意一点发射无限强的激光束，会造成多少伤害？
items.model_answer:
If you fired an “infinitely powerful” laser into the sky, the first thing to say is that this isn’t physically possible in our universe. “Infinite power” would mean delivering unlimited energy per unit time, and the laws of physics break down long before that. But as a thought experiment, the result would be catastrophic and not at all like a normal laser beam shooting cleanly into space.

The air would not stay transparent. A sufficiently intense laser ionizes the atmosphere almost instantly, turning the beam path into an expanding channel of plasma hotter than the surface of the Sun. Instead of a neat beam, you would get a violent column of glowing, exploding air. The surrounding atmosphere would absorb huge amounts of energy, producing a blast wave far beyond any conventional explosion. In practice, the air itself becomes the target.

If you keep increasing the power, the energy density becomes so extreme that matter near the source is vaporized immediately, including the laser device, the ground around it, and likely a large region of Earth’s surface. The beam would trigger intense X-rays and gamma rays from the plasma, and the event would resemble a high-energy astrophysical disaster more than a weapon.

At truly absurd levels, gravity becomes important. Energy has mass-equivalent through E = mc², so if enough energy is concentrated into a small enough region, it could form a black hole. An actually infinite-power beam would imply infinite energy flow, which is not compatible with a stable physical situation. In any realistic extension of known physics, you do not get “a really bright laser to space”; you get the destruction of the local environment, likely the atmosphere in the beam path, and possibly a gravitational collapse if the energy is concentrated enough.

So the direct answer is: you would not simply punch a beam into the sky. The atmosphere would turn into a violently exploding plasma channel almost instantly, the surroundings would be annihilated, and at the limit of truly infinite power, the scenario stops making physical sense at all.

items.question: What If One Person Owned All the Money in the World?
human_answers: So you've somehow found a way to gather all the world's money. We won't worry about how you did it—let's just assume you invented some kind of money-summoning magic spell. [Image: image] Physical currency—coins and bills—represents just a small percentage of the world's wealth. In theory, you could edit all the property records on Earth to say that you own all the land and edit all the banking records to say you own all the money. But everyone else would disagree with those records, and they would edit them back or ignore them. Money is an idea, and you can't make the entire world respect your idea. Getting all the world's cash, on the other hand, is much more straightforward. There's a certain amount of cash in the world—it's about $4 trillion—and you want it all. It won't necessarily do anything for you, since—without the cooperation of the outside world—you probably won't be able to spend it. But maybe you can swim around in it, like Scrooge McDuck in his giant room full of gold. [Image: image] So you cast your magic spell and summon all the money. The pile of cash is the size of the Empire State Building, but heavier. You probably don't want to be standing under it, so let's assume you're standing over here, off to the side: [Image: image] The vast majority of the weight in the pile is coins, and the biggest single contributor is the US penny. Despite periodic efforts to kill off the penny (http://www.retirethepenny.org/), the US Mint keeps producing more of them. [Image: image] There are probably 150 billion pennies[1]A 1996 GAO report mentioned a US Mint estimate of the number of pennies in circulation: 132 billion. If you're excited by phrases like "General Accounting Office", "auditing standards", and "Subcommittee on Domestic and International Monetary Policy", you can read the report here (http://gao.gov/assets/110/106568.pdf). If you're so excited about penny statistics that the GAO report isn't enough for you, you're in luck: There's another way to derive this number. We can get an idea of the number of pennies in circulation by looking at all the change in our pockets, counting the dates, and using that to estimate a loss rate. In 1999, some statisticians recorded the dates on 1,000 pennies they had lying around, and published the data in the book Workshop Statistics: Discovery with Data and Fathom, page 389 (http://books.google.com/books?id=wGMRja1vE0kC&lpg=PA389&pg=PA389#v=onepage&q&f=false). By plotting the frequency with which they saw pennies of various ages against the frequency we'd expect from US Mint production numbers, we can estimate the rate at which older pennies drop out of circulation per year. Using their numbers, I come up with an estimate of about 190,000,000,000 pennies in circulation. We can then apply the same formula to previous dates, and come up with a number for 1996, to check against the GAO number. (I have a lot of spare time on my hands.) Surprisingly, this produces an estimate that's still about 190,000,000,000. Either number (190 billion or 132 billion) is probably a reasonable estimate, but if you're serious about your penny statistics—and if you've read this far, you must be—you should probably go with the US Mint guess. After all, they presumably know a thing or two about counting pennies. currently in circulation, for a total weight of over 300,000 tons. In total, US coins and bills are responsible for about 30% of the pile's weight, while the European Union—which has barely been minting coins for a decade—contributes 15%. Unfortunately for you, the pile doesn't stay a pile for long,[2]When you pour lots of loose material in a heap, it tends to form a cone. Different materials will form cones with different slopes; the steepness of the slope for a given material is called its angle of repose. I've never found the exact angle of repose for coins—or had enough of them to test it—but a forum poster with the username Master of Coin (who claims to be well-acquainted with "how piles of coins 'slish' about") says (http://asoiaf.westeros.org/index.php/topic/78114-the-hobbit-a-long-expected-spoiler-movie-thread/?p=3985923) that it's probably no more than 5 or 10 degrees. and what seems like a safe distance isn't so safe. In 1919, a tank of molasses in Boston collapsed. Molasses is thick, so you might think it would flow out slowly, but it didn't. The wave of molasses swept down the streets too fast to outrun, demolishing buildings and killing 21 people. Something similar happens with the pile of coins. As it collapses, the pile spreads outward, a wave of money carrying a staggering amount of momentum. The pennies, quarters, loonies, and euros scour the landscape in an expanding ring. Within seconds, the wave of coins engulfs you and you die. [Image: image] There are ways to avoid this. You could, say, build a wall around the coins to contain them. Unfortunately, then you might face a problem worse than death: Building code violations. Heavy skyscrapers need ground strong enough to support them. Places with large skyscrapers, like those in Manhattan, need bedrock sturdy enough to hold them up.[3]For a long time, people said that this was why there was a gap in Manhattan's skyline—the bedrock wasn't strong enough to support skyscrapers in the middle. However, a 2011 paper in the Journal of Economic History (http://journals.cambridge.org/action/displayAbstract?fromPage=online&aid=8429737) says that this is a myth, and the bedrock had little influence on the location of skyscrapers. A search through this giant PDF of NYC building codes (http://www2.iccsafe.org/states/newyorkcity/Building/PDFs/Chapter%2018_Soils%20and%20Foundations.pdf) suggests that if we went ahead with this plan, we would be in serious danger of violating section 1804 ("ALLOWABLE BEARING PRESSURES"). Which makes me wonder: Did Scrooge McDuck ever have to worry about this stuff? [Image: image]
items.original_question: 人们有时会说“如果我拥有世界上所有的钱……”来讨论如果他们没有财务限制他们会做什么。但我很好奇，如果一个人拥有世界上所有的钱，会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If one person owned all the money in the world, it would not mean they literally owned all real wealth, but it would still break the economy.

Money is mainly a tool for exchange. Real wealth is food, land, factories, energy, skills, houses, machines, and labor. So even if one person held every dollar, euro, yen, and so on, they would not instantly “own everything.” Other people would still physically control farms, businesses, homes, and their own ability to work.

But the immediate problem is that everyone else would have no money to buy or sell with. Normal trade would freeze because money is what lets people exchange goods efficiently. Workers could not be paid, customers could not buy products, and businesses could not operate in the usual way. Banks would also fail to function if all money balances were concentrated in one place.

What happens next depends on whether that person spends the money.

If they just hoarded it, the result would be extreme deflation and economic collapse. Prices would crash because nobody else had cash to spend. Production would fall, unemployment would soar, and people would quickly switch to alternatives like barter, private credit, local currencies, or direct government rationing.

If they started spending it, they could temporarily control a huge share of economic activity, because whoever receives the money can then transact again. In effect, the owner of all money would decide where demand exists. That would give them enormous power over markets and politics. But even then, they could not buy things if people refused to sell, if governments intervened, or if social order broke down.

In reality, governments and central banks would not allow this situation to continue. They could create new money, redenominate the currency, freeze accounts, impose confiscation, or replace the monetary system entirely. Modern money is largely a social and legal system, not just piles of cash. If one person captured all of it, states would simply change the rules.

So the short answer is: one person owning all the money would cause a severe monetary crisis, but not permanent ownership of the world’s real wealth. Society would likely respond by creating a new money system, and the value of that person’s monopoly would quickly collapse.

items.question: What If Everything except Earth Were Made of Antimatter?
human_answers: This one doesn't end well for us. But—unlike most scenarios involving the word "antimatter"—the end is surprisingly slow and drawn-out. [Image: image] The whole universe is matter, as far as we can tell. No one is sure why (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baryon_asymmetry) there's more matter than antimatter, since the laws of physics are pretty (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CP_violation#CP-symmetry) symmetrical, and so there's no reason to expect there to be more of one than the other.[1]Although when it comes down to it, there's no reason to expect anything at all. It's possible that galaxies are made of antimatter, and we just haven't noticed because we haven't tried to touch them. This is a cool idea, but if there are zones of matter and zones of antimatter, we should see a telltale gamma-ray glow from the boundary between the zones. So far, we haven't (http://www.researchgate.net/publication/1746009_When_Clusters_Collide_Constraints_On_Antimatter_On_The_Largest_Scales) seen that, although another telescope (http://arxiv.org/abs/1401.7258) might help. [Image: image] If the rest of the universe were swapped out for antimatter, we'd be in trouble. Outer space isn't really "space";[2]As far as I know, it really is "outer", for what that's worth. it's full of a thin gas.[3]Technically, plasma.​[4]Technically, there's also a substantial quantity of solid grains of dust.​[5]Look, there's a bunch of little bits that are hard to see, ok?.​[6]Ok, they're not always (https://www.flickr.com/groups/northernlight/) hard to see (https://www.google.com/search?q=1833+leonids&tbm=isch). The Earth's magnetic field (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magnetic_Fields) protects us from the solar wind, and would protect us from an anti-solar wind, too. A tiny fraction of the particles from the Sun do reach the Earth, funneled down by our magnetic field, and create the aurora. In this scenario, the aurora would get a lot brighter, but most of the time not bright enough to really cause problems. Meteorites would be the real problem. The Earth sweeps up space dust as it travels around its orbit.[7]Unfortunately for us, antimatter is probably (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_interaction_of_antimatter) attracted to matter by gravity. About 100 tons of dust per day enters the atmosphere in the form of tiny grains, most weighing about 10^-5 grams. An additional similar (http://books.google.com/books?id=eqd4e34uE-MC&pg=PA78) average per-day amount arrives in giant clumps all at once (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicxulub_impactor). This inflow of antimatter dust would collide with the top of our atmosphere and be annihilated. The interactions between the nuclei and antinuclei and protons and antiprotons would be complex,[8]A lot (http://www.iaps.inaf.it/sz/integral2013/talks-posters/40-2013_10%20Antimatter%20Universe_von%20Ballmoos.pdf) of the energy would be carried away by neutrinos (http://turtlepedia.wikia.com/wiki/Neutrinos). but the end result would be a lot of gamma rays, which would turn into a lot of heat. This steady flow of material would be worst around dawn, when your house was facing in the direction of Earth's motion. The heat and light added by the antimatter would most likely be enough to tip the Earth into a "runaway greenhouse (http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v504/n7479/full/nature12827.html?WT.ec_id=NATURE-20131212)" scenario, turning the Earth into something resembling Venus. But the big asteroids would get us first. Even a relatively small object like the Chelyabinsk meteor (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelyabinsk_meteor) would deliver as much energy as the meteor that killed the dinosaurs.[9]Although it would deliver it to the top of the atmosphere, so in some ways it wouldn't be as bad. Fairly large asteroids enter the atmosphere every few months (http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v503/n7475/full/nature12741.html)—mostly unnoticed. If they were all antimatter, each one would trigger a tremendous pulse of energy in the sky and ignite a massive firestorm.[10]If an antimatter meteor is large enough, encountering a cloud could launch some of it backward without completely destroying it (http://books.google.com/books?id=gI-nZdadvJ4C&pg=PA140). However, it's hard to come up with a practical (http://weeklyworldnews.com/headlines/43206/asteroid-to-bounce-off-earth-today/) scenario in which a meteor would exhibit this effect in Earth's atmosphere—unless it were so large that it would have basically destroyed the planet anyway. Right now, it's still an open question whether any significant percentage of the stuff in the sky is made of antimatter. It's probably not, but we'd need to build another orbiting gamma-ray telescope to really be sure. However, it's easy to use a telescope to rule out one possibility: That everything in the sky is antimatter. [Image: image] If you have a telescope, maybe you can get that result published.
items.original_question: 如果除了地球之外一切都是反物质怎么办？
items.model_answer:
If everything except Earth were made of antimatter, Earth would not last long.

The key fact is that when matter and antimatter touch, they annihilate and turn into energy, mostly high-energy gamma rays and other particles. If Earth stayed ordinary matter while the atmosphere, Moon, Sun, planets, interplanetary dust, and the rest of the universe were antimatter, then the boundary where Earth met its surroundings would immediately become a gigantic annihilation zone.

The first problem would be the atmosphere. If only Earth itself were matter but the air above it were antimatter, then every contact between Earth’s surface and the air would produce continuous annihilation. The same would happen all through the oceans’ surfaces and in the upper atmosphere. The energy release would be enormous—far beyond nuclear weapons on a global scale. Earth’s surface would be blasted by intense radiation and heat, and the planet would rapidly be stripped, melted, and likely partly vaporized.

Even if you tried to rescue the scenario by saying Earth includes its own normal-matter atmosphere, it still would not help for long. The solar wind from an antimatter Sun, antimatter meteoroids, and antimatter gas and dust in space would hit Earth’s magnetosphere and upper atmosphere and annihilate. The incoming radiation would be lethal. More importantly, the Sun itself being antimatter would still shine almost normally in terms of gravity and large-scale astrophysics, because antimatter is expected to behave gravitationally like matter. So Earth would keep orbiting it, but ordinary sunlight from an antimatter Sun would not be dangerous by itself—photons are just photons. The danger comes from any actual antimatter particles reaching Earth.

The Moon would be catastrophic too if it were antimatter. Its gravitational pull would still be the same, so it would orbit Earth as usual, but any dust, solar wind, or exchanged particles between Earth and Moon would annihilate. If Earth ever physically contacted antimatter matter on a large scale, the explosion would be devastating.

Would the entire universe explode at once? No. Matter and antimatter only annihilate when they meet. Empty space would keep many objects separated. Stars, galaxies, and planets made of antimatter could exist and look much like ordinary ones from a distance. In fact, an antimatter galaxy would emit the same ordinary light as a matter galaxy. The main observable difference would be intense gamma rays at the boundaries where matter and antimatter regions mix.

So in this scenario, the universe as a whole could still exist, but Earth specifically would be in extreme trouble because it is immersed in antimatter surroundings. Unless Earth were somehow protected by a perfect barrier that prevented any antimatter from touching it, the planet would quickly become uninhabitable and probably be destroyed or at least severely ablated by annihilation at its boundary with the rest of the world.

In short: if everything except Earth were antimatter, gravity and orbits would mostly work normally, but contact with the surrounding antimatter would release so much energy that Earth would be rapidly sterilized, scorched, and likely torn apart.

items.question: What If You Teleported to the Surface of the Sun for One Nanosecond?
human_answers: Believe it or not, this wouldn't even warm you. The temperature of the surface of the Sun is about 5,800 K,[1]Or °C. When temperatures start having many digits in them, it doesn't really matter. give or take. If you stayed there for a while, you'd be cooked to a cinder, but a nanosecond is not very long—it's enough time for light to travel almost exactly a foot.[2]A light-nanosecond is 11.8 inches (0.29981 meters), which is annoyingly close to a foot. I think it would be nice to redefine the foot as exactly 1 light nanosecond. Because we don't have enough unit confusion in the world already. This raises some obvious questions, like "Do we redefine the mile to keep it at 5,280 feet?" and "Do we redefine the inch?" and "Wait, why are we doing this?" But I figure other people can sort that out. I'm just the idea guy here. [Image: image] I'm going to assume you're facing toward the Sun. In general, you should avoid looking directly at the Sun, but it's hard to avoid when it takes up a full 180 degrees of your view. [Image: image] In that nanosecond, about a microjoule of energy would enter your eye. A microjoule of light is not a lot. If you stare at a computer monitor with your eyes closed, then open them and shut them quickly, your eye will take in about as much light from the screen during your reverse blink[3]Is there a word for that? There should be a word for that. as it would during a nanosecond on the Sun's surface. During the nanosecond on the Sun, photons from the Sun would flood into your eye and strike your retinal cells. Then, at the end of the nanosecond, you'd jump back home. At this point, the retinal cells wouldn't even have begun responding. Over the next few million nanoseconds (milliseconds) the retinal cells—having absorbed a bunch of light energy—would get into gear and start signaling your brain that something had happened. [Image: image] You would spend one nanosecond on the Sun, but it would take 30,000,000 nanoseconds for your brain to notice. From your point of view, all you would see was a flash. The flash would seem to last much longer than your time on the Sun, only fading as your retinal cells quieted down. The energy absorbed by your skin would be minor—about 10-5 joules per cm2 of exposed skin. For comparison, according to the IEEE P1584 standard (as quoted (http://www.arcadvisor.com/faq/threshold-incident-energy-second-degree-burn.html) on ArcAdvisor.com), holding your finger in the blue flame of a butane lighter for one second delivers about 5 joules per cm2 to the skin, which is roughly the threshold for receiving a second-degree burn. The heat during your Sun visit would be five orders of magnitude weaker. Other than the dim flash in your eyes, you wouldn't even notice. But what if you got the coordinates wrong? The Sun's surface is relatively cool. It's hotter than, like, Phoenix,[citation needed (https://www.google.com/search?tbm=isch&q=gibson+citation)] but compared to the interior, it's downright chilly. The surface is a few thousand degrees, but the interior is a few million degrees.[4]The corona, the thin gas high above the surface, is also several million degrees, and no one knows why (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corona#Coronal_heating_problem). What if you spent a nanosecond there? [Image: image] The Stefan-Boltzmann law (http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/thermo/stefan.html) lets us calculate how much heat you'd be exposed to while inside the Sun.[5]There's also direct pressure from the heavy particles, protons and stuff, bouncing around, but the radiation turns out to be the dominant component. I'm going to hijack this note to ask another question: How does this transporter work, anyway? When you teleport somewhere, presumably it does gets rid of the matter that was in the way, so you don't end up combining yourself with whatever was there. A simple solution is to have the teleporters swap matter between the two locations. Kirk gets teleported down to the planet, a Kirk-sized chunk of air gets teleported up to the Enterprise. So what would happen if an AJ-shaped chunk of Sun-interior gets teleported to snowy Colorado, then we just left it there? The protons inside the Sun bounce around at speeds of about 350 km/s (about half of the Sun's escape velocity at that depth, for weird and deep (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virial_theorem) reasons.) Freed from their crushingly hot neighborhood, the whole collection of protons would burst outward, pouring light and heat energy into their surroundings. The energy released would be somewhere between a large bomb and a small nuclear weapon. It's not good. You would exceed the IEEE P1584B standard for second-degree burns after one femtosecond in the Sun.[6]Although it wouldn't be a second-degree burn until many picoseconds later, since the definition of a second-degree burn is one which damages some of the underlying layers of tissue—and in the first few femtoseconds, light wouldn't have time to reach the underlying tissue. A nanosecond—the time you're spending there—is 1,000,000 femtoseconds. This does not end well for you. There's some good news: Deep in the Sun, the photons carrying energy around have very short wavelengths—they're mostly a mix of what we'd consider hard and soft X-rays.[7]<what_if_book_reference>I wonder if there are more soft or hard x-ray photons in the universe.</what_if_book_reference> This means they penetrate your body to various depths, heating your internal organs and also ionizing your DNA, causing irreversible damage before they even start burning you. Looking back, I notice that I started this paragraph with "there's some good news." I don't know why I did that. [Image: image] In Greek legend, Icarus (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icarus) flew too close to the Sun, and the heat melted his wings and he fell to his death. But "melting" is a phase change which is a function of temperature, a measure of internal energy, which is the integral of incident power flux over time. His wings didn't melt because he flew too close to the Sun, they melted because he spent too much time there. Visit briefly, in little hops, and you can go anywhere. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 当我大约 8 岁的时候，在科罗拉多州寒冷的天气里铲雪时，我希望自己能立即被传送到太阳表面，只持续一纳秒，然后立即被传送回来。我想这足以让我暖和起来，但又不足以伤害我。实际上会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If you somehow teleported to the Sun’s visible “surface” for one nanosecond, you would still die essentially instantly.

The key point is that the Sun’s surface, the photosphere, is about 5,500°C to 6,000°C. Even though one nanosecond is extremely short, the environment is so intense that you would be hit by an enormous burst of thermal radiation, and you would also be surrounded by superheated plasma rather than breathable gas. Your skin and outer tissues would begin to vaporize almost immediately. You would not have time to consciously perceive anything, since human reaction times are millions of times longer than a nanosecond.

However, one nanosecond is so brief that you would not have time to be completely “incinerated away” in the everyday sense during that interval alone. The damage would begin at the surface first: extreme heating, ionization, and explosive expansion of exposed material. If you were returned after exactly one nanosecond, your body would already have suffered catastrophic thermal and radiation damage, almost certainly incompatible with life.

Gravity would not be the main issue on that timescale. The Sun’s surface gravity is about 28 times Earth’s, but over only a nanosecond it would not have time to significantly accelerate or crush you. The dominant effect is the heat and radiation.

So the careful answer is: you would not vanish instantly, but the solar environment would start destroying your body immediately, and a one-nanosecond visit would still be lethally damaging.

items.question: What If Auto Racing Had Only One Rule: The Driver Must Survive?
human_answers: The best you'll be able to do is about 90 minutes. There are lots of ways you could build your vehicle—an electric car,[1]With wheels designed to dig into the pavement on turns. a rocket sled, or a carriage that runs along a rail on the track—but in each case, it's pretty easy to develop the design to the point where the human is the weakest part. The problem is acceleration. On the curved parts of the track, drivers will feel powerful G forces.[2]Which you can broadly call either "centrifugal" or "centripetal" forces, depending on exactly which type of pedant you want to annoy. The Daytona Speedway in Florida has two main curves, and if the vehicles go around them too fast, the drivers will die from the acceleration alone. [Image: image] For extremely brief periods, such as during car accidents, people can experience hundreds of Gs and survive. (One G is the pull you feel when standing on the ground under Earth's gravity.) Fighter pilots can experience up to 10 Gs during maneuvers, and—perhaps because of that—10 Gs is often used as a rough limit for what people can handle. However, fighter pilots only experience 10 Gs very briefly. Our driver would be experiencing them, in pulses, for minutes and probably hours. There's a good NASA document on the physical effects of acceleration here (http://ntrs.nasa.gov/archive/nasa/casi.ntrs.nasa.gov/19930020462.pdf), and a particularly helpful chart in Figure 5 here (http://history.nasa.gov/conghand/mannedev.htm). But the most fun data comes from John Paul Stapp. Stapp was an Air Force officer who strapped himself into a rocket sled and pushed his body to the limit, taking careful notes after every run. You can read a great essay (http://www.ejectionsite.com/stapp.htm) about him on the Ejection Site (http://www.ejectionsite.com/). The whole story is fascinating, but my favorite line is, "... Stapp was promoted to the rank of major [and] reminded of the 18 G limit of human survivability ..." Stapp aside, the data shows that for periods on the order of an hour, normal humans can only handle 3-6 Gs of acceleration. If we limit our vehicle to 4 Gs, its top speed on the turns at Daytona will be about 240 mph. At this speed, the course will take about 2 hours to complete—which is definitely faster than anyone has driven it in an actual car, but not by that much. But wait! What about the straightaways? The vehicle will be accelerating during the turns, but coasting on the straightaways. We could instead accelerate the vehicle up to a higher speed while on straight segments, then decelerate it back down when approaching the end. This would result in a speed profile like this: [Image: image] This has the additional advantage that—with some clever back-and-forth maneuvering on the track—the driver can be kept at a relatively constant acceleration through the whole trip, hopefully making the forces easier to endure. [Image: image] Keep in mind that the direction of the acceleration will keep changing. Humans can survive acceleration best if they're accelerated forward, in the direction of their chest, like a driver accelerating forward. The body is least capable of being accelerated downward toward the feet, which causes blood to pile up in the head. To keep our driver alive, we'll need to swivel them around so they're always being pressed against their back. (But we have to be careful not to change direction too fast, or the centrifᵫtal[3]Splitting the difference. force from the swiveling of the seat will itself become deadly!) [Image: image] The fastest modern Daytona racers take about 3 hours to finish the 200 laps. If limited to 4 Gs, our driver will finish the course in a little under an hour and 45 minutes. If we raise the limit to 6 Gs, the time drops to an hour and 20. At 10 Gs—well past human tolerability—it would still take an hour. (It would also involve breaking the sound barrier on the backstretch.) So, barring dubious concepts like liquid breathing (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_breathing), human biology limits us to Daytona finishing times over an hour. What if we drop the "survive" requirement? How fast can we get the vehicle to go around the track? Imagine a "vehicle" anchored with Kevlar straps to a pivot in the center, reinforced with a counterweight on the other side. In effect, this is a giant centrifuge. This lets us apply one of my favorite weird equations,[4]See footnote [8] in article #86 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/86/). which says that the edge of a spinning disc can't go faster than the square root of the specific strength[5](tensile strength divided by density) of the material it's made of. For strong materials like Kevlar, this speed is 1-2 km/s. At those speeds, a capsule could conceivably finish the race in about 10 minutes—although definitely not with a living driver inside. Ok, forget the centrifuge. What if we build a solid chute, like a bobsled course, and send a ball bearing (our "vehicle") rocketing down it? Sadly, the disc equation strikes again—the ball bearing can't roll faster than a couple km/s or it will be spinning too fast and will tear itself apart. Instead of making it roll, what if we make it slide? We could imagine a diamond cube sliding along a smooth diamond chute. Since it doesn't need to rotate, it could potentially survive more accelerations than a rolling ball bearing. However, the sliding would result in substantially more friction than the ball bearing example, and our diamond might catch fire (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WWpm6_Y7ASI). [Image: image] To defeat friction, we could levitate the capsule with magnetic fields, and make it progressively smaller and lighter to accelerate and steer it more easily. Oops—we've accidentally built a particle accelerator. And while it doesn't exactly fit the criteria in Hunter's question, a particle accelerator makes for a neat comparison. The particles in the LHC's beam go very close to the speed of light. At that speed, they complete 500 miles (30 laps) in 2.7 milliseconds. Wikipedia lists (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_motor_racing_tracks) about 850 motor racing tracks. The LHC beam could run the equivalent of a full Daytona 500 on each of those 850 tracks, one after another, in about 2 seconds, before the drivers had made it to the first turn. [Image: image] And that's really as fast as you can go.
items.original_question: 如果你抛开赛车比赛的所有规则，举办一场比赛，只是让一个人以尽可能快的速度绕赛道 200 倍，那么什么策略会获胜呢？假设赛车手必须生存。
items.model_answer:
If auto racing had only one rule—“the driver must survive”—the sport would still exist, but it would become a very different kind of engineering competition. It would not turn into pure chaos, because survival alone imposes strong constraints on car design, track choice, speed, and race strategy. But it would become much less about close wheel-to-wheel spectacle and much more about risk management, vehicle protection, and minimizing the chance of a fatal crash.

The first big change would be in vehicle design. If survival were the only requirement, teams would build cars like armored survival capsules with huge crash structures, enclosed cockpits, advanced restraint systems, fire suppression, redundant controls, and probably active safety systems designed to prevent impacts in the first place. Aerodynamics would matter, but not just for speed—for stability. Cars would likely be heavier, tougher, and less fragile than modern race cars. Open-wheel designs would mostly disappear, because exposed wheels and exposed drivers create dangerous crash dynamics. Something closer to an ultra-safe prototype, or even a reinforced autonomous-looking shell around the driver, would make more sense.

Second, speed would not simply rise without limit. At first glance, “survive” sounds permissive: go as fast as you want as long as you don’t die. But in practice, survival probability drops sharply with impact energy, and crash energy scales roughly with the square of speed. That means every increase in speed makes fatal accidents much harder to guard against. So teams would face a tradeoff: go faster and risk exceeding the protection envelope of the car, or go slower and dramatically improve survival odds. If the only hard constraint is survival, rational teams would try to find the highest speed at which the probability of death remains acceptably close to zero. That could still be very fast on some tracks, but not absurdly fast everywhere.

Track design would also change. If there were no rules about track limits, contact, or layout, the safest way to race fast would be on wide tracks with enormous runoff areas, energy-absorbing barriers, minimal fixed obstacles, and gentle corner radii. Street circuits would make little sense. Narrow tracks lined with walls, trees, poles, or elevation traps would be avoided because they increase the chance that a survivable mistake becomes fatal. In fact, the “best” racing environment under this rule might look more like an enormous paved test facility than a traditional circuit.

Racecraft would change too. Without rules against blocking, contact, or dangerous maneuvers—other than the survival requirement—drivers would be much more cautious around one another, because another car is one of the biggest threats to survival. Close pack racing, especially at high speed, would be irrational unless the cars were engineered to survive multi-car impacts reliably. Drafting trains, side-by-side cornering, and aggressive overtakes might become rare, because they raise uncertainty. The safest competitive strategy might be to spread out, avoid traffic, and win through consistency and controlled speed rather than direct combat.

That said, the lack of any rule besides survival could also produce ugly incentives. Teams might exploit gray areas by making cars that are survivable for the driver but dangerous for everyone else, unless “the driver” is understood to mean every driver involved. If survival is judged only per entrant, then ramming or destabilizing competitors could become attractive if your own car is tank-like enough to protect you. So the exact interpretation matters enormously. If the rule means every driver must survive every race, then the sport would strongly favor non-contact formats and conservative safety margins. If it means only that your own driver must survive, the sport could become strategically hostile and ethically disturbing.

There is also the issue of uncertainty. Survival is not binary in the way a technical regulation is. Engineers can never guarantee survival in every conceivable crash, only reduce fatality risk. So enforcement becomes difficult. Would a team be penalized only after a death occurs? That would be a terrible governance model, because the first failure is irreversible. More realistically, the sport would evolve toward probabilistic safety engineering: crash testing, simulation, biomechanical limits, and design standards that demonstrate that likely accident scenarios are non-fatal. But once that happens, the “one rule” would naturally expand into many implied rules, because survival has to be operationalized.

In the long run, the sport would probably converge on something like this: extremely safe enclosed vehicles, highly controlled tracks, fewer sudden interactions, and heavy use of technology to keep cars stable and separated. It might become closer to high-speed time trialing or endurance testing than today’s dramatic racing. The winner would still be the fastest, but only within a tightly optimized envelope where fatal outcomes are engineered to be vanishingly unlikely.

So the direct answer is: auto racing with only the rule “the driver must survive” would not eliminate competition, but it would shift the entire sport toward safety-dominated design. Cars would become armored survival machines, tracks would become forgiving, drivers would race less aggressively, and the spectacle would likely become less chaotic but more technically sophisticated. In trying to maximize speed under a survival constraint, the sport would end up reinventing many of the safety principles that modern racing already uses—just with even more extreme emphasis.

items.question: What If Your Income Materialized around You in Cash?
human_answers: First, let's think about coins. The US federal minimum wage in the US is \$7.25/hour, which is about \$15,000/year for a full-time job. If you earn the minimum wage, you make a penny every 5 seconds during work hours, or every 20 seconds if you average it over your whole week. [Image: image] Someone making minimum wage in pennies would earn about 30 lbs of pennies per workday. Two weeks' worth of pay in pennies would fill a small carry-on suitcase. At 150 lbs, the suitcase would probably be too heavy to pick up. However, if they were paid in quarters instead of pennies, two weeks' pay would only weigh about 3 lbs. If paid in a typical mix of loose change,[1]The makeup of a "mix of loose change" depends on your spending habits. Lots of people have calculated this to estimate the amounts of change in a jar. One of the more careful theoretical calculation I've seen, which considers prices and sales tax, comes from Dan Kozikowski (http://dfkoz.tumblr.com/post/20389927354/whats-a-pound-of-change-worth). Since I've spent way too much time on this question over the years, for the record: If you're ever trying to guess the value of coins in a jar, my suggestion would be \$13.05/lb and \$468/gallon if the person doesn't use quarters for laundry or parking, \$9.53/lb and \$336/gallon if they do, and \$16.75/lb and \$611/gallon if they discard pennies. the US federal minimum wage is about one plastic water bottle full of coins per workday, and the median household earns three or four water bottles per workday. [Image: image] A CEO of a large company might make \$40,000 per workday (http://news.yahoo.com/median-ceo-pay-crosses-10-million-2013-104644141--finance.html). Assuming an 8-hour workday, that's 130 pennies per second. If paid in a mix of loose change, the CEO would earn about a water bottle of coins per minute, and a duffel bag full of loose change every hour, or 600 water bottles per workday: [Image: image] If you're a CEO working in a 300 ft2 office, the change would accumulate on the ground at a rate of about only half an inch per day. (If it were pennies, it would be more like 3" per day). It would mean frequently getting up to adjust your desk so it stayed on top of the pile, and I can't imagine your chair would be too stable, but it seems like it might be manageable. Lugging those 150-kg duffel bags to CoinStar every hour would be a hassle. If we allowed paper money, things would get easier. A dollar bill has a volume of about 1.55 mL, which means that a CEO paid in dollar bills would only need one large-ish duffel bag for a day's pay. If paid in \$100 bills, a CEO would only need a couple (http://xkcd.com/1070/) of duffel bags to carry home their year's salary. In either case, at 60-70 lbs, a duffel bag full of bills would be a little on the heavy side. [Image: image] Now, there are people who make a lot more than "typical CEOs". Mark Zuckerberg, Warren Buffett, and Bill Gates all made in the neighborhood of \$10 billion in 2013 (http://www.wealthx.com/articles/2013/revealed-billionaires-who-made-the-biggest-financial-gains-in-2013/). During the workday, that's a duffel bag full of \$100 bills every half-hour. Going back to our earlier metric, that's 25 water bottles full of change—one minimum-wage worker's daily salary—per second of the workday. [Image: image] If randomly dispensed from the ceiling in the form of loose change, Mark Zuckerberg's income would pile up at an inch every minute. There would be so many coins hitting the ground per second that it would meld into white noise.[2]The Mark Zuckerberg Money Pump would require over a kilowatt of power just to hoist the coins up to his ceiling and drop them. But that's not a problem. Even a penny is worth enough to pay for the electricity to hoist itself several thousand miles upward (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=1+penny+%2F+%28cost+of+electricity%29+%2F+%28penny+mass+*+earth+gravity%29). The downward force from the coins falling on Mark's head and shoulders would certainly be annoying, but not debilitating. It would be possible for him to walk around, but if he sat still for an hour, he'd be buried. [Image: image] It does sound awful.
items.original_question: 如果人们的收入以现金的形式实时出现在他们身边会怎样？你需要赚多少钱才会陷入真正的麻烦？
items.model_answer:
If your income literally materialized around you in cash, the main consequences would be practical, economic, and legal.

At the personal level, you would quickly have a storage and security problem. Even a modest salary in physical bills takes up space and attracts theft risk. If you were paid, say, $50,000 per year entirely in $100 bills, that is 500 bills, which is manageable. But higher incomes, frequent payments, or smaller denominations would become bulky fast. You would need safes, transport, counting, and banking arrangements just to use your income normally.

Economically, it would depend on where the cash came from. If the cash appeared without being taken from an employer’s account and without being printed within the normal monetary system, then it would effectively be new money creation. If this happened only to you, you would become unusually wealthy with limited broader impact at first. If it happened to everyone, the money supply would rise sharply, and inflation could follow because there would be more money chasing the same goods and services. In extreme cases, prices would adjust upward until the “real” value of income was not much improved.

There is also the issue of denomination and authenticity. If the cash were perfect legal tender, banks and stores could accept it. If it merely resembled cash but had no recorded issuance, it could trigger anti-counterfeiting investigations. Modern economies rely on traceable payroll records, taxes, and bank transfers, so unexplained physical cash would create serious accounting problems.

Legally, you would still owe income tax in most systems, because taxation is based on income received, not the form it takes. You would need to document how much materialized, when, and likely deposit it. Repeated unexplained cash deposits could draw scrutiny for money laundering or fraud unless the phenomenon were publicly understood and recognized.

Physically, if the cash appeared “around you,” there could be immediate hazards. Bills appearing in open air are harmless, but coins or dense stacks materializing in occupied space could cause injury or property damage. Large sums appearing all at once could bury objects, block doors, or create fire and sanitation issues depending on the setting.

So the short answer is: if your income materialized around you in cash, you would gain a strange form of payment, but also inherit major problems of security, storage, taxation, banking, and possibly inflation. If the cash was truly newly created money, the wider effect would be inflationary; if it was just your ordinary income converted into physical currency, the main effect would be inconvenience and risk rather than new wealth.

items.question: What If You Used Lasers to Evaporate the Rain before It Hit the Ground?
human_answers: Stopping rain with a laser is one of those ideas that sounds totally reasonable, but if you— [Image: image] While the idea of a laser umbrella might be appealing, it— [Image: image] Ok. The idea of stopping rain with a laser is a thing we're currently talking about. [Image: image] It's not a very practical idea. First, let's look at the basic energy requirements. Vaporizing a liter of water takes about 2.6 megajoules,[1]It takes more energy if the water is colder, but not much more. Heating the water up to the edge of boiling only takes a little of the 2.6 megajoules. Most of it goes into pushing it over the threshold from 100°C water to 100°C vapor. and a big rainstorm might drop half an inch of rain per hour. This is one of those places where the equation isn't complicated—you just multiply (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=2.6+megajoules%2Fliter+*+1+cm%2Fhour) the 2.6 megajoules per liter by the rainfall rate and you get laser umbrella power requirement (watts per square meter protected). It's weird when units work out so straightforwardly: \[2.6\tfrac{\text{megajoules}}{\text{liter}}\times0.5\tfrac{\text{inches}}{\text{hour}}=9200\tfrac{\text{watts}}{\text{square meter}}\] 9 kilowatts per square meter is an order of magnitude more power than is delivered to the surface by sunlight, so your surroundings are going to heat up pretty fast. In effect, you're creating a cloud of steam around yourself, into which you're pumping more and more laser energy. In other words, you'd be building a human-sized autoclave (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoclave). Needless to say, autoclaves are not really a popular place to live (http://boston.craigslist.org/search/hhh?sort=rel&query=autoclave+you+can+live+in). But it gets worse! Vaporizing a droplet of water with a laser is more complicated than it sounds.[2]And to be honest, it sounds pretty complicated. There are many (http://www.opticsinfobase.org/ao/abstract.cfm?uri=ao-24-11-1631), many (http://pubs.rsc.org/en/Content/ArticleLanding/2003/CP/b210609d#!divAbstract), many (http://authors.library.caltech.edu/10136/1/SAGao84.pdf) papers on this subject,[3]Quote from the article Explosion of a Water Droplet by Pulsed Laser Heating (http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/02786828708959148) by J. C. Carls and J. R. Brock: "... in practice, heating a droplet to very high temperatures before substantial motion occurs ... might be difficult." Other, out-of-context quotes from that same paper: "The droplet seems to maintain its basic shape and does not appear to be shattering", "The particles formed previously will probably be vaporized.", "By acting strangely, the equation of state is saying that all is not well", "" "Avalanche breakdown", "extremely low and sometimes negative pressures", "the most dynamic response possible", and "Notice the very high temperatures". and the general gist is that it takes a lot of energy—delivered fast—to vaporize the droplet without just splattering it apart into little droplets. Here's a video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bRbHDtPbHe0) of a droplet getting zapped by a laser pulse; you can see that it splatters the droplet, more than vaporizing it. The upshot is that cleanly vaporizing a droplet would probably take more than the already-unreasonable (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoclave) amounts we were considering. Then there's the problem of targeting. In theory, this is probably solvable. Adaptive optics (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adaptive_optics) allow for extremely fast and precise control of beams of light. Covering an area of 100 square meters (which Zach also asked about in his full letter) would require something like 50,000 pulses per second. This is slow enough that you wouldn't run into any direct problems with relativity, but the device would—at minimum—need to be a lot more complicated than just a laser pointer on a swiveling base. It might seem easier to forget about targeting completely and just fire lasers in random directions.[4][Image: image] If you aim a laser beam in a random direction, how far will it go before it hits a drop? This is a pretty easy question to answer; it's the same as asking how far you can see in the rain, and the answer is at least several hundred meters (http://www.researchgate.net/publication/258316669_Review_of_the_mechanisms_of_visibility_reduction_by_rain_and_wet_road/links/00b7d527b4f9da2560000000). Unless you're trying to protect your whole neighborhood, firing powerful lasers in random directions probably won't help. And, honestly, if you are trying to protect your whole neighborhood ... [Image: image] ... firing powerful lasers in random directions definitely won't help.
items.original_question: 用雨伞或帐篷阻止雨水落在某物上是很无聊的。如果你试图用激光来阻止雨，在每个进入的水滴到达地面十英尺之前瞄准并蒸发它，会怎么样？
items.model_answer:
In any realistic sense, you couldn’t do it on a useful scale.

Rain contains an enormous amount of water, and evaporating water takes a huge amount of energy because of water’s latent heat of vaporization. To evaporate just 1 kilogram of liquid water, you need about 2.3 megajoules of energy, and that’s before accounting for inefficiencies, beam spreading, atmospheric absorption, and the fact that the drops are moving through turbulent air.

A moderate rainstorm over even a small area involves a surprisingly large mass flow of water. For example, rainfall of 10 mm per hour over 1 square kilometer is 10,000 cubic meters per hour? Actually, 10 mm is 0.01 m, so over 1,000,000 m² that is 10,000 m³? No: 0.01 × 1,000,000 = 10,000 m³, yes. Since water is about 1000 kg/m³, that is 10 million kilograms of water per hour. Evaporating that would require on the order of 2.3 × 10^13 joules per hour, which is roughly 6 gigawatts of continuous power, comparable to several large power plants, just to stop a moderate rain over one square kilometer. Heavy rain would require much more.

There are also practical problems beyond raw energy. A laser powerful enough to dump that much energy into falling raindrops would also heat the surrounding air, create turbulence, ionization, and probably plasma effects before efficiently evaporating all the droplets. The beam would be scattered and absorbed by the very rain, mist, and water vapor you are trying to remove. Even if you could target individual drops, there are far too many of them, and they keep being replaced by more falling from above.

If you somehow partially evaporated the rain, you would not simply make it disappear harmlessly. You would increase humidity dramatically, likely producing hot, saturated air, fog, steam, or recondensation nearby. In other words, the water would still be in the local atmosphere and could just come down again or shift where it falls.

So the basic answer is: with enough energy, yes, in principle you can evaporate raindrops with lasers. But to prevent rain from hitting the ground over any meaningful area, the required power is so immense, and the atmospheric complications so severe, that it is not a practical or efficient idea.

items.question: What If Every River in America Froze in Midsummer?
human_answers: This is another question that turns out even worse than I expected. [Image: image] For starters, pretty much every animal in the water would die. This would wipe out several fish species completely (this site (http://wwf.panda.org/about_our_earth/ecoregions/lower_mississippi_river.cfm) lists a number of species found only in the Mississippi and its tributaries) and seriously damage many others. Then all the ice would start to melt. Melting ice takes a lot of heat energy, but the ice in this scenario would be spread out in thin strands across the country, so it would all melt pretty fast.[1]Strangely, solid ice usually melts faster than snow—not only in terms of weight, but in terms of inches melted per day.[2] Or[3]Whoa, I can nest footnotes! centimeters. This seems a little counterintuitive, since ice is a lot denser than snow, so it requires a lot more energy to melt a given volume. But snow reflects a lot more light than solid ice, keeping it from absorbing energy, and its air pockets help insulate it. As ice melts, if it stays in contact with water, the water speeds up the melting, since water can transfer heat more efficiently than air. This can be demonstrated by a simple household experiment (http://www.cockeyed.com/science/moment/colander.shtml). Snow is partly protected from this effect because it can't conduct heat in from the edges as easily. This would cause some localized cooling of the air, but we're talking about a relatively small amount of heat energy compared to the environment's overall energy budget.[4]To estimating the river volume, I found a book (http://www.amazon.com/Water-Crisis-Guide-Worlds-Resources/dp/0195076281) that collected estimates of the total world surface water volume in rivers (Chapter 2). It didn't have a breakdown of that number by continent, but it had total discharge rates by continent, so I just used that as a proxy to figure out how to apportion the water between the continents and came up with 16.5% for North America. To get a rough idea, we can apportion that water by surface area (I found a page saying Canada has 9% of the world's freshwater discharge, which seems consistent, although using two numbers from different sources like this creates large potential for error. That leaves 7.5% for the rest of the continent. Dividing up that 7.5% by land area between the US and Central America, the US has about 5%, which works out to 77 km3 of water. [Image: image] We can use data on iceberg melt rates (http://journals.ametsoc.org/doi/pdf/10.1175/1520-0485%281980%29010%3C1681%3AOTEOAI%3E2.0.CO%3B2) to estimate how quickly individual rivers would melt. Small streams would melt in days in all but the coldest areas, while ice in larger rivers would take longer. But before that could happen, things would get weird. To help me out with this question, I talked to Charlie Hohn (http://coyot.es/slowwatermovement), a Vermont field naturalist with an interest in river behavior. I brought Zoe's question to him, and he made a lot of interesting observations. He pointed out that the water feeding into the rivers—from tiny rivulets and raindrops and melting snow all over the watershed—would suddenly find its path blocked by a wall of ice. [Image: image] But all that water still has to go somewhere. And if the riverbed is full, it will go somewhere else. "Any place with rain or snowmelt would have horrific flooding because the water would have nowhere to go," Charlie told me. "Water would shoot down narrow canyons, and once it hit the floodplain it would probably jump into old river channels where they exist, but in many areas that would mean towns and farms." The problems would get worse as the ice melted and broke up, starting upstream and progressing down the river. The floating ice would pile up, damming the water and creating huge lakes. Charlie notes that even a small ice dam can cause terrible flooding. When the Winooski river in Vermont was clogged by an ice dam in 1992, the water spilled over the banks and flooded Montpelier in a matter of minutes (http://www.montpelier-vt.org/community/351/Flood-of-1992.html). And that's just a tiny river, he says. "The Winooski here is narrow enough to throw a rock across, and usually only a few feet deep. In a dry year you could wade across in summer in shorts without getting them wet. So scale that up to the Mississippi and 12-foot-thick ice." As part of its normal meandering, the Mississippi has been trying for 150 years to jump its banks and flow down the Atchafalaya river's route. The Atchafalaya offers a steeper path to the Gulf of Mexico, but if it captured the Mississippi's flow, it would leave the major ports of New Orleans and Baton Rouge high and dry. The Army Corps of Engineers has been trying to stop it (http://www.americaswetlandresources.com/background_facts/detailedstory/LouisianaRiverControl.html). [Image: image] Charlie says that if the Mississippi froze solid, "you'd have the Atchafalaya disaster, without a doubt." And the problems wouldn't be limited to the Mississippi. "The California delta system would also flood, causing a collapse of most of California's water system—though if the aqueducts and reservoirs froze, it wouldn't matter that you couldn't get water from the delta." If man-made reservoirs do freeze in this scenario (which I guess depends whether they count as "rivers") the ice could damage the dams by expanding in the turbines. Whether or not the reservoir froze,[5]We spent a while debating whether, if Lake Meade froze (and expanded), the Hoover Dam would burst due to the expansion. My gut feeling is that it wouldn't, but I'm really not sure. I think we should just try it. the dams could collapse, causing cataclysmic flooding. And where there aren't dams to collapse, the ice would create them ... and when ice dams break up, the result can be pretty spectacular (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ezcgPAptbIk). According to Charlie, the vegetation around the rivers would handle the sudden freeze pretty well, but the effect on the broader ecosystem would be huge and complex. "If there were salmon in the rivers, the bears would feast on them when they thawed. But later, if the fishery crashed, there would be a bunch of desperate hungry bears unleashed on the environment." He mentions that salmon spend part of their life cycle in the ocean, so some of them would survive the rivers freezing. "But if their food were gone, the fishery would still fail. Then again, with all the dams destroyed, maybe it would be a net benefit for salmon ... which is kind of sad." Although agriculture would take a serious hit, humans would probably make it through ok. We wouldn't run out of drinking water; we get a lot of it from underground aquifers, and there would be plenty of quickly-melting ice lying around in most areas. In the worst case scenario, people could just use hair dryers to melt ice to make drinking water for only pennies (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=%28334+J%2Fg%29+*+%28water+density%29+*+%282+liters%2Fday%29+*+%28price+of+electricity%29+to+USD%2Fday) per person per day. We'd probably limp through the scenario tattered but alive, buying food overseas. At least, most of us would. I think the most horrifying part of this summer freeze wouldn't be the large-scale, long-term devastation. It would be the immediate consequences. As a kid, I spent summers swimming in the James River (https://www.google.com/search?tbm=isch&q=james+river+richmond) in Virginia. Now, thanks to Zoe, every time I set foot in a river ... [Image: image] ... I'm going to feel a faint chill.
items.original_question: 如果美国所有的河流在仲夏时节立即结冰，会发生什么？
items.model_answer:
If every river in America suddenly froze in midsummer, the result would be a continent-scale environmental and infrastructure crisis.

First, this would imply an extraordinary and physically unrealistic cold event or some unknown mechanism removing heat from flowing water. Rivers in summer carry large amounts of thermal energy, so freezing all of them at once would require a massive energy extraction. That alone would likely mean the surrounding air and land were also experiencing severe temperature disruption. So the river ice would not be an isolated curiosity; it would signal a major breakdown of normal climate conditions.

The immediate effects would hit water supply systems. Many cities draw drinking water from rivers directly or indirectly, and intake structures, pumps, and treatment facilities could fail if blocked by ice. Power plants that rely on river water for cooling could be forced to reduce output or shut down. Barges and inland shipping on the Mississippi, Ohio, Missouri, Columbia, and other major rivers would stop abruptly, disrupting fuel, grain, fertilizer, coal, and industrial transport.

Ecologically, the shock would be devastating. Fish and aquatic invertebrates adapted to warm-season conditions could die in large numbers from rapid freezing, oxygen disruption, and habitat loss. River plants and wetlands would be stressed or destroyed. Migratory and breeding cycles for birds, amphibians, and insects would be thrown off. In many places, river-connected agriculture would also suffer because irrigation access could be interrupted at the peak of the growing season.

Flooding would become a serious risk, especially if the freeze happened unevenly. Ice jams can block channels and force water over banks, damaging towns, bridges, levees, and farmland. If the rivers later thawed quickly, a second crisis could follow: sudden high flows, erosion, infrastructure damage, and contamination from overwhelmed sewage and industrial systems.

Weather and regional climate would also shift. Rivers exchange heat and moisture with the atmosphere; widespread summer ice would alter local temperatures, humidity, and fog patterns. Areas near large river systems could become cooler at first, but if this event reflected a broader atmospheric anomaly, crop-killing cold could extend far beyond riverbanks. Agriculture across the Midwest, South, and West could face severe losses.

Economically, the effects would be enormous. Transportation delays, crop losses, power disruptions, water shortages, ecological damage, and emergency response costs would likely total hundreds of billions of dollars or more, depending on duration. If the freeze lasted only a day or two, the damage would still be severe; if it persisted for weeks, it could trigger a national emergency with long-term food and energy consequences.

So, if every river in America froze in midsummer, the country would face simultaneous failures in water access, transport, power generation, ecosystems, and agriculture. The frozen rivers themselves would be dangerous, but the deeper implication would be even more alarming: something extreme enough to freeze them would mean the broader environment was undergoing a profound and possibly catastrophic disturbance.

items.question: What If You Made a Lava Lamp with Real Lava?
human_answers: This is a surprisingly reasonable idea, by What If standards. I mean, it's not that reasonable. At the very least, I'm guessing you would lose your teaching license, and possibly some of the students in the front row. But you could do it. [Image: image] Just a warning: I'm going to be linking to a lot of videos (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K2x7FGzjbqQ) of lava flowing and people poking it with sticks (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SbcM7lh6DSQ), so you may have a hard time getting to the end of the article without getting sidetracked into watching a bunch of them (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6M-YX-r0Ll4) like I did while writing it. You have a few choices for transparent materials that could hold the lava without rupturing (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a6pXf05Ph9Q) and splattering half the classroom with red-hot droplets. Fused quartz glass would be a great choice. It's the same stuff they use in high-intensity lamp bulbs, the surface of which can easily get up to mid-range lava (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kHO389dvj6Y) temperatures.[1]This bulb (http://www.amazon.ca/Philips-400w-GY9-5-Short-Light/dp/B0062ATTRW), for example, can supposedly handle bulb temperatures of up to 1000°C, which is hotter than many types of lava. Another possibility is sapphire, which stays solid up to 2,000°C, and is commonly used as a window (http://www.newport.com/Sapphire-Optical-Windows/378626/1033/info.aspx) into high-temperature chambers.[2]That link wasn't a lava video, but this (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v_VyKplXtOM) is. [Image: image] The question of what to use for the clear medium (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=scGvM_VoPwk#t=31) is trickier. Let's say we find a transparent glass that melts[3]Some people say glass is a liquid that flows very slowly. Other people smugly point out that this is actually wrong. Then another group of people dissects how we know it's wrong, and where this incorrect idea got started. And then at the end of the chain, a Metafilter user steps back and asks some supremely insightful questions about what's really going on here (http://www.metafilter.com/141772/MetaFolkloreFilter#5676767) as we variously repeat and debunk these kinds of factoids. at low temperatures. Even if we ignore the impurities from the hot lava that would probably cloud the glass, we're going to have a problem.[4]And later, when the school board finds out, we'll have another. Molten glass is transparent (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1WmJOhbpyKY). So why doesn't it look transparent?[5]Which sounds sorta contradictory. "This music is loud, but it doesn't sound loud." The answer is simple: It glows. Hot objects give off blackbody radiation (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-QhU8eMR4IQ); molten glass glows just like molten lava does, and for the same reason. So the problem (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bWswq8PmRII) with a lava lamp is that both halves of it will be equally bright (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xsJn8izcKtg), and it will be hard to see the lava. We could try having nothing (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xiYzYaLM-hQ) in the top half of the lamp—after all, when it's hot enough, lava bubbles (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EFVQhcuT2U0) pretty well on its own. Unfortunately, the lamp itself would also be in contact with the lava. Sapphire might not melt (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2dww24LeoEk) easily, but it will glow, making it hard to see whatever the lava was doing inside. [Image: image] Unless you hooked it up to a really bright bulb, this lava lamp would cool down quickly. Just like individual blobs of lava, the lamp would solidify and stop glowing within the first minute, and by the end of the class period (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zf4wKY8PJtg) you'd probably be able to touch it without being burned. A solidified lava lamp is just about the most boring thing (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TszHiC6fjDg) in the world. But the scenario made me wonder: If making a lamp out of molten lava wouldn't be very exciting, then what about a volcano made of lamps (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7V2_aMG3YsI)? [Image: image] This is probably the most useless calculation I've ever done,[6]Ok, there's no way that's true. but ... what if Mount Saint Helens (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jxvisqt-U-8) erupted again today, but instead of tephra,[7]The technical term for "whatever crap comes out of a volcano." it spewed compact fluorescent bulbs? Well, if it did, the mercury (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cFvijBpzD_Y) released into the atmosphere would be several orders of magnitude larger than all manmade emissions combined.[8]45% of which (http://www.chem.unep.ch/mercury/Atmospheric_Emissions/UNEP%20SUMMARY%20REPORT%20-%20CORRECTED%20May09%20%20final%20for%20WEB%202008.pdf) come from gold mining. [Image: image] All in all, I think making a lava lamp out of lava would be kind of anticlimactic, and would much rather go find some actual lava and poke it with a stick. I also think that it's probably good that Mount Saint Helens didn't erupt compact fluorescent bulbs. And I think that if I were in Ms. Johnstone's class, I'd try to sit toward the back of the room. Lastly, for old time's sake, I'd like to share one final link with you: The music video for Rick Astley's "Never Gonna Give You Up." (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q8NXO6YxBmU#t=3)
items.original_question: 如果我用真正的熔岩制作一盏熔岩灯会怎么样？我可以使用什么作为透明介质？我能站在多近的距离观看它？
items.model_answer:
If you tried to make a lava lamp with real lava, it would not work as a normal lava lamp, and it would be extremely dangerous.

Real lava is molten rock, typically around 700 to 1,200 °C or more. A regular lava lamp works because two liquids with different densities expand and contract gently as they are heated by a small bulb. Real lava is nothing like that. It is far too hot to be contained in ordinary glass, metal, or household materials. Most glass would soften, crack, or shatter, and many containers would fail from the heat.

Even if you used a very high-temperature container, real lava would not flow in the smooth blobs seen in a lava lamp. Molten rock is much denser and often much more viscous than the wax in a lava lamp. As it cools, it would quickly begin to solidify into rock, especially near the container walls. Instead of rising and falling in neat globules, you would likely get a partly molten mass, crust formation, trapped gases, and possibly violent cracking or splattering.

There is also the issue of heating. Keeping lava molten would require an enormous and continuous heat source, more like an industrial furnace than a lamp bulb. Without that, it would just cool into solid rock. With such a heat source, the outside of the device would also become dangerously hot.

So the realistic result is not a decorative lamp but a high-temperature rock furnace, with major risks of burns, fire, toxic gases, pressure buildup, and container failure. In short: a real-lava lava lamp would be more like a miniature volcano experiment than a lamp, and it would almost certainly be impractical and hazardous.

items.question: What If Every Child's First Laugh Created an Immortal Fairy?
human_answers: "There are always a lot of young ones," explained Wendy, who was now quite an authority, "because you see when a new baby laughs for the first time a new fairy is born, and as there are always new babies there are always new fairies. They live in nests on the tops of trees; and the mauve ones are boys and the white ones are girls, and the blue ones are just little sillies who are not sure what they are." —Peter Pan Interestingly, fairies in the Peter Pan mythology definitely don't live forever. At the end of the book, Peter comes to visit Wendy a year after their adventures. Wendy asks about Tinker Bell, and Peter says he can't remember her and assumes she's died, and Wendy observes that fairies don't live very long.[1]When she expressed a doubtful hope that Tinker Bell would be glad to see her he said, "Who is Tinker Bell?" "O Peter," she said, shocked; but even when she explained he could not remember. "There are such a lot of them," he said. "I expect she is no more." I expect he was right, for fairies don't live long, but they are so little that a short time seems a good while to them. This suggests that at any given time, there are probably be far fewer fairies than humans in the Peter Pan universe, since they have the same birth rate and shorter lifespans. [Image: image] But Mira's scenario assumes immortal fairies, so let's talk about immortal fairy demographics. A fairy is created by every[2]Approximately, anyway, but we'll round up by assuming that all babies laugh. newborn baby. The total number of humans who have ever lived is somewhere around 100-120 billion,[3]There are various groups who have estimated this, and they all tend to come up with a number around in this range. If you take a set of estimates for ancient human population (Wikipedia has a table of them (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population_estimates)) and assume a birth rate near the biological maximum before the 20th century (35 to 45 births per 1,000, according to this paper (http://www.researchgate.net/publication/231918377_The_Use_of_Historical_Demography_in_Ancient_History)), you can derive a similar number yourself. meaning 100-120 billion fairies have been created. How much do all those fairies weigh? Tinker Bell, the main fairy from the Peter Pan universe, seems to be a little under six inches tall. In a scene in Hook, Tinker Bell (played by the 5 foot 9 inch Julia Roberts) fits comfortably in a 1/12 scale dollhouse, suggesting a height of 5.75 inches. As another data point, the statue of Tinker Bell (http://www.madametussauds.com/london/newsandevents/tinkerbell/) at Madam Tussaud's wax museum is 5.5 inches. This suggests that fairies in Peter Pan are pretty close to 1/12th scale. If fairies are 1/12th the size of humans, then they weigh \( \left( \tfrac{1}{12\text{th}}\right) ^3=\tfrac{1}{1728\text{th}} \) as much as us, which means Julia Roberts's Tinker Bell is probably around 35 grams.[4](two mice) As of 2015, total fairy biomass would be about 4 million tons. That's less than humans or horses (http://xkcd.com/1338/), and probably comparable to the total mass of all humpback whales (http://iwc.int/estimate).[5]Fairies also probably outweigh wild birds. At these numbers, fairies would be a minor piece of the ecosystem, although possibly a pretty annoying one. [Image: image] But it wasn't always the case. In the early days of our species, our high birth rates (and death rates) plus our low population mean that we would have accumulated fairies quickly. The exact numbers depend on when the modern human (fairy-generating) species developed, but by the time the last ice age was over, the accumulated fairies could have outweighed our tiny living human population 10 to 1. [Image: image] Once our population started growing following the agricultural revolution (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic_Revolution), we would have quickly outstripped fairies in terms of weight. In 2015, fairy biomass would be down to about 1.2% of human biomass, and by the mid-21st-century, they'd bottom out at less than 1%. But as long as humans keep reproducing, the fairy population would keep growing. If we assume the human population will level off (http://www.un.org/esa/population/publications/longrange2/WorldPop2300final.pdf) at around 9 billion partway through this century, then the share of mass occupied by fairies would continue rising steadily. If our population stays at a stable 9 billion indefinitely, by 2100, they'll be back above 1% of human biomass, and they'll reach 2% by the year 3000. In the year 100,000, if our species is somehow still around, they'll outweigh us. This makes things interesting. Let's assume fairies need to eat. If fairies weigh about as much as us, they'd presumably be consuming a similar share of food and water. So even if the Earth can support 400 million tons of human, it may not be able to support 400 million tons of human and another 400 million tons of fairy. This suggests that, sometime in the next hundred millennia, the growing fairy population would start to crowd out the human population. But if fairies crowd out humans, that would in turn reduce the growth rate of the fairies, slowing down the replacement process. The end result (in this idealized model) would be that the fairy population growth would taper off as the human population declined. The situation would never quite reach a stable equilibrium, because every 1,728 human births would create one human's weight in fairies, reducing the Earth's total human carrying capacity by 1. But since the rate of fairy creation would slow down as the human population shrank, the process would stretch out for a very long time. This odd situation would only exist because fairies—in Mira's scenario—are immortal. The scenario would change dramatically if we introduced a fairy death rate. Perhaps fairies don't age or experience natural deaths, but can still die from other causes. What would kill the fairies? Who knows.[6]J. M. Barrie introduces a fairy-killing mechanism in Peter Pan; any time anyone says "I don't believe in fairies", a random fairy dies. In a world of immortal fairies, this could serve as an effective feedback. If no one has heard of fairies, no one will say they don't believe in them, and their population will grow. As fairies start to be common enough to be noticed, people will have a reason to say they don't believe in them, and their population will drop.
