A geostationary satellite must sit above the equator, and under this rule, equatorial nations could claim that satellites stationed above them are in their sovereign territory no matter how high up they are. That would let a small set of countries monopolize some of the most valuable orbital slots. In the real world, this issue was hinted at by equatorial claims in the past, but it was never generally accepted precisely because it would undermine open access to space.

Military tensions would rise sharply. A country might argue that foreign reconnaissance satellites passing overhead are violating its sovereign territory, much as military aircraft would be if they entered national airspace. That could justify attempts to jam, seize, or destroy satellites. Since many satellites are dual-use, serving both civilian and military roles, the distinction would blur fast. Space would likely become more militarized and unstable, not less.

Science would also suffer. Space telescopes, planetary probes, and crewed missions often depend on crossing many orbital paths without asking territorial permission each time. Even observing Earth from orbit could be framed as unauthorized surveillance within another country’s infinite vertical domain. International cooperation on missions like the ISS would become far harder, because the station’s orbit crosses over many countries.

There are also geometry problems. If sovereignty extends upward forever from borders drawn on a curved rotating Earth, then states effectively own narrowing or widening three-dimensional wedges extending into space. Near the poles, where longitudinal borders converge, these claims would become awkward and dense. Orbital mechanics does not respect political boundaries, so legal geography would clash with physical reality.

The Moon and planets would raise another question: would a country’s upward column continue only away from Earth, or as a fixed region of space extending infinitely? If taken literally, the claim becomes absurd, because distant celestial bodies and spacecraft trajectories could intersect someone’s territorial “column.” That shows why the idea breaks down physically as well as legally.

So the likely overall outcome is that modern space activity would be drastically reduced, fragmented, and politicized. Satellite networks would be less reliable, launch access would depend heavily on diplomacy, military conflict risks would increase, and a few geographically advantaged states could gain outsized control over orbit. In short, if national airspace extended forever into space, space would no longer be a shared operational domain; it would become a patchwork of territorial barriers, and the space age as we know it would be far harder to sustain.

items.question: What If You Crashed a Comet into the Ocean to Cool the Earth?
human_answers: No. In fact, it's honestly sort of impressive to find a solution that would actively make the problem worse in so many different ways. [Image: image] Dropping a comet into the ocean to cool the planet, famously suggested by the 2002 Futurama episode None Like It Hot,[1]I'm used to stuff making me feel old, but the fact that this episode aired 20 years ago is distressing in multiple ways. wouldn't work for a few reasons. One is that dropping things from space creates heat. When water—or anything else—falls, it gains kinetic energy. When it stops falling, that energy has to go somewhere. Generally, it turns into heat. Water that goes over Niagara Falls, for example, gains enough kinetic energy during the 50-meter plunge to warm it up by about 0.1°C by the time it reaches the bottom. (This added heat is minor compared to the cooling effects of evaporation on the way down, so the actual temperature at the bottom is likely colder.) Outer space is a lot higher up than Niagara Falls,[citation needed] so the plunge down into the atmosphere at the bottom of Earth's gravity well adds a lot more than 0.1 degrees worth of heat. A chunk of ice from space that falls to Earth gains enough energy to warm the ice up, melt it, boil it into vapor, and then heat the vapor to thousands of degrees. If you built an icy waterfall from space, the water would arrive at the bottom as a river of superheated steam. [Image: image] Small chunks of ice falling from space disintegrate and boil away before they reach the ground, warming the upper atmosphere. Large comets can reach the ground intact and be vaporized on impact as their kinetic energy is converted to heat all at once. This heat energy would be about 100 times greater than the energy needed to bring even a very cold comet up to room temperature, so a comet falling from space would heat the Earth 100 times more than it cooled it. [Image: image] But let's suppose you figure out a way to lower the comet slowly, using some kind of magical crane,[2]Magical storks deliver babies, magical cranes deliver comets. and gently set the comet in the ocean. [Image: image] Comets are more dust than ice, but they're not particularly dense. A tiny piece of a comet would float for a short time until it became waterlogged, melted, and broke apart. A full-size comet wouldn't be strong enough to support its own weight, and would collapse like a drying sand sculpture. [Image: image] If the comet were placed in the ocean,[3]It actually wouldn't have much effect on global sea level, but the influx of cold water on the surface—and the dust released into the air—could definitely mess with the atmosphere. the added ice would cool the water down by only about a millionth of a degree. If you set the comet on land, it would soak up heat from the atmosphere—which contains much less stored heat than the oceans—briefly cooling the air by an average of one or two thousandths of a degree. Okay, so we just need thousands of comets, right? Each one will cool the air a little bit. With a large enough supply of comets, we can keep the Earth nice and cool, as long as we make sure they're lowered slowly. [Image: image] Unfortunately, comets would affect the Earth's temperature in another way. In addition to dust and water, they contain a small amount of CO2, which would be released into the atmosphere as the comet melted. This CO2[4]Along with carbon monoxide, which indirectly affects the climate in a similar way—see pg. 718-719 of the IPCC WG1 AR5 report (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/02/WG1AR5_Chapter08_FINAL.pdf) for more. would change Earth's radiation balance, trapping heat near the surface and raising the planet's temperature. After a few years, the comet's greenhouse effect would have trapped more heat than the ice absorbed, and over the decades to follow, the extra heat would keep piling up. The CO2 released from the comet would raise the temperature of the Earth for centuries. It wouldn't just cancel out the cooling effect of the ice—over time, the comet's greenhouse effect would deliver as much heat as if you'd just let it slam into the planet and vaporize.[5]Although letting a comet slowly decay on the surface would definitely be preferable to a high-speed impact, as any dinosaur from the end of the Cretaceous can tell you. It's okay. Despite all this, your scenario could fix global warming. Remember that hypothetical crane that lets you lower comets to the surface? Well, if you hooked it up to a generator, you could use the slowly-descending comet to produce electricity. [Image: image] One comet, lowered from space down to the surface, could supply the entire world's energy consumption for a year. Sure, it would release a little CO2, but it would be nothing compared to the pollution from our current sources of energy. A comet crane generator could cut our energy-related greenhouse gas emissions to almost zero. The comet isn't the important part, the crane is. Sadly, we don't have the technology to build comet-lowering cranes—certainly not in time to help mitigate climate change. But harvesting orbital energy like this is a neat idea! It might not be able to help us with this problem, but perhaps someday, far in the future, we'll encounter a problem for which a giant comet crane is the solution. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 我可以通过捕获一颗彗星并将其扔进海洋来冷却地球吗，就像一杯水中的冰块一样？
items.model_answer:
In principle, crashing a comet into the ocean would not be a practical or safe way to cool Earth. The immediate effects would be catastrophic, and any cooling benefit would be uncertain, brief, or outweighed by the damage.

A comet could affect climate in two main ways. First, a large impact would throw huge amounts of water vapor, salt, dust, and possibly sulfate-containing material into the atmosphere. If enough fine particles reached the stratosphere, they could reflect some sunlight and temporarily cool the planet, somewhat like a giant volcanic eruption. Second, if the comet delivered a lot of water, it would slightly increase ocean mass, but that would not meaningfully cool the climate system. Water vapor is also a greenhouse gas, so the atmospheric effects could even add warming in some phases.

The problem is that the energy of impact would be enormous. Even a modest comet, moving at tens of kilometers per second, would release far more energy than the world’s nuclear arsenal. Hitting the ocean would not make it safe. It would generate extreme shock waves, massive tsunamis, intense heating, and widespread destruction around ocean basins. A sufficiently large impact could inject so much steam and debris into the atmosphere that it would disrupt weather, damage the ozone layer, and collapse agriculture. That might produce short-term cooling, but in the same way that an asteroid winter cools Earth: by causing a global disaster.

There is also a scaling problem. To noticeably offset modern global warming, you would need a very large and carefully controlled change in Earth’s radiation balance. A comet impact is the opposite of controlled. Small comets would mostly cause regional devastation without enough atmospheric dust to change global temperature much. Large comets might cool the planet temporarily, but only through catastrophic atmospheric pollution and sunlight blocking. The cooling would likely last years, not solve the underlying greenhouse gas buildup, and could be followed by rebound warming once the dust settled.

So the direct answer is: yes, a comet impact could potentially cool Earth for a short time by lofting sunlight-blocking material into the atmosphere, but it would do so as a planet-scale disaster, not as a usable climate intervention. It would be far more dangerous than the warming it was meant to reduce.

items.model_answer:
If the existence of God were scientifically proven, the biggest change would be that “God exists” would stop being mainly a matter of faith, philosophy, or theology and become a matter of established knowledge. But that would not automatically settle the most important follow-up questions. Science might prove that some divine being exists without proving which religion, if any, has understood that being correctly, what that being wants, whether it intervenes in human life, or what moral obligations follow.

In science, “proof” usually means overwhelming, reproducible evidence rather than absolute logical certainty. So if there were clear, testable, independently verified evidence for God, the effects would be enormous across many fields. Philosophy would be transformed because major debates about metaphysics, causation, consciousness, and the origin of the universe would have to incorporate a confirmed divine reality. Theology would shift from arguing over whether God exists to interpreting the nature, intentions, and attributes of the proven God. Some religious traditions would claim vindication, while others might need major revision.

Society would likely react unevenly. Many believers would feel confirmed, but not all religions would benefit equally. If the scientific evidence pointed to a God unlike the one described in a given tradition, that tradition could face crisis rather than triumph. Some atheists and agnostics would change their views, though others might still reject worship, arguing that existence does not imply worthiness, goodness, or authority. A proven God could be seen less as an object of faith and more as a fact of reality.

Politics and law would become especially complicated. Governments would face pressure from citizens to align laws with what they believed the proven God required. But pluralism would still matter, because even with God’s existence established, disagreement would remain about interpretation. There could be renewed conflicts over education, human rights, bioethics, and the relation between church and state. Some societies might become more religiously unified; others might become more polarized.

Science itself would not end. Instead, it would gain a new subject of inquiry. Researchers would ask how this God is detected, whether divine action follows regular patterns, whether miracles are measurable, and how divine existence fits with physical law. If God acted in observable ways, that would open entirely new areas of investigation. If God existed but rarely intervened, the practical impact on everyday science might be smaller than expected.

Psychologically and culturally, a proof of God could alter how people think about death, purpose, morality, and human significance. It might reduce some forms of existential uncertainty while increasing others. People would still ask: Why did God create us? Why is there suffering? What happens after death? Scientific proof of existence would not necessarily answer those questions.

So the most careful answer is this: if God were scientifically proven, it would be one of the most important discoveries in human history, but it would not end religion, philosophy, or moral debate. It would resolve one question while making many others more urgent.

items.model_answer:
To run Santa Claus’s global delivery operation in the real world, you would need a system so far beyond current human logistics that it would require either radically advanced physics, a complete reinterpretation of the story’s assumptions, or both.

If we take the traditional version literally, Santa must deliver presents to essentially all children who celebrate Christmas in one night. Even with rough assumptions, that means visiting on the order of 100 million households worldwide. Time zones help, but not enough: the useful delivery window is still only about 24 to 36 hours at best, and much less if Santa must arrive while children are asleep. That means millions of deliveries per hour, thousands per second, continuously, without error.

The first requirement would be extraordinary navigation and routing. Santa would need a real-time global optimization system far superior to anything used in airline scheduling, parcel networks, or military command systems. It would have to account for geography, weather, air traffic, roof access, building type, local customs, security systems, and whether a household should receive gifts at all. This alone is a colossal data and computation problem, though in principle advanced AI and global sensing could help.

The second requirement is impossible speed by ordinary transportation standards. A sleigh moving sequentially between all households would need to travel at hypersonic or orbital-scale effective speeds, and likely much faster, depending on route assumptions. At those speeds, the atmosphere becomes a major problem: air drag, shock heating, sonic booms, and enormous energy consumption would destroy a conventional vehicle. So either Santa’s craft must avoid normal aerodynamic interaction, use some kind of field propulsion, exploit spacetime shortcuts, or use teleportation-like movement. A normal reindeer-powered sleigh cannot do this.

The third requirement is handling the gift payload. If each household receives even a modest mass of presents, the total cargo would be in the millions of tons. No single sleigh could carry that by conventional means. So Santa would need either matter compression, on-demand fabrication, distributed local warehousing, or a magical/infinite-capacity cargo system. A more realistic engineering reinterpretation would be that gifts are manufactured regionally in advance and Santa only supervises final delivery, rather than physically hauling everything from the North Pole.

The fourth requirement is impossible acceleration tolerance. If Santa actually moved from house to house at the speeds implied by one-night delivery, the accelerations during stopping and starting would be lethal to both Santa and the reindeer unless inertia itself were somehow controlled. So the operation would require inertial damping, continuous rather than impulsive motion through nonclassical transit, or duplication of Santa so that no single body experiences the full mission profile.

The fifth requirement is entry and placement. Delivering into homes without waking anyone means bypassing locked doors, alarm systems, apartment buildings, and houses without chimneys. In practical terms, Santa would need a universal access technology: either tiny autonomous delivery devices, temporary phasing through matter, robotic indoor navigation, or prior permission through smart-home infrastructure. The classical chimney model is not scalable to modern urban housing.

A sixth requirement is a global manufacturing and supply chain. Toys and gifts must be designed, built, packaged, matched to recipients, and quality-checked. This is more plausible than the delivery itself, because modern industry already runs massive seasonal production systems. Santa’s “workshop” would in reality need to resemble a planetary-scale network of automated factories, suppliers, data centers, and fulfillment hubs, with elves functioning more like a specialized labor force of engineers, robotic technicians, and planners.

A seventh requirement is information management. Santa would need a database of children, preferences, behavior, addresses, and gift eligibility, updated continuously and governed somehow across every culture and legal system. In modern terms this is a surveillance and privacy challenge on an unprecedented scale. The famous “naughty or nice” list is less a whimsical ledger than a gigantic global behavioral scoring system.

From a physics standpoint, the literal version only works if at least one of these is true: Santa can travel faster than practical atmospheric flight allows, Santa can manipulate time so that one night contains much more subjective working time, Santa can create copies of himself or autonomous agents, Santa can compress or locally generate payload mass, or Santa uses nonclassical access to homes and routes. In other words, the operation requires either magic or technologies equivalent to violating major practical constraints of energy, materials, aerodynamics, and perhaps relativity.

If you wanted to make Santa’s operation semi-realistic without invoking pure magic, the most plausible model is this: a globally distributed network of automated factories and warehouses produces gifts in advance; vast fleets of drones, robots, and local couriers perform most deliveries; AI handles routing and personalization; and “Santa” is a symbolic coordinator or a small number of flagship operators who appear only ceremonially. In that version, the miracle is not one sleigh circling the world, but an ultra-optimized, planet-scale logistics system.

So the direct answer is that running Santa Claus’s global delivery operation would take superhuman computation, nonclassical transportation, impossible payload management, global manufacturing infrastructure, and either advanced physics beyond what we have or a complete redesign of the myth into a distributed logistics network.

items.model_answer:
If the speed of light were 100 times faster than it is now, the universe would still work by the same basic laws of physics, but many important effects of relativity, electromagnetism, astronomy, and even daily technology would become much less noticeable at human scales.

A good way to think about it is that the speed of light, \(c\), is not just “how fast light moves.” It is also the built-in conversion factor connecting space, time, energy, mass, and causality. So making \(c\) 100 times larger would ripple through a lot of physics.

At everyday speeds, relativity would become far less important. Right now, objects moving close to the speed of light experience strong time dilation and length contraction. If \(c\) were 100 times larger, then our usual speeds—cars, planes, rockets, even planetary motion—would be an even tinier fraction of \(c\). That means Newton’s laws would be an even better approximation than they already are. It would be much harder to notice relativistic effects in particle accelerators too, because particles would need to move much faster before those effects became significant.

Mass-energy equivalence would change numerically in a dramatic way. Since \(E = mc^2\), increasing \(c\) by a factor of 100 increases \(c^2\) by a factor of 10,000. So one kilogram of mass would correspond to 10,000 times more rest energy than it does now. In that sense, matter would contain vastly more energy. But that does not automatically mean ordinary life becomes explosive or that everything releases more energy in practice. What matters is whether physical processes can access that energy. Nuclear reactions and particle interactions would have to be reconsidered in the full context of changed constants, not just by plugging into \(E=mc^2\).

Electromagnetism would also be affected because the speed of light is tied to the electric constant and magnetic constant through
\[
c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \epsilon_0}}.
\]
So if \(c\) became 100 times larger, at least one of those constants would need to change unless other definitions of units were altered. That would affect atomic structure, chemistry, and how strong electromagnetic interactions are, depending on what is held fixed. This is the biggest complication: changing \(c\) alone is not really a fully self-contained change, because many “constants” are linked. Some changes would be physically meaningful, while others might just reflect a different choice of units.

If we interpret the question in the usual meaningful way—keeping dimensionless constants like the fine-structure constant roughly the same while making the relativistic speed scale larger—then atoms and chemistry could remain broadly similar, but relativistic and light-travel-time effects would shrink.

Astronomy would feel much “smaller” in a communication sense. Light from the Sun currently takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. If light were 100 times faster, it would take only about 4.8 seconds. Signals to the Moon would take about 0.013 seconds instead of about 1.3 seconds round trip per leg being around that scale. Communication with planets and spacecraft would be far less delayed. Looking at distant stars would still mean looking into the past, but not as far into the past for a given distance. The observable universe, in terms of how far signals could have traveled in a given time, would be much larger.

Causality would still exist in the same basic sense—nothing could send information faster than the new speed limit—but that limit would be much less restrictive for practical purposes. A civilization could coordinate across planetary distances much more easily. Space travel would also be more forgiving relativistically: a spaceship could travel much faster before encountering severe time dilation, and the energy cost from relativistic effects would kick in later. Still, interstellar travel would remain hard because the stars are so far away.

Gravitation would be affected in general relativity because \(c\) also appears there. Gravity propagates at the speed of light, and the structure of spacetime depends on \(c\). A larger \(c\) would generally make gravity look more Newtonian over a wider range of situations, and relativistic gravity effects such as black hole horizons and gravitational wave timing would be altered. The radius of a black hole horizon, for fixed mass, scales like \(1/c^2\), so if \(c\) were 100 times larger, the Schwarzschild radius of the same mass would be 10,000 times smaller. Black holes would be much more compact.

In short, if the speed of light were 100 times faster, everyday life might seem surprisingly similar at first, but the universe would be less relativistic at accessible speeds, communication across space would be much faster, black holes would be smaller for the same mass, and many deep physical scales would shift. The biggest caveat is that changing \(c\) alone is not a simple isolated tweak: because it is woven into many equations, the full consequences depend on what other constants are assumed to stay fixed.

items.model_answer:
If humans were placed on a planet that had oxygen but a different overall atmosphere, whether they could survive would depend on much more than “is there oxygen?”

Humans need not just oxygen to be present, but the right partial pressure of oxygen, the right total air pressure, and an atmosphere that is not toxic. On Earth, oxygen makes up about 21% of the air, and that works because the total atmospheric pressure is also suitable. If the new planet had oxygen but the total pressure were too low, humans could still suffocate because there would not be enough oxygen entering the lungs. If the pressure were too high, oxygen itself could become harmful, causing oxygen toxicity. A very dense atmosphere could also make breathing mechanically difficult.

The other gases matter too. If the atmosphere contained large amounts of carbon dioxide, methane, ammonia, sulfur compounds, chlorine-containing gases, or other reactive chemicals, it could poison or damage human lungs and blood chemistry even if oxygen were available. Even an inert gas mixture can be dangerous if pressures are wrong; for example, high nitrogen pressure can cause narcosis, and unusual gases could affect voice, heat transfer, or nervous system function.

There are also indirect effects. Different atmospheric density changes how sound travels, how fire behaves, and how quickly humans lose or retain heat. Different pressure and composition can alter evaporation from the skin and lungs, making temperature regulation harder. If the atmosphere had more oxygen than Earth, fires would ignite more easily and burn more intensely. If it had less, combustion and perhaps some biological processes would be harder.

So the short answer is: humans would not automatically be able to live there just because the planet had oxygen. They could survive only if the atmosphere’s composition and pressure fell within a narrow range compatible with human physiology, and if the other gases were non-toxic. Otherwise they would need breathing support, pressurized habitats, or protective suits.

items.original_question: 如何彻底摧毁一座城市，而不为4000年后的人类留下任何线索？背景 我想彻底烧毁一座城市。一切不得残留，尘归尘，尘归尘。尽管我是一个超自然的存在，但我希望这一切以自然的方式发生。我还希望这次破坏不会留下任何痕迹，以便 4000 年后人类可以利用这些痕迹来确定到底发生了什么。然而，该事件可能会留下痕迹，让他们猜测发生了什么，但绝对不应该导致确切的原因。细节 完全烧毁一座城市（阅读：摧毁，但我喜欢火）。该市地处海拔以上，属半干旱气候。该事件可能不会留下任何线索。这意味着 4000 年后的人类无法准确识别发生了什么。然而，破坏可能会留下痕迹，让人们想知道到底发生了什么。主要的一点是，这座城市本身应该成为一个传说，也就是说，毁灭地点不应该留下任何可以证明被毁城市存在的痕迹。不过，如果人们知道发生了某种自然灾害也很好，但最好他们不确切知道是什么类型的自然灾害。 事件时间：公元前 2,000 年（大约）。销毁最好在 24 小时内发生。优选地，破坏方法可以摧毁主要用岩石和粘土类物质建造的城市。我有什么选择？有什么可以利用的自然灾害吗？这是否可能以自然的方式实现？请发挥创意。我本以为是“从天而降的火”，但陨石撞击的痕迹要持续 4000 多年。编辑 1：我删除了以下要求，以使更多答案成为可能：该区域不存在火山活动或地震活动。编辑2：答案和评论的数量非常多，谢谢！我重写了要求/细节，使事情更加清晰。我还在其中两个添加了“最好”一词，这意味着应该可以提供更多的答案。只要记住“最好”...还要注意，这个问题首先谈论两个城市。我将其更改为一个城市，因为：如果它适用于一个城市，那么它可能适用于任意数量的城市。
items.model_answer:
If you wanted a city destroyed so thoroughly that archaeologists 4,000 years later would likely misread the cause, the key would not be “maximum destruction” in the abstract. It would be to create a destruction pattern that looks, in the long run, like something else. Archaeologists do not recover events directly; they infer them from partial material traces after erosion, rebuilding, scavenging, fires, floods, chemistry, and time have altered the evidence. So the most effective way would be to combine near-total destruction with heavy overprinting of the physical record.

The easiest way to make the cause hard to read would be to destroy the city in multiple stages using different mechanisms. For example, first shatter structures with blast or earthquake-like ground motion, then burn large parts of it, then inundate it with water and sediment, and finally leave it exposed to collapse and scavenging. Four thousand years later, investigators might argue over whether the city fell to war, earthquake, accidental fire, flood, abandonment, or some combination. Archaeological interpretation becomes uncertain when distinct signatures overlap.

A simple fire alone usually leaves recognizable signs: ash layers, carbonized beams, reddened mudbrick, heat-cracked stone, and sometimes bodies trapped in place. A military sack can leave weapons, trauma on skeletons, breach patterns, and selective burning. An earthquake leaves wall-fall orientations, pancaked masonry, crushed occupants, and sudden abandonment horizons. A flood leaves sorted sediment, water-laid deposits, and specific damage patterns. If you stack these on top of each other, especially in the right order, the record becomes ambiguous. A city hit by structural collapse and then burned can look different from one burned and then collapsed. Add later flooding, and many of the decisive clues get buried, dispersed, or chemically altered.

To maximize later confusion, you would also want to eliminate the most obvious diagnostic evidence. Remove bodies if possible, because mass graves, trauma, and demographic anomalies strongly suggest warfare, massacre, or plague. Remove weapons and obvious military debris. Strip valuable metals, because looting signatures can suggest post-destruction human activity but obscure who destroyed the site. If archives exist, destroy those too, because inscriptions and records often preserve the clearest account of cause. A city can be materially ambiguous but textually obvious; without texts, interpretation becomes much harder.

Then the ideal finishing step would be burial under a thick, rapid sediment layer. This is one of the best ways to preserve the city as a ruin while also confusing causation. If heavy sediment arrives after the destructive event—through diverted river flow, engineered flooding, landslide, volcanic ashfall, or coastal inundation—it can lock in a mixed destruction horizon and make later investigators focus on the burial event rather than the original trigger. They may say “the city was destroyed by flood” when in fact the flood merely sealed a city already wrecked by conflict or internal demolition.

Paradoxically, total obliteration is not the best route. If you vaporized everything or erased the site completely, there might be little for archaeologists to study, and they would simply say the city disappeared or was never substantial at that location. To be misread, the site has to survive enough to tell a misleading story. The ideal ruin is one with abundant remains but scrambled causality.

A strong candidate scenario would therefore be this: destabilize buildings so they collapse in a way resembling seismic destruction, ignite widespread but not uniform fires, clear away the bodies and military indicators, then rapidly bury the whole area under flood deposits or imported sediment. Over centuries, weathering, rebuilding on the margins, robbing of stone, and groundwater chemistry would further erase the sequence. Four thousand years later, archaeologists might plausibly conclude that an earthquake caused urban collapse, followed by accidental fire and later flooding, even if the true cause had been deliberate human destruction.

So the shortest answer is: you would not try merely to destroy the city; you would try to curate the ruins. The best way to ensure future misinterpretation would be to layer several destructive processes, remove the clearest forensic indicators, and then bury the site in a way that preserves destruction but obscures sequence.

items.question: What If a Birdlike Species Almost Never Touched the Ground?
human_answers: Evolution Since the defining feature is not nesting on ground, the starting point should be the nesting behaviour. There should be a strong pressure to reduce time spent on the ground such as predators or competition for suitable locations with other species.

Most creature designs, if anthropomorphized, can be thought of as a balance between seizing opportunities and fearfully avoiding mishaps. As a result, most designs are very flexible, adapting to new situations as they come.

I think any answer to this question really hinges on how earth-like you want your planet to be and how earth-like you want the rest of your fauna and flora to be. Since you don't place any restrictions on these, I'll take the liberty to assume these factors...
So here's where we can start: Some birds (megapodes) are superprecocial , i.e. they can fly on the day they hatch.
items.original_question: 一种从不接触地面的鸟 正如我们目前所知，鸟类在地面上筑巢并产卵。有着锋利牙齿的人和物生活在地面上。也有一些东西有爪子和喙在空中，但较少。我想知道是否存在一种像鸟一样的动物，一生都在空中度过，死后才落到地上。我已经知道鸟类可以在空中睡觉，但我需要帮助：找出一种方法来解释我的鸟类（或蝙蝠，或其他什么）如何进化到永远不会接触地面 - 我缺乏一个令人信服且可信的故事。粮食情况。除非我也有飞行植物（考虑到能量方程，不太可能），否则它必须是捕食其他飞行生物的食肉动物，或者从地面抓取动物。更具体地说，我担心生命的第一阶段。也许是给新生儿准备一个类似袋鼠的育儿袋？最后，为了故事相关的目的，我更愿意让这只飞行的野兽尽可能大。你认为它能长到多大并且仍然全天候飞行？ （上图：诺斯罗普仍然制造出最好的羽蛇神）后期编辑：感谢大家提供了大量的好建议！ 感谢您的所有回答，我希望在这种情况下我能接受另外两个回答。除了我接受的@VilleNiemi 的答案之外，我认为@Ivy_Lynx 的答案值得更多的支持，我也从@CortAmmon 那里得到了一些有趣的想法。
items.model_answer:
If a birdlike species almost never touched the ground, it would likely evolve into something extremely specialized for an aerial or arboreal lifestyle, with its whole body, behavior, and ecology shaped around avoiding landing on flat terrestrial surfaces.

Its anatomy would probably favor efficient long-duration flight. You would expect long, high-aspect-ratio wings if it spent much of its life soaring, or highly maneuverable wings if it lived in dense forest canopies. Its feet might become less useful for walking and more useful for clinging, hanging, or perching vertically, since ground locomotion would matter very little. The legs could become short and light, reducing drag and weight. If it nested, slept, and fed above ground, the species might only use branches, cliffs, floating vegetation, or even the air itself during key parts of its life cycle.

Its feeding strategy would also shift. A species that rarely lands would need food it could catch or access without standing on the ground: flying insects, fruit plucked in flight, fish skimmed from water, nectar from hovering, or prey taken from branches or the air. It might evolve a bill and neck adapted for snatching food while moving, and a digestive system suited to frequent small meals if it had high flight energy demands.

Reproduction would be a major constraint. Eggs are hard to manage without some stable resting place, so unless the species evolved live birth or some very unusual brooding strategy, it would still need to land somewhere to nest—most likely in trees, cliffs, caves, or other elevated surfaces rather than on the ground. Juveniles might be especially vulnerable, because young often cannot remain airborne continuously. That means the life cycle would probably include at least brief periods of non-flight, even if healthy adults almost never touch the ground.

Its senses and nervous system would likely become tuned for constant three-dimensional movement. Excellent vision, rapid balance correction, and precise spatial memory would be important. Social behavior could also adapt: flocking, aerial mating displays, and even sleeping in safe elevated sites or while gliding might emerge.

Ecologically, such a species would be very vulnerable to changes in airspace and perch availability rather than to ground predators alone. Forest loss, cliff disturbance, storms, and reductions in aerial prey could be more serious threats than terrestrial competition. It might avoid many ground-based predators and parasites, but pay for that with very high energy needs and narrow habitat requirements.

So in short, a birdlike species that almost never touched the ground would become highly optimized for life in the air or above the ground, with reduced walking ability, specialized feeding and nesting behavior, strong flight adaptations, and a lifestyle constrained mainly by how it reproduces and rests without relying on terrestrial surfaces.

human_answers: Absolutely! Pigs are dangerous animals.
I'm going to disagree with a lot of people here and say that, while not impossible, it would be very very difficult to use pigs. This isn't about the size of the pig nor its strength.
items.original_question: 骑猪的骑兵可能吗？最近，我的邻居让我很不高兴。我发现他计划以某种方式改进他的投石机，以便将肮脏的东西扔到河对岸。我告诉他我的猪骑骑兵会攻击他。我必须向你坦白一件事……我还没有任何骑猪的骑兵……！能有骑猪的骑兵吗？如果大人太重的话，我可以派小孩和矮人去战斗。我想要最少的东西（否则我会有安装在沙发上的骑兵，更舒服）：沿着想要的方向行走，当敌人在那里时不要逃跑，甚至如果可能的话向他们冲锋。是否可以？
items.model_answer:
If you tried to build a pig cavalry, the basic idea would fail for the same reasons armies have almost never used pigs as mounts: pigs are strong and smart, but they are badly suited to riding, discipline, and sustained movement.

First, a cavalry animal has to tolerate a rider, respond reliably to commands, stay calm in noise and chaos, move quickly over distance, and be trainable as a unit. Pigs are poor fits on most of those requirements. Their backs are not built to comfortably carry a human the way horses, camels, or even some ponies are. An average pig’s body shape makes riding awkward, and larger pigs still would not provide the same stable, efficient platform as a horse. You might be able to sit on a very large pig briefly, but doing it effectively in military conditions is another matter.

Speed is another major problem. Pigs can sprint surprisingly fast for short bursts, but they are not endurance animals in the cavalry sense. Cavalry historically relied on mobility over long distances, rapid maneuver, and the ability to charge or reposition repeatedly. Pigs overheat more easily, tire differently, and would struggle with long campaigns, rough marching, and sustained battlefield use.

Temperament and trainability would also undermine the project. Pigs are intelligent, but intelligence does not automatically mean they make good mounts. They are independent, food-motivated, often stubborn, and not naturally inclined to coordinated group movement under a rider’s control. Training a few pigs to perform tricks or carry loads is plausible; training hundreds into a disciplined mounted force that can handle shouting, weapons, blood, and explosions is far less plausible.

There are also practical issues. Saddles, tack, and control systems would have to be reinvented because standard cavalry equipment would not fit well. Feeding and managing pigs on campaign would be inefficient. Pigs can root, wander, panic, or become hard to control at exactly the wrong time. In muddy or confined terrain they might do better than expected, but not enough to outweigh the disadvantages.

So the likely result is that a “pig cavalry” would become more of a novelty, parade force, or comic disaster than a real military arm. At best, you might create a small unit of riders on specially bred giant pigs for very short-range transport, spectacle, or intimidation. At worst, the animals would throw riders, ignore commands, scatter under stress, and turn your cavalry charge into confusion almost immediately.

In short: you could probably put people on pigs, but you could not realistically replace horse cavalry with them. The experiment would expose why successful cavalry animals need a very specific mix of anatomy, endurance, and temperament that pigs do not have.

items.model_answer:
If everyone on Earth vanished except 35 people, the immediate result would be silence, infrastructure failure, and then a rapid collapse of modern civilization.

At first, the survivors would not die simply because there are too few of them. The real problem would be that nearly everything in the modern world depends on billions of people continuously operating, repairing, transporting, farming, refining, and coordinating. Thirty-five people cannot keep that system running.

In the first hours to days, power grids would begin failing. Most electrical systems need constant balancing and oversight. Some plants would shut down automatically; others could fail dangerously if not managed. Water systems would stop working in many places because pumps, purification plants, and pressure systems require electricity and maintenance. Internet and phone networks might continue briefly in some areas, but they too would soon break down. Fires, industrial accidents, gas leaks, and transportation crashes could occur without anyone to respond.

Food would not disappear immediately. There would be enormous stockpiles of canned food, packaged food, bottled water, and medicine left behind. If the 35 survivors were smart and near an intact city or warehouse, they could live off existing supplies for quite a long time. Their best strategy would be to gather in one safe, temperate location with access to clean water, stored food, fuel, tools, medical supplies, and shelter. A hospital, distribution center, or well-equipped rural area might be ideal. They would need to avoid dangerous sites such as unattended nuclear plants, chemical facilities, flood-prone cities, and areas at risk of wildfire.

Nuclear power is one of the biggest medium-term dangers people imagine. Most modern reactors are designed to shut down automatically and have backup safety systems, so they would not all instantly explode. But over time, with no staff, some facilities could suffer serious failures, especially once backup power and cooling systems degrade. That could contaminate some regions, though it would not make the whole planet uninhabitable.

Agriculture would mostly stop in an industrial sense. Fields would go unharvested, livestock would die or escape, and supply chains for seeds, fertilizer, fuel, and machinery would collapse. With only 35 people, however, total food demand is tiny by planetary standards. They would not need industrial agriculture at first. Later, if they wanted a long-term future, they would need to relearn and maintain small-scale farming, animal husbandry, sanitation, and basic manufacturing.

The biggest long-term issue is not food or shelter but population biology and social resilience. Thirty-five people is a dangerously small gene pool for rebuilding humanity, especially if the sex and age distribution are unfavorable. If the group includes too few women of childbearing age, or too many people beyond reproductive age, humanity may simply end within one generation. Even if the mix is favorable, severe inbreeding risk would emerge over time. Thirty-five is likely below or near the lower edge of what could plausibly sustain a genetically healthy long-term population without advanced reproductive technology, stored gametes, or exceptional planning.

Knowledge would also become fragile. Modern science and engineering exist not just in books but in networks of specialists, factories, laboratories, and education systems. Some knowledge could be preserved in libraries and digital archives, but much would become unusable without the industrial base behind it. The survivors could preserve parts of civilization if they were highly skilled and coordinated, but they would almost certainly fall back to a much simpler technological level within years or decades.

So the likely outcome is this: the 35 survivors could probably stay alive for quite a while if they were lucky, organized, healthy, and geographically well placed. But global civilization would collapse almost immediately, most technology would decay, and the human species would be at serious risk of eventual extinction. If those 35 were unusually well chosen for age, health, skills, and genetic diversity, they might found a tiny remnant society. If not, humanity would probably disappear.

items.model_answer:
A Cold War submarine after 50 years on the seafloor would usually look like a dark, corroded, partly collapsed metal hull covered with marine growth, with its condition depending heavily on depth, water chemistry, and whether it carried a reactor or weapons.

From a distance, the basic shape would often still be recognizable, especially if it were a large steel military submarine resting intact on soft sediment. The hull would likely be coated in rust, mineral deposits, bacteria-driven corrosion products, and deep-sea organisms. Paint and markings would mostly be gone. Any exposed rubber, seals, cables, and plastics would be degraded, though some synthetic materials might persist surprisingly well in cold deep water.

The steel structure would not simply vanish in 50 years, but it would be significantly weakened. Salt water relentlessly corrodes steel, and in many wrecks microbes accelerate the process by forming “rusticles” or similar corrosion structures. Openings, damaged areas, weld seams, and thinner outer fittings would deteriorate fastest. Railings, propeller guards, masts, sonar domes, and external piping might be bent, missing, or collapsed. If the submarine sank violently or imploded on descent, it could be a badly shattered debris field instead of a recognizable boat. If it reached the bottom largely intact, pressure itself would not keep crushing it once internal and external pressures equalized, but prior implosion damage could be severe.

The seafloor setting matters a lot. In deep, cold, low-oxygen water, decay can be slower, so much of the pressure hull might remain for decades. In shallower, more oxygen-rich water, corrosion and biological activity would be faster. If partly buried in sediment, some sections could be preserved better while exposed portions corrode more aggressively. Nets, fishing damage, or currents could also alter the wreck over time.

Inside, the submarine would be flooded unless some compartments remained sealed for a time. Interiors would be dark, silt-filled, and coated with corrosion. Machinery would be heavily rusted and often fused in place. Organic materials such as paper, food residues, textiles, and human remains would mostly decompose, though cold, deep, low-oxygen conditions can preserve some things longer than people expect. Sediment could blanket decks and equipment. Batteries, fuels, lubricants, hydraulic fluids, and other hazardous materials might still be present in altered or leaking form.

A nuclear-powered Cold War submarine adds another layer. The reactor compartment would still exist physically, but surrounding structures would be corroding like the rest of the vessel. The reactor fuel would remain radioactive long after 50 years, though the hazard to the outside environment would depend on whether protective barriers had failed and whether radionuclides were leaking into surrounding water and sediment. If nuclear weapons were aboard, their metal casings and components would also be degrading, creating contamination concerns even if no nuclear explosion were possible.

So the short answer is: after 50 years, a Cold War submarine on the seafloor would most likely be a recognizable but heavily corroded wreck—encrusted, weakened, possibly partly collapsed, and potentially still hazardous environmentally, especially if it contained a reactor, fuel, or weapons.
